courses.subject: ATSC(GEOG)
courses.title: Hidden Figures in the Atmospheric Sciences
courses.description: Critical examination of the history of the atmospheric sciences in the U.S. with a focus on the foundational contributions of African-American, Asian-American, Hispanic-American, and Native American scientists. In addition, the key roles of women, the LGBTQ community, people with physical disabilities, and neurodiverse people in the atmospheric sciences are highlighted.

courses.subject: ATSC(GEOG)
courses.title: Synoptic Meteorology and Climatology
courses.description: Theory and observations to understand mid-latitude weather systems. Focus is on application of quasi-geostrophic theory in weather forecasting. Analysis and interpretation of weather maps and numerical models. Development and life cycle of cyclones, fronts, and jet streams.
courses.course_objectives: By the end of the course, students will be able to describe the role of atmospheric circulation in the climate system, with a focus on the synoptic and dynamics of mid-latitude weather systems. Students will learn to effectively employ advanced analysis tools in weather forecasting, with a focus on mid-latitude weather systems. By the end of the course, students will be expected to cogently employ fundamental conceptual models to diagnose the genesis and evolution of cyclones. Students are expected to formulate and effectively communicate a weather discussion in oral and written forms.

courses.subject: ATSC(GEOG)
courses.title: Tropical Meteorology and Climatology
courses.description: An investigation of the weather and climate of the tropics, including its interactions with the tropical oceans and the extratropical atmosphere. Topics include the Hadley Cell, the ITCZ, monsoons, equatorial waves, tropical oscillations, and climate change, with particular emphasis on the theory, observations, modeling, and forecasting of tropical cyclones.

courses.subject: ATSC(GEOG)
courses.title: Tropical Meteorology and Climatology
courses.description: An investigation of the weather and climate of the tropics, including its interactions with the tropical oceans and the extratropical atmosphere. Topics include the Hadley Cell, the ITCZ, monsoons, equatorial waves, tropical oscillations, and climate change, with particular emphasis on the theory, observations, modeling, and forecasting of tropical cyclones.
courses.offeredText: Offered summer semester every odd-numbered year.

courses.subject: ATSC(GEOG)
courses.title: Satellite Meteorology and Climatology
courses.description: Application of satellite remote sensing in meteorology and climatology. Applications include clouds, atmospheric water vapor and precipitation, the Earth's radiation budget, sea and land surface temperatures.
courses.course_objectives: Complete a survey regional to global scale meteorological-climate processes and how these processes are linked to human and environmental systems. Demonstrate and communicate a fundamental understanding of physical and remote sensing concepts and methodologies applied in meteorological/climate analysis and forecasting. Complete a rigorous review of current and future observational and prediction systems/methodologies for meteorological and climate studies. Engage in inquiry-based learning and hands-on application of meteorological and climate satellite data through modules and scenarios.

courses.subject: ATSC(GEOG)
courses.title: Physical Climatology
courses.description: Advanced, quantitative study of Earth's physical climate.  Includes global energy balance, surface-atmosphere energy exchanges, surface hydrology and water budget at various temporal and spatial scales. Methods of measuring and modeling are discussed.  Case studies are used to illustrate how the physical processes govern the climate system.
courses.prerequisiteText: ATSC(GEOG) 3110 or ATSC(GEOG) 3120-3120L or ATSC(GEOG) 4140/6140 or ATSC(GEOG) 4160/6160 or ENGR(ATSC)(GEOG) 4161/6161-4161L/6161L or GEOG(ENGR) 4112/6112 or permission of department

courses.subject: ATSC(GEOG)
courses.title: Hydrometeorology
courses.description: Hydrometeorology bridges atmospheric sciences and hydrology, including formation and distribution of liquid and solid precipitation, floods, and drought, and impacts on water resources. Topics address the observing, modeling, and forecasting of fluxes, flow, and storage of liquid water, ice, and water vapor, including interactions between the land surface and atmosphere.
courses.course_objectives: Students will establish a well-rounded background in the intersection of atmospheric and hydrologic sciences. Students will learn the tools and methods for observation, modeling, and prediction of liquid and solid precipitation, soil moisture, snow/ice cover. Students will understand the application of instrumentation for in situ and remotely sensed observations in hydrometeorology. Students will demonstrate application of observations and tools to address the role of water in human activities, particularly those impacts associated with floods and drought at local and regional scales.

courses.subject: ATSC(GEOG)
courses.title: Applied Climatology in the Urban Environment
courses.description: Do cities create their own thunderstorms?  Will pollution from emerging mega-cities change climate?  Exploration of fundamental concepts of the urban-climate system, observational and modeling strategies for studying the urban-climate system, and context for how human activity in the built environment is changing Earth's weather and hydro-climate.
courses.prerequisiteText: ATSC(GEOG) 3110 or ATSC(GEOG) 3120-3120L or permission of department | Graduate Prerequisite | ATSC(GEOG) 3110 or ATSC(GEOG) 3120-3120L or permission of department

courses.subject: ATSC(GEOG)
courses.title: Mesoscale and Radar Meteorology/Climatology
courses.description: Fundamental theory, analysis, and exercises on mesoscale weather phenomena and principles of radar meteorology. A major topical focus will be thunderstorms, mesoscale convective systems, and tornadic supercells. Other topics will include mesoscale classification, observing systems, the boundary layer, circulations, flooding, mesoscale tropical systems, mesoscale modeling, short-range forecasting/nowcasting, and mesoscale climatology.

courses.subject: ATSC
courses.title: Internship in Atmospheric Sciences
courses.description: Placement of students in employment and/or training environment where they will utilize atmospheric sciences and related techniques in approaching practical problems relevant to the organization’s mission. An initial orientation and a post-internship evaluation with the internship committee are required.

courses.subject: ATSC
courses.title: Programming for Atmospheric Scientists
courses.description: An introduction to computer programming for atmospheric scientists. Students will learn to navigate the scientific computing environment and work with several computing languages. A study of applications of scientific computing for modeling atmospheric processes and data analysis. The course will be hands-on and focused around several practical programming assignments.
courses.prerequisiteText: (GEOG 1111 and GEOG 1111L) or (GEOG(ATSC) 1112 and GEOG(ATSC) 1112L) or permission of department

courses.subject: ATSC
courses.title: Atmospheric Dynamics II
courses.description: A quantitative investigation of atmospheric phenomena, including boundary-layer dynamics; balanced dynamics theory; atmospheric waves; geostrophic adjustment theories; atmospheric instabilities and cyclogenesis theories; frontogenesis theories; jet stream dynamics; introduction to finite difference methods; survey of tropical dynamics and middle atmosphere dynamics.
courses.prerequisiteText: GEOG(ENGR) 4112/6112 or permission of department | Graduate Prerequisite | GEOG(ENGR) 4112/6112 or permission of department

courses.subject: ATSC
courses.title: Introduction to Data Assimilation
courses.description: Introduction to the concepts, theory, and computational methods of data assimilation in the atmospheric and related sciences. Topics include the history of data assimilation, the “rejectionproblem,” adjustment to balance, balance constraints, nonlinearnormal mode initialization, variational data assimilation, Kalman filter methods and applications to different disciplines and data types.

courses.title: Capstone in Atmospheric Sciences
courses.description: The capstone allows B.S. Atmospheric Sciences majors to synthesize knowledge within the atmospheric sciences or between the atmospheric sciences and other disciplines while enhancing students’ appreciation of the discipline and connecting their education with future goals. This course allows the department to assess the learning outcomes of this major.

courses.subject: ATTR
courses.title: Prevention and Care of Conditions in Sports Medicine
courses.description: Overview of the field of sports medicine to include an introduction to the prevention, evaluation, and treatment of acute and chronic athletic related conditions.
courses.course_objectives: Describe the role and function of an athletic trainer and members of the comprehensive sports medicine team. Describe the principles related to injury prevention, care, and management for optimal recovery. Identify emergency medical situations and apply the appropriate first aid measures. Describe basic human anatomy and how it applies to injuries and illness. Identify and treat common conditions seen in sports medicine. Identify and apply basic rehabilitation principles.
courses.topical_outline: Legal Liability Injury Prevention Protective Equipment Injury and Illness Classifications and Mechanisms Non-orthopedic Conditions Environmental Conditions Wound Care Injury Evaluation and Recognition Therapeutic Interventions and Rehabilitation

courses.subject: ATTR
courses.title: Prevention and Care of Conditions in Sports Medicine Laboratory
courses.description: Course will allow students to gain basic skills to be used in the prevention, evaluation, and treatment of conditions commonly found in sports medicine.
courses.course_objectives: Select, apply, and fit appropriate protective equipment in order to prevent and/or minimize the risk of injury to the head, torso, spine, and extremities for safe participation in sport and/or physical activity. Select, fit, and educate a patient with an appropriate gait assistive device. Assess environmental factors to determine safety of physical activity in a variety of environmental conditions. Demonstrate basic clinical examination and wellness assessment techniques. Demonstrate basic taping and wrapping techniques of the extremities. Demonstrate appropriate management techniques for emergent conditions of the spine and extremities. Demonstrate a basic understanding of therapeutic interventions.
courses.topical_outline: Protective Equipment Principles of Fitness and Conditioning Assistive Devices Taping and Wrapping Techniques Wellness and Injury/Illness Assessment Techniques Emergent treatment of the spine and extremities Wound Care

courses.subject: ATTR
courses.title: Clinical Anatomy for Athletic Training I
courses.description: This course will complete advanced study to include gross and surface anatomy, biomechanical principles, and functional anatomy of the spine and upper extremities.
courses.course_objectives: At the completion of the course, the student will be able to apply anatomical terminology and concepts of orientation planes, directions, and joint motions. At the completion of the course, the student will be able to describe the structure and function of human body systems. At the completion of the course, the student will be able to identify human anatomical structures in gross cadaver specimens. At the completion of the course, the student will be able to describe the normal structures and interrelated functions of the body systems. At the completion of the course, the student will be able to identify the origin, insertion, action, innervation, and blood supply of muscles in the upper extremity. At the completion of the course, the student will be able to identify the origin, insertion, action innervation, and blood supply of muscles of the head, face, and spine. At the completion of the course, the student will be able to apply the principles and concepts of body movement, including functional classification of joints, joint biomechanics, normal ranges of joint motion, joint action terminology, muscular structures responsible for joint actions (prime movers, synergists), skeletal muscle contraction, and kinesthesis/proprioception. At the completion of the course, the student will be able to describe normal biomechanical function of the upper extremity. At the completion of the course, the student will be able to describe normal biomechanical function of the spine. At the completion of the course, the student will be able to describe cell adaptations (e.g., atrophy, hypertrophy, hyperplasia, metaplasia, and dysplasia). At the completion of the course, the student will be able to analyze the normal physiological responses of the human body to trauma and inactivity of specific body tissues (ligaments/capsules, muscles, tendons, and bones). At the completion of the course, the student will be able to describe the healing process of body structures.
courses.topical_outline: Introduction to Body Dissection Anatomical Terminology Cellular Anatomy and Physiology Bone Physiology Muscle Physiology Nerve Physiology Cartilage Physiology Ligament Physiology Cervical Spine Thoracic Spine and Thorax Lumbar Spine Shoulder Elbow Wrist and Hand

courses.subject: ATTR
courses.title: Clinical Anatomy for Athletic Training II
courses.description: This course will complete advanced study to include human gross and surface anatomy, biomechanical principles, and functional anatomy of the lower extremities, brain, spinal cord, and internal organs.
courses.course_objectives: At completion of this course, students will be able to apply anatomical terminology and concepts of orientation planes, directions, and joint motions. At completion of this course, students will be able to describe the structure and function of human body systems. At completion of this course, students will be able to identify human anatomical structures in gross cadaver specimens. At completion of this course, students will be able to identify the origin, insertion, action, innervation, and blood supply of muscles in the lower extremity. At completion of this course, students will be able to identify the origin, insertion, action innervation, and blood supply of muscles of the pelvis. At completion of this course, students will be able to apply the principles and concepts of body movement, including functional classification of joints, joint biomechanics, normal ranges of joint motion, joint action terminology, muscular structures responsible for joint actions (prime movers, synergists), skeletal muscle contraction, and kinesthesis/proprioception. At completion of this course, students will be able to describe normal biomechanical function of the lower extremity and pelvis. At completion of this course, students will be able to describe the normal structures and interrelated functions of the body systems. At completion of this course, students will be able to demonstrate knowledge of the normal anatomical structures of the human body systems and their physiological functions, including the cardiovascular, respiratory, digestive, urogenital, endocrine, brain, spinal cord, and special sensory systems. At completion of this course, students will be able to analyze the normal physiological responses of the human body to trauma and inactivity of specific body tissues (ligaments/capsules, muscles, tendons, and bones). At completion of this course, students will be able to describe the healing process of body structures.
courses.topical_outline: Principles of Neuroanatomy Brain Spinal Cord Internal Organs (cardiovascular, respiratory, digestive, urogenital, endocrine) Hip/Pelvis Knee Foot, Ankle, and Lower Leg

courses.subject: ATTR
courses.title: Clinical Anatomy for Athletic Training
courses.description: Advanced study of human anatomy to include gross cadaver dissection and surface anatomy, biomechanical principles, and functional anatomy of the extremities, brain, spine, and internal organs.
courses.course_objectives: Apply anatomical terminology and concepts of orientation planes, directions, and joint motions. Describe the structure and of the anatomical structures of the human body systems and their physiological functions. Analyze the normal physiological responses of the human body to trauma and inactivity of specific body tissues. Describe the structure and function of human body systems. Identify human anatomical structures. Identify the origin, insertion, action, and innervation of muscles in the trunk and extremities. Apply the principles and concepts of body movement, including functional classification of joints, joint biomechanics, joint action terminology, muscular structures responsible for joint actions (prime movers, synergists), skeletal muscle contraction, and kinesthesis/proprioception. Describe cell adaptations (e.g., atrophy, hypertrophy, hyperplasia, metaplasia, and dysplasia).
courses.topical_outline: Introduction to Body Dissection Anatomical Terminology Bone Physiology Muscle Physiology Nerve Physiology Cartilage Physiology Ligament Physiology Cervical Spine Thoracic Spine and Thorax Lumbar Spine Shoulder Elbow Wrist and Hand Principles of Neuroanatomy

courses.subject: ATTR
courses.title: Introduction to Athletic Training Clinical Practice
courses.description: Students will learn foundational clinical skills needed for the prevention, evaluation, and treatment of orthopedic and non-orthopedic conditions.

courses.subject: ATTR
courses.title: Clinical Medicine I
courses.description: The first course in a series designed to introduce students to the pathophysiology, evaluation, treatment, and relevant pharmacology for non-orthopedic conditions in Athletic Training.

courses.subject: ATTR
courses.title: Clinical Medicine II
courses.description: The second course in a series designed to introduce students to the pathophysiology, evaluation, treatment, and relevant pharmacology for non-orthopedic conditions in Athletic Training.

courses.subject: ATTR
courses.title: Therapeutic Interventions I
courses.description: Students will be introduced to the foundations, theories, and techniques regarding treatment interventions.  Interventions include pain modulation, pharmacology, and therapeutic modalities.

courses.subject: ATTR
courses.title: Therapeutic Interventions II
courses.description: Students will be introduced to the foundations, theories, and techniques regarding treatment interventions to include therapeutic exercise and therapeutic modalities.

courses.subject: ATTR
courses.title: Therapeutic Interventions III
courses.description: Students will be introduced to the foundations, theories, and techniques regarding treatment interventions to include therapeutic modalities, complementary and alternative medicine therapies, and joint stabilization.

courses.subject: ATTR
courses.title: Clinical Evaluation and Treatment: Emergent Conditions
courses.description: Students will learn skills and techniques required to recognize, examine, diagnose, and manage acute and emergent life or limb threatening conditions.

courses.subject: ATTR
courses.title: Clinical Evaluation and Treatment:  Spine and Trunk
courses.description: Designed to teach students pathomechanics, recognition, evaluation, treatment, and therapeutic interventions of conditions found in the cervical, thoracic, and lumbar spine, pelvis, trunk, and temporomandibular joint.

courses.subject: ATTR
courses.title: Clinical Evaluation and Treatment:  Brain
courses.description: Focuses on integrative study of the brain. Topics of this course include anatomy, neuroscience, and neuroplasticity, and the recognition, evaluation, treatment, and interventions of acute, chronic, and degenerative conditions.

courses.subject: ATTR
courses.title: Clinical Evaluation and Treatment: Foot, Ankle, and Lower leg
courses.description: Designed to teach students pathomechanics, recognition, evaluation, treatment, and therapeutic interventions of conditions found in the lower extremity.

courses.subject: ATTR
courses.title: Clinical Evaluation and Treatment:  Knee and Hip
courses.description: Designed to teach students pathomechanics, recognition, evaluation, treatment, and therapeutic interventions of conditions found in the knee and hip.

courses.subject: ATTR
courses.title: Clinical Evaluation and Treatment:  Shoulder
courses.description: Designed to teach students biomechanics, pathomechanics, recognition, evaluation, treatment, and therapeutic interventions of conditions found in the shoulder.

courses.subject: ATTR
courses.title: Clinical Evaluation and Treatment:  Elbow, Wrist, and Hand
courses.description: Designed to teach students biomechanics, pathomechanics, recognition, evaluation, treatment, and therapeutic interventions of conditions found in the elbow, wrist, and hand.

courses.subject: ATTR
courses.title: Evidence-Based Practice I
courses.description: Introduces the athletic training student to research methods to facilitate translation of scientific inquiry to clinical practice.

courses.subject: ATTR
courses.title: Evidence-Based Practice II
courses.description: Introduces the athletic training student to statistical analysis of scientific inquiry.

courses.subject: ATTR
courses.title: Evidence-Based Practice III
courses.description: Teaches students clinically-applicable statistical analysis in order to critically evaluate research and determine the impact on clinical practice.

courses.subject: ATTR
courses.title: Evidence-Based Practice IV
courses.description: Prepares students to disseminate scientific research.

courses.subject: ATTR
courses.title: Advanced Research Skills in Athletic Training
courses.description: Prepares students to undertake independent research by introducing advanced literature review skills, scientific writing techniques, and methodology design and implementation. Additionally, students will gain an advanced understanding of statistical analyses related to common clinical sports medicine research designs.

courses.subject: ATTR
courses.title: Psychological and Social Considerations in Healthcare
courses.description: Students will be prepared to identify, support, and refer patients with psychological disorders or concerns. Students will learn to embed empathy into their practice with respect to cultures, values, and the socioeconomic status of patients.

courses.subject: ATTR
courses.title: Clinical Imaging and Diagnostic Procedures
courses.description: Provides students with fundamental clinical knowledge of commonly utilized diagnostic procedures in sports medicine.

courses.subject: ATTR
courses.title: Special Populations and Disabilities
courses.description: Designed to introduce athletic training students to the evaluation, treatment, and medical considerations of those with developmental and physical disabilities as they participate in physical activity and sport.

courses.subject: ATTR
courses.title: Injury Prevention, Performance Enhancement, and Wellness
courses.description: Provides students with advanced theories and policies of public health, prevention and treatment programs in the communities, evaluation and integration of epidemiological data, and injury prevention techniques, as well as theories, concepts, and techniques regarding return to activity progression and training.

courses.subject: ATTR
courses.title: Healthcare Management
courses.description: Introduces students to the business and administrative responsibilities of athletic training.

courses.subject: ATTR
courses.title: Special Topics in Athletic Training
courses.description: Designed to prepare students for advanced clinical practice through selected topics related to theory, research, or athletic training clinical practice.

courses.subject: ATTR
courses.title: Clinical Integration I
courses.description: Designed to integrate didactic knowledge and clinical practice through collaboration, problem-solving, and critical thinking. The primary focus of this course will be the evaluation and treatment of emergent conditions, neurological conditions, or spinal injuries.

courses.subject: ATTR
courses.title: Clinical Integration II
courses.description: Designed to integrate didactic knowledge and clinical practice through collaboration, problem-solving, and critical thinking. The focus of this course will be the evaluation and treatment of orthopedic and non-orthopedic conditions.

courses.subject: ATTR
courses.title: Clinical Integration III
courses.description: Designed to integrate didactic knowledge and clinical practice through collaboration, problem-solving, and critical thinking.  This is a capstone course to prepare students for autonomous clinical practice.

courses.subject: ATTR

courses.subject: ATTR
courses.title: Internship in Athletic Training
courses.description: Professional practice of athletic training under the direct supervision of a credentialed professional. Professional work and responsibilities will be dependent upon clinical site and may include the domains of an athletic trainers’ clinical practice.

courses.subject: BCHE(BIOE)
courses.title: Biopharmaceutical Engineering
courses.description: Introduces students to the fundamentals of developing, optimizing, and manufacturing large-molecule biologic pharmaceuticals with an emphasis on therapeutic proteins, therapeutic antibodies, and antibody modifications. Course will cover the regulatory and ethical landscape of biopharmaceuticals, along with the biopharmaceutical industry in general.
courses.course_objectives: Students will be able to describe the regulatory and manufacturing pathways of pharmaceutical and biopharmaceutical products, including comparing and contrasting the two. Students will be able to describe key types of biopharmaceutical products and classify existing biopharmaceutical therapeutics on the market into their respective categories. Students will be able to explain key features of innate and adaptive immunity and link these features to biopharmaceutical (antibody) therapeutics or potential therapeutic targets. Students will be able to describe and illustrate antibody structure, function, modifications, and compare/contrast different methods of antibody development. Students will be able to describe and evaluate the different methods of biopharmaceutical (protein) production. Students will be able to create a work portfolio demonstrating knowledge of bio/pharmaceutical topics, including proposing and completing a semester-long individual project related to a self-selected topic in biopharmaceutical engineering.
courses.topical_outline: Regulatory pathways for pharmaceutical and biopharmaceutical industries in the United States Steps in manufacturing pharmaceutical and biopharmaceutical products Ethical considerations in the bio/pharmaceutical industry Types of biopharmaceutical products The innate and adaptive immune system Antibody function and structure Antibodies with modified structures Technology used in antibody development Recombinant DNA technology Protein production systems DNA mutagenesis methods Scaling-up biopharmaceutical production and manufacturing

courses.subject: BCHE(BIOE)
courses.title: Animal Cell Biomanufacturing
courses.description: Biochemical engineering concepts related to large-scale animal cell biotechnology and scalable manufacturing of cellular products, such as recombinant proteins, monoclonal antibodies, viral vaccines, therapeutic cells, and gene therapy vectors. Working in small groups, students will address a range of contemporary problems.
courses.course_objectives: Students will understand the benefits and limitations of animal cell culture. Students will apply mathematical models to cell growth and product synthesis. Students will identify, formulate, and solve problems related to the scale-up of biomanufacturing processes. Students will design a biomanufacturing system, component, or process to meet desired needs. Students will communicate effectively via a group setting about contemporary bio-manufacturing processes.
courses.topical_outline: 1. Introduction to Animal Cell Biotechnology 2. Effective technical communication 3. Library instruction 4. Primary vs. immortalized cell lines 5. Cell metabolism, proliferation, and death in culture 6. Microcarrier culture 7. Adaptation to serum-free suspension culture 8. Animal cell bioreactors: Complications and considerations 9. Genetic modification and stability 10. Modeling growth and substrate utilization 11. Scale-up vs. scale-out 12. In situ monitoring 13. Viral vaccine separation and purification 14. Product separation efficiency 15. Viral purification methods 16. Quality control 17. Regulatory aspects and GMP 18. Validation and product stability 19. Advances in biotechnology
courses.prerequisiteText: BCHE 3520 | Graduate Prerequisite | Permission of department

courses.subject: BCHE
courses.title: Introduction to Biochemical Engineering Design
courses.description: Introduction to biochemical engineering processes, types of process units, process flow sheets, mass and energy balance calculations, process simulation, and basics of plant design economics.
courses.course_objectives: Students will learn basic biochemical engineering concepts. Students will learn about biochemical engineering processes, including process flow sheets, process units, and their functions. Students will understand the stepwise methodology to solve material balance problems. Students will understand degree of freedom analysis for solving material balance problems. Students will be able to solve material balance problems in biochemical engineering process for single and multiple process units. Students will be able to solve energy balance problems with and without a chemical reaction. Students will understand the basics of biochemical process design. Students will generate process flow sheets for a given biochemical engineering design process. Students will understand the importance of ethics, code, and safety in engineering design. Students will learn concepts related to feasibility and economic evaluation of design. Students will develop the ability to identify, formulate, and solve engineering design and analysis problems. Students will apply the concepts learned to design a biochemical engineering process in the course project.

courses.subject: BCHE
courses.title: Kinetics and Reactor Design
courses.description: The fundamentals of engineering science and design related to chemical, environmental, and biocatalytic homogeneous reactions. An introduction to chemical and enzymatic kinetics, collection and analysis of rate data, isothermal reactor design, bioreactor design, energy balance, and runaway reactions.
courses.prerequisiteText: CHEM 1212 and BIOL 1107 and BCHE 2910 | Pre or

courses.subject: BCHE
courses.title: Mass Transport and Rate Phenomena
courses.description: Mass transport and rate phenomena in the analysis of engineering problems in biological systems.
courses.course_objectives: Students will solve problems involving calculations of mass and mole fraction, molecular weight, partial pressure, and relative humidity; apply correct units in problems and identify when unit conversions are needed. Students will solve gas-phase problems using the Ideal Gas Law and gas-liquid equilibrium problems using Raoult’s Law and Henry’s Law. Students will solve biological and chemical kinetics problems involving zero, first, and second order reversible and irreversible reactions (single or multiple reactions). Students will solve macro-scale material balance (species, atomic, and molar) problems under steady and unsteady state conditions with and without reactions. Students will solve molecular and interphase mass transfer problems under steady and unsteady state conditions involving calculations of molar velocity and flux, using Fick’s Law, and estimating mass transfer coefficients.
courses.topical_outline: Review of Biological and Chemical Calculations Mixtures Gas-Liquid Equilibrium Terms in Biological and Chemical Kinetics Zeroth, First, and Second Order Reversible Reactions Multiple Reaction Kinetics Introduction of Macroscopic Material Balances Steady-State Systems Unsteady-State Systems Reactive Systems Definitions of Velocities and Fluxes Fick's Law Differential Material Balances Interphase Mass Transfer
courses.prerequisiteText: (MATH 2700 or MATH 2700E) and (ENGR 1140 or ENGR 1140H) and (CHEM 1212-1212D and CHEM 1212L) | Pre or

courses.course_objectives: Students will understand kinetics/reactor design, unit operations such as filtration or mechanical separation, biosensing, or biochemical fuel cells. Students will model systems and interpret the experimental results. Students will comprehend the physical system and define key parameters. Students will conduct experiments. Students will adjust/modify the experimental protocol. Students will analyze and interpret experimental results including statistical analysis. Students will complete written laboratory reports. Students will present results orally.

courses.subject: BCHE
courses.title: Biochemical Process Control
courses.description: Theories and knowledge of chemical/biochemical process control systems	focusing on dynamic behavior of processes, feedback control, and applications to biological systems.
courses.course_objectives: Students will understand dynamic behavior of processes and feedback control in Chemical/Biochemical Engineering. Students will be able to apply knowledge of math, science, and engineering to formulate mathematical descriptions of chemical/biochemical processes. Students will understand controllers for process operations and be able to select controllers for a specific application. Students will be able to design and conduct control experiments and analyze the dynamic response results. Students will be able to design and test simple control loops for practical uses. Students will be able to use engineering tools for control analysis, tuning, and troubleshooting. Students will acknowledge applications of process control in biological systems and be aware of the need for life-long learning.

courses.subject: BCHE
courses.title: Biochemical Engineering
courses.description: Design and analysis of enzymatic and microbial biological reaction systems.
courses.course_objectives: Students will understand the physiology of cells and microbes. Students will understand the theory of bioreactor design. Students will develop/design bioreactors. Students will understand GEO's and their applications. Students will understand the principles of bioprocessing.
courses.topical_outline: 1. Enzyme kinetics 2. Microbial growth kinetics in batch, fed batch, and continuous systems 3. Design of enzyme and microbial biological reactors

courses.subject: BCHE
courses.title: Bioprocess Design and Simulation
courses.description: Design and modeling of chemical/bioprocess systems, including unit operations and reactor design principles. Process simulation and process economics applied to chemical/bioprocessing systems. Plant layout and process safety of bio/chemical plants will be included.
courses.course_objectives: Students will acquire the principles and methodologies of process design of various unit operations (e.g., reactors, separation units, material handling) in the context of bio/chemical manufacturing plants. Students will develop skills and learn modern computational techniques to model and simulate unit operations for equipment sizing and process optimization. Students will analyze and assess process efficiency, plant safety (HAZOP analysis), and mitigation measures. Students will conduct equipment costing and plant economics and interpret production cost, product selling price, and return on investments. Students will develop plant design reports and recommend suggestions on the feasibilities of selected bio/chemical manufacturing plants.
courses.topical_outline:
- General design considerations - Process design principles - Process flow, synthesis, and development - Equipment design, simulation, and cost of:
a) Material handling equipment - Equipment design, simulation, and cost of:
b) Heat transfer equipment - Equipment design, simulation, and cost of:
c) Chemical/bioreactors - Equipment design, simulation, and cost of:
d) Separation equipment - Computation tools in process design and plant simulation - Analysis of equipment sizing and costing - Material selection and fabrication - Plant economics, ROI, and profitability - Bio/chemical process safety - Hazard evaluation (HAZOP analysis) and risk analysis (LOPA) - Design reports and interpretations

courses.description: Course introduces graduate students who do not have an undergraduate degree in an engineering discipline to the fundamental aspects of bioengineering. courses.course_objectives: By the end of the course, the student should be able to perform mass and energy balance calculations. By the end of the course, the student should be able to understand basic reactor design and apply to solve model problems.

courses.title: Cancer Bioinformatics
courses.description: This course teaches a fundamentally novel framework of cancerbiology.  Throughout this course, students will learn how theinitial and seemingly harmless stressors induced by chronicinflammation or ROS accumulation can lead to increasinglymalignant development of neoplastic cancer tumors as a result ofadaptation to the also evolving microenvironment.

courses.subject: BCMB(BINF)
courses.title: Computational Methods in Bioinformatics
courses.description: Computational methods, including development and implementation of computer codes, used to solve biological problems; development and solution of statistical and mathematical biological models.  Topics include bio-sequence comparison and analysis, functional site prediction, structure prediction and analysis, and biological data analysis.

courses.subject: BCMB(CHEM)
courses.title: Physical Biochemistry
courses.description: The principles of physical chemistry applied to biological molecules and systems, including current approaches in structural biology.
courses.course_objectives: Students will analyze raw data to identify the best mathematical model that describes these data and calculate high confidence estimates for key kinetic and equilibrium constants. Students will calculate the relative contributions of entropy, enthalpy, heat, and work to chemical equilibria. Students will evaluate the contributions of molecular interactions and conformational entropy to protein stability. Students will describe the theoretical concept of energy and how this applies to biological systems at an atomic scale. Students will compare and contrast modern biophysical methods that evaluate biochemical mechanisms. Students will explain how microscopic properties affect macroscopic behaviors of molecules. Students will compare and contrast cooperativity and allostery and give examples of how each can influence protein function.
courses.topical_outline:
1. Thermodynamics: State functions, Energy, enthalpy, entropy, Gibbs free energy, The Laws of thermodynamics, Chemical potential and Equilibrium, Calorimetry, Buffers and pH, Electrochemical potential and ion transport, Redox reactions and the Nernst equation, Electron transport and bioenergetics

2. Kinetics: Chemical Kinetics, Zero, first, second, and higher order reactions, Determining Rate Laws, Consecutive Reactions, Complex Reactions and Approximations, Real World Kinetics, Enzyme Kinetics, Introduction to Enzyme functions, Michaelis-Menten Mechanism, Interpreting Enzyme Kinetic Data, Enzyme Inhibition

3. Quantum theory: Fundamentals of quantum theory, Quantum theory - Particle in a box

4. The role of physical chemistry in current biochemical techniques: Electronic spectroscopy and fluorescence, Nuclear magnetic resonance spectroscopy, Surface Plasmon resonance, Separations, Mass spectrometry and proteomics

courses.subject: BCMB(CHEM)
courses.title: Advanced Physical Biochemistry
courses.description: Principles in physical chemistry and biophysics to biological macromolecules, including structural biology, hydrodynamics, electronic and magnetic resonance spectroscopy, and crystallography.

courses.subject: BCMB(CHEM)
courses.title: Advanced Topics in Protein Structure-Function Relationships
courses.description: The relationship of protein structure to biological function, including protein folding, conformation, stability, and enzyme mechanisms.

courses.subject: BCMB(CHEM)
courses.title: Bioimaging Using X-rays, Neutrons, and Electrons
courses.description: The basic principles of X-ray and neutron diffractions,cryo-electron microscopy, and other complementary imaging methodswill be introduced. The strengths and limitations of these methods will be studied. Examples of recent use of theseindividual or combined tools in advancing the understanding ofbiological systems will be highlighted.

courses.subject: BCMB(CHEM)
courses.title: Fundamental Principles of NMR Spectroscopy
courses.description: Practical, theoretical, and instrumental aspects of 1D and 2D NMRspectroscopy, including pulsed Fourier transform techniques,proton and carbon-13 techniques used in the analysis of organiccompounds and macromolecules.  Instrumentally, the focus is onthe operation of NMR spectrometers presently available at theUniversity of Georgia.

courses.subject: BCMB(CHEM)
courses.title: NMR Spectroscopy of Biomolecules
courses.description: NMR spectroscopy with applications to proteins and other biopolymers.  Special attention will be given to methods of structure determination.

courses.subject: BCMB(ENTO)(BTEC)
courses.title: Biotechnology
courses.description: Applied aspects of biochemistry and molecular biology in various fields, with emphasis on the use of recombinant DNA methods and protein engineering.
courses.course_objectives: Students will identify unmet needs that could be addressed using biological products. Students will describe the sources and types of biomaterials that are commercially available. Students will summarize fundamental technologies that form the basis of modern biotechnology. Students will become familiar with examples of biotech companies across the domains of life science. Students will analyze biotech company data to make and defend mock investment decisions and determine returns on investment. Students will survey literature and patents to select a discovery around which to form a mock biotech company. Students will conceptualize the mock company from scientific discovery through to a business plan. Students will become familiar with leadership roles in biotech companies, including the information and decision-making for which each executive is responsible Students will communicate orally and in writing about the company, including the founding discovery, the market, and the business model. Students will employ a “shark tank” style approach to evaluate mock companies both scientifically and in terms of investment potential.

Genome Editing

courses.description: The structure and function of biological molecules, enzymology,metabolism and bioenergetics, and molecular biology.
courses.course_objectives: Students will be able to explain how biological macromolecules (proteins, nucleic acids, carbohydrates, lipids) are synthesized and metabolized. Students will be able to explain the relationship between biological macromolecular structure and function. Students will be able to explain how enzymes function, including their mechanisms and regulation. Students will be able to explain the energetics of biochemical reactions. Students will be able to explain the idea of "flux" and its relationship to the function and regulation of metabolic pathways. Students will be able to predict how chemical and physical parameters affect biological processes. Students will be able to apply the knowledge above to analyze, interpret, and evaluate biochemical data for solving biochemical problems.

courses.subject: BCMB
courses.title: Genomics and Bioinformatics
courses.description: A focus on the remarkable impact that genome sequencing projectsis having on virtually all aspects of biochemistry, as well as onmedicine and biotechnology.  An introduction to a broad range of'omic' topics, including functional genomics, microarrays,proteomics, physiological genomics, and bioinformatics.
courses.course_objectives: Students will explain how the genome sequences of microbes, of humans and of environments, are determined. Students will describe how genome sequence information is used to provide insights into how a human cell functions, which diseases a human is susceptible to and how this is affected by interactions with microbes, and how the human species evolved. Students will describe how DNA is used to create synthetic life and to produce long term data storage systems. Students will solve problems using bioinformatics tools and techniques including sequence comparison, structure modeling, and multimodal data analysis. Students will perform practical bioinformatics analyses using real biological datasets. Students will visualize and interpret biological data to generate a hypothesis or to a conclusion. Students will integrate diverse biological data types for protein and gene function prediction. Students will delineate the various ways that gene expression is regulated. Students will explain how basic research discoveries can lead to revolutionary biotechnologies. Students will design hypothetical experiments that apply biotechnologies to address problems
courses.topical_outline:
Topics include genome projects, genome sequencing and annotation, gene expression and the transcriptome, proteomics, functional genomics, SNPs, metabolomics, and computational
genomics. An outline of the syllabus is as follows:
1. Genome Projects: Organization and Objectives

2. Genome Sequencing and Annotation

3. Gene Expression and the Transcriptome

4. Proteomics and Functional Genomics

- Structural Proteomics
- Functional Genomics
5. SNPs and Variation

6. Integrative Genomics

courses.subject: BCMB
courses.title: Biochemistry and Molecular Biology I
courses.description: A comprehensive treatment of biochemistry and molecular biology stressing structures of biological molecules, including proteins, nucleic acids, carbohydrates, and lipids, enzymology and selected aspects of metabolism and bioenergetics.
courses.course_objectives: Students will apply an understanding of basic thermodynamics to chemical reactions in biological systems. Students will explain how proteins and enzymes achieve specificity and affinity. Students will describe common elements of enzyme mechanisms and explain and give examples of how coupled reactions are used in enzyme mechanisms. Students will describe basic enzyme kinetics and noncovalent inhibition mechanisms. Students will illustrate the principles that underlie the application of common analytical methods in biochemistry. Students will describe structures, functions, and transport of lipids and carbohydrates in living systems, including examples of dysfunction.
courses.topical_outline: The topical outline for the course has not changed. Topics will include the chemistry of life, thermodynamics of biological systems, macromolecular structure and function, membrane transport and bioenergetics, and enzyme kinetics and regulation. An outline of the syllabus is as follows: 1. The Chemistry of Life: Organic chemistry of biological molecules, Weak chemical forces, Water as a solvent, Acid/base equilibria and pH 2. Thermodynamics of Biological Systems: Thermodynamics principles, Heat, work, energy, enthalpy, and entropy, Chemical equilibria, High-energy compounds and coupled reactions 3. Structure and Function of Biological Macromolecules: Amino acids, polypeptides, and proteins, Carbohydrates, polysaccharides, and cell surfaces, Lipids and biological membranes, Nucleotides nucleic acids, and gene expression 4. Membrane Transport and Bioenergetics: Membrane organization, Passive and facilitated diffusion, Channels and pores, Primary and secondary active transport 5. Enzyme Kinetics and Regulation: Chemical kinetics and catalysis, Enzyme kinetics and specificity, Cooperativity and allostery, Enzyme mechanisms

courses.subject: BCMB
courses.title: Biochemistry and Molecular Biology II
courses.description: A comprehensive treatment of biochemistry and molecular biology stressing aspects of metabolism, metabolic regulation, bioenergetics, and recombinant DNA methodologies.
courses.course_objectives: Students will describe different metabolic pathways in terms of their chemical reactions, regulation, and energetic driving forces, and explain how they are used by living organisms from microbes to humans. Students will apply thermodynamic and kinetic principles to explain the molecular driving forces in biochemical reactions. Students will explain how energy is obtained, stored, transformed, and harnessed in biological systems. Students will describe how information is stored, retrieved, and transmitted in biological systems, including the processes of replication, transcription, translation, gene expression and DNA repair mechanisms. Students will analyze and interpret figures from primary literature on experiments related to nucleic acid structure and function. Students will describe the different levels of biological organization from single microbial cells to complex higher organisms.
courses.topical_outline:
Topics include primary metabolic pathways, bioenergetics, photosynthesis, respiration, replication, transcription, and translation and specific subtopics are:
- Glycolysis 
- Tricarboxylic Acid Cycle 
- Oxidative Phosphorylation 
- Photosynthesis 
- Gluconeogenesis 
- Fatty Acid Catabolism 
- Lipid Biosynthesis 
- Amino Acid Metabolism 
- Nucleotides
- Metabolic Integration 
- DNA Replication/Repair 
- Transcription 
- Translation

courses.subject: BCMB
courses.title: Human Biochemistry and Disease
courses.description: Integrated treatment of human biochemistry and selected topics on the biochemical basis of human disease.  Examples will be given of inheritable and acquired disorders.
courses.course_objectives: Students will elaborate on the interplay of the four biomolecules of life and assess their impact on cellular, organ, and whole system (patho)physiology as well as their ability to be manipulated by modern medicine. Students will compare and contrast organelle/tissue/organ specific biochemistry and metabolism and their role in whole system health and opportunities for intervention in disease states. Students will describe biochemical aspects of immune system function and assess the role of different components of the immune system in human health. Students will examine the nervous system from a biochemistry perspective and discuss the influence of biochemistry in understanding and treating neural developmental, psychiatric, and degenerative diseases. Students will analyze the role of iron, copper, and heme in red blood cell life cycle and metabolism and apply that knowledge to recognizing related pathophysiology. Students will investigate the function and dysfunction of other selected organ systems. Students will appraise primary literature to comprehend and critique current theories of and therapies for human disorders.
courses.topical_outline: Macromolecular structure and function in human processes and systems, including: - Fertilization, Implantation, and Early Development - Sexual Differentiation - Endocrine (Reproductive, Thyroid and Adrenal) - Nervous system - Muscular system, including Cardiac Biochemistry and Vascular Biology - Digestion, Glucose Homeostasis, and Diabetes - Hepatic and Integrative Metabolism - Immune system - Connective Tissue and Calcium Homeostasis - Blood and Acid-Base Balance - Heme Metabolism, Red Blood Cell Development, and Hemoglobinopathies - Trace Metal Metabolism and Related Disorders - Stem Cells and Stem Cell-Based Therapies - Cell Signaling

courses.subject: BCMB
courses.title: Human Biochemistry II
courses.description: Exploration of advanced topics in medicine from a molecular standpoint, with a focus on the mechanistic basis for acquired and infectious diseases.
courses.course_objectives: Students will elaborate on the interplay of the 4 biomolecules of life, taught in prerequisite courses, and assess their impact on cellular, organ, and whole system as well as their ability to be manipulated by modern medicine, representing novel opportunities for intervention in disease states Students will describe vertebrate development through somitogenesis and explain the involvement of the Notch pathway. Students will recall the hallmarks of cancer and how the Notch pathway is involved in T cell Acute Lymphoblastic Leukemia. Students will explain how stem cells can be applied in disease modeling, disease mechanism discovery, cell replacement therapy, and drug discovery. Students will evaluate the benefits and limitations of different stem cell technologies, including the ethical dimensions. Students will compare the cellular and biochemical mechanisms of common neurodegenerative diseases. Students will describe the role of cellular stress responses in the process of aging. Students will evaluate alignment between biochemical and cell biological data and models. Students will develop a conceptual and mechanistic understanding of hemoglobin structure-function and impacts on hemoglobinopathies and plasmodium biochemistry and metabolism. Students will evaluate merits and limitations of breakthroughs in gene therapy and genome editing therapeutic approaches to these diseases. Students will evaluate results from primary literature with respect to current theories of and therapies for human disorders Students will explain key scientific results in oral and visual formats to varied audiences.

courses.description: Faculty-supervised independent or collaborative inquiry into fundamental and applied problems within a discipline that requires students to gather, analyze, and synthesize and interpret data and to present results in writing and other relevant communication formats.
courses.course_objectives: Students will develop research questions and/or hypotheses. Students will design and conduct appropriate experiments or investigations. Students will analyze and interpret data using appropriate tools and approaches. Students will contextualize research within the primary literature and/or databases. Students will present scientific results in an appropriate context and in a variety of ways (e.g., group meetings, final report), including via visual representations of data (figures, graphs, tables), orally and in writing. Students will develop awareness of the ethical dimensions of science and responsible conduct of research.
courses.topical_outline: During the process of completing the research course sequence, students accomplish authentic biochemistry and molecular biology research, which involves developing science practice skills and learning about and applying principles related to the responsible and ethical conduct of their particular research project. Students must apply through a sponsoring faculty member to conduct research. Each research experience is an independent collaboration between the faculty member and the student. The faculty mentor and student develop their own work plan and determine specific expectations and milestones (i.e., individualized syllabus). The student receives guidance and feedback on their work during individual and group meetings. The student presents their results in a final journal article style report.

courses.subject: BCMB
courses.title: Project Management
courses.description: Covering the principles of project management as applied to the discovery and development of therapeutics within the pharmaceutical and biotechnology industries. Through an integrated approach, students will learn about the philosophy regarding and principles of project management and gain hands-on experience with project management software and collaborative platforms.
courses.course_objectives: Students will develop a comprehensive understanding of project management principles and methodologies as applied to therapeutic discovery and development. Students will be equipped with practical skills to plan, execute, monitor, and close projects within the pharmaceutical and biotechnology sectors. Students will apply risk management, resource allocation, and budgeting strategies to real-world therapeutic discovery projects. Students will foster effective leadership and teamwork abilities for managing multidisciplinary project teams in a therapeutic research environment. Students will be equipped capabilities in stakeholder communication, reporting, and documentation essential for successful project delivery. Students will use tools and technologies for project tracking, data management, and collaborative work in drug discovery pipelines.
courses.topical_outline:
Module 1: Foundations of project management in therapeutic discovery
•	Introduction to project management: Definition, key concepts, and the project lifecycle initiation, planning, execution, monitoring & control, closure).
•	The therapeutic discovery pipeline: An overview of the stages from target identification to clinical trials from the perspective of management to understand the Product Development Lifecycle (PDL).
•	Defining the project: Scope, goals, and success criteria for a therapeutic project.
•	Stakeholder analysis: Identifying and managing the expectations of internal (researchers, management) and external (investors, regulatory bodies) stakeholders. Module 2: Project planning and execution
•	Project scope and objectives: Defining clear project goals and deliverables.
•	Work Breakdown Structure (WBS): Decomposing large therapeutic projects into manageable tasks.
•	Scheduling and timelines: Creating and interpreting visual project schedules using Gantt charts. Identifying the longest sequence of tasks that determines the project's duration using the Critical Path Method (CPM).
•	Data management and digital tools: Utilizing project management software, data analytics, and potentially AI/blockchain technologies to track progress, manage data silos, and improve decision-making.
•	Resource allocation and budgeting: Assigning personnel and financial resources and creating a project budget: matching people and resources to project tasks. Module 3: Financial management
•	Funding models: A comparison of funding for start-ups (venture capital) versus larger corporations.
•	Project implementation, monitoring and control: Implementing the project plan. Monitoring project expenditures and controlling costs using Key Performance Indicators (KPIs) to track progress and make data-driven decisions.
•	Change management: Handling changes to the project scope or plan.
•	Project closure: The process of officially closing a project, documenting lessons learned, and archiving project data. Module 4: Risk and quality management
•	Risk identification and assessment: Identifying potential risks in therapeutic projects, such as scientific failure, clinical trial setbacks including enrollment challenges, supply chain disruptions, or regulatory delays.
•	Funding challenges: Evaluating and responding to changes in financial circumstances, collaborating with scientific leads to adjust plans as necessary, ensuring program continuity under revised funding conditions through clear communication, rigorous expenditure management, or, if required, program cancellation.
•	Risk mitigation and contingency planning: Developing strategies to minimize or respond to project risks.
•	Quality management in a regulated environment: Ensuring adherence to Good Laboratory Practices (GLP), Good Clinical Practices (GCP), and other regulatory standards.
•	Problem-solving and adaptability: Thriving when faced with unexpected scientific results, regulatory changes, or market shifts by quickly adjusting plans and solutions.
•	Ethical considerations: Addressing ethical dilemmas in therapeutic research and project management. Module 5: Leadership, team management, and communication
•	Leadership in therapeutic projects: The role of the project manager as a leader. Strategies for managing and motivating a team. Fostering collaboration and communication within cross-functional teams. Grasping the relationship between individual projects and the overall company portfolio, ensuring alignment with strategic goals, and productively function within a framework of multiple interrelated projects.
•	Effective communication: Developing strong communication plans for different audiences, including presentations and project status reports.
•	Negotiation and conflict resolution: Handling disagreements and fostering a collaborative environment. 
•	Regulatory communication: Understanding the documentation and reporting requirements for regulatory bodies like the FDA. Methods to support students in meeting learning outcomes:
•	Interactive lectures
•	Case study analysis: Students will analyze a real-world therapeutic project, identifying its successes, failures, and management challenges.
•	Project plan development: Students will work in teams to develop a comprehensive project plan for a hypothetical therapeutic development project (after the discovery phase) to be assigned by the instructors. This will include a WBS, Gantt chart, budget, and risk management plan.

courses.subject: BCMB
courses.title: Organizational Leadership in Biotechnology and Pharmaceuticals
courses.description: This course examines the unique leadership opportunities and challenges that arise in pharmaceutical and biotechnology companies. Students will integrate industry-specific leadership theories, regulatory and geopolitical landscapes, innovation management, and strategic organizational practices, preparing them for leadership roles in these dynamic and complex sectors.
courses.course_objectives: Students will develop a deep understanding of the classic and contemporary leadership theories in the context of pharma/biotech organizations. Students will identify and develop skills needed to lead cross-functional, multicultural teams, and global teams, across both internal organization and with outside partners. Students will explain the regulatory, ethical, geopolitical and compliance challenges that inform and drive the decision-making processes. Students will examine innovation and product differentiation strategies in highly competitive and regulated environments to address significant unmet clinical needs. Students will develop strategic thinking for sustainable growth and competitive advantage, balancing scientific risk, capital requirements and commercial potential. Students will understand the capital intensity of therapeutics discovery and development and communicate the scientific “reason to believe” to the financial community. Students will assess individual leadership competencies, including but limited to meeting management, decision-making and conflict resolution, to create a professional leadership growth plan to meet the industry workforce’s needs.
courses.topical_outline: 1	Pharma & Biotech Workforce and its Evolving Leadership Needs Balancing Cultural Diversity in Achieving Corporate Goals 2	Leadership Theories: Application in Regulated Industries 3	Organizational Structure: R&D, Manufacturing, and Commercial Operations 4	Regulatory Environment: Compliance, Risk, Global Standards, and ethical challenges 5	Leading Innovation: Product Development, Digitalization, and AI 6	Strategic Leadership 7	Developing, Retaining, and Leading High-Performing Teams leadership 8	Inclusive Leadership in Pharma/Biotech 9	Leading Change and Organizational Transformation 10	Ethical Leadership and Corporate Social Responsibility (CSR) in Pharma/Biotech 11	Stakeholder Engagement and Relationships Building: Investors, Regulators, Patients, and Partners 12	Crisis Leadership: Regulatory Actions, Supply Chain Disruptions, Recalls, and Public Health Emergencies 13	Life-Long Learning and Leadership

courses.description: An introduction to foundational programming techniques, data organization, and computational analysis approaches commonly used across the biomedical and informational sciences fields. This course uses open-source lessons and curricula developed by The Carpentries organization (https://carpentries.org/). Students will gain an understanding of the command-line interface and how this can be used to manipulate files and perform data analysis tasks on their computers.
courses.course_objectives: Students will be able to explain how to use command-line computing interfaces and demonstrate the use of common Unix commands and shell scripts. Students will be able to compare and contrast the benefits and drawbacks of command-line versus graphical interfaces. Students will understand the basic principles of automated version control systems (Git) and explain how to apply these systems to common computational tasks. Students will develop a working knowledge of Python programming fundamentals and common programming applications of this language. Students will develop a working knowledge of R programming and the use of the R studio graphical interface, with an emphasis on using R for data cleaning, organization, and visualization. Students will understand how specific data science tools and workflows are commonly applied across diverse scientific disciplines such as Ecology, Genomics, Social Science, and Library Science.

courses.subject: BINF
courses.title: Single Cell Analysis and Bioinformatics
courses.description: Course will cover single-cell data, spanning genes, proteins, and phenotypes. Students will engage in hands-on data analysis experiments, device fabrication, protein electrophoresis, and protein signal processing, emphasizing practical application. Students will undertake a final project addressing contemporary disease problems through single-cell analysis, applying acquired bioinformatic skills to process data.
courses.course_objectives: Students will be able to appraise single-cell analysis techniques and their significance in modern biology, critiquing different techniques and their ability to unravel cellular diversity and extract meaningful insights into health and disease. Students will be able to compare and contrast of key single-cell analysis methods, including scRNA-seq, scDNA-seq, epigenomics, and protein analysis, and differentiate the principles and practical applications of each. Students will be able to execute protocols focused on microfluidic device fabrication, protein electrophoresis techniques, and protein signal processing using MATLAB, and interpret the performance of microfluidic experiments and data analysis. Students will be able to demonstrate proficiency in using state-of-the-art bioinformatics tools for single-cell data analysis, including data preprocessing, quality control, normalization, clustering, and interpretation, ensuring the ability to analyze and interpret single-cell datasets. Students will be able to examine the application of single-cell analysis in diverse research fields, including developmental biology, cancer research, immunology, and neurobiology, through the examination of case studies and real-world examples. Students will be able to construct a class presentation that assesses the challenges and limitations in single-cell analysis and proposes innovative solutions, investigating the evolving landscape of single-cell biology research.
courses.topical_outline:
Week 1: Introduction to Single-Cell Analysis 

Overview of single-cell analysis and its significance in biology and medicine

Historical development and key milestones in single-cell analysis Week 2: Single-Cell Isolation Techniques 

Microfluidic techniques for single-cell isolation

Fluorescence-activated cell sorting (FACS) and its applications Week 3-4: Single-Cell RNA Sequencing (scRNA-seq) 

Principles of scRNA-seq

Sample preparation, library preparation, and sequencing platforms

Data analysis pipelines for scRNA-seq (e.g., quality control, normalization, clustering)

Practical scRNA-seq data analysis exercises Week 5-6: Single-Cell Protein Analysis 

Mass spectrometry-based methods for single-cell protein analysis

Antibody-based techniques (single cell western blot)

Hands-on lab sessions on single-cell protein analysis Week 7-8: Single-Cell DNA Sequencing 

Single-cell DNA sequencing methods (scDNA-seq)

Applications in genomics, cancer research, and evolutionary biology

Data analysis challenges in scDNA-seq Week 9-10: Single-Cell Epigenomics 

Single-cell DNA methylation analysis

Single-cell ATAC-seq (Assay for Transposase-Accessible Chromatin with sequencing)

Role of epigenetic diversity in development and disease Week 11-12: Spatial Transcriptomics 

Introduction to spatial transcriptomics techniques (e.g., in situ hybridization, spatial transcriptomics platforms)

Analyzing spatially resolved single-cell data

Case studies and applications Week 13-14: Integration of Single-Cell Data 

Combining scRNA-seq, scDNA-seq, and other single-cell omics data

Multi-omics data integration methods

Systems biology and network analysis Week 15-16: Emerging Trends and Student Presentations 

Discuss current trends in single-cell analysis research

Allow students to present on a single-cell analysis topic of their choice

Discuss potential research proposals and projects
