courses.title: Applied Data Science for Wastewater Epidemiology
courses.description: Focusing on topics such as water safety and quality, wastewater management, and disease transmission, the course offers a comprehensive exploration of the importance of advanced data science in shaping public health strategies. Through hands-on experiences with microbiological and -Omics data, students will develop skills to interpret complex data sets effectively.
courses.course_objectives: Students will be able to describe and discuss some of the most important environmental and public health challenges we face in water and sanitation across the globe, including the commonly used methods to approach these issues such as experimental design and implementation, data analysis tools, computational modeling, and statistical assessment. Students will be able to identify gaps in the application of bioinformatics to actionable approaches for real-world scenarios. This will also result in learning to search, review, and assess relevant cutting edge journal articles. Students will be able to interpret metagenomics and metatranscriptomics data sets enabling them to make informed inferences about microbial community dynamics, potential pathogenicity, and overall environmental health impacts. Students will be able to describe and appraise connections of quantitative microbial and -Omics data sets by applying techniques such as quantitative microbial risk assessment and machine learning for predictive analysis. Students will be able to design and complete a final project with -Omics data of their own or using a given data set to demonstrate their understanding of innovative approaches to water and sanitation problems.
courses.topical_outline:
Introduction to water and sanitation related issues across the globe Commonly used methods for tackling these issues and related challenges:
o	Experimental design and implementation 
o	Sample processing
o	Data analysis- quantitative and qualitative
o	Data application- risk assessments, modeling Global public health ethics and responsibilities Current strengths of bioinformatics applications in public health
o	Broad-brush approach to environmental sampling
o	Identification of unexpected targets Current weakness of bioinformatics applications in public health and potential solutions
o	Overcoming proportion data (relative abundance)
o	Recovery accuracy, particularly for amplicon-based sequencing
o	Reproducibility (lack of replication) Hypothesis testing using omics data. Determining viability and infectivity using omics data Achieving absolute quantification using omics data Integrating omics data for standard quantitative microbial risk assessment Integrating omics data, quantitative data, and covariates using AI/machine learning for risk prediction Discussion- is a catch-all using bioinformatics possible for quantitative application? Final semester project: students will utilize the tools and knowledge gained throughout the semester to produce a quantitative analysis and actionable solutions from bioinformatics data sets.

courses.subject: BINF
courses.title: Network Science for Complex Biological Systems
courses.description: The use of network science in understanding complex systems, from the intricate networks of neurons to genetic interactions in our cells. Students gain an intuition for types of biological problems that network science can be used to address, emphasizing problem-solving through data analysis, and exploring frontiers.
courses.course_objectives: Students will learn the use of structural and functional brain networks extracted from non-invasive neuroimaging data (fMRI, MEG, MRI, DTI, DSI) in determining fundamental organizational principles of neuronal processes. Students will learn to review evidence for alterations in these network structures in psychiatric disease, neurological disorders, and brain injury. Students will learn the use of dynamic networks in understanding cognitive functions including learning and lexical processing, and emerging applications of network control theory for an understanding of cognition and clinical interventions. Students will learn programming skills such as MATLAB, Python, or R. Students will learn how to peer-review journal articles and write reviewer reports. Students will learn to perform a network-based research project and bring it from initial data through to a final publication. Students will learn from one another and from the discussion occurring in this class. The discussion occurring in this class is likely to inform our research in the coming years, and we very much hope it also changes the way each of you thinks about thinking.
courses.topical_outline: •	Introduction to the course •	Types of networks and their validity •	Mesoscale network statistics •	Mesoscale network dynamics •	Spatial embedding of networks •	Generative models •	Network control •	Algebraic topology •	Cross-species comparisons •	Development and aging •	Disease, brain, symptoms •	Behavior from actions to knowledge •	Final semester project We will place particular emphasis on (i) network methods, (ii) data objects amenable to network methods, (iii) neurophysiological perturbations of such data, and (iv) current frontiers and open mathematical problems. Final semester projects will be 4-6 weeks long. Students will engage in research projects applying ideas and tools learned in class to real data (either from their current lab or from a public database). Every student will present orally to the class and submit a final written report/paper.

courses.subject: BINF
courses.title: Computational Methods in Population Genomics
courses.description: Bioinformatic tools and approaches for the analysis of population genomic data for understanding population structure, past demography, predicting the effects of mutations on organisms, mechanisms of adaptation, and domestication.

courses.subject: BINF
courses.title: Statistical Inference for the Life Sciences
courses.description: Introductory statistics for students in the life sciences, including probability, discrete and continuous random variables, distributions, expectations, maximum likelihood, Bayesian inference, hypothesis testing, and linear regression. These topics will be mixed with applications of the statistical concepts to biological data. Statistical inference and real data analysis are implemented.
courses.course_objectives:
Students will learn concepts of statistical inference, particularly maximum likelihood and Bayesian inference, and
apply techniques to biological data. Students will be able to write and run computer simulations that will strengthen their knowledge of statistical concepts.
courses.topical_outline: Probability Random variables Probability distributions Expectation Maximum likelihood Hypothesis testing Bayesian inference Linear regressions

courses.subject: BINF
courses.title: Statistical Inference for the Life Sciences
courses.description: Introductory statistics for students in the life sciences,including probability, discrete and continuous random variables,distributions, expectations, maximum likelihood, Bayesianinference, hypothesis testing, and linear regression. Thesetopics will be mixed with applications of the statisticalconcepts to biological data. Statistical inference and real dataanalysis are implemented.

courses.subject: BINF
courses.title: Bioinformatics Algorithms
courses.description: A hands-on course in which students will design and implementselected bioinformatics algorithms under the guidance of theinstructor.

courses.subject: BINF
courses.title: Python Programming for Bioinformatics
courses.description: An introduction to foundational Python programming skills, including data structures, data organization, data visualization, and supplementary Python packages commonly used across the biomedical and informational sciences fields (such as NumPy, SciPy, Pandas, Matplotlib, and Scikit-learn). No prior experience with Python is required for enrollment.
courses.course_objectives: Students will be able to explain the most common types of Python data structures and statements. Students will be able to demonstrate a working knowledge of Python programming fundamentals and common programming applications of this language Students will be able to demonstrate a working knowledge of common Python packages (including but not limited to NumPy, SciPy, Pandas, Matplotlib, and Scikit-learn) and argue how each package can be applied to common problems in the biomedical and informational sciences. Students will be able to distinguish the basic principles of data visualization in scientific programming Students will be able to select and weigh the use of specific Python tools and workflows across diverse scientific disciplines. Students will be able to design and complete a Python programming capstone project using the skills learned in the course, applied toward a problem of relevance to the student’s graduate research.
courses.topical_outline: Python Fundamentals Lists, Loops, and Conditionals Analyzing Data from Multiple Files Creating Functions Errors and Exceptions Debugging and Defensive Programming Plotting and visualizing data using Python Best practices for code formatting and commenting NumPy features and applications SciPy features and applications Pandas features and applications Matplotlib features and applications Scikit-learn features and applications

courses.subject: BINF
courses.title: Introduction to Grant Writing
courses.description: Introduction to the principles of successful grant writing. Students are expected to develop a grant proposal in NIH or NSFformat.

courses.subject: BINF
courses.title: Data Visualization for Life Sciences Research
courses.description: Exploration of best practices for data visualization across biomedical and life science disciplines. Through hands-on exercises and real-world case studies, students will develop skills for displaying research data in compelling visual formats. Emphasis will be placed on translating data into compelling narratives that resonate with diverse audiences, with a particular focus on developing informative figures for peer-reviewed manuscripts and scientific presentations.
courses.course_objectives: Students will be able to discuss the fundamental principles of data visualization and their importance in communicating complex biological concepts effectively. Students will be able to examine various types of biological data, including molecular, ecological, and genomic data, and differentiate suitable visualization techniques in each category. Students will be able to implement best practices for data cleaning, preprocessing, and data wrangling to prepare biological data for visualization. Students will be able to compare and contrast the most common data visualizations used to highlight specific biological trends and patterns. Students will be able to select and critique techniques for effectively incorporating color, labels, and annotations to enhance the interpretability of visualizations while avoiding common pitfalls. Students will be able to describe and use the principles of data storytelling and how to create compelling narratives using different visualizations. Students will be able to appraise ethical considerations and best practices in data visualization, including accurately representing data, avoiding biases, and ensuring data privacy.
courses.topical_outline: Why is data visualization so important? Bad visualizations, and what they can teach us about best practices Principles of effective data storytelling Color theory and its application in life sciences visualizations Overview of common visualization tools and software Overview of common types of charts, plots, and graphs Design principles for creating clear and informative charts and graphs Tips and tricks for labels, annotations, and figure organization Ethical considerations in data communication and visualization AI and machine learning-driven visualization Case studies on specialized visualization tools and techniques in the life sciences

courses.subject: BINF
courses.title: Building Your Science Communication Toolbox
courses.description: Students will develop a foundational skill set for science communication via hands-on assignments and active learning exercises. Students will learn how to develop and refine an elevator pitch, identify target audiences, and use storytelling skills to communicate compelling scientific narratives in both written and visual formats.
courses.course_objectives: Students will be able to define science communication and discuss the different forms it may take. Students will be able to demonstrate how to assess and define a target audience. Students will be able to design and develop a personalized “elevator pitch” for communicating scientific research. Students will be able to compare and contrast the features and applications of different digital media tools and platforms. Students will be able to compare and contrast the utility of digital tools and in-person science communication activities, and argue when one approach may be preferred over the other. Students will be able to appraise and defend the key elements of narrative storytelling. Students will be able to differentiate how to use various assessment mechanisms and metrics for evaluating the success of science communication goals.
courses.topical_outline: What is Science Communication? Defining your audience Elucidating your professional “brand” and online presence Fundamentals of narrative storytelling Introduction to digital media tools and platforms Adapting your science communication to different formats: written, visual, and audio “Offline” science communication strategies Interacting with journalists and the media Communicating science to policymakers Assessment tools and metrics for evaluating success

courses.subject: BINF
courses.title: Special Problems in Bioinformatics
courses.description: Research or intensive study in a specialized area of bioinformatics under the direction of a faculty member.
courses.course_objectives:
Students will be able to identify a topic of interest and a faculty mentor with expertise in that area.   

Criteria for the topic or related project are determined by the faculty mentor and may vary from project to project. Since this course is in directed study format, there is no attendance policy. The student will be expected to meet with the faculty mentor on a regular basis to review progress on the project. Students will be able to construct a course plan to learn advanced aspects in bioinformatics research. Students will be able to demonstrate mastery of the concepts through writing and/or oral communication. Students will be able to design, develop, and complete a final project that uses concepts from the area of interest.
courses.topical_outline: Intensive study in a specialized area of bioinformatics. Graduate students enrolled in the course will work under the direction of a faculty mentor to develop and implement a specific plan for each course.

courses.subject: BINF
courses.title: Bioinformatics Lab Rotation
courses.description: Students will be exposed to research topics and techniques byparticipating in the research projects of Bioinformatics facultymembers.
courses.prerequisiteText: Must be in the Institute of Bioinformatics MS or PhD programs

courses.subject: BINF
courses.title: Systems Biology
courses.description: Broad introduction to mathematical modeling for molecularprocesses in living systems.

courses.subject: BINF
courses.title: Advanced Software Carpentries for Scientific Programming
courses.description: An introduction to foundational programming techniques, data organization, and computational analysis approaches commonly used across the biomedical and informational sciences fields. This course uses open-source lessons and curricula developed by The Carpentries organization (https://carpentries.org/). Students will gain an understanding of the command-line interface and how this can be used to manipulate files and perform data analysis tasks on their computers.
courses.course_objectives: Students will be able to explain how to use command-line computing interfaces and demonstrate the use of common Unix commands and shell scripts. Students will be able to compare and contrast the benefits and drawbacks of command-line versus graphical interfaces. Students will be able to explain the basic principles of automated version control systems (Git) and investigate how to apply these systems to common computational tasks. Students will be able to demonstrate a working knowledge of Python programming fundamentals and common programming applications of this language. Students will be able to demonstrate a working knowledge of R programming and the use of the R studio graphical interface, with an emphasis on using R for data cleaning, organization, and visualization. Students will be able to select and argue for the use of specific data science tools and workflows in different scientific disciplines such as Ecology, Genomics, Social Science, and Library Science. Students will be able to design and execute a scientific programming project using the skills learned in the course, applied toward a problem of relevance to the student’s graduate research.
courses.topical_outline: The Unix Shell Version Control with Git Programming with Python Programming with R and R Studio Introduction to Data Analysis Workflows in Ecology, Genomics, Geospatial data, Social Sciences, and Library Sciences Scientific Programming Capstone Project

courses.subject: BINF
courses.title: Advanced Software Carpentries for Scientific Programming
courses.description: An introduction to foundational programming techniques, data organization, and computational analysis approaches commonly used across the biomedical and informational sciences fields. This course uses open-source lessons and curricula developed by The Carpentries organization (https://carpentries.org/). Students will gain an understanding of the command-line interface and how this can be used to manipulate files and perform data analysis tasks on their computers.
courses.course_objectives: Students will be able to explain how to use command-line computing interfaces and demonstrate the use of common Unix commands and shell scripts. Students will be able to compare and contrast the benefits and drawbacks of command-line versus graphical interfaces. Students will be able to explain the basic principles of automated version control systems (Git) and investigate how to apply these systems to common computational tasks. Students will be able to demonstrate a working knowledge of Python programming fundamentals and common programming applications of this language. Students will be able to demonstrate a working knowledge of R programming and the use of the R studio graphical interface, with an emphasis on using R for data cleaning, organization, and visualization Students will be able to select and argue for the use of specific data science tools and workflows in different scientific disciplines such as Ecology, Genomics, Social Science, and Library Science. Students will be able to design and execute a scientific programming project using the skills learned in the course, applied toward a problem of relevance to the student’s graduate research.
courses.topical_outline: The Unix Shell Version Control with Git Programming with Python Programming with R and R Studio Introduction to Data Analysis Workflows in Ecology, Genomics, Geospatial data, Social Sciences, and Library Sciences Scientific Programming Capstone Project

courses.subject: BINF
courses.title: Laboratory Group Meeting
courses.description: A weekly meeting of a faculty laboratory group where research progress and current literature are discussed.
courses.course_objectives: The successful graduate student will have an opportunity to present current research results to faculty and peers, be able to effectively communicate those results, and receive feedback. The successful student will be able to construct and evaluate experimental approaches to research problems. The successful graduate student will read primary literature directly relevant to work done in the laboratory and be able to critically assess that literature.
courses.topical_outline: The topical outline will depend on the faculty member leading the group meeting. In each case, the topics will focus on relevant areas of bioinformatics research.

courses.subject: BINF
courses.title: Case Studies in Systems Biology
courses.description: Shared research experience in systems biology.  Each semester the research case study will be either on the biological clock,hot-pathogen interactions, or marine metagenomics.  Project willinclude genomics experiments involving microfluidics, networkidentification, and genomic analysis. Emphasis will be placed ontransformative research accomplished on the clock, host-pathogensystem, or marine ecosystem.

courses.subject: BINF
courses.title: Bioinformatics Colloquium
courses.description: Students will attend bi-weekly seminars covering a range oftopics in Bioinformatics.  In alternate weeks preceding eachseminar, students will discuss a relevant paper from the primaryliterature.
courses.course_objectives: The Institute of Bioinformatics seminar series will expose students to cutting edge research on a large range of topics. In order to add depth to the breadth of this experience, students will be assigned readings a week in advance of each seminar speaker's visit and expected to discuss the topic of the research paper and seminar with the speaker.
courses.topical_outline: Will vary with semester

courses.subject: BINF
courses.title: Current Topics in Bioinformatics
courses.description: Students will attend weekly seminars on current topics in bioinformatics covering relevant papers from the primary literature.
courses.course_objectives: Graduate students will learn to read, discuss, critically evaluate, and present on primary literature covering a current topic in bioinformatics.
courses.topical_outline: Will vary with semester

courses.subject: BINF
courses.title: Doctoral Research
courses.description: Research while enrolled for a doctoral degree under the direction of faculty members.

courses.subject: BINF
courses.title: Doctoral Dissertation
courses.description: Dissertation writing under the direction of the major professor.

courses.subject: BIOE(BCHE)
courses.title: Bioelectroanalytical Techniques
courses.description: Analyze and design chemical and biological systems relevant to the chemical, biomedical, biotechnological, and pharmaceutical industries using bioanalytical and electroanalytical techniques.

courses.subject: BIOE(CHEM)
courses.title: Soft Materials
courses.description: Introduction to soft condensed matter, including the general aspects of chemistry, physical properties, structure and dynamics, and applications of soft materials (including polymers, colloids, liquid crystals, amphiphiles, gels, and biomaterials).  Emphasis is placed on the molecular forces related to self-assembly.
courses.prerequisiteText: CHEM 2211 or PHYS 1212 -1212L or ENGR 3140 or permission of department

courses.subject: BIOE
courses.title: The Bioengineering Professional Persona
courses.description: Exploration, analysis, and application of the elements comprising the bioengineering professional persona along with those elements’ centrality to the process of becoming a world-class bioengineer. Topics include rhetorical strategies for communicating with diverse audiences across various genres and media as well as the sociotechnical ethics of modern engineering work.
courses.course_objectives: Upon completion of the course, students will be familiar with and adept at analyzing, developing, devising, and delivering bioengineering content via a variety of writing- and speaking-related deliverables. Upon completion of the course, students will be able to recognize specific rhetorical situations, the objectives that arise out of them, and the types of written documents and presentations most suitable to a given scenario. Upon completion of the course, students will be able to analyze stakeholders and suit format, content, and tone accordingly in written documents and presentation slide decks. Upon completion of the course, students will be able to design writing- and speaking-related deliverables that are structurally, mechanically, and aesthetically effective and that conform to expected standards for professional communication. Upon completion of the course, students will be able to identify and explain the fundamental concepts of social policy through the prism of professional ethics and communication at the local, national, and global scales. Upon completion of the course, students will be able to interpret interconnections among and differences between social institutions, groups, or individuals as pertaining to professional ethics and communication.
courses.topical_outline:
1. Basics of analysis and development 
• Stakeholder-centeredness and purpose 
• Refresher on mechanical and stylistic considerations 2. General structure and organization
• User-friendly organization
• Standard deliverable structures
Low-stakes writing assignments: active-learning case studies such as “The Propeller Car: Writing to a Misguided Reader,” “The AutoHen Email Exchange,” guided peer review for the high-stakes assignment below 3. Genres and associated rhetoric
• Correspondence (email)
• Statements of purpose and job-related materials
• Technical descriptions for professional scenarios
• Research reports on engineering-research or engineering-ethics topics
• Lab reports
• Proposals
High stakes writing assignment: cover letter or personal statement/state of purpose for professional scenarios (the job search, applying for graduate or medical school) 4. Interpreting and visualizing data
• The logic of interpretation: what do the data mean?
• Drawing appropriate conclusions
• Choosing visual schemes
Low-stakes writing assignments: creating infographics, choosing the appropriate graphic, data-interpretation exercises; “The Korean Skyscraper Incident” (research, vetting sources, and writing about complex physical phenomena); guided peer review for the high-stakes assignment below; guided slide review for the high-stakes assignment below; midterm team evaluation
High-stakes writing assignments: “Three Levels of Explanation” — explaining a bioengineering topic (concept, process, or device) for a high-school STEM club, a panel of reviewers with any of the UGA Innovation Gateway's startup programs, and a technical class of the writer’s peers; final slide deck for the first presentation (selected science current events topics) 5. Slide decks, visual aids, and delivery
• Slide and poster design
a. Color and font choices
b. Balancing text and imagery
• Delivery
a. Vocal volume and variety
b. Eye contact and overall body language
c. General enthusiasm and audience engagement 6. Professional ethics and communication
• General principles of professional ethics
• Documenting source material (citing, plagiarism)
• Case studies and analysis: Henrietta Lacks; the Bhopal chemical disaster; Jeffrey Wigand and the socio-personal costs of whistleblowing; Theranos, Elizabeth Holmes, and biotech startup fraud; et al.
Low-stakes writing assignments: “What information needs citing?” exercise; exercise on creating appropriate paraphrases; drafting abstracts for the high-stakes assignments; analysis of the writing that went on during the space shuttle Challenger disaster; final team evaluation
High stakes writing assignments: collaborative report on a research or ethics topic (students’ Capstone design projects; the ethics of gene and cell therapy; antibacterial coatings; CRISPR/Cas9 technology; advantages and controversies surrounding cochlear implants; etc.); slide deck for a presentation on the report described above
courses.prerequisiteText: ENGL 1050H or ENGL 1060H or ENGL 1102 or ENGL 1102E or ENGL 1102S or ENGL 1103

courses.subject: BIOE
courses.title: Engineering Physiology
courses.description: Mathematical and engineering sciences are used to highlightprinciples governing the function of physiological systems.Simulation of normal and diseases states are used inunderstanding, devising, and testing systems for intervention.
courses.course_objectives: Students will combine knowledge of math and physiology quantitatively to describe physiological systems. Students will use simulation software such as STELLA to model the normal and diseased behavior of physiological systems. Students will design and conduct experiments in silica, as well as analyze and interpret the results. Students will appreciate the complexity and interconnectedness of physiological systems. Students will communicate effectively. Students will understand the importance of the relationships between science, technology, people and community- local and global.
courses.topical_outline: - Defining engineering physiology - Physiological modeling - Modeling with STELLA - Homeostasis - Introduction to feedback control - Introduction to endocrinology - Introduction to the nervous system - Cell membrane potential - Hodgkin-Huxley model of action potential - Cardiovascular system circuitry - Body fluids - Physical and flow properties of blood - The cardiac cycle - Energetics of the heart - Fundamentals of electrocardiology - Circulation - Regulation
courses.prerequisiteText: ENGR 2170 and ENGR 3160 and (BIOL 1104 or BIOL 1104H or BIOL 1108 or BIOL 1108H) | Pre or

courses.subject: BIOE
courses.title: Tissue Engineering
courses.description: The fundamentals of science and engineering design related to replacement organs and tissues.
courses.prerequisiteText: BCHE 3520 and (BCMB 3100 or BCMB 3100E or BCMB 3100H) | Graduate Prerequisite | Permission of department

courses.subject: BIOE
courses.title: Human Factors and Ergonomics in Biomedical Device Design
courses.description: Introduction of the application of human factors and ergonomics in the design of biomedical devices as well as the regulatory framework for device pre-market approval.

courses.subject: BIOE
courses.title: Human Factors and Ergonomics in Biomedical Device Design
courses.description: Introduction of the application of human factors and ergonomics in the design of biomedical devices, as well as the regulatory framework for device pre-market approval.

courses.subject: BIOE
courses.title: Biomaterials
courses.description: Biomaterials and groundwork for topics such as mechanical, chemical, and thermal properties of replacement materials and tissues.  Implantation of materials in the body is studied for the biological point of view.
courses.course_objectives: Students will apply fundamentals of engineering science to the application of materials for medical application. Students will describe and understand physiology of tissues and organs and their engineering performances. Students will develop design criteria for solving problems toward medical applications. Students will have developed creative thinking skills and formulation of conceptual solutions. Students will have reinforced communication skills. Students will have a greater understanding of the need to engage in life-long learning.
courses.topical_outline:
1. Natural and synthetic polymeric materials
2. Wound healing
3. Foreign body response
4. Tissue engineering

courses.subject: BIOE
courses.title: Biomedical Engineering Laboratory
courses.description: This course is intended to connect basic science, materials, and engineering principles with specific biomedical applications through experiential learning.

courses.subject: BIOE
courses.title: Biomechanics
courses.description: The application of engineering principles to solid mechanics and to body dynamics is discussed. The student should understand the mechanics of the musculoskeletal system.
courses.course_objectives: Students will apply fundamentals of engineering science to understand movement of the human body. Students will describe and understand physiology of bone and its relationship to engineering performance. Students will develop design criteria for solving problems in medical applications.
courses.topical_outline: • Statics Analysis of Human Models and Ergonomics Applications • Kinematics/Kinetics of the Human Body • Gait Analysis and Calculations of Intersegmental Loading • Nonlinear Mechanics of Biological Tissue, Including Bone, Muscle, Ligament/Tendon

courses.subject: BIOE
courses.title: Regulations and Ethics in Biomedical Engineering
courses.description: Ethical issues in biomedical engineering: responsible conduct of research, concepts of good lab and clinical practices, ethical issues, and case studies. Food and Drug Administration (FDA) regulatory pathways and approval procedures. Commercialization and technology transfer.
courses.prerequisiteText: (BCMB 3100 or BCMB 3100E or BCMB 4010/6010) and BCHE 3520

courses.subject: BIOE
courses.title: Capstone Design I
courses.description: This capstone design course is the first in a two-semestersequence that is project-based and focused on problem framing,stakeholder analysis, concept generation, and project managementskills. The projects are designed to provide students with asignificant design experience in engineering prior to graduation.
courses.course_objectives: Students will perform professionally exhibiting integrity, accepting responsibility, taking initiative, and providing leadership necessary to ensure project success. Students will establish relationships and implement practices with team members, academic advisors, industrial advisors, and clients that support high performance and continuous improvement. Students will plan, monitor, and manage project schedule, resources, and work assignments to ensure timely and within budget completion. Students will utilize prior knowledge, independent research, published information, patents, and original ideas in framing problems and generating solutions.
courses.topical_outline: Projects will be developed in collaboration with industry partners and faculty consultations.

courses.subject: BIOE
courses.title: Capstone Design II
courses.description: This capstone design course is the second in a two-semestersequence that is project-based and focused on concept selection,development, prototyping, and testing.  The projects are designedto provide students with a significant design experience inengineering prior to graduation.
courses.course_objectives: Students will produce design products that meet important performance requirements while satisfying relevant societal and professional constraints. Students will make design decisions based on product design requirements, product life-cycle considerations, life-cycle cost, resource availability, and associated risks. Students will demonstrate effective use of contemporary tools for engineering and business analysis, fabrication, testing, and design communication. Students will test and defend performance of a design or design product with respect to the design requirements. Students will use formal and informal communications with team, advisor, and clients to document and facilitate progress and to enhance impact of design products. This includes a written report, a poster, and an oral presentation. Students will assess and pursue personal professional growth in concert with project requirements and personal career goals. Students will understand the interaction of biological engineering with other disciplines in the design process.
courses.topical_outline: 1. Projects will be developed in collaboration with industry. 2. Partners and faculty consultations.

courses.subject: BIOE
courses.title: Faculty-Mentored Undergraduate Research I
courses.description: Faculty-supervised independent or collaborative inquiry into fundamental and applied problems within a discipline that requires students to gather, analyze, and synthesize and interpret data and to present results in writing and other relevant communication formats.

courses.subject: BIOE
courses.title: Faculty-Mentored Undergraduate Research II
courses.description: Faculty-supervised independent or collaborative inquiry into fundamental and applied problems within a discipline that requires students to gather, analyze, and synthesize and interpret data and to present results in writing and other relevant communication formats.

courses.subject: BIOE
courses.title: Faculty-Mentored Undergraduate Research III
courses.description: Faculty-supervised independent or collaborative inquiry into fundamental and applied problems within a discipline that requires students to gather, analyze, and synthesize and interpret data and to present results in writing and other relevant communication formats.

courses.subject: BIOE
courses.title: Undergraduate Research Thesis (or Final Project)
courses.description: Faculty-supervised independent or collaborative inquiry into fundamental and applied problems within a discipline that requires students to gather, analyze, and synthesize and interpret data. Students will write or produce a thesis or other professional capstone product, such as a report or portfolio that describes their systematic and in-depth inquiry.

courses.subject: BIOE
courses.title: Regenerative Medicine, Cell Manufacturing, and Society
courses.description: Designed to introduce advanced students working in cell biology and regenerative medicine research to ethical, policy, and social issues relevant to the field, specifically stem cell research.

courses.subject: BIOE
courses.title: Multiscale Biomechanics
courses.description: Designed for students to study advanced concepts in multiscale biomechanics at the molecular and cellular levels. Advanced biomolecular and cellular biomechanics topics will be covered. Students will learn advanced theoretical and advanced experimental topics related to biomechanics.

courses.subject: BIOE
courses.title: Advances in 3-D Cell-Based Biosensors
courses.description: Advances in three-dimensional cell-based sensors as well as the associated signal readout technologies with emphasis on application in drug discovery and non-clinical development.
courses.offeredText: Not offered on a regular basis.

courses.subject: BIOE
courses.title: Biofabrication and 3D Printing
courses.description: Introduction to the field processing of natural and synthetic polymers as well as biofabrication and 3-D printing of devices.  Students will learn properties of polymeric materials and how to design medical devices and structures, such as implants, scaffolds, catheters, and stents from polymers.
courses.prerequisiteText: ENGG(CHEM) 4615/6615 or CHEM 8420 or permision of department

courses.subject: BIOE
courses.title: Biocompatibility of Materials
courses.description: Introduces graduate students to the fundamental aspects of biomaterial-tissue interactions, experimental design for biocompatibility testing methods, and related translational research and regulatory evaluation requirements. The course also allows students to build on these concepts through literature research, project proposal writing, and project management planning.
courses.course_objectives: Upon completion of this course, students will be enabled to provide a foundation in contemporary biomaterial-interface principles and their use in modern medical devices. Upon completion of this course, students will be enabled to discuss cellular and molecular aspects of the host response to biomaterials. Upon completion of this course, students will be enabled to discuss methodology and regulatory requirements for biocompatibility testing evaluation. Upon completion of this course, students will be enabled to develop critical analysis of biomaterials through a research project proposal writing and project management planning. Upon completion of this course, students will be enabled to develop critical scientific literature review and effective written/verbal communication.
courses.topical_outline: Introduction to biomaterials and medical device materials Cellular and molecular interactions with surfaces Reactions of biological molecules on biomaterials Inflammation, wound healing, and foreign body response Systemic and immune toxicity of implanted materials Methods of testing biological performance and biocompatibility (in vitro, in vivo) Regulatory guidelines for biocompatibility of materials testing for medical device applications Translational research, clinical performance, and interdisciplinary aspects of biomaterials and medical device development Technical scientific writing and verbal presentation Research project proposal and project management planning

courses.subject: BIOE
courses.title: Advanced Biomaterials
courses.description: Advanced concepts of biomedical engineering, materials science, and chemistry, including interactions between materials and blood/bacteria/cells/tissues and the development of biomaterials, their clinical applications, and animal models used to evaluate biomaterials.

courses.subject: BIOE

Lectures providebiological background and describe classical and more recentmodels. Hands-on exercises in Matlab are used to develop skillsin generating, analyzing, and utilizing systems models.

courses.subject: BIOE
courses.title: Advanced Biomedical Instrumentation
courses.description: The study of advanced concepts in biomedical instrumentation from a systems viewpoint. Advanced physiological and electro-physiological concepts will be covered in this course. Students will learn advanced theoretical and advanced biomedical instrumentation concepts.

courses.subject: BIOE

courses.description: Advanced directed readings in special topics in biological engineering in an area(s) of interest to the student.

courses.subject: BIOL(CBIO)(VPAT)
courses.title: Electron Microscopy
courses.description: Instrument theory and theory of specimen preparation for both transmission and scanning electron microscopy. Fundamentals of X-ray microanalysis, image processing, and image analysis.

courses.subject: BIOL(CBIO)
courses.title: Electron Microscopy Laboratory
courses.description: Operation of both transmission (TEM) and scanning electron microscopes (SEM).  Preparation of specimens (ultramicrotomy, critical point drying, negative staining) for examination in both TEM and SEM.  Basics of X-ray microanalysis.

courses.subject: BIOL(FANR)
courses.title: Biology of the South Pacific
courses.description: The study of natural history on location throughout the SouthPacific, with particular emphasis on New Zealand and Australia.During visits to nature reserves and parks, rain forests, coralreefs, coastlines, and mangrove forests, the animal, plant, andinsect species will be identified, and the geological settingwill be explained. Human migration and exploitation of theenvironment will also be discussed.

courses.subject: BIOL(WILD)
courses.title: Animal Behavior
courses.description: Principles of animal behavior integrating genetic, physiological, developmental, and evolutionary aspects. Topics include communication, reproduction, sociality, foraging, defense, migration, habitat selection, and learning.

courses.subject: BIOL
courses.title: Concepts in Biology
courses.description: Course topics explore chemistry of life, environmental endocrinedisruptors' effects on gene expression, genetic testing, immunity,and effects of global nutrient cycling on climate change andeutrophication. Students apply principles to real-worldsituations, identify, interpret, and evaluate valid sources ofscientific information, and apply that information to everydaydecision-making.
courses.course_objectives: Students will be able to apply principles of biology to support real world decisions like genetic testing or purchasing habits. Students will be able to integrate ideas and communicate understanding about biology with others in a format which is adapted to particular circumstances and audiences, addresses issues in the context of the larger community and environment, and allows them to apply societal ethics to scientific inquiry and findings. Students will be able to identify and evaluate the credibility of valid sources of scientific information. Students will be able to develop and effectively express scientific ideas in a written form for a general audience. Students will learn to work effectively with others in a group and develop and cultivate an interest in current science issues. Students will be able to model the process whereby researchers test a scientific claim, including composing a valid scientific argument.

courses.title: Organismal Biology
courses.description: In this general biology course, students will study organismsfrom an ecological and evolutionary perspective. Emphasis is onstructure and function, pathways and transformation of energy andmatter, and the importance of biodiversity. Students will applycore biological concepts to contemporary challenges, emphasizinginteractions between humans and their environment.
courses.course_objectives: Students will identify relationships between core biological concepts and predict outcomes of situations based on those relationships. Students will effectively communicate, verbally and in-writing, to a general audience about core biological concepts and relationships between them. Students will identify and apply knowledge about biology in various scenarios to improve human and environmental health. Students will be able to think critically about scientific information, and the relevance of scientific information to your career path. Students will have confidence in your ability to understand and make decisions about biology in your daily life.

courses.title: Principles of Biology I
courses.description: This course focuses on information flow and evolution. The flow of information within biological systems, how genetic information influences traits of organisms and is passed to the next generation, and how populations evolve over time will be examined.
courses.course_objectives: Students will examine information flow in biological systems at different scales and over time. Students will develop and use models of information flow in biological systems. Students will interpret data and figures related to information flow in biological systems. Students will use quantitative reasoning to analyze scenarios involving information flow in biological systems.

courses.subject: BIOL
courses.title: Principles of Biology II
courses.description: Students will examine how biological systems function, and how energy moves within and between these systems. We will explore biology across multiple scales including biochemistry, molecular biology, cell biology, physiology, population biology, and community ecology.
courses.course_objectives: Students will explore the structure and behavior of biological systems. Students will understand how energy is transformed and transferred across different levels of biological organization. Students will improve their data literacy by learning how to use models, analyze graphical information, and communicate quantitative data. Students will examine how structure impacts the function of biological organisms or systems. Students will interrogate how processes at different levels of biological organization impact each other.
courses.topical_outline:
This course will examine energy transfer, and the relationships between structure and function in biological systems at five scales:

• Molecular and Biochemical Scale
• Cellular scale
• Organismal scale (i.e., anatomy and physiology)
• Population and community scale
• Ecosystem scale

An emphasis will be placed on how these systems are organized and behave, and how these systems respond to the changes in their environment. The relationships and interactions between processes at these scales will also be investigated.
courses.prerequisiteText: (BIOL 1107 and BIOL 1107L) or (BIOL 2107H and BIOL 2107L) or permission of department

Students will evaluate new scientific findings and how the Internet, media, and businesses may dramatize and misrepresent those findings. Students will identify, innovate, and implement a public outreach strategy. Students will communicate to influence personal and public opinion and policies with a strong commitment and knowledge base.

courses.description: Examination of the organization and behavior of biological structures and systems, including how these systems capture and process energy and how they interact with and respond to environmental influences.

By the end of this course, students should be able to analyze and interpret data and figures. By the end of this course, students should be able to use available evidence to support or refute a claim. By the end of this course, students should be able to identify and describe ways in which human activity alters the structure and function of biological systems. By the end of this course, students should be able to communicate biological concepts and reasoning in written and oral forms.

courses.description: This course is intended for students considering careers in medicine. courses.subject: BIOL
courses.title: Professional Development for Biology Careers
courses.description: Course prepares students for careers in biology by developing skills for career exploration, job search strategies, and professional development. Students will investigate hiring trends and learn how to leverage college experiences. Students will develop their personal brand and learn how to tailor their resumes/interview strategies.
courses.course_objectives: Students will learn to analyze key trends in life science employment sectors and their impacts on employment opportunities for undergraduates majoring in biology. Students will learn to identify potential career paths within the biological sciences, using online tools and professional networking resources to research and evaluate opportunities. Students will develop a professional brand that aligns with personal interests, career goals, and industry expectations, with a focus on effective self-presentation in the job market. Students will learn to design resumes and cover letters for specific job opportunities and create tailored interview strategies to maximize success in competitive hiring environments.

Students will become well-practiced in laboratory skills. Students will be able to critically interpret results. Students will gain practice communicating results through scientific writing and oral presentation.

courses.course_objectives: Students will define the scope of planning required to conduct biological field research. Students will design and execute adaptive research plans to collect biological data in the field. Students will understand the drivers and impacts of select environmental issues. Students will synthesize collected data and present the findings of experimental results.

Students will engage in active reflection in order to develop as an instructor.

courses.subject: BIOL
courses.title: Science and Health Writing
courses.description: Students will analyze the ways that scientists’ and health professionals’ messages must change with the audiences they address, whether scientific, lay, or government. Students will explore topics of interest in a science or health field, and they will communicate about that topic through different writing formats and strategies.
courses.course_objectives: Students will apply public health and communication theories to tailor messages for particular science and health rhetorical situations. Students will assess and synthesize relevant published and unpublished sources of information as evidence for message. Students will create clear and persuasive textual, visual, and oral communications founded in rhetorical theory. Students will collaborate in groups to create an intervention plan to respond to a particular public health issue.
courses.topical_outline:
- Conduct interviews with researchers, practitioners, patients
- Engage with generative AI though strategies and practice
- Create essays that bring together a variety of sources (peer reviewed articles, reputable websites such as the WHO, interviews, etc.) to communicate the importance of an area of healthcare or scientific research
- Create visual communications
- Collaborate on a project to identify a community need and create an intervention using communication and public health theories

courses.subject: BIOL
courses.title: Scientific Research Writing
courses.description: Students will examine recent peer-reviewed scientific writing, consider the strategies of successful scientific writers, learn writing conventions of scientific journals, and workshop student writing. If an undergraduate student is engaged in research (e.g., Undergraduate Research in Biology), the student can work on the required research paper during the course. Graduate students can work on a current research paper during the course.
courses.course_objectives: Students will develop an argument for the importance of a scientific research question and contextualize it within a broader scientific research conversation. Students will assess and synthesize relevant published and unpublished sources of information. Students will create clear and persuasive communications for scientific writing rhetorical situations. Students will design visual communications to represent data Students will demonstrate effective oral communication skills to practice delivering textual messages.
courses.topical_outline:
- Analyze and evaluate published scientific research articles 
- Develop a research proposal
- Compose a scientific article, which includes developing an argument, contextualizing work with current research, visualizing data, and interpreting of findings
- Create a scientific research poster using data visualization strategies
- Present scientific research poster

courses.subject: BIOL
courses.title: Biomedical Applications of Molecular Biology Laboratory Skills
courses.description: Students will gain hands-on experience in molecular cloning, bacterial and mammalian cell culture, reporter assays, and protein analysis. The course culminates in linking molecular biology to translational organoid models, emphasizing experimental design, data analysis, and biomedical application. This class is offered in a Study Abroad setting.
courses.course_objectives: Students who complete this course will be able to design and execute molecular cloning experiments, including plasmid mapping, primer design, bacterial transformation, and colony screening. Students who complete this course will be able to perform DNA purification, quality control, and mammalian transfection with appropriate biosafety practice. Students who complete this course will be able to conduct quantitative assays (e.g. luciferase, Western blot) to measure protein expression and analyze data critically. Students who complete this course will be able to integrate molecular findings with translational applications by linking reporter assays to organoid-based models. Students who complete this course will be able to communicate scientific reasoning effectively through written reflections and experimental proposals. Students who complete this course will be able to recognize ethical considerations in biomedical research.
courses.topical_outline:
Week 1
•	Plasmid design, cloning strategies, and bacterial transformation
•	Colony screening and plasmid purification Week 2
•	DNA purification and QC
•	Mammalian transfection and reporter gene assays Week 3
•	Protein harvest, SDS-PAGE, and Western blot
•	Immunodetection and densitometry
•	Translational mini-module: linking reporter assays to patient-derived organoid models
courses.prerequisiteText: [(BIOL 1107 and BIOL 1107L) or (BIOL 2107H and BIOL 2107L)] and [(CHEM 1212-1212D and CHEM 1212L) or (CHEM 1412-1412D and CHEM 1412L)]

courses.description: Topics will vary by semester and instructor.  This course isintended to allow faculty to cover timely, advanced topics ofspecial interest to biology majors, particularly focusing onrecent discoveries and technical literature.

courses.subject: BIOL
courses.title: Internship in Biology
courses.description: Supervised work experience with public agencies, private industry, mass media, or non-profit organizations in the area of the biological sciences.  Examples of work experience include traineeships in scientific investigation, environmental impact assessment, financial analysis, mass media, biotechnology law,and informatics. In addition to an off-campus workplace and supervisor, students must identify a UGA faculty member to serveas an academic interface/coordinator. Students must submit a proposal or other documentation (e.g., letter from supervisor)outlining their duties and responsibilities to the facultycoordinator who must approve it.

courses.title: Undergraduate Research in Biology
courses.description: Laboratory research conducted under the supervision of a faculty member in biological sciences.  Arrangements must be made in advance. A final paper/report is required to receive credit toward the Biology major.

courses.subject: BIOL
courses.title: Tropical Biology
courses.description: Biological concepts pertaining to the tropics through intensive field study.

courses.subject: BIOS(EPID)
courses.title: Spatial Epidemiology
courses.description: Spatial modeling in infectious, chronic, and environmentalepidemiology.  Methods for disease mapping, detection anddelineation of disease clusters, and linking disease outcome toenvironmental exposures are considered.  Parameter estimation,inference, and diagnostic testing for geostatistical, random field, and point process models are described.

courses.subject: BIOS(PHAR)
courses.title: Biostatistical Applications for the Pharmaceutical and Biotechnology Industries
courses.description: Biostatistical issues regarding the introduction and regulatory agency (FDA) approval of new drugs, biologics, medical devices, and combination products, and their postmarket surveillance are considered. Data quality assurance, experimental design, clinical trials, power and sample size determination, uncertainty assessment, regression, survival analysis, and variable and model selection are considered.

courses.subject: BIOS(STAT)
courses.title: Survival Analysis
courses.description: Methods for comparing time-to-event data, including univariate parametric and nonparametric procedures, regression models, diagnostics, group comparisons, and use of relevant statistical computing packages.
courses.prerequisiteText: [(STAT 4210 or STAT 4110H) and STAT 4510/6510] or permission of department | Graduate Prerequisite | [(STAT 6220 or STAT 4230/6230 or STAT 6320 or STAT 6420 or BIOS 7020) and STAT 4510/6510] or permission of department

courses.subject: BIOS(STAT)
courses.title: Intermediate Mathematical Statistics
courses.description: Calculus-based introduction to probability and mathematicalstatistics for students in Biostatistics, Epidemiology and otherfields requiring a technical understanding of statisticalinference. Random variables, expectation, laws of large numbersand central limit theorem. Point estimation, confidence intervals, and hypothesis testing for statistical models with public health and biomedical applications.

courses.subject: BIOS(STAT)
courses.title: Multilevel and Hierarchical Models
courses.description: Multilevel and hierarchical models for social and biologicalsciences.  Empirical Bayes, James-Stein, maximum likelihood, andBayesian estimation of model parameters.  Interpreting anddiagnosing multilevel models, model building, and uncertaintyassessment.

courses.subject: BIOS(STAT)
courses.title: Clinical Trials
courses.description: Drug development and FDA approval procedures; randomization;blindness; phase I-IV clinical trials; multicenter trials;bioequivalency; sample size determination; design and analysis;cross-over design; repeated measurements design; survivalanalysis; meta analysis.

courses.subject: BIOS
courses.title: Elementary Biostatistics
courses.description: Basic concepts of statistics with applications in health and life sciences. Descriptive statistics, principles of statisticalinference, uncertainty assessment, hypothesis testing, publichealth surveys, and biomedical experimental design areconsidered. Methods include t-tests, simple linear regression,and categorical data analysis.
courses.course_objectives: Students will be able to produce graphical summaries of data. Students will be able to identify the principles of statistical inference, including parameter estimation and uncertainty assessment. Students will be able to describe the importance of randomization in public health surveys and biomedical experiments. Students will be able to communicate the results of biostatistical analyses, draw substantive conclusions from the results of hypotheses tests. Students will be able to distinguish between prospective and retrospective studies. Students will be able to use statistical software. Students will be able to apply Bayes Theorem to diagnostic tests, public health survey design, and analysis of contingency tables.
courses.topical_outline: 1. Descriptive statistics 2. Basic probability concepts 3. Bayes Theorem and diagnostic procedures 4. Public health surveys 5. Principles of statistical inference 6. Biomedical experiments 7. One-sample and two-sample t-test 8. Chi-square tests for contingency tables 9. Simple linear regression

courses.description: Students will develop statistical literacy in public health. Course will provide the fundamentals of biostatistics and will apply them to public health research. Topics will include exploratory data analysis, probability theory, and how to interpret the statistical output.

courses.title: Foundations of Biostatistics
courses.description: Students will develop statistical literacy in public health. Course will provide the fundamentals of biostatistics and will apply them to public health research. Topics will include exploratory data analysis, probability theory, and how to interpret the statistical output.

courses.subject: BIOS
courses.title: Applied Biostatistics for Public Health I (Online)
courses.description: Students will apply statistical knowledge to relevant issues in health promotion and behavior. Application includes the use of a statistical package with programming capabilities.

courses.subject: BIOS
courses.title: Applied Biostatistics for Public Health II (Online)
courses.description: Students will apply statistical knowledge to relevant issues in environmental health science. Application includes the use of a statistical package with programming capabilities.

courses.subject: BIOS
courses.title: Graduate Student Seminar
courses.description: Advanced supervised experience in an applied setting.  This course may not be used to satisfy a student's approved program of study.

courses.subject: BIOS
courses.title: Introductory Biostatistics I
courses.description: Introductory statistics with applications to medical and biological problems. Topics to be covered include biostatisticaldesign in health research, data collection and management, and introductory concepts and methods of statistical data analysis.

courses.subject: BIOS
courses.title: Introductory Biostatistics I
courses.description: Introductory statistics with applications to medical andbiological problems. Topics to be covered include biostatisticaldesign in health research, data collection and management, andintroductory concepts and methods of statistical data analysis.

courses.subject: BIOS
courses.title: Introductory Biostatistics II
courses.description: Introduction to a variety of statistical tools with applicationsin public health and the biological sciences, including surveysampling, multiple regression, experimental design, categoricaldata analysis, logistic regression, and survival analysis. Motivating examples will be drawn directly from the literature inthe health, biological, medical, and behavioral sciences.
courses.prerequisiteText: BIOS 7010 or BIOS 7010E or permission of department

courses.subject: BIOS
courses.title: Introductory Biostatistics II
courses.description: Introduction to a variety of statistical tools with applications in public health and the biological sciences, including simple and multiple regression, experimental design, categorical data analysis, logistic regression, and survival analysis. Motivating examples will be drawn directly from the literature in the health, biological, medical, and behavioral sciences.
courses.course_objectives: Students will learn to apply public health research, practice, and ethics to inform biostatistical analyses. Students will learn to describe concepts of probability, random variation, and commonly used probability distributions. Students will learn to execute exploratory data analyses including the production of tabular summaries, graphical displays, and descriptive statistics. Students will learn to identify the appropriate statistical procedure for statistical analysis based on study objectives, study design, and the types of variables involved. Students will learn to apply common statistical procedures including simple and multiple regression, analysis of variance, analysis of contingency tables, non-parametric methods, logistic regression, and survival analysis using at least one statistical software package.
courses.topical_outline: 1.	Simple and Multiple Regression 2.	Analysis of Variance 3.	Categorical Data Analysis 4.	Logistic Regression 5.	Survival Analysis
courses.prerequisiteText: BIOS 7010 or BIOS 7010E or permission of department

courses.subject: BIOS
courses.title: Biostatistical Applications for the Pharmaceutical and Biotechnology Industries
courses.description: Biostatistical issues regarding the introduction and regulatoryagency (FDA) approval of new drugs, biologics, medical devices,and combination products, and their postmarket surveillance areconsidered.  Data quality assurance, experimental design,clinical trials, power and sample size determination, uncertaintyassessment, regression, survival analysis, and variable and modelselection are considered.

courses.subject: BIOS
courses.title: Master's Thesis
courses.description: Thesis writing under the direction of the major professor.

courses.subject: BIOS
courses.title: Research Data Management and Computing
courses.description: Introduction to concepts and techniques of research datamanagement in public health and biomedicine; use of computers and statistical programs to process and analyze biomedical andhealth-related data.

courses.subject: BIOS
courses.title: Regression and Analysis of Variance
courses.description: Regression and analysis of variance (ANOVA) for biomedical andpublic health data.  Simple and multiple regression models areconsidered, including data transformation, weighted regression,diagnostics, and model selection.  Contrasts, multiplecomparison, missing, and unbalanced data are considered forexperimental designs including one-way and multi-way ANOVA,randomized block, and Latin squares.

courses.subject: BIOS
courses.title: Linear and Generalized Linear Models
courses.description: Extension of linear models to data with heterogeneous varianceand correlated repeated measures.  Mixed effects, log-linear, and generalized linear models are considered. Statistical inference is carried out using quasi-likelihood, conditional likelihood, marginal likelihood, and generalized estimating equations. Applications in public health and biomedical research.

courses.subject: BIOS
courses.title: Longitudinal Data Analysis
courses.description: Introduces students to statistical models and methods for theanalysis of longitudinal data, including univariate andmultivariate repeated measures analysis of variance, generallinear model for correlated continuous data, generalized linearmodels, generalized estimating equations, and generalized linearmixed effects models.

courses.subject: BIOS
courses.title: Advanced Biostatistics
courses.description: Recent developments in biostatistical research aimed at analysesof biomedical and public health data.  Emphasis is given to their motivation, statistical properties, computation, practicalapplications, comparison to alternative techniques, andopportunities for future research.

courses.subject: BIOS
courses.title: Categorical Data Analysis
courses.description: Introduction to analysis of categorical data including log-linear models, logistic regression, probit models, graphical models and casual inference.  Motivating examples will be drawn directly from the literature in the health, biological, medical, and social sciences.

courses.subject: BIOS
courses.title: Multivariate Design for Public Health
courses.description: Multivariate analysis of data from designed experiments in public health.  Topics include descriptive statistics, graphicalmethods, experimental design, Hotelling's T-square, multivariateanalysis of variance, orthogonal contrasts, profile analysis,repeated measures, and discriminant analysis.

courses.subject: BIOS
courses.title: Reproducible Research: Statistical Methods and Practices
courses.description: Basic definitions, approaches, and current issues in reproducibleresearch; metrics for assessing reproducibility for binary,continuous, multivariate, and meta-analysis data; best practicesfor statistical design and analysis of reproducible studiesinvolving simple group comparisons, regression and prediction,large database analyses, bioinformatics, and unsupervisedclustering; current examples drawn from literature throughout.

courses.subject: BIOS
courses.title: Biosatistical Consulting I
courses.description: Biostatistical consulting skills needed to assist clients,formulate statistical models, explain analyses and results, andwrite reports in language understandable to the investigators inpublic health and biomedicine.  Practice of biostatisticalconsulting as it relates to human subjects research, focusing onethical treatment of human subjects.

courses.subject: BIOS
courses.title: Biostatistical Consulting II
courses.description: Biostatistical consulting skills needed to collaborate withinvestigators in public health and biomedicine.  Practice ofbiostatistical consulting as it relates to ethical conduct ofresearch and proposals for extramural research support.

courses.subject: BIOS
courses.title: Monte Carlo Methods and Bayesian Computation
courses.description: Introduces Monte Carlo methods, including Monte Carlo integration, variance reduction, and optimization. The Bayesian framework of inference and the Markov Chain Monte Carlo method (MCMC) will be used to estimate posteriors.

courses.subject: BIOS
courses.title: Advanced Biostatistical Inference
courses.description: Following an overview of probability measures and distribution functions, modes of convergence, laws of large numbers and central limit theorems, decision theory, hypothesis testing, and Bayesian inference are considered.  Emphasis is given to results needed to develop and evaluate biostatistical methodsrather than rigorous mathematical proofs.

courses.subject: BIOS
courses.title: Asymptotic Biostatistical Inference
courses.description: Asymptotic inference for maximum likelihood estimators, M-estimators, U-statistics, and nonparametric and semiparametric models.  Consistency, asymptotic normality, and asymptotic efficiency are considered.  Both independent and dependent data cases are included. Emphasis is given to results needed to develop and evaluate biostatistical methods rather than rigorous mathematical proofs.

courses.subject: BIOS
courses.title: Special Topics in Biostatistics
courses.description: Selected topics concerning recent developments in biostatisticsare covered.

courses.subject: BIOS
courses.title: Problems in Biostatistics
courses.description: Analysis of contemporary biostatistical methods, theory, andapplications.

courses.subject: BIOS
courses.title: Doctoral Research
courses.description: Research while enrolled for a doctoral degree under the direction of faculty members.

courses.subject: BIOS
courses.title: Graduate Student Seminar
courses.description: Advanced supervised experience in an applied setting for studentsat the doctoral level. This course may not be used to satisfy astudent's approved program of study.

courses.subject: BIOS
courses.title: Biostatistics Graduate Seminar
courses.description: Provides graduate students with exposure to current biostatistical research, topics relevant to their graduate school experience, and future academic opportunities. In a journal club, students will critique seminal papers in statistics and biostatistics.

courses.subject: BIOS
courses.title: Doctoral Dissertation
courses.description: Dissertation writing under the direction of the major professor.

courses.subject: BMSC(VPHY)(RBIO)
courses.title: Neurobiology of Disease
courses.description: Molecular and cellular mechanisms underlying the pathophysiology and therapeutics of neurological disorders, including neurodegenerative diseases, psychiatric disorders, and traumatic injury. The course will include discussion of general principles of disease mechanisms such as protein aggregation, metabolic dysfunction, neuroinflammation, and genetic and environmental risk factors relevant to each disease.
courses.course_objectives: Students will learn to examine the pathophysiology and causes of neurological diseases and how this information is used to develop therapeutic strategies. Students will learn to assimilate the literature about our understanding of disease mechanisms for individual diseases covered in this course. Students will understand the broad concepts of functional deficits and the mechanisms involved in each neurological disease covered in the course. Students will investigate, analyze, synthesize, and write knowledgeably and coherently on one neurological disease covered in the course in a written course report.
courses.topical_outline: 1.	General mechanisms of neurodegenerative diseases: genetic and environmental risk factors, protein misfolding, metabolic syndrome, mitochondrial dysfunction, neuroinflammation, neurotransmitter imbalance 2.	Non-motor autonomic dysfunction in ND and gut-brain microbiome axis 3.	Principles of neurotherapeutics 4.	Alzheimer’s disease 5.	Parkinson’s disease 6.	Amyotrophic lateral sclerosis and Huntington’s disease 7.	Multiple sclerosis and myelin disorders 8.	Mood disorders 9.	Substance abuse disorders/Addiction 10.	Neurotoxicology- Exposure induced disorders and syndromes 11.	Brain tumors and emerging anticancer treatment 12.	Stroke, Spinal cord injury, and Traumatic brain injury 13.	Epilepsy and neuropathic pain 14.	Autism spectrum disorder/intellectual disability 15.	Sleep disorders
courses.prerequisiteText: Courses in Physiology or Cell Biology or Biochemistry required

courses.subject: BMSC
courses.title: Companion Animal Behavior and the Human-Animal Relationship
courses.description: Exploration of the process of domestication for five different companion animals: the cat, dog, horse, rabbit, and parrot.  The student will learn the behavior of the wild ancestors and the current domestic animals and explore various aspects of the human-animal bond and human-animal relationship, as well as the place of animals in various human religions. Introduction to the training techniques and tools used for the training of dogs and horses. Students will use the information they have learned and engage in discussions of the welfare of these five species when under human care, both as general concepts and as specific issues.

courses.subject: BMSC
courses.title: Basic Medical Histology
courses.description: Cells organize to form tissues. The body is composed of four basic tissues that together form organs. Organs interact to create organ systems. Introduction to the four basic tissues, identification of these tissues in different organ systems, and gaining an appreciation for how the function of an organ is dependent on its structure.
