courses.subject: DANC
courses.title: Issues in Dance Education and Pedagogy
courses.description: Survey of selected topics in dance education, emphasizing learning theories, history of dance in education, diversity and gender issues, scientific principles and theories related to the teaching of dance, including cognitive science and motor learning applications, and assessment. Includes 4-8 hours of community or K12 school field experience.
courses.course_objectives: Students will differentiate between various types of learners in the dance classroom. Students will identify a common language among genres from which to observe, analyze, and teach movement. Students will apply foundational pedagogical knowledge in an applied teaching setting. Students will analyze selected historical and contemporary challenges in the dance education field and how they apply to their own learning and teaching practices. Students will apply practical and theoretical information from various critical perspectives to the building of their own informed teaching philosophy. Students will synthesize theoretical and practical information in order to see themselves as teachers/professionals, rather than students.
courses.topical_outline: Situating the learner and learning: Personal, historical, and critical perspectives in dance education Instructional practices; The art and science of effective dance teaching Implementation of learned practices: Community or K12 teaching practicum Implementation of learned practices: Creating a Teacher's Visionary Statement
courses.prerequisiteText: Permission of department | Graduate Prerequisite | Permission of department

courses.subject: DANC
courses.title: Senior Choreographic Project
courses.description: Guided creation of an original choreographic work as a capstone project as part of a fully produced concert production of peer works. Student will write a brief project proposal and post-project analysis/reflection and assist in duties required for concert production.
courses.course_objectives: By the end of this course, students will imagine a choreographic vision and communicate it in a written statement. By the end of this course, students will apply selected crafting devices to movement studies and phrases. By the end of this course, students will critically review/analyze the choreographic drafts of their peers. By the end of this course, students will compose a draft and final version of a choreographic work. By the end of this course, students will analyze the effectiveness of their own work in progress and make resulting edits. By the end of this course, students will communicate effectively with their peers whom they hired as performers in their work. By the end of this course, students will communicate persuasively and clearly with their hired peer performers in leading them in choreographic process. By the end of this course, students will make aesthetic value assessments as to how their work is communicating their intended idea. By the end of this course, students will reflect on critical feedback and create revisions and changes to a choreographic work in process.
courses.topical_outline: Drafting initial proposal Revision and final proposal Explore possible movement studies and phrases Create rough draft of work Editing and peer review Reflection of work in progress Faculty showing of work in progress Technical rehearsals and lighting design Final performance and assessment Post-project analysis/reflection

courses.subject: DMAN
courses.title: Introduction to Disaster Management
courses.description: An introduction to emergency operations and disaster management - from mitigating and planning for disasters to responding to and recovering from them. Students will learn how their personal and community emergency preparedness can be improved, and about the careers and opportunities available in disaster management.

courses.subject: DMAN
courses.title: Disasters and Society
courses.description: Exploration of the connections between disasters and societies. Upon completion of the course, students will have a broad understanding of the core theories and frameworks that guide emergency and disaster management, including mitigation, planning, preparedness, response, recovery, and research. Students will conduct hands-on, in-class exercises and learn from leading experts in the field of disaster management.
courses.course_objectives: Students will be able to identify how social systems interact with hazards and disaster events. Students will be able to interpret major historical disasters and analyze their scale and scope of impact. Students will be able to describe key methods used to prevent, manage, and respond to disasters. Students will be able to explain key theories related to the study of disaster research, including vulnerability.
courses.topical_outline:
1. Overview of disasters and society
a. Natural hazards
b. Technological and human-caused hazards
c. Historical disaster events
d. The impacts of climate change
e. Fostering individual and community resilience
2. Key concepts, methods, and theories of disaster management
a. The National Incident Management System (NIMS)
b. The Incident Command Systems (ICS)
c. The disaster management cycle
d. Emergency response and triage
e. Scenario-based role-play and tabletop exercises
3. The history and future of emergency and disaster management
a. The evolution of disaster management in the U.S.
b. Disaster law and policy
c. Disaster ethics and research
d. Jobs and careers in emergency and disaster management
e. The future of disaster management

courses.description: Introduction to policies and practices intended to minimize losses from hazards and disasters. There is a growing demand for this knowledge and skillset. The costs to people and societies by hazards continue to challenge managers at all levels - from government and the private sector to NGOs and grassroots movements.

courses.subject: DMAN
courses.title: International Aspects of Disasters
courses.description: An overview of disasters and disaster management from an international perspective, with a focus on social vulnerability. Content will address a number of issues, including the relationship between disasters and social systems, how disasters are dealt with in different countries, and the interactions between nations during disasters.

courses.subject: DMAN
courses.title: Disasters, Media, and Pop Culture
courses.description: This highly interactive course focuses on representations of disasters in media and pop culture. Issues discussed will include disaster news, social media, symbolism, film, music and disasters, and disaster literature. Students will learn how these issues relate to applied topics in disasters, such as warning communication and policy framing.

courses.subject: DMAN
courses.title: How to Survive the Apocalypse
courses.description: Apocalypses signal an end of times, and they are seen in the histories, present, and futures of life on Earth. In this course, we examine what it means to survive - and prevent - an apocalypse! Together, we draw from diverse disciplinary perspectives, including human-environment geography, environmental studies, sustainability, and disaster management.

courses.subject: DMAN
courses.title: Methods in Disaster Research
courses.description: Designed to prepare students for a broad range of methods used in the study of hazards and disasters. Topics include quick response fieldwork training, ethics, introduction to SPSS, and basic GIS. Students will practice forming research questions, strategies for data collection, and conducting analyses.

Content will address critical issues, including how Federalism influences disaster response, the legal impact of a declared Public Health Emergency, and contemporary ethical challenges that might be faced during disaster management.

courses.subject: DMAN

courses.description: An overview of disaster mental health, including information about: traumatic stress brought on by disasters and the impact that has on individuals and communities; the role of the public mental health system; the importance of continuity of operations (COOP) to ensure that routine services continue and behavioral health support for disaster survivors and responders is provided; disaster mental health skills and interventions; various disaster mental health training models that are used; and the importance of self-care for all disaster responders.

courses.title: Consumer Financial Planning
courses.description: Consumer problems encountered during and after school years. Howthe economy functions, wise purchase decisions, managing money,evaluating sales and advertising practices, and guarding againstunwise buying practices. Instructional approaches for teachingfinancial planning in workforce education.
courses.course_objectives: Students will be able to discuss what will be gained from the study of personal finance. Students will be able to describe the goals of financial planning. Students will be able to forecast interest rates, inflation, and the state of the economy. Students will be able to examine careers and other key factors that affect income. Students will be able to explain how to plan financially over one's lifetime. Students will be able to review types of financial records and statements pertinent to success in personal financial management. Students will be able to review all phases of personal income taxation. Students will be able to discuss the specifics of managing expenditures. Students will be able to examine the specifics of budgeting and adopt a cash-flow approach to the subject of budgeting. Students will be able to make effective use of today's changing financial services industry to earn maximum interest on money. Students will be able to discuss credit use and credit cards. Students will be able to describe the planned use of credit and non-credit card borrowing. Students will be able to discuss what happens should one become overextended using credit. Students will be able to evaluate major expenditures and the use of long-term credit. Students will be able to consider several ways to save money when purchasing goods and services. Students will be able to detail steps in the planned buying process. Students will be able to compare leasing with financing. Students will be able to cover aspects related to the housing expenditure and home-buying process. Students will be able to plan for personal health care and recognize that health insurance is really a health care plan. Students will be able to conduct a comprehensive study of investment fundamentals.
courses.topical_outline: Orientation; importance of personal finance Financial planning Managing taxes Budgeting and cash flow management Managing your cash Credit use and credit cards Planned borrowing Automobiles and other major purchases The housing expenditure Health care planning Investment fundamentals and portfolio management

courses.subject: ECHD(EPSY)
courses.title: History of Psychology and the Evolution of Contemporary Practice
courses.description: Exploration of the history of psychology and the development of the four specialty areas of contemporary practice: clinical, counseling, industrial/organizational, and school psychology.  Major figures and corresponding systems are studied, including contemporaneous political and cultural events, movements, and counter-movements. The influence of women and minorities will be emphasized.
courses.course_objectives:
To understand and appreciate the major figures and systems in psychology’s history. To understand and appreciate contemporaneous political and cultural movements and events that affected systems and theorists. To understand and appreciate the role of underrepresented groups (LGBT, women, and people of color) in the history of psychology. To understand and appreciate how psychology has impacted society. To understand and appreciate how history has evolved into contemporary practice. To understand and appreciate the foundations of specific specialties within psychology.
a. How to provide a survey of your specialty.
b. Examine the historical development of your specialty, including the social and political forces that shaped the profession. Identify and examine the contributions of important figures in your specialty.
c. Begin the process of establishing a professional identity within your specialty.
d. Students will become familiar with professional organizations that are central to specialties.
courses.topical_outline:
The hallmark of doctoral training is the (guided) individual pursuit of knowledge. Although one is challenged and supportive by various professionals (faculty, supervisors, committee members), ultimately it is up to the doctoral student to establish an independent (although inter-connected) professional path. This is true in research and in clinical practice. Required Texts:
1. Selected readings available electronically and posted on ELC.
2. Guthrie, R. V. (2004). Even the rat was white: A historical view of psychology (2nd Ed.). Boston, MA: Pearson/Allyn & Bacon.
3. Benjamin, L. T. (2014). A brief history of modern psychology. Hoboken: Wiley, 2014.
4. Free online textbook/resource http://psychclassics.yorku.ca.
5. You will pick a text or primary source on History and Systems; you must notify the instructor of your choice.

Students will have enhanced awareness of similarities and differences of the helping professions. Students will understand how to identify with goals and behavioral codes of the marriage and family therapy profession.

courses.subject: ECHD

courses.description: Exploration of eight major world religions and the salience of religion and spirituality in regard to mental health practice. Discussion on the integration of religion and/or spirituality into counseling spaces and the introduction of culturally appropriate intervention skills specifically related to religion and spirituality.
courses.course_objectives: Describe the basic tenets of eight major world religions. Articulate the legal, ethical, and professional issues confronting mental health practitioners. Exhibit the ability to attend to religion and spirituality in the counseling space. Demonstrate awareness, knowledge, and skills regarding advocacy processes needed to address institutional, societal, and attitudinal barriers that impede access, equity, and success for clients who identify with less privileged religious traditions and other marginalized clients. Document self-awareness of how behaviors, values, and attitudes regarding religion and spirituality affect performance in counseling.

courses.subject: ECHD
courses.title: Systems Bases of Behavior and Counseling
courses.description: Course examines systems basis of behavior and counseling concepts, research, and evidence-based practices equipping students with the awareness, knowledge, and skills to identify and effect systems change for enhancing mental health across people groups with various backgrounds on individual, institutional, and societal/ cultural levels to support counselors’ roles as advocates.
courses.course_objectives: Students will develop a working understanding of theories, concepts, and research associated with systems and their relevance to behavior, mental health, and systems change. Students will identify individual, organizational, societal, and systemic factors that influence quality of life and mental health among people groups across a range of backgrounds. Students will develop identify and generate counseling strategies, informed by theory and research relevant to systems bases of behavior, for enhancing counseling experiences and the overall quality of life of people across varied backgrounds. Students will explore and examine socially constructed identities, including their own (enhancing self-reflective skills and personal awareness), in the context of counseling practice.
courses.topical_outline:
This course supports core competencies in the Master’s in Psychology and Counseling Accreditation Council’s (MPCAC) requirements for profession-wide competencies which detail that certain competencies are required for all students who graduate from programs accredited by this entity in counseling and psychology. Programs must provide opportunities for all of their students to achieve and demonstrate each required profession-wide competency. The competencies serve as foundations upon which later competencies are built and demonstrated in through the practice of the profession, each competency is considered critical and necessary for graduates in programs accredited by this entity in counseling and psychology. The specific requirements for each competency are articulated in MPCAC’s Accreditation Manual.  Because science is at the core of mental health counseling and psychology, programs must demonstrate that they rely on the current evidence-base and theory when training students in specified competency areas. From MPCAC’s standards, this course provides background for building competencies in MPCAC’s Standard B.2.j., elements (ii.) knowledge of individuals in the context of their environment and how the environment (e.g., geographical, ideological, demographic, familial, institutional) affects functioning, (ii.) understanding of the use of systems changes (whether prevention or intervention) to enhance the functioning of individuals, families, groups, organizations, and/or institutions. Completion of this required course as part of the master’s degree in mental health counseling is a necessary first step for seeking licensure to practice as a counselor.
•	Systems Bases of Behavior Foundational Concepts
•	Systems Bases of Behavior and Mental Health 
•	Systems Influences on Mental Health and Quality of Life
•	Systems Bases of Behavior and Mental Health Prevention and Intervention
•	Systems Bases of Behavior and Counselor’s Role in Systems Change

courses.subject: ECHD
courses.title: Social Justice and Liberation Frameworks in School and Community Settings
courses.description: Review of social justice and liberation frameworks in school and community settings, with an emphasis on theoretical approaches and their connection to social change. A focus on the mechanisms of privilege, oppression, and social change leadership is provided, in addition to a community-based project that implements course learning.

courses.title: Social Psychology and Counseling
courses.description: Examination of social psychological perspectives on human behavior, with attention to social perception and cognition, social influence, self-conception and identity formation, anti-social and pro-social behavior, intersections with personality, counseling and other human services, and "positive" psychology.

courses.subject: ECHD
courses.title: Advanced Multicultural Counseling
courses.description: Course supports doctoral students in health service psychology as scientist-practitioners with empirical research, theories, paradigms, and ethical practice relevant to multicultural counseling and psychology. Emphasis on culturally responsive clinical skills and systems bases of behavior. Particular focus on scholars of multicultural psychology and counseling and translating theory to practice.
courses.course_objectives: Students will gain an awareness of theories, concepts, and evidence-based associated with multicultural counseling and psychology research and clinical practice. Students will develop a knowledge of a range of skills (i.e., approaches to assessment, intervention, interviewing, etc.) to facilitate multicultural practice and research in psychology with individuals, groups, and communities across diverse backgrounds and experiences. Students will apply broader scholarship and theory relevant to systems bases of behavior and interdisciplinary discourse that may have an impact on counseling psychology research and practice. Students will develop an awareness of the growth areas in  multicultural research and practice as well as the future direction for multicultural counseling and psychology. Students will develop ongoing recognition and understanding of the self as a cultural being, holding multiple intersecting, fluid, and complex social identities, and of the lifelong process involved with developing a multicultural orientation in research and practice areas (clinical, training, supervision, teaching, and service).
courses.topical_outline:
This course supports core competencies in the American Psychological Association’s requirements for profession-wide competencies which detail that certain competencies are required for all students who graduate from programs accredited in health service psychology. Programs must provide opportunities for all of their students to achieve and demonstrate each required profession-wide competency. The competencies serve as foundations upon which later competencies are built, each competency is considered critical and necessary for graduates in programs accredited in health service psychology. The specific requirements for each competency are articulated in APA’s Implementing Regulations. Because science is at the core of health service psychology, programs must demonstrate that they rely on the current evidence-base when training students in the following competency areas. From APA’s standards, this course provides background for building competencies in APA’s Standard II.B.1.b, elements (ii.) ethical and legal standards; (iii) individual and cultural diversity; (iv) professional values, attitudes, and behaviors; (v) communication and interpersonal skills; and (ix) consultation and interprofessional/interdisciplinary skills. Completion of this required course as part of the doctoral degree in Counseling Psychology is a necessary first step for seeking licensure to practice as a psychologist and for advancing future responsive evidence-based research in health service psychology.
•	MC Counseling and Psychology Theory & Concepts 
•	Self and Systems Assessment in Cultural Contexts
•	Multicultural Care
•	Intersectionality 
•	Identity Development Models
•	Ethical Issues in Multicultural Counseling and Psychology
•	Cultural Analysis 
•	Culture and Intervention
•	Psychological Assessment and Service Delivery

courses.subject: ECHD

courses.subject: ECHD

courses.description: Current trends, issues, and research related to contemporary college student affairs practices. Organizational patterns, models, and structures; professional standards; personnel practices; and innovations in program and service delivery.

courses.subject: ECHD
courses.title: Introduction to Research Methods in Student Affairs Leadership
courses.description: An overview of research methods applied within educational contexts, specifically student affairs and higher education, settings, practice, and leadership.
courses.course_objectives: Students will understand how to describe the role of research for guiding practice. Students will understand how to describe basic research procedures. Students will understand how to initiate research questions and statement of problem in the area of student affairs leadership research interest. Students will understand how to critically analyze the components of student affairs leadership research studies. Students will understand how to develop an overall knowledge of various quantitative and qualitative student affairs research methodologies. Students will understand how to complete a structured literature review locating and retrieving relevant studies related to a topic of research interest within student affairs leadership. Students will understand how to outline a research study related to a topic of research interest within student affairs leadership.
courses.topical_outline: Foundation of the Course Introduction to Research The Role of Literature Research Questions and Purpose of the Study Scholarly Writing & Research Ethics Literature Review Writing Research Introduction Framing & Research Paradigms Role of Theory in Research Theoretical Framework Selecting Research Methodologies Qualitative Study Quantitative Study Mixed Method Other Considerations in Method Positionality Statement Validity/Reliability/Trustworthiness Issues in Research Method Research Presentation

courses.subject: ECHD
courses.title: Organizational Development and Consultation in Higher Education
courses.description: Organizational development strategies and consultation approaches designed to strengthen higher education organizations.

courses.subject: ECHD
courses.title: Applied Quantitative Methods in Student Affairs
courses.description: An introduction to the conceptual and theoretical foundations of quantitative research methods in student affairs. Provides a holistic view and makes explicit the fundamental assumptions and interests of quantitative research methods in student affairs resulting in students having a deeper understanding and increased competency.

courses.subject: ECHD
courses.title: Advanced Theories of College Student Development
courses.description: Major theories of college-student psychosocial, intellectual, moral, and ego development; measurement of developmental constructs; and effects of college attendance on each domain. Differences attributable to gender, socioeconomic background, sexual orientation, age, and ethnicity.

courses.subject: ECHD
courses.title: Applied Qualitative Methods in Student Affairs Leadership
courses.description: An introduction to the conceptual and theoretical foundations of qualitative research methods in student affairs. Provides a holistic view and makes explicit the fundamental assumptions and interests of qualitative research methods in student affairs, moving all students toward deeper understanding and increased competency.
courses.course_objectives: Students will understand how to articulate understanding of social science philosophy supporting qualitative research. Students will understand how to defend the role of qualitative research in student affairs leadership. Students will understand how to reflect on the role of identities and ethics in research processes. Students will understand how to review various paradigms and designs appropriate for qualitative research. Students will understand how to devise data collection methods for qualitative research in student affairs leadership. Students will understand how to simulate data analysis strategies for qualitative research in student affairs leadership. Students will understand how to compose strategies for representing qualitative data in student affairs leadership.
courses.topical_outline: Overview and Paradigms Conceptual and Theoretical Frameworks Researcher Positionalities and Subjectivities Research Design Data Collection: Research Site Data Collection: Sampling Data Collection: Recruiting Participants Data Collection: Ethical Considerations Data Collection: Forms of Data Data Analysis Data Representation, Trustworthiness, and Answerability Reporting Findings

courses.subject: ECHD
courses.title: Environmental Assessment and Milieu Management
courses.description: Theories and techniques for assessing human environments in educational settings and strategies to influence them.
courses.offeredText: Offered summer semester every year. Offered fall

courses.subject: ECHD
courses.title: Application of Research Methods in Student Affairs Leadership
courses.description: An opportunity for students to prepare to apply research methods within educational contexts, specifically student affairs and higher education settings, practice, and leadership, with the aim of designing their own research study plan and proposal.
courses.course_objectives: Students will understand how to apply research methods within educational contexts, specifically student affairs and higher education settings, practice, and leadership. Students will understand how to design a research study plan and proposal. Students will understand how to develop an introduction, literature review, and methodology for a student affairs leadership dissertation. Students will understand how to argue and defend the worthiness and soundness of the study by developing a prospectus defense. Students will understand how to obtain any necessary IRB trainings. Students will understand how to develop an IRB proposal for the study. Students will understand how to devise strategies for developing and maintaining a consistent writing habit.
courses.topical_outline: Student Affairs leadership prospectus outline Literature review chapter of a student affairs leadership dissertation Introduction chapter of a student affairs leadership dissertation Methodology chapter of a student affairs leadership dissertation Student Affairs leadership dissertation outline Writing a student affairs leadership dissertation Defending a student affairs leadership prospectus Defending a student affairs leadership dissertation IRB training and student affairs leadership study ethics IRB student affairs leadership study submissions

courses.subject: ECHD
courses.title: Leadership and Policy Development in Student Affairs
courses.description: The theoretical foundations, research findings, and contemporary practices related to the processes of leadership and policy-making in college student affairs division. Specific attention will be given to analyzing the role of leadership in the institution and the effects of policy implementation.

courses.subject: ECHD
courses.title: Legal Issues in Student Affairs Leadership
courses.description: Course designed to orient student affairs leaders to ethical, legal, professional, and contemporary issues within the context of student affairs administration, practice, and leadership in a higher education setting.
courses.course_objectives: Students will understand how to locate the governance structure, policies, and legal resources at one’s institution, including those most informed on the laws of country, state, or province, and regulations that both influence and govern higher education. Students will understand how to describe and interpret the procedures and processes required to engage with the governance structure. Students will understand how to apply the law to policies and practices carried out by individuals working in higher education. Students will understand how to explain how policy is developed and applied, including how policies may promote or discourage equitable practice. Students will understand how to engage with law, policy, and governance outside of the university and apply it to university systems. Students will understand how to demonstrate the ability to remain current with changing policies and to connect the institution’s constituents to the systems occurring outside the institution.
courses.topical_outline: Introduction to the American Court System and Opinions Overview of Higher Education Law The College and Government Legal Planning, Dispute Resolution, and the College’s Authority and Liability The College and Legal Issues of its Employees The College and Legal Issues of its Faculty Academic Freedom and Freedom of Expression Legal Status of Students and Their Academic Issues Sexual Harassment Employees and Students with Disabilities Housing, Campus Security, Support Services, Student Files, and Records (FERPA) Student Organizations, Fraternities and Sororities, Student Press, Athletics, and Admissions and Financial Aid

courses.subject: ECHD
courses.title: Staffing Practices in Student Affairs
courses.description: Research and theory in staff recruitment and selection, new position orientation, staff supervision, staff development and continuing education, and performance appraisal.

courses.subject: ECHD
courses.title: Student Affairs Leadership Development
courses.description: Students will apply material learned to writing about current trends, issues, and research related to contemporary organizational patterns, models, and structures; professional standards; personnel practices; and innovations in program and service delivery. Students will consider their own career trajectories and understand the role of senior student affairs officers and leaders.
courses.course_objectives: Students will understand how to reflect on the historical roots of student affairs profession. Students will understand how to compare and contrast current issues with historical trends and integrate into one’s student affairs leadership practice. Students will understand how to integrate foundational philosophies, models, and theories related to the profession. Students will understand how to apply scholarship in professional contexts to enhance practice. Students will understand how to argue contributions made by the profession to higher education communities and beyond. Students will understand how to critique contemporary social and cultural issues in student affairs and situate them into leadership practice. Students will understand how to build a student affairs leader identity and career plan.
courses.topical_outline: Conceptualizing Student Affairs Leadership Identity Student Affairs Leadership Career Trajectory: Various Roles Student Affairs Leadership Career Trajectory: Resume/CV, Cover Letter, and Vision Statement Student Affairs Leadership Career Trajectory: Job Talks Student Affairs Leadership Preliminary/Comprehensive Exam Prep Session: Review of History Student Affairs Leadership Preliminary/Comprehensive Exam Prep Session: Review of Theories and Research Student Affairs Leadership Preliminary/Comprehensive Exam Prep Session: Review of Practice and Leadership Innovations and Rethinking Student Affairs Leadership

courses.description: Theories, models, issues, and practices in contemporary college student affairs administration.

Course content willfocus on the application of student development and learning theoryand the impact of college environments on college students.

courses.subject: ECHD

courses.description: Advanced overview of the theories of counseling and student development. Examination of sociocultural (e.g., racial/ethnic,gender, sexual orientation, disability) and social justicetheories of counseling and student development.

courses.subject: ECHD
courses.title: Foundations of Counseling Psychology
courses.description: History, development, and current issues related to the profession of counseling psychology. Philosophical and cultural assumptions, legal and ethical considerations, and implications of selected research topics.

courses.subject: ECHD
courses.title: Theories of Counseling Psychology
courses.description: Basic theoretical foundations for the profession of counseling psychology. Counseling and psychotherapy, career development, human development, and cultural diversity perspectives.

courses.subject: ECHD
courses.title: Assessment in Counseling Psychology
courses.description: The administration and interpretation of psychological measure of intellectual, social, and personality characteristics of individuals. The ethical use of test results in counseling individuals from diverse populations.

courses.subject: ECHD
courses.title: Advanced Psychodiagnosis
courses.description: Use of selected appraisal instruments and techniques, with an emphasis on outcome assessment and the relationship between assessment and psychodiagnosis. Students will become familiar with the DSM classification system and achieve proficiency in making diagnoses.

courses.subject: ECHD
courses.title: Consultation in Human Systems
courses.description: Application of social psychological research and systems theory to organizational development.  Emphasis will be on the role of the counseling psychologist as a consultant and the development of consultation and group leadership skills necessary to work with teachers, clients, patients, families, groups, administrators, and personnel in agencies, organizations, or institutions.

courses.subject: ECHD
courses.title: Process of Counseling Psychology Supervision
courses.description: Each student will supervise two master's-level students in Individual Counseling Practicum. The supervisory sessions will be recorded and critiqued in the supervision course. An updated and systematic understanding of the problems of supervision will be accomplished through a review of the literature.

courses.subject: ECHD
courses.title: Counseling Psychology Supervision Practicum
courses.description: This course is for the advanced counseling psychology doctoral student who has had a didactic course in supervision and will provide closely directed experiences in supervising master's-level students in counseling practice.

courses.subject: ECHD
courses.title: Ethics and Professional Issues
courses.description: Introduction and application of the APA Ethical Principles of Psychologists and Code of Conduct. Ethical decision-making and professional judgment will be explored using case studies and select articles. Legal and jurisdictional information and reference to universal principles will be explored.

courses.subject: ECHD
courses.title: Internship in Counseling
courses.description: Supervised individual and small group counseling conducted atpredetermined P-16 site settings. A field placement that provides direct opportunities to integrate theory and advanced practice with an emphasis on social justice and multicultural implications.
courses.course_objectives:
Upon completion of this course, doctoral trainee will be able to analyze, process, and improve one's own counseling skills with individuals and small group members. Upon completion of this course, doctoral trainee will be able to receive and implement constructive feedback from instructors, supervisors, and other students to assist in advancing counseling skills. A special emphasis is placed on the ACA Multicultural Competencies (1992) and the ACA Advocacy Competencies (2002). Upon completion of this course, doctoral trainee will be able to demonstrate the ability to give constructive feedback in group supervision sessions, with specific skills in developing multicultural and social justice case conceptualization. Upon completion of this course, doctoral trainee will be able to complete a thorough self-assessment of personal strengths and challenges as they are evident during the internship. Upon completion of this course, doctoral trainee will gain understanding of one's own personality and biases, as well as of one's impact upon others in professional interactions. Specifically, be able to understand how these personal biases and social locations of privilege and oppression influence practice. Upon completion of this course, doctoral trainee will be able to demonstrate knowledge of and commitment to the ethical code of the profession. Develop a personal ethical decision-making model that integrates multicultural and social justice factors. Upon completion of this course, doctoral trainee will be able to demonstrate understanding of and ability to advocate for clients from diverse ethnic, cultural, and social backgrounds. 
Describe the specific multicultural and social justice implications of working with these clients (e.g., counselor and client locations of privilege and oppression). Upon completion of this course, doctoral trainee will be able to integrate current research in the field and describe how these research implications influence both theory and practice with clients.
courses.topical_outline: Clinical Skills in counseling (e.g., active listening, rapport-building, case conceptualization, treatment planning, structuring sessions) Ethical issues in counseling (e.g., confidentiality, duty to warn, dual relationships) Multicultural and diversity issues in counseling Giving and receiving feedback Research as applied to clinical practice Self-knowledge and awareness Tape and case study review of counseling sessions Note: Supervision will be provided by both a university and site supervisor on counseling practice

courses.subject: ECHD
courses.title: Equity, Diversity, and Inclusion in Student Affairs
courses.description: Exploration of concepts of equity, diversity, and inclusion in student affairs scholarship and practice. Exploring power, privilege, and oppression associated with socially constructed identities, we will approach inclusion from a framework that emphasizes individual, organizational, and systemic strategies with a specific focus on student affairs practice and scholarship.
courses.course_objectives: As a result of this course, students will understand theories and scholarship highlighting individual, organizational, and systemic barriers to inclusion and equity in student affairs practice. As a result of this course, students will be able to critically explore their own socially constructed identities (e.g., race, gender, sexual orientation, class, religion, ability) in the context of their student affairs scholarship and practice. As a result of this course, students will be able to develop strategies for becoming a culturally competent student affairs scholar and practitioner. As a result of this course, students will be able to identify and articulate their scholarly philosophy related to equity, diversity, and inclusion in student affairs scholarship and practice.
courses.topical_outline:
This course will be broken into four major units, each highlighting specific scholarship and strategies related to equity, diversity, and inclusion in student affairs. Each unit will highlight scholarship about a variety of social identities, including, but not limited to, race, gender, sexual orientation, nationality, class, ability, age, and religion. UNIT 1: Individual attitudes, behaviors, and skills
a.) Cycles of socialization and liberation
b.) Microaggressions UNIT 2: Organizational barriers and strategies
a.) Multicultural Organizational Development Theory
b.) Organizational culture in student affairs (e.g., stated and unstated norms and expectations) UNIT 3: Systemic barriers and strategies
a.) College/university and student affairs structures and practices (e.g., hiring and promotion practices, organizational charts)
b.) Laws, policies, and procedures influencing diversity and equity in student affairs (e.g., Title IX, affirmative action) UNIT 4: Cultural influences
a.) Contextual and societal beliefs and practices
b.) News and media influences
c.) National laws and policies external to higher education

courses.title: Tropical Ecological and Cultural Systems
courses.description: Characteristics of tropical ecosystems, tropical biological communities, and human cultures in the tropics; how they differ from those in the temperate zone, and the implications for conservation and development.

courses.subject: ECOL(BIOL)(IDIS)
courses.title: Population Biology of Infectious Diseases
courses.description: Ecology and evolution of infectious diseases that affectfree-living animals, plants and human populations. Topics include pathogen life history and transmission modes, epidemiology and impacts on hosts, evolution of resistance and virulence, emerging infectious diseases, and the role of parasites in wildlife conservation.
courses.course_objectives: Students will develop a knowledge base to match important concepts of biology of parasites and infectious diseases with real-world examples. Students will increase their ability to apply quantitative approaches to studying infectious disease dynamics at the population level. Students will be able to articulate the historical development and current research in the field of disease ecology. Students will be able to provide examples of taxonomic and biological diversity of parasitic organisms and host responses to infection. Students will be able to explain examples of the importance of parasites in wildlife conservation and management. Students will demonstrate, through theory and examples, the role of ecology and evolution in predicting disease emergence and responding to epidemics.
courses.topical_outline:
PART 1. THE BASICS: EPIDEMIOLOGY AND PARASITE BIOLOGY
Introduction: Basic terminology and diversity of parasites
Population growth, population regulation, and statistical epidemiology
Population biology of microparasites
Rinderpest in the Serengeti, dead seals in the North Sea
Measles and childhood diseases: herd immunity and vaccination
Parasitic helminths: T.tenuis and red grouse
Helminths of humans: Ascaris, filariasis and hookworm
Rots, scabs, smut, and blight: the biology of plant pathogens
Invertebrate pathology: forest pest cycles and insect mushrooms PART 2. ECOLOGICAL HETEROGENEITY
Parasites and host behavior
It bit me: vector-borne pathogens, ticks and mosquitoes
Birds, bees, and STDs
Complex dynamics and social mixing
Key hosts and superspreaders
Patterns of spatial spread
Metapopulation biology of disease
Community effects and multi-host pathogens
Keeping the herds healthy: predators and infectious disease PART 3. HOST IMMUNITY AND PATHOGEN EVOLUTION
Vertebrate immunity: innate and adaptive
Population dynamics of the immune response
Immunity and resistance in plants and invertebrates
Evolution of host resistance: tradeoffs and constraints
Parasites and sexual selection
Evolution of pathogen virulence
Molecular phylogeny of pathogens
Host-parasite coevolution and cospeciation PART 4. CONSERVATION, CONTROL, AND EMERGING INFECTIOUS DISEASES
Influenza, Ebola, BSE; emergent pathogens and disappearing cures
Worms in a warmer world; parasites and global change
Evaluating disease risks to threatened wildlife
Drug treatment and drug resistance
Role of host-pathogen evolution in disease emergence
Darwinian medicine

courses.description: An introduction to the effects of contaminants on aquaticorganisms and terrestrial wildlife, types of contaminantsimpacting ecosystems, fate and transport of contaminants in theenvironment, and the effects of contaminants at various levels of biological organization ranging from biochemical reactions in the cell to the population level.
courses.course_objectives: Students will understand how to identify sources and types of contaminants affecting ecosystems. Students will understand how to predict the fate of environmental contaminants. Students will understand how to explain how chemicals are absorbed, digested, metabolized, and excreted. Students will understand how to assess the toxic effects of contaminants at the biochemical, cellular, organismal, and population levels. Students will understand how to identify toxicity testing procedures and biomonitoring methods.

courses.subject: ECOL(ENTO)
courses.title: Agroecology and Sustainable Farming
courses.description: Exploration of the principles and practices of sustainable agriculture and their integration with ecological concepts. Students will develop a deep understanding of how agriculture affects environmental health, economic viability, and social equity. Through lectures, discussions, and self-driven research projects, students will learn how to evaluate sustainability in agriculture.
courses.course_objectives: Focuses on introducing students to new topics as well as gaining new skills in navigating the scientific literature. The main outcomes for learners are: Define and explain the principles of sustainable agriculture and their relationship with ecological, environmental, social, and economic sciences. Understand the concept of agroecology and its role in promoting resilient and sustainable food systems including as part of climate change adaptation and maintaining food security. Gain confidence in reading, interpreting, and summarizing concepts from primary literature (scientific papers). Build presentation and discussion skills (both written and oral) about sustainable agriculture. Acquire a breadth of basic knowledge of the different topics that shape sustainable agroecology by generating a written body documenting self-driven research on a topic of your choosing within sustainable agriculture.
courses.topical_outline:
Introduction to Sustainable Agriculture and Ecology
•	Definition of sustainable agriculture and its importance
•	Historical context and evolution of agricultural practices
•	Principles of agroecology and their relationship to ecological concepts
•	Systems thinking in agriculture: understanding interconnections Environmental Impacts of Agriculture

•	Land sparing vs land sharing Sustainable Agricultural Systems

•	Agroforestry and silvopasture systems
•	Urban agriculture, hydroponics, and rooftop gardening Soil, Water, and Waste
•	Soil degradation and erosion prevention, cover cropping, and crop rotation
•	Composting, secondary products, and food waste
•	Soil and water testing and nutrient management
•	Water consumption and water policy Crops, Countries, and Industries
•	Case studies of certain example crops, industries, and countries
•	Students generate and choose project ideas Biodiversity and Conservation in Agriculture
•	Importance of biodiversity in agricultural ecosystems
•	Habitat restoration and wildlife-friendly farming practices
•	Integrating native plants and pollinators in agricultural landscapes Agroecology and Resilient Food Systems
•	Principles of agroecology: diversity, efficiency, and resilience
•	Food sovereignty and security in a changing climate
•	Case studies of agroecological projects around the world Sustainable Agriculture and Global Challenges
•	Climate change and its impacts on agriculture
•	Mitigation and adaptation strategies for sustainable agriculture
•	Role of sustainable agriculture in achieving the Sustainable Development Goals Policies and Regulations
•	Government policies and incentives for sustainable agriculture
•	International agreements and organizations promoting sustainable agriculture
•	Barriers to implementing sustainable agriculture and potential solutions Project Work, Finals Review, and Presentations

courses.subject: ECOL(FANR)
courses.title: Restoration Ecology
courses.description: As an applied science, restoration ecology uses ecological theory to guide the restoration of degraded ecosystem structures, functions, and/or services. This course examines principles from systems theory and population, community, landscape, and ecosystem ecology. It links those principles to restoration social contexts and values, and to decision-making, planning and implementation.
courses.course_objectives: Students will learn to understand and analyze ecosystem degradation and restoration from a systems perspective. Students will learn to apply fundamental ecological principles to analyze problems and inform practice in restoration ecology. Students will explore and appreciate the history and plurality of rationales, values, goals, and tradeoffs associated with restoration. Students will learn to identify how both ecological theory and values are translated into planning and action through restoration methods and decision-making. Students will gain deeper appreciation of ongoing challenges, tensions, and dilemmas in restoration ecology by studying and evaluating primary literature and case studies.
courses.topical_outline: Top-1. Ecosystems as Systems TOP-1.1. Systems ecology & basics of complexity theory TOP-1.2. How systems change: feedbacks, thresholds, degradation, resilience, regime shifts TOP-1.3. Social-ecological systems TOP-2. Restoration Perspectives and Planning: What do we want, and why do we want it? TOP-2.1. Evolution of past and current schools of thought TOP-2.2. Multiple values, multiple goals TOP-2.3. Ecosystem services
courses.prerequisiteText: ECOL 3500-3500L or ECOL 3505H-3505L or FANR 3200 or FANR 3200W or permission of department

courses.subject: ECOL(FISH)(WASR)
courses.title: Freshwater Ecosystems
courses.description: Exploration of freshwater ecosystems (lakes, streams, wetlands), their biota, physical and chemical properties, and linkages between terrestrial and aquatic ecosystems.
courses.prerequisiteText: (ECOL 3500 and ECOL 3500L) or (ECOL 3505H and ECOL 3505L) or (FANR 3200W and FANR 3200L)

courses.subject: ECOL(FISH)(WASR)
courses.title: Freshwater Ecosystems Lab
courses.description: Students will learn research methods in aquatic ecology including, sampling techniques, water chemistry analysis, experimental design, and data analyses. Students will become familiar with approaches to assess the condition of freshwater systems and will develop written and oral communication skills through laboratory activities.
courses.course_objectives: Students will have a greater understanding of the ecological structure and function of freshwater ecosystems. We will accomplish this goal by studying the basic physics, chemistry, and biology of freshwater ecosystems through a lens of systems ecology. Students will be able to identify and describe current threats to freshwater ecosystems. We will accomplish this goal by using the assigned readings, lectures, activities, and discussions to study the ways in which freshwater ecosystems can become degraded. Students will be able to read, understand, and apply information presented in peer-reviewed literature. When finished with the course, you should be confident in reading primary literature, understanding the information presented therein, and applying scientific findings to answer new questions about freshwater ecosystems.
courses.prerequisiteText: (ECOL 3500 and ECOL 3500L) or (ECOL 3505H and ECOL 3505L) or (FANR 3200W and FANR 3200L)

courses.title: Perspectives on Integrative Conservation and Sustainability
courses.description: Ecological issues of conservation and development.
courses.course_objectives: Graduate students interested in conservation will be exposed to a diversity of conservation perspectives.
courses.topical_outline: conservation of endangered species through biomonitoring, natural history studies, development of habitat conservation plans applications of science to management and policy restoration ecology global warming and carbon sequestration projects environmental ethics conservation and urban environments coastal conservation and management how ecological research can help mitigate environmental disasters land-market responses to conservation the role of botanical gardens in conservation effectively combining social and ecological science to address conservation issues

courses.subject: ECOL(IDIS)
courses.title: Evolutionary Medicine
courses.description: An introduction to the rapidly emerging field of evolutionary medicine. The aim is to better understand the evolutionary nature of human health and disease. The course will apply central concepts from evolutionary biology (such as life history theory, coevolution, genomic conflict, constraints, and trade-offs) to problems in medicine and public health, including antibiotic resistance, aging, cancer, autoimmune disease, and pathogen virulence.
courses.course_objectives: Students will learn how to use evolutionary principles to identify why we are vulnerable to common diseases. Students will learn how to evaluate the consequences of pathogen evolution for disease outcomes, treatment, and control. Students will learn how to apply evolutionary principles for novel treatments of cancer and infectious diseases. Students will learn how to evaluate data (graphical and tabular information) in order to formulate hypotheses about mechanisms underlying disease. Students will learn how to apply scientific thinking to assess evidence for different hypothesis regarding specific conditions, such as the menopause or aging. Students will learn how to create testable hypotheses to assess the impacts of evolutionary history in chronic diseases and reproductive health.
courses.topical_outline: Why we get sick? Human evolution and host defense Genetics of susceptibility and personalized medicine Aging Reproduction Cancer and chemotherapy Autoimmunity Microbiomes Circadian rhythms Pathogen virulence Emerging pathogens Vaccines and evolution Drugs and evolution Evolution-proof control

courses.subject: ECOL(IDIS)
courses.title: Fundamentals of Disease Biology II
courses.description: The fundamentals of infectious disease biology focusing on microparasite infections (e.g., viruses, bacteria). Taught in four-week modules, the course covers essential concepts in ecology, evolution, immunology, biochemistry, cell biology, and metabolism as they relate to specific infectious diseases. Each module is self-contained, and students can register to receive credit for one or more modules.

courses.subject: ECOL(MARS)
courses.title: Methods in Marine Ecology
courses.description: In-depth understanding of ecological processes and interactionsin marine and estuarine environments. Students will runexperiments and gather and analyze data.

courses.subject: ECOL(PBIO)(CRSS)(FORS)
courses.title: Terrestrial Biogeochemical Cycling
courses.description: Plant processes which mediate biogeochemical cycling on land.  Includes survey of global element cycling, functions of essential elements, element acquisition, translocation and loss by plants, litter decomposition, and methods of estimating standing stocks of elements in and transfer rates of elements between ecosystem components.

courses.title: Population Ecology
courses.description: Advanced ecological theory to biological populations. Mathematical and evolutionary treatment of population growth and regulation, niche theory, foraging theory, predator-prey theory, habitat selection, and competition.
courses.course_objectives: After completion of this course, students will know the basic concepts and ideas of theoretical population ecology.

Individual variation
Structured populations
Density-dependence

Evolution of aging

Natural selection 2 SECTION 3: INTERACTING POPULATIONS

Directly transmitted disease
Vector-borne disease

courses.subject: ECOL(PBIO)(WILD)
courses.title: Modeling Population Ecology
courses.description: Review of some commonly used mathematical approaches to modeling ecological populations, including single species approaches (discrete and continuous time), age/stage structure, species interactions, spatial structure, harvesting, and management.

courses.subject: ECOL(PBIO)
courses.title: Plant Reproductive Ecology
courses.description: Pollination ecology, breeding systems, patterns of gene flow via pollen and seed dispersal, flower arrangement and phenology, and implications of reproductive biology for demography.  Group and individual laboratory projects.
courses.offeredText: Not offered on a regular basis.

courses.subject: ECOL(WILD)
courses.title: Concepts and Approaches in Ecosystem Ecology
courses.description: Ecosystem biogeochemical processes and the organism-organism,organism-environment interactions that regulate them.  Therelationship of ecosystem structure and function to foodwebs,global change, scaling, nonlinearity, self-organization, andapproaches to study these.

courses.subject: ECOL(WILD)
courses.title: Endangered Species Practicum
courses.description: Introduces the United States Endangered Species Act and its application, using a practicum model in which students draft five-year status reviews of protected species in partnership with the United States Fish and Wildlife Service. Students learn relevant environmental policy, apply principles of conservation biology, and develop practical skills in conservation.
courses.course_objectives: Students will understand how to explain the history and core elements of the Endangered Species Act (ESA) and related laws and policies, and how they are applied in practice by federal and state agencies. Students will understand how to apply an understanding of conservation biology to species status and recovery assessment, including effective synthesis of natural history information, demographic and genetics data, species threats, and conservation actions. Students will understand how to find and synthesize relevant literature and write clear effective reports.
courses.topical_outline:
Students learn about federal and state policies, delve into species natural history, ecology, and population status, and develop skills in applied research, information synthesis, and report writing. Module 1 will be taught in the first 3 weeks of class. Modules 2 and 3 will be taught concurrently as students conduct research for 5-year reviews and draft 5-year reviews. Module 1: Laws and policies for endangered species, and their application:
• History of the ESA
• Sections of the ESA
• Species listing, downlisting, delisting, petitioning
• FWS and NOAA structure and organization
• Federal agency (“Section 7”) consultation
• Habitat conservation plans, candidate conservation agreements
• Related environmental laws
• State protection of species in Georgia and beyond Module 2: Applied conservation biology:
• Species taxonomy, systematics, and nomenclature
• Understanding and interpreting species natural history, habitat, and trait information
• Understanding and interpreting population trends, distribution, abundance, and demographic data
• Understanding and interpreting genetics data
• Threats to imperiled species
• Conservation actions for species protection Module 3: Practical skills used in conservation management:
• Sections of the 5-year review
• Kinds of reports, papers, and documents related to imperiled species
• Searching peer-reviewed and grey literature
• Summarizing and adapting existing literature (without plagiarizing)
• Essential rules for clear writing
• Reviewing, editing, and revising reports Mini module: how to get a job in a federal or state wildlife agency
courses.offeredText: Not offered on a regular basis.

courses.subject: ECOL
courses.title: Ecological Basis of Environmental Issues
courses.description: This course builds on foundational ecological principles (organism, population, community, ecosystem) to engage students with real-world sustainability challenges, emphasizing how humans use and manage resources at local and global scales. It applies key ecological concepts to critical environmental issues, including population growth, climate change, water resources, and energy.
courses.course_objectives: Students will understand the scientific process, and describe how scientists reach consensus, and how our understanding of the natural world changes over time. Students will define and understand basic ecological principles at different levels of complexity, including organisms, populations, communities, and ecosystems, and gain an understanding of the range of ecosystem services provided by the natural world. Students will describe the complexity and interconnectedness of natural systems, and how the natural world simultaneously is impacted and supports humans. Students will discuss historical drivers of the earth’s climate and gain an understanding of how the current climate is affected by natural processes and on-going anthropogenic change. Students will understand how data are presented and interpreted, such as through maps, graphs and tables, and use these data to predict ecological, economic, and social outcomes relevant to human well-being.
courses.topical_outline: Introduction: Sustainability and complex problem solving Population growth and demographic transitions Ecological principles of energy flow (e.g., photosynthesis), trophic interactions, succession and disturbance Biodiversity including evolution, ecosystem services, species invasions, infectious diseases, extinction and conservation Natural resource use and sustainability, including forests, freshwater, agriculture and fisheries Energy including non-renewable and renewable energy The Earth’s climate and climate change: causes and consequences Environmental issues and concerns including water scarcity, pesticide use, pollution, infectious diseases, and resource extraction The interactions among ecological, economic, and social spheres that lead to decision making Environmental justice, ethics, and policy

courses.subject: ECOL
courses.title: Ecological Basis of Environmental Issues Laboratory
courses.description: Builds on lecture (Ecological Basis of Environmental Issues) themes by providing students opportunities to investigate natural systems and explore ways human activities affect the environment. Students practice collecting, analyzing, and interpreting environmental data and develop information literacy skills throughout the semester. Students will also research a sustainability issue, explain its impact on the environment, and propose solutions across scales.
courses.course_objectives: Students will apply scientific principles to understand how natural systems and human activities affect the earth’s capacity to sustain life. Students will describe linkages between organisms and their environment. Students will communicate consequences of various human activities on the environment. Students will analyze the reliability of information and use scientific evidence to support claims. Students will evaluate ethical and moral issues involved with environmentally sustainable decision making related to land use and the environment.

courses.subject: ECOL
courses.title: Ecological Basis of Environmental Issues Laboratory
courses.description: Builds on lecture (Ecological Basis of Environmental Issues) themes by providing students opportunities to investigate natural systems and explore ways human activities affect the environment. Students practice collecting, analyzing, and interpreting environmental data and develop information literacy skills throughout the semester. Students will also research a sustainability issue, explain its impact on the environment, and propose solutions across scales.
courses.course_objectives: Students will apply scientific principles to understand how natural systems and human activities affect the earth’s capacity to sustain life. Students will describe linkages between organisms and their environment. Students will communicate consequences of various human activities on the environment. Students will analyze the reliability of information and use scientific evidence to support claims. Students will evaluate ethical and moral issues involved with environmentally sustainable decision making related to land use and the environment.

courses.subject: ECOL
courses.title: Our Planet: Ecological Basis of Life and Death
courses.description: Course uses case studies to explore human impacts on ecological and evolutionary processes that underlie life (e.g., reproduction, mating systems, life histories) and death (e.g., predation, disease, decomposition) across a diversity of species. Human-environment interactions that impact ecological populations, species interactions, and students’ daily lives will be emphasized.
courses.course_objectives: Through this course, students will improve their ability to think critically about natural processes and how they are affected by human-induced environmental change at various levels (individuals to ecosystems). Through this course, students will improve their ability to apply scientific reasoning to explain complex phenomena, particularly those ecological phenomena that are relevant to students’ daily lives. Through this course, students will improve their ability to Interpret quantitative data through figures and graphs. Through this course, students will improve their ability to evaluate and predict how human-environment interactions affect biodiversity. Through this course, students will improve their ability communicate effectively through speech (i.e., oral presentation and classroom participation during activities). By the end of this course, students will have experience incorporating logic and scientific inference into their decision making.

a.	Plants and Herbivores
i.	Herbivore weapons and adaptations
ii.	Anti-herbivory defenses and adaptations; Case Study 17: Invasive herbivores – causes and mitigation strategies

b.	Predators and Prey
i.	Predator weapons and adaptations
ii.	Anti-predator defenses and adaptations; Case Study 18: Invasive predators - causes and mitigation strategies

c.	Trophic interactions: Green food web IV.	Death: Parasitism and Disease
a.	Ecto- vs. endo-parasites; Case Study 19: Habitat fragmentation and Lyme Disease

a.	Organic matter in the soil; Case Study 21: Climate impacts on thawing permafrost

b.	Soil and fossil fuel formation; Case Study 22: Fossil fuel extraction and climate

c.	Trophic interactions: Brown food web
i.	Microorganisms; Case Study 23: What is compost and why does it help a garden?
ii.	Scavengers

courses.subject: ECOL
courses.title: Global Climate Change: Past, Present, and Future
courses.description: Introduction to climate, climate change, and the influence of terrestrial ecosystems and humans on climate.

courses.subject: ECOL
courses.title: Water Sustainability in the Anthropocene
courses.description: A systems-focused conceptual basis for environmental problem solving, specifically addressing water issues. Systems approaches to sustainability, challenges of Anthropocene environmental change, and solutions to connected water-food-energy problems are explored. Focus on local to regional watersheds, water quality and quantity, biodiversity loss, communication, and systems change.

courses.subject: ECOL
courses.title: Global Change and Emerging Infectious Diseases
courses.description: Emerging infectious diseases are a significant threat to modern society. This course will examine the rise of new pathogens in the late twentieth and twenty-first centuries in the context of global environmental trends, including changes to trade and travel, land use, the distribution of wealth and poverty, and climate change.

courses.subject: ECOL
courses.title: Introduction to Ecological Data Science
courses.description: Introduction to the management, analysis, interpretation, and communication of ecological data. Students will practice critically evaluating data-based claims, developing and implementing analytical workflows (i.e., data import, cleaning, statistical analysis, and visualization) to solve data-based ecological problems, and interpreting and communicating findings from data.
courses.course_objectives: By completing this course, student should be able to critically and logically evaluate data-based claims in scientific literature, the popular press, and social media. By completing this course, student should be able to apply appropriate analytical approaches and statistical tests to different types of ecological data. By completing this course, student should be able to develop proficiency in the use of computational tools (e.g., R & RStudio) to effectively manage, organize, analyze, model, interpret, and visualize ecological data. By completing this course, student should be able to communicate the outcomes of data-based analyses verbally, graphically, and in written form. By completing this course, student should be able to integrate principles of open science and data ethics into analytical workflows and when communicating ecological information.
courses.topical_outline:
This course is organized around seven core data science principles that are explored through an ecological lens: data management, data analysis, data visualization, coding, modeling, reproducibility, and ethics. 

Within these areas, specific topics include:
Data Management
•	Data organization, handling, and storage best practices
•	Setting up and using RStudio projects
•	Importing, viewing, and exporting raw and modified data Data Analysis
•	Data tidying and transformations
•	Variability, distributions, and sample size
•	Logic, probability, and hypothesis testing
•	Designing experiments
•	Making inferences and critically evaluating results Data Visualization 
•	Graph types and visualization matches 
•	Graph mechanics and creation
•	Interpreting graphs
•	Ensuring accessibility of graphical information Coding (e.g., using R and RStudio)
•	Computational thinking
•	Reading, writing, and refining code Modeling
•	Model selection, assumptions, and data needs
•	Applying parametric and non-parametric statistical models
•	Interpreting statistical outputs, relationships between variables, and uncertainty Reproducibility
•	Data provenance and metadata
•	Reproducibility and version control Ethics
•	Responsible conduct and data integrity
•	Data sovereignty and open science
•	Uncertainty reporting, misinformation, and social consequences of data interpretation

courses.subject: ECOL
courses.title: Field Methods in Animal Ecology
courses.description: Course provides training in field-based animal ecology, introducing students to field techniques, and generating meaning from field collected data to address scientific questions. Course emphasizes the scientific process: making observations, asking questions, proposing hypotheses, designing fieldwork, data collection and analysis, and oral and written communication.
courses.course_objectives: Students will be able to demonstrate an understanding of a range of concepts in ecology. Students will be able to design field studies to address scientific questions and hypotheses. Students will be able to effectively collect, record, analyze, and interpret scientific evidence and experimental data. Students will be able to solve practical problems in field settings. Students will be able to communicate effectively using a range of formats relevant to professional scientists.
courses.topical_outline: Week 1: An introduction to field ecology and the scientific method Week 2: Field survey and sampling strategies; data collection and record keeping Week 3: Use of R for analysis of field collected data Week 4: Resource availability: size frequency analysis Week 5: Minimal disturbance wildlife surveying 1; camera trapping Week 6: Minimal disturbance wildlife surveying 2; correlation and regression-based models Week 7: Community ecology 1; pitfall trapping Week 8: Community ecology 2; diversity indices and ordination Week 9: Size and recruitment; distribution analysis; information theory Week 10: Wildlife trapping and handling 1; capture-mark-recapture Week 11: Wildlife trapping and handling 2; capture-mark-recapture Week 12: Wildlife trapping and handling 3; population estimation Week 13: Population estimation and projections Week 14: Experimental field ecology: giving up density Week 15: Ecological applications
courses.prerequisiteText: (BIOL 1108 and BIOL 1108L) or permission of department | Pre or

courses.subject: ECOL
courses.title: Apprenticeship in Ecology
courses.description: Supervised training in methodology (field, lab, or other) related to ecological topics. The course applies to students who are developing new skills in some area of ecology where initial work in that area requires training by qualified personnel.

courses.subject: ECOL
courses.title: Environment and Humans
courses.description: Macro-environmental problems currently faced by humans placing them in historical perspective, and relating them to the natural laws and ecological processes which govern the outcome of human-environmental interactions.
courses.offeredText: Not offered on a regular basis.

courses.subject: ECOL
courses.title: Tropical Field Ecology
courses.description: An interdisciplinary field program in tropical habitats,exploring and comparing tropical environments, their naturalhistory, their biological wealth, and the ecological patterns,processes, and interactions that characterize tropical systems. Students will develop competence in recognition and observationof tropical organisms in the wild.  Analysis of the interplay oftropical nature and human society, the threats to tropicalbiodiversity, and current conservation approaches in the tropics.
courses.course_objectives: Students will be able to understand the patterns and processes of geography, climate, geology, soils, and vegetation in the tropics. Students will be able to recognize the interplay of nature and human society in shaping tropical landscapes. Develop an understanding of tropical agricultural practices and their ecological consequences. Students will understand how to be aware of global patterns of biodiversity, with special reference to latitudinal gradients. Students will understand how to be aware of the issues surrounding conservation, loss of habitat, global warming, invasive species, and sustainable development in the tropics. Critically assess aspects of sustainability. Students will gain proficiency in natural history and the observation of tropical organisms in the wild. Students will be able to recognize and identify major groups of tropical organisms, including plants, insects, birds, mammals, intertidal marine invertebrates, and fish. Use standard reference works on taxonomy of tropical flora and fauna. Students will be able to understand how to apply skills of observation and taxonomy to identify unfamiliar species in unexplored sites. Students will understand how to work competently and safely within various tropical environments, including forest, riparian habitats, marine habitats, and agricultural zones; understand risks to health and safety, and apply measures to minimize risks. Students will be aware of current focus areas of research in tropical ecology and understand the issues.
courses.topical_outline: Tropical climates, global circulation patterns, and seasonality in the tropics Geography and agriculture in Costa Rica Geological origins of Central America Tropical soils and soil processes Tropical plant families: bryophytes, ferns, and angiosperms Tropical forest ecology: issues and the evidence Insect diversity in the tropics Costa Rican amphibian families: natural history, reproduction, and acoustic signaling Amphibian conservation Tropical mammals: evolution of the major groups Systematics and ecology of Costa Rican bats Tropical birds: major families, and recognition of birds in the field
courses.prerequisiteText: (BIOL 1108 or BIOL 2108H) and permission of department
courses.offeredText: Offered summer semester every year. Offered fall

courses.subject: ECOL
courses.title: Neotropical Ecology, Conservation, and Sustainability
courses.description: Course explores fundamentals of tropical ecology and Neotropical conservation, focusing on biodiversity, ecological processes, and sustainability. Through field trips and discussions, students develop skills in observing tropical habitats and assessing human impacts like habitat loss and climate change. Hands-on experiences equip students to propose solutions for sustainable Neotropical conservation.
courses.course_objectives: Students will be able to describe the characteristics of the various tropical biomes and differentiate between them by identifying floral and faunal diversity. Students will be able to identify common plant and animal taxa and understand their natural history within an ecological and evolutionary context. Students will be able to define and critically assess aspects and the practice of sustainability in the tropics through applied case studies and field excursions (e.g., sustainable agriculture, development, tourism, forestry, and energy). Students will be able to understand the principles of tropical conservation, how they are implemented, and potential solutions for how conservation practices can more effectively protect future biodiversity and ecosystem services. Students will formulate and debate proposals for alternative management practices in Costa Rican legislation or policies that are needed for the protection of tropical ecosystems.
