Students will develop insight into basic principles and theories of policy making, decision making, and management of higher education. Students will acquire knowledge about significant issues and problems confronting administrators in higher education. Students will identify basic concepts of organization, including similarities and dissimilarities of higher education with (a) for-profit organizations and (b) elementary and secondary schools. Students will review and evaluate the literature and research studies related to the organization and governance of higher education.
courses.topical_outline: A. Basic Theories of Higher Education Organization B. Organizational Patterns at the System Level C. Organizational Patterns at the Institutional Level D. Evolving Structures and Functions in Higher Education

courses.subject: EDHI
courses.title: Social Theory and Higher Education
courses.description: Social theories about higher education are explored, including theories that cover the relation of higher education to states and to markets, organizational theories, professionalization theories, theories about student issues such as financial aid, social stratification as well as implications of postmodern and feminist theories.

courses.subject: EDHI
courses.title: College Choice, Access, and Success
courses.description: Focuses on the diverse set of theoretical frameworks and methodological approaches that researchers have been using to understand factors affecting high school graduates' educational and occupational outcomes as it relates to college enrollment decisions. Special attention will be paid to issues of access and success as well as the policies, interventions, and initiatives developed to address them.
courses.course_objectives: Students will be able to explain the diverse set of theoretical frameworks and methodological approaches that have been used to understand factors affecting the educational outcomes of high school students as related to college enrollment decisions. Students will be able to explain the diverse set of theoretical frameworks and methodological approaches that have been used to understand factors affecting the occupational outcomes of high school students as related to college enrollment decisions. Students will critique the research literature and develop alternative considerations for theories and explanations of college access, progression, and graduation.
courses.topical_outline: • Sociological and behavioral economic theories • College access and success • College choice as it relates to poverty, minority status, race, and ethnicity • The transition from high school to college, community colleges, and labor markets • Inequality in educational opportunity • Policies, interventions, and initiatives that address inequality in college choice

courses.subject: EDHI
courses.title: College Choice, Access, and Success
courses.description: Focuses on the diverse set of theoretical frameworks and methodological approaches that researchers have been using to understand factors affecting high school graduates' educational and occupational outcomes as it relates to college enrollment decisions. Special attention will be paid to issues of access and success as well as the policies, interventions, and initiatives developed to address them.
courses.course_objectives: Students will be able to explain the diverse set of theoretical frameworks and methodological approaches that have been used to understand factors affecting the educational outcomes of high school students as related to college enrollment decisions. Students will be able to explain the diverse set of theoretical frameworks and methodological approaches that have been used to understand factors affecting the occupational outcomes of high school students as related to college enrollment decisions. Students will critique the research literature and develop alternative considerations for theories and explanations of college access, progression, and graduation.
courses.topical_outline: • Sociological and behavioral economic theories • College access and success • College choice as it relates to poverty, minority status, race, and ethnicity • The transition from high school to college, community colleges, and labor markets • Inequality in educational opportunity • Policies, interventions, and initiatives that address inequality in college choice

courses.subject: EDHI
courses.title: The American Professoriate
courses.description: Social organization, social stratification, and change of theAmerican professoriate by way of classical and contemporaryreadings. The transition of new faculty members from graduateschool to the initial academic appointment.

courses.subject: EDHI
courses.title: Leadership in Higher Education
courses.description: Administrative leadership concepts, principles, and practices in United States colleges and universities. Interpretation and evaluation of theory and research in leadership, administration, and management.

courses.subject: EDHI
courses.title: Strategy and Management in Higher Education
courses.description: Consideration of how higher education institutions developand implement strategy, including drawing on the base of theory,research, and cases from business. Topics include industrystructure; competition and differentiation; integration,diversification, and expansion; market selection and businessplans; developing and maintaining brands; strategic management;organizational culture; and organizational change.

courses.subject: EDHI
courses.title: Doctoral Dissertation
courses.description: Dissertation writing under the direction of the major professor.

courses.subject: EDHI
courses.title: Comparative Higher Education
courses.description: Higher education systems and institutions outside North America.

courses.subject: EDHI
courses.title: Policy Studies in Higher Education
courses.description: Analyzing, interpreting, and evaluating selected policy issues related to the continued improvement and development of institutions, programs, and services in higher education. Policy analysis and research at public and institutional levels.

courses.subject: EDHI
courses.title: Critique of Educational Literature in Higher Education
courses.description: Critical interpretation and evaluation of theory and research. Each student will make critical reviews of scholarly studies in his/her field of specialization.

courses.subject: EDHI
courses.title: Internship in Higher Education
courses.description: Problems encountered in a work-study program applying higher education principles at a selected institution.
courses.offeredText: Not offered on a regular basis.

courses.subject: EDIT(QUAL)
courses.title: Introduction to Q Research Methodology
courses.description: An overview of the history, philosophy, principles, and practice of Q methodology, a mixed methods research approach used in the study of subjectivity. Concepts and theories covered include subjectivity theory, concourse theory, abductive logic, and self-reference in the context of understanding people's viewpoints and how they influence behavior.

courses.subject: EDIT(QUAL)
courses.title: Introduction to Q Research Methodology
courses.description: An overview of the history, philosophy, principles, and practice of Q methodology, a mixed methods research approach used in the study of subjectivity. Concepts and theories covered include subjectivity theory, concourse theory, abductive logic, and self-reference in the context of understanding people's viewpoints and how they influence behavior.
courses.offeredText: Not offered on a regular basis.

courses.subject: EDIT
courses.title: Teaching and Learning with Technology
courses.description: The computer and its educational applications for preservice teachers.  Computer-based education in the areas of instruction, text and data processing, multimedia, and telecommunications.  Emphasis on integrating computer tools into class instruction.

courses.subject: EDIT
courses.title: Teaching and Learning with Technology
courses.description: The computer and its educational applications for preserviceteachers. Computer-based education in the areas of instruction,text and dataprocessing, multimedia, and telecommunications.Emphasis on integrating computer tools into class instruction.

courses.subject: EDIT
courses.title: Special Problems in Instructional Technology
courses.description: Independent study of selected problems in instructional technology.

courses.subject: EDIT
courses.title: Innovation Through Design and Technology
courses.description: Technologies that support communication, collaboration, creativity, innovation, critical thinking, research, and problem solving in the workplace. Emphasis on making critical decisions about technology's role in the workplace and leadership development in use of technology in varied fields.

courses.subject: EDIT
courses.title: Innovation Through Design and Technology
courses.description: Technologies that support communication, collaboration, creativity, innovation, critical thinking, research, and problem solving in the workplace. Emphasis on making critical decisions about technology's role in the workplace and leadership development in use of technology in varied fields.

courses.subject: EDIT
courses.title: Mentoring K12 Students Through Technology
courses.description: Students will design, develop, and assess enrichment activitiesfor K12 learners, with a directed focus on identifying learnerneeds and development of project-based learning activities.Students will serve as academic mentors for K12 learners acrossthe state of Georgia via online communication tools.

courses.subject: EDIT
courses.title: Introduction to Digital Learning
courses.description: Introduction to ideas, concepts, and strategies for using digitaltechnologies to enhance and support learning and performance in avariety of contexts. The course focuses on models for integration, specific applications, and how they can be usedin classroom and other learning contexts.

courses.subject: EDIT
courses.title: Introduction to Digital Learning
courses.description: Introduction to ideas, concepts, and strategies for using digitaltechnologies to enhance and support learning and performance in avariety of contexts. The course focuses on models for integration, specific applications, and how they can be usedin classroom and other learning contexts.

courses.subject: EDIT
courses.title: Design and Development Tools
courses.description: Students learn a variety of tools appropriate for computer-based development. These include graphics, media, and software development tools. Students are required to write a contract for the specific tools to be learned.

courses.subject: EDIT
courses.title: Introduction to Instructional Design
courses.description: Systematic procedures for designing, developing, evaluating, and revising instruction to meet identified goals and objectives.

courses.subject: EDIT
courses.title: Introduction to Instructional Design
courses.description: Systematic procedures for designing, developing, evaluating, and revising instruction to meet identified goals and objectives.

courses.subject: EDIT
courses.title: Instructional Development
courses.description: Developing instructional materials for a defined context applying a learner-centered, systematic design philosophy.  Working within a team environment while applying contemporary learning theories. courses.subject: EDIT
courses.title: Introduction to Instructional Message Design
courses.description: Course explores the application of message design principles to the development of instructional materials. Iterative design, including user testing, is emphasized to refine and enhance instructional effectiveness. Key principles related to memory, perception, concept learning, attitude change, and learner engagement are integrated to create user-centered instructional communications.
courses.course_objectives: At the end of the course, students will be able to identify message design principles as they apply to “good” design. At the end of the course, students will be able to identify, describe, and differentiate among major message design principles, and cite their origins and applications. At the end of the course, students will be able to apply design principles to practical application exercises. At the end of the course, students will be able to use proper evaluation techniques – including qualitative and quantitative methods, analytics, user-testing, etc. – to examine the effectiveness of instructional message design. At the end of the course, students will be able to critique media materials by applying message design principles. At the end of the course, students will be able to develop adaptable message design strategies that leverage iterative design principles for continuous improvement in practical applications.

courses.title: Advanced Evaluation Methods in Learning, Design, and Technology
courses.description: Planning, conducting, analyzing, and reporting systematic formative and summative evaluations. Students will apply a systems thinking approach to evaluation across K-12, higher education, and industry.
courses.course_objectives: Articulate and defend a definition of product evaluation. Contrast the objectives and methodologies of formative and summative product evaluation, emphasizing their relevance in the design of learning experiences. Distinguish between/among the following as they related to instructional products: (a) measurement and evaluation; (b) input, context, process, and product criteria; (c) extrinsic and intrinsic evaluation; (d) norm-reference and criterion- referenced measurement; and (e) learner verification. Write effective assessment items and test their validity and reliability. Describe sources, applications, advantages, and limitations of at least six alternative evaluation models as they relate to instructional products. Describe rationale, methods, and instrumentation for four facets of evaluation with the context of instructional product evaluation, specifically documentation, formative evaluation, assessment of immediate effectiveness, and impact evaluation. Evaluate a real-world training program by gathering data using the assessment items generated in the evaluation plan. Synthesize and present actionable recommendations for the training program, grounded in data-driven insights from the evaluation process.

courses.title: Embodied Learning and Instructional Technology
courses.description: This course will explore the theoretical and philosophical roots of embodied cognition and ecological psychology as they relate to instructional technology. Students will apply design principles to develop embodied learning experiences with technology and implement instructional strategies that engage the sensorimotor system in a variety of content areas.
courses.course_objectives: Students will describe mind-body dualism and how it impacts current perspectives of learning. Students will explain how learning occurs from an embodied perspective of cognition and how it differs from traditional views of cognition. Students will identify technologies that support learning from an embodied perspective and describe how those tools could be used in various learning contexts. Students will apply the principles of embodied learning to create activities that use technology to foster learning in a given content area. Students will implement embodied learning experiences using techniques associated with responsive teaching.

courses.description: Developmental forum for establishing, clarifying, and evolving students' perspectives on instructional technology research. Heighten awareness of critical issues in the field and areas of disciplined inquiry.
courses.course_objectives: Students will have an improved understanding of the processes of research. Students will understand how to appreciate the varied forms of disciplined inquiry used in the instructional systems field. Students will understand how to discuss how research interests evolve via disciplined inquiry. Students will understand how to articulate how existing research and theory influences the perspectives of scholars. Students will understand how to recognize how disciplined inquiry can advance a field collectively, as well as the perspectives of individual researchers. Students will understand how to explore, in-depth, the research and theory relevant to an area of personal interest. Students will understand how to identify alternative research problem statements within a given problem area. Students will understand how to discuss the implications of problem statements for research methods.

courses.title: AI in Educational Technology
courses.description: Artificial intelligence in educational technology, focusing on AI across educational settings. Foundational concepts of AI and machine learning. Theoretical perspectives, historical development, current state, and future potential of AI for learning. Application of AI across P-12, higher education, and other educational settings. Ethical considerations, privacy protection, and responsible AI use.
courses.course_objectives: Students will describe foundational concepts and historical development of AI and machine learning in educational technology. Students will analyze the historical development, key terms, concepts, and promising applications of AI and machine learning in educational technology, including the use of AI tools for teaching and learning. Students will critically review the foundations of generative AI and ChatGPT, explain the types of data outputs they produce, and evaluate their applications in educational technology. Students will develop the skills to analyze and apply AI and machine learning educational technologies in various educational contexts, including P-12, higher education, learning design, etc. Students will develop familiarity with the current state of research in AI in educational technology and critically evaluate and analyze research findings in this area. Students will explore and implement AI and machine learning applications in P-12 and higher education, focusing on subject-specific applications, productivity enhancements through prompt engineering, assignment redesigns, student engagement, individualized feedback, and educational data analysis. Students will explore and address ethical compliance and risk aspects of AI in educational technology, such as fairness, transparency, and privacy protection, as well as unique perspectives on AI, including human-centered AI, explainable AI, and AI education for young children.

courses.title: Educating Young Adolescents

The concept of a separate organization and program for young adolescents, types of curricular plans for the middle grades, 
aspects of teaching in the middle grades, and the organization and staffing of middle grades schools. A supervised field 
experience is included.
courses.course_objectives: Students will understand the unique cognitive, physical, social, emotional, and moral characteristics of young adolescents as individuals and members of groups. Students will understand how ethnicity, language, religion, socioeconomic status, gender, geographic origin, sexual orientation, and physical and mental exceptionalities may influence student lives. Students will understand the implications of young adolescent development for successful middle grades programs and schools. Students will understand how prior learning, differing family background, and diverse cultural backgrounds influence young adolescent learning. Students will understand the role of interdisciplinary and grade-level team planning in developing curriculum. Students will use content standards when designing curriculum. Students will incorporate the ideas, interests, and experiences of young adolescents in curriculum.

There is an emphasis on the landmark legal precedents that have shaped special education law. School-based practices and policies that are driven by such laws, such as determining eligibility and placement, developing Individualized Education Plans, and planning for transition services are also explored.

courses.subject: EDSE
courses.title: Observation and Assessment Techniques
courses.description: Directed experiences in observing, recording, and assessing behavior and interaction among children and families, and examination of program assessment.
courses.course_objectives: Students will know about and understand the goals, benefits, and uses of child assessment. Students will know about and use systematic observations, documentation, and other effective assessment strategies in a responsible way, in partnership with families and other professionals, to positively influence children’s development and learning. Students will apply theories of child development, both typical and atypical, and apply current research with emphasis on cognitive, motor, social-emotional, communication, adaptive, and aesthetic development in learning situations, family and community contexts. Students will identify specific disabilities, including the etiology, characteristics, and classification of common disabilities in young children, and describe specific implications for development and learning in the first years of life. Students will involve families in assessing and planning for individual children, including children with special needs. Students will select and use a variety of informal and formal assessment instruments and procedures, including observational methods, to make decisions about children’s learning and development. Students will develop and use authentic, performance-based assessments of children’s learning to assist in planning, to communicate with children and parents, and to engage children in self-assessment. Students will involve families as active participants in the assessment process. Students will communicate assessment results and integrate assessment results from others as an active team participant in the development and implementation of the individual education program (IEP) and individual family service plan (IFSP). Students will monitor, summarize, and evaluate the acquisition of child and family outcomes as outlined on the IFSP or IEP. Students will implement culturally unbiased assessment instruments and procedures. Students will identify levels of assessment and basic psychometric principles. Students will identify and critically evaluate formal and informal instruments and observations techniques for screening, diagnosis, and program planning. Students will plan and conduct community screening for infants, toddlers, and preschoolers with special needs. Students will plan and conduct transdisciplinary play-based assessments. Students will summarize assessment results in written reports and discussion with other professionals and families.
courses.topical_outline: • Assessment principles & purposes • Framework for assessment; family involvement • Collaboration throughout the assessment process • Screening process • Assessment approaches with young children; Standardized/Norm Ref. • Standardized tests such as: Peabody Picture Vocabulary Test III, Brazelton Neonatal Assessment Scale, Rosetti Infant Toddler Scale, Denver Developmental Screening Test II, Bayley Scale of Infant Development, Battelle Developmental Inventory 2 • Ecological assessment and assessing environments • Criterion referenced assessments • Informal assessments • Transdisciplinary Play-Based Assessment • Kidwatching • Assessment report writing and interpreting results to parents
courses.prerequisiteText: Students must be enrolled in a professional program to register for this course

courses.subject: EDSE
courses.title: Dyslexia and Other Learning Disabilities
courses.description: Characteristics of individuals with dyslexia and other learning disabilities across the lifespan. Students will gain an understanding of neurological functions in individuals with dyslexia and other learning disabilities and its impact on learning. Historical perspectives and contemporary issues surrounding dyslexia and related disabilities will also be addressed.
courses.course_objectives: Students will be able to define terminology related to dyslexia, language, and the brain. Students will be able to explain the relevant laws (IDEA, ADA AA) pertaining to individuals with dyslexia and other learning disabilities. Students will be able to explain historical perspectives and contemporary issues surrounding dyslexia and related disabilities (e.g., dysgraphia, dyscalculia, language impairment). Students will be able to explain the functions of the various parts of the brain in reading and how those functions are impaired in students with dyslexia. Students will be able to identify areas of deficit (phonological awareness, phonemic awareness, orthography, decoding, fluency, reading comprehension, spelling) associated with dyslexia and other learning disabilities. Students will be able to describe the comorbidity of dyslexia and other learning disabilities, and how this impacts teaching and learning. Students will be able to explain the similarities and differences between dual language learners and individuals with dyslexia and other learning disabilities. Students will be able to explain how to support individuals with dyslexia and other learning disabilities as they transition into postsecondary settings.

courses.subject: EDSE
courses.title: Designing Reading Interventions for Special Education
courses.description: The focus of this course is on translating evidence-based teaching methods related to literacy instruction for students with reading disabilities (e.g., dyslexia, DLD, LD) into guidelines for instruction and intervention. The emphasis is on applying an understanding of the English language and reading development to the implementation of structured literacy.
courses.course_objectives: Upon completion of the course, students will be able to explain the difference between structured literacy approaches and balanced or whole-language-based approaches. Upon completion of the course, students will be able to explain how an understanding of the alphabetic principle undergirds reading acquisition. Upon completion of the course, students will be able to explain the reciprocal relationship between phonemic awareness and phonics instruction. Upon completion of the course, students will be able to identify, pronounce, classify, and compare all consonant and vowel phonemes of English. Upon completion of the course, students will be able to design and implement explicit, systematic, cumulative, teacher-directed reading instruction. Upon completion of the course, students will be able to develop lesson plans that reflect an understanding of English orthography—from basic spelling patterns (e.g., CVC, CCVC, CVCC, CVCe) to more complex spelling patterns (e.g., vowel di- and tri-graphs, soft and hard sounds), including multisyllabic words. Upon completion of the course, students will be able to implement decoding and encoding routines to promote automatic word reading and accurate spelling. Upon completion of the course, students will be able to teach the spelling of regular and irregular words using systematic, alphabetic, and morphologically based practices. Upon completion of the course, students will be able to implement a variety of techniques and methods for building students’ oral reading fluency. Upon completion of the course, students will be able to implement informal diagnostic surveys of phonemic awareness, decoding skills, oral reading fluency, and spelling. Upon completion of the course, students will be able to state the IDA’s professional dispositions and practices, including doing no harm, maintaining public trust through the use of best practices, respecting confidentiality, objective reporting, and respecting the intellectual property of others.

courses.subject: EDSE
courses.title: Developmentally Appropriate Programming and Curricula for Infants and Toddlers
courses.description: An overview of developmentally appropriate practices for infants and toddlers with and without disabilities. Content will focus on early development, interactions and collaboration with families, interdisciplinary collaboration, and routines-based intervention for infants and toddlers in home-based and inclusive, center-based settings.
courses.course_objectives: Students will understand how to explain the historical, legal, and philosophical foundations of services for very young children with and without exceptional learning needs. Students will understand how to describe early development in the areas of social-emotional, communication, adaptive skills, cognitive skills, and motor skills. Students will understand how to explain the influence of medical issues and risk factors on the early development of infants and toddlers. Students will understand how to explain the importance of interactions and experiences for early brain development. In collaboration with families, students will understand how to plan developmentally and individually appropriate lessons and activities for infants and toddlers with and without disabilities. In collaboration with families, students will understand how to design a developmentally and individually appropriate program for infants and toddlers that supports parent confidence and competence. Students will understand how to explain early learning standards and various mainstream curricula and how they can be used to guide instruction in infant/toddler programs. Students will understand how to explain the importance of cultural competence in working with very young children and their families. Students will understand how to describe issues around transition from early intervention to preschool-based services for young children with disabilities and their families.

courses.description: This course addresses developmentally appropriate practices for children ages 3-5 years who are typically and atypically developing, including relevant theories of early learning, play, preschool curricula, emergent literacy and numeracy, social and emotional development, and classroom design.
courses.course_objectives: Upon completion of this course, students will be able to critique models, theories, philosophies, and trends of early childhood education/special education. Upon completion of this course, students will be able to describe the impact of language on all areas of development, including behavior and utilize strategies to support the language development of young children. Upon completion of this course, students will be able to utilize resources (including GELDS) and academic content knowledge to create developmentally appropriate lesson plans across disciplines for typically and atypically developing children. Upon completion of this course, students will be able to develop and create lesson plans to support learning for children experiencing a variety of needs and abilities. Upon completion of this course, students will be able to describe characteristics of a learning environment that creates a supportive social-emotional environment for young children and strategies to supportive effective behavior management in the classroom. Upon completion of this course, students will be able to collaborate and partner with peers to promote professional growth and development of educational philosophies and teaching abilities.

Upon completion of this course, students will be able to utilize resources (including GELDS) and academic content knowledge to create developmentally appropriate lesson plans across disciplines for typically and atypically developing children. Upon completion of this course, students will be able to develop and create lesson plans to support learning for children experiencing a variety of needs and abilities. Upon completion of this course, students will be able to describe characteristics of a learning environment that creates a supportive social-emotional environment for young children and strategies to supportive effective behavior management in the classroom. Upon completion of this course, students will be able to collaborate and partner with peers to promote professional growth and development of educational philosophies and teaching abilities.
courses.topical_outline: Theories of child development and educational models Developmentally appropriate programs Lesson planning Early childhood environments Assessing children’s learning Early childhood curriculum domains (e.g., cognitive, language, physical, social-emotional) Play-based learning Organizing children’s learning over time

courses.subject: EDSE
courses.title: Methods in Teaching Infants and Young Children with Developmental Delays Birth through 5
courses.description: Exploring foundations and programming for infants, toddlers, and young children with developmental delays, including developmentally appropriate practice, activity-based instruction, and other naturalistic evidence-based instructional practices.
courses.course_objectives: This course is designed for undergraduate students in the Birth through Age 5 Teacher Certification program. Upon completion of this course, students will understand foundations and policy for early intervention and preschool special education. Upon completion of this course, students will identify components of appropriate and effective individualized intervention for young children with disabilities (e.g., evidence-based practice). Upon completion of this course, students will identify program models in Birth through 5, including service delivery and methods for team collaboration. Upon completion of this course, students will identify the interface between developmentally appropriate practices (NAEYC) and best practices as they relate to young children with disabilities. Upon completion of this course, students will discuss the rationale for family-focused, culturally sensitive intervention, including IFSP/IEP development. Upon completion of this course, students will plan for instruction across developmental domains using an activity-based approach. Upon completion of this course, students will use naturalistic teaching techniques with young children with disabilities to facilitate integrated growth and learning in all developmental domains. Upon completion of this course, students will identify methods to facilitate interaction between children with and without disabilities. Upon completion of this course, students will design appropriate social and physical learning environments. Upon completion of this course, students will plan for transitions from Part C to Part B programs, and from preschool to kindergarten.

courses.subject: EDSE
courses.title: Literacy Instruction for Students with Intellectual and Developmental Disabilities
courses.description: Examination of evidence-based strategies, curricula, and assessment techniques for planning and implementing comprehensive literacy instruction for students with intellectual and developmental disabilities. Techniques for promoting literacy development with augmentative and alternative communication (AAC) systems will be addressed.
courses.course_objectives: Students will identify domains in comprehensive literacy instruction and the role of each in literacy development for students with intellectual and developmental disabilities (I/DD). Students will identify evidence-based strategies and curricula for supporting literacy development for students with I/DD. Students will identify and adapt assessments to inform literacy programming and instruction for students with I/DD. Students will implement literacy assessments and interpret assessment data to inform instructional planning in literacy for students with I/DD. Students will design literacy instruction that addresses concepts of print, sight word reading, vocabulary, oral and receptive language, listening comprehension, and/or reading comprehension. Students will implement literacy instruction utilizing evidence-based practices, including explicit and systematic instruction, for students with I/DD. Students will adapt literacy instruction to promote literacy and language development for students with I/DD who utilize AAC.
courses.topical_outline:
1. Current research trends literacy instruction for students with intellectual and developmental disabilities (I/DD) 2. Comprehensive reading instruction for students with I/DD
a) Role of literacy components in development, planning, and instruction
b) Literacy curricula and adaptations for students with I/DD 3. Literacy assessment for students with I/DD 4. EBP for implementing literacy instruction with students with I/DD 5. Writing instruction for students with I/DD 6. Assistive technology to support literacy for students with I/DD
a) Augmentative and alternative communication (AAC)
b) Other assistive technology 7. Training support personnel to implement literacy instruction for students with I/DD with fidelity

courses.title: Practicum in Intensive Reading Intervention
courses.description: Students will apply structured literacy techniques to address the needs of struggling readers. Students will develop and deliver a one-on-one, structured literacy reading intervention program. Emphasis will be placed on the implementation of evidence-based reading techniques, ongoing progress monitoring of student performance, and reflective instructional decision-making.
courses.course_objectives: Students will apply specific, evidence-based instructional strategies based upon a structured literacy approach for the teaching of reading. Students will master strategies associated with increasing opportunities to respond (OTR) in order to provide intensive intervention. Students will administer reading diagnostic assessments for the purpose of instructional planning. Students will develop an intervention plan that includes evidence-based components. Students will implement key aspects of reading intervention that address decoding, written expression, and comprehension. Students will teach strategies to struggling readers for the purpose of improving reading, writing, spelling, and handwriting performance.

courses.description: Behavioral psychology learning principles and procedures in the design of instructional programs to teach basic life skills.  Focus is on data-based instructional strategies that facilitate skill acquisition, fluency, maintenance, and generalization.
courses.course_objectives: Define and exemplify the principles and procedures of applied behavior analysis used in assessing a learner's performance on a target skill and in teaching tat skill. Design teaching sequences which incorporate the basic components of instructional programs, including specific attentional responses, and which are responsive to the learner's cognitive, sensory and physical disabilities. Critically discuss one-to-one and group instructional arrangements in teaching discrete trial and response chain tasks to students with developmental disabilities. Conduct concept and task analyses. Design instructional programs employing the following procedures: including, physical prompting and fading, system of least prompts, most-to-least prompt hierarchy, graduated guidance, progressive time delay, constant time delay, incidental teaching, and-model, and naturalistic time delay Critically evaluate the procedures listed under objective. Discuss approaches to creating positive learning environments and strategies for facilitating observational and incidental learning. Discuss programming strategies, including career/vocational and transition models, which facilitate behavior generalization and maintenance. Demonstrate the ability to teach students with mental retardation/developmental disabilities in a variety of place settings and include formative evaluation as a means for determining the effectiveness of instructional programs. Design instructional programs that use specific attentional responses and instructive feedback to facilitate incidental learning. Design and implement "errorless" instructional programs that teach learners with disabilities a functional skill. Write the results of the instructional program in accordance with APA (1994) publication guidelines. Present the results of the instructional program to the seminar in a professional manner. Design and implement sensory stimulation programs for individuals with extensive needs. Demonstrate the ability to integrate selected related services into the instructional day of students with mental retardation/developmental disabilities. Discuss the impact of multiple disabilities on the behavior on individuals with disabilities. Discuss conditions and utilize assessment instruments that ensure maximum performance for students with mental retardation/developmental disabilities. Utilize research-supported instructional strategies and practices, including the functional embedded skills approach, community- based instruction, task analysis, multisensory, and concrete/manipulative techniques and provide             instruction in these areas. Design instructional programs that teach culturally responsive functional life skills relevant to independence in the community, personal living, and employment, including assessing public transportation, cooking, shopping, laundry, functional reading, and sexuality. Demonstrate and assist students in the use of alternative and augmentative communication systems.

courses.title: Basic Principles of Applied Behavior Analysis
courses.description: Behavioral analysis as applied to socially significant behavior. Emphases include skills curricula, social behavior across cultures, school- and community-based instruction, generalization of skills, and validation of intervention procedures.
courses.course_objectives:
Course Objectives and Related CEC Knowledge (K) and Skill (S) Competencies in the Area of Behavioral Disorders (BD): Upon completion of this course, the student will be able to:  
1. Articulate historical and current trends in applied  behavior analysis and social learning theory. Define, select, and prioritize target behaviors. BD6.S2, BD6.S3, BD6.S4, MR2.K5, LD4.K5 Design and implement data collection procedures and Behavioral Intervention Plans (BIP). BD6.S2 Produce and analyze graphic displays of dependent measures. BD6.S2 Conduct functional analyses. BD6.S2, BD6.S3, MR3.K4, MR6.K1, MR6.K2 Articulate the common elements of effective social skills curricula and analyze selected social skills curricula. BD6.K, BD4.S5, EC6.S2 Discuss learning constructs and social behavior as related to diversity and multiculturalism. BD6.K1, EC7.S3 Design a generalization-based social skills program. BD4.S4, MR4.S4 Define internal and external validity and list related threats. Describe single-subject research designs and their strengths/weaknesses. Articulate definitions and develop appropriate applications related to operant reinforcement, punishment, time-out, stimulus control, extinction, generalization, self-management, contracting, token economics, shaping, chaining, and task analysis. BD6.K1, BD6.K3, MR4.K3, LD6.S1 BD4.S4, BD6.S2, BD4.S10 Critically analyze literature on social behavior with respect to internal and external validity. EC8.S5
courses.topical_outline: History and origins of applied behavior analysis. Trends and advancement in conceptualization and philosophy. Relationship to Social Learning Theory Bandura. Perspectives on addressing antisocial behavior. Includes discussion of psycho-educational and other models seen in schools. Identification and measurement of behavior. Establishing measurement systems. Reporting data in graph form. Visual analysis of time series graphs. Overview of single subject research designs and analysis of graphical data for common designs. Including techniques for analyzing graphed data in the published literature. Design of formative evaluation plans to monitor intervention. Functional behavior assessment and experimental functional analysis. Use of reinforcement to increase pro-social behaviors. Use of reinforcement to decrease anti-social behaviors. Using punishment to reduce behavior. Programming for stimulus control and generalization.

courses.subject: EDSE
courses.title: Instructional Design for Students with Autism Spectrum Disorder
courses.description: Readings, discussions and activities related to the design ofeffective and efficient instructional programs for students withASD.  Topics include how to adapt the learning environment,including: the physical organization of the setting; use ofvisual schedules, modifications that address fine motordifficulties; and strategies to reduce sensory challenges.
courses.course_objectives: Students will be able to describe and explain the characteristics of autism that should be considered when designing instruction for these learners. Students will be able to design the physical environment for students with autism, including use of adaptations and modifications, visual schedules, and work systems. Students will be able to evaluate instructional strategies for students with ASD based on assigned readings. Students will be able to review a student file, conduct a teacher interview, and observe the student in an educational setting with the purpose of selecting IEP objectives. Students will be able to write instructional IEP objectives for students with ASD. Students will be able to select appropriate teaching procedures, including visual supports, to teach selected objectives (for academic, self-help, alternative behaviors, and other functional skills). Students will be able to conduct progress monitoring, teach others (e.g., paraprofessionals) to conduct instruction and monitor progress. Students will be able to plan instruction for a small group of diverse students. Students will be able to determine antecedents and consequences, characteristics of autism, and skill deficits that may contribute to behavior problems and design antecedent- and/or consequence-based interventions to decrease problem behaviors and increase appropriate replacement behaviors.
courses.topical_outline: 1. Historical and current contexts related to teaching and autism spectrum disorders 2. Basics of teaching; assessing interventions for students with autism 3. Assessment of functional, academic, and problem behaviors for students with autism (including conducting interviews and observations) 4. Using visuals and writing related objectives (including use and measurement of schedules, work systems, instruction, priming, and prompts; 5 sessions) 5. Using and fading prompts for individuals and groups (2 sessions) 6. Teaching self-help and adaptive skills 7. Functional behavior assessment for problem behaviors 8. Function-based interventions for problem behaviors 9. Academic interventions (e.g., reading, writing, and math-specific interventions) 10. Teaching adults to implement interventions and collect data
courses.prerequisiteText: (EDSE 2000 or EDSE 2000E) and permission of department

courses.subject: EDSE
courses.title: Internship in Special Education
courses.description: Supervised culminating field experience related to teaching individuals with disabilities.
courses.course_objectives: Upon completion of this internship, the student will be able to prepare accurate formal social assessment reports on students with E/BD based on behavioral-ecological information. Upon completion of this internship, the student will be able to implement procedures for assessing both appropriate and problematic social behaviors of students with E/BD. Upon completion of this internship, the student will be able to use exceptionality-specific assessment instruments appropriately for assessing students with E/BD. Upon completion of this internship, the student will be able to identify and use prevention and intervention strategies as early as appropriate for use with students with E/BD. Upon completion of this internship, the student will be able to delineate and apply the goals and intervention strategies and procedures related to a variety of theoretical approaches to students with E/BD. Upon completion of this internship, the student will be able to use technology applicable to students with E/BD. Upon completion of this internship, the student will be able to plan, organize, and implement individualized student programs appropriate to the cognitive and affective needs of the student with E/BD with special consideration to use of reinforcement systems and environmental conditions. Upon completion of this internship, the student will be able to select, develop, adopt, and evaluate curriculum materials and technology applicable to students with E/BD. Upon completion of this internship, the student will be able to establish a consistent classroom routine for students with E/BD. Upon completion of this internship, the student will be able to delineate and apply appropriate management procedures when presented with spontaneous management problems applicable to students with E/BD. Upon completion of this internship, the student will be able to stablish classroom rules, as well as a means for enforcing these rules, that are applicable to students with E/BD. Upon completion of this internship, the student will be able to integrate academic instruction, affective education, and behavior management for individual students and groups of students with E/BD. Upon completion of this internship, the student will be able to use student-initiated learning experiences and integrate them into ongoing instruction for students with E/BD. Upon completion of this internship, the student will be able to monitor intragroup behavior changes from subject to subject and activity to activity applicable to students with E/BD. Upon completion of this internship, the student will be able to select a functional classroom design (e.g., functional seating, work area, storage) that is effective for students with E/BD. Upon completion of this internship, the student will be able to use a variety of nonaversive techniques (including voice modulation, facial expressions, planned to ignore, proximity control, and tension release) for the purpose of controlling targeted behavior and maintaining attention of students with E/BD. Upon completion of this internship, the student will be able to develop and implement a systematic behavior management plan for students with E/BD using a variety of behavioral principles (including observation, recording, charting establishment of timelines, intervention technique hierarchies, and schedules of reinforcement). Upon completion of this internship, the student will be able to select target behaviors to be changed and identify the critical variables affecting the target behavior (such is subsequent events and antecedent events). Upon completion of this internship, the student will be able to designate certain pupil behaviors as either appropriate or inappropriate for a specific age group based on observation and social validation. Upon completion of this internship, the student will be able to define and use skills in problem solving and conflict resolution.
courses.topical_outline:
Internship Activities and Evaluation Policies and Procedures Notebook Activities: This notebook is to be compiled by the intern within the first two weeks of the first day of the internship, and shall include sections for the written policies and procedures (with accompanying forms) in the categories of prereferral, parental and student notifications, referral, assessment, IEP, placement, evaluation, and discipline. Evaluation: The presence of written policies, procedures and accompanying forms for each area above. Student Profiles and Assessment Activities: The intern will read the files of all students served in the classroom, and conduct assessments on at least three students. Standardized, informal, criterion-referenced, curriculum-based, and functional assessments will be administered to help determine present levels of functioning. Decisions about specific assessment tools to be administered will be made by the student intern and supervisor(s). This information is to be compiled into a student profile (using a pseudonym) for each student assessed. Demographic information including a pseudonym, grade level, chronological age, parental information

¨ Relevant medical information
¨ Services received through special education, general education, and related services
¨ Levels of functioning in math, language arts, speech, all other academics, vocational skills
¨ Social skills, excessive behaviors
¨ Motivational factors, reinforcement survey
¨ Familial issues Evaluation: The presence of complete information on each of the above elements IEP Development Activities: Student interns will develop Individualized Education Plans for two students with learning disabilities during the semester. Each IEP should include: Present level of performance, annual goals and short-term objectives, the special education and related services that will be provided and the extent to which the child will participate in general education programs, plans for starting the services and the anticipated duration of the services, plans for evaluating whether the goals and objectives are being achieved, and, if appropriate, a transition plan. Informal and/or formal assessments should be administered to complete each IEP and, if possible, feedback from the parents or guardians of the student the semester. Lesson plans are to be developed for each observation, including the criteria below. Evaluation of Lesson Plans: Lesson plans will be evaluated within the following format. Activities: Students will develop a leadership project in either advocacy or inclusion. For either area, the intern is to prepare an outline of the proposed activities, including (a) rationale, (b) the goal(s) of the project, (c) a detailed description of the planned activities to meet the goal(s), (d) the method for evaluating the outcomes with respect to the goal(s), and (e) implications for future. The intern should design this project with the assistance of the supervisor and cooperating teacher. Examples of projects include: Developing and implementing an in-service for teachers to enhance their understanding of behavioral disorders; initiating a co-teaching approach that involves general education teachers and students and students with behavioral disorders in a joint project (e.g., service learning, mentoring); and developing an in-service for general education teachers in the area of strategies to improve academic success. Evaluation: The project outline will be evaluated by the supervisor and supervising teacher. The final write up of the project shall be 10-15 pages, including references and APA style. The written project shall be evaluated with respect to a-e above.

courses.subject: EDSE
courses.title: Behavior Analysis Across the Lifespan
courses.description: Course focuses on the application of behavior analysis to address a wide variety of clinical issues. Course is intended to provide exposure to non-autism related content and expand student’s understanding of the applicability of behavior analysis beyond the narrow clinical scope of autism, particularly children with autism.
courses.course_objectives: Provide a description of behavior analysis to address pediatric disorders. Identify the behavioral mechanisms measured when addressing academic/school-aged behavioral concerns and classroom performance. Demonstrate familiarity with applications of behavior analysis to address behavioral concerns faced by elder adults. Provide a description of behavior analysis as a means of addressing behavioral deficits such as communication deficits, self-advocacy deficits, and social skills deficits. Produce a summary of a researcher or non-autism related topic of their choosing.
courses.topical_outline: Pediatric feeding disorders Sleep, elimination, compliance ADHD School-based instruction Pediatric obesity Communication Social skills and jobs Sports, health, and fitness Self-advocacy Psychological suffering Behavioral gerontology

courses.subject: EDSE
courses.title: Staff Training and Supervision in Behavior Analysis
courses.description: Skills behavior analysts need as supervisors and consultants, including ABA technologies to change and improve practitioner, educator, and caregiver behaviors. The fundamentals for developing effective supervisory and consulting relationships. Students receive instruction on assessing skills, developing performance objectives, and providing training and feedback.
courses.course_objectives: Students will be able to define and provide examples of the concepts and principles of ABA directly related to consultation and supervision. (Behavior Analyst Certification Board [BACB] Task List B-1, 4, 5, 8, 12, I-01) Students will be able to demonstrate competency in training supervisees and consultees in the implementation of behavior analytic procedures (e.g., selecting supervision goals, evaluating the effects of supervision, stating reasons for supervision). (BACB Task List I-01, 02, 04, 05, 07, 08) Students will be able to conduct assessment activities directly related to consultation and supervision, ensuring they are culturally and linguistically relevant. (BACB Task List F-3, 4, I-02, 03, 06, 08) Students will be able to develop and implement training plans to foster effective performance using behavior analytic technologies. (BACB Task List H-9, I-01, 02, 03, 04, 05, 06, 07, 08) Students will be able to demonstrate personnel supervision and management skills directly related to consultation and supervision, including skills demonstrating cultural responsiveness. (BACB Task List H-9, I-02, 03, 04, 05, 06, 07, 08)
courses.topical_outline: Behavioral consultation and models of consultation Goals and assumptions underlying supervisory and consulting behaviors Developing effective collaborative and supervisory relationships Consultation and supervision practice—developing treatment plans and training protocols, progress monitoring Training others on behavior analytic practices Developing and evaluating intervention plans and goal setting in consultation and supervision Assessment in consultation and supervision The use of dimensions of ABA in consultation and supervision Evidence- and competency-based supervision Collaboration with non-ABA professionals Performance feedback in consultation and supervision

courses.subject: EDSE
courses.title: Philosophical Underpinnings and Concepts in Behavior Analysis
courses.description: Designed to give future behavior analysts a solid foundation in the underlying philosophical and basic concepts associated with human behavior and learning. In doing such, the course will sample literature from philosophy as well as from basic science.

courses.subject: EDSE
courses.title: Translational Behavior Analysis
courses.description: Course focuses on the bridge between basic and applied behavior analysis. Students will work through several topics, tracing the basic roots, discussing behavioral mechanisms underlying each topic, and finishing with a discussion of its utility in clinical contexts.
courses.course_objectives: Describe the link between basic and applied research as relevant to individuals with disabilities. Identify behavioral mechanisms underlying many of the applied practices utilized in the assessment and treatment of behavioral excesses and deficits. Provide a description of the role translational research plays in the science of behavior.
courses.topical_outline: Relapse: Evaluation of variables that lead to or mitigate the re-emergence of behavior following response extinction/reduction Response Variability: Evaluation of the variables that allow for and promote response variability Persistence: Evaluation of variables that increase response strength, resulting in persistent operant behavior Behavioral Economics: Investigation of how response requirement and reinforcement magnitude combine to impact response allocation

Educators will explore key aspects of learning and teaching, reflect on their own learning processes and those of others, and apply their knowledge to equitably meet the diverse learning needs of P-12 students in a variety of educational settings and contexts.

courses.title: History of Childhood and the Family in the United States
courses.description: An examination of the changing experiences and forms of childhood and family life, as mediated by class and ethnicity, over the course of United States history. Students will seek to relate those changing experiences and forms to their political, economic, and schooling contexts, and to consider explanations for their historical alterations.

courses.subject: EDUC(LACS)

courses.description: An overview of important patterns and issues in education relating to Hispanic/Latino students K-12 and post-secondary, statewide and nationally. Includes history, cultural context, policy issues and trends, challenges faced by Latinos in school, implications for practice, and current research.

Connections to written expression, discourse writing, and special populations in varied contexts are explored.

courses.subject: EDUC
courses.title: Politics and American Education
courses.description: Education is inherently political. Historical and contemporary analyses of public education, its changing purposes, curricular battles, federal and state policy conflicts, constitutional cases, multicultural issues, and privatization efforts are explored.
courses.course_objectives: Explain the social policy connections between education and politics in the United States. Analyze historical and cultural influences and impacts on local, state, and national education, policies, and practices. Critique the constitutional freedoms and legal protections of students and teachers. Explain conflicts over education among local, state, and the federal government, Congress, and state legislatures. Discuss the different and competing ideologies that inform education policy and curricular decisions. Deconstruct historical and contemporary multicultural conflicts and public schooling. Analyze conflicts over education and curricula initiated by external interest groups. Critique the public-school privatization movement, its related interest groups, and the role of state legislatures and philanthropies in education reform.
courses.topical_outline:
A. Topics for Reading
1. Reading and Thinking Critically
2. Learning to Read and Evaluate Historical and Political Arguments
3. Learning Historical Rootedness in Contemporary Problems
4. Ideology Critique
5. Developing Social Justice Arguments B. Topics for Writing
1. Learning to Write Critically
2. Organization and Development
3. Grammar and Citation Format C. Content Outline
1. Outside environmental influences on learners, including culture, family structure and background, home language, SES, and peers
2. Institutionally and historically rooted forms of racism, sexism, classism, and homophobia in educational institutions and policies
3. Political and cultural conflicts over the purposes and goals of educational institutions
4. Conflicts related to education and the federalist nature of American government
5. Major court cases impacting education
6. Case studies related to state political conflicts over public school curricula
7. How major political and social events affect public schooling
8. How inequalities and inequities are institutionally perpetuated
9. School privatization

courses.subject: EDUC
courses.title: International Educational Experiences in the Classroom and Community
courses.description: Designed for students enrolled in a study abroad experience.  Students will examine the teaching profession in an international context, engage in observations and analyses of how culture and context impact public education systems, and make comparisons to the United States. This course has a required field experience component.

courses.subject: EDUC
courses.title: Educational Experiences in Classroom and Community
courses.description: Students will explore the role of public education in a complex and diverse democratic society through course readings, class discussions, and active involvement in schools. Students will also examine various perspectives on controversial issues in education and consider the impact of policy and practice on students, teachers, schools, and society.

courses.subject: EDUC
courses.title: Educational Experiences in Classroom and Community (Honors)
courses.description: Exploration of the role of public education in a complex and diverse democratic society through course readings, class discussions, and active involvement in schools. Students will also examine various perspectives on controversial issues in education and consider the impact of policy and practice on students, teachers, schools, and society.

courses.title: Faculty-Mentored Undergraduate Research I
courses.description: Faculty-supervised independent or collaborative inquiry into fundamental and applied problems within a discipline that requires students to gather, analyze, and synthesize and interpret data and to present results in writing and other relevant communication formats.

courses.subject: EDUC
courses.title: Faculty-Mentored Undergraduate Research II
courses.description: Faculty-supervised independent or collaborative inquiry into fundamental and applied problems within a discipline that requires students to gather, analyze, and synthesize and interpret data and to present results in writing and other relevant communication formats.

courses.subject: EDUC
courses.title: Faculty-Mentored Undergraduate Research III
courses.description: Faculty-supervised independent or collaborative inquiry into fundamental and applied problems within a discipline that requires students to gather, analyze, synthesize, and interpret data and to present results in writing and other relevant communication formats.

courses.subject: EDUC
courses.title: Undergraduate Research Thesis (or Final Project)
courses.description: Faculty-supervised independent or collaborative inquiry into fundamental and applied problems within a discipline that requires students to gather, analyze, and synthesize and interpret data. Students will write or produce a thesis or other professional capstone product, such as a report or portfolio that describes their systematic and in-depth inquiry.

courses.subject: EDUC
courses.title: Research in the College of Education
courses.description: Varied opportunities in research in education and relatedhuman-service fields, including special seminars, presentations,participation in research projects, and other activities.  Designed to introduce undergraduate students to research in these areas.
courses.offeredText: Not offered on a regular basis.

courses.subject: EDUC
courses.title: Immigrants, Migrants, and Refugees: Education and Policy In Global Perspective
courses.description: Examination of the motives for and dynamics of populationmovements of immigrants, migrants, and refugees and theirimplications for schools and society in the United States and other countries.  Takes an interdiscipinary approach to study relations among policy and practice, population shifts, and education in sociocultural, political, and historical context.

courses.subject: EDUC
courses.title: Academic and Social Achievement in Instructional Conversations - Culturally Responsive Pedagogy
courses.description: Designed for pre-service and in-service teachers, this non-traditional, hybrid course will explore the theory and practice underpinning the culturally-responsive pedagogy, InstructionalConversations (IC). Students will participate in a four-day institute, respond to readings, engage in observations and applied practice in P-12 classrooms, and reflect on their practice through online interactions.

courses.subject: EDUC
courses.title: Clinical Internship in Education
courses.description: Supervised experience in an educational setting appropriate to educator preparation programs.
courses.course_objectives: This course is designed to provide a field experience for the preservice teacher. The student will be in a classroom setting daily and will be responsible for almost all regular teacher duties.
courses.topical_outline: Demonstrate professionalism in the school setting (punctuality, attendance, dependability, confidentiality, and collaboration), effective management techniques, thoughtful and thorough planning, accurate and varied assessment techniques, professional parent-teacher relations, create an integrated unit.

courses.subject: EDUC
courses.title: Classroom-Based Research
courses.description: Students will investigate professional teaching standards toguide their classroom inquiries as they assemble tools,strategies, and methodologies for classroom-based research. Thecourse is designed to encourage experienced teachers toarticulate theories upon which their practice is based, critiquethose theories, and prepare for advanced graduate degreeprograms. Students must be practicing teachers when they takethis course.
courses.course_objectives:
Students will be able to identify and examine local/state/national standards for professional development of teachers. Students will be able to design action research plans based on professional development standards. Students will be able to identify and use research tools and methodologies to carry out classroom-based inquiries. Students will be able to practice different strategies of writing up data. Students will be able to produce visual representation of data as a means of communicating student achievement to
stakeholders.
courses.topical_outline: a. Professional development standards b. Grounded and a priority theory c. Research questions d. Data sources e. Teacher research as professional development f. Assessment g. Action research methods h. Writing strategies

courses.subject: EDUC
courses.title: Foundations of School Climate
courses.description: Examination of school climate, the quality and character of school life, grounded in an interdisciplinary framework. Explores perspectives on measuring school climate, the connection of school climate and educational outcomes, and methods of school climate improvement. Emphasis on evidence-based practices for developing safe and supportive learning environments for all students.

courses.subject: EDUC
courses.title: Graduate Student Seminar
courses.description: Advanced supervised experience in an applied setting. This course may not be used to satisfy a student's approved program of study.

courses.subject: EDUC
courses.title: Comparative and International Education
courses.description: Theory, policy, and practice in selected educational systems.  Examines data and models from educational systems around the world.  Critiques important themes:  race, ethnicity, class, and gender; the role of education in national development; cross-cultural research; and major development in the methodology of comparative education.

courses.subject: EDUC
courses.title: History of Education in the United States
courses.description: Examination of changing forms, philosophical orientations, and operations of education in the United States from its colonial origins to the present.  Includes consideration of both formal and informal education, though the emphasis is on formal institutions.  Encompasses education from early childhood through various forms of adult education, and education of majority and minority populations.

courses.subject: EDUC
courses.title: Gender and Education
courses.description: Issues, research, theory, and policy on gender and education.  Gender effects in socialization, schooling, and lifelong learning are analyzed for their implications for individuals, society, and culture.

courses.subject: EDUC
courses.title: Sociological Theories of Education
courses.description: Theories of social structure, stratification, and social change.  Relationships among social institutions and educational processes and outcomes, and how various social institutions contribute to the maintenance of existing structured inequalities.

courses.subject: EDUC
courses.title: Multicultural Education for the 21st Century
courses.description: Racial and cultural identity; ways oppression appears instudents' lives, schooling policies, and practices; connectionsbetween gender, race, class, and cultural marginalization andeducation; relationships of empowerment to social changes,assessment, and evaluation; and associations among knowledgeconstruction, culture, and learning.

courses.subject: EDUC
courses.title: Examining Race and Culture in Education Reform and Policy
courses.description: How race and culture have historically shaped and continue to shape school reform and policy formation. Encourages students to explore and critically examine the underlying assumptions about the purpose of schooling, and the beliefs that undergird educational reform systems historically, and in contemporary society.
courses.course_objectives:
Students will develop an interdisciplinary perspective - historical, philosophical, anthropological, and sociological - on race and culture in education reform and policy. Students will develop an understanding of the policy process and efforts to create reform in education. Students will explore the ideological basis undergirding efforts to bring about reform in education. Students will develop critical assessments and insight regarding educational reform along with dimensions of race, culture, gender, and class. Students will develop critical assessments of insight regarding educational reform targeted towards individuals from
various racial, cultural, ethnic, and linguistically diverse groups.
courses.topical_outline:
Students will develop an interdisciplinary perspective - historical, philosophical, anthropological, and sociological - on race and culture in education reform and policy. Students will develop an understanding of the policy process and efforts to create reform in education. Students will explore the ideological basis undergirding efforts to bring about reform in education. Students will develop critical assessments and insight regarding educational reform along with dimensions of race, culture, gender, and class. Students will develop critical assessments of insight regarding educational reform targeted towards individuals from
various racial, cultural, ethnic, and linguistically diverse groups.

courses.subject: EDUC
courses.title: Social Class, Poverty, and Economics in Education and Communities
courses.description: This course immerses students in social, psychological, embodied, economic, political, and place-based aspects of social class, poverty, and economics in education in the U.S. and across the globe. Students will create concrete action plans for teaching, learning, and working with youth in K-12 classrooms, communities, and other contexts.
courses.course_objectives: Students will interpret broad social, political, historical, economic, ecological, and land-based contexts that shape their own social classed lives and experiences. Students will critique children’s and adult literature, media, and history through a class analysis and compare to working-class, wage-poor, and indigenous perspectives. Students will recognize and articulate different class-based orientations in school policies and curriculum including meritocracy, neoliberalism, egalitarianism, collectivism, communalism, humanism, and posthumanism. Students will analyze the assumptions in humanist and posthumanist theories as they are related to policies and curriculum in schools and communities. Students will explain how ethics, ontology, and epistemology are embedded in different ways educators and youth workers approach relationships, curriculum, structures, and policies. Students will analyze existing educational materials, environments, and curriculum from a class- and economics-focused perspective. Students will develop and assemble educational materials that encourage expansive and critical inquiries into the way social class and economics operate in the everyday lives of youth, families, educators, and all youth workers.
courses.topical_outline: 1.Personal experiences of social class inside and outside schools, then situated within larger social, economic, and political contexts; 2.Historical and contemporary perspectives on social class/education/labor (Indian Boarding Schools; Antebellum slavery; convict leasing; immigration; modern day slavery; capitalism in the U.S.; neoliberal capitalism and schooling); fundraising;  and implications for creating educational environments, designing lessons and units, and shaping an ethico-onto-epistemology that is class-sensitive in schools; 3.Children’s literature and lessons about social class, poverty, and the prevalence of middle-class normativity and affluent desirability; 4.Language use in the classroom by teachers, students, and families as markers of social class, middle-class normativity, and classism; 5.Social class and classism in popular culture and discourses circulating in schools and classrooms; 6.Place-based and land-based teaching and learning as an integral part of class-sensitive teaching, class-based healing, and wellbeing; 7.Curriculum development around work, workers, economics, class, poverty, wealth, histories, housing, transportation, literature, language, popular culture, ecology, geography, family-school relationships, etc. and classism on local and global scales; 8. Action plan construction regarding preferred policies, practices, routines, relationships, content, curriculum, pedagogies, and shaping a class-sensitive material and discursive environment.
