courses.description: Faculty-supervised independent or collaborative inquiry into fundamental and applied problems within a discipline that requires students to gather, analyze, and synthesize and interpret data and to present results in writing and other relevant communication formats.

courses.subject: ELEE
courses.title: Undergraduate Thesis in Electrical Engineering
courses.description: Students who successfully complete this course will produce a research project/thesis approved by the instructor and a reader.
courses.offeredText: Not offered on a regular basis.

courses.subject: ELEE
courses.title: Undergraduate Research Thesis (or Final Project)
courses.description: Faculty-supervised independent or collaborative inquiry into fundamental and applied problems within a discipline that requires students to gather, analyze, and synthesize and interpret data. Students will write or produce a thesis or other professional capstone product, such as a report or portfolio that describes their systematic and in-depth inquiry.

courses.subject: ELEE
courses.title: Optoelectronic Devices
courses.description: Fundamentals of semiconductor materials, p-n and metal-semiconductor junctions, photon absorption in semiconductors, optical detection devices, light emitting diode operation, diode laser design, optical modulators, and physical device fabrication.
courses.offeredText: Not offered on a regular basis.

courses.subject: ELEE
courses.title: Microwave Remote Sensing
courses.description: Basic concepts of microwave remote sensing, including wave propagation, scattering, and reflection from natural Earth environments as well as emerging methodologies, such as GNSS-R and signals of opportunity.
courses.course_objectives: After successfully completing this course, the students will be able to understand how microwave remote sensing complements optical (visible and infrared) observations. After successfully completing this course, the students will be able to explain the fundamental difference between active versus passive microwave remote sensing. After successfully completing this course, the students will be able to describe the interaction of waves with natural Earth environments such as soil, vegetation, snow, ice, and water bodies. After successfully completing this course, the students will be able to understand and apply the governing physics (radiative transfer theory and analytical wave theory) to land observations. After successfully completing this course, the students will be able to interpret and derive surface roughness and vegetation scattering models to apply measured microwave data. After successfully completing this course, the students will be able to understand future directions in microwave remote sensing, such as signals of opportunity.
courses.topical_outline: Introduction to Microwave Remote Sensing Wave Propagation Remote Sensing Antennas Microwave Dielectric Properties of Natural Earth Materials Radar Scattering Microwave Radiometry and Radiative Transfer Surface Scattering Models and Land Observations Volume Scattering Models and Land Observations

courses.subject: ELEE
courses.title: Nonlinear Control Systems
courses.description: Examines how nonlinear systems can be analyzed as well as controlled. In particular, we will discuss various notions of stability and develop general theories on how to establish stability properties for nonlinear systems. Various applications will be covered in different engineering disciplines.

courses.subject: ELEE
courses.title: Instrumentation Programming
courses.description: Students will learn to write custom computer programs that interface with laboratory instruments. The course will cover advanced topics such as interfacing with dynamic link libraries and using queues and state space models to control program execution. The course is intended for graduate students who will be performing experimental work.

courses.subject: ELEE
courses.title: Autonomous Mobile Robots and Manipulation
courses.description: Teaches students to understand the fundamental principles of robotics and expose students to the latest robotics research. The course will cover advanced topics such as differential kinematics, localization, mapping, motion planning, soft robotics, and robotic perception, as well as current research topics in robotics.
courses.prerequisiteText: (MATH 2250 or MATH 2250E) and MATH 3000 and permission of department

courses.subject: ELEE
courses.title: Nanoelectronics: Electronic, Opto-Electronic, and Thermo-Electronic Transport in Nanostructures
courses.description: Provides graduate students with knowledge and understanding of the physical background and applications of nanoelectronics. Covers electrical, thermoelectric, and optical properties of materials and nanostructures, fabrication of nanostructures, and nanoelectronic devices, as well as their applications.
courses.prerequisiteText: PHYS 1010 or ELEE 4270 or ELEE 4020 or ELEE 4260/6260 or CHEM 8930 or permission of department

courses.subject: ELEE
courses.title: MEMS Design
courses.description: Exploration of the world of microelectromechanical systems (MEMS) through awareness of material properties, microfabrication technologies, structural behavior, sensing techniques, actuation schemes, fluid behavior, electronic circuits, and feedback systems. Lectures will be augmented with homework assignments and design projects.
courses.prerequisiteText: This class is open to all Engineering and Science graduate students.

courses.subject: ELEE
courses.title: Fiber Optic Sensors
courses.description: Fiber optic sensors is a promising and fast growing technology. The unique properties of fiber optics solve the bottleneck of electronic sensors. The principle, design, and applications of various fiber optic sensors. Topics including distributed sensors, interferometric sensors, evanescent-field sensors, and wavelength-modulated sensors will be covered.
courses.offeredText: Not offered on a regular basis.

courses.subject: ELEE
courses.title: Advanced Wireless Communication
courses.description: Course covers wireless communication fundamentals, focusing on four areas: wireless basics, including channel modeling, modulation, and capacity; channel capacity and coding; MIMO fundamentals; and emerging topics. The goal is to understand key physical layer blocks and explore advancements in wireless communication.
courses.course_objectives: Students will understand basic and advanced topics on wireless communication and its fundamentals. Students will have in-depth analysis on wireless system performance, metrics, and evaluation. Students will be able to use math tools to model wireless channel, wireless capacity, and access efficiency. Students will be able to read papers in the general area of 5G and beyond. Students will be able to design and evaluate a wireless system in practice Students will have knowledge of wireless technology and its application in 5G and beyond era.
courses.topical_outline:
Wireless Communication Fundamentals 
a. Wireless channel modeling and measurement 
b. Communication system overview and blocks 
c. Wireless modulation and demodulation techniques
d. Wireless signal detection, estimation, and likelihood methods Channel Capacity and Information Theory
a. Channel coding and capacity of channels
b. Multiple access technology and interference management MIMO and Its Fundamentals 
a. Spatial multiplexing 
b. Diversity 
c. Space-time codes
d. Multi-user communication Selected Topics in Emerging Areas 
a. 5G and beyond 
b. Intelligent reflective surfaces 
c. UAV communication 
d. Satellite communication

courses.subject: ELEE
courses.title: Advanced Motor Drives
courses.description: There is an increasing demand for high-performance motor drives in home appliances, automotive, and industrial applications. Principles, design, and applications of motor drive systems. Topics including power electronics, advanced torque controls, sensorless controls, permanent magnet synchronous machines, and switched reluctance machines will be covered.
courses.offeredText: Not offered on a regular basis.

courses.subject: ELEE
courses.title: Microwave Photonics
courses.description: This interdisciplinary course provides the exposure to the theoryand technologies behind the marriage of the fields of microwaveand photonics, as well as its emerging applications in military,civilian, and commercial areas. Students will learn the skillsthat are essential for designing and characterizing microwavephotonic devices and systems.

courses.subject: ELEE
courses.title: Advanced Optics and Photonics
courses.description: Advanced topics in optics and photonics. Topics covered include nonlinear-optics, optical response of materials and optical fiber, and electro-optic effects in photonic devices. Applications of photonic technologies in signal processing and emerging applications will be discussed.
courses.course_objectives: Upon completion of this course, students should be able to calculate the optical response of different nonlinear materials. Upon completion of this course, students should be able to describe different applications of nonlinear optics. Upon completion of this course, students should be able to describe and explain different linear and nonlinear effects in optical fiber. Upon completion of this course, students should be able to describe and explain different electro-optic effects in photonic devices. Upon completion of this course, students should be able to understand the applications of photonics in various areas. Upon completion of this course, students should be able to apply basic fiber optics principles and devices to solve problems. Upon completion of this course, students should be able to understand how photonics connects to our life and the society.
courses.topical_outline: Maxwell’s equations Gaussian beams Second and third harmonic generation Raman processes Four-wave mixing Optical cavities and lasers Optical properties of materials Linear effects in optical fiber Nonlinear effects in optical fiber Electro-optic effect Optoelectronic devices Photonic signal processing Emerging applications of photonics

courses.subject: ELEE
courses.title: Biological Microscopy
courses.description: An interdisciplinary introduction to modern biological microscopy techniques. Students will be introduced to all aspects of preparing and imaging biological samples. Students will prepare samples for fluorescence imaging and use different microscopes. Specific topics covered will change from year to year.

courses.subject: ELEE
courses.title: Advanced Power System Analysis
courses.description: Power system reliability and resiliency rely on steady-state and dynamic analyses. Course will offer an in-depth exploration of power system steady-state analyses. Major topics are power flow, unit commitment, economic dispatch, electricity market, distribution systems, and microgrids. Students are expected to work on project during this course.
courses.course_objectives: At the completion of this course, students should be able to demonstrate a comprehensive understanding of power system analysis techniques, preparing them for research and applications in interdisciplinary settings. At the completion of this course, students should be able to develop a solid foundation to pursue further studies in power system analysis, encompassing both system modeling, optimization, and computation. At the completion of this course, students should be able to recognize and understand emerging technologies and methodologies in the realm of power system analysis. At the completion of this course, students should be able to articulate complex problems and solutions related to power system analysis through clear technical writing and oral communication for class projects and discussions.
courses.topical_outline: Overview of power system analysis Power system steady-state modeling Power flow: formulations and algorithms Optimization overview for power system applications Unit commitment and economic dispatch Distribution systems and microgrids

courses.subject: ELEE
courses.title: Advanced Power Electronics
courses.description: Power electronics systems span smart homes and buildings, manufacturing systems, smart grids, and electrified transportation. Principles, design, and applications of power electronics systems. Topics include modeling, control, and design of power electronics with applications to smart grids, manufacturing systems, and electric vehicles.

courses.subject: ELEE
courses.title: Advanced Topics in Wireless Communication
courses.description: The course covers wireless communication basics, including channel modeling, modulation, and capacity. It explores coding theory, multiple access technology, and MIMO techniques. Emerging topics are also discussed.
courses.course_objectives: Students will understand basic concepts related to random variables, including probability density function, moments, characteristic functions, as well as conditional expectation. Students will grasp the theoretical results of convergence and central limit theorem. Students will understand the definition of random processes and related concepts, including stationarity, correlation, and power spectrum density. Students will comprehend basic linear system theory and the frequency domain analysis of random processes. Students will implement related algorithms on real applications in Engineering.
courses.topical_outline: Wireless Communication Fundamentals Channel Capacity and Information Theory MIMO and its Fundamentals Selected Topics in Emerging Areas

courses.subject: EMAT
courses.title: Foundations of Mathematics Education
courses.description: Role of mathematics in society; contemporary issues in mathematics education; role of professional mathematics educator, including ethical and effective practice; social, historical, and philosophical perspectives and methods of inquiry in analysis of mathematics education issues; and sociological and psychological bases for learning mathematics.  Technologies used in teaching mathematics.
courses.offeredText: Not offered on a regular basis.

courses.subject: EMAT
courses.title: Children's Mathematical Learning
courses.description: Children's mathematical learning from pre-numerical stages through the acquisition of advanced numerical and spatial processes and operations.  Research-based development of a theory of children's learning.  Includes field component.

courses.subject: EMAT
courses.title: Mathematics Teaching and Curriculum in PreK-5th Grade
courses.description: Mathematics teaching and curriculum in preK through 5th grade.  Content and materials appropriate for preK through 5th grade mathematics curriculum is integrated with an analysis of mathematics teaching, including the use of technology.  Includes a field component.

courses.subject: EMAT
courses.title: Special Problems in Mathematics Education
courses.description: Topics in mathematics education.

courses.subject: EMAT
courses.title: Technology in Teaching Elementary School Mathematics
courses.description: Use of technological tools in teaching elementary mathematics.  Current computer software for mathematical explorations.
courses.offeredText: Not offered on a regular basis.

courses.subject: EMAT
courses.title: Mathematics Methods for PreK-Grade 8
courses.description: Content, methods, and materials appropriate for preK through 8thgrade mathematics instruction. Integration of instruction andassessment and appropriate use of technology.

courses.subject: EMAT
courses.title: Mathematics in Context
courses.description: An analysis of high school mathematics that arises in commercial and non-commercial workplace settings. Topics come from algebra, geometry, statistics, and other branches of mathematics.
courses.offeredText: Not offered on a regular basis.

courses.subject: EMAT
courses.title: Contemporary School Mathematics
courses.description: The contemporary secondary and collegiate mathematics curriculum, with an emphasis on data handling, modeling, infinite processes, stochastic processes, and discrete mathematics.
courses.offeredText: Not offered on a regular basis.

courses.subject: EMAT
courses.title: Problem Solving in Mathematics
courses.description: Mathematical problems with emphasis on exploring various mathematical contexts, on posing and extending problems, and on communicating mathematical problems and solutions.

courses.subject: EMAT
courses.title: Reasoning and Proving in Secondary Mathematics
courses.description: Investigates reasoning and proving at the middle and high school levels with an emphasis on supporting students’ capacities to reason and prove. Provides opportunities to deepen understandings of reasoning and proving across curricular topics.

courses.subject: EMAT
courses.title: Historical and Cultural Foundations of Mathematics
courses.description: Development of mathematics across time, geography, and cultures with attention to the content of school mathematics.
courses.course_objectives: Students will learn more mathematical content AND learn more mathematical content that is relevant for teaching high school and middle school students, and the cultural origins and perspectives of the content. Students will learn more effective strategies for teaching mathematics AND learn more ways to affirm students who are underrepresented in the mathematics professions by recognizing the contributions of diverse cultures to mathematics. Students will gain the necessary expertise to incorporate technological resources (e.g., WWW, interactive e-mail) into the teaching of mathematics AND gain expertise in selecting and evaluating resources that reflect diverse cultures.

courses.subject: EMAT
courses.title: Technology and Secondary School Mathematics
courses.description: Mathematical investigations appropriate to the secondary school using various technology tools.
courses.offeredText: Not offered on a regular basis.

courses.subject: EMAT
courses.title: Technology Enhanced Instruction in Secondary School Mathematics
courses.description: Use of technology in mathematics instruction and development of materials for mathematics instruction enhanced by technology.
courses.offeredText: Not offered on a regular basis.

courses.subject: EMAT
courses.title: Advanced Explorations with Technology in Mathematics Instruction
courses.description: Use of technology in mathematics instruction, with an emphasis on the organization of materials for secondary mathematics courses.
courses.course_objectives: To become familiar with and operational on MacIntosh computer systems To use application software to solve mathematics problems To use application software to create mathematics demonstrations To use application software to construct new ideas of mathematics for yourself To engage in mathematical investigations using software applications To engage in some independent investigations of mathematics topics from the secondary school curriculum or appropriate for that level To communicate mathematics ideas that arise from mathematics applications on the MacIntosh To communicate mathematics ideas via the MacIntosh applications To use general tools such as word processing, paint programs, and spreadsheets on the MacIntosh to facilitate mathematics investigations and communication about mathematics investigations
courses.topical_outline:
This course is an extension of Technology and Secondary School Mathematics and Technology Enhanced Instruction in Secondary School Mathematics. We will continue the course aims of Technology Enhanced Instruction in Secondary School Mathematics to go more depth with the use of various software applications to engage in mathematics investigations, to organize pedagogical demonstrations, and to set up problem explorations, and we will continue to emphasize the development of material that might be used with secondary school students. The change from Technology and Secondary School Mathematics and Technology Enhanced Instruction in Secondary School Mathematics is that each student, or possibly teams of students, in the course will select, develop, and carry out a major project. The students will use application software owned by the Department of Mathematics Education and will carry out the course using primarily MacIntosh computers. The emphasis is on exploration of various mathematics contexts to learn mathematics, to pose problems and problem extensions, to solve problems, and to communicate mathematical demonstrations. The following software will be used:
1. Graphing Calculator 2.3
2. Geometer's Sketchpad
3. Excel
4. xFn
5. Microsoft Word
6. Other software as needed
7. Hand-held devices Communication will be facilitated via e-mail and the course homepage, and each student should have an e-mail account. Projects/Course Requirements: Develop and carry out one major project. This must be carefully planned and approved by the instructor.
courses.offeredText: Not offered on a regular basis.

courses.subject: EMAT
courses.title: Teaching Secondary School Mathematics I
courses.description: Introductory ideas about mathematics education, including current mathematics standards and policy documents, learning theories, and teaching strategies. Students will explore how secondary students think about and learn mathematics, examine how to select and modify tasks, use appropriate technology, and apply their learning in an accompanying field experience.

courses.subject: EMAT
courses.title: Field Experience in Secondary School Mathematics I
courses.description: Students will work one-on-one with secondary school pupils toinvestigate their mathematical thinking and learn to communicatemathematically with pupils.

courses.subject: EMAT
courses.title: Connections in Secondary Mathematics I
courses.description: Explores various secondary mathematics topics with a modeling and data analysis approach and an explicit focus on ways of reasoning that connect critical concepts of secondary mathematics. A problem solving approach will be used to foster and explore topics including function, rate of change, and algebra.

courses.subject: EMAT
courses.title: Teaching Secondary School Mathematics II
courses.description: Using data to assess secondary students' learning and issues of equity in mathematics education. Students will examine various assessments and data to facilitate learning through mathematics tasks, questioning techniques, manipulatives and technology, and differentiating instruction to teach diverse student populations in a field experience.

courses.subject: EMAT
courses.title: Field Experience in Secondary School Mathematics II
courses.description: Students will work with small groups of secondary school pupilsto implement lessons and assess student learning.

courses.subject: EMAT
courses.title: Connections in Secondary Mathematics II
courses.description: Exploration of secondary mathematics topics related to number and measurement with an explicit focus on reasoning that connects critical topics of secondary mathematics to one another and to problem situations. Sample topics include proportional reasoning, number theory, and probability.

courses.subject: EMAT
courses.title: Teaching Secondary School Mathematics III
courses.description: Planning lessons and units, facilitating discourse, and applying theories of learning and teaching. Students will explore how to create plans for student learning, use culturally appropriate pedagogies, negotiate classroom norms, use instructional technology appropriately, and apply their learning in an accompanying field experience.

courses.subject: EMAT
courses.title: Field Experience in Secondary School Mathematics III
courses.description: Students will teach in whole class settings in area middle andhigh schools. They will plan and implement lessons that usediscourse strategies and technology to alleviate educationalinequities.

courses.subject: EMAT
courses.title: Connections in Secondary Mathematics III
courses.description: Exploration of various secondary mathematics topics with an explicit focus on ways of reasoning that connect critical concepts of secondary mathematics. A problem solving approach will be used to foster and explore topics including similarity, transformations, conics, linear systems, and sequences and series.

courses.subject: EMAT
courses.title: Teaching and Learning Undergraduate Mathematics
courses.description: Provides mathematics and mathematics education students with astudy of current issues in the teaching and learning ofundergraduate mathematics. Course topics will include exploringimportant ways of thinking at the undergraduate mathematicslevel. Other topics will include an overview of undergraduatepedagogies and instructional design.
courses.course_objectives: Students will understand unifying mathematical ways of thinking that connect major undergraduate mathematics topics. Students will gain knowledge of how students come to develop those ways of thinking. Students will recognize examples of student activity that illustrate those ways of thinking. Students will understand various pedagogies associated with the teaching of undergraduate mathematics. Students will analyze the affordances and constraints of the aforementioned pedagogies. Students will identify current and critical issues in the teaching and learning of undergraduate mathematics. Students will recognize the importance of improving the teaching and learning of undergraduate mathematics.
courses.topical_outline:
Unifying ways of thinking for Algebra and Precalculus:
- The role of variation
- The role of invariance
- The role of representations Unifying ways of thinking for Calculus:
- Accumulation
- Rate of change Unifying ways of thinking for Differential Equations:
- Rate of change
- Dynamical systems Unifying ways of thinking for Statistics:
- Variance
- Sampling Undergraduate mathematics pedagogies
- Traditional strategies, including lecture and recitation
models
- Alternative strategies, including online and hybrid
- TA training Current and pressing issues in the teaching and learning of
undergraduate mathematics
- Evolves with field issues

courses.title: Professional Seminar in Teaching Mathematics
courses.description: Issues identified from the student teaching experience in mathematics with consideration of various avenues for professional development.

courses.subject: EMAT
courses.title: Faculty-Mentored Undergraduate Research I
courses.description: Faculty-supervised independent or collaborative inquiry into fundamental and applied problems within a discipline that requires students to gather, analyze, synthesize, and interpret data and to present results in writing and other relevant communication formats.

courses.subject: EMAT
courses.title: Faculty-Mentored Undergraduate Research II
courses.description: Faculty-supervised independent or collaborative inquiry into fundamental and applied problems within a discipline that requires students to gather, analyze, synthesize, and interpret data and to present results in writing and other relevant communication formats.

courses.subject: EMAT
courses.title: Faculty-Mentored Undergraduate Research III
courses.description: Faculty-supervised independent or collaborative inquiry into fundamental and applied problems within a discipline that requires students to gather, analyze, synthesize, and interpret data and to present results in writing and other relevant communication formats.

courses.subject: EMAT
courses.title: Undergraduate Research Thesis (or Final Project)
courses.description: Faculty-supervised independent or collaborative inquiry into fundamental and applied problems within a discipline that requires students to gather, analyze, synthesize, and interpret data. Students will write or produce a thesis or other professional capstone product, such as a report or portfolio that describes their systematic and in-depth inquiry.

courses.subject: EMAT
courses.title: Teaching Number Systems in the Middle Grades
courses.description: A quantitative measurement approach to the study of numbersystems for middle grades mathematics. Methods of teaching numbersystems are based in students' quantitative reasoning in thecontext of using appropriate technology. Evaluation through theexamination of mathematics content, with emphasis on mathematicaloperations, models, and problem solving.
courses.prerequisiteText: MATH 2200 or MATH 2250 or MATH 2250E | Graduate Prerequisite | MATH 2200 or MATH 2250 or MATH 2250E | Undergraduate

courses.subject: EMAT
courses.title: Teaching Geometry and Measurement in the Middle Grades
courses.description: Explore middle grades mathematics topics with an explicit focuson teaching methods for developing middle grades students’ waysof reasoning about geometric, measurement, and statisticalconcepts. Examine how to select and modify tasks to meet theneeds of all students and use technology appropriately forteaching and learning.
courses.prerequisiteText: EMAT 5320/7320 or EMAT 5320E/7320E | Graduate Prerequisite | EMAT 5320/7320 or EMAT 5320E/7320E

courses.subject: EMAT
courses.title: Teaching Algebra in the Middle Grades
courses.description: A quantitative approach to the study of essential topics inmiddle grades mathematics, particularly regarding algebra andchange. A critical analysis of pedagogical methods that supportmiddle grades students’ sense making and problem solving.
courses.prerequisiteText: EMAT 5280/7280 or EMAT 5280E/7280E | Graduate Prerequisite | EMAT 5280/7280 or EMAT 5280E/7280E | Undergraduate

courses.subject: EMAT
courses.title: Student Teaching in Secondary School Mathematics
courses.description: Supervised mathematics teaching in a secondary school.
courses.course_objectives: Students will learn how to communicate to different students who learn in different ways. Students will learn how to present traditional mathematics concepts in ways that engage students. Students will learn how to use various instructional techniques for the classroom. Students will learn how to organize lessons into coherent units and courses. Students will learn how to incorporate practical applications into mathematics lessons. Students will learn how to motivate students who do not care about math. Students will learn how to manage a mathematics classroom.
courses.topical_outline: 10 weeks of supervised student teaching in mathematics (Grades 7-12), including at least 2 weeks of full-time teaching Taking initiative Learning about the school and community Meeting weekly with all student teachers and mentors in the school Visiting other classes and teachers—mathematics and other subject areas Making two videotapes of yourself and discussing them with mentor and supervisor Responding to weekly e-mail prompts Experimenting with teaching Seeking out constructive critiques
courses.prerequisiteText: EMAT 4900/6900 and EMAT 4900L/6900L and EMAT 4910/6910 | Graduate Prerequisite | EMAT 6360

courses.subject: EMAT
courses.title: Student Teaching in Secondary School Mathematics (Honors)
courses.description: Supervised mathematics teaching in a secondary school.
courses.course_objectives: Honors students will, in addition to their regular student teaching goals, learn to be critical and reflective teachers, learn to use action research to improve teaching, and learn to develop and/or refine larger curriculum units.
courses.topical_outline: Students will negotiate, in advance, with their supervising faculty member specific projects to be completed during student teaching. These projects will reflect the student's interests and areas of needed growth. Possible projects might include an action research project or the development and implementation of a curriculum unit. Students will enroll in 3 hours of honors student teaching for each project, up to a maximum of 6 hours.
courses.prerequisiteText: EMAT 4900/6900 and EMAT 4910/6910 and permission of Honors

courses.subject: EMAT
courses.title: College Mathematics Teaching Internship
courses.description: Supervised work in mathematics education in undergraduateinstructional contexts.

courses.subject: EMAT
courses.title: Pivotal Pedagogical Practice in 6-12 Mathematics I
courses.description: Exploration of current trends in mathematics teaching. Pivotal concepts include classroom discourse, teaching all students rigorous mathematics, and creating a motivating and inclusive space to do mathematics. Topics are grounded in social, historical, and philosophical perspectives on mathematics teaching and learning.
courses.course_objectives: Students will understand how to use research-based strategies to create a motivating and inclusive space to facilitate student learning in mathematics. Students will understand how to reflect on teaching practice through a research lens on classroom discourse and culture and identify areas of strengths and weaknesses of such practices. Students will understand how to use artifacts of teaching to analyze students’ classroom experiences. Students will understand how to discuss how social, historical, and philosophical perspectives influence current trends in teaching and learning.
courses.topical_outline: Brief history of mathematics teaching and learning Tools and strategies to enhance learning mathematics for all students Facilitating productive mathematical discourse Hidden biases and assumptions that influence teaching mathematics and assessing mathematics learning Planning for research-based instructional practice Creating motivating and inclusive classroom environments

courses.subject: EMAT
courses.title: Pivotal Pedagogical Practice in 6-12 Mathematics II
courses.description: Building on Pivotal Math Pedagogy I, this course is a deep exploration of students’ mathematical thinking to support their needs and success. Consideration of current state and national trends and foci in mathematical instruction. Examination of current curriculum and technology resources with appropriate connections to research and policy.
courses.course_objectives: Students will understand how to use effective technology, research-based resources, innovative teaching strategies, and knowledge of mathematics to facilitate student learning in mathematics. Students will understand how to reflect on teaching practice through a research lens on students’ mathematical thinking and identify areas of strengths and weaknesses of such practices. Students will understand how to use artifacts of teaching to analyze students’ mathematical thinking and plan for instruction.
courses.topical_outline: Selecting and teaching worthwhile mathematical tasks Tools and strategies to enhance learning mathematics for all students Recent research-based resources for teaching including technology and curricula Formative and summative assessment of mathematics learning Planning for instructional practice guided by students’ mathematical thinking

courses.subject: EMAT
courses.title: Timely Topics and Trends in Mathematics Education
courses.description: The relevance of mathematics is always evolving. This course will explore timely topics, ideas, and trends in secondary mathematics. These topics could include modeling, financial literacy, school data and assessment, discourse, and decision making. These topics, ideas, and trends will be tied to the life and practice of teachers.
courses.course_objectives: Students will understand how to identify timely topics, ideas, and trends in secondary mathematics education. Students will understand how to critically analyze timely topics, ideas, and trends in secondary mathematics education. Students will understand how to relate timely topics, ideas, and trends to the learning of secondary mathematics content. Students will understand how to connect timely topics, ideas, and trends to standards for secondary mathematics content. Students will understand how to reflect on their teaching practice in light of timely topics, ideas, and trends in secondary mathematics education.
courses.topical_outline: Specific topics will be dependent on the ideas and trends covered in the course. Introduction of the topic History of the topic Research and relevance of the topic to secondary mathematics or society Connections of the topic to classroom practice and curriculum Importance of the topic for the teaching and learning of mathematics including its use

courses.subject: EMAT
courses.title: Mathematical Knowledge for Teaching: Ratio, Proportion, and Algebraic Reasoning
courses.description: Students will examine secondary mathematics topics that include ratio, proportional reasoning, relationships to linear functions, the multiple roles of variable, making sense of equations, and the utility, types, and representations of functions. The course will review research on students’ reasoning and instructional strategies for fostering proportional and algebraic reasoning.
courses.course_objectives: Students will understand how to address and investigate basic concepts in secondary pre-algebra and algebra courses, including ratio, proportional reasoning, the different uses of variable, equations and equality, and linear, quadratic, and exponential functions. Students will understand how to engage in weekly problem-solving activities by solving ratio, proportion, and function problems. Students will understand how to review and synthesize the research literature on students’ understanding of ratio, proportion, variable, equations, and functions. Students will understand how to review and synthesize the research literature on effective instruction of ratio, proportion, variable, equations, and functions. Students will understand how to communicate and reason mathematically, make connections across representations, including tables, functions, and graphs, and develop and present justifications and proofs. Students will understand how to design and analyze tasks and activities that promote the learning of key concepts related to ratio, proportion, variable, equations, and functions. Students will understand how to use general tools such as word processing, spreadsheets, and the Internet to facilitate mathematical investigations and to communicate about mathematical investigations. Students will understand how to explore mathematics using a variety of technologies including online graphing calculators and online geometric and algebraic construction software.
courses.topical_outline: The use of variables and symbolic representations Ratios, rates, and proportions and their connections to fractions and linear functions Equality, equations, and solution techniques for solving equations Linear, quadratic, and exponential functions Research on students’ reasoning about ratio, proportion, and algebra Research on the effective instruction of ratio, proportion, and algebra Research on the use of representations and manipulatives in supporting mathematical reasoning in ratios, proportion, and algebra Best practices for enacting graphing, modeling, argumentation, and other current priority topics in the 6-12 pre-algebra and algebra classroom Connections to precalculus, calculus, and other college-level mathematical ideas

courses.subject: EMAT
courses.title: Mathematical Knowledge for Teaching: Quantitative Reasoning
courses.description: Students will explore various secondary mathematics topics including function, rate of change, and modeling. Quantitative reasoning will be explored as a connecting thread of these topics with an additional emphasis on instructional strategies for fostering and promoting secondary students’ quantitative reasoning.
courses.course_objectives: Students will understand how to engage in mathematical, epistemological, curricular, and pedagogical investigations. Students will understand how to address and investigate basic concepts in the secondary mathematics curriculum, differentiating between what is critical to a concept and what is a conventional practice. Students will understand how to reflect on the content knowledge necessary for a mathematics teacher, and the role content knowledge plays in teaching. Students will understand how to communicate and reason mathematically, engage in problem solving, investigate different representations, and make mathematical connections. Students will understand how to design and analyze instructional tasks focusing on connecting concepts and ways of reasoning. Students will understand how to use technological tools in doing, exploring, and communicating mathematics. Students will understand how to use general tools such as word processing, spreadsheets, and the Internet to facilitate mathematical investigations and to communicate about mathematical investigations. Students will understand how to use application software to solve mathematical problems, create mathematical demonstrations, and construct new ideas of mathematics.
courses.topical_outline: Amounts of change as a foundation to rate of change Different functions classes, such as linear, quadratic, cubic, logarithmic, exponential, and trigonometric Various coordinate systems and the quantities that constitute them Critical data analysis including representational practices Instructional design principles for quantitative reasoning

courses.subject: EMAT
courses.title: Mathematical Knowledge for Teaching: Geometric Reasoning
courses.description: A deep examination of geometry topics designed for secondary mathematics teachers. Pedagogical and instructional strategies will accompany investigation of concepts of geometry. Reasoning and proof will provide a foundation for geometric explorations.
courses.course_objectives: Students will understand how to use dynamic software to test conjectures and conduct geometric investigations. Students will understand how to use tools and technology to perform geometric constructions based on properties. Students will understand how to apply geometric concepts in modeling situations. Students will understand how to derive and explain geometric formulas such as area and volume. Students will understand how to prove theorems involving similarity and congruence. Students will understand how to connect Euclidean properties to coordinate geometry.
courses.topical_outline: Euclidean geometry including congruence and similarity Geometric transformations Axiomatic systems Constructions Pythagorean Theorem Measurement Connections to algebra Conjecturing, reasoning, and proof Optional extensions include fractals, tiling, robotics, and visualization

courses.subject: EMAT
courses.title: Mathematical Knowledge for Teaching: Statistical Reasoning
courses.description: Students will formulate statistical questions, collect and analyze data, and interpret results. They will develop a deep conceptual understanding of the statistics they will teach to K-12 students. A focus of the class will be dealing creatively with messy data and students’ thinking about variability and statistical processes.
courses.course_objectives: Students will understand how to formulate statistical questions, collect and analyze data, and interpret results. Students will understand how to identify variability in the world around us. Students will understand how to use technology to reformulate messy data and choose appropriate methods for analysis. Students will understand how to use the interrogative cycle to question data presented by the media or other sources. Students will understand how to interpret and discuss inference in the simple linear regression model test of independence and homogeneity. Students will understand how to design and analyze data from experiments, observations, and surveys. Students will understand how to perform statistical analysis including measuring and interpreting center and spread of a data set.
courses.topical_outline: Sample statistics and population parameters Case vs. Aggregate Descriptive statistics Confidence intervals and significance tests Statistical investigation and interrogation Comparing groups Linear regression Use of technology Statistical arguments and communication Statistical dispositions and connection to the Mathematical Practices Emerging approaches and issues in statistics and data science

courses.subject: EMAT
courses.title: Research on the Teaching and Learning of Mathematics
courses.description: Addresses how teachers can use research in mathematics education to support instruction. Using the case of a core strand of mathematics, the course examines research on how students learn mathematical ideas, common student challenges and difficulties, what is effective in supporting students’ learning, and productive pedagogical strategies for fostering mathematical thinking.
courses.course_objectives: A student who successfully completes this course will identify the unifying ideas of a mathematical strand (e.g., algebra) as enacted in the 6-12 curriculum. A student who successfully completes this course will describe and characterize how mathematical ideas (e.g., from algebra) are represented, communicated, and connected. A student who successfully completes this course will identify what research indicates about the strategies, representations, and communication methods teachers can use to support their students’ understanding of mathematical (e.g., algebraic) ideas. A student who successfully completes this course will identify key shifts students make in their understanding of mathematical (e.g., algebraic) concepts. A student who successfully completes this course will identify and address the conceptions and difficulties students demonstrate with mathematical (e.g., algebraic) ideas.
courses.topical_outline: General research on mathematical (e.g., algebra and algebraic) reasoning The use of literal symbols and symbolic representations in particular mathematical topics Research on students’ understanding of important aspects of ideas in the mathematical strand Research on the use of representations and manipulatives in supporting mathematical reasoning Students’ abilities and research on patterns and generalization as appropriate to their understanding of mathematical ideas Students’ understanding of proportional reasoning and research on effective ways to foster proportional reasoning Instruction of the big ideas undergirding the mathematical strand (e.g., for algebra, function families, including linear, quadratic, exponential, and higher-order polynomial and other functions) Best practices for enacting graphing and modeling and other current priority topics in the 6-12 algebra classroom Connections to precalculus, calculus, and other college level mathematical ideas

courses.subject: EMAT
courses.title: National Trends in STEM Education
courses.description: An examination of trends and issues in STEM education from historical and current perspectives. National, state, and local concerns regarding public education, changing demographics in schools, curriculum standards, teaching, and professionalism will be studied. Students will critically examine persistent problems in middle and high school STEM education and determine promising solutions.
courses.course_objectives: A student who successfully completes this course will critically examine and understand selected issues and trends. A student who successfully completes this course will identify and understand persistent and current issues related to STEM education and schooling. A student who successfully completes this course will examine recent changes in STEM education associated with national, state, and local initiatives. A student who successfully completes this course will develop an inclusive view of equity and diversity in STEM education to include issues of race, gender, culture, language, SES, disability, sexual orientation, and differentiated learning. A student who successfully completes this course will develop an informed opinion based on new information, data, and experiences with issues pertaining to the STEM education of each and every student. A student who successfully completes this course will identify and investigate a current trend or issue in STEM education and explore its implications for STEM teaching, learning, and research. A student who successfully completes this course will participate in a STEM teaching and learning community. A student who successfully completes this course will consider ways to create and guide a rigorous and appropriate STEM learning environment for students.
courses.topical_outline:
History of STEM Education National Standards for Mathematics and Science Current Trends and Issues:
o The Corporate Reform Movement: Public, Private, and Charter Schools
o Tests, Testing, and Achievement Gaps
o Opportunity Gaps and Poverty
o Teacher Effectiveness
o Teaching by Tracks: Block Scheduling, Advanced Placement, Dual Enrollment, Remedial Support, Online Courses Promising Solutions:
o Motivation and Positive STEM Identities
o Solutions: Classrooms Structures
o Solutions: School Structures: Access and Equity in STEM

courses.title: Geometry and Problem Solving
courses.description: A deep examination of mathematical topics designed for future elementary school teachers. Length, area, and volume. Geometric shapes and their properties. Probability. Elementary number theory. Applications of elementary mathematics.
courses.course_objectives: To strengthen and deepen knowledge and understanding of measurement, basic geometry, elementary probability, and some elementary number theory and how they are used to solve a wide variety of problems In particular, to strengthen the understanding of and the ability to explain why various procedures and formulas in mathematics work To strengthen the ability to communicate clearly about mathematics, both orally and in writing To promote the exploration and explanation of mathematical phenomena To show that many problems can be solved in a variety of ways
courses.topical_outline: Geometry and measurement: Length, area, and volume, and the fundamental principles that govern them; Understanding why various formulas for areas and volumes work; The relationship between perimeter and area; Measurement in different units and scaling; Basic geometric shapes and their properties, including the Pythagorean Theorem (for right triangles) and the sum of the angles in triangles; Constructions with straightedge and compass; Angles; Symmetry; Congruence and similarity, including applications to measurement; Platonic solids Probability: Understanding and calculating probability, including conditional probability; Combinations and Pascal's triangle Number Theory: Greatest common divisor and least common multiple; Prime numbers; Decimal representations of rational and irrational numbers; Irrationality of the square root of 2

courses.subject: EMAT
courses.title: Algebra and Problem Solving
courses.description: A deep examination of topics in mathematics that are relevant for elementary school teaching. Probability, number theory, algebra and functions, including ratio and proportion. Posing and modifying problems.
courses.course_objectives: To strengthen and deepen knowledge and understanding of probability, elementary number theory and algebra, and how they are used to solve a wide variety of problems In particular, to strengthen the understanding of and the ability to explain why various procedures and formulas in mathematics work To strengthen the ability to communicate clearly about mathematics, both orally and in writing To promote the exploration and explanation of mathematical phenomena To show that many problems can be solved in a variety of ways; To learn to pose and modify mathematical problems
courses.topical_outline: Probability: Understanding and calculating probability, including conditional probability; Combinations and Pascal's triangle; Expected value Number Theory: Greatest common divisor and least common multiple; Prime numbers; Divisibility tests; Decimal representations of rational and irrational numbers; Irrationality of the square root of 2 Algebra and functions, including ratio and proportion as part of the study of linear functions; Applications of ratio and proportion, such as adjusting for inflation with the Consumer Price Index The course will emphasize solving a wide range of problems as well as posing and modifying problems; Computer technology will be used

courses.description: Students will reflect on their graduate program to identify, analyze, and discuss the main learning goals for the program. They will continue to consider these ideas in order to transform them in ways that they can incorporate into and impact their practice. The course includes a capstone project.
courses.course_objectives: Students will understand how to identify key ideas and concepts constituting their graduate program experience. Students will understand how to critically analyze, connect, compare, and contrast key ideas and concepts constituting their graduate program experience. Students will understand how to relate key ideas and concepts constituting their graduate program experience to the learning of mathematics. Students will understand how to relate key ideas and concepts constituting their graduate program experience to standards for secondary mathematics content. Students will understand how to reflect on their teaching practice in light of key ideas and concepts constituting their graduate program experience to standards for secondary mathematics content. Students will understand how to identify key reflective practices for continuous learning and development as teachers.

courses.subject: EMAT
courses.title: Mentoring in Mathematics Education
courses.description: Theories and practices needed to guide mathematics teachers atall educational levels to improve their teaching practices.Perspectives on content-focused mentoring for pre-service andin-service mathematics teaching.  Mathematical, psychological,pedagogical, and curricular foundations for coaching effectivemathematics instruction.  Strategies for developing aconstructive, collaborative approach to helping mathematicsteachers improve.
courses.course_objectives: Deepen their understanding of, and commitment to, effective mentoring in mathematics education. Be able to locate, analyze, and use relevant literature and resources to strengthen their theoretical and practical readiness for mentoring other mathematics teachers. Understand roles and strategies for helping mathematics teachers to change their teaching practices. Be able to apply mentoring processes within simulated situations. Complete initial preparations and plans for their mentoring internship.
courses.topical_outline:
Objective 1
a. Establishing the needs and potential benefits related to an effective program of mentoring in mathematics education
b. Building a positive philosophy for “teachers coaching other teachers”
c. Examining the nature of an effective mentoring relationship as a partnership for professional development in mathematics education Objective 2
a. Identifying and studying appropriate literature that provides relevant information for effective mentoring in mathematics education
b. Identifying and studying resources to support mentoring mathematics teachers
c. Examining the dimensions, variables, and factors that might affect the mentoring situation and its outcomes
d. Studying relevant recommendations from professional societies
e. Reviewing research related to teacher change and to improved mathematics teaching and learning Objective 3
a. Characterizing high quality mathematics teaching and learning, and a standards-based mathematics curriculum and assessment program
b. Roles for a mathematics teaching mentor
c. Improving the teacher’s knowledge for improved teaching, including mathematics, psychology of learning, mathematics curriculum, assessment, and classroom pedagogical knowledge
d. Assisting a mathematics teacher to assess their own needs and practices, and indicators of professional growth and improvement of teaching and learning Objective 4
a. Reviewing models (e.g., video examples) of effective mentoring in mathematics teaching
b. Addressing specific scenarios of teachers needing and wanting to improve their teaching of particular mathematical topics
c. Developing a variety of coaching strategies to stimulate and support teachers in their teaching of particular mathematical topics Objective 5
a. Communicating with a colleague to develop a coaching partnership situation that could serve as an internship in mentoring
b. Planning and developing the particular foci for the coaching partnership that will later serve as the internship in mentoring
c. Securing institutional permissions and commitments for the internship situation

courses.title: Strategic Management
courses.description: Traditional corporate strategy combined with principles oflarge-scale organizational change to produce an overview ofstrategic management as a process for adapting the firm to itschanging environment.  Topics include practical issues related tomental frameworks and human behavior, environmental andcompetitor analysis, and change implementation.
courses.course_objectives: Course seeks to develop students' capacity to think strategically about a company, its business position, how it can gain sustainable competitive advantage, and how its strategy can be implemented and executed successfully. Course builds students' skills in conducting strategic analysis in a variety of industries and competitive situations and provides a strong understanding of the competitive challenges of a global market environment. Course gives students hands-on experience in crafting business strategy, reasoning carefully about strategic options, using what-if analysis to evaluate action alternatives, and making strategic decisions that can be implemented successfully. Course should also improve students' ability to manage the organizational processes by which strategies get formed and executed, and build confidence in being able to perform the tasks of a strategy-maker and strategy-implementer. Course hones managerial judgment in assessing business risks and improves students' ability to create results-oriented action plans.

courses.subject: EMBA
courses.title: Change Management
courses.description: Course explores theories, frameworks, practical interventions, and best practices associated with successfully designing, implementing, and institutionalizing organizational change, and studies rapidly changing global marketplace companies with a “change ready” culture and related capabilities who are positioned to thrive while others are at risk.
courses.course_objectives: Students will be able to identify factors contributing to the rapid pace of change in today’s business environment. Students will be able to list multiple reasons employees may not readily embrace change. Students will be able to select tactics and techniques to increase employee openness to change. Students will be able to identify and describe theories, interventions, and/or models associated with organizational change. Students will be able to create and detail an organizational intervention to address a specific challenge and/or opportunity relevant to their employer, business, and/or industry.
courses.topical_outline: In today’s dynamic, rapidly changing global marketplace, companies with a “change ready” culture and related capabilities are positioned to thrive while others are at risk. Accordingly, professionals who can lead major change within their organizations are well positioned for prosperous careers. To this end, this graduate-level course explores theories, frameworks, practical interventions, and best practices associated with successfully designing, implementing, and institutionalizing organizational change. The course is dynamic in that it weaves a high degree of student interaction, group exercises, expert speakers, and practical assignments to achieve the learning outcomes of the course.

courses.course_objectives: By the end of this course, students will have learned critical language to interrogate contemporary entertainment media, especially issues of visual media texts and storytelling. By the end of this course, students will have learned about issues of textual form, economic contexts, historical antecedents, and cultural/ideological discourses for understanding contemporary entertainment media. By the end of this course, students will have a theoretical language drawn from the field of media studies and media literacy, which will inform subsequent coursework in the Entertainment and Media Studies Department.

courses.subject: EMST
courses.title: Writing for Entertainment Media
courses.description: In this introductory writing course, students learn narrative structure, writing, and storytelling for visual entertainment media. Students are required to write and workshop documents and short scripts both in groups and individually.
courses.course_objectives: Upon completing this course, students will be able to develop script writing conventions and formats (such as master scene format, dual column format, beat sheets, and treatments). Upon completing this course, students will be able to draft a short script that can be used in future Entertainment and Media Studies courses. Upon completing this course, students will be able to execute the process of creative production, from brainstorming, drafting, and receiving critiques. Upon completing this course, students will be able to master writing in active voice. Upon completing this course, students will be able to demonstrate the basic premises of narrative theory and structure and be capable of applying that structure to a variety of visual media.
courses.topical_outline: 1. Narrative structure for visual media 2. Finding/developing good stories 3. Characterization and character development 4. Story development documentation 5. Short form script writing 6. The art of giving and receiving notes and rewriting
courses.prerequisiteText: (EMST 3010 or EMST 3010H) and permission of major

By the end of the semester, students will cultivate the habit of keeping up with industry news and developments.

courses.subject: EMST
courses.title: Production Basics
courses.description: Methods of visual storytelling that include structural elements  pre-production, production, and postproduction for entertainment media. Emerging methods and concepts for visual storytelling.
courses.course_objectives: Students will demonstrate knowledge of how to translate an original, student-written short screenplay into a visual story. Students will demonstrate knowledge and practice of preproduction, production, and postproduction. Students will demonstrate knowledge of proper and professional use of production equipment, including but not limited to pre-production, budgeting, set protocol, location safety, basic sound recording, basic camera usage, and basic editing. Students will demonstrate knowledge of the use of proper production terminology. Students will demonstrate knowledge and practice of production team etiquette, protocol, and organization. Students will demonstrate knowledge of proper production paperwork, including but not limited to storyboards, cast/crew calls, location releases, shot logs, batch lists, shooting scripts, budgets, and invoices.
courses.topical_outline: 1. On-set protocol and professionalism 2. Professional paperwork and front office procedures 3. Production workflow 4. Sound recording and design 5. Lighting design 6. Safety procedures and team dynamics 7. Post-production techniques, team dynamics, and finishing 8. Production department hierarchies and responsibilities
courses.prerequisiteText: (EMST 3110 or EMST 3110H) and EMST 3150 and permission of major

courses.description: Strategies of critical analysis of entertainment media as artistic, scholarly, and professional practice. Students will learn the language of visual analysis and components of media aesthetics as they apply to a variety of entertainment media and will discuss visual media literacy, meaning, and interpretation as analytical viewing practices.
courses.course_objectives: Upon completing this course, student will be conversant in the basic vocabulary of visual media components, including cinematography, editing, sound, and mise-en-scène. Upon completing this course, student will be able to apply critical and/or theoretical frameworks to the analysis of genre, form, and media across platforms and in western and non-western contexts. Upon completing this course, student will describe, interpret, and analyze visual media and connect aesthetic form to cultural and thematic meaning.
courses.topical_outline: 1. Analysis of visual media 2. Visual media literacy and interpretation 3. Genre and theme 4. Film and television aesthetic styles 5. Western and global form and style 6. Digital media and video games
courses.prerequisiteText: (EMST 3110 or EMST 3110H) and EMST 3150 and permission of major

courses.subject: EMST
courses.title: WWII Documentary Filmmaking
courses.description: Provides students an experiential learning opportunity by participating in the film production as a crew member. Students and WWII Foundation’s production team will visit important landmarks in WWII history to shoot a documentary film. Also, all participants will complete their own short documentary after the trip.
courses.course_objectives: Students will be able to understand the storytelling structure and techniques for documentary films. Students will be able to demonstrate the skills and techniques of a documentary film shoot: Directing, camera operation, audio recording, and editing as a production crew member. Students will be able to comprehend the documentary film production processes including pre-production, production, and post-production as a creator of a short documentary.
courses.topical_outline:
Pre-Travel Meetings
1.  Orientation: Overview, Itinerary, Introducing WWII Foundation’s summer project
2.  Group Session: Organizing group, developing a story, assigning roles
3.  Workshop: documentary filmmaking Travel and Production
1.  Daily Meeting
a.  Students are required to participate in the daily meeting in the morning.
b.  Before/during breakfast to discuss the daily shooting schedule
c.  Students will be assigned specific roles and assignments of the day such as shooting a b-cam for the interview, collecting b-roll footages in the certain area/location, assisting WWII Foundation production crew. Shooting as a Crew Member
1.  All students will experience documentary field production by shadowing and observing the WWII production. Students also will be assigned with collaboration of the program director to shoot certain footage by the director of the WWII Foundation.
2.  Students will perform their roles during the shoot.
3.  Students will communicate with the program director and the WWII Foundation production crew to successfully complete their roles. Shooting as a Group Member
1.  A group of students (3-4 students in each group) will create their own documentary films during the travel. Each group will develop their own story, shoot, and edit a short documentary film (10-15 minutes). Students will utilize the WWII Foundation’s resources – local history, locations, interviewees, logistics and production schedule. Pre-Travel Meeting (Pre-Production). Post-Travel Meeting
1.  Students will screen and discuss the group project.
2.  The program director will give feedback for each project and post-production process.

courses.title: Directing I
courses.description: Analysis and practice of directing narrative film and episodic television using the single camera shooting style. courses.subject: EMST
courses.title: Directing II

courses.subject: EMST
courses.title: Cinematography I
courses.description: A hands-on course that trains students in the aesthetic and technical aspects of camera and lighting for episodic television and narrative film production. Students will be exposed to a variety of lighting and camera styles and the instruments and equipment used to plan and execute them.
courses.course_objectives: This is an intensive, hands-on course that examines the technology and aesthetics of lighting and motion picture camera work, as well as the techniques, the thought processes, and the methodology of how a scene gets lit, made ready to shoot, and shot. Students will complete weekly camera and lighting exercises, with an emphasis on understanding the relationship between time, budget, and working efficiently with each department of a production crew.
courses.topical_outline:
Fundamentals of Lighting: An exploration of the process, requirements, and tools of the lighting process. Special emphasis on quality of light, direction relative to subject, and fill ratios. Exposure Theory: An examination, through shooting exercises and tests, of film/sensor response to light, brightness perception, ISO/ASA speeds, and lighting source distance. Basic Scene Lighting: Analysis and practice of three- and five-point lighting, contrast, mood, and genre lighting. Composition and Shot Size: An examination of aspect ratios, frame axes, camera angles, depth cues, and focal points. These principles will be taught through in-class execution of wide, medium, and close up shots. Dynamic Range and Contrast Ratios: Discussion of various cameras and sensors and their ability to handle a wide range of brightness in a scene followed by testing and in-class exercises. Special emphasis on the minimum amount of light a camera needs, highlights, and gamma and knee settings. Camera Placement and Camera Movement: Classroom shooting exercises that explore how to manipulate time, space, and aesthetic distance through camera movement and camera placement.
Special emphasis on how the camera impacts narrative meaning. Color Theory: An analysis of hue, value, and color temperature and their narrative impact on story and the
emotional response of the audience. Color mixing and stylistic choices in color control will also be explored.

courses.subject: EMST
courses.title: Cinematography II
courses.description: Builds on Camera and Lighting I, focusing on broadening the understanding and execution of the aesthetic and technical practices of motion picture cinematography. The cinematographer as the leader of the camera department and grip and electric departments is also examined.
courses.course_objectives: This course is built upon an integrated approach to understanding and applying advanced camera and lighting concepts through praxis. Students will apply the principles of lighting and camera taught in Cinematography I through class exercises and short films outside of class in preparation for the MFA Thesis in film.
courses.topical_outline: Grip and Electricity: An exploration of light controls, flags and cutters, diffusers and holding clamps, as well as electrical supply systems, power sources, distribution equipment, and electrical safety. Painting with Light: An examination of mood, full range of tones, color control, and color balance, as well as quality of light and relative size of radiating sources and lenses. Understanding Lenses: A survey of focal length, field of view, lens speed, depth of field, and the impact these have on image, light, and the perspective of the viewer. Special emphasis on the relationship between lens choice and story. Light Meters and Gray Scale: An analysis of foot candles, sensors, f and t stops, and how the use of a gray card impacts color balance and exposure during production and post-production. Filtration and Gels: An examination of color balance and color temperature and its impact on image, mood, and story. Correcting light balance will also be discussed and practiced through in-class shooting and testing. Dollies and Tracking: An analysis of how the physical movement of the camera with a constant focal length changes the perspective of composition and audience emotion. Motivated camera movement will be practiced through exercises where the camera follows alongside, in front of, and behind subjects. The Team and Set Operations: An exploration of how the director of photography leads the camera and grip and electric departments while seamlessly working with other departments in pre-production and production. The process of blocking, rehearsing, lighting, and shooting will also be explored.

Students will synthesize interdisciplinary insights gained from speaker presentations to enrich their understanding of complex educational issues and inform their own research practices. Students will enhance their skills in professional engagement by interacting with invited speakers and through scholarly presentation, posing insightful questions, and articulating thoughtful responses during seminar discussions.
courses.topical_outline: Overview of the seminar topic and its theoretical relevance in the field Selection and application of research methodology for the seminar topic Specific discussion of transformative applications to engineering education practice

courses.course_objectives: Students will critically analyze and synthesize advanced theories, methodologies, and findings related to the special topic, demonstrating an ability to integrate interdisciplinary perspectives and articulate well-informed insights. Students will describe the necessary process design and conduct a research project or applied study that addresses a complex issue within the scope of the special topic, employing appropriate methodologies and presenting findings in a professional format. Students will effectively communicate complex ideas related to the special topic and collaborate with peers to solve problems, lead discussions, and present findings, fostering a deeper understanding of the topic through diverse viewpoints and teamwork.
courses.topical_outline:
I. Overview of the special topic and its relevance in the field

a. Key theories, models, and concepts
b. Interdisciplinary connections and their implications II. Advanced Methodologies and Analytical Techniques

a. Research methods and tools specific to the special topic
b. Critical approaches to data analysis and interpretation
c. Ethical considerations in research and application III. Case Studies and Applied Examples

a. Examination of real-world applications or case studies
b. Critical evaluation of successes and challenges
c. Lessons learned and their broader implications IV. Research and Project Development

a. Designing a research or applied project
b. Proposal writing and methodological justification
c. Execution and documentation of findings V. Collaboration, Communication, and Future Directions

a. Collaborative activities: group discussions, debates, or peer reviews
b. Exploring future trends, open questions, and implications for the field
