courses.prerequisiteText: Second year and above student standing

courses.subject: EPID
courses.title: Epidemiological Aspects of Global Health Problems
courses.description: Introductory overview of public health problems.  A survey of abroad range of public health problems facing the developing worldand an exploration of a variety of possible solutions.  Thiscourse is uniquely suited for students interested in studyingabroad or volunteering in the global community.

courses.subject: EPID
courses.title: Faculty-Mentored Undergraduate Research I
courses.description: Faculty-supervised independent or collaborative inquiry into fundamental and applied problems within a discipline that requires students to gather, analyze, and synthesize and interpret data and to present results in writing and other relevant communication formats.

courses.subject: EPID
courses.title: Faculty-Mentored Undergraduate Research II
courses.description: Faculty-supervised independent or collaborative inquiry into fundamental and applied problems within a discipline that requires students to gather, analyze, and synthesize and interpret data and to present results in writing and other relevant communication formats.

courses.subject: EPID
courses.title: Faculty-Mentored Undergraduate Research III
courses.description: Faculty-supervised independent or collaborative inquiry into fundamental and applied problems within a discipline that requires students to gather, analyze, and synthesize and interpret data and to present results in writing and other relevant communication formats.

courses.subject: EPID
courses.title: Undergraduate Research Thesis (or Final Project)
courses.description: Faculty-supervised independent or collaborative inquiry into fundamental and applied problems within a discipline that requires students to gather, analyze, and synthesize and interpret data. Students will write or produce a thesis or other professional capstone product, such as a report or portfolio that describes their systematic and in-depth inquiry.

courses.subject: EPID
courses.title: Master's Research
courses.description: Research while enrolled for a master's degree under the direction of a faculty member.

courses.subject: EPID
courses.title: Graduate Student Seminar
courses.description: Advanced supervised experience in an applied setting.  This course may not be used to satisfy a student's approved program of study.

courses.subject: EPID
courses.title: Fundamentals of Epidemiology
courses.description: Introduction of principles and methods of epidemiology,emphasizing study design.  Measures of morbidity and mortality,data sources, observational and experimental designs, datainterpretation, quantitative methods to determine riskassociations, controlling for confounding factors, andapplications of epidemiology will be covered.  Community health,environmental epidemiology, infectious, noninfectious and chronicdisease epidemiology are considered.

courses.subject: EPID
courses.title: Fundamentals of Epidemiology
courses.description: Principles and methods of epidemiology, emphasizing study design. Measures of morbidity and mortality, data sources, observational and experimental designs, data interpretation, quantitative methods for risk associations, controlling for confounding factors, and applications of epidemiology will be covered. Community health, environmental epidemiology, infectious, noninfectious and chronic disease epidemiology are considered.

courses.subject: EPID
courses.title: Introduction to Epidemiology II
courses.description: Strategies for investigation of etiologic hypotheses, includingstudy design, data collection, quantitative assessment andcontrol of confounding and other biases, evaluation of effectmodification, and interpretation and reporting of study resultswill be covered in detail. Topics will include analysis of datafrom cross-sectional, case-control, and cohort study designs.

courses.subject: EPID
courses.title: Introduction to Epidemiology II
courses.description: Students will develop an understanding of the theoretical basis and practical tools of epidemiologic research. Strategies for investigation of etiologic hypotheses, including study design, data collection, quantitative assessment and control of confounding and other biases; evaluation of effect modification and interpretation and reporting of study results will be covered in detail.
courses.offeredText: Offered every year. Offered every even-numbered year. Offered every odd-numbered year.

courses.subject: EPID
courses.title: Current Topics in Epidemiology
courses.description: Current topics in epidemiology. The course will consist of presentations given by faculty to discuss their current research, and discussion of important recent papers from the primary research literature.

courses.subject: EPID
courses.title: Epidemiological Aspects of Health Disparities
courses.description: Introductory survey of the growing problem of racial and ethnic disparities in health and health care facing the public health and health care systems in the United States. Reviews a number of topics and challenges students to think critically about them.

courses.subject: EPID
courses.title: Introduction to Coding for Public Health
courses.description: Introduction to several commonly used programming languages used in public health research and practice.
courses.course_objectives: Students will be able to perform public health coding and data analysis tasks using reproducible, efficient, automated, and documented workflow. Students will be able to apply appropriate statistical analysis methods to the data. Students will be able to generate figures and tables that convey results and conclusions based on statistical analysis results and audience needs. Students will be able to assess the strengths and weaknesses of different programing languages for a given task.
courses.topical_outline: Overview of programming for public health Installing and running R and SAS Principles of reproducible workflows Common variable and data structures Data importing Data cleaning Data exploration Generating figures and tables Basic statistical analysis of data Common programming workflows and algorithms Further applied topics of coding in public health
courses.prerequisiteText: Enrolled in the MPH or MS or PhD in Epidemiology and Biostatistics or permission of department

courses.subject: EPID
courses.title: Introduction to Coding for Public Health
courses.description: Introduction to several commonly used programming languages used in public health research and practice.
courses.course_objectives: Students will be able to install and update software on their computers. Students will be able to proficiently load data and perform initial exploratory data analyses. Students will be able to perform common public health coding and data analysis tasks using reproducible, efficient, automated, and documented workflow. Students will be able to apply appropriate common statistical analysis methods to the data. Students will be able to generate high-quality figures and tables that properly convey results and conclusions based on statistical analysis results and audience needs. Students will be able to assess the strengths and weaknesses of different programing languages and choose the appropriate one for a given task.
courses.topical_outline: Overview of programming for public health Installing and running R and SAS Principles of reproducible workflows Common variable and data structures Data importing Data cleaning Data exploration Generating figures and tables Basic statistical analysis of data Common programming workflows and algorithms Further applied topics of coding in public health
courses.prerequisiteText: Enrolled in the MPH or MS or PhD in Epidemiology and Biostatistics or permission of department

courses.subject: EPID
courses.title: Principles and Methods of Field Epidemiology I
courses.description: Course provides cross-cutting competencies needed to practice as an epidemiologist. Topics covered include outbreak and cluster investigations, proper analysis of outbreak data, and communication of findings. In covering these areas, students will use and enhance competencies in epidemiologic investigations, data management, survey analysis, and public health communication.
courses.course_objectives: Studenta will integrate scientific knowledge from diverse sources in the planning and conduct of field investigations. Students will demonstrate knowledge of the basic principles of human biology, disease pathology, and its related social determinants of health in the development of a field investigation. Students will describe the key phases of planning and conducting an outbreak or cluster investigation and define the key aims of the investigation. Students will critically assess survey data collection instruments, apply best practices for data entry, and use data management techniques to analyze data from a field investigation or surveillance data. Students will conduct analysis and develop inferences supported by the study findings including the use of appropriate statistical methods. Students will communicate public health information in a clear and concise manner to lay audiences with diverse health literacy levels and policymakers.
courses.topical_outline: Surveillance Defining an outbreak Planning and conducting an outbreak investigation Survey Design Outbreak Data Analysis and Reporting Tools for field investigations

courses.subject: EPID
courses.title: Principles and Methods of Field Epidemiology I
courses.description: Course provides cross-cutting competencies needed to practice as an epidemiologist. Topics covered include outbreak and cluster investigations, proper analysis of outbreak data, and communication of findings. In covering these areas, students will use and enhance competencies in epidemiologic investigations, data management, survey analysis, and public health communication.
courses.course_objectives: Students will integrate scientific knowledge from diverse sources in the planning and conduct of field investigations. Students will demonstrate knowledge of the basic principles of human biology, disease pathology, and its related social determinants of health in the development of a field investigation. Students will explain the key phases of planning and conducting an outbreak or cluster investigation and define the key aims of the investigation. Students will critically assess survey data collection instruments, apply best practices for data entry, and use data management techniques to analyze data from a field investigation or surveillance data. Students will conduct analysis and develop inferences supported by the study findings including the use of appropriate statistical methods. Students will communicate public health information in a clear and concise manner to lay audiences with diverse health literacy levels and policymakers.
courses.topical_outline: Surveillance Defining an outbreak Planning and conducting an outbreak investigation Survey Design Outbreak Data Analysis and Reporting Tools for field investigations
courses.prerequisiteText: EPID 7010 or EPID 7010E or permission of department

courses.subject: EPID
courses.title: Principles and Methods of Field Epidemiology II
courses.description: Concepts and methods of field epidemiology. These methods are utilized in the context of outbreak investigations, community health assessments, and disaster response. The practical application of epidemiologic concepts to solve public health problems will be emphasized.

courses.subject: EPID
courses.title: Public Health Surveillance
courses.description: An introduction to public health surveillance and its history, purposes and objectives, activities, elements, data sources, models, actions, reports, evaluation, and ethical and legal issues.
courses.prerequisiteText: EPID 7010 or EPID 7010E or permission of department

courses.subject: EPID
courses.title: Public Health Surveillance
courses.description: An introduction to public health surveillance and its history, purposes and objectives, activities, elements, data sources, models, actions, reports, evaluation, and ethical and legal issues.
courses.prerequisiteText: EPID 7010 or EPID 7010E or permission of department

courses.subject: EPID
courses.title: Introduction to Coding in R, Data Science and Simulation for Public Health and the Life Sciences
courses.description: Introduction to programing in R with a focus on data analysis, visualization, and simulation. Students will learn to examine data and think algorithmically, as well as develop intuition for key study design and statistical concepts.
courses.prerequisiteText: BIOS 7010 or BIOS 7010E or permission of department

courses.subject: EPID
courses.title: Reproductive and Perinatal Epidemiology for Public Health Practice
courses.description: The epidemiology of major reproductive and perinatal outcomes, with particular emphasis on current research, controversial issues, methodologic approaches, and public health practice, including policies; programs; and behavioral, screening, and treatment interventions.
courses.prerequisiteText: EPID 7010 or EPID 7010E or permission of department

courses.subject: EPID
courses.title: Adolescent Health
courses.description: Adolescence is characterized by marked physical, cognitive, social, and emotional changes that impact adult health. Focus is on the epidemiology of major health issues and outcomes among adolescents, with particular emphasis on current research, controversial issues, methodologic approaches, and public health practice, including policies, programs, and prevention and treatment interventions.
courses.course_objectives: Students will be able to evaluate the public health impact of adolescent health outcomes. Students will know how to examine epidemiologic trends in adolescent health. Students will be able to describe biologic and physiologic aspects of adolescent development and adolescent health outcomes. Students will be able to assess the contribution of sociodemographic, behavioral, and biologic risk factors to adolescent health outcomes and explain potential mechanisms. Students will be able to synthesize major concepts of adolescent health epidemiology, including theories, important outcomes and exposures and their measurement, and methodologic challenges related to research design and interpretation and evaluation of public health interventions. Students will be able to appraise strengths and limitations of different forms of evidence, tools, and systems used to measure and monitor adolescent health. Students will be able to critically evaluate epidemiologic research and findings about selected adolescent health outcomes. Students will be able to analyze economic, social, and political issues influencing development and implementation of public health practice measures that address adolescent health. Students will be able to demonstrate competence in applying epidemiologic findings to public health policies, programs, and controversies.
courses.topical_outline: Adolescent brain development Adolescent biopsychosocial development Family, peer, and romantic relationships in adolescence Public health approaches in adolescent health Adolescent alcohol, tobacco, and substance use Eating behaviors, physical activity, and obesity Adolescent sexual behavior and sexual education HIV, sexually transmitted infections, and pregnancy Mental health and suicide Adolescent violence and injury Incarcerated youth Sexual and gender minority adolescents Legal and ethical issues in adolescent healthcare and research
courses.prerequisiteText: EPID 7010 or EPID 7010E or permission of department

courses.subject: EPID
courses.title: Public Health and Healthcare Ethics
courses.description: Survey of ethical issues facing healthcare providers in the United States and the public health system. Students will be required to think critically about ethical issues in health care today, analyze complex situations, develop a personal position, and will be active participants leading weekly discussions from the reading.

courses.subject: EPID
courses.title: Fundamentals of Public Health Ethics
courses.description: An introduction to ethical issues with a focus on public health research.

courses.subject: EPID
courses.title: Cohort Study Design, Implementation, and Analysis
courses.description: The conceptual framework for cohort studies, their conduct, basic concepts of time, exposure, and outcome. Analytic methods covered in the course will include analysis of age, period, and cohort effects, analysis of incidence rates, analysis of repeated measures, and analysis of time-to-event data.
courses.prerequisiteText: EPID 7010 or EPID 7020 or BIOS 7010 or BIOS 7020

courses.subject: EPID
courses.title: Case-Control Study Design, Implementation, and Analysis
courses.description: The conceptual framework for case-control studies, their conduct, basic concepts of time, exposure, and case and control selection. Analytic methods covered in the course will include contingency tables to assess confounding and effect modification, assessment of bias and logistic regression methods.

courses.subject: EPID
courses.title: Epidemiology Teaching Practicum
courses.description: Designed for doctoral students to develop and practice teaching skills in epidemiology. Under faculty supervision, students will develop a syllabus, choose textbooks, develop lectures, prepare and grade homework, write and grade exams, and hold office hours. Students will be mentored to develop a personal teaching style.

courses.subject: EPID
courses.title: Clinical Trial Methods, Implementation, and Analysis
courses.description: The conceptual framework for design and implementation of intervention studies. A detailed understanding of experimental design options; methods of randomization; blinding; developing interventions and controls; measuring outcomes and adverse effects; follow-up; compliance and ethical issues pertinent to clinical trials will be emphasized.

courses.subject: EPID
courses.title: Causal Inference in Epidemiology
courses.description: Teaches advanced epidemiology students to synthesize biologic content, epidemiologic designs, and statistical analysis into a coherent research plan.  The didactic portion of the course will cover causality in epidemiology, scientific method, including hypothesis testing and interval estimation, sample size estimation, sampling strategies, and advanced regression models.

courses.subject: EPID
courses.title: Clinical Epidemiology and Evidence-Based Practice
courses.description: Principles of clinical epidemiology and their application to healthcare settings. Topics will include critical appraisal of the medical literature, diagnosis, screening and prevention, therapy, prognosis, systematic review and meta-analysis, basic decision and cost-utility analysis, and clinical decision rules.

courses.subject: EPID
courses.title: Digital Tools and Technologies for Public Health Research and Practice
courses.description: Provides a comprehensive overview of key concepts in digital health, mobile and eHealth, and the use of digital technologies for public health research and practice. Topics will include using digital tools for participant recruitment, data collection, research and intervention implementation and disease surveillance, and data visualization and dissemination.
courses.prerequisiteText: EPID 7010 or EPID 7010E or permission of department

courses.subject: EPID
courses.title: Screening and Prevention
courses.description: Topics of primary prevention, secondary prevention, and tertiary prevention in the public health and clinical setting. The instructor has served on the U.S. Preventive Services Task Force (USPSTF), the group that makes recommendations for preventive services at the federal level. Topics include cancer screening, cardiovascular prevention, and prevention at the community level.
courses.prerequisiteText: EPID 7010 or EPID 7010E or permission of department

courses.subject: EPID
courses.title: Screening and Prevention
courses.description: Topics of primary prevention, secondary prevention, and tertiary prevention in the public health and clinical setting. The instructor has served on the U.S. Preventive Services Task Force (USPSTF), the group that makes recommendations for preventive services at the federal level. Topics include cancer screening, cardiovascular prevention, and prevention at the community level.
courses.prerequisiteText: EPID 7010 or EPID 7010E or permission of department

courses.subject: EPID
courses.title: Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analysis
courses.description: Students will learn how to do systematic reviews andmeta-analyses of screening, prevention, diagnosis, andtherapeutic topics. Systematic reviews are the foundation of anevidence-based approach to practice in many disciplines. Whilemost of the examples will be in healthcare, the methods learnedare broadly applicable.
courses.prerequisiteText: BIOS 7010 or BIOS 7010E or permission of department

courses.subject: EPID
courses.title: Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analysis
courses.description: Students will learn how to do systematic reviews and meta-analyses of screening, prevention, diagnosis, and therapeutic topics. Systematic reviews are the foundation of an evidence-based approach to practice in many disciplines. While most of the examples will be in healthcare, the methods learned are broadly applicable.
courses.prerequisiteText: BIOS 7010 or BIOS 7010E or permission of department

courses.subject: EPID
courses.title: Molecular Epidemiology
courses.description: Introduction to the basic concepts and technologies from geneticsand molecular biology, and the diverse ways they are marshalledto solve practical problems in disease spread and riskidentification.
courses.course_objectives: Students will be able to understand the elements of the ethical treatment of human subjects research. Students will be able to organize and conduct biostatistical collaboration meetings with researchers. Students will be able to formulate and implement a data analysis plan based on study objectives, the study design, and data provided by the researchers. Students will be able to present clear and concise oral and written reports of the statistical data analyses to various audiences, including statistical team members and non-statistician researchers. Students will be able to investigate and apply advanced statistical methods that they have not previous encountered in graduate courses.
courses.topical_outline: Students will provide statistical consulting on applied problems in public health and biomedicine, including data analysis. Written and oral reports detailing the results of those analyses will be presented at the end of the semester.  In addition, topical discussions will be carried out on: Training in Human Subjects Research; Systematic ways to plan and execute effective statistical collaborations; Critical Evaluation of Objectives and Data; Formulating a statistical analysis plan Data Organization and Summary; Conduction data analysis; Writing Statistical Information for Non-Statisticians (emphasized throughout the course); Researching Advanced Statistical Topics (as required by projects);

courses.subject: EPID
courses.title: Cancer Epidemiology
courses.description: Reviews fundamentals of cancer epidemiology, including classicdescriptive cancer epidemiology, basic cancer biology, etiologyof common and uncommon human cancers, major and minor riskfactors for cancer, screening techniques for early detection,cancer biomarkers, and current research.  Epidemiologicmethodology and surveillance techniques, including cancerregistries, will be covered.

courses.subject: EPID
courses.title: Cardiovascular Disease Epidemiology
courses.description: Course covers relevant cardiovascular disease pathophysiology, risk factors for CVD, methodological issues in CVD research, including measures of CVD endpoints and relevant exposures, major population-based studies of CVD, CVD prevention strategies, treatment of CVD and major CVD trials, and current CVD-related epidemiological research.

courses.subject: EPID
courses.title: Infectious Disease Epidemiology
courses.description: Introduction to infectious disease epidemiology, the branch of epidemiology that investigates epidemics, studies transmission dynamics of infectious diseases, and evaluates control measures for infectious diseases with a particular focus on the population level. This course draws on the disciplines of biology, immunology, social science, mathematics, and biostatistics.
courses.course_objectives: Illustrate the importance of infectious disease epidemiology in the world today. Compare the determinants of infectious disease transmission dynamics including host behavior, host immunity, and pathogen biology. Design non-pharmaceutical and pharmaceutical public health interventions for outbreaks. Analyze how epidemiologic methods are applied during outbreaks.
courses.topical_outline: Principles of Infectious Disease Epidemiology Tracking and forecasting outbreaks, public health decision-making, interventions, and epidemiological trials Outbreak health disparities and public health inequities Pandemic dynamics including emergence, epidemiology, public health interventions, and the disparate impact The future of pandemic preparedness
courses.prerequisiteText: EPID 7010 or EPID 7010E or permission of department

courses.subject: EPID
courses.title: Infectious Disease Epidemiology
courses.description: Introduction to infectious disease epidemiology, the branch of epidemiology that investigates epidemics, studies transmission dynamics of infectious diseases, and evaluates control measures for infectious diseases with a particular focus on the population level. This course draws on the disciplines of biology, immunology, social science, mathematics, and biostatistics.
courses.prerequisiteText: EPID 7010 or EPID 7010E or permission of department

courses.subject: EPID
courses.title: Dynamical Systems Approach to Infectious Disease Epidemiology
courses.description: The spread and control of infectious diseases taking a population level and dynamical systems approach.
courses.prerequisiteText: BIOS 7010 or BIOS 7010E or permission of department

courses.subject: EPID
courses.title: Dynamical Systems Approach to Infectious Disease Epidemiology
courses.description: The spread and control of infectious diseases taking a populationlevel and dynamical systems approach.
courses.prerequisiteText: BIOS 7010 or BIOS 7010E or permission of department

courses.subject: EPID
courses.title: Analysis of Infectious Disease Data
courses.description: A variety of approaches for analyzing and interpreting data commonly encountered in infectious disease studies are covered, such as case counts, longitudinal measures of prevalence and incidence, time-series data, and more.
courses.prerequisiteText: BIOS 7010 or BIOS 7010E or permission of department

courses.subject: EPID
courses.title: Social Epidemiology
courses.description: Examination of how society and social organizations influence health and well-being of individuals and populations. In particular, it studies the frequency, distribution, and social determinants of states of health in populations, going beyond individual risk-factor analysis to the study of the social context in which the health-disease phenomenon occurs.

courses.subject: EPID
courses.title: Special Topics in Epidemiology
courses.description: Selected topics concerning recent developments in epidemiologyare covered.

courses.subject: EPID
courses.title: Problems in Epidemiology
courses.description: Analysis of contemporary epidemiological methods, theory, andapplications.

courses.subject: EPID
courses.title: Doctoral Research
courses.description: Research while enrolled for a doctoral degree under the direction of faculty members.

courses.subject: EPID
courses.title: Graduate Student Seminar
courses.description: Advanced supervised experience in an applied setting for studentsat the doctoral level. This course may not be used to satisfy astudent's approved program of study.

courses.subject: EPID
courses.title: Epidemiology Doctoral Seminar
courses.description: Provides doctoral students an opportunity to be exposed to topics directly relevant to their graduate school experience and future academic opportunities. In addition, this course includes a journal club component where students will critique landmark epidemiologic papers and other topical papers chosen by various faculty members.

courses.subject: EPID
courses.title: Doctoral Dissertation
courses.description: Dissertation writing under the direction of the major professor.

courses.subject: EPSY(ECHD)
courses.title: Development Across the Lifespan for School/Counseling Psychologists and Educators
courses.description: A study of developmental trajectories, systems, timing, malleability, plasticity, and typical and atypical development. Developmental theory and its application across the lifespan for educators and psychologists. Focuses on biological, physical, cognitive, and psychosocial development during prenatal period, infancy, early childhood, adolescence, and adulthood in context.

courses.subject: EPSY
courses.title: Critical Thinking and Creative Problem-Solving for Life
courses.description: A sequence of experiences leading to increased personal creative behavior and critical thinking with an emphasis on service-learning for nurturing creative talent in elementary-aged students.

courses.subject: EPSY
courses.title: Exploring Learning and Teaching
courses.description: Future educators will understand how opportunities, access, and engagement intersect to contribute to P-12 student success. Educators will explore key aspects of learning and teaching, reflect on their own learning processes and those of others, and apply their knowledge to equitably meet the diverse learning needs of P-12 students in a variety of educational settings and contexts.

courses.subject: EPSY
courses.title: Exploring Learning and Teaching (Honors)
courses.description: Future educators will understand how opportunities, access, and engagement intersect to contribute to P-12 student success. Educators will explore key aspects of learning and teaching, reflect on their own learning processes and those of others, and apply their knowledge to equitably meet the diverse learning needs of P-12 students in a variety of educational settings and contexts.
courses.offeredText: Not offered on a regular basis.

courses.subject: EPSY
courses.title: Exploring Teaching and Learning Practicum
courses.description: An early community or school field experience for students who wish to engage in clinical experience. Provides an option to satisfy elements of the university's experiential learning requirement for undergraduates.
courses.offeredText: Not offered on a regular basis.

courses.subject: EPSY
courses.title: Child and Adolescent Development for Education
courses.description: Cognitive, sociocultural, emotional, and moral development from infancy through adolescence, with particular emphasis placed on developmental issues in the context of educational settings.
courses.prerequisiteText: Any course with EPSY, PSYC, ECHD, or CHFD prefix

courses.subject: EPSY
courses.title: Child and Adolescent Development for Education (Honors)
courses.description: Child and adolescent development is examined in-depth from aneducational perspective. Cognitive, emotional, moral, and socialaspects of development are emphasized.
courses.prerequisiteText: Any course with prefix EPSY, PSYC, ECHD, or CHFD and permission of Honors
courses.offeredText: Not offered on a regular basis.

courses.subject: EPSY
courses.title: Child and Adolescent Development for Education
courses.description: Cognitive, sociocultural, emotional, and moral development from infancy through adolescence, with particular emphasis placed ondevelopmental issues in the context of service-learning in an educational setting.
courses.prerequisiteText: Any course with EPSY, PSYC, ECHD, or CHFD prefix

courses.subject: EPSY
courses.title: Child Development and Teaching in the Sciences
courses.description: Students in this course will use developmental science to explore the foundations of early child development. These principles will be applied to P-5 science education, with special emphasis on best teaching practices in the sciences, such as agricultural science education.

courses.subject: EPSY
courses.title: Psychology of Habit
courses.description: The psychology of habit formation and change. Students learn how habitual behavior relates to goals, intentions, and self-control. Students apply habits principles to their daily lives to support academic success, health, and well-being.

courses.subject: EPSY
courses.title: Science and Practice of Health and Well-Being
courses.description: A study of the science and practice of health and well-being, which is situated within the field of positive psychology. Students engage in a series of evidence-based practices designed to develop skills and habits supporting health and well-being. Students work on building conditions enabling a person to flourish.

courses.subject: EPSY
courses.title: Independent Study in Educational Psychology
courses.description: Independent study agreed upon by the student and sponsoring professor.
courses.course_objectives: Students will demonstrate acquisition of knowledge or skills regarding a topic in educational psychology.
courses.topical_outline: Determined by student and instructor.

courses.subject: EPSY
courses.title: Independent Study in Educational Psychology
courses.description: Independent study agreed upon by the student and sponsoring professor.
courses.course_objectives: Students will demonstrate acquisition of knowledge or skills regarding a topic in educational psychology.
courses.topical_outline: Determined by student and instructor.

courses.subject: EPSY
courses.title: Research-Based Experiences in Educational Psychology
courses.description: Through lectures and field-based experiences, students will learn the foundations of educational psychology research.Students will learn about practical research methods and engagein empirical projects related to assessment and interventionpractice. The course will be valuable to students wishing topursue graduate degrees in education and psychology.

courses.subject: EPSY
courses.title: Research-Based Experiences in Educational Psychology (Honors)
courses.description: Through lectures and field-based experiences, students will learn the foundations of educational psychology research. Students will learn about practical research methods and engage in empirical projects related to assessment and intervention practice. The course will be valuable to students wishing to pursue graduate degrees in education and psychology.
courses.prerequisiteText: Permission of department and permission of Honors

courses.subject: EPSY
courses.title: Foundations of Human Development for Education
courses.description: The interactive influences of biology, family, culture, and extended environment on children's and adolescents' emotional, social, and cognitive development during the school years. The implications of regularities and diversity in development for teaching and learning and on principles of educational practice to enhance development.

courses.subject: EPSY
courses.title: Foundations of Human Development for Education
courses.description: The interactive influences of biology, family, culture, and extended environment on children's and adolescents' emotional, social, and cognitive development during the school years. The implications of regularities and diversity in development for teaching and learning and on principles of educational practice to enhance development.

courses.subject: EPSY
courses.title: Social-Emotional Learning (SEL) in the Classroom and Beyond
courses.description: Theories and practices are examined that focus on social-emotional learning (SEL) among educators, children, and youth in diverse contexts. Students will examine pre-kindergarten through high school SEL programs and consider not only school-based approaches but community-based and youth empowerment approaches.
courses.course_objectives: Students will understand how to identify key components and stages of social and emotional learning (SEL) and explain why it is important. Students will understand how to characterize their own social and emotional competencies. Students will understand how to recognize factors that may impact the development and use of SEL across contexts. Students will understand how to identify SEL needs in diverse situations (e.g., emergency settings, trauma-informed practice) and for children and youth with diverse requirements. Students will understand how to create a safe, emotionally supportive, and responsive environment for children and youth, and consider a variety of culturally responsive strategies for teaching and practicing SEL in daily practice. Students will understand how to assess SEL in a variety of contexts and at different developmental stages.
courses.topical_outline:
What is SEL? SEL in early childhood, middle childhood, and adolescence Why is SEL important? SEL for diverse populations
a. Disparate identification of problems and distribution of resources/services across children and youth Factors that influence the development of SEL
a. Individual
b. Home
c. Broader context including classrooms/schools, neighborhoods SEL in emergency situations Determining the SEL environment Culturally responsive strategies for teaching and practicing SEL
a. Home
b. School
c. Other contexts SEL assessment
courses.prerequisiteText: Students must be enrolled in a professional program to register for this course

courses.subject: EPSY
courses.title: Social-Emotional Learning (SEL) in the Classroom and Beyond
courses.description: Theories and practices are examined that focus on social-emotional learning (SEL) among educators, children, and youth in diverse contexts. Students will examine pre-kindergarten through high school SEL programs and consider not only school-based approaches but community-based and youth empowerment approaches.
courses.course_objectives: Students will understand how to identify key components and stages of social and emotional learning (SEL) and explain why it is important. Students will understand how to characterize their own social and emotional competencies. Students will understand how to recognize factors that may impact the development and use of SEL across contexts. Students will understand how to identify SEL needs in diverse situations (e.g., emergency settings, trauma-informed practice) and for children and youth with diverse requirements. Students will understand how to create a safe, emotionally supportive, and responsive environment for children and youth, and consider a variety of culturally responsive strategies for teaching and practicing SEL in daily practice. Students will understand how to assess SEL in a variety of contexts and at different developmental stages.

courses.subject: EPSY
courses.title: Foundations of Cognition for Education
courses.description: Cognitive psychology as applied to education. Cognitive theories, models, and processes are applied to the teaching and learning of school skills and content areas. Processes such as attention, critical thinking, concept formation, language, memory, and problem solving are examined. Cognitive psychology principles are used to examine and refine instructional methods.
courses.course_objectives: Students will be able to define the impact of cognition and particularly the learning process. Students will be able to analyze how cultural and learner differences influence cognition and the educational process. Students will understand the Behavioral, Cognitive, and Constructivist views of learning. Students will be able to identify issues related to motivating students. Students will learn cognitive teaching strategies for creating interesting learning environments. Students will understand issues related to cognition, intelligence, and classroom assessment. Students will refine their own philosophy of teaching and use cognitive principles in evaluating a unit of instruction. Students will apply the cognition concepts they have learned in the course to answer questions about educational issues. Students will present empirical research and write a paper in APA style. Students will use a variety of their computer skills, including PowerPoint presentation software. Students will analyze relationships between cognition and technology. Students will apply cognition concepts to real world problem solving, and learning educational skills (including reading, writing) and content areas (including mathematics, science, and social studies).
courses.topical_outline:
1. Foundations of Cognitive Science
-	early history
-	recent history
-	structure of cognition: cognitive processes
-	perception, learning, and memory 2. Cognitive Development
-	mental growth and intelligence assessment
-	qualitative shifts: classical views
-	qualitative shifts: contemporary views 3. Curriculum Applications: Language and Literacy
-	beginning to read
-	early writing
-	advanced reading and writing 4. Curriculum Applications:  Mathematics, Science, Social Studies, Art, Music, and Physical Education
-	developmental and cognitive models
-	instructional strategies 5. Models of Instruction and Technology Supported Cognition
-	changing practices
-	learning environments
-	instructional design
-	computer-based instruction

courses.subject: EPSY
courses.title: Multicultural Psychology
courses.description: To prepare scientist-practitioners, from a social justice framework, this course is designed to provide students with an opportunity to critically examine privileged and marginalized cultural identities, intersectionality, and social justice engagement. The course will cover historical and current psychological and interdisciplinary literature related to the four categories, as well as popular media and individual lived experiences.
courses.course_objectives: Students will examine how their own identities affect how they understand and interact with people different from themselves. Students will increase their culture-specific knowledge about persons/clients from various racial and ethnic groups, giving special attention to relevant gender and class issues. Students will apply models, frameworks, and techniques to help increase one’s skill level in working with racial and ethnic group members and systems that serve racial and ethnic minorities. Students will demonstrate effective interpersonal skills and the ability to manage difficult communication well.
courses.topical_outline:
This course supports core competencies in the American Psychological Association’s requirements for profession-wide competencies which detail that certain competencies are required for all students who graduate from programs accredited in health service psychology. Programs must provide opportunities for all of their students to achieve and demonstrate each required profession-wide competency. The competencies serve as foundations upon which later competencies are built, each competency is considered critical for graduates in programs accredited in health service psychology. The specific requirements for each competency are articulated in APA’s Implementing Regulations. Because science is at the core of health service psychology, programs must demonstrate that they rely on the current evidence-base when training students in the following competency areas. From APA’s standards, this course provides background for building competencies in APA’s Standard II.B.1.b, elements (ii.) ethical and legal standards; (iii) individual and cultural diversity; (iv) professional values, attitudes, and behaviors; (v) communication and interpersonal skills; and (ix) consultation and interprofessional/interdisciplinary skills. Completion of this required course as part of the doctoral degree in Educational Psychology with an area of emphasis in School Psychology is a necessary first step for seeking licensure to practice as psychologist in Georgia. courses.subject: ERSH
courses.title: Survey of Latent Variable Models
courses.description: Survey of statistical models for analyzing latent variables. Topics include path analysis, confirmatory factor analysis, structural equation modeling, latent class modeling, item response theory, and diagnostic classification models. Emphasis on applications in educational research.
courses.course_objectives: Students successfully completing the course will be able to explain the purpose of latent variable models in educational research. Students successfully completing the course will be able to determine when a latent variable model is appropriate in a research context. Students successfully completing the course will be able to select appropriate latent variable techniques to answer research questions of interest. Students successfully completing the course will be able to use software to analyze latent variable models and obtain results. Students successfully completing the course will be able to statistically and practically interpret model results. Students will be able to utilize proper analytical models to estimate causal effects in different types of designs. Students will be able to summarize published research that focuses on study design for causal effects. Students will be able to perform, interpret, and defend statistical power analyses of different types of designs for causal inferences.

courses.description: Categorical data analysis with emphasis on practical applications in educational research and on the use of computing packages for analysis of such data.  Topics include contingency table analyses, generalized linear models, logistic regression, and loglinear models.  These techniques are applied to data sets from educational research.

courses.description: Procedures for analyzing large-scale data sets. Students will learn various data analysis strategies unique to large-scale data sets. Students will conduct secondary data analyses using national and international data sets. Large-scale data sets provide useful resources for both substantive and psychometric research in education.

courses.subject: ERSH

courses.description: Introduction to structural equation modeling techniques,including path models, confirmatory factor analysis, and fullstructural models. Emphasis will be placed on conducting andinterpreting computer analyses, critiquing SEM research, andcurrent research on the methodology.

This course is relevant for students in psychology, sociology, education, business, and other social sciences.

courses.title: Rasch Measurement Theory for Rating Scales
courses.description: Extends the measurement topics introduced in Rasch Measurement Theory to rating scales. This course specifically addresses the modeling of rating scale data scored in ordered categories, such as Likert scales.  Problems encountered in rater-mediated assessments (e.g., writing) that require judgments are also examined.

courses.subject: ESCI
courses.title: Physical Sciences for Middle School Teachers
courses.description: The course is intended for future middle school teachers to understand basic physical sciences concepts. Course content  addresses the state Science Standards. The course covers both physics and chemistry concepts, including matter, mechanics, thermodynamics, waves, and E&M.
courses.course_objectives: Students will have a firm grasp of big ideas in physical sciences for teaching at middle school level. Students will be able to perform hands-on activities, inquiry-based investigations, computer modeling, and science content reading and comprehension. Students will also be aware of popular middle school students’ misconceptions. With these experiences, students will be able to teach middle school physical sciences at a highly competent level.
courses.topical_outline: Structure and Properties of Matter: distinguish between atoms and molecules and between substances and mixtures; identify movement and characteristics of particles in solids, liquids, and gases; recognize physical changes and chemical changes. Force and Motion: determine the relationship between position, time, velocity and acceleration; understand the effect of balanced and unbalanced forces on the motion of an object in one and two dimensions; demonstrate the effect of simple machines; apply Newton’s laws to different contexts; understand the concept of potential and kinetic energy and energy conservation and transformation. Heat and Temperature: distinguish heat and temperature; understand the particle model of phases and phase change; apply ideal gas laws to different contexts. Electricity and Magnetism: understand and construct basic series and parallel circuits; understand static electricity and electric field; understand the relationship among current, voltage, and resistance; represent magnetic field; understand electromagnetic induction. Sound and Light: demonstrate geometric optics in terms of reflection and refraction; identify the characteristics of electromagnetic and mechanical waves; describe how the behavior of waves is affected by medium; understand the physics behind musical instruments.
courses.prerequisiteText: Students must be enrolled in a professional program to register for this course

courses.subject: ESCI
courses.title: Science Teaching Methods in the Middle Grades
courses.description: Science teaching methods using classroom, laboratory, and field experiences.  Development of a range of strategies appropriate for use with middle grades students. Special attention to examples and problems drawn from the physical sciences.
courses.course_objectives: By the end of this course, students will be able to determine ways of promoting “science for all” in your classroom. By the end of this course, students will be able to recognize characteristics of teaching science as inquiry. By the end of this course, students will be able to conduct a scientific investigation. By the end of this course, students will be able to ask questions to elicit students’ ideas about science concepts. By the end of this course, students will be able to use teaching strategies that encourage students’ interest and learning in science. By the end of this course, students will be able to plan a unit of science instruction based on a model conceptual change teaching. By the end of this course, students will be able to plan a unit of science instruction that integrates at least one other subject area. By the end of this course, students will be able to critically reflect on your own and others’ teaching, noting areas of strength as well as needed improvement.

courses.course_objectives: Students will develop, through experiences, an understanding of contemporary interdisciplinary scientific inquiry with the goal of enhancing middle and secondary students’ communication and literacy skills in reading, writing, art, and mathematics. Students will develop age-appropriate science inquiry-based instructional activities and performance assessments consistent with inquiry learning. Students will explore how inquiry can be woven into lessons that address national and state (including QCC, CRCT, and Stanford 9) science standards.

courses.course_objectives: By the end of this course, the learner should be able to present and defend her/his beliefs about science teaching and learning in grades PreK-8. By the end of this course, the learner should be able to identify elements of equitable instruction in the classroom. By the end of this course, the learner should be able to recognize characteristics of teaching science as inquiry. By the end of this course, the learner should be able to conduct a scientific investigation. By the end of this course, the learner should be able to demonstrate proficiency in the process skills common to PreK-8 science. By the end of this course, the learner should be able to evaluate alternative strategies for managing instructional space, time, and materials. By the end of this course, the learner should be able to identify professional publications that provide information about instruction in PreK-8 science. By the end of this course, the learner should be able to evaluate science curriculum materials.

Articulate their own pedagogical decisions and rationales for implementing various methods with secondary students. Communicate and collaborate with colleagues, school personnel, and university instructors in a professional manner.

courses.subject: ESOC
courses.title: Teaching Social Studies in the Middle Grades
courses.description: Lesson planning, implementation, and formative classroom assessments to foster equity-orientated, interdisciplinary social studies classrooms. Students will apply planning and teaching tasks to demonstrate competencies in connecting the curriculum to the world, questioning techniques, and use of the inquiry approach in social studies.
courses.course_objectives: Develop a critical inquiry stance toward middle grades social studies teaching and learning. Make interdisciplinary and curricular connections between the social studies content standards (i.e., economics, geography, history and political sciences) when designing lessons, planning curriculum, and implementing assessments. Develop news media literacy skills to enhance the relevancy of social studies lessons for the advancement of student engagement and understanding. Incorporate an understanding of students’ ideas, interests, and experiences along with their ethnicity, race, language, religion, socioeconomic status, gender, geographic origin, sexual orientation, and physical and mental exceptionalities within the lesson designs and instruction. Incorporate ways to teach social studies using an inquiry approach to pedagogical practice and methodological designs. Develop questioning techniques that promote student engagement and critical thinking in social studies. Use an equity-orientation for lesson planning to formatively assess middle grades students within the planning, teaching, and assessment cycle. Develop an appreciation for the complexity and challenges of implementing meaningful social studies learning in the middle grades classroom.
courses.topical_outline: Instructional planning that encompasses economics, geography, history, and political science in the study of social studies News media literacy skills development in alignment with middle grades social studies curriculum Strategies for the effective incorporation of relevant references to the world in middle grades social studies Pedagogical practices that foster active participation and engagement among middle grades students Assess students’ understanding of interdisciplinary social studies content using formative assessments

courses.description: Lesson planning, implementation, and formative classroom assessments to foster middle grades students’ understanding of the global world. Teaching and planning tasks will deepen students understanding of the history, politics, economics, and geographies of Europe, Australia, Canada, Latin American, Asia, Africa, and Southwest Asia.
courses.course_objectives: Align middle grades social studies content standards when designing lessons, planning curriculum, and implementing assessments. Use backwards design for lesson planning to formatively assess middle grades students within the planning, teaching, and assessment cycle. Design formative assessments based on knowledge of their characteristics, uses, and limitations to promote student growth, match instructional goals, and foster engagement in middle grades social studies. Analyze and select sources for an interdisciplinary approach to middle grades social studies content and classroom activities that are differentiated for students. Incorporate the unique cognitive, physical, social, emotional, and moral characteristics of students in middle grades as individuals and members of groups within lesson planning, instruction, and assessment. Incorporate understandings of how prior learning, differing family background, historical and contemporary contexts, and diverse cultural backgrounds influence learning within their lesson and assessment designs. Develop middle grades lessons that are creative, incorporate critical thinking, and follow the guidelines of an inquiry design approach to social studies.
courses.topical_outline: Introduce meaningful curricular decisions, pedagogical practices, and assessment designs for middle grades social studies. Introduce lesson planning approaches for middle grades social studies that lead students to transferable learning outcomes. Inquiry-orientated, social studies learning experiences that promote high student engagement and critical thinking. Pedagogical practices and corresponding assessment strategies that foster active participation and engagement among all students. Assess students’ understanding of the middle grades social studies content using formative assessments.

courses.subject: ESOC
courses.title: Teaching Geography
courses.description: Geographic principles and the history of geography in the school curriculum; the literature of the field, including textbooks; the application of special techniques; and geographic evaluation.
courses.course_objectives: Students will expand and demonstrate knowledge of content and modes of inquiry that are essential to the study of geography. Students will engage with ideas and information about human and spatial geography needed to teach in social studies classrooms. Students will practice using geographic skills to prepare lessons for teaching geography in social studies classrooms. Students will interpret and create a geography curriculum that reflects state, local, and national content standards. Students will develop knowledge of instructional materials and methods that reflect creative use of geographic knowledge and skill for teaching geography in elementary, middle, and high school settings. Students will use knowledge of social, linguistic, and cultural diversity to create an equitable and culturally responsive classroom. Students will develop an understanding of and learn to design types of assessments based on knowledge of their characteristics, uses, and limitations to promote student growth and match instructional goals. Students will articulate clear and defensible rationales for curricular and instructional decision-making. Students will learn to vary their instructional roles (i.e., instructor, facilitator, audience), instructional strategies, and materials to support active student engagement in worthwhile learning for all students. Students will engage in collaborative inquiry around major issues related to teaching geography.

Students will interpret and create a geography curriculum that reflects state, local, and national content standards. Students will develop knowledge of instructional materials and methods that reflect creative use of geographic knowledge and skill for teaching geography in elementary, middle, and high school settings. Students will use knowledge of social, linguistic, and cultural diversity to create an equitable and culturally responsive classroom. Students will develop an understanding of and learn to design types of assessments based on knowledge of their characteristics, uses, and limitations to promote student growth and match instructional goals. Students will articulate clear and defensible rationales for curricular and instructional decision making. Students will learn to vary their instructional roles (i.e., instructor, facilitator, audience), instructional strategies, and materials to support active student engagement in worthwhile learning for all students. Students will engage in collaborative inquiry around major issues related to teaching geography.

courses.subject: ETAP
courses.title: The Socioemotional Wellness for Practitioners
courses.description: This interdisciplinary course explores socioemotional wellness as a foundation for sustainable professional practice. Designed for graduate students in education, social work, public health and, medicine it integrates theory and reflective practice to develop emotional intelligence, prevent burnout, and cultivate personal and collective wholeness within high-demand, service-oriented professions.
courses.course_objectives: Students will analyze connections between socioemotional wellbeing and professional performance. Students will identify evidence-based strategies to sustain wellness and prevent burnout. Students will apply reflective and restorative practices to enhance self-awareness and emotional regulation. Students will evaluate systemic and cultural influences on practitioner wellbeing. Students will create a personalized wellness framework to support long-term personal and professional balance.
courses.topical_outline: The Practitioner as a Person: overview of course; defining socioemotional wellness and wholeness; exploring practitioner identity. The Science of Wellbeing: foundations of emotional intelligence, stress physiology, and the mind-body connection. Systems of Care and the Cost of Caring: understanding burnout, compassion fatigue, and vicarious trauma. Mindfulness and Self-Regulation Practices: exploration of mindfulness, breathwork, and embodied awareness as resilience tools. Boundaries and Balance: establishing professional boundaries and navigating emotional labor. Cultural Contexts of Wellness: examining how race, gender, and culture shape wellness experiences and expectations. Trauma-Informed and Healing-Centered Practice: applying trauma-informed principles to sustain personal and community wellbeing. Midterm Reflection and Integration: guided reflection; developing insights from personal practice logs and class discussions. The Role of Community and Connection: building professional support systems and collective care networks. The Spiritual Dimension of Wholeness: exploring purpose, meaning-making, and alignment in professional life. Environmental and Organizational Wellness: analyzing workplace cultures and institutional supports for wellbeing. Creative and Restorative Practices: engaging art, movement, and creativity as wellness modalities. Practicing with Wellness in Mind: integrating socioemotional wellness into career practices. Designing a Personal Wellness Framework: developing individualized and context-specific wellness plans. Integration and Legacy: final presentations and collective reflection on sustaining wellness beyond the course.

courses.title: Spaces of Writing, Inquiry, and Leadership for Equity in Education
courses.description: Emphasizes the lifelong power of inquiry and writing and the importance of teacher leadership and equity in education. Immersed in a community of writers and inquirers, students will investigate inquiry-based and writing pedagogies and also design their own inquiry projects.
courses.course_objectives: Students will be able to investigate theories and practices of inquiry-based pedagogies. Students will be able to read and examine theories of writing and writing pedagogies. Students will be able to explore how writing and inquiry can facilitate teacher leadership. Students will be able to study theories and practices of equity in education. Students will be able to design classroom spaces and practices for inquiry and for writing. courses.subject: ETES
courses.title: Robotics for Teachers
courses.description: Fundamentals of robotic control systems and hands-on robotics activities for enhancing STEM learning.
courses.course_objectives: Students who successfully complete this course will be able to identify grade-appropriate science, technology, engineering, and mathematics (STEM) content that can be enhanced with robotics activities. Students who successfully complete this course will be able to design learning activities incorporating robotics that enhance STEM content specified by current Georgia Department of Education standards for grade-appropriate instruction. Students who successfully complete this course will be able to explain the function of robotics controllers, sensors, and actuators. Students who successfully complete this course will be able to describe the underlying principles of robotic control systems and programming. Students who successfully complete this course will be able to analyze basic robotics tasks and develop hardware and software solutions. Students who successfully complete this course will be able to describe and assemble basic logic structures used in programming robotics systems to accomplish specified tasks. Students who successfully complete this course will be able to describe and critique robotics hardware and software available for school use. Students who successfully complete this course will be able to prepare recommendations for robotics hardware, software, and learning activities given a set of learning objectives and budget and time constraints. Students who successfully complete this course will be able to describe the instructional approaches that could benefit from use of robotics to support learning of STEM content. Students who successfully complete this course will be able to identify significant streams of research on use of robotics to enhance learning in instructional settings. Students who successfully complete this course will be able to assess the effectiveness of including robotics in STEM learning activities.

courses.subject: ETES
courses.title: Communication Systems
courses.description: Communication technology in business and industry.  Use of microcomputer applications for computer graphics, desktop publishing, electronic presentation, and telecommunications, including layout and design principles and procedures, graphic production systems, photographic processes, societal impacts, and innovative technologies.
courses.course_objectives: Students will be able to describe the underlying principles of graphic and printing reproduction processes. Students will be able to analyze basic layout and design problems and design appropriate solutions. Students will be able to demonstrate a variety of composition techniques. Students will be able to demonstrate applications of microcomputers in graphic communications. Students will be able to demonstrate techniques for using continuous tone photography, digital photography, and electronic capture and transmission of photographic images. Students will be able to demonstrate correct use of web page construction and website management. Students will be able to produce well designed video materials using appropriate techniques for capturing, editing, and packaging media for distribution. Students will be able to demonstrate teamwork processes when solving technical communications problems. Students will be able to recognize the historical perspective of communication technology and recognize the impact of communication technologies on societies and cultures. Students will be able to describe the fundamentals of voice, data, and video communication systems. Students will be able to explain the various instructional approaches for teaching communication systems as a component of technology education and workforce education. Students will be able to identify significant streams of research relevant to communication systems. Students will be able to assess the effectiveness of various curriculum models for communication systems instruction in technology education and workforce education.
courses.topical_outline: Principles of communication systems Technological impacts Audio and video communications Broadcast systems Message design Optic systems Photography and digital imaging systems Message transfer and product conversion Technical design and illustration Web development Digital video Macromedia Flash Applications in education settings Strategies for technology education communication systems instruction

courses.subject: ETES
courses.title: Principles of Technology
courses.description: Technological literacy acquired through applied physics concepts and laws.  Special emphasis on teaching the integration of mathematics, science, and technology scholarship.
courses.course_objectives: Students who successfully complete this course will be able to provide instruction in applied physics using a unified concepts approach. Students who successfully complete this course will be able to describe the fundamental concepts and theory of work, rate, resistance, and force transformers. Students who successfully complete this course will be able to define fundamental terminology pertaining to applied physics. Students who successfully complete this course will be able to demonstrate fundamental operating procedures for using applied physics laboratory equipment. Students who successfully complete this course will be able to describe what force, pressure, voltage, and temperature differences have in common. Students who successfully complete this course will be able to predict what happens in a system when the forces are balanced and when forces are unbalanced. Students who successfully complete this course will be able to measure force in mechanical, fluid, electrical, and thermal systems. Students who successfully complete this course will be able to demonstrate how thermal power and thermal rate are the same. Students who successfully complete this course will be able to describe the nature of energy in mechanical, fluid, electrical, and thermal systems. Students who successfully complete this course will be able to determine the relationship between work and energy. Students who successfully complete this course will be able to explain why force transformers form a unifying principle in mechanical, fluid, and electrical systems.

courses.subject: FANR(BINF)(GENE)
courses.title: Functional Genomics
courses.description: Fundamentals and practical applications of functional genomics in biological research.  Lecture- and paper-based discussion on topics including gene discovery, genome sequencing, transcript profiling by microarray, and next-generation sequencing (RNA-Seq), regulation of gene expression, forward and reverse genetics, proteomics, metabolomics, correlation network analysis, and ecological genomics.
courses.course_objectives: By the end of this course, students will demonstrate a comprehensive understanding of current and emerging omics technologies, including their principles, methodologies, and applications in the life sciences. By the end of this course, students will gain proficiency in using various functional genomics tools, enabling them to conduct advanced research and analysis in genomics. By the end of this course, students will be able to integrate omics approaches into traditional research disciplines such as biochemistry, development, ecology, genetics, and physiology, enhancing their interdisciplinary research capabilities. By the end of this course, students will develop critical thinking and problem-solving skills through homework exercises and literature paper discussions. By the end of this course, students will enhance their ability to communicate scientific findings effectively and collaborate with peers and experts in the field of omics technologies.
courses.topical_outline: Introduction to Functional Genomics Recombinant DNA Technology Gene Discovery Expressed Sequence Tags Microarray Next-generation Sequencing Technologies Regulation of Gene Expression Alternative mRNA Splicing Micro-RNAs and Small RNAs Forward and Reverse Genetics Proteomics Metabolomics Correlation Networks Ecological Genomics

courses.subject: FANR(ECOL)(GEOG)
courses.title: Natural History of Georgia
courses.description: An introduction to the science of natural history and biota ofGeorgia, as well as the impacts of humans on regional and national resources (overfishing, human-driven extinctions).  Students will gain familiarity with the geography, geology, plants, and animals (especially vertebrates) of the Appalachians, Piedmont, Coastal Plain, and islands of Georgia.

courses.subject: FANR(ECOL)
courses.title: Agent-Based Modeling in Ecology and Management
courses.description: Theory and applications of agent-based models (ABM) for ecosystem science and management. Students will develop an understanding of the conceptual foundation for designing models, coding models, conducting simulation experiments in NetLogo, and analyzing a model to develop a theory for complex adaptive systems. No coding/programming background is required.

courses.subject: FANR(GEOG)
courses.title: International Issues in Natural Resources and Conservation
courses.description: Introduction to international natural resource policy concentrating on endangered species, international trade, multiple land-use and conservation planning, eco-tourism, sustainability, and environmental education.  Conservation continuum is explored from protectionist to utilitarian perspectives. Three case studies (Africa, Asia, Europe) are investigated to understand how policies affect areas they claim to protect.
courses.offeredText: Not offered on a regular basis.

courses.subject: FANR(MARS)
courses.title: Natural Resources Conservation
courses.description: Introduction to the general principles and contemporary issuesrelated to ecology and management of wildlife, fish, forests, andrangelands; natural resources recreation and tourism;conservation of water, wetlands, and soil resources; andrenewable and non-renewable energy.  Students will acquire theknowledge necessary to advance beyond the simplistic portrayal ofenvironmental dilemmas offered by mass media and gain a firmerbasis for environmental stewardship, responsible citizenship, andaction on environmental issues.

courses.subject: FANR(WILD)
courses.title: Human Dimensions of Natural Resources and Wildlife Conservation
courses.description: Course covers major concepts, theories, and disciplinary perspectives in human dimensions of natural resources, wildlife, and fisheries conservation. You will learn how to identify underlying causes of stakeholder conflicts and conservation problems, possible solutions to conflicts, and reasons why policies or management actions may or may not resolve conflicts.
courses.course_objectives: Upon completion of this course, students will be able to identify and explain key concepts and theories from psychology, sociology and economics that are applied in human dimensions research. Upon completion of this course, students will be able to use human dimensions concepts and theories to understand the drivers of conservation conflicts. Upon completion of this course, students will be able to evaluate potential solutions to conservation conflicts that take into account multiple, differing perspectives of key stakeholders. Upon completion of this course, students will be able to identify and appraise the psychological, sociological, and economic determinants of stakeholders’ behaviors through active listening. Upon completion of this course, students will be able to increase stakeholder engagement in conservation solutions through interpersonal communication.
courses.topical_outline: Human Dimensions of Natural Resources: Introduction and Overview The Public Trust Doctrine and Legal Trends in Wildlife Management Stakeholder Engagement in Decision Making Structured Decision-Making and Stakeholder Engagement Attitudes, Beliefs, Values, and Emotion: The Social Psychology of Conservation Social Psychology Models: Theory of Planned Behavior, Value-Belief-Norm Model, Theory of Reasoned Action Using Facts and Knowledge to Resolve Conservation Problems Applying Sociology to Conservation Problems Environmental and Ecological Economics Conservation Criminology Designing a Human Dimensions Study Quantitative Research Techniques Writing Survey Questions and Designing Surveys Designing and Pretesting Survey Questions to Test Psychological and Sociological Constructs Designing Economic Valuation/Stated Preference Questions Rules, Regulations, and Trade Bans Market-Based Conservation Incentives Community-Based Conservation Outreach, Education, and Communication Private Ownership of Wildlife/Game Ranching Ethics in Conservation

courses.subject: FANR
courses.title: Fundamentals of Sustainable Development
courses.description: The principles of sustainable development and various applied tools which are typically used for measuring social, economic, and environmental impacts of a policy initiative at any level. Human-environment interactions are also emphasized along with real-world applications of sustainability principles and tools at various levels.

courses.subject: FANR
courses.title: Introduction to Natural Resource Statistics
courses.description: Introduction to the collection, quantification, and analysis of natural resources data, including descriptive statistics, probability/uncertainty, and inference. Topics include sampling, basic experimental design, exploratory data analysis, hypothesis testing, and data visualization. Students will use a variety of software tools for analysis and reporting using realistic datasets.
courses.course_objectives: After finishing this course, students will be able to characterize a dataset with descriptive stats and standard graphs. After finishing this course, students will be able to generate testable statistical hypotheses from data summaries in two or more variables. After finishing this course, students will be able to select and perform an appropriate statistical test for these hypotheses. After finishing this course, students will be able to communicate results effectively using standard textual and visual idioms. After finishing this course, students will be able to recognize common errors and misrepresentations in statistical communications.
courses.topical_outline: Intro: Why Do We Measure the Natural World? Basics of Statistics; Sampling and Distributions Sample Design, Randomization, Observational vs. Manipulative Experiments Describing Data: Summary Statistics (Intro to R I) Visualizing Data I: Center, Variability, Outliers (Intro to R II) Visualizing Data II: Scatterplots, Correlation, Distributions, Simple Linear Regression Writing about Data: Communicating Assumptions, Methods, Predictions, and Limitations Sampling Distributions for Proportions and Means Statistical Inference: Hypothesis Tests on Proportions and Means Confidence Intervals for Means Making the Case: Interpreting and Visualizing Coefficients and Uncertainty Hypothesis Tests for Two Groups Contingency Analysis

courses.subject: FANR
courses.title: Forest Ecosystem Services
courses.description: Forest ecosystems sustain life and provide aesthetic/spiritual services. This course provides an overview and basic understanding of forest ecosystem services from interdisciplinary and international perspectives. Internet-based lectures are prepared by faculty from several United States and Brazilian universities, and these faculty also lead both web-based and on-campus discussions.
