courses.prerequisiteText: ENGL 1101 or ENGL 1101E or ENGL 1101S or permission of department

courses.subject: GRMN
courses.title: Germania
courses.description: Explores the diverse histories and cultures of pre-national Germany from the Germanic barbarians through the Holy Roman Empire to the Thirty Years' War (1618-48). Emphasis on history, archaeology, art, and architecture, as well as their historical, religious, and political context. Taught in German.

courses.subject: GRMN
courses.title: German Courtly Literature
courses.description: Reading and analysis of representative lyric and epic texts from the medieval German "Blütezeit" (1150-1250). Explores the origins and development of German/European secular society in the courtly ideals of love and romance, knighthood and femininity, war and redemption. Taught in German.

courses.subject: GRMN
courses.title: The Age of Reformation
courses.description: Multi-media investigation of the period of massive intellectual and religious transition between 1350 and 1600 in the German-speaking lands. Emphasis on the Catholic conciliar movement; the Protestant Reformation and Sectarianism; and the rise and spread of Northern Humanism. Includes close-readings of German texts. Taught in German.

courses.subject: GRMN
courses.title: Introduction to German Cinema
courses.description: Survey of history of German cinema; investigation of particulardirectors, periods, and styles; relationship between German andother national cinemas. Course includes a required weekly filmscreening. Taught in English.

courses.subject: GRMN
courses.title: German Poetry
courses.description: A historical survey of German poetry or focus on particular poets, periods, or themes. Poems will be explored in their historical and cultural context but also engaged with as living works of art. There will be a performance and creative component. Taught in German.

courses.subject: GRMN
courses.title: Revolution, Revolt, and Nationlism in the Nineteenth Century
courses.description: Discussion of texts by German/Austrian writers and artists who responded to and participated in political movements of the nineteenth century. Texts address the Napoleonic Wars, democratic visions, the mid-century revolts, women's rights, Jewish emancipation, and the rise of nationalism. Taught in German.

courses.subject: GRMN
courses.title: The German Romantic Age
courses.description: What is Romanticism? How do artistic disciplines vary in their expression of Romantic ideals? Works include nineteenth-century poems, fairy tales, short fiction, letters, brief philosophical texts, music, and art. Taught in German.

courses.subject: GRMN
courses.title: German for Reading Knowledge
courses.description: Review of grammar, idioms, and vocabulary; practice in translating moderately difficult technical and non-technical German texts into correct English. Does not apply to the major or minor in German or language certificates.  Satisfies language requirement for graduate students.

courses.subject: GRMN
courses.title: Contemporary Issues in German Culture, Society, and Literature
courses.description: Selected contemporary topics in the culture, civilization, language, or literature of German-speaking countries.  Taught in English.

courses.subject: GRMN
courses.title: German Film and Visual Culture
courses.description: Berlin is a living city of art. This course introduces students to historical and contemporary German film, art, and visual culture (street art, museums, music/cinema venues, architecture, urban design). It addresses social, political, and demographic changes and investigates how these changes are reflected in German art.
courses.course_objectives: Students will be able to identify traits of German art movements and changing aesthetics from the 20th and 21st centuries with examples from German cinema and visual culture. Students will be able to analyze changing representations of Germans and German history and culture in German film, art, and visual culture in and around Berlin through place-based learning. Students will be able to engage with local Berliners and Berlin sights and learn to navigate an international city; the program will help students become global citizens aware of cultural differences.
courses.topical_outline: Art in the City - Neighborhood walking tour, historic “Karl-Marx-Allee”  - City art walking tour  Weimar Berlin and its Art Movements I  - Expressionism, Dadaism, Surrealism - Bauhaus archive and museum + meeting with artist  Weimar Berlin and its Art Movements II - Bauhaus, New Objectivity in Art and Cinema - Neue Nationalgalerie (Modern Arts Museum)  Art + Popular Film in Weimar Berlin - Film Archive and museum: Kinemathek, organized tour  - Film screening  Nazi Aesthetics  - Propaganda, Sculptures, Architecture - Olympia Stadium  Postwar German Film and Art - Zero Hour and Beyond in Art and Cinema - Optional: individual afternoon exhibits for small groups  All day excursion to Potsdam - Potsdam Filmmuseum and (art) city tour  All day excursion to Potsdam - Babelsberg Film Studio  Art and Film in Cold War Germany - Photography and Film in the BRD and the GDR - Photography Museum - Meeting with contemporary digital artist  Art and Film today: Contemporary German Film - Contemporary German Film + guest filmmaker - Group movie theater visit at Kino International (Engl.)  Transnational Art in Berlin  - Transnational Berlin + project proposal + discussion - Transnational art exhibition + meeting with artist  Transnational Berlin, work on group projects, + afternoon on-site work  On-site work for final projects

courses.subject: GRMN
courses.title: Berlin: The Capital in the 20th Century
courses.description: Through the lens of cultural history, students will investigate how key events of Germany’s turbulent 20th century played out in Berlin and are reflected in popular culture, literature, journalism, and architecture. Taught on location in Berlin in English.
courses.course_objectives: Students will have gained an overview of key debates and themes in culture and politics in Germany, especially how they manifested in Berlin, during different eras of the 20th century: The Weimar Republic, the Third Reich, the occupation period, the FRG and the GDR, and Reunified Germany/Berlin. Students will have gained an overview of the major sociopolitical differences between the different periods of German history during the 20th century. Students will have practiced contextualizing a cultural text in the surrounding sociopolitical debates of a particular era in German history of the 20th century. Students will have become acquainted with a non-US-based view on Cold War issues determined by opposing German perspectives (the GDR's and the FRG's). Students will have used media technology to collaborate on Berlin-themed film, photography, and essay projects for the course website. Students will have become an expert on a “Berlin cultural landmark” during their project work –  defined as a location/space/physical object/local tradition/technological innovation intrinsically connected to Berlin. Students will have engaged in cross-cultural exchanges with Berliners and tourists in Berlin on subjects concerning German/Berlin history, Berlin local culture, and others during their project work. Students will have spent three weeks on location in Berlin, a period during which they will have had the opportunity to connect the course content to their own personal experience of the city.
courses.topical_outline: Weimar Berlin (1918/9-1933) I: The Origins of the Weimar Republic Weimar Berlin (1918/9-1933) II: Life during the Weimar Republic; The advent of Mass Culture, New Woman, new Man Weimar Berlin (1918/9-1933) III: The fall of the Weimar Republic Third Reich Berlin (1933-1945) I: The Nazi Takeover Third Reich Berlin (1933-1945) II: Repression, deportation, and the Holocaust Third Reich Berlin (1933-1945) III: Albert Speer, and the “World Capital Germania” Zero Hour Berlin - The Airlift (1945-1949): The end and a new beginning, Occupation zones, The Berlin airlift Postwar Berlin (1949-1961): The Cold War in Berlin The Wall: The events of 1961 Divided City I (1961-1989): Living in East Berlin Divided City II (1961-1989): Living in West Berlin Unification Berlin I (1989-1990): The events of 1989 Unification Berlin II (1989-1990): The political unification of 1990 Unified Berlin (1990-now): Living in unified Berlin

courses.subject: GRMN
courses.title: German Writer/Filmmaker-in-Residence
courses.description: Course will be taught by the visiting Max Kade Foundation Writer-in-Residence or Filmmaker-in-Residence. Course is focused on a topic of their choice, usually involving their own work, though not exclusively. Taught in German.

courses.subject: GRMN
courses.title: Discourses of Post-War Literature
courses.description: Post-war German-speaking literature and ideas. Traces literary themes and topics and analyzes their social, political, and cultural context. Includes aftermath of World War II (philosophical, political, cultural, economic), feminism, new politics of the 60s/70s, terrorism, foreigners/guestworkers/immigrants, East and West Germany, Generation X. Taught in German.

courses.subject: GRMN
courses.title: The Wild Berlin of Bertolt Brecht (Honors)
courses.description: Focuses on German playwright Bertolt Brecht (1898 - 1956), one of the most influential figures in twentieth-century drama. Discussion of Brecht's political and artistic development during his Berlin years, a period of explosive political constellations and artistic controversy. Involves the discussion of art, music, film, and drama from the period.

courses.subject: GRMN
courses.title: Post-War Women Writers
courses.description: The construction of gender, history, and representation in novels, poems, and essays of post-war women writers from German-speaking countries. Explores how femininity and feminism inform lives and texts. Taught in German.

courses.subject: GRMN
courses.title: Memory, History, Narrative
courses.description: Personal and historical memory in literary texts. Discussion of "Geschichte" in its multiple meanings of history and story, questions of literary representation, and role of gender. Longer narratives supplemented by short stories, essays, interviews, and music that illuminate socio-historic contexts.  Taught in German.

courses.subject: GRMN
courses.title: The Wall
courses.description: The Berlin Wall as a site of history and imagination within the context of post-war politics, culture, and everyday life. Discussion of the physical border and the persistence of mental "walls" between East and West Germans. Prose supplemented by political documents, interviews, films, and music. Taught in German.

courses.subject: GRMN
courses.title: Authorities and Law in Modern German Society and Culture
courses.description: A cross-cultural exploration of current perceptions and interactions of authorities (e.g., police) with the public through examination of laws and regulations. Specific focus on protecting youth, religious neutrality in schools, migration, and immigration. Explores crime and morality in literature and popular media such as television crime dramas. Taught in German.

courses.subject: GRMN
courses.title: Literature in Music, Music in Literature
courses.description: Explores the synthesis of the verbal and musical arts in German culture from a dual perspective: literary content of musical genres (such as minne- and meistersang, Lutheran hymn, cantata, opera, folk song, lied), and musical structures and themes in certain literary works. Taught in German.

courses.subject: GRMN
courses.title: German Film
courses.description: The history of German film and its political, social, and cultural contexts. Includes expressionism, nazi film, post-war "Heimatfilm," new German cinema, the post-wall comedy wave, and the contemporary state of German film making. Taught in German.

courses.subject: GRMN
courses.title: Children's and Youth Literature
courses.description: Examines the representation of childhood in German juvenile literature in various genres. Issues of identity and self-realization in traditional and contemporary children's literature. Focuses on stories that reflect upon the art and value of storytelling, as well as the nature and function of creative imagination. Taught in German.

courses.subject: GRMN
courses.title: The Jewish Experience in German Culture
courses.description: Contributions of Jews and Jewish culture to the German-speaking world. Emphasis on how Jewish writers, thinkers, and artists portray their experiences and identities. Responses of Jews and non-Jews to discrimination, emancipation, assimilation, the Holocaust, and the Jewish presence in Germany today. Taught in English.

courses.subject: GRMN
courses.title: Introduction to Goethe's Life and Works
courses.description: Taking Goethe's late autobiographical writing Dichtung und Wahrheit as point of departure, this course explores the life and work of Goethe, focusing on dramatic, novelistic, and poetic genres for which he is renowned and considering their aesthetic, historical, and cultural implications. Taught in German; English as necessary.

courses.subject: GRMN
courses.title: The German Fairy Tale Tradition
courses.description: Traditional folk fairy tales by Jacob and Wilhelm Grimm and literary fairy tales by Clemens Brentano, Ludwig Tieck, Johann Wolfgang von Goethe, Friedrich de la Motte Fouqué and others in their social and cultural contexts. Taught in German.

courses.subject: GRMN
courses.title: German Fairy Tales
courses.description: Traditional folk fairy tales by Jacob and Wilhelm Grimm and literary fairy tales by Clemens Brentano, E.T.A. Hoffmann, Ludwig Tieck, Johann Wolfgang von Goethe, Friedrich de la Motte Fouqué, Michael Ende, and others in social and cultural contexts. Representations of fairy tales in film and TV. Taught in English.

courses.subject: GRMN
courses.title: Transnational Germany: Contemporary German Film, Literature, Art, and Popular Culture
courses.description: Course investigates post-Cold War transnational cultural productions in Germany. Representative works (prose, film, art, comedy) will be discussed in the sociopolitical context of their creation, supplemented with scholarly, historical, and journalistic readings. Course scrutinizes competing notions of nation/citizenship/ethnicity/multilingualism in artistic work.
courses.course_objectives: By the end of this course, students should be able to identify German cultural developments and the dynamic politics and changing discourses as related to German minorities and transnational art. By the end of this course, students should be able to analyze and contextualize such discourses, minority art, and changing representations of minorities via selected German film, literature, and art. By the end of this course, students should be able to comprehensively evaluate various materials (minority discourses and transnational art in Germany) before establishing a conclusion on the meaning of an individual piece of work. By the end of this course, students should have engaged and analyzed multiple opposing viewpoints or arguments. By the end of this course, students should be able to support their own conclusion about a particular work and its critical interpretation with sound reasoning and judgment. By the end of this course, generally, students should be able to interpret a range of material and develop nuances of a certain discourse through their engagement with various critical texts. By the end of this course, students should be able to express concepts and thoughts in verbal forms. By the end of this course, students should be able to identify and apply appropriate theoretical frameworks or methodologies as discussed in the course (such as cultural studies approaches) to their inquiries in class. By the end of this course, students should be able to organize and synthesize the theoretical and artistic course materials to develop and create their own research projects. By the end of this course, students should be able to effectively develop, express, and exchange ideas in written, oral, and/or visual form. By the end of this course, students should be able to tailor their communication style appropriately for our academic setting. By the end of this course, students should be able to analyze the impact of human behaviors on the physical and/or social environment of people. By the end of this course, students should be able to reflect upon how one’s social identities and roles shape one’s worldview and interactions. By the end of this course, students should have developed an awareness, appreciation, and knowledge of cultures and communities beyond one’s own. By the end of this course, students should be able to creatively synthesize and/or transform ideas that they learned in the German context. By the end of this course, students should be able to consider various—at times contradictory—viewpoints on social or artistic German works when designing their research projects. By the end of this course, students’ final research projects should reflect their creative and original response to a research question. By the end of this course, students should plan, initiate, manage, and complete a research project in small groups, all in consultation with the faculty member. By the end of this course, students should be able to address a problem or issue related to the course in their research projects. By the end of this course, students should be ready to consider and incorporate peer feedback and faculty comments into their projects
courses.topical_outline:
This course investigates post-1989 transnational cultural productions in Germany (film, visual art, comedy, and prose). Representative artistic works such as poems, short stories, short and feature films, sketches, art, and music will be discussed in the sociopolitical context of their creation and analyzed in groups and individually. More specifically, the transformative period of the Wende and post-Wende Germany (post-Cold War Germany) will be discussed from a transnational perspective, providing insights into transnational artwork made in Germany. Selected scholarly, historical, and journalistic readings will help participants to lead the class discussions as they relate to shifting and competing notions and questions of the nation and nationality, citizenship, ethnicity, and multilingualism in Germany. Pre-1990:
Cem Karaca (music & lyrics)
Birol Denizeri, Mojca Posavec (short stories) 1990s:
Pepe Danquart, Der Schwarzfahrer, 1993
May Ayim, Blues in schwarz weiss (poems), 1995 Early 2000s:
Wladimir Kaminer, Schönhauser Allee, 2002 Post-2010:
Yasemin Samdereli, Almanya: Willkommen in Deutschland, 2011
Olga Grjasnowa, Der Russe ist einer der Birken liebt, 2012
Ilker Catak, Sadakat (Fidelity), 2015
Serdar Somuncu, select comedy/satire pieces Post-2020:
Fatih Akin, Rheingold, 2022
Moshtari Hilal, Hässlichkeit, 2023 Other texts/critical readings:
Deniz Göktürk, et al., eds. Germany in Transit, 2007 (and in German 2011)
Fatima El-Tayeb, Undeutsch, 2016

courses.subject: GRMN
courses.title: Creativity vs. Crisis: 1920s Berlin in Literature, Film, and Art
courses.description: Marked by a variety of political, economic, and social changes, Berlin was the political capital and cultural center of the Weimar Republic. This course explores Germany's dynamic post-WWI period that allowed for thematic and stylistic experimentation and innovation in German art and culture amidst various crises.
courses.course_objectives: By the end of this course, students should be able to identify German cultural/political/social developments (including changing gender roles, changing art movements/aesthetics, increasing political tensions) in the Weimar Republic. By the end of this course, students should be able to analyze and contextualize the changing representations and discourses of German cultural/political/social developments via selected German film, literature, and art. By the end of this course, students should be able to comprehensively evaluate materials (Weimar Germany and its art and artistic movements amidst economic, political, and social crises) before establishing a conclusion on the meaning of individual works. By the end of this course, students should be able to engage and analyze multiple opposing viewpoints or arguments. By the end of this course, students should be able to support their own conclusion about a particular (art)work and its critical interpretation with sound reasoning and judgment. By the end of this course, generally, students should be able to interpret materials and develop nuances of a particular discourses through their engagement with various critical texts. By the end of this course, students should be able to express concepts and thoughts in verbal forms. By the end of this course, students should be able to identify and apply appropriate theoretical frameworks or methodologies as discussed in our course (such as cultural studies approaches) to their inquiries in class. By the end of this course, students should be able to organize and synthesize theoretical and artistic materials to develop and create their own research projects/inquiries. By the end of this course, students should be able to effectively develop, express, and exchange ideas in written, oral, and/or visual form. By the end of this course, students should develop, support, and effectively express ideas in written and oral form using German language with clarity and precision. By the end of this course, students should be able to tailor their communication style appropriately for our academic setting. By the end of this course, students should be able to analyze the impact of human behaviors on the physical and/or social environment of people. By the end of this course, students should be able to reflect upon how one’s social identities and roles shape one’s worldview and interactions. By the end of this course, students should have developed an awareness, appreciation, and knowledge of cultures and communities beyond one’s own. By the end of this course, students should be able to creatively synthesize and/or transform ideas that they learned in the German context. By the end of this course, students should be able to consider various—at times contradictory—viewpoints on social or artistic works when designing their research projects/critical inquiries. By the end of this course, students’ final research projects should reflect their creative and original response to a research question. By the end of this course, students should plan, initiate, manage, and complete a research project in small groups, all in consultation with the faculty member. By the end of this course, students should be able to address a problem or issue related to the course topic in their research projects. By the end of this course, students should be ready to consider and incorporate peer feedback and faculty comments into their final project.
courses.topical_outline:
The Weimar Republic (1919-1933) is known for its world-famous cinema, architecture and design, vibrant art and cabaret scene, and artists, as much as for being a time of political upheaval in a new and unstable democracy. Marked by a variety of political, economic, and social changes caused by the lost war, a flourishing art scene, a new urban culture, changing gender roles, two inflations, and much more, Berlin was the political capital and cultural center of the Weimar Republic. In this course, we will explore this dynamic time for German cultural productions, which allowed for thematic and stylistic experimentation and innovation.
The main aim of this course is to introduce undergraduate students to German literature, culture, and media of the Weimar Republic. While engaging with cultural products, we will address aspects of the various changes and shifts in Germany’s first democracy. 
In the first half of the semester, the material to be discussed ranges primarily from 1918/19 (the end of WWI and the beginning of the Weimar Republic) to 1933 (the end of the Weimar Republic and the beginning of the Third Reich). We will discuss these materials (advertisements, films, literary works, and other texts) as case studies to make further inquiries into the period. Selected films and textual works will be viewed/read in excerpts or in their entirety. The course will be accompanied with selected readings about the individual cultural products and Weimar movements such as Bauhaus, Expressionism, New Objectivity, etc. In the later sections of the semester, we will watch and analyze some episodes of the contemporary Netflix show “Babylon Berlin” and create evaluations and criticisms of the show with our newly gained expertise in this period. Historical background:
- The end of WWI
- The beginning (and end) of the Weimar Republic
- Challenges to everyday life in the beginning of the Weimar Republic The city: technology, modernization, and life in the metropolis Berlin
- Art: Otto Dix, George Grosz (selected art works)
- Poetry: Erich Kästner
- Architecture & design: Bauhaus, the “Frankfurt Kitchen”
- Film: Walter Ruttmann, Berlin: Symphonie einer Großstadt (1927) (excerpts) New gender roles & “the crisis of masculinity”
- Film: Robert Wiene, Das Cabinet des Dr Caligari (1920), Richard Oswald, Anders als die anderen (1919), Ernst Lubitsch, Ich möchte kein Mann sein (1918) & Die Austernprinzessin (1919) (excerpts)
- Texts: magazines and other print media
- Advertisement
- Art: Hannah Höch, Otto Dix
- Literature: Irmgard Keun and Vicky Baum (The Artificial Silk Girl (1932) and Grand Hotel (1929)) (excerpts) „Freizeit“ (free time/hobbies) and body culture
(All texts are from the Weimar Sourcebook)
- Sports/athletics
- The movies
- Nature
- Urban flânerie and Georg Simmel (excerpts) Americanization
- Louise Brooks
- „Girl culture“ Art: dada, expressionism, new objectivity
- Texts and art (various examples) The end of the Weimarer Republik, beginning of the Third Reich in film
- Film: Fritz Lang, M (1931), Hans Steinhoff, Hitler Youth Quex (1933) Youth Literature, main text:
- Erich Kästner, Emil and the Detectives (1929) The afterlife of Weimar Berlin in various media today
- Music, Musicals, Other media (various examples) Streaming Weimar Berlin: Netflix’s Babylon Berlin (2017-today)
- TV-Series/Netflix Serie: Babylon Berlin (1. season, 2017) excerpts
- Scholarly literature on Babylon Berlin
- Journalistic texts on Babylon Berlin

courses.subject: GRMN
courses.title: Directed Study in German
courses.description: Independent study, research, and substantial final project under the direction of individual faculty members.

courses.subject: GRMN
courses.title: Advanced German Conversation and Composition
courses.description: Vocabulary building and review of grammar. Emphasis on common errors of English speakers and on distinctions in meaning.
courses.course_objectives: Students will read, listen, speak, and write in German at the advanced level (ACTFL Intermediate High/Advanced Low, CFR B2/C1). Students will express informed knowledge and opinions about important events, people, issues, and artistic works in modern German/Austrian society and culture. Students will independently read/view/listen, analyze, evaluate, summarize, and present on materials from authentic German-language media.
courses.topical_outline: I. German grammar, usage, and vocabulary review and development for spoken and written communication II. Important issues in modern/contemporary German/Austrian society and culture III. A modern German/Austrian novel IV. German/Austrian works in other artistic media, most notably film/video and music

courses.subject: GRMN
courses.title: Magic, Monsters, and the Occult in German Literature
courses.description: Texts that address themes from occult science and philosophy such as magic, alchemy, and secret societies by Johann Wolfgang von Goethe, Friedrich Schiller, E.T.A. Hoffmann, Friedrich de la Motte Fouqué, Gustav Meyrink and excerpts from works by Paracelsus and other occult scientists and philosophers. Taught in German.

courses.subject: GRMN
courses.title: Theory and Practice of German Theater
courses.description: Overview of major developments in German-speaking theater. Students will be introduced to various dramaturgical models and analytic approaches (semiotic, phenomenological, social) before analyzing representative texts and performances. Theoretical insights will then be applied to the production of a play. Taught in German; readings in German and English.
courses.offeredText: Not offered on a regular basis.

courses.subject: GRMN
courses.title: German Political Songwriting: 1945 to Today
courses.description: An introduction to German political songwriting since 1945. Using songwriting to access the cultural history of the Federal Republic and the German Democratic Republic, course participants discuss sociopolitical issues such as identity, race, gender, migration, political dissent, generational conflict, and sexuality as prevalent in both Germanies at various times.
courses.course_objectives: Students will describe and understand German culture from a decentered, non-U.S. perspective. Students will analyze the history and prevalent themes of popular music and songwriting in Germany of the last 70 years. Students will interpret works of important songwriters from 1945 to today. Students will critically appraise the political ambitions of German music artists on both sides of the Iron Curtain during different periods of the Cold War. Students will improve language proficiency on the intermediate-advanced level in speaking, listening, reading, and writing. Students will analyze scholarly and journalistic writing on intercultural and historical topics. Students will conduct research for a scholarly project in the target language.
courses.topical_outline:
1. Syllabus. Introduction to the course. Overview: German-German history 1945-today. The form of the "song," songwriter and songwriter. 2. The 2000s. Afro-German Identities. Everyday racism.
Readings: Tyron Ricketts, "Afrodeutsch" (song lyrics), Dirke on Hip Hop Made in Germany 3. The 2000s. Turkish-German Identities. Female gender roles, "Gangstas" and "Kanakstas"
Readings: Song lyrics by Aziza-A, Eko Fresh, and Ebru Düzgn (Ebow), SPIEGEL article on Guest Workers 4. The 2000s. Debates around normalization of history and national pride.

courses.subject: GRMN
courses.title: Goethe and Islam
courses.description: The influence of Islam on Goethe was profound. This course examines various literary responses, such as his "Mahomets Gesang" or the "West-östlicher Divan"; considers how Islamic and Qur'anic thought is reflected elsewhere in his oeuvre; and investigates Muslim responses to Goethe (especially that of Muh. Iqbal). Taught in German.

courses.subject: GRMN
courses.title: The Language and Literature of the German-American Experience
courses.description: Exploration of the language, culture, and autochthonous literature of German-Americans during the peak years of German immigration to the U.S. in the 19th and early 20th centuries. Central themes include bilingualism, cultural contact, and the duality of identity inherent in the immigrant experience. Taught in German.
courses.course_objectives: Students will gain an understanding of the history of German immigration to the United States, and of the social, cultural, and political institutions established by German Americans in the United States. Students will gain understanding of the language and literary tradition of German Americans, during the 19th and early 20th centuries. Students will benefit from a broad overview of the theoretical approaches and experimental methods to studying language maintenance or language shift, as caused by language-external factors. Students will engage with primary demographic sources used to reconstruct contemporary German American social, cultural, and political institutions, including German-language literature, newspapers, travel logs, meeting minutes, court records, and audio corpora that represent contemporary language use; and German-language ego documents (diaries, letters, personal ledgers). Students will analyze evidence of German English bilingualism, including dialect influence, the effects of standard language ideology, cross-linguistic transfer, and also independent linguistic innovations. Students will identify and analyze cross-cultural differences between German Americans and their Yankee neighbors, through contemporary literature and meta-linguistic discourse, and apply these historical cultural lessons to modern (cross-)cultural contexts.
courses.topical_outline: 1.	Introduction: Emigration and Immigration 2.	(European) German Perspectives on America 3.	Anti-immigrant Sentiment 4.	The World Wars 5.	The Temperance Movement 6.	German-American Dual Identity: Language and Citizenship 7.	Assimilation and Post-vernacularity 8.	Modern Analogs: Spanish in the Americas and Turkish in Germany

courses.subject: GRMN
courses.title: Germany and the French Revolution
courses.description: The political and literary reception of the French Revolution in Germany. Includes representative literature of German classicism, travelogues and journalistic writings by German Jacobins, and political and sociological essays from 1775 to 1806. Focuses on the relationship between politics and aesthetics. Taught in German.

courses.subject: GRMN
courses.title: The Holocaust in German Literature and Film
courses.description: Literary and cinematic representations of the Holocaust from post-war to contemporary Germany. Topics include: artistic versus historical truth, moral and ethical dimensions, representation in different media. Additional readings address the social, political, and cultural significance of the Holocaust in German society. Taught in German.

courses.subject: GRMN
courses.title: 20th- and 21st-Century Texts and Contexts
courses.description: Significant works, authors, topics, genres, or movements in 20th-and 21st-century literature examined within their specifichistorical contexts.

courses.subject: GRMN
courses.title: Special Topics in German Studies or Linguistics
courses.description: Intensive reading and study of a genre, period, or topic.

courses.subject: GRMN
courses.title: Senior Seminar
courses.description: Capstone course for German majors, minors, and advanced students. Selected topics in German literature and culture. Required for German majors.
courses.course_objectives: Students will engage in the German language at an advanced level in speaking, reading, writing, and listening. Students will understand, analyze, and critically evaluate texts, films, and other authentic German-language media on the seminar topic. Students will discuss contemporary debates and issues related to the seminar topic. Students will develop a project (individual or group) with a formal oral and written presentation as an experiential aspect of the student's intellectual engagement with the course topic.
courses.topical_outline: Explores in German at an advanced level a topic of representative importance within the field of German studies and/or for a broad understanding of German culture

courses.subject: GRMN
courses.title: Elective Affinities:  Literature and Philosophy in Dialogue (Honors)
courses.description: Since time immemorial, literary writers and philosophers haveengaged in an intense dialogue and intellectual exchange.  Howhave the discourses of literature, poetry, and philosophymutually influenced and complemented each other?  Figuresconsidered may include Plato, Kleist, Hoelderlin, Kierkegaard,Schopenhauer, Nietzsche, Kafka, Hesse, Arendt, Adorno, Celan andGadamer.  Taught in English.

courses.subject: GRMN
courses.title: Vienna: Literature, Art, Music, Culture
courses.description: The golden age of Viennese culture, from the fin-de-siecleliterature of the cafes to the rise of expressionism, theinfluence of psychoanalysis, and the ravages of the war. Figuresconsidered include: Mozart, Schubert, the Strauss dynasty,Schnitzler, Hofmannsthal, Mahler, Freud, Wittengenstein, Kafka,Altenberg, Polgar, Trakl, Kraus and Musil. Taught in German.

courses.subject: GRMN
courses.title: Image and Word: Reading Culture Through the Visual Arts
courses.description: An exploration of various stages of German and Austrian culturethrough the visual arts.  Attuned to the relation between wordand image, we interpret exemplary paintings, poetry and prosefrom the rich German and Austrian artistic traditions.  Figures: Duerer, Friedrich, Klimt, Lasker-Schueler, Schiele, Kokoschka,Kiefer, Beuys, Hoech, Rilke, Celan, and Richter. Taught in German.

courses.subject: GRMN
courses.title: Historical Sociolinguistics
courses.description: Provides an overview of the extra-linguistic factors that affect language use in historical languages; provides anintroduction to conducting sociolinguistic inquiry on linguisticvarieties for which direct linguistic evidence is limited. Emphasis is placed on quantifiable methods for correlating extra-linguistic factors with observable changes in language useover time. Taught in English.
courses.prerequisiteText: LING 4690/6690 or LING(ANTH) 4860/6860 or permission of department | Graduate Prerequisite | Graduate student standing

courses.subject: GRMN
courses.title: Internship
courses.description: Designed for students interning at a company with a German-speaking working environment. Students apply and deepen their German language skills and cultural knowledge while gaining hands-on work experience in a professional work/business environment.
courses.prerequisiteText: GRMN 3010 or GRMN 3015 or permission of department

courses.subject: GRMN
courses.title: Contemporary Issues in German Business and Politics
courses.description: Builds detailed, specialized knowledge of cutting-edge issues in contemporary German/European public and corporate life. Current events and student-teacher consensus will determine thematic foci. Intended to foster competence in reading "newspaper" German and development of a good formal written style with emphasis on rhetoric and idioms. Taught in German.
courses.course_objectives: Students will demonstrate knowledge on a variety of topics in German society and current events, politics, the economy, international affairs, technology, and culture that are of general interest to the German public today. Students will navigate a variety of German online news sources to investigate current events topics in Germany. Students will demonstrate confidence, clarity, and fluency in spoken German. Students will illustrate skills in written German and demonstrate a critical understanding of current events topics. Students will comprehend and utilize high-frequency verbs and nouns and technical terms relevant to recent developments in politics, the economy, business, international affairs, society, culture, and technology in Germany. Students will lead in-depth discussions on the current events topic researched as a final project for the class.
courses.topical_outline:
Parliamentary democracy
German political parties
Globalization vs. German national and regional interests
Globalization and German culture
Germany's media reporting of domestic and global current events
Migration in Germany and political responses 
German youth culture
Major German companies and international mergers

courses.subject: GRMN
courses.title: Survey of German Literature and Film
courses.description: Concise overview of German literary history and the history ofGerman film.

courses.subject: GRMN
courses.title: Medieval German Courtly Literature
courses.description: Representative narrative texts from the classical period ofMiddle High German literature (c. 1150-1250). Focus on Arthurianromance as both the paradigmatic genre of medieval aristocraticself-representation and the prototype of the modern European novel.

courses.subject: GRMN
courses.title: Early Modern German Literature, 1400-1700
courses.description: Broad overview of German literature from approximately 1400 to1700, including Neo-Latin writings by German authors. Readingsfrom Humanism, Reformation, and Baroque represent the developmentof forms and aesthetics within the historical and cultural context.

courses.subject: GRMN
courses.title: 18th-Century Texts and Contexts
courses.description: Significant works, authors, movements, genres, or topics in18th-century literature and culture examined within theirspecific historical context.
courses.offeredText: Not offered on a regular basis.

courses.subject: GRMN
courses.title: Classics and Romantics
courses.description: Interpretation and analysis of works from the late 18th through early 19th centuries considered in their social, cultural, andhistorical contexts. Studies of individual authors, specificgenres, significant topics, or literary constellations.

courses.subject: GRMN
courses.title: 19th-Century Texts and Contexts
courses.description: Significant works, authors, movements, genres, or topics in 19th-century literature and culture examined within theirspecific historical contexts.

courses.subject: GRMN
courses.title: The Fin-de-Siecle: Its Roots and Aftermath
courses.description: What cultural, social, and political conditions gave rise to the fin-de-siecle spirit in the 19th and 20th centuries? Placing the phenomenon in a comparative context, this seminar explores theperiod's vibrant literature, its arts (Jugendstil), and the riseof crucial intellectual movements (psychoanalysis, relativism,aestheticism), including their persistence in the present.

courses.subject: GRMN
courses.title: German Gothic Literature
courses.description: Broad overview of the development of Gothic horror literature in Germany from the 18th to the 20th century in its historical and cultural contexts. Study of 18th- and early 19th-century aesthetic theory, which inspired German authors of horror literature. Given in German.

courses.title: Master's Research
courses.description: Research while enrolled for a master's degree under the direction of faculty members.

courses.title: Graduate Student Seminar
courses.description: Advanced supervised experience in an applied setting.  Thiscourse may not be used to satisfy a student's approved program ofstudy.

courses.subject: GRMN
courses.title: Master's Thesis
courses.description: Thesis writing under the direction of the major professor.

courses.subject: GRMN
courses.title: Teaching with Technology
courses.description: Professional development in language pedagogy with a focus onenhancing teaching through technology. Assessment of howtechnologies can enrich student learning and be effectivelyintegrated into syllabi and curricula.

courses.subject: GRMN
courses.title: Directed Reading and/or Projects
courses.description: Individual study, reading, or project under the direction of a project director.

courses.subject: GRMN
courses.title: German Cinema
courses.description: History of German cinema; investigation of particular directors,periods, and styles; relationship between German and othernational cinemas. The course includes a required weekly filmscreening.

courses.subject: GRMN
courses.title: Proseminar: Text and Interpretation
courses.description: An introduction to German literary studies. Techniques and methods of interpretation of literary works. Topics include:genres and literary periodization, literary theories, researchmethods.

courses.subject: GRMN
courses.title: Seminar in German Literature
courses.description: Intensive investigation of a particular genre, theme, topic, or author.

courses.subject: GRMN
courses.title: Seminar in German Studies
courses.description: Intensive investigation of a particular theme or topic.

courses.subject: GRNT(HPAM)
courses.title: Economics of Aging
courses.description: An overview of the economics of aging from a multidisciplinary perspective. We examine the consequences of population aging globally. Topics include demographics, economic status of elders, labor market activity, retirement, intergenerational conflict, private and public pensions, and an evaluation of current income and health policies for elders.

courses.subject: GRNT
courses.title: Aspects of Aging
courses.description: An overview of aging from the biological, psychological, social, and economic perspectives. We will discuss the factors involved in adjustments to the aging process and cover topics including retirement, race/ethnicity, global aging, family, death and bereavement, finances, sexuality, and health. Students will critically examine their own perceptions on aging.
courses.course_objectives:
Student will be able to provide an overview of the field of gerontology across majority and under-represented populations. Student will be able to articulate and discuss the major themes, challenges, and issues in aging across cultures. Student will be familiar with the physical, social, and psychological attributes that identify the multidisciplinary approach to aging.
in developed nations Student will have insight into their own perceptions and judgments on aging and how culture and society influence these. Student will be able to analyze how diversity influences the aging process. Student will be able to examine the intersection of age, gender, class, and race/ethnicity on political, social, cultural, and economic issues of society. Student will be able to understand global aging by assessing the importance of the country/cultural context on aging. Student will be able to discuss the portrayal of aging (especially minority elders and women) in the media and evaluate how this influences their own perception of aging.
courses.topical_outline: Demographics of aging Ageism Global Aging Health Promotion for older adults Physical aging/Chronic conditions Mental health and aging Caregiving Social supports Death, dying, and bereavement Minority Aging Public policies for older adults Intersection of age, gender, class, and race/ethnicity

courses.subject: GRNT
courses.title: Diversity in Aging: A Service-Learning Experience
courses.description: Service-learning and critical reflection will be used to apply theory and explore the diversity of lived experiences, challenges, strengths, and opportunities present in older age.

courses.subject: GRNT
courses.title: Diversity in Aging: A Service-Learning Experience
courses.description: Service-learning and critical reflection will be used to apply theory and explore the diversity of lived experiences, challenges, strengths, and opportunities present in older age.

courses.subject: GRNT
courses.title: Medical Care of Older Adults
courses.description: Course introduces students to medical care for older adults, focusing on unique health needs, care models, and age-related challenges in healthcare.
courses.course_objectives: Students will learn to describe the basic physical and cognitive changes with aging. Students will learn to identify and explain various healthcare models tailored to the needs of older adults. Students will learn to analyze the social, economic, and environmental factors that impact health outcomes in older adults. Students will learn to develop strategies to support autonomy and informed decision-making for older patients. Students will learn to describe effective management approaches for common chronic conditions affecting older adults. Students will learn to develop effective communication skills tailored to interacting with older adults, their families, and interdisciplinary care teams.
courses.topical_outline: Fundamentals of physical and cognitive changes with aging Understanding Key Care Models Ageism in Healthcare Promoting Autonomy in Aging Ethical Advocacy Social Determinants of Health Management of Chronic Conditions and Caring for Comorbidities Addressing Polypharmacy Addressing Cognitive Health Needs Ensuring Safety in Care Supporting Family and Caregiver Needs Integrating End-of-Life Care Principles Cultural Competency in Gerontology Effective Communication Skills
courses.prerequisiteText: BIOL 1103 or BIOL 1103E or BIOL 2103H or BIOL 1107 or BIOL 1107E or BIOL 2107H

courses.subject: GRNT
courses.title: End of Life and Aging
courses.description: Provides a foundation for understanding death, dying, and bereavement, with a focus on older adults. We will examine the end of life in the socio-cultural, interpersonal, and public health context. Foundational knowledge will be applied to current controversies.
courses.course_objectives: Students will learn to summarize the major theories of death and dying. Students will learn to examine societal attitudes toward death. Students will learn to categorize the dying process, specifically as it relates to older adults. Students will learn to evaluate end of life care in the context of the healthcare system and the legal system. Students will learn to analyze how the diversity of ethnicity, religious preferences, gender, culture, and other factors affect the perspectives, attitudes, practices, and experiences of individuals and their families at the end of life.

courses.title: Early Life Influences on Aging
courses.description: An in-depth exploration of how early life events and experiences during critical periods of development lead to outcomes of health and well-being or disease in later life. Includes discussion of the accumulation of social determinants of health across the lifespan and at sensitive periods in development.

courses.subject: GRNT
courses.title: Global Aging
courses.description: The world is aging, but the experiences of aging vary across the globe. The purpose of this course is to compare and contrast aging across the globe through macro perspectives and micro perspectives. We will incorporate concepts from public health, policy, sociology, and demography to examine gerontology across the globe.

courses.description: The systems, structures, and behaviors that support and promote health across the lifespan; focuses on health from pre-natal development through older age.

courses.subject: GRNT
courses.title: Health Communication and Aging
courses.description: Principles of health communication for older adult consumers of information. Includes medical communication, health literacy, medical decision-making, and strategies for improving communication.
courses.course_objectives: Students will be able to describe age-related changes in sensory systems that can affect communication. courses.title: Cognition and the Aging Brain
courses.description: Introduction to changes in cognitive function across the lifespan, with corresponding changes in neurological structures and behaviors that promote cognitive vitality.
courses.course_objectives: Students will identify the basic parts of the nervous system and basic brain structure. Students will describe how the brain supports the various behaviors that support activities of daily living. Students will discuss the ways in which the brain changes with age and the degree to which neurological aging impacts behavior. Students will examine the ways in which cognition changes with age. Students will identify a set of public health evidence for aging populations that promote cognitive vitality. Students will critique the evidence supporting behaviors that promote cognitive vitality.

courses.description: The epidemiology, biology, clinical characteristics, treatment, and public health implications of Alzheimer’s disease and related dementias among older adults.
courses.course_objectives: Students will learn to differentiate amongst the term's symptoms, clinical syndromes, and etiologies for neurodegenerative diseases. Students will learn to describe the epidemiology of Alzheimer’s disease and related dementias. Students will learn to identify neuropathological changes associated with neurodegenerative diseases. Students will learn to discuss the public health implications of neurodegenerative diseases.

courses.description: A course for the advanced undergraduate who wishes to participate in supervised research and/or clinical experience.
courses.course_objectives: Students will be able to explain pertinent theories and empirical research in the student's area(s) of interest. Students will be able to formulate conceptual hypotheses that guide research. Students will be able to design a basic, methodologically sound research project. Students will be able to demonstrate skills necessary to conduct empirical research (e.g., data entry, coding, transcribing, survey design, scientific writing, ethical participant recruitment). Students will be able to employ best practices in professionalism when working with older adults in a research and/or clinical setting. Students will be able to use HIPAA rules and regulations when working with protected health information. Students will be able to generate an IRB proposal for a research study. Students will be able to create educational materials (e.g., brochures, infographics, handouts, guides) for dissemination in the community that follow best practices in health education and accessibility. Students will be able to propose and adapt SMART goals to ensure project deadlines are met. Students will be able to demonstrate skills necessary to effectively work on a collaborative project (e.g., giving and/or receiving constructive feedback in a respectful and supportive manner; communicating with team members in a professional, respectful, clear, and timely manner). Students will be able to implement clinic policies and procedures when conducting clinical tasks.
courses.topical_outline: The format for this course is nontraditional and topics will vary; therefore, the course will address 3-5 of the above learning objectives depending on the students' particular project and experiential learning interests.

courses.subject: GRNT
courses.title: Early Life Influences on Aging
courses.description: An in-depth exploration of how early life events and experiences during critical periods of development lead to outcomes of health and well-being or disease in later life. Includes discussion of the accumulation of social determinants of health across the lifespan and at sensitive periods in development.
courses.course_objectives: Students will be able to interpret health outcomes in later life from a developmental trajectory perspective. Students will be able to evaluate the scholarly evidence for early life influences on health in later stages of life. Students will be able to compare and contrast normative developmental stages across the lifespan, including how their disruption impacts health in older adulthood. Students will be able to evaluate current public health initiatives with regard to how effectively they address determinants of health from a lifespan health-development perspective. Students will be able to assess interventions aimed at reducing adversity and/or increasing resilience with reference to structural inequality and the macro systems within which they are implemented. Students will be able to develop an intervention to either decrease adversity or increase resilience for a particularly vulnerable group.
courses.topical_outline:
Defining Health:
1. Reductionist vs. holistic models
2. Overview of a life-course health-development framework Early Life Development:
1. Historical context of developmental science
2. Applying a developmental framework to health
3. Basics of prenatal development
4. Developmental origins of health and disease (DoHaD) model
5. Infancy and early childhood cognitive, social, and emotional development
6. Attachment as a foundational piece of lifespan health development
7. Fetal origins of major adult health diseases – e.g., CVD, diabetes (including mental health)
8. Prenatal programming of weight set point and metabolism Adversity and Resilience:
1. The biology of stress and resilience
2. Influence of relationships with early caregivers on health and wellbeing across the lifespan
3. Adverse Childhood Events (ACEs) and adult physiological and mental health
4. Lifespan stress and stigma as threats to health
5. Interventions for resilience and prevention of ACEs
6. Social and cultural contributions to resilience across the lifespan
7. Resilience and aging well Never Stop Developing:
1. Adult development as a continuation of early life development
2. Relationships
3. Identity
4. Cognition
5. Sensation and perception

courses.description: The goal of this community-based research course is to provide students with an overview of theories, principles, and strategies associated with Community-Based Participatory Research (CBPR) within the context of public health and lifespan health. CBPR is an approach to conducting research to address community-level needs.
courses.course_objectives: Students will be able to assess and articulate the value of community organization engagement in research and evaluation. Students will be able to identify strengths and limitations in community-based research, including scientific and ethical strengths and limitations. Students will be able to critique peer review journal articles related to the fidelity and scientific-contributions of community-based research principles, process, and implementation. Students will be able to apply the basic steps in community engaged research: collaborative identification of community need, conception of research questions, identification of data collection instruments (qualitative and quantitative), and collaborative data analysis and dissemination (with community partners).

courses.subject: GRNT
courses.title: Death, Dying, and Bereavement
courses.description: Provides a foundation for understanding death, dying, and bereavement, with a focus on older adults. We will examine the end of life in the socio-cultural, interpersonal, and public health context. Foundational knowledge will be applied to current controversies.
courses.course_objectives: Students will learn to summarize the major theories of death and dying. Students will learn to examine societal attitudes of death. Students will learn to categorize the dying process, specifically as it relates to older adults. Students will learn to examine the end of life in the context of the healthcare system and the legal system. Students will learn to analyze how the diversity of ethnicity, religious preferences, gender, culture, and other factors affect the perspectives, attitudes, practices, and experiences of individuals and their families at the end of life. Students will learn to analyze classic and current research and theories about death, dying, and bereavement. Students will learn to apply theories and evidence-based practice to current issues in death and dying. Students will learn to evaluate and debate ethical issues at the end of life.
courses.topical_outline: Meaning of death and societal attitudes about the end of life Theories of death and dying Historical and philosophical perspectives of the end of life Cross cultural death, dying, and bereavement rituals The principles of palliative care End of life and the healthcare systems End of life and the legal system Epidemiology and patterns of care at the end of life Controversies in the end of life

courses.subject: GRNT
courses.title: Women and Aging: Biological, Social, and Psychological Perspective
courses.description: Examination of the multi-dimensional impacts of aging on women, incorporating biological, social, and psychological perspectives. Students will gain comprehensive insights into the aging process, its physiological change, and psychological societal implications. This content will specifically focus on the unique experiences and challenges faced by women as they age.
courses.course_objectives: Summarize key demographic trends related to aging and gender. Explain the multi-system physiological changes (endocrine, skeletal, cognitive, immunological, etc) that women experience during the aging process. Apply knowledge of societal expectations and cultural factors to analyze the impact on the aging experience of women in various cultures. Analyze the role of gender disparities in science and medicine, focusing on how they affect access to healthcare and health outcomes for aging women. Analyze the economic challenges faced by older women, considering gender-specific factors such as the gender pay gap and caregiving responsibilities. Critically review empirical evidence on women’s aging to identify gaps in knowledge, and propose new research questions or areas of investigation. Develop strategies to enhance the overall well-being of aging women, considering the social, psychological, and biological aspects of aging.
courses.topical_outline: Overview of the demographic trends and statistical data related to aging and gender Historical perspectives on women's roles and expectations in different societies and their implications on aging Understanding the multi-system physiological changes and health challenges experienced by aging women Hormonal changes, menopause, and their impacts on health and well-being Understanding common health issues in aging women and preventive measures Behavioral strategies for improving health and wellbeing Social roles, expectations, and stereotypes affecting aging women Mental health issues, coping strategies, and resilience in older women Intersectionality: Considering factors like race, ethnicity, and socioeconomic status in aging experiences Social support, caregiving, and intergenerational relationships Aging, sexuality, and body image

courses.subject: GRNT
courses.title: Professional Practice in Neuropsychology and Aging
courses.description: Course covers key neuropsychology principles with a focus on aging. Case-based learning will prepare students for clinical internship, fellowship, and entry-level independent practice. Topics include brain-behavior relations in aging, cognitive assessment and diagnostic formulation, intervention strategies, and the roles/impacts of laboratory, imaging, medications, and comorbidities on cognitive aging.
courses.course_objectives: Students will learn to discuss the ethical and legal considerations in neuropsychological practice, with a focus on aging populations. Students will learn to apply psychometric concepts to real world scenarios. Students will learn to collaborate effectively in interdisciplinary teams, integrating neuropsychological findings with laboratory results, imaging, and biomarkers. Students will learn to identify appropriate referral pathways for genetic testing, medication management, and other specialty interventions in neuropsychology. Students will learn to conduct thorough case conceptualizations that address differential diagnosis, sociocultural factors, and medical comorbidities. Students will learn to formulate treatment recommendations that align with both clinical findings and sociocultural considerations in neuropsychology. Students will develop skills in professional negotiation for job offers, contracts, and work conditions in neuropsychology.

This course will be taught by one instructor, usually the ILS Graduate Coordinator, during the first seven weeks of the fall semester. Instructional materials will include, but not be limited to, the primary scientific literature, other published articles or written material, online resources, and videos.

courses.subject: GRSC
courses.title: Critical Reading of the Primary Scientific Literature
courses.description: Designed to teach entering graduate students how to deconstruct and understand primary scientific literature at a level of awareness needed for becoming successful graduate students and professional scientists, and in a manner that fosters critical thinking skills. Topics emphasize both foundational and emerging topics across the breadth of research in the Integrated Life Sciences (ILS) program.
courses.course_objectives: The primary literature is the primary medium of scientific communication. The ability to effectively access the literature in diverse fields within Life Sciences is essential for the ability to pursue research projects in whatever direction they may lead. First-year ILS graduate students will be introduced to the primary research literature through the in-depth analysis of papers selected from across the breadth of the ILS program. This analysis will include discussions of all aspects of the selected papers both in student-only groups and in class groups led by faculty members, as well as student-led discussions and presentations and weekly writing assignments. The successful student will be able to read the primary scientific literature and be able to summarize and convey their analysis to a small group, both in writing and orally.
courses.topical_outline:
Students will read and discuss papers in multiple areas of research within the scope of the ILS program, as determined by the participating departmental and interdisciplinary research groups within ILS. 

Research in the ILS-affiliated departments and institute-based graduate programs includes (but is not limited to) the following areas: Biochemistry, molecular biology, genetics, genomics, bioinformatics, cellular biology, immunology and infectious diseases, neuroscience, plant biology, evolutionary biology, microbiology, pharmacology, and environmental and ecosystem studies. Each week, the students will investigate papers that may encompass one or more of these areas. Papers are selected to both provide grounding in key concepts in each field, as well as to provide an introduction to the breadth and diversity of the scientific literature, and to highlight emerging concepts and topics of research. The primary goal of the course is to develop skills in critical reading of the primary literature.

This course will be taught in the fall semester in sections of 10-15 students. Each section is taught by two instructors, usually from two different departments within the ILS program. Instructors are paired with the goal of providing diversity in research areas and complementary approaches to scientific research. Instructional materials will be primary articles and review articles taken from the scientific literature. 

This topical outline is the general plan for the course; the exact order and specific papers assigned for each lecture will be announced to the class in advance by the instructor.

courses.subject: GRSC
courses.title: Experiential Professional Development Graduate Internship
courses.description: This course allows graduate students to integrate their academic learning with the development of practical knowledge and skills through supervised work in a professional setting. Permission of the Graduate School as well as the student’s faculty advisor is required.
courses.course_objectives: Students will gain hands-on experience in a professional field in organizational settings, such as higher education, industry, government, or the non-profit sector. Students will work in settings that demonstrate the ways in which graduate training can be applied to meet the needs of the host organization. Students will participate in structured mentoring activities that broaden exposure to potential career paths in the host organization beyond the scope of the intern’s immediate work duties. Students will integrate new professional experiences into their educational program through reflective activities. Students will consider meaningful insights for future growth as highlighted by the internship experience. Students will broaden their professional networks to include individuals in career paths beyond traditional academic roles.
courses.topical_outline:
Specific responsibilities and activities for the internship will be determined by the host organization, with
consideration given to the goals and qualifications of the student intern. Students will complete a Learning Contract with the host organization, outlining clear objectives and expected outcomes of the internship. Students will provide a written report at the end of the internship experience detailing:
a. Progress towards objectives in the learning contract;
b. Impact of the internship experience on career planning/goals; and
c. Anticipated next steps towards their career goals. The Graduate School will encourage host sites to develop internship experiences which include some routine tasks but must also involve higher-order duties that align with graduate-level skillsets and provide students with broader exposure to the field. Host units must also commit to providing the student with structured mentorship during the internship, with the aim of fostering learning above and beyond the supervisory relationship. A range of activities may satisfy this requirement, such as formal trainings, informational interviews, weekly check-in meetings, shadowing experiences, exploratory projects, guided readings, and so on. A reasonable expectation is that roughly 10-15% of the student’s time is devoted to these types of activities.

Students will complete oral work geared towards promoting effective communications in day-to-day situations and functional tasks Students will improve their oral proficiency by focusing on using the proper rendition of the language Students will increase their reading proficiency by completing authentic readings of gradually increasing complexity including some literary texts Students will expand their cultural knowledge through more detailed and nuanced cultural discussions
courses.topical_outline: Feelings and emotions - Direct and indirect questions Conditionals Simple and complex verb formations Adverbs and adverbial expressions Repetition and reduplication Tense variations Hausa music and songs Comparatives and superlatives Personal names and titles Ceremonies and their preparations Simple proverbs and poems Weekly Course Outline will be provided as well as the assignments and exercises for the week and their due dates. The readings will be distributed throughout the course, and taken mainly from Nigerian/Hausa textbooks, newspapers, and creative writings.

courses.subject: HDFS
courses.title: Lifespan Development
courses.description: Physical, cognitive, social, and emotional development of individuals from conception to the end of life from ecological and life-span perspectives.
courses.course_objectives: Students will use core concepts, integrative elements, and cross-cutting themes as they learn to identify major developmental changes, behaviors, and issues during infancy, childhood, adolescence, adulthood, and later life (e.g., factors influencing development, physical, cognitive, and socioemotional development) that promote individual well-being and optimal development. Students will use core concepts, integrative elements, and cross-cutting themes as they learn to reflect on and explain how individual (e.g., race, religion, ethnicity, gender, and class) and social factors influence development and how family, community, societal, and historical contexts contribute to developmental outcomes (e.g., ecological systems) as you consider, engage, and analyze opposing viewpoints or arguments. Students will use core concepts, integrative elements, and cross-cutting themes as they learn to think critically about the knowledge gained in class to address contextual and societal issues and to apply this knowledge to your own personal and professional development and to the lives of others. You will support your own conclusion, decision, or action with sound reasoning and judgment.
courses.topical_outline:
Each major section will illustrate aspects of development for infants, children, adolescents, and mid-and later-life adults within an ecological framework, including family influences, and incorporate theory, research methods, application, and cultural diversity issues. 1. Introduction to Life-Span Development 
a. Overview
b. Research Methods
c. Theories
d. Influence of Socio-contextual factors on development (e.g., race, religion, ethnicity, gender, and class)  
e. Mutual influence of physical, cognitive, and socioemotional development across the lifespan 2. Factors Influencing Development
a. Genes, Environment, Evolution   
b. Gene-environment Interaction and Heritability  
c. Early Environmental Influences on Development-- Prenatal, Perinatal, Early Postnatal 3. Physical Development  
a. Endocrine and Nervous Systems, Brain Development 
b. Growth, Fine and Gross Motor, Coordination, Strength, Endurance, Speed  
c. Reproduction   
d. Health and Safety Issues (e.g., Impact of Physical Health on Behavior, Developmental Stages) 4. Cognitive Development   
a. Perception and Attention   
b. Cognition and Language   
c. Learning, Memory, and Information Processing   
d. Intelligence and Creativity (e.g., Cognitive Development Theories, Neurodevelopmental Factors, Brain development during childhood and adolescence , Effects of trauma on cognitive and emotional growth, Neuroplasticity and its implications for recovery) 5. Social-Emotional Development   
a. Self-concept/Identity, Personality, and Temperament   
b. Gender Roles and Sexuality   
c. Social Cognition and Moral Development   
d. Attachment and Social Relationships   
e. The Family   
f. Achievement (e.g., Social Environment: How socio-economic status, peer relationships, and community resources influence behavioral health. The impact of social isolation and support systems.) 6. Promoting Well-being in the Midst of During Challenges   
a. Psychological Disorders   
b. Risk, Coping, and Resilience   
d. Death and Dying

courses.subject: HDFS
courses.title: Research Unlocked: Skills for Understanding and Applying HDFS
courses.description: An introduction to research in the field of Human Development and Family Science and the skills necessary for understanding and interpreting research, as well as integrating research into writing across the curriculum.
courses.course_objectives: Across all content, students will learn to write for the discipline. Students will demonstrate an understanding of the contribution of original research in human development. Students will explain the strengths and weaknesses of various research methods in assessing human behavior. Students will successfully locate, read, and summarize published research related to a given topic. Students will distinguish between qualitative and quantitative paradigms of research. Students will distinguish between types of measurement and causal relationships. Students will critically evaluate the adequacy of a scientific study’s sampling, measurement, and design. Students will critically consume scientific research to make and defend evidenced-based interpretations. Students will compile components of empirical research articles for summary and synthesize research in a literature review.
courses.topical_outline: Course introduction Why does research matter? Finding, reading, and evaluating empirical sources Ethical principles in research Types of research: Qualitative, Quantitative, and Evaluation Sampling basics: Who participates in research studies? Measurement Basics and Causal Relationships: surveys, observations, etc. Statistics Basics: Basic probability and statistical significance Data visualization: Making sense of tables and figures Drawing conclusions from the data Research Implications What happens next? Literature Review

courses.subject: HDFS
courses.title: Professional Development for Careers in Human Development and Family Science
courses.description: Students will learn about the professional and academic fields and study of human development and family science.
courses.course_objectives: Students will be able to identify scholarly strengths and contributions of HDFS faculty to the field. Students will understand how to assess career paths related to HDFS experiential learning. Students will be able to identify professional skills and competencies practiced in the HDFS field as a practitioner/scholar.
courses.topical_outline: What is HDFS as a field? History and legacy of human development History and origins of family science Current and future trends of human development Current and future trends of family science Career paths, including the professional skills and competencies practiced in the HDFS field as a practitioner/scholar

courses.subject: HDFS
courses.title: Self and Society: Identity and Human Flourishing
courses.description: The examination of the ways in which contexts interact with individual and social identities and how those interactions influence life trajectories across the life course in human and family development.
courses.course_objectives: Students will learn to identify how the interaction of context and identity influence individual and family life trajectories and outcomes. Students will learn to apply theoretical perspectives to the course content. Students will explore the social significance and intersection of personal and family identities. Students will consider the implications of course content for research, policy, and practice.
courses.topical_outline: Individual and social identities across the life course Cycle of socialization and understanding social identities Theoretical perspectives on how our personal identities interact at the individual, societal/institutional, and cultural levels Implications of cumulative advantage and disadvantage for human flourishing Implications for research, policy, and practice

courses.subject: HDFS
courses.title: Human Sexuality Across the Life Span
courses.description: Students will learn how to define human sexuality and identifyand analyze attitudes and diverse perspectives based onsubstantive and theoretical information, with emphasis on howdevelopment and interactions across the life span are affected byfamilial, social, cultural, and psychological factors.
courses.course_objectives: Students will be able to describe human sexual development (physical, cognitive, and socioemotional), behavior, and attitudes across the lifespan. Students will understand how diverse sexual belief systems influenced by race, ethnicity, class, gender, sexual orientation, and religion influence the expression of human sexuality in families, intimate relationships, and societies. Students will know how to examine and discuss sensitive issues related to diverse behaviors, coercion, and sex for commercial purposes. Students will know how to communicate openly and effectively about issues related to human sexuality. Students will know how to make responsible sexual decisions.
courses.topical_outline:
Defining human sexuality by reflecting and examining how diverse sexual belief systems influenced by race, ethnicity, class, gender, sexual orientation, and religion influence the expression of human sexuality in families, intimate relationships, and societies.
