courses.subject: HDFS
courses.title: Introduction to Behavioral Health
courses.description: The psychological, social, and biological factors that contribute to mental and behavioral health, as well as the strategies for intervention, prevention, and treatment will be addressed. You will learn about behavioral health principles, ethical practices in behavioral health, and skills and attitudes needed to promote well-being in individuals and communities.
courses.course_objectives:
Students will integrate concepts of behavioral health into prevention and intervention strategies grounded in ethical and evidenced-based practices within the healthcare field. 
a. Recognize ethical issues and apply different ethical perspectives to ethical dilemmas in a variety of settings. 
b. Reflect upon how one's social identities and roles shape one’s worldview and interactions Students will develop knowledge, skills, and attitudes in interdisciplinary collaboration and holistic approaches to behavioral health care. Students will simultaneously develop personal and professional skills to support your own well-being and mitigate burnout.
courses.topical_outline: Introduction to behavioral health within the context of human development and family systems Ethical practices in behavioral health Mechanisms of behavioral change Prevention and intervention science Self-of-the-provider and clinician well-being Collaborative care Behavioral health, disability, and neurodistinct-ness Human flourishing within diverse settings

courses.subject: HDFS
courses.title: Substance Use and Other Addictive Behaviors within Family Systems
courses.description: Diagnosis, treatment, and recovery of substance use, and other addictive behaviors will be addressed through biological, psychological, and family science theories. Emphasizing a holistic, person-centered approach, it covers stigma, ethics, and cultural factors, equipping students with practical skills to support individuals and families in clinical, community, and healthcare settings.
courses.course_objectives: Students will apply key concepts, theories, and evidenced-based practices in behavioral health within the context of the prevention and intervention of substance use disorders and other addictive behaviors. Students will understand the biological, psychological, social, and other contextual factors that contribute to the development, progression, prevention, and intervention of substance use disorders and other addictive behaviors in individuals and families. Students will develop ethical practices based on awareness of social stigma and cultural considerations, grounded in holistic person-centered approaches that support individuals and families through their journey towards long-term health. Students will strengthen your professional skills in clinical and community settings to address behavioral health needs and challenges related to substance use disorders and other addictive behaviors in order to support individuals and their families.
courses.topical_outline: Prevention and early intervention strategies with individuals and families Define substance use disorders and other addictive behaviors (e.g., diagnostic criteria, risk factors, etc.) Familial, cultural, socioeconomic, and environmental factors of substance use disorders, addictive behaviors, and recovery Discuss social narratives, assumptions, and expectations around substance use disorders, addictive behaviors, and recovery Practice creating a nonjudgmental, supportive therapeutic environment Ethical challenges in the treatment of substance use disorders and addictive behaviors (e.g., confidentiality, client autonomy, informed consent, etc.) Effective prevention programs and strategies for at-risk populations, including (e.g., adolescents , individuals with trauma histories, those with family histories of substance use disorders and other addictive behaviors) Early intervention and screening (e.g., reducing the long-term impact of substance use disorders, other addictive behaviors, family and community-based initiatives, policy-level interventions aimed at reducing the prevalence of addiction and promoting behavioral health, etc.) Practical communication and counseling skills for working with clients and families dealing with substance use disorders, addictive behaviors, and behavioral health issues Ethical decision-making and cultural humility in client and family interactions Reflective practices to assess and improve one's clinical competencies when working with individuals affected by substance use disorders and other addictive behaviors

courses.description: Individual and family development during middle and later years. Emphasis is on importance of physical, psychological, and social development within multigenerational relationships.
courses.course_objectives: Students will develop an understanding of the field of gerontology. Students will develop an awareness of aging within contexts of historical, biological, physiological, psychological, cultural, and social research. Students will develop an understanding of and the ability to apply gerontological theories and concepts to "real-life" situations.
courses.topical_outline: 1. Aging and agism 2. Theories, methods, and ethics in aging research 3. Aging demographics: numbers, trends and diversity in aging 4. Aging across the lifespan a. Finances and economics f. Retirement/work 5. Housing, Leisure, and the Family a. Housing/transportation b. Leisure, recreation and education c. Family and social support 6. Death and dying 7. Policies and programs

courses.subject: HDFS
courses.title: Infant and Toddler Development
courses.description: Physical, cognitive, social, and emotional development of children from prenatal development through age three.
courses.course_objectives: Students will acquire basic knowledge and recognition of the theories and principles of infants’ physical, cognitive, social, and emotional development. Students will understand the interaction between biological and environmental factors that shape growth and development through age three. Students will gain awareness about infants with variable developmental trajectories. Students will articulate the ways in which context and culture contribute to child development and recognize diverse cultural values that parents and families have for developing infants. Students will describe developmentally appropriate caregiving in infancy. Students will obtain skills in observing, recording, analyzing, and using data gathered from and about infants. Students will develop abilities in critical thinking through multiple modalities (e.g., reading, presentation, and group discussions) to become an educated consumer of scientific information about prenatal and infant development.
courses.topical_outline:
Historical and contemporary perspectives on infant development Sociocultural contexts of infant development Prenatal development Birth and the newborn Physical and motor development Brain development Cognitive and language development Social/Emotional development Parenting and caregiving Diverse developmental characteristics and pathways in prenatal development and infancy Topics specific to infancy (may include):
a. Attachment
b. Nursing and nutrition
c. Sleep
d. Maternal and child health
e. Prenatal risks
f. Parental leave

courses.subject: HDFS
courses.title: It’s Complicated:  Intimate Relationships in the 21st Century
courses.description: Students will learn how to improve their own relationships by studying the science behind relationships: the good, the bad, the ugly, and how to fix it when it is not working. Students will explore what draws people together, the processes in how they either stay together or break up, and both the advantages and disadvantages to learning how to be in a relationship in a contemporary context.
courses.course_objectives: Students will select appropriate theories and methods used to generate knowledge about intimate relationships. Students will identify and discuss the basic processes of forming and maintaining relationships. Students will discuss the process by which relationships are dissolved and enhanced. Students will prepare high-quality oral and written presentations regarding the current fund of knowledge about interpersonal relationships. Students will apply knowledge about the influences on relationships, such as gender, personality, conflict, relationship beliefs, and meaning making in relationships, as well as how power and violence are manifested in relationships.
courses.topical_outline: Couples research Theories that inform relationship science Gendered power Attraction Personality's influence on relationships Communication in couples Couple conflict Relationship beliefs Meaning making in relationships Relationship stressors Friendships Couple maintenance and interventions Dating in the digital age

courses.title: Family Policy: Bridging Theory and Practice
courses.description: Students will learn about the interdependence between familyfunctioning and public policies at the local, state, and federallevels. The course will include theoretical frameworks forconceptualizing family policy, roles professionals can play inbuilding family policy, and approaches professionals can use inimplementing these roles.
courses.course_objectives: Students will understand family policy concepts. Students will understand the challenges to developing and implementing family policies. Students will understand family policy models and theoretical frameworks. Students will understand strategies for analyzing family policies. Students will understand how to track a family policy. Students will understand how to examine the intended and unintended consequences of family policies. Students will understand how to practice using appropriate resources to investigate family policy issues.

courses.subject: HDFS
courses.title: Medical Terminology for Healthcare Professionals
courses.description: Students will learn medical terminology relevant to clinical healthcare settings and the practice of child life in hospitals. Students will learn parts of words (roots; combining forms; suffixes; prefixes) to prepare for terminology in subspecialties of pediatric healthcare and will practice using developmentally appropriate language for children of different ages.
courses.course_objectives: By the end of this course, students will demonstrate mastery of common medical terms (including diseases, treatments, and medical equipment) in pediatric healthcare. By the end of this course, students will define common medical terms in specific specialty areas of pediatric healthcare. By the end of this course, students will define common medical procedures used in pediatric healthcare. By the end of this course, students will explain medical terminology and medical procedures to children and adolescents of different ages using developmentally appropriate language.
courses.topical_outline:
I. Introduction to medical terminology II. Medical terminology for specific body systems
a. The human body

g. The digestive and urinary systems
h. The nervous system

a. Radiology unit

c. Cardiology unit
d. Hematology/oncology unit

f. Neurology unit
g. General pediatrics unit
h. Endocrine unit
i. Intensive care unit IV. Final case study and learning activity projects

courses.subject: HDFS
courses.title: Health Technology, Ethics, and Human Development
courses.description: The ways in which bioethical and human developmental theoretical perspectives and information can assist in considering the implications of medical technologies for human flourishing. An empirically driven approach to learning about new medical technologies and assessing their utility. Practical implications for those who plan to work in a medical or therapeutic field or contribute to the creation or implementation of medical or health care policy.
courses.course_objectives: Students will understand how to identify cutting edge medical technologies that have profound implications for human development. Students will understand how to evaluate the various ways in which the medical technologies present both opportunities and ethical issues/dilemmas for people. Students will understand how to apply theory to evaluate current global and domestic policies related to the medical technologies discussed. Students will understand how to deliberate individually and collaboratively, using their understanding of principles and theories of optimal human and family development, about what they believe should be society’s reaction to the advent of these new medical technologies.
courses.topical_outline:
Introduction to Moral Principles in Bioethics and Bioethical Theories Review of Relevant HDFS Theories Emerging and relevant lines of research and medicine that have implications for human development and flourishing. Selected Topics may include:
o	Artificial Reproductive Technologies (may include but not limited to: gamete harvesting and storage, pre-conception genetic testing, preimplantation genetic diagnosis/screening, embryonic transfer of mitochondrial DNA, embryo implantation choices and regulation, choices related to unused embryos through in-vitro fertilization, collaborative reproduction and surrogacy, and/or prenatal cell-free DNA testing)
o	Human Milk Banking and Biotechnology
o	Gene Editing/CRISPR Technology
o	Stem Cell Research and Technology
o	Genetic Testing for Future Disease Probability
o	Pharmacogenomics
o	Vaccines
o	Organ Transplant and Donation
o	Xenotransplantation and Transgenesis
o	Hormone Treatment for Gender Dysphoria/Transgender Athletic Competition
o	Prosthetics and Other Skeletal Enhancements
o	End-of-Life Body Preservation/Choices

courses.subject: HDFS
courses.title: Creativity and Mindfulness in Behavioral Health
courses.description:
Mindfulness and creativity inform communication with individuals and families within the context of healthcare, prevention, and intervention. Students will engage in creative processes, supported by empirical evidence that foster coping and adaptation
to support individuals and family systems across the lifespan.
courses.course_objectives: Students will holistically define creativity and mindfulness and recognize appropriate uses of the terms within the context of healthcare across the lifespan. Students will apply HDFS theory to support the development of creative and mindfulness-based interventions. Students will engage creativity and mindfulness techniques in fields of interest (i.e., OT, PT, child-life, nursing, research) by engaging in active learning. Students will engage in experiential learning, helping them understand how creativity and mindfulness practices will feel to their future healthcare patients.
courses.topical_outline: Introduction and Defining Creativity and Mindfulness Foundations for Prevention and Interventions Creativity and Mindfulness Across the Lifespan (Prevention and Intervention) Creativity and Mindfulness in Family Stress and Coping (Mental Health) Creativity and Mindfulness in Healthcare (Intervention and Prevention) Creativity and Cognition Creative Arts Therapy Neurodistinct HDFS Theory and Prevention HDFS Theory and Intervention

courses.subject: HDFS
courses.title: Child Life Theory and Practice
courses.description: The child life profession will be examined, including history,theory, clinical practice, techniques, and interventions, alongwith experiential-learning with children and families coping with illness.
courses.course_objectives: Students will demonstrate understanding of the history and evolution of the role of Child Life Specialists in healthcare settings. Students will acquire knowledge of the Child Life profession through reviewing the Official Documents of the Child Life Council. Students will identify key components of Patient and Family Centered Care as it relates to the Child Life role. Students will demonstrate understanding of the role of play and therapeutic play in daily Child Life interventions. Students will identify types of preparation and methods utilized in preparing children and families to cope with stressful situations in health care settings. Students will demonstrate an understanding of the link between developmental theory and Child Life practice. Students will demonstrate an understanding of the benefits and techniques of coping and distraction for hospitalized children and families. Students will explore the various areas/populations and environments of Child Life practice in and outside the hospital. Students will identify various indirect responsibilities of a Child Life Specialist, including administrative tasks, budgeting, statistics, and charting. Students will identify the role of Child Life Specialist in assisting patients and families in grief and bereavement.
courses.topical_outline:
I. Overview of Child Life Profession and Professional Organization II. Child Life Documentation to include:
Official Documents of the Child Life Council
Code of Ethical Responsibility
Child Life Competencies
Standards of Clinical Practice
Child Life Mission, Values, and Mission Statement
Code of Professional Practice III. History of Child Life and Its Development in the Evolution of Children’s Healthcare IV. Developmental Theories in Relation to Child Life V. Child Life’s Role in Facilitating Play/Medical Play/Therapeutic Play VI. Impact of Illness, Injury, and Healthcare on Patients and Families VII. Child Life Specialist's Role in Preparation Along with Historic and Current Perspectives VIII. Child Life’s Role in Coping/Distraction Techniques IX. Scope of Child Life Practice X. Family Centered Care XI. Child Life Administration XII. Child Life Specialist's Role in Grief and Bereavement Situations XIII. Child Life in Alternative Settings XIV. Future Directions

courses.subject: HDFS
courses.title: More than a Four-Legged Friend: The Benefits of Animal-Assisted Interventions
courses.description: Examination of the benefits of animal-assisted interventions (AAI) in healthcare and community settings. The significance of the human-animal bond and its relevance in therapeutic interventions will be explored. Information about the history, evolution, ethical and safety considerations, and animal welfare will also be studied. Course is designed for students pursuing careers in healthcare, social work, counseling, education, or other health and human service fields.
courses.course_objectives: Demonstrate a comprehensive understanding of animal-assisted interventions (animal-assisted therapy, animal-assisted education, and animal-assisted activities) and its benefits in various settings. Explore the developmental and psychosocial effects of AAI across the lifespan. Analyze the similarities and differences between therapy animals, service animals, facility dogs, and emotional support animals. Evaluate best practice when partnering with animals in professional practice. Apply academic skills and knowledge to address a community need, issue, or problem (service-learning). Develop self-reflective practice by critically reflecting on the service-learning activity.
courses.topical_outline: The Conceptualization of the Human-Animal Bond Historical Perspective and Evolution Therapeutic Roles, Psychosocial Health Effects, and Wellness Benefits Theoretical and Developmental Perspectives Ethical and Safety Considerations Research, Evidence Based Practice, Public Policy Hippotherapy and Therapeutic Riding AAI in Various Settings (healthcare settings, schools) AAI for Populations Across the Lifespan

courses.description: Theoretical concepts and behavioral skills as applied to prevention and intervention work with help-seeking individuals and families.
courses.course_objectives: Students will learn how to apply new and traditional theories and techniques to prevention and intervention work with families. Students will learn how to identify, read, and apply current research about family life, prevention, and intervention. Students will be encouraged to engage in interdisciplinary collaboration and holistic approaches to behavioral health care. Students will develop knowledge, skill, and attitudes in interdisciplinary collaboration and holistic approaches to behavioral health care.

courses.course_objectives: Students will learn how to apply new and traditional theories and therapies to family situations. Students will learn how to identify, read, and apply current research about family life, therapy, and intervention. Students will learn how to discuss training and supervision issues in family therapy. Students will learn to communicate how new and traditional theories translate to practice in both oral and written presentations. Students will learn how to critically evaluate family therapy theories and techniques with respect to different family forms, culture, ethnicity, gender, and presenting problem. Students will learn how to identify the ways culture, gender, and ethnicity influence family structure and apply appropriate interventions to demonstrate the importance of being a culturally competent therapist.
courses.topical_outline: 1. Foundations in Family Therapy 2. Basic Techniques in Intervention 3. Fundamental Concepts in Family Intervention 4. Systems theory 5. courses.subject: HDFS
courses.title: Therapeutic Benefits of Play
courses.description: Individual and group programming for children and adolescents based upon current theory, research, and developmentally appropriate practice. Special emphasis will be placed upon the integration and implementation of therapeutic activities, including art, music, movement, and dramatic and medical play, particularly in the healthcare context.
courses.course_objectives: Students will compare and contrast classical and contemporary theories of play and their role in development. Students will differentiate the stages of child development and the associated stages of play. Students will demonstrate an understanding of the value and characteristics of play, with an emphasis on the therapeutic aspects of play. Students will identify developmentally appropriate toys and materials that can be incorporated into either a permanent or traveling playroom. Students will demonstrate effective observation and assessment of children's play. Students will demonstrate the ability to plan and implement developmentally appropriate play activities for children in traditional and non-traditional settings, with an emphasis on the healthcare context. Students will compile a collection of creative activity ideas and materials to use with children in the areas of music and movement, art, sensory, dramatic play, and technology. Students will identify methods for modifying play activities for children with limited mobility and/or cognitive delays. Students will be familiar with the psychological, behavior, and physiological benefits of therapeutic play in the healthcare context.

1. Orientation to Course 2. Classical and Contemporary Theories of Play 3. Developmental Stages of Play 4. The Development of Dramatic Play 5. Value and Characteristics of Play 6. What is Therapeutic Play? 7. Therapeutic Play Activities Incorporating Art, Music, Movement, Technology, Outdoors, Animal-Assistance, and Sensory Aspects 8. Using Play as Preparation in Healthcare Context 9. Using Play as Coping in Healthcare Context 10. Using Play as Normative Activity in Healthcare Context 11. Psychological, Behavior, and Physiological Benefits of Therapeutic Play in Healthcare Context 14. Including Parents and Siblings in Play 15. Planning and Implementing Therapeutic Play Activities to Meet Developmental and Therapeutic Needs of Individual
Children

courses.description: Families and their relationship with schools and communities, with consideration of how historical events related to issues of diversity impact these relationships. Implications for selected areas of practice, including school counseling, teaching, community development, and advocacy, are emphasized.
courses.prerequisiteText: HDFS 2100 or HDFS 2100E or HDFS 2100H | Graduate Prerequisite | Permission of department
courses.offeredText: Not offered on a regular basis.

courses.subject: HDFS
courses.title: Aging and Social Inequalities
courses.description: The dynamic interplay between aging, inequalities and privilegeoccurs through interpersonal interactions, societal institutions,and social policies.  In addition to contemporary Westernliterature examining aging, gender, race-ethnicity, and socialclass, we also will consider aging in cross-cultural andhistorical perspectives through the use of comparative andhistorical readings and discussions.
courses.prerequisiteText: HDFS 3710 or HDFS(FHCE) 4500/6500 or permission of department | Graduate Prerequisite | Permission of department
courses.offeredText: Not offered on a regular basis.

courses.subject: HDFS
courses.title: Study Tour in Human Development and Family Science
courses.description: Selected topics in human development and family science. Combined with site visits to relevant locations.
courses.prerequisiteText: Permission of department | Graduate Prerequisite | Permission of department

courses.subject: HDFS
courses.title: Applied Community Internship in Human Development and Family Science
courses.description: Supervised professional practice in settings with employedpersons in a Human Development and Family Science or related field.
courses.course_objectives: Students will be able to apply their HDFS coursework in a learning environment. Interns are expected to develop an understanding of the respective mission, policies, and services of their sponsoring agencies. Interns are expected to develop professional skills and work habits that will allow them to transition into their chosen careers. Students will build upon their existing knowledge base in family science and/or Family Life Education to further develop their skills. Students will apply their knowledge of family science and/or Family Life Education in a professional setting. Students will evaluate their performance as well as their strength and growth areas in the workplace. Students will learn the experiences of those who work in family science settings and/or Family Life Education settings. Students will share their internship experiences with their cohort through topical group meetings. Students will reflect on their experience through creation of structured weekly logs, weekly assignments, a professional portfolio, as well as a project relevant to their internship experience.
courses.topical_outline: Complete and submit weekly assignments Complete and submit mid-term and final self-rating evaluation Prepare paper or project summarizing the experience Prepare a professional portfolio
courses.prerequisiteText: (HDFS 2100 or HDFS 2100E or HDFS 2100H) and (HDFS 2200 or HDFS 2200E or HDFS 2200H) and HDFS 2400 and 6 hours of HDFS courses at the 3000-level or above and permission of department

courses.subject: HDFS
courses.title: Applied Community Internship in Human Development and Family Science
courses.description: Supervised professional practice with a community-based human or family-service related partner. Student and community partner will conduct a needs-assessment to identify a community need. Students will also connect their course learning goals through reflection and critical analysis via bi-weekly reflective journals submitted to the course instructor.
courses.course_objectives: Students will be able to apply their HDFS coursework in a learning environment. Interns are expected to develop an understanding of the respective mission, policies, and services of their sponsoring agencies. Interns are expected to develop professional skills and work habits that will allow them to transition into their chosen careers. Students will build upon their existing knowledge base in family science and/or Family Life Education to further develop their skills. Students will apply their knowledge of family science and/or Family Life Education in a professional setting. Students will evaluate their performance as well as their strength and growth areas in the workplace. Students will learn the experiences of those who work in family science settings and/or Family Life Education settings. Students will share their internship experiences with their cohort through topical group meetings. Students will reflect on their experience through weekly assignments, a professional portfolio, a project relevant to their internship experience.
courses.topical_outline: Complete and submit weekly assignments Complete and submit mid-term and final self-rating evaluation Prepare paper or project summarizing the experience Prepare a professional portfolio Develop a project that benefits the organization, consumers, or community of the agency
courses.prerequisiteText: (HDFS 2100 or HDFS 2100E or HDFS 2100H) and (HDFS 2200 or HDFS 2200E or HDFS 2200H) and HDFS 2400 and 6 hours of HDFS courses at the 3000-level or above and permission of department

courses.subject: HDFS
courses.title: Internship in Human Development and Family Science
courses.description: Supervised professional practice in programs for children under six with employed persons with a degree in Human Development andFamily Science or a related field.
courses.prerequisiteText: Permission of department | Graduate Prerequisite | Permission of department

courses.subject: HDFS
courses.title: Applied Research Internship in Human Development and Family Science
courses.description: Supervised experience with faculty in qualitative and/orquantitative research in a topical area related to humandevelopment and family science. With mentorship and feedback from faculty, students will generate and disseminate developmentalknowledge over the life span, fostering research and itsapplication to enhance quality of life.
courses.prerequisiteText: (HDFS 5110 or HDFS 5110W or PSYC 3980 or SOCI 3600) and permission of department

courses.subject: HDFS
courses.title: Pre-Practicum for Clinical Practice
courses.description: Fundamental skills of couple and family therapy and clinic procedures; case assessment, treatment planning, and management. Case observation, role play, and video reviews.
courses.course_objectives: Students will learn to demonstrate fundamental therapy skills (e.g., building therapeutic alliance, conducting an intake, informed consent process). Students will learn to demonstrate appropriate screening for telehealth fit. Students will learn to demonstrate clinic procedures such as documentation, Electronic Health Record processes, and emergency and high-risk assessment/procedures.
courses.topical_outline: 1. Therapeutic alliance 2. Informed consent 3. Conducting an intake 4. Telehealth screening 5. Documentation (Progress notes vs. Psychotherapy notes, Treatment Plans, etc.) Mandated Reporting assessment and procedures Mental health emergency scenarios (voluntary vs. Involuntary hospitalizations) and other crisis situations

courses.subject: HDFS
courses.title: Interdisciplinary Practice
courses.description: Course facilitates the development of competencies in multidisciplinary collaboration. Specifically, the course builds students’ ability to integrate clinical foci, develop a shared language for similar and/or parallel processes, collaborate with affiliated or complementary disciplines, and differentiate between the disciplinary scope of practice and potential collaborators.
courses.course_objectives: Students will identify connections and tensions among contextual factors, epistemic foundations, values, and techniques. Students will foster creativity and flexibility in case conceptualization through working with multiple clinical and affiliated perspectives. Students will synthesize ideas and characteristics from multiple clinical disciplines and affiliated fields to solve problems from different perspectives. Students will discern clinical areas of focus within their own scope of practice from those requiring consultation and/or collaboration with other disciplines. Students will identify the specific ways stress, mental health, relationship issues, and financial issues co-exist.
courses.topical_outline: Multidisciplinary, transdisciplinary, and interdisciplinary clinical work Scope of practice Co-therapy, Consultation, and Collaboration

courses.subject: HDFS
courses.title: Evidence-Based Practice Treating Traumatic Stress
courses.description: Course introduces evidence-based models for the treatment of traumatic stress. Models covered are designed for use with a wide range of individuals, couples, and families across the lifespan. Content on assessment, crisis intervention, and adaptation for telemental health settings is covered.
courses.course_objectives: Students will learn to identify effective assessments for traumatic stress and PTSD. Students will learn to demonstrate relationally oriented case conceptualization of traumatic stress treatment. Students will learn to demonstrate relationally oriented clinical practice skills specific to traumatic stress. Students will learn to critically evaluate evidence based relational therapy practice theories and techniques with clients across the lifespan.
courses.topical_outline:
1. Trauma, Traumatic Stress, PTSD, and Complex PTSD 2. Assessment of traumatic stress – adults and children 3. Introduction to Evidence Based Models for treating traumatic stress:  
     a. Cognitive Processing Therapy 
     b. Eye Movement Desensitization and Restructuring  
     c. Prolonged Exposure Therapy 
     d. Narrative Exposure Therapy 
     e. Trauma-Focused CBT 4. Working with Children and Trauma/Complex PTSD 5. Assessment for adaptation of covered models for telemental health

courses.subject: HDFS
courses.title: Psychopathology and Relational Assessment throughout the LifeSpan
courses.description: Course facilitates the development of competencies in diagnosis using the DSM-5 to assess, diagnose, and treat major mental health issues. Relational assessment to identify and assess psychopathology and relational functioning across the lifespan, including addiction, suicide, trauma, abuse, intra-familial violence, and managing acute chronic medical conditions, utilizing CFT philosophy.
courses.course_objectives: Students will complete a comprehensive assessment, identify symptoms/symptom formation using the DSM 5-TR, formulate diagnoses, differential diagnoses, and articulate treatment recommendations. Students will understand the biopsychosocial contributions and effects of psychopathology within families. Students will conduct relational assessment using both observational data as well as established instruments. Students will understand the influence of age, gender, culture, economics, and sexual orientation on psychopathology and the assessment of psychopathology throughout the life span.
courses.topical_outline: 1. Introduction to psychopathology in families and the biopsychosocial model 2. Diagnostic criteria for DSM 5-TR categories of mental disorders 3. Diagnostic criteria for DSM 5-TR categories of substance use and dependence disorders 4. Diagnostic criteria for DSM 5-TR neurodevelopmental disorders 5. Diagnostic criteria for DSM 5-TR categories of trauma, stressor, and dissociative disorders 6. Diagnostic criteria for DSM 5-TR categories of personality disorders 7. Diagnostic criteria for DSM 5-TR sexual dysfunction disorders 8. Assessments and measures of psychopathology and relational assessment 9. A life-span perspective on psychopathology

courses.subject: HDFS
courses.title: Couple Therapy
courses.description: Course examines key issues associated with effective couple therapy and develops students’ competencies in treatment approaches specifically designed for use with a wide range of diverse couples, including same-sex couples, and includes a focus on evidence-based practice.
courses.course_objectives: Students will be able to demonstrate relationally-oriented couple case conceptualization and clinical practice skills for effective practice with couples and intimate relationships. Students will be able to evaluate relational interaction patterns. Students will be able to select appropriate relational interventions for intimate relationships. Students will be able to articulate ethical issues related to practice with couples and intimate relationships.
courses.topical_outline: 1. Emotionally Focused Couple Therapy 2. Cognitive Behavioral Couples Therapy 3. Gottman Method 4. Acceptance and Commitment Therapy 5. Imago 6. Therapy with polyamorous relationships 7. Brief overview of sex therapy

courses.subject: HDFS
courses.title: Theories of Human Development
courses.description: Theoretical and historical perspectives used in the study of human development across the lifespan.

courses.subject: HDFS
courses.title: Theories of Family Relationships
courses.description: Theoretical and philosophical perspectives used in the study of families.

courses.subject: HDFS
courses.title: Issues in Family Relationships
courses.description: Integration of classic and current research literature on families from an ecological, life-span perspective.

courses.subject: HDFS
courses.title: Masters-Level Research Methods in Human Development and Family Science
courses.description: Research design in selected areas of family and consumer sciences.  Emphasis on common problems incurred in measurement and data analysis.
courses.course_objectives: Students will gain or increase understanding of the foundations of research (e.g., ethics, formulation of research questions, development of measurement strategies and the internal validity of research). Students will gain or increase understanding of research strategies (e.g., experimental, correlational, survey research, single-case, natural, and quasi-experimental designs). Students will gain or increase understanding of the data collection and interpretation processes. Students will gain or increase understanding of the processes involved in writing research papers and proposals.
courses.topical_outline: 1. Introduction to Class 2. The Conceptualization to Operalization to Data Analysis Model 3. Research Strategies and Problem Identification 4. The Literature and Problem Identification 5. The Hourglass Model 6. Turning Hypotheses Into A Study 7. Validity 8. Experimental Designs 9. Quasi-Experimental and Single-Participant Designs 10. Correlational Approaches 11. Survey Research 12. Sampling and Research Procedures 13. Interpretation and Dissemination of Research Results

courses.subject: HDFS
courses.title: Master's Research
courses.description: Research while enrolled for a master's degree under the direction of faculty members.

courses.subject: HDFS
courses.title: Graduate Student Seminar
courses.description: Advanced supervised experience in an applied setting.  Thiscourse may not be used to satisfy a student's approved program ofstudy.

courses.subject: HDFS
courses.title: Directed Study in Human Development and Family Science
courses.description: Directed reading and/or research under supervision of the instructor.

courses.subject: HDFS
courses.title: Non-Thesis Clinical Project in Child Life
courses.description: Development of a non-thesis clinical project and a final written report describing the development process, under the direction of the major professor. Specific components of the non-thesis clinical project include defending the clinical project proposal, creating appropriate content and design to meet the needs of the audience, conducting readability analyses, collaborating with community partners to review and revise the project, writing a final report of the clinical project, and completing the final defense.

courses.subject: HDFS
courses.title: Socioculturally Attuned Family Therapy and Third Order Change
courses.description: Facilitates competencies in applying clinical knowledge to the range of life experiences based on biopsychosocial, contextual, and societal position (e.g., power, privilege, and oppression as related to identities); applying models of family therapy from a critical lens to work with various populations, including those from multicultural, marginalized, and/or underserved communities.
courses.course_objectives: Students will be able to identify the elements of a relational, process-oriented approach to cultural humility that integrates cultural sensitivity with attention to societal processes of power, privilege, and equity. Students will be able to define third order thinking and change. Students will be able to apply sociocultural attuned family therapy as a transtheoretical lens across the major models and theories of couple and family therapy. Students will be able to examine clinical guidelines that promote equitable and socio-culturally attuned practice.
courses.topical_outline:
1. Guiding principles for socioculturally attuned family therapy (ANVIET) 2. Third Order Thinking and Change 3. Third Order Ethics 4. Application of a Sociocultural family therapy lens to major family therapy models 
     a. Structural 
     b. Strategic 
     c. Experiential 
     d. Attachment 
     e. Transgenerational 
     f. Cognitive Behavioral Therapy 
     g. Solution Focused 
     h. Collaborative 
     i. Narrative

courses.subject: HDFS
courses.title: Masters Couple and Family Therapy Practicum
courses.description: Supervised practice in the application of relational intervention/couple and family therapy skills.
courses.course_objectives: Students will learn how to integrate clinical services with other professional activities such as record keeping, supervision, information and referral, in-service, and staff meetings. Students will learn how to integrate CFT theories, sensitivity to diversity, and human development theories into therapeutic practice. Students will learn how to diagnose and assess client systems, develop treatment plans, and deliver therapeutic interventions systemically and contextually. Students will learn how to apply the appropriate professional and ethical standards, as well as legal mandates, appropriate to the clinical setting. Students will learn how to integrate issues of diversity into the practice of couple and family therapy.
courses.topical_outline: This course entails the practice of couple and family therapy and supervision of clinical work. Conducting relational therapy (CFT) Live supervision of cases Supervision of recorded sessions Case conceptualization presentations Discussion of self of therapist issues that impact clinical effectiveness

courses.subject: HDFS
courses.title: Masters Couple and Family Therapy Internship
courses.description: Supervised internship in the practice of relational intervention/couple and family therapy.
courses.course_objectives: Students will learn to integrate clinical services with other professional activities such as record keeping, supervision, information and referral, in-service, and staff meetings. Students will learn to integrate CFT theories, sensitivity to marginalized populations, and human development theories into therapeutic practice. Students will learn to diagnose and assess client systems, develop treatment plans, and deliver relational therapeutic interventions systemically and contextually. Students will learn to apply the appropriate professional and ethical standards, as well as legal mandates, appropriate to the clinical setting. Students will learn to integrate issues of diversity into the practice of couple and family therapy.
courses.topical_outline: This course entails the practice of couple and family therapy and supervision of clinical work. Conducting relational therapy (CFT) Live supervision of cases Supervision of recorded sessions Case conceptualization presentations Discussion of self of therapist issues that impact clinical effectiveness

courses.subject: HDFS
courses.title: Systems Theory and Couple and Family Therapy Theory
courses.description: Investigation of the foundations and critical epistemological issues of MFT, including the historical development of the Couple and Family Therapy (CFT) relational/systemic philosophy, the theoretical and empirical foundations of relational intervention, and the biopsychosocial framework. Major models of early couple and family therapy such as Bowenian, Strategic, Structural, and Contextual are explored.
courses.course_objectives: Students will demonstrate Couple & Family Therapy (CFT) relational/systemic philosophy through case conceptualization using the biopsychosocial framework, early relational theories, and therapies. Students will demonstrate foundations and critical epistemological issues of CFT. Students will demonstrate clinical practice skills using the theoretical and empirical foundations of relational intervention. Students will critically evaluate early family therapy theories and techniques with respect to different family forms, culture, ethnicity, gender, and presenting problem. Students will identify the ways culture, gender, and ethnicity influence families and apply appropriate interventions.
courses.topical_outline: Epistemological Foundations in Family Therapy Biopsychosocial Framework Basic Techniques in Relational Intervention Fundamental Concepts in Family Intervention Systems theory Psychodynamic Structural models Strategic models Intergenerational models

courses.subject: HDFS
courses.title: Contemporary Family Therapy
courses.description: Investigation of theory, research, and practice of constructivist and social constructionist family therapies, and contemporary models of CFT, including evidence-based practice. Major models of contemporary couple and family therapy such as Solution Focused, Narrative, and Common Factors.
courses.course_objectives: Students will investigate contemporary conceptual foundations of CFT. Students will demonstrate relationally oriented case conceptualization using contemporary models of CFT. Students will demonstrate relationally oriented clinical practice skills using contemporary models of CFT. Students will critically evaluate post-modern family therapy theories and techniques with respect to different family forms, culture, ethnicity, gender, and presenting problem.
courses.topical_outline: 1. Experiential Models of Family Therapy 2. Solution-Focused Brief Therapy 3. Narrative Family Therapy 4. Collaborative Language Systems 5. Critical Theories (feminist, queer, critical decolonizing, critical social theory) 7. Internal Family Systems 8. Common Factors

courses.subject: HDFS
courses.title: Qualitative Methods In Family Science
courses.description: Practical knowledge for conceptualization and designs of qualitative research projects, including data collection, analysis (including manual and digital methods), presentations, publications, and writing. Students develop skills in individual, dyadic, triadic interviewing, ﬁeldwork, focus groups, ethnography, and participatory action research.

courses.subject: HDFS
courses.title: Introduction to Applied Statistics in Human Development and Family Science
courses.description: Foundations for statistical reasoning and applications (e.g., SPSS), with an emphasis on the application of developmental and family research. Students will gain understanding of basic statistical concepts and analytical procedures (e.g., descriptive statistics, statistical significance, standard deviation, correlations, t-tests, cross tabulations, analysis of variance, and regression).

courses.subject: HDFS
courses.title: Practicum in Child Life
courses.description: Supervised practice in the application of child life interventions in a hospital or therapeutic setting.
courses.course_objectives: Students will apply their knowledge of child life in a professional setting. Students will learn from the experiences of those who work in child life clinical settings. Students will build upon their existing knowledge base in child life to further develop their skills. Students will evaluate their performance as well as their strength and growth in the workplace.
courses.topical_outline:
This course entails the practice in the application of child life interventions in the hospital or therapeutic setting. Includes: 
•	Live supervision of cases •	Conducting case reviews and presentations •	Self-reflection and goal setting

courses.subject: HDFS
courses.title: Master's Thesis
courses.description: Thesis writing under the direction of the major professor.

courses.subject: HDFS
courses.title: Ethics in Couple and Family Therapy
courses.description: Investigation of the foundations of ethical decision-making in relational therapy. Course addresses the development of a CFT identity and socialization and facilitates the development of competencies in ethics in CFT practice, including understanding and applying the AAMFT Code of Ethics and understanding legal responsibilities.
courses.course_objectives: Students will learn to identify professional guidelines, ethical codes, and legal regulations relevant to the practice of CFT. Students will learn to distinguish between the ethical tensions in individual practice vs. relational/systemic clinical practice. Students will learn to apply AAMFT Code of Ethics and legal regulations to clinical case studies. Students will learn to develop personal ethical decision-making models
courses.topical_outline: 1. CFT Professional Identity 2. Scope of practice 3. Professional Organizations 4. Licensure 5. MFT Ethical values and codes 6. Ethical decision-making models 7. Legal responsibility and liabilities of clinical practice, telehealth, and research 8. Building an ethical workplace culture

courses.subject: HDFS
courses.title: College Teaching in Human Development and Family Science
courses.description: This is a teaching-support seminar designed to familiarize graduate teaching assistants with the principles of higher education pedagogy and the resources and support services available to them at UGA. Students learn about different teaching approaches that are effective and appropriate for their particular teaching assignments and practice using teaching techniques.
courses.course_objectives: Students will describe the different duties that may be assigned to you in your role as a TA, and comply with relevant Federal, State, and UGA policies and procedures (e.g., FERPA). Students will identify campus resources to support both your instructional duties and your students’ learning. Students will use evidence-based strategies to effectively and efficiently complete instructional tasks (including skills related to planning and presenting lessons, developing assessments or rubrics, grading and giving feedback, and using eLC in your role as TA). Students will explain how your role is critical to building an inclusive learning environment for all students. Students will intentionally reflect on your teaching practices and strategies, particularly as it relates to human development and family science.
courses.topical_outline: •	Instructional Resources •	Teaching in Human Development and Family Science •	Instructional Strategies for Inclusive Excellence (e.g., Active Learning) •	Assessment Strategies •	Creation of Instructional Portfolio •	Teaching Observation

courses.subject: HDFS
courses.title: Internship in Human Development and Family Science
courses.description: Supervised professional practice in settings with employedpersons with a degree in Human Development and Family Science orrelated field.

courses.subject: HDFS
courses.title: Hospital Internship in Child Life
courses.description: Supervised professional practice in a hospital or other healthcare setting with children birth–age 18, with employed Certified Child Life Specialists.

courses.subject: HDFS
courses.title: Family Psychopathology and Assessment throughout the Life Span
courses.description: Prepares students to identify and assess psychopathology in families throughout the life span using a biopsychosocial family systems framework.

courses.subject: HDFS
courses.title: Mechanisms of Change in Couple and Family Therapy
courses.description: Focuses on change in a relational context. Models of change, factors related to change, and interventions related to change will be discussed. Students will have the opportunity to critically examine these interventions and models within the contexts of gender, ethnicity, socioeconomic status, and applicability to specific presenting problems.
courses.course_objectives: Students will become familiar with general systems theory and cybernetics Students will become familiar with the contributions systems theory and cybernetics have made to family therapy. Students will become familiar with the foundational models of couple and family therapy. Students will be able to evaluate and critique the theories and models presented. Students will have an understanding of research findings related to the therapy models.
courses.topical_outline: 1. Course Introduction 2. Historical Context of Couple and Family Therapy 3. General Systems Theory 4. Critiques of Systems Theory 5. Cybernetics 6. Critiques of Cybernetics 7. Structural Therapy 8. Research Findings on Structural Therapy 9. Critiques of Structural Therapy 10. Strategic Therapy 11. Behavioral Therapy 12. Intergenerational Therapy Models 13. Functional Family Therapy 14. Emotionally Focused Therapy 15. Experiential Therapy Models & Psychoanalytic Based Therapy Models 16. Non-specific Factors of Change 17. Introduction to Postmodern Models of Therapy 18. Integration vs. Eclecticism 19. How Does Change Occur?

courses.subject: HDFS
courses.title: Contemporary Approaches to Couples and Family Therapy Across the Life Span
courses.description: Post-modern theories examining and intervening with individuals and families across the life span. Narrative therapy, collaborative language systems and solution-focused therapy will be presented. Discussion of how cultural contexts influence the constructs of race, class, gender, and sexual orientation and interpersonal power.

courses.subject: HDFS
courses.title: Couple and Sex Therapy
courses.description: Designed to help students gain an advanced understanding of the role of sexuality in human relationships and to learn interventions and approaches to treating sexual problems. Additionally, the students will learn various theoretical applications to common problems presented in couple therapy.

courses.subject: HDFS
courses.title: Global Mental Health: Systemic Applications to Contemporary Challenges
courses.description: Advanced core course in HDFS, MFT specialization, uses a social justice orientation to address global mental health with an emphasis on systemic applications to contemporary challenges. Evidence-based clinical interventions will be introduced in prevention, intervention, and translational sciences. Implications for the design and conduct of trials will be integrated.

courses.subject: HDFS
courses.title: Behavioral Medicine and Family Therapy
courses.description: Designed to provide graduate students with extensive knowledge of theory, research, and practice in behavioral medicine and foundations of medical family therapy.
courses.offeredText: Offered summer semester every odd-numbered year.

courses.subject: HDFS
courses.title: Advanced Family Theories
courses.description: Course focuses on conceptual frameworks used to study diverse families. Assumptions, limitations, and empirical examples of family theories will be discussed. Course activities will challenge students to critically interpret applications of family theories. The course also explores cutting-edge theoretical orientations in family science that inform a social justice orientation.

courses.subject: HDFS
courses.title: Philosophy of Science in Human Development and Family Science
courses.description: Integration of literature on history and philosophy of science as it pertains to the study of human development and families across the life span.

courses.subject: HDFS
courses.title: Principles of Life-Span Human Development
courses.description: Integration of theoretical and research literature as it pertains to study of human development over the life span with an emphasis on contextual-systemic approaches to family and individual development.

courses.subject: HDFS
courses.title: Ecological Perspective on Individual and Family Diversity
courses.description: Theoretical, historical, and philosophical perspectives on diversity and similarity in individual and family development.  Considers transactions among families and individuals and other significant contexts as moderated by diversity.  Emphasizes implications for service delivery, treatment, policy, and marriage and family therapy.

courses.subject: HDFS
courses.title: Structural Equation Modeling for Family and Social Sciences
courses.description: This course focuses on latent variable modeling techniques. Topics include confirmatory factor analysis, structural equation models, and means and covariance structures. Students will learn appropriate use of these techniques as they are applied in the family and social sciences. Students will learn to fit models using statistical software packages.
courses.course_objectives: Students will acquire an understanding of how SEM (and related latent variable models) can be used in human development and other social and behavioral research. Students will gain an appreciation of the conceptual and, at least at a basic level, the mathematical, basis of SEM. Students will develop the ability to formulate and evaluate models with your own data. Students will become proficient in using Lavaan or another software package for the analysis of models. Students will gain the ability to understand and critically evaluate research articles using SEM. Students will gain the skills necessary to conduct and write publishable research reports using SEM. Students will gain the foundations upon which to learn more advanced SEM topics.
courses.topical_outline: 1.	Course introduction & psychometrics 2.	Defining constructs; Scale setting & identification 3.	Confirmatory factor analysis 4.	Parcels & parceling 5.	Model fit, model comparison, & statistical power 6.	Multiple-group models: Evaluating measurement invariance 7.	Multiple-group models: Comparing latent parameters across groups 8.	Latent regression models & structural equations 9.	Latent variable mediation & moderation 10.	Latent variable representation of interdependent data 11.	Hierarchical structural models; Multi-trait, multi-method models 12.	Longitudinal CFA & SEM; Introduction to latent growth curve modeling 13.	Reporting Structural Equation Modeling results

courses.subject: HDFS
courses.title: Quantitative Methods in Human Development and Family Science
courses.description: Quantitative research processes, conceptualization of research problems, research designs, selection of appropriate methods of data collection, consideration of alternative data analysis strategies, interpretation of findings, and research writing.  Research on marital and family therapy included.

courses.subject: HDFS
courses.title: Qualitative Methods in Human Development and Family Science
courses.description: Qualitative research processes, conceptualization of research problems, research design, selection of appropriate methods of data collection, consideration of alternative data analysis strategies, interpretation of findings, and research writing.  Research in marital and family therapy included.

courses.subject: HDFS
courses.title: Applied Regression Analyses in HDFS
courses.description: Applied quantitative analyses in human development and family science, with a focus on foundational concepts of linear regression. Students will learn about conceptual issues in this area and develop skills in the proper application of linear regression methods to empirical data in human development and family science.
courses.course_objectives: Students will learn the basic assumptions underlying regression analyses, when to use particular regression techniques, and how to interpret statistical output from regression analyses. Students will learn how to conduct their own regression analyses using statistical software packages. Students will be able to understand basic assumptions of regression analyses in human development and family science. Students will be able to determine appropriate regression techniques for testing particular models and hypotheses. Students will be able to interpret results of linear regression analyses. Students will be able to distinguish between mediational and moderation models and when to use them. Students will be able to implement regression analyses in research using data from human development and family science. Students will be able to critically evaluate research that employs regression analyses.
courses.topical_outline: Foundational Assumptions of Regression Analyses Applications of Regression Analyses for Human Development and Family Science Review of Correlations Data Visualization Simple Linear Regression Conducting Simple Linear Regression Analyses Multiple Linear Regression Conducting Multiple Linear Regression Analyses Regression Diagnostics Covariates and Statistical Control Mediation Analyses in Regression Moderation Analyses in Regression Probing Statistical Interactions Categorical Independent Variables in Regression Logistic Regression

courses.subject: HDFS
courses.title: Multilevel Modeling for Family and Social Sciences
courses.description: This course focuses on multilevel regression models. Multilevel models are used in studies where individuals are nested within communities and/or where individuals are measured repeatedly over time. The course emphasizes application of multilevel regression models in family/community research and introduces statistical modeling.
courses.course_objectives:
Students will understand the conceptual application of multilevel regression analysis.

2. Students will learn proper use of multilevel regression models for their research studies where individuals are nested within communities and/or where individuals are measured repeatedly over time.

3. Students will learn proper interpretations and evaluations of multilevel models.

4. Students will become familiar with statistical software packages. Students will learn proper use of multilevel regression models for their research studies where individuals are nested
within communities and/or where individuals are measured repeatedly over time. Students will learn proper interpretations and evaluations of multilevel models. Students become familiar with statistical software packages such as HLM, SAS, and Mplus.
courses.topical_outline: 1. Intra-class correlation, reliability coefficients, and within/between group relations 2. Alternative multilevel models 3. Random intercept and slope models in detail 4. Model comparisons and hypothesis testing 5. Centering (group mean and grand mean) 6. Design effect and power in multilevel models 7. Estimation 8. Growth curve models as multilevel models 9. Latent trajectory class analysis 10. Multilevel models with categorical outcomes

courses.subject: HDFS
courses.title: Categorical and Dyadic Data Analysis for Family and Social Sciences
courses.description: Quantitative analysis for family/social sciences research topics includes dependent variables that are categorical or otherwise inappropriate for typical regression methods, data that are interdependent (i.e., dyadic data), and classification techniques assessing unmeasured/latent group membership explaining heterogeneity among individuals. Students will also learn to perform statistical analyses.
courses.course_objectives: By the end of this course, students will develop the ability to understand and critically evaluate research using techniques covered in this class. By the end of this course, students will develop the skills necessary to apply one or more of these techniques with your own data. By the end of this course, students will develop the ability to interpret and present results using one or more of these techniques. By the end of this course, students will develop the foundations upon which to learn more advanced techniques toward the three topics covered in this course.
courses.topical_outline: 1.	Course overview; Review of OLS regression 2.	Topic 1: Categorical (manifest) dependent variables •	Logistic regression •	Generalized Linear model; Categorical variables in MLM and SEM 3.	Topic 2: Dyadic data analysis •	Overview of Interdependent Data; Introduction to Dyadic Data Analysis •	Actor-Partner Interdependence Models (APIM) •	Longitudinal APIM •	Social Relations Models (SRM) •	SRM with roles •	One with Many; Intro to Social Network 4.	Topic 3: Classification Techniques (i.e., Latent group membership) •	Cluster Analysis •	Finite Mixture Modeling: Latent Class Analysis •	Finite Mixture Modeling: Latent Profile Analysis

courses.subject: HDFS
courses.title: Longitudinal Structural Equation Modeling for Family and Social Sciences
courses.description: This course focuses on several topics related to longitudinal continuous and categorical data analysis. Topics include analysis of change, analysis of panel data, longitudinal couple data, latent transition models, and survival mixture models. Examples from the family, social, and behavioral sciences are used.
courses.course_objectives: Students will understand/develop the types of complex hypotheses and research questions for which advanced analytical procedures for panel data are used. Students will perform a number of advanced longitudinal analytical procedures, including higher-order latent growth curve modeling, difference-score growth modeling, mixture modeling and transition analysis, and the combination of these procedures from a structural equation modeling (SEM) perspective. Students will read and evaluate research articles in the area of behavioral science for which these advanced analytical procedures are used.
courses.topical_outline: 1. Orientation to Course 2. Path Analysis, Causation, Indirect, Direct and Total Effects, Mediation, and Moderation 3. Longitudinal CFA, Scale Setting, Factor Invariance, Auto-Correlation, and Methods Factor 4. Stability and Change – Residualized Change 5. Autoregressive Models and Cross-lagged in Panel Data 6. Stability and Change – Absolute Change, Change Scores, and Latent Change 7. Comparison of Residualized Change and Absolute Change 8. Growth Curve Models, Recent Extensions, and Advances 9. Comparison of Auto-Regressive Models and Growth Curves, Associated Models 10. Higher-Order Growth Curves and Advances 11. Mixture Modeling and Advances 12. Longitudinal Transitions, Transitions Across Latent Classes 13. Analysis of Longitudinal Couple Data – APIM, Dyadic Growth, and Common-Fate Models

courses.subject: HDFS
courses.title: Meta-Analysis for Family and Social Sciences
courses.description: Meta-analysis in HDFS/related social sciences. This course covers all steps of performing a meta-analysis, including developing research questions, searching for literature, coding effect sizes and study characteristics, analyzing meta-analytic data, and preparing a publishable manuscript. Students will use Excel, SPSS, Mplus, and/or R packages at various steps of meta-analytic review.

courses.subject: HDFS
courses.title: Practicum in Couple and Family Therapy
courses.description: Supervised experience in couple and family therapy.
courses.course_objectives: The purpose of practicum is to facilitate student’s growth in clinical knowledge and expertise as well as aid the student in the development of their personal theory of change. This objective will be met through supervision of therapy and interaction with the supervisor and other students in the class.
courses.topical_outline:
This course is a practicum for couple and family therapy students seeing clients and getting supervision of that
clinical work. Class sessions consist of case presentations and discussion of case material.

courses.subject: HDFS
courses.title: Supervision of Couple and Family Therapy
courses.description: Methods of supervision in couple and family therapy.
courses.course_objectives: Students will teach advanced doctoral students and supervisors-in-training (SIT) the content of family therapy supervision. Students will support the continual exploration of SIT's in supervisory practice. Students will supervise doctoral student SIT's supervision of family therapists. Students will create a context of growth, critical analysis, and excitement about the field of family therapy training and supervision.
courses.topical_outline:
1. Introduction: Logistics, Contracts, Expectations, AAMFT SIT
Contract 2. Discussion of Contracts, Structure, Evaluations 3. Discussion of History and Ethics 4. Cultural Issues 5. Sexual Orientation and Gender 6. Psychoanalytic and Transgenerational Models 7. Comparing Models and Creating Your Own 8. Purposive Systemic Models 9. Integrative and Postmodern Models 10. Relationships, Power, Problems, and Complexity 11. Methods and Interventions: Tapes and Case Consultations 12. Supervision Settings: Issues and Differences 13. Teaching and Supervising Supervisors

courses.subject: HDFS
courses.title: Applied Supervision of Couple and Family Therapy
courses.description: Supervision of the practice of systemic supervision for clinical doctoral students.
courses.course_objectives: Students will supervise doctoral student SIT's supervision of family therapists. Students will apply critical systemic thinking to complex ethical dilemmas and legal responsibilities of the supervisors of direct clinical practice. Students will demonstrate competencies in relational/systemic supervision of clinical practice. Students will demonstrate knowledge of relevant research to clinical populations being served by Master's-level clinical trainees. Students will demonstrate competency in navigating multicultural content in the practice of supervision and assist Master's-level clinical trainees in developing cultural humility when providing intervention with clients. Students will demonstrate competency in evaluation and assessment of Master's-level clinical trainee’s ability to use a systemic framework in case conceptualization, intervention model selection, goal development, case presentation, assessment, and evaluation.
courses.topical_outline: This course is a practicum for couple and family therapy supervisors in training (SITs) supervising Master's-level clinicians and getting supervision of that supervision experience. Class sessions consist of case presentations, discussion of case material, and live observation of supervision of Master's-level clinical trainees.

courses.subject: HEBR

courses.description: Readings in the Bible, in Hebrew, with an emphasis on fluidity, vocabulary development, and understanding how to capture nuance in translation.

courses.subject: HFIM
courses.title: Introduction to Hospitality and Food Industry Management
courses.description: Major components and organizational structure of the hospitalityand food industry. An introduction to hospitality and foodindustry business management principles, sales and marketingprinciples, financial planning and budgeting principles, andbusiness ethics.

courses.subject: HFIM
courses.title: Hospitality and Food Industry Marketing
courses.description: Analysis of services provided to consumers in the hospitality and food industry and the application of fundamental consumer marketing and research concepts to these services, including lodging, food services, and special events.
courses.prerequisiteText: HFIM 2500 and (AAEC 2580 or AAEC 2580E or ECON 2106 or ECON 2106E or ECON 2106H)

courses.description: Analysis of services provided to consumers in the hospitality and food industry and the application of fundamental consumer marketing and research concepts to these services, including lodging, food services, and special events.

courses.subject: HFIM
courses.title: Hospitality and Food Industry Human Resource Management
courses.description: Application of human resource management in hospitality and foodindustry environments; recruitment, selection, training,compensation, motivation, and performance appraisals; laborrelations and government regulations specific to the hospitalityand food industry.
courses.course_objectives: Students will analyze and apply key human resource management principles related to recruitment, selection, training, and retention, assessing their impact on workforce performance in the hospitality industry. Students will collaboratively design a training program tailored to the needs of a hospitality organization, incorporating principles of adult learning and industry-specific requirements. Students will evaluate strategies for creating a positive workplace culture, improving employee motivation, and managing performance in hospitality and food service operations. Students will illustrate employment laws, labor relations, and government regulations specific to the hospitality and food sectors, assessing their impact on workplace policies and decision-making. Students will analyze emerging workforce trends in the hospitality industry and develop strategies to address key workplace challenges, including the integration of technology, workplace ethics, and employee turnover.
courses.topical_outline:
Fundamental Employment Laws and Applications Job Analysis and Job Design Employee Recruiting, Selection, and Retention Plans and
Actions Workplace Orientation and Culture Employee Training and Development Incentives, Benefits, and Compensation Evaluating Employee Performance Dealing Effectively with Conflict, Turnover, Discipline, and
Exits

courses.subject: HFIM
courses.title: Hospitality and Food Industry Professional Development
courses.description: Professional development preparation to facilitate effectivecareer management. Must be completed prior to internships.

courses.subject: HFIM
courses.title: Hospitality and Food Industry Law and Liability
courses.description: Survey of the primary laws and regulations that apply to thehospitality and food industry and how to effectively manage thecommon legal issues/liabilities faced by hospitality and foodmanagers.

courses.subject: HFIM
courses.title: Hospitality and Food Industry Financial Management
courses.description: Financial concepts, principles, and analysis related to the function of firms in the hospitality and food industry, including financial statements, budgeting, and investment analysis.

courses.description: Introduction to building systems and facilities management forhospitality and food industry establishments. Explores theengineering and maintenance requirements peculiar to thehospitality and food industry. Special emphasis onsustainability, building operating systems, and resource management.

courses.subject: HFIM
courses.title: International Food Culture and Cuisine
courses.description: Exploration of multiple world cultures using food, language, religion, geography, communication, and politics, among other attributes, and compare/contrast with our own diverse cultures here in the United States.
courses.course_objectives: By the end of this course, students will be able to illustrate the role of intercultural communication. By the end of this course, students will be able to compare and contrast the foods and world cultural relationship of other ethnic groups. By the end of this course, students will be able to recognize the similar and diverse ways in which international food customs and traditions differ among the groups in the United States and globally. By the end of this course, students will be able to critique the relationship of food customs to food safety, government regulations, and religious restrictions. By the end of this course, students will be able to identify through self-examination of individual cultural uniqueness.
courses.topical_outline: Introduction to Food and Culture Traditional Health Beliefs Intercultural Communication Food and Religion Native American Culture and Cuisine Regional American Cuisine Cuisine Around the World

courses.description: An overview of the components of hotel and lodging operations; ahistorical view of the development of the hotel and lodgingindustry; an understanding of the functions of front andback-of-the-house hotel and lodging operations; classificationsof hotel and lodging products and services; and trends in hotel and lodging development and operations.

courses.subject: HFIM
courses.title: Hospitality Beverage Management
courses.description: This is an introductory-level course designed to acquaint the student with many products and processes pertaining to the world of beverages. Through lectures, demonstrations, and hands-on experiences, the student will learn proper techniques of effective beverage management. Through actual tastings, they will compare and contrast the most common products served in beverage operations. Also examined will be the health, legal, and moral obligations attendant with the service and consumption of spirited beverages.

courses.subject: HFIM
courses.title: Hospitality and Food Industry Organizational Behavior and Leadership
courses.description: Course provides a comprehensive analysis of human behavior and examines how employee behavior affects organizational performance. Course will provide students a framework for understanding how culture, employee motivation, job design, leaderships and communication, conflict, and team development impact performance.
courses.course_objectives: By the end of this course, students will be able to describe how enduring personality traits and psychological   characteristics influence a manager’s behavior and how these relate to and impact the organizational culture of a hospitality organization. By the end of this course, students will be able to describe the role of managers in implementing strategy to achieve the goals and objectives of a hospitality organization. By the end of this course, students will be able to describe the types of organizational structures that are appropriate in a hospitality setting. By the end of this course, students will be able to describe how motivation theories can be applied in the hospitality context to maximize employee productivity, retention, professional development, and satisfaction. By the end of this course, students will be able to explain leadership attributes contribute to the effectiveness of hospitality managers. By the end of this course, students will be able to explain how effective group leadership contributes to the effectiveness of hospitality organizations. By the end of this course, students will be able to describe how hospitality managers can encourage and facilitate collaborative cross-functional decision-making.
courses.topical_outline: Organizational behavior and management in a hospitality setting Individual differences personality and ability The hospitality experience of work: Values, attitudes, and moods Perception attribution and the management of diversity Learning in organizations Nature of hospitality work and motivation Job design and goal setting Performance appraisal, pay, and hospitality careers Hospitality stress and work-life linkages Effective work groups and teams Leading hospitality organizations Communication Decision making The hospitality organizational structure and culture Power, politics, and conflict in hospitality settings Organizational change and development
