courses.subject: HIST
courses.title: World War II in History and Memory
courses.description: Examination of how the public memory of World War II changed in different countries in Asia, Europe, and North America from the immediate aftermath of the war to the present.

courses.subject: HIST
courses.title: Histories of the Soviet People
courses.description: The Soviet Union was a diverse federation of fifteen proto-states, peopled by myriad ethnic groups speaking nearly two hundred languages and dialects. While Russians in many ways occupied the center, the non-Russian peoples of the Soviet Union are central to understanding the country’s form and fate. These are their histories.
courses.prerequisiteText: One course in HIST or POLS or INTL or CMLT or RUSS or SOCI or JOUR or COMM

courses.subject: HIST
courses.title: Holocausts in History
courses.description: The Jewish Holocaust 1933-1945, emphasizing historical precedents and consequences.  Traditional religious anti-Semitism, biologically-based racism, and extreme nationalism will be investigated as sources of modern genocidal behavior.

courses.subject: HIST
courses.title: History of Science and Religion in Western Society
courses.description: The historical interaction of science and religion in WesternSociety from antiquity to the present. Key historical episodesinclude the rise of Greek natural philosophy, science in medieval Christendom and Islam, the Galileo affair, religion in the Enlightenment, the Darwinian challenge, and religious implicatons of modern physics.

courses.subject: HIST
courses.title: Newton, Einstein, Bohr: History and Philosophical Lessons of Modern Physics
courses.description: Introduction to the history of modern physics and its underlying philosophy for both science and non-science majors.  Basic concepts of classical physics, relativity, and quantum mechanics are explained through their history, which combines intellectual, biographical, and cultural approaches.  Shows how philosophical ideas shaped the development of science and how the latter, in turn, changed human views of the world.

courses.subject: HIST
courses.title: History of Russian Science from Eastern Exploration to the Space Age
courses.description: An introduction to the role of science and technology in Russian history: the Imperial Academy, universities, disputes over Darwinism, the Soviet system of research, the fiasco of Lysenkoism in biology, successes in physics, and the unexpected triumph of Soviet space exploration.

courses.subject: HIST
courses.title: The Nuclear Age: Science, Bombs, and the World Order in the Twentieth Century
courses.description: An exploration of the role of nuclear energy and weapons in the history of the twentieth century, from the humble origins of the science of radioactivity and atomic nucleus, through the drama of World War II's race for the atomic bomb, to the nuclear-centered world politics and diplomacy of the Cold War.

courses.subject: HIST
courses.title: The History of Oil: Energy, Labor, and Politics
courses.description: Course traces the history of the political, economic, and social history of oil in the twentieth and twenty-first centuries. It details the impact of oil on the rise and fall of empires and nations, the social ramifications of the oil industry on local cultures and societies, the role of petrostates in modern geopolitics, and the contribution of the oil industry to the economic and environmental crises.
courses.course_objectives: By the end of this course, students will be able to arrive at conclusions about the history of oil gathering and weighing evidence, logical argument, and listening to counter argument. By the end of this course, students will be able to write stylistically appropriate papers and essays. Students will be able to analyze ideas and evidence, organize their thoughts, and revise and edit their finished essays. By the end of this course, students will be able to identify how the history of oil shaped diverse social and cultural attitudes toward labor and environment, energy and consumption, and empire and power, encouraging them to understand diverse worldviews and experiences. By the end of this course, students will be able to apply appropriate methodological approaches to their analysis of primary sources and to organize their evidence to show historical continuities and discontinuities. By the end of this course, students will be able to generate their own research question or topic, locate suitable primary and secondary sources, and synthesize their ideas in novel ways. By the end of this course, students will be able to initiate, manage, complete, and evaluate their independent research projects in stages and to give and receive constructive feedback through the peer review process.
courses.topical_outline: 1. Fossil Capital: Steam, Coal, and the Petroleum Industry 2. The Breakup of Big Oil: The Standard Oil Monopoly and the Texas Oil Boom 3. The Oil Wars: Carbon Conflict in the Dutch East Indies, Russia, and Iran 4. Petronationalism: The Seven Sisters in Latin America and the Middle East 5. A World Safe for Oil: Conspiracies and Military Coups in Venezuela and Iran 6. America’s Kingdom: Oil, Labor Conflict, and Communism in Saudi Arabia 7. Pyramids in the Sand: Petrodollars, Weapon Sales, and Economic Development 8. The Red Sheikh: Nationalism, Third Worldism, and the Rise of OPEC 9. The Energy Crisis: Peak Oil, Producer Markets, and Environmental Catastrophism 10. The Oil Shock: Yom Kippur War, Oil Boycott, and Iranian Revolution 11. Hydrocarbon Horizons: Supply Shocks and New Frontiers in Shale Production 12. The Long Gulf War: Production Quotas and War in the Persian/Arab Gulf 13. Blood and Oil: Resources, Markets, and Wars in Iraq and Ukraine 14. Renewable Revolutions: Climate Change, Green Energy, and Fracking Debates 15. Blessings and Curses: Wealth, Corruption, and Dictatorship in Contemporary Petrostates 16. The End of Growth: Economic Necessities vs. Environmental Limitations

courses.subject: HIST
courses.title: A Global History of Drugs
courses.description: Exploration of drugs and medicines as commodities in thenineteenth and twentieth centuries. How different cultures and societies across the world have shaped the meanings of drugs and medicine, and how drugs and medicines have conversely influenced peoples' habits and social relationships across the globe.

courses.subject: HIST
courses.title: A Global History of Drugs
courses.description: Exploration of drugs and medicines as commodities in the nineteenth and twentieth centuries. How different cultures and societies across the world have shaped the meanings of drugs and medicine, and how drugs and medicines have conversely influenced peoples' habits and social relationships across the globe.

courses.subject: HIST
courses.title: Democracy in Modern Europe
courses.description: An exploration of the role of nuclear energy and weapons in the history of the twentieth century, from the humble origins of the science of radioactivity and atomic nucleus, through the drama of World War II's race for the atomic bomb, to the nuclear-centered world politics and diplomacy of the Cold War.

courses.subject: HIST
courses.title: History of Islam in Africa
courses.description: Examination of the history of Muslim Africa. The rise and spread of Islam as well as the European conquest and occupation. Examines issues of race, gender, and slavery and requires students to analyze primary sources and historical debates in formal essays.

courses.subject: HIST
courses.title: The History of Orientalism
courses.description: Images and symbolism used by Europeans and Americans to define the Islamic Middle East.  The history of the Middle East through representation--stereotypes, myths, fairy tales, novels, films, and news coverage--particularly the ramifications of these images on Western foreign policy towards the Islamic Middle East.
courses.course_objectives: By the end of this course, students will be able to arrive at conclusions about the history of Orientalism by gathering and weighing evidence, logical argument, and listening to counter argument. By the end of this course, students will be able to write stylistically appropriate papers and essays. Students will be able to analyze ideas and evidence, organize their thoughts, and revise and edit their finished essays. By the end of this course, students will be able to identify how the history of Orientalism shaped diverse social and cultural attitudes toward religion and civilization, race and ethnicity, and empire and domination, encouraging them to understand diverse worldviews and experiences. By the end of this course, students will be able to apply appropriate methodological approaches to their analysis of primary sources and to organize their evidence to show historical continuities and discontinuities. By the end of this course, students will be able to generate their own research question or topic, locate suitable primary and secondary sources, and synthesize their ideas in novel ways. By the end of this course, students will be able to initiate, manage, complete, and evaluate their independent research projects in stages and to give and receive constructive feedback through the peer review process.
courses.topical_outline: The European Discovery of Islam in the Middle Ages Islam and the Renaissance Changing Views of the Middle East in the Age of Enlightenment Romanticism and the Golden Age of Orientalism Knowledge and Imperialism Orientalism and Imperial Administration Orientalism and "Scientific" Racism Orientalists and Arabophiles Zionism and Orientalism The Middle East through American Eyes The Current Debate on Orientalism as a Discipline
courses.prerequisiteText: Any HIST course or ENGL 1101 or ENGL 1101E or ENGL 1101S or ENGL 1102 or ENGL 1102E or ENGL 1102S or POLS 1101 or POLS 1101E or POLS 1101H or POLS 1101S

courses.subject: HIST
courses.title: Law and Society in Colonial India
courses.description: Exploration of the relationship between law and society in colonial India. Features cases relating to marriage and divorce, property and inheritance, sedition, and criminal conspiracy woven through the lives of ordinary people in nineteenth and twentieth century India.
courses.course_objectives: Students will be able to describe the relationship between law and society in colonial India throughout the nineteenth and twentieth centuries and the changes in this relationship over this time, in 3-4 sentences. Students will be able to analyze primary source legal materials from the nineteenth and twentieth centuries in the Indian subcontinent (case-law, statutes, legal reporting in historical newspapers) developed through scaffolding assignments such as journal entries, presentations, and class discussions throughout the course. Students will be able to identify the historical implications of contemporary legal developments in India including changes in marriage, divorce, property, and inheritance laws as well as provisions in criminal law and criminal procedure retained from the colonial period such as sedition and describe the significance of adopting a legal historical perspective on these developments.
courses.topical_outline: Introduction: Law and the Establishment of the East India Company The Role of Legal Intermediaries in the Making of Indian Law Law and Social Reform in the Early 19th century: The Debate over Sati Rukhmabai’s Case: The Restitution of Conjugal Rights and Legal Reform Meet the Abrahams: Law and Indigenous Agency in Colonial-Era Courts Jurisdictional Jostling: Forum Shopping from Bombay to Baroda Utilitarianism, Macaulay and the Indian Penal Code The Rise and Fall of the Criminal Jury Trial in India The End of Company Rule and the Trial and Exile of Bahadur Shah Zafar The Role of Lawyers in the Indian Freedom Struggle Ambedkar, Gandhi and the Debates over Political Equality The Great Trial of 1922: Gandhi in Court The India and Pakistan Partition and the Legal Regimes of Evacuee Property The 1970s Emergency and the Role of the Indian Supreme Court Conclusion and Wrap Up

courses.subject: HIST
courses.title: Studies in Middle Eastern History since 1600
courses.description: A special issue or topic not otherwise offered in the history curriculum. Topics, methodology, and instructors will vary from semester to semester. Representative topics include: "Modern Shi'ism," "War and Society in the Modern Middle East," and "The Ottomans and Europe."
courses.course_objectives: By the end of this course, students will be able to arrive at conclusions about Middle Eastern history by gathering and weighing evidence, logical argument, and listening to counter argument. By the end of this course, students will be able to write stylistically appropriate papers and essays. Students will be able to analyze ideas and evidence, organize their thoughts, and revise and edit their finished essays. By the end of this course, students will be able to identify how selected topics in the History of the Middle East shaped diverse social and cultural attitudes toward race, religion, gender, or morality, encouraging them to understand diverse worldviews and experiences. By the end of this course, students will be able to apply appropriate methodological approaches to their analysis of primary sources and to organize their evidence to show historical continuities and discontinuities. By the end of this course, students will be able to generate their own research question or topic, locate suitable primary and secondary sources, and synthesize their ideas in novel ways. By the end of this course, students will be able to initiate, manage, complete, and evaluate their independent research projects in stages and to give and receive constructive feedback through the peer review process.
courses.topical_outline: Will vary from instructor to instructor and from topic to topic Sample outline on "Modern Shi'ism" What is Shi`ism The Geography of Sectarian Difference The Creation of the Modern Shi`i Hierarchy Shi`ism and Modernity in Iran Shi`ism and the Formation of the Iraqi State The Lebanese Shi`a: Out of the Margins Shi`ism in the Gulf The Iranian Revolution The Contemporary Shi`i Revival
courses.prerequisiteText: HIST 2701 or HIST 2701H or HIST 2702 or HIST 2702H or HIST 3561 or HIST 3562 or HIST 3564 or HIST 3580

courses.subject: HIST
courses.title: The Crusades
courses.description: The origins and development of the Crusades from 1095 until the fall of Acre in 1291. The origins of Crusading, the concepts of just war and Jihad, and the Byzantine and Islamic responses to the Crusades.
courses.prerequisiteText: HIST 2301 or HIST 2311H or HIST 2701H or HIST 3330 or HIST 3561 or HIST 3570H or HIST 4330/6330 or HIST 4345 or HIST 4371/6371

courses.subject: HIST
courses.title: The Arab-Israeli Conflict
courses.description: Exploration of the origins and development of the struggle forland between Jews and Palestinians, and how that struggle spreadthroughout the Arab Middle East.  We will begin by exploring thegrowth of Zionism among Russian and European Jews in thenineteenth century as well as the beginnings of nationalism amongArabs in Palestine under the Ottoman Empire.  From there we willcontinue with issues of statehood, nationalism, colonialism andthe continuation of the conflict to today.
courses.prerequisiteText: Any HIST course or ENGL 1101 or ENGL 1101E or ENGL 1101S or ENGL 1102 or ENGL 1102E or ENGL 1102S or POLS 1101 or POLS 1101E or POLS 1101H or POLS 1101S

courses.subject: HIST
courses.title: Studies in Asian History
courses.description: A special issue or topic not otherwise offered in the history curriculum.  Topics, methodology, and instructors will vary from semester to semester.  Representative topics include "Japan and the Samurai," "Women, Gender and Family in Traditional Japan," and "Court and Countryside in Japan's Golden Age."

courses.subject: HIST
courses.title: The World of the Samurai
courses.description: The evolution of Japan's warrior tradition from earliest times to the late nineteenth century.  The role of warriors in society, the ethics and values of the samurai, and the nature of warfare as these developed and changed during the millennium that has become known as the Age of the Samurai.

courses.subject: HIST
courses.title: The Chinese Industrial Revolution
courses.description: Chinese economic history in world perspective, from the medievalcommercial revolutions to the 19th-century crisis. The rise ofEuropean-dominated industrial capitalism was a reversal oflong-term trends of a China-centered world system. A comparativeapproach will explain how the Chinese and European economictrajectories diverged between labor intensive commercializationand land-intensive capitalism.

courses.subject: HIST
courses.title: Everyday Life in Ming China
courses.description: A cultural history of the Ming dynasty (1368-1644), focusing onthe structures of everyday life. Topics will include the cultureof commerce, conspicuous consumption, artistic production, urbanspaces, technologies of gender, and literary masterpieces.

courses.subject: HIST
courses.title: Japan: The Golden Age of the Imperial Court
courses.description: The world of Japan's late classical age, focusing on the culture, the social structure, and the political evolution of the imperial court.

courses.subject: HIST
courses.title: Warriors and Warlords in Medieval Japan
courses.description: Japan's medieval world, focusing on the evolving political, social, and cultural make-up of the country from the 13th through the 16th centuries.

courses.subject: HIST
courses.title: Themes in Comparative History
courses.description: A special subject not otherwise offered in the history curriculum.  Topics, methodology, and instructors vary from semester to semester.

courses.subject: HIST
courses.title: Modern Medievalisms
courses.description: What were the Middle Ages like after they ended? Examination of how modern cultures have imagined the medieval past —from the Victorians and their Viking heroes to Monty Python,Derrida, Game of Thrones, and white nationalism — and how theMiddle Ages are still shaping the present as a result.
courses.prerequisiteText: One 2000-level HIST course or one 3000-level HIST course or one 4000-level HIST course

courses.subject: HIST
courses.title: Statelessness in Global History
courses.description: Instances of statelessness and refugeedom dominate headlines today. But what does “statelessness” mean? Rather than solely focusing on contemporary legal interpretations of statelessness, this course emphasizes twentieth century global, regional, and national histories within which statelessness emerged as a political and legal category.
courses.course_objectives: Students will be able to distinguish between different categories of displacement, including refugeedom and statelessness. Students will be able to locate nationality not only as an international legal category, but as emerging from within national and regional histories. Students will be able to articulate in concrete terms, the challenges associated with writing histories of statelessness – access to archival materials, the ethics of conducting oral history interviews with displaced persons, and confidentiality. Students will be able to draw links between legal histories of displacement and contemporary developments such as climate-change induced displacement.
courses.topical_outline: Introductions Identifying Keywords – “migrant,” “refugee,” “alien,” “stateless person” The History of Nationality as an International Legal Category and the Role of Empire The Role of Passports as Travel Documents and Identity Documents World War II and the Right to Have Rights The Legal History of the UN Conventions on the Status of Refugees and the Status of Stateless Persons Partitions and the Creation of Stateless Populations The Cold War and the Uneven Development of the International Refugee Regime The UNHCR Case Files as a Historical Source The UK and its Asylum Policies: A Historical Perspective Working with Materials from UGA Special Collections Climate Refugees: A new legal category to address statelessness? Conclusions and Presentations

courses.subject: HIST
courses.title: The People Behind Public Policy
courses.description: Who really makes public policy? For the past thirty years, historians of public policy have broadened the scope of understanding who really shapes public policy, emphasizing the importance of race, gender, class, and power. We will explore more top-down accounts of top leaders and their advisors as well as lawmakers, lobbyists, activists, and ordinary people, all of whom have had important roles in coming up with, advocating, passing, amending, and repealing policies.
courses.course_objectives: Students will learn the importance of the different stages of policymaking, from recognizing a problem through implementation. Students will learn to consider the importance of race, gender, class, and power to the different stages of policymaking. Students will learn how to analyze how those and other categories shaped public policies that continue to shape what it means to live, work, and be a resident or citizen. Students will know how to research and write an historically focused policy brief attuned to the many people involved in making or changing public policy.
courses.topical_outline: A “progressive” world order Economic Crisis & Reform Democracy & Decolonization Neoliberalism in a Multi-Polar World

courses.subject: HIST
courses.title: Marx and Marxist History (Honors)
courses.description: This course on Marx covers five issues: revolutions, thetransition from feudalism to capitalism, industrial and monopolycapitalism, women and capitalism, and contemporary capitalism.Includes extensive readings from Marx and Engels along withselections from later Marxists.

courses.subject: HIST
courses.title: History and Film
courses.description: We are living in a post-literate age.  Most people now get their history from films instead of books.  How film, using a different vocabulary than that of books, recreates the past.
courses.prerequisiteText: Any HIST course or ENGL 1101 or ENGL 1101E or ENGL 1101S or ENGL 1102 or ENGL 1102E or ENGL 1102S or POLS 1101 or POLS 1101E or POLS 1101H or POLS 1101S

courses.subject: HIST
courses.title: Oral History Methods and Theory
courses.description: Exploration of the methods and theory of oral history. Studentswill learn about the discipline’s rise in the 1960s and 1970s (intandem with social history) and engage ethical and theoreticaldebates within the discipline. They then will conduct, process,and analyze an oral history interview, putting theory into practice.

courses.subject: HIST
courses.title: Museum Registration Methods
courses.description: The course will review the history and methods of museum registration and collections management.
courses.course_objectives: Students who complete this course will develop an understanding of the history of museum registration. Students will learn about cataloguing and records management of museum collections. Students will learn how to develop a museum collections management policy.
courses.topical_outline:

courses.subject: HIST
courses.title: History Internship
courses.description: This course is for the history major who is accepted into aninternship program to gain experience in an institution ororganization and who wants to earn academic credit for history-related research work in conjunction with the internship. Ascholarly research paper is required. Enrollment is subject toapproval of the course application.
courses.course_objectives: Introduces the history major to professional career interests Students will gain practical experience and learn how the major relates to a particular career path Students will gain work skills and networking capabilities related to their field of internship
courses.topical_outline:
The student, along with a faculty instructor, will devise a course proposal and topical outline directly related to the internship position and research component of the course. Examples of internships and related research projects have included - radio internship: study of war-time Nazi radio propaganda; Washington semester internship: historical research on topics in lobbying and legislation. The course proposal will provide a description of the internship, how it relates to the discipline of history, and
how course objectives relate to the practical internship experience and academic research. A schedule for communication between the faculty instructor and student should be determined and included. The topical outline of the academic paper will include a thesis statement, preliminary bibliography, and required or recommended publications. The scholarly paper must be 15-20 pages.

courses.subject: HIST
courses.title: Professional Development Internship in History
courses.description: Students will partner with an internship sponsor with the purpose of obtaining practical applications for the skills they have developed as part of their History degree at the University of Georgia.
courses.course_objectives: This course is designed to reinforce and practice the soft skills learned in the history classroom, via practical experience, on-the-job training, and exploration of career opportunities in various history-related fields. This course will help students compete more effectively on the job market. Students will be able to put into practice the skills they have learned in the history classroom. Students will be able to evaluate various career paths/options. Students will have been able to improve their professional skills in collaboration with local communities and industries.
courses.topical_outline: This course is designated for the undergraduate internship but will meet formally four times a semester. Students will choose from many different types of professional internships. Examples might include: communications internships, program assistant internships, and internships with archives, institutes, and historical societies. 1) Research and reporting methods 2) Collaborations with community partners 3) Historical writing for a public audience 4) Professional development: resume, publications, conferences

courses.subject: HIST
courses.title: Directed Readings in History
courses.description: Individual study, reading, or projects under the direction of a project director.

courses.title: Faculty-Mentored Undergraduate Research I
courses.description: Faculty-supervised independent or collaborative inquiry into fundamental and applied problems within a discipline that requires students to gather, analyze, and synthesize and interpret data and to present results in writing and other relevant communication formats.

courses.subject: HIST
courses.title: Faculty-Mentored Undergraduate Research II

courses.subject: HIST
courses.title: Faculty-Mentored Undergraduate Research III
courses.description: Faculty-supervised independent or collaborative inquiry into fundamental and applied problems within a discipline that requires students to gather, analyze, and synthesize and interpret data and to present results in writing and other relevant communication formats.

courses.subject: HIST
courses.title: Senior Thesis in History
courses.description: Students research and write an original and substantial thesisunder faculty mentorship. Students formulate their own researchquestions, identify and analyze primary sources, synthesizehistoriography, present and discuss their work as part of theresearch process, and explain the significance of their findingsfor understanding the past and present.
courses.course_objectives: By the end of this course, students will be able to arrive at conclusions about a specific historic subject by gathering and weighing evidence, logical argument, and listening to counter argument. By the end of this course, students will be able to write stylistically appropriate historical research essays. Students will be able to analyze ideas and evidence, organize their thoughts, and revise and edit their finished essays. By the end of this course, students will be able to identify how the history of a specific historical topic -- which will vary according to instructor -- shaped diverse social and cultural attitudes toward categories like race and ethnicity, gender and sexuality, and religion and culture, encouraging them to understand diverse worldviews and experiences. By the end of this course, students will be able to apply appropriate methodological approaches to their analysis of primary sources, using such sources to support their own original analysis of a particular historical topic and organizing their evidence to show historical continuities and discontinuities. By the end of this course, students will be able to generate their own research question or topic, locate suitable primary and secondary sources, and synthesize their ideas in novel ways. By the end of this course, students will be able to initiate, manage, complete, and evaluate their independent research projects in stages and to give and receive constructive feedback through the peer review process.

Themes in Military History A Brief Survey of Military History Using the Library Finding a Topic and Finding Sources Reading History Historical Analysis The Mechanics of Research and Writing Individual Work on Bibliographies and Prospectuses Class Presentations Individual Work on Papers Organizing a Research Paper Writing Well Individual Meetings with Instructor Individual Work on Papers Final Paper Presentations

courses.title: Undergraduate Research Thesis (or Final Project)

Students will be able to analyze ideas and evidence, organize their thoughts, and revise and edit their finished essays. courses.subject: HIST
courses.title: The Medieval Middle East: An Introduction
courses.description: The history of the medieval Islamic world from the seventh to thefifteenth century, covering the major political, religious, andsocial developments of the period.

courses.subject: HIST
courses.title: Master's Research
courses.description: Research while enrolled for a master's degree under the direction of faculty members.

courses.subject: HIST
courses.title: Graduate Student Seminar
courses.description: Advanced supervised experience in an applied setting.  Thiscourse may not be used to satisfy a student's approved program ofstudy.

courses.subject: HIST
courses.title: Area Colloquium
courses.description: Readings and discussions on major themes in the history and historiography of a geographical area.  Time period and area will vary with the instructor.

courses.subject: HIST
courses.title: Master's Thesis
courses.description: Thesis writing under the direction of the major professor.

courses.subject: HIST
courses.title: Writing and Composition
courses.description: This course supports M.A. students through the thesis-writing process, combining historical research and writing with project management skills. Through sequenced assignments and collaborative activities, students refine their scholarship, time management, and revision strategies, culminating in an article-length thesis based on original primary research.
courses.course_objectives: Students will be able to develop and refine advanced research, analytical, and writing skills necessary to produce an article-length thesis. Students will be able to engage critically with primary sources and situate their findings within relevant historiographic debates. Students will be able to gain practical project management strategies for large-scale academic writing. Students will be able to produce successive drafts of their thesis, incorporating substantive feedback at each stage. Students be able to complete and submit a polished thesis on schedule.
courses.topical_outline: •	What is a thesis? •	Conducting Primary Source Research •	Identifying Secondary Sources •	Making a Writing Plan •	Time Management and Motivation •	Crafting an Argument •	Using Evidence •	Staying on Track •	Editing •	Formatting

courses.subject: HIST
courses.title: Professional Development for Historians
courses.description: This professionalization seminar offers graduate studentshands-on preparation for launching careers as historians in theacademy and other settings. The course covers the trajectory ofcareer development from conference paper submissions to jobapplication dossiers.

courses.subject: HIST
courses.title: History, Mapping, and Spatial Analysis
courses.description: GIS is a technology that allows users to store and analyzeinformation spatially. Exploration of its usefulness to historians and how to employ it in our own work. Over the length of the semester, students will work on a mapping project related to their own interests and research.

courses.subject: HIST
courses.title: Museum Ethics and Controversies
courses.description: This course will explore ethical issues pertaining to museums, including practices relating to collecting and exhibiting artifacts, institutional governance and funding, and education and public programs. Students will interpret, assess, and critique current professional standards for museum ethics, including the examination of emerging ethical issues in museums and collections.
courses.course_objectives: Students who complete this course will develop an understanding of the history of museum ethics Students will learn best practices for implementing ethical standards as museum professionals Students will develop an understanding of the issues, controversies, and theorists that have helped define museum ethics
courses.topical_outline: Why the need for Ethical Standards in Museums? Ethical Collecting Loot Deaccessioning Practices Repatriation Public Stewardship Ethical Labor Practices Responsible Fundraising Navigating Board Politics and Conflicts Climate Change and Collections Making Your Mission Matter Ethical Educational Programming

courses.subject: HIST
courses.title: Museum Exhibitions
courses.description: Exploration of practices used in the development, research, and design of museum exhibitions. The course will also consider the history of object display in the United States and examine major turning points in the development of museum exhibitions.
courses.course_objectives: Students will learn best practices for developing museum exhibitions Students who complete this course will develop an understanding of the history of museum exhibitions Students will develop an understanding of the issues and theories relating to museum exhibition design
courses.topical_outline: History of Museum Display World’s Fairs and Museum Exhibitions The Museum Exhibit in the 20th Century 21st Century Interventions in Museum Exhibition Pivotal Museum Exhibits Developing Your Exhibit’s “Big Idea” Writing for the Public Researching for Exhibitions Writing Object Labels Interactive Display Exhibition Design Installation Practices Audience Engagement and Programming Managing Loan Exhibitions Marketing Your Exhibition for Travel Deinstallation Practices

courses.subject: HIST
courses.title: Theory and Practice of History
courses.description: Methods of research and fundamental theoretical issues pertaining to practicing the science of history, with emphasis on the development of writing skills.

courses.subject: HIST
courses.title: Independent Reading Colloquium
courses.description: Readings on major themes in the history and historiography of a geographical area or topic.  Time period, area, and topic will vary with the instructor.  Offered on request.
courses.offeredText: Not offered on a regular basis.

courses.subject: HIST
courses.title: Teaching History in Colleges and Universities
courses.description: The variety of methods appropriate to instruction in college-level survey history courses. Students will develop syllabi and course materials in preparation for teaching their own surveys.

courses.subject: HIST
courses.title: Seminar in Early American History
courses.description: A research seminar in early American history.  Native Americans, Spanish and French borderlands, British settlement, elaboration of colonial institutions, colonial wars, the American Revolution, and the rise of the new nation.

courses.subject: HIST
courses.title: Seminar in Middle Period United States History
courses.description: A research seminar in which students should produce a potentially publishable paper upon some topic relating to the American South, the American Civil War, or Reconstruction.

courses.subject: HIST
courses.title: United States Women, Politics, and History
courses.description: This interdisciplinary course investigates reform and thechanging meaning of gender from the Colonial to Post Modernperiod. An emphasis upon real rather than ideological politics is the focus of discussions of change and continuity. Other major themes include the meaning of politics and the evolution of women's politics.

courses.subject: HIST
courses.title: Seminar in Recent United States History
courses.description: Social, intellectual, cultural, and political developments in United States history since 1900.

courses.subject: HIST
courses.title: Colloquium in Southern History
courses.description: Focuses on historiographical analyses of key events and circumstances in southern history from slavery to the Sunbelt.  Heavy emphasis on critical reading of secondary texts and historiographical writing.

courses.subject: HIST
courses.title: State and Society in Modern America
courses.description: Major themes, historiographical debates, and methods in United States sociopolitical history since 1865.

courses.subject: HIST
courses.title: Colloquium in United States Cultural History
courses.description: Offers an in-depth examination of the major themes and debatesin, as well as theories and methods of, American cultural history of the nineteenth to twenty-first centuries.

courses.subject: HIST
courses.title: The Early American Continent
courses.description: We have for generations conflated the British colonies with allof early America.  This course instead explores the entirecontinent, from Sitka to St. Augustine, and all the people living there, including native peoples, Russians, Spanish, French, and British. Students will emerge with a clearer sense of the continuities and discontinuities in early American history and with a broad synthetic and comparative framework.
courses.offeredText: Not offered on a regular basis.

courses.subject: HIST
courses.title: Colloquium in North American History and United States History to 1865
courses.description: Major themes and current historiography in North American and United States history to 1865.

courses.subject: HIST
courses.title: Colloquium in United States History: 1865 to the present
courses.description: Major themes and current historiography in United States history from 1865 to the present.

courses.subject: HIST
courses.title: Colloquium in Latin American and Caribbean History
courses.description: Major themes and historiography in Latin American and Caribbean history from pre-Columbian times to the present.

courses.subject: HIST
courses.title: Seminar in Early Modern Europe
courses.description: Research seminar that will allow graduate students to workextensively on a particular theme in early modern Europeanhistory, 1350-1815.

courses.subject: HIST
courses.title: Seminar in Nineteenth-Century European History
courses.description: Selected research topics in nineteenth-century European diplomatic, political, social, economic, and intellectual history.  Topics vary.

courses.subject: HIST
courses.title: Colloquium in Premodern European History
courses.description: The gradual discovery of the individual in premodern Europe. The areas of religion, politics, law, art, and literature.  Readings will range from Plato and Thomas Aquinas to Dante and Leonardo da Vinci.

courses.subject: HIST
courses.title: Colloquium in Early Modern Europe
courses.description: Major themes and current historiography of Europe from 1500-1800.

courses.subject: HIST
courses.title: Colloquium in Modern European History
courses.description: Major themes and current historiography of Europe from 1800 to the present.

courses.subject: HIST
courses.title: The Cold War
courses.description: Graduate research seminar, focused on the development and writing of a significant work of original historical research touching, in some way, on the Cold War. The topic can be interpreted broadly in theme and geography.
courses.course_objectives: Students will learn to assess the potential and the shortcomings of a source base. Students will learn to design a research question with the care and precision required of professional work. Students will learn to organize and write on a deadline, as well as the essential skills of collaboration and generous peer review.
courses.topical_outline: Origins of the Cold War- 19th century through the Russian Revolution Wilson, Lenin, and the "Third World" American anti-communism and the first Red Scare Great Depression and Stalin’s Great Break Transformations of WWII China and the Communist Bloc The Nuclear Age and the Nuclear Age The Science-State and the Military-Industrial Complex The Cold War university McCarthyism and the Second Red Scare Decolonization and the Cold War Cold War in the Global South 1954, 1968, and the international communist movement Détente Cold War Culture—Spies, Sport, Propaganda Decline of the Soviet Bloc “The End of History” and the post-Cold War settlement

courses.subject: HIST
courses.title: Seminar in Twentieth-Century Europe
courses.description: Research in twentieth-century European history.  Topics will vary according to the interests of the students and instructors.

courses.subject: HIST
courses.title: Colloquium in Asian History
courses.description: Readings on and discussion of major issues in the history and historiography of Asia.  Countries and periods of focus will vary from semester to semester.

courses.subject: HIST
courses.title: Colloquium in Pacific World History
courses.description: This graduate colloquium introduces students to the historiography of the Pacific World, loosely defined. We will examine transnational connections among Asia and the Americas, emphasizing the modern period. Major topics include capitalism and labor, colonialism and resistance, global migration and diasporas, race and gender relations, and war and memory.
courses.course_objectives: Students will learn and practice how to analyze scholarly texts. This includes locating scholarly texts within a historiography, identifying key debates that inform their research questions, and critically analyzing the significance of their arguments and evidence. Students will have learned how to write book reviews and historiographical essays. Students will be able to give scholarly presentations and lead seminar discussions.
courses.topical_outline: What is the Pacific? Early Encounters in the “Age of Exploration” Imperialism and Colonialism Global Migrations and Diasporas Commodities and Capital in Circulation Race, Labor, and Gender World War I and World War II The End of Empire Pax Americana and the Cold War

courses.subject: HIST
courses.title: Colloquium in Comparative History
courses.description: Readings and discussion of major topics in the theory and practice of comparative history.

courses.subject: HIST
courses.title: Colloquium in World History
courses.description: Methods, traditions, concepts, and literature of world history.

courses.subject: HIST
courses.title: Colloquium on Gender in History
courses.description: Recent scholarship on gender in a geographic area. The time period of the subject matter will vary with the instructor.

courses.subject: HIST
courses.title: The Atlantic World, 1500-1900
courses.description: Examination of the shared history of Europe, Africa, and theAmericas during the period of colonization and globalization.Between the era of exploration and the age of revolutions, thesecivilizations interacted through conquest, trade, emigration, and cultural exchange, giving rise to a distinctly Atlantic World.

courses.subject: HIST
courses.title: Colloquium in Atlantic World History
courses.description: Exploration of the historiography of the world-making exchanges between  Europe, Africa, and the Americas since colonization. From the era of exploration to the age of revolutions and nation-building, the civilizations of these continents interacted through conquest, trade, migration, and cultural exchanges that gave rise to a distinctly Atlantic World.

courses.subject: HIST
courses.title: Economy as History
courses.description: This graduate colloquium focuses on the feedback loop between“societies” and “economies.” It asks how particular ideas andsocial arrangements have shaped the forms that economies havetaken and how economies have impacted conceptual categories andhuman relationships.

courses.subject: HIST
courses.title: Colloquium in Warfare in History
courses.description: The history of warfare in the context of the warring societies from ancient to modern times.  Topics depend on interest of the instructor.

courses.subject: HIST
courses.title: Gastric Geographies: Food as Power in World History
courses.description: This course explores food and drug delivery systems and the rise of empire. Topics include slave trade goods (cocoa, sugar, coffee, tobacco) and the European scientific renaissance, modern European states, French Revolution, World War I, and the Arab Spring.
courses.course_objectives: Students will be able to understand civil logistics, and its relationship to economics through a geographical lens. Students will be able to account for the growth and expansion of empires as wars over foodways. Students will be able to understand the neuroscience of addiction, and its relationship to the Atlantic Slave Trade. Students will be able to examine how food insecurity has contributed to revolution.
courses.topical_outline: 1.	Kawkaw & the Classic Maya period, 250-900 2.	Sugar: staple of Persia, the Caliphate & the Serene Republics 3.	Slavery & shipbuilding: Portugal, the Netherlands, & Britain 4.	Tropical Drugs & the Birth of Biological Sciences 5.	Tobacco, slavery, and the American Revolution 6.	Coffee & Imperial Wars in the Caribbean & Africa 7.	Phytophthora Infestans & the birth of Free Trade 8.	Crimean War & American Civil War 10.	Britain’s Flour Empire: Argentina, Canada, & Australia 11.	Drugs and the Scramble for Empire post-1865 12.	World War I: A War over Bread 13.	Revolutions & Bread: Russian Revolution & Arab Spring 14.	Applying food and war to contemporary issues

courses.subject: HIST
courses.title: Colloquium in Environmental History
courses.description: Introduction to the discipline of environmental history. Readings will seek to expose students to the variety of methodological approaches employed by environmental historians.  Though much of the reading will focus on the United States environmental history, there will also be a significant world component to the course.

courses.subject: HIST
courses.title: Colloquium in the History of the Senses
courses.description: An introduction to the theory and practice of sensory history in a global context, employing an interdisciplinary and cross-cultural approach.
courses.course_objectives: By the end of this course, graduate students in history will have an advanced understanding of the historiography of the sub-discipline of sensory history. By the end of this course, graduate students in history will have an advanced understanding of the core theories of sensory history, drawn from a variety of social science disciplines. By the end of this course, graduate students in history will demonstrate understanding on a discrete question in sensory history.
courses.topical_outline: 1.	A Survey of the Subfield of Sensory History 2.	Cultural Anthropology of the Senses 3.	Theories of Sensory Perception and Epistemology 4.	Sight: Reimagining Visual Experiences 5.	Sound: Recovering Sonic Worlds 6.	Smell: Reconstructing Olfactory Impressions 7.	Taste: Re-experiencing Gustatory Experiences 8.	Touch: Re-sensing Haptic Environments 9.	Synesthesia: Blurring Sensory Boundaries 10.	Research Presentations

courses.subject: HIST
courses.title: Colloquium on Science and Society
courses.description: Introduction to the Social and Cultural History of Science. Study of the role and practice of science in ancientand modern societies, interaction with religion, politics, andculture, and social consequences of the development ofscientific knowledge.  Readings reflect the variety ofmethodological approaches pursued by historians of science.

courses.subject: HIST
courses.title: Colloquium in History, Museums, and Collections
courses.description: An in-depth examination of the history, issues, methods, and debates in museum studies, including the ethics of collecting.

courses.subject: HIST
courses.title: Colloquium in Public History
courses.description: Examination of the role of public history in the historical profession. In addition to exploring the historiography of the field of public history, the course introduces students to methodsused in the discipline. Students will examine major issues ofpast decades that have shaped the field in the 21st century.

courses.description: Historical and contemporary significance of herbs, spices, and medicinal plants in human culture and commerce; chemical and biological characteristics; commercial production techniques; application in modern and traditional medical systems.

courses.subject: HORT(CRSS)(ENTO)(PATH)
courses.title: Organic Agricultural Systems
courses.description: Philosophy, policies, and practices related to organic agriculture, including the history and development of organic agriculture, current USDA National Organic Program standards, fundamental crop management techniques (horticultural focus), and the organic market. Practical experiences, such as growing crops and sampling methods, are integrated with lecture material.
courses.course_objectives: Students will be able to summarize and explain the basic principles of organic systems. Students will gain applied experiences in organic food production from crop planning to harvest through the care of greenhouse and field crops. Students will further develop critical thinking skills by analyzing and critiquing current literature, regulatory documents, and marketing information related to organic food production. Students will improve their ability to work cooperatively with peers via group activities, class discussions, presentations, and interactions with industry representatives. Graduate students will become familiar with primary and peer-reviewed literature in sustainable agriculture. Graduate students will relate an independent research project to the broader goals and challenges of organic agriculture. Graduate students will gain experience with undergraduate classroom instruction through a class presentation/lesson based on their independent research project.

Students will be responsible for growing several ornamental crops in a greenhouse.
courses.course_objectives: After completing this course, the student will be able to apply the principles of greenhouse site selection. After completing this course, the student will be able to compare and contrast the relative merits and problems associated with the numerous types of greenhouses and be able to select the proper type for their particular needs. After completing this course, the student will be able to design the specifications for greenhouse heating, cooling, and air movement systems. After completing this course, the student will be able to understand the day-to-day operations of producing crops in greenhouses, including substrate selection and preparation; pasteurization of substrates; general greenhouse sanitation; principles and methods of irrigation and fertilization; enrichment of the atmosphere with carbon dioxide; irradiance, photoperiod, and temperature regulation; and chemical regulation of plant growth. After completing this course, the student will be able to seek and analyze alternatives and their costs for each aspect of establishing and operating a greenhouse business.

courses.subject: HORT
courses.title: Plant Phenotyping Technologies
courses.description: Covers the concepts and practical skills for plant phenotyping, from traditional methods to modern advancements. Includes imaging systems, data management, Python programming for phenotypic analysis, and lab activities focused on research experiments, imaging, data analysis, presentations, and scientific writing. Suitable for beginners and those with programming experience.
courses.course_objectives: By the end of this course, students should be able to introduce and explain the principles of plant phenotyping technologies, including the ability to identify the advantages and limitations of each type of system. By the end of this course, students should be able to list, explain, and quantify multiple critical plant phenotypes and analyze the phenotypic traits in digital images by developing a Python program. By the end of this course, students should be able to design and implement a plant imaging system for a specific real-world application and have the ability to diagnose its limitations and interpret the data. By the end of this course, students should be able to work on a research project in a team with independent responsibility and perform self-reflection. By the end of this course, students should be able to present and document the project results in professional oral presentations and scientific reports.
courses.topical_outline:
1. Introduction of plant phenotyping
• Introduction to phenotyping, including its importance and applications in agriculture
	o Shoot, root, fruit, and seed phenotypes
	o Importance in breeding, crop protection, product quality control, etc.
• Overview of traditional and modern phenotyping methods 2. Essential knowledge basics about plant phenotyping equipment
• Basics in optical systems and electronic systems
	o Components of an optical system, what is light, how photons are captured and transformed into information
• Basics in camera systems
	o RGB camera, 3D camera, image distortion, color calibration
• Spectral imaging technology
	o Multispectral, hyperspectral
• High-throughput plant phenotyping
	o Introduction of automation systems, robotics, remote sensing 3. Process and interpretation of plant phenotyping data
• Basics in data management
	o How data is stored, organized, corrected, and analyzed
• Basics in Python programming language. (Lectures and labs might be hosted in the computer lab if not all the students have a laptop)
	o Python Hello World. Will be taught using Google Colab notebooks
• Basics in computer vision algorithms and spectral analysis
	o The famous OpenCV library
• Experiment design and project preparation
	o How to design your own plant phenotyping experiments based on what you need and what you have

Through hands-on experiences, students will deepen their understanding of horticultural practices. Students will develop and hone skills in communicating horticultural science effectively. Students will craft, analyze, and improve their capacity to convey scientific concepts within the realm of horticulture to a wider audience.
courses.course_objectives: Upon completion of the course, students will apply and enhance inter-cultural communication skills across diverse countries. Upon completion of the course, students will analyze the intricate agricultural systems prevalent in the host countries. Upon completion of the course, students will utilize hands-on experiences to comprehend and integrate new learning and teaching methodologies. Upon completion of the course, students will evaluate personal growth through exposure to novel cultural environments.

courses.description: An in-depth look at how research is approached, conducted, andcarried out in traditional horticultural programs. Topics willinclude preparation, the hypothesis, reason, design, observation,and data interpretation.

courses.subject: HORT
courses.title: Design, Analysis, and Interpretation of Horticultural Data
courses.description: This active learning course provides students with a comprehensive understanding of experimental designs commonly used in horticultural research. Students will explore key principles of experimental planning, statistical analysis, and data visualization through lectures and hands-on activities, and will learn to design robust experiments in lab, greenhouse, and field settings. Students bring and share their own research data or data from others to conduct analysis and visualization learned from the class.
courses.course_objectives: Students will explain concepts of common experimental design in horticultural research and apply analysis of variance (ANOVA) for their own data. Students will determine adequate statistical methods and visualization techniques to explore, analyze, and visualize horticultural data. Students will interpret data and figures in scientific papers. Students will design data-driven solutions to assist their own study for publication.
courses.topical_outline: Week 1: Experimental design & ANOVA (1): CRD, RCBD, latin square, factorial design, tests of significance (LSD vs. HSD) Week 2: Experimental design & ANOVA (2): split-plot design, covariance, random effects, repeated measures, pipeline Week 3: Regression, correlation & multivariate analysis Week 4: Creating figures for scientific papers (part 1): Principal component analysis, clustering, heatmap, path analysis Week 5: Creating figures for scientific papers (part 2): Meta-analysis, litera-ture trend analysis, and how to write the stats section Week 6: Student project presentations

courses.course_objectives: Students will be able to examine and discuss topics in plant growth and development, particularly issues that are pertinent to economic plants. Students will be able to evaluate the physiological processes of growth, juvenility, maturity, flower initiation and development, embryogenesis, fruitset, senescence, dormancy, and environmental effects on growth and development using current review articles and the primary literature.
courses.topical_outline: Growth and differentiation, polarity Cell wall biosynthesis and regulation Embryogenesis Seed germination and dormancy Leaf development Shoot types and growth patterns, bud break and dormancy Juvenility and maturity, phase change Floral induction and development, reproductive strategies Regulation of fruiting Effects of temperature, chilling, freezing and heat stress on plant growth and development Effects of water and drought on plant growth and development Effects of light, photomorphogenesis, and photoperiodism on plant growth and development

courses.description: Introduction to the fundamentals of research study design, methods, and data collection. Additional focus on utilizing publicly available secondary data to improve analytic skills. Topics include conceptualization, hypothesis formation, sampling, observation/measurement, design and operationalization, secondary data analysis, and translating knowledge into action.
courses.course_objectives: Students will understand how to identify health research questions and develop research objectives to address the gap in literature. Students will understand how to critically assess public health/health services research articles published in peer-reviewed journals. Students will understand how to select appropriate study designs and analysis strategy for health services research. Students will understand how to develop a proposal for a primary research project. Students will understand how to identify common challenges encountered during health research and discuss ways to address them. Students will understand how to describe the process for conducting ethical health research. Students will understand how to manage and analyze data using statistical software packages. Students will understand how to describe results and discuss the results in the context of the current literature. Students will understand how to demonstrate professional writing skills. Students will understand how to develop professional communication, teamwork, and leadership skills. Students will understand how to collaborate with colleagues in health service research through different platforms such as local regional and national conferences, and manuscript preparation for peer-reviewed journals.

courses.subject: HPAM
courses.title: Cases in Health Economics and Economic Evaluation
courses.description: Course presents a series of case studies based on recent events and/or policy changes. Applying analytical tools used in economics and economic evaluation, students will analyze the case-study scenarios and derive their implications on healthcare market. Short-term and medium-term outcomes of the events or policy changes will be evaluated.
courses.course_objectives: Students will understand how to identify important market implications of changes that happened in the real-life scenarios presented. Students will understand how to describe and explain the appropriate tools to be used for analyzing the case and to derive policy options. Students will understand how to interpret results of data analysis to evaluate the effect of public health programs, policies, and changes presented in the cases. Students will understand how to analyze the effect of changes indicated in the case scenario to understand effects on the behavior of patients, healthcare providers, and healthcare facilities. Students will understand how to examine utility and social welfare aspects of economic evaluation. Students will understand how to design economic evaluation of alternative health interventions, including analysis of alternative pharmaceuticals to select the most cost-effective intervention. Students will understand how to clearly, concisely, and analytically communicate the expected outcomes of the case study scenarios to relevant stakeholders and policy options being suggested to address the concerns.

Design economic evaluation of alternative health interventions, including analysis of alternative pharmaceuticals, to select the most cost-effective intervention. Clearly, concisely, and analytically communicate the expected outcomes of the case study scenarios to relevant stakeholders and policy options being suggested to address the concerns.
courses.topical_outline: The market for healthcare and possible factors that affect demand and supply of healthcare services and products in the short-run and in the medium-run For each case scenario in health economics, evaluating the effect of the events or changes on supply, demand, and market environment Analyzing the effect of policy changes on provider and consumer behavior The market for health insurance and effects of policy changes on health insurance market Costing of healthcare services and interventions and understanding how to perform program cost analysis and cost-of-illness analysis Estimating the benefits of preventive services including vaccinations Conducting cost-benefit analysis of alternative interventions on preventive services Estimating the effectiveness of health interventions and how to deal with health outcomes that happen over a longer period of time Analyzing cost-effectiveness of alternative health interventions and pharmaceutical products

courses.title: Comparative Healthcare Systems
courses.description: A framework for students to analyze how health care is organized and delivered in settings around the world. The course will engage students in a comparative analysis of health indicators in different countries. Students will undertake a detailed analysis of health care delivery, financing, and workforce issues.

courses.subject: HPAM
courses.title: Leadership and Management of Public Health Organizations and Non-Governmental Organizations
courses.description: Public health professionals assume leadership roles in organizations and are responsible for planning, organizing, staffing, coordinating, reporting, and budgeting activities. This course will expose students to concepts in modern public health administrative issues, analyze management techniques and perspectives using case-studies, and examine core competencies related to leadership, communication, and management.
courses.course_objectives: Students will understand how to examine the foundational theories and practices of leadership within the context of public health. Students will understand how to describe personal values, behaviors, and practices and their impact when leading teams, collaborations, and initiatives in public health. Students will understand how to identify the differences between effective leadership and managerial approaches in public health. Students will understand how to critique approaches for managing conflict and navigating polarities in public health. Students will understand how to assess approaches for managing conflict and navigating polarities in public health. Students will understand how to evaluate leadership strategies in stakeholder engagement that emphasize collaboration and inclusivity in public health contexts. Students will understand how to explain ethical challenges in public health leadership. Students will understand how to design a personal development plan for public health managerial and leadership capacity.

courses.subject: HPAM
courses.title: Fundamentals of Health Care Accounting
courses.description: Provides students with a foundation for understanding and applying financial accounting, budgeting, and reporting concepts in health care organizations. After mastering essential accounting terminology and principles of electronic spreadsheets, students will learn how to prepare, analyze, and interpret income statements, balance sheets, cash flow statements, and operating budgets.

courses.subject: HPAM
courses.title: Finance for Health Administration
courses.description: Introduction to financial management, financial analysis, and financial decision-making within the healthcare environment. Basic financial management concepts will be explored to answer questions such as which projects to finance, how to finance short-term operations, and how to finance long-term projects within the healthcare setting.
courses.course_objectives: Students will understand how to define the objectives of financial management within a healthcare organization. Students will understand how to assess the tools and skills needed to make the decision to allocate capital on competing projects within a healthcare setting. Students will understand how to describe the funding mechanisms needed to maintain ongoing daily operations within an organization. Students will understand how to evaluate capital markets and how and when to access those markets in order to acquire capital used to finance healthcare operations, building of facilities, or other initiatives. Students will understand how to analyze problems in healthcare financial management.

courses.subject: HPAM
courses.title: Healthcare Law and Ethics
courses.description: This course strengthens students' and practitioners' knowledge on foundational and current issues in law and ethics that impact the policies and practice of various sectors in healthcare. It allows students to identify and appropriately assess legal, ethical, and human rights issues that underlie the healthcare industry.
courses.course_objectives: Students will understand how to evaluate the constitutional underpinnings of health prevention and interventions. Students will understand how to discuss the limitations of the legal system to address and resolve conflict and the role of ethical analysis. Students will understand how to examine the differences between legal and ethical issues in healthcare. Students will understand how to compare and contrast the respective roles of local, state, tribal, and federal governments with respect to healthcare inequities and disparities. Students will understand how to interpret the balance between individual rights and governmental interests in protecting the human health. Students will understand how to develop system-level interventions that utilize the application of legal and ethical principles to the interests in clinical and population health.

courses.subject: HPAM
courses.title: Healthcare Finance for Public Health Practitioners
courses.description: Course provides a working knowledge of financial management for managers and administrators who work or plan to work in public health and not-for-profit organizations. Course includes discussions on basics of financial accounting, costs and controls, budgeting, financial analysis, revenue, and revenue sources for governmental and not-for-profit organizations.
courses.course_objectives: Students will be able to explain generally accepted accounting principles and other appropriate standards. Students will be able to gather, interpret, and report financial data and communicate data and information according to standards. Students will be able to develop budgets and financial data according to prescribed submission formats and specifications. Students will be able to use cost, managerial accounting, and economic evaluation approaches and apply these skills to the practice of public health. Students will be able to assess budget activities and their relationship to the operational and program goals of the organization. Students will be able to explain basic financial and business processes including accounts payable, accounts receivable, and time accounting. Students will be able to apply principles of financial management to promote financial accountability and transparency. Students will be able to explain the role of audits for program improvement. Students will be able to analyze process of identifying new funding sources, revenue streams, and product lines, as well as strengthening and maintaining existing ones. Students will be able to examine the relationship between strategic planning, budgeting, and financial management.
