courses.title: Physical Diagnosis
courses.description: Veterinary clinical diagnostic procedures.  Techniques and procedures necessary to perform physical diagnosis on the animal are practiced in the clinic on normal and abnormal animals.

courses.subject: LAMS
courses.title: Principles of Anesthesia
courses.description: Principles and application of anesthesia to large and small animals.

courses.subject: LAMS
courses.title: Equine Dentistry
courses.description: An introduction to equine dentistry. Topics to be covered include: instrumentation, sedation, handling, floating with hand and power tools.  Extraction of deciduous and permanent teeth via intraoral extraction and various surgical techniques.  The labs will involve both cadaver skulls and live horses.
courses.prerequisiteText: Course will be open to students in the second, third, or fourth years of the veterinary curriculum

courses.subject: LAMS
courses.title: Large Animal Medicine I: Urology, Hematology, Endocrinology
courses.description: Medical aspects of the urinary tract, hematology, andendocrinology of large domestic animals.

courses.subject: LAMS
courses.title: Problems in Large Animal Medicine
courses.description: A problem-based course using cases submitted to the DDI service.Students (in a small group of 3-4 along with a facilitator) will develop their learning objectives, and using the resources of the CVM, accomplish their learning objectives and provide a solution to the questions posed by practitioners.

courses.subject: LAMS
courses.title: Clinical Techniques in Large Animal Medicine and Surgery
courses.description: Introduction to procedures commonly performed during diagnosis and treatment of large animal cases.  The course consists of lectures describing the procedures and their clinical use and interactive case discussions illustrating the application of these concepts.

courses.subject: LAMS
courses.title: Clinical Techniques in Large Animal Medicine and Surgery Laboratory
courses.description: An introduction to procedures commonly performed during diagnosis and treatment of large animal cases.  The course is the laboratory companion to Clinical Techniques in Large Animal Medicine and Surgery, and laboratories will be timed to demonstrate the techniques described during lectures.

courses.subject: LAMS
courses.title: Veterinary Obstetrics
courses.description: Pregnancy and its abnormalities. Parturition, diagnosis,treatment, and prevention of dystocia in cow, mare, ewe/doe, sow,dog, and cat.  Cesarean section and fetotomy.  Postparturientproblems.

courses.subject: LAMS
courses.title: Ruminant Internal Medicine: Respiratory Diseases
courses.description: Pathophysiology, etiology, diagnosis, treatment, and preventionof cardiopulmonary diseases of ruminants will be covered.
courses.prerequisiteText: 2nd year or above DVM student | Pre or

courses.subject: LAMS
courses.title: Large Animal Theriogenology Selective
courses.description: This is a comprehensive course that encompasses the didactic aspects of large animal theriogenology.

courses.subject: LAMS
courses.title: Advanced Topics in Equine Cardiovascular, Respiratory, and Hemolymphatic Disease
courses.description: To complement skills and core foundational knowledge gained in the first three years of the DVM program, this course will discuss the pathophysiology, diagnosis, and management of common cardiovascular, respiratory, and hemolymphatic diseases affecting horses. Clinical reasoning and key concepts will be reinforced in case discussions.
courses.course_objectives: By the end of the course, students will be able to perform a complete cardiovascular and respiratory examination on horses. By the end of the course, students will be able to identify abnormal clinical and clinicopathologic findings associated with cardiovascular, respiratory, and hemolymphatic diseases in horses and correctly correlate to the underlying pathophysiology. By the end of the course, students will be able to identify cardiac murmurs or arrhythmias, and attribute significance based on history, physical examination, and murmur characteristics. By the end of the course, students will be able to formulate an appropriate diagnostic plan for horses with cardiovascular, respiratory, or hemolymphatic disease. By the end of the course, students will be able to acquire and interpret a base-apex electrocardiogram. By the end of the course, students will be able to acquire and interpret diagnostic imaging of the cardiovascular and respiratory systems of horses. By the end of the course, students will be able to prepare a list of relevant differential diagnoses for cardiovascular, respiratory, or hemolympathic diseases in horses based on the signalment, history, clinical signs, and examination findings. By the end of the course, students will be able to formulate an appropriate treatment plan for horses with cardiovascular, respiratory, or hemolympathic disease. By the end of the course, students will be able to provide recommendations for biosecurity (including preventative strategies if relevant) to manage respiratory disease in an outbreak setting.
courses.topical_outline:
1. Respiratory examination (comparative) 2. Diagnostic approach to respiratory disease 3. Respiratory disease of the Performance horse URT focus 4. Sinusitis 5. Strangles 6. Viral respiratory diseases 7. Biosecurity - control of highly contagious respiratory pathogens 8. Foal pneumonia/R. equi 9. Broncho pneumonia 10. Pleuropneumonia 11. Fungal, parasitic, and miscellaneous (EMPF) disorders of the respiratory system 12. Equine Asthma/EIPH 13. Cardiovascular examination 14. Clinical approach to acquired valvular disease and heart failure 15. Congenital cardiac disease (comparative) 16. Clinical approach to dysrhythmias 
Infective cardiac disease- comparative (endocarditis, myocarditis, pericarditis) 17. Clinical approach to toxins that cause cardiac disease 18. Clinical approach to the diagnosis and treatment of hematologic abnormalities 19. Infectious and neoplastic diseases of the hemolymphatic system 20. Vasculitis/Thrombophlebitis: Purpura hemorrhagica/other causes of vasculitis/lymphangitis 21. Clinical approach to toxins that cause hemolymphatic disease
courses.prerequisiteText: Enrollment in the Doctor of Veterinary Medicine curriculum

courses.subject: LAMS
courses.title: Advanced Topics in Equine Neurology, Endocrinology, and Ophthalmology
courses.description: To complement skills and core foundational knowledge gained in the first three years of the DVM program, this course will discuss the pathophysiology, diagnosis, and management of common cardiovascular, respiratory, and hemolymphatic diseases affecting horses. Clinical reasoning and key concepts will be reinforced in case discussions.
courses.course_objectives: By the end of the course, students will be able to perform and use neurologic examination findings to localize the neurologic lesion(s) within the nervous system (e.g., make a neuroanatomic diagnosis). By the end of the course, students will be able to prepare a list of relevant differential diagnoses based on the neuroanatomic diagnosis, the patient’s signalment, and the rate of progression of the signs. By the end of the course, students will be able to formulate an appropriate diagnostic plan. By the end of the course, students will be able to describe the pathogenesis of common neurologic diseases in horses. By the end of the course, students will be able to formulate a therapeutic plan (and preventative strategies if relevant) to manage common neurologic diseases in horses. By the end of the course, students will be able to recognize the presenting complaint(s), clinical signs, and clinicopathologic abnormalities associated with the common equine endocrinopathies. By the end of the course, students will be able to formulate an appropriate diagnostic plan for equine endocrinopathies. By the end of the course, students will be able to describe the pathogenesis of common equine endocrinopathies. By the end of the course, students will be able to formulate a therapeutic plan (and preventative strategies if relevant) to manage common equine endocrinopathies. By the end of the course, students will be able to recognize the presenting complaint(s) and clinical signs associated with common ocular diseases of horses. By the end of the course, students will be able to formulate an appropriate diagnostic and therapeutic plan for the common ocular diseases of horses.
courses.topical_outline: 1. Equine neurologic examination 2. Differential diagnosis and treatment of common equine neurologic diseases 3. Neonatal encephalopathy 4. Traumatic brain injury 5. Disorders of energy metabolism in horses 6. Equine pituitary pars intermedia dysfunction 7. Endocrinopathic laminitis 8. Equine thyroid disorders 9. Anhidrosis 10. Common equine corneal diseases 11. Equine recurrent uveitis 12. Squamous cell carcinoma 13. Case investigations
courses.prerequisiteText: Enrollment in the Doctor of Veterinary Medicine curriculum

courses.subject: LAMS
courses.title: Equine Clinical Diagnostic Imaging
courses.description: Radiographic and ultrasonographic imaging of osseous and soft tissue disorders of the musculoskeletal, abdominal, and thoracic systems.

courses.subject: LAMS
courses.title: Large Animal Advanced Anesthesia
courses.description: How the unique anatomy and physiology of large animal species impact drug choices and overall anesthetic management. Pharmacology of sedative and anesthetic drugs, selection of drugs and techniques, equipment, considerations of specific diseases, and recognition and treatment of common anesthetic complications will be covered.
courses.course_objectives: By the end of the course, students will be able to identify potential problems for anesthetic management from patient signalment (species, breed, age, sex, weight), laboratory data, and a brief description of the proposed medical or surgical procedure. By the end of the course, students will be able to use physical and chemical restraint in large animal species and discuss the anesthetic management including ideal goals, anesthetic drugs, appropriate monitoring, and supportive therapy. By the end of the course, students will be able to describe behavioral and pharmacologic effects, method of administration, interactions, and possible complications of sedative and anesthetic drugs, such as anticholinergics, sedatives, tranquilizers, opioids, dissociative and inhalant anesthetics. By the end of the course, students will be able to choose an adequate protocol for standing sedation, including drugs and physical restraint. By the end of the course, students will be able to monitor large animal patients under general anesthesia and explain the values obtained from capnography, pulse oximetry, and anesthetic agent analyzers. By the end of the course, students will be able to recognize and treat common anesthetic complications, such as hypoventilation, hypoxemia, hypotension, and hypothermia. By the end of the course, students will be able to perform common nerve blocks, such as epidural, paravertebral, cornual, and periocular nerve blocks.
courses.topical_outline: Course introduction and overview Preanesthetic evaluation, sedation, and analgesia Standing sedation in the horse General intravenous anesthesia in the equine patient Inhalation anesthesia in horses Management of intra-anesthetic complications and recovery from anesthesia in horses Local anesthetic techniques in large animal species Physical restraint, sedation, and anesthesia in ruminants Physical restraint, sedation, and anesthesia in pigs Physical restraint, sedation, and anesthesia in camelids Case discussion
courses.prerequisiteText: Enrollment in the Doctor of Veterinary Medicine curriculum

courses.subject: LAMS
courses.title: Large Animal Cardiology
courses.description: Review and discussion of clinical signs, diagnosis, and treatmentof the most common cardiac diseases of large animals.  Lectureswill review "core" cardiology, sound recordings and ECG used tosimulate normal and abnormal cardiac findings, and consist ofaudience participation (keypad interaction) case presentations.

courses.subject: LAMS
courses.title: Large Animal Digestive Diseases
courses.description: The diagnosis, treatment, and prognosis of diseases of the equineand food animal digestive systems.

courses.subject: LAMS
courses.title: Advanced Topics in  Equine Gastroenterology and Dentistry
courses.description: To complement skills and core foundational knowledge gained in the first three years of the DVM program, this course will discuss the pathophysiology, diagnosis, and management of common dental and gastrointestinal tract diseases affecting horses. Clinical reasoning and key concepts will be reinforced in case discussions.
courses.course_objectives: By the end of the course, students will be able to recall and explain the normal anatomy of the equine digestive tract, including dental anatomy. By the end of the course, students will be able to recognize the cause, clinical signs, and physical findings of horses with gastrointestinal and dental disease. By the end of the course, students will be able to formulate a diagnostic plan and interpret results used in the work up of dental and gastrointestinal diseases. By the end of the course, students will be able to recognize normal and common abnormal ultrasonographic findings of the gastrointestinal tract of horses. By the end of the course, students will be able to prepare a list of differential diagnoses for equine abdominal pain, based on etiologic categories (obstructive, inflammatory, strangulating or other), age, signalment, onset (acute, chronic, recurrent colic), and anatomic location. By the end of the course, students will be able to discuss the treatment, prognosis, and prevention for the most common causes of dental disease in horses. By the end of the course, students will be able to discuss the risk factors, treatment, prognosis, and prevention for the most common causes of gastrointestinal disease in horses. By the end of the course, students will be able to decipher when to send a horse to a referral institution or specialty practice for additional diagnostics or treatment for equine abdominal pain.
courses.topical_outline: 1. Review of anatomy, physiology, clinical exam 2. Diagnostic plan for the acute equine abdomen 3. Ultrasonography of the equine gastrointestinal tract 4. Non-strangulating obstructions 5. Strangulating obstructions 6. Intestinal inflammatory disease 7. Peritonitis 8. When referral is indicated 9. Equine dentistry
courses.prerequisiteText: Enrollment in the Doctor of Veterinary Medicine curriculum

courses.subject: LAMS
courses.title: Equine Lameness and the Foot
courses.description: Significant lameness as a clinical problem, identification of thelame limb, and diagnostic techniques used to identify the cause. The equine foot is discussed in terms of its form and functionin relation to disease with emphasis on relating the symptoms,diagnosis and treatment to basic principles. Individual diseasesand cases are discussed.

courses.subject: LAMS
courses.title: Advanced Topics in Ruminant Medicine and Surgery
courses.description: To complement skills and core foundational knowledge gained in the first three years of the DVM program, this course will discuss the pathophysiology, diagnosis, and management of common diseases affecting cattle, small ruminants, and New World Camelids. Clinical reasoning and key concepts will be reinforced in case discussions.
courses.course_objectives: By the end of the course, students will be able to recognize the presenting complaint(s), clinical signs, and physical findings associated with common cardiovascular, respiratory, gastrointestinal, urogenital, endocrine, neurologic, and musculoskeletal diseases of ruminants. By the end of the course, students will be able to formulate a differential diagnosis list relevant to the body system(s) affected. By the end of the course, students will be able to formulate and interpret an appropriate diagnostic plan relevant to the problem list and body system(s) affected. By the end of the course, students will be able to describe the pathogenesis of common diseases of ruminants. By the end of the course, students will be able to formulate a therapeutic plan (and preventative strategies if relevant) to manage common cardiovascular, respiratory, gastrointestinal, urogenital, endocrine, neurologic, and musculoskeletal diseases of ruminants.
courses.topical_outline: 1. Cardiovascular and respiratory disease 2. Gastrointestinal tract disease 3. Reproductive and urologic disease 4. Endocrine disease 5. Neurologic disease 6. Musculoskeletal disease 7. Case investigations
courses.prerequisiteText: Enrollment in the Doctor of Veterinary Medicine curriculum

courses.subject: LAMS
courses.title: Advanced Techniques in Ruminant Medicine and Surgery
courses.description: To expand on didactic knowledge acquired in ruminant medicine and surgery, students will learn clinical safe practices, perform physical examination techniques, diagnostics, and therapeutic and surgical procedures commonly used in ruminant clinical practice.
courses.course_objectives: By the end of the course, students will be able to appropriately integrate clinical safe practices as skills expand. By the end of the course, students will be able to perform a complete clinical examination. By the end of the course, students will be able to perform a standing flank laparotomy in a cow or steer. By the end of the course, students will be able to pass an orogastric tube in a cow or steer. By the end of the course, students will be able to perform a rectal examination in a cow or steer. By the end of the course, students will be able to perform a basic foot trim and apply a claw block. By the end of the course, students will be able to perform a breeding soundness exam on a bull and cow. By the end of the course, students will be able to determine pregnancy and stage of estrus. By the end of the course, students will be able to perform a transabdominal ultrasound exam of a goat. By the end of the course, students will be able to identify obstruction of the lower urinary tract of a goat.
courses.topical_outline: 1. Clinical examination 2. Bovine flank laparotomy, orogastric tube, rectal exam 3. Lameness and the foot 4. Theriogenology/Obstetrics 5. Transabdominal ultrasonography of the goat and urinary tract evaluation
courses.prerequisiteText: Enrollment in the Doctor of Veterinary Medicine curriculum

courses.subject: LAMS
courses.title: Large Animal Emergency Medicine and Surgery
courses.description: Clinical rotation in large animal emergency medicine and surgery. Students will participate in the admission, work-up, and treatment of large animal emergencies after hours.  Additionally, participants will help with treatments on critical patients in the hospital and take part in topic and case-based rounds.

courses.subject: LAMS
courses.title: Advanced Topics in the Equine Musculoskeletal and Integumentary Systems
courses.description: To complement skills and core foundational knowledge gained in the first three years of the DVM program, this course will discuss the pathophysiology, diagnosis, and management of common musculoskeletal and integument diseases affecting horses. Clinical reasoning and key concepts will be reinforced in case discussions.
courses.course_objectives: By the end of the course, students will be able to perform a complete musculoskeletal and/or lameness examination. By the end of the course, students will be able to use musculoskeletal and/or lameness examination findings to localize the musculoskeletal disease within a specific limb(s). By the end of the course, students will be able to prepare a list of relevant differential diagnoses based on the localization of the musculoskeletal disease. By the end of the course, students will be able to formulate an appropriate diagnostic, therapeutic (both medical and surgical), and rehabilitation plan for a horse with musculoskeletal disease. By the end of the course, students will be able to describe the pathogenesis of wound healing as it relates to skin, muscle, bone, and tendon/ligament. By the end of the course, students will be able to formulate a diagnostic and therapeutic plan for a horse with a dermatopathy, cutaneous mass, or wound. By the end of the course, students will be able to obtain and interpret radiographic and ultrasonographic images of the musculoskeletal system.
courses.topical_outline: 1. Equine musculoskeletal examination 2. Equine subjective and objective lameness assessment 3. The pre-purchase examination and performance evaluation 4. Advanced diagnostic imaging for musculoskeletal evaluation 5. Equine foot conditions and shoeing 6. Equine bone conditions 7. Equine joint conditions 8. Myopathies 9. Equine soft tissue injuries (tendinitis/desmitis) 10. Equine axial skeleton conditions 11. Equine rehabilitation techniques 12. Foal orthopedic diseases 13. Wounds, synovial sepsis, osteomyelitis 14. Skin/subcutaneous lesions and masses 15. Bandaging/coaptation 16. Case investigations
courses.prerequisiteText: Enrollment in the Doctor of Veterinary Medicine curriculum

courses.subject: LAMS
courses.title: Equine Surgery II: Soft Tissue Surgery
courses.description: Diseases of the digestive, respiratory, integumental, andreproductive systems in which surgery may be a treatment.Emphasis on diagnostic techniques, surgical decision making,surgical techniques, and postoperative care.

courses.subject: LAMS
courses.title: Advanced Topics in Equine Urogenital System and Neonatology
courses.description: To complement skills and core foundational knowledge gained in the first three years of the DVM program, this course will discuss the pathophysiology, diagnosis, and management of common reproductive, neonatal, and urogenital diseases affecting horses. Clinical reasoning and key concepts will be reinforced in case discussions.
courses.course_objectives: By the end of the course, students will be able to recall and explain the normal anatomy, function, and pathophysiology of the equine reproductive and urogenital tracts. By the end of the course, students will be able to identify and classify common urogenital diseases affecting horses, including urinary obstruction, reproductive disorders, and congenital anomalies. By the end of the course, students will be able to understand the indications for diagnostic testing and be able to interpret and apply the basic diagnostic tests used in the work up of equine urogenital disease. By the end of the course, students will be able to formulate appropriate treatment plans for common urogenital diseases, including pharmacological and surgical interventions. By the end of the course, students will be able to develop an understanding of obstetrical intervention and be able to discuss specific management principles for treatment of dystocia. By the end of the course, students will be able to develop an understanding of medical management of the dam and the fetus/neonate in late gestation and in the immediate postpartum period. By the end of the course, students will be able to discuss preventive measures and management strategies to reduce the incidence of urogenital diseases in horses.
courses.topical_outline: 1. Review of pregnancy and parturition 2. Disorders of pregnancy and fetal monitoring 3. Abortion investigation 4. Equine dystocia 5. Surgical management of dystocia 6. Frenotomy 7. Review of urinary diseases 8. Urogenital imaging 9. Neonatology
courses.prerequisiteText: Enrollment in Doctor of Veterinary Medicine curriculum

courses.subject: LAMS
courses.title: Advanced Techniques in Equine Medicine and Surgery
courses.description: To complement didactic knowledge acquired in the body system-specific electives offered in large animal medicine and surgery, students will learn clinical safe practices, perform physical examination techniques, diagnostics, and therapeutic and surgical procedures commonly used in equine clinical practice.
courses.course_objectives: By the end of the course, students will be able to appropriately integrate clinical safe practices as skills expand. By the end of the course, students will be able to perform a complete cardiopulmonary clinical examination. By the end of the course, students will be able to perform a complete gastrointestinal clinical examination. By the end of the course, students will be able to perform a complete neurologic clinical examination. By the end of the course, students will be able to perform a complete ophthalmic clinical examination. By the end of the course, students will be able to perform a complete reproductive clinical examination. By the end of the course, students will be able to perform a basic lameness evaluation and identify the affected limb(s). By the end of the course, students will be able to appropriately place routine standing wraps. By the end of the course, students will be able to obtain basic radiographic and ultrasonographic images of the limbs. By the end of the course, students will be able to perform a routine equine dental. By the end of the course, students will be able to formulate a plan for a dystocia. By the end of the course, students will be able to perform an equine castration.
courses.topical_outline: 1. Cardiopulmonary clinical examination 2. Gastrointestinal clinical examination 3. Neurologic clinical examination 4. Ophthalmic clinical examination 5. Reproductive clinical examination 6. Lameness and the foot 7. Equine bandaging and rehabilitation 8. Musculoskeletal imaging 9. Equine dentistry 10. Theriogenology/Obstetrics 11. Equine castration
courses.prerequisiteText: Enrollment in the Doctor of Veterinary Medicine curriculum

courses.subject: LAMS
courses.title: Bovine Surgery
courses.description: The course discusses diseases of the digestive, musculoskeletal, reproductive systems in which surgery may be a treatment.  Emphasis is placed on diagnostic techniques, surgical decision making, surgical techniques, and post-operative care.

courses.subject: LAMS
courses.title: Artificial Insemination, Embryo Transfer, and  Advanced Reproductive Technologies
courses.description: A combination of lectures and labs will introduce students to Artificial Insemination (AI), Embryo Transfer (ET) in large animals, and other Advanced Reproductive Aechnologies (ART). Students will perform AI and actively participate in the practical management and performance of an ET program.
courses.prerequisiteText: Third-year student standing in the College of Veterinary Medicine

courses.subject: LAMS
courses.title: Large Animal Advanced Clinical Anesthesia
courses.description: Clinical training in large animal anesthesiology. Students willexamine, evaluate, and provide anesthesia and analgesia forclinical patients in the large animal hospital. Practical skillsand knowledge of problem-solving techniques will be emphasized.

courses.subject: LAMS
courses.title: Large Animal Internal Medicine
courses.description: A three-week clinical rotation in the large animal internalmedicine of horses, ruminants, and pigs.

courses.subject: LAMS
courses.title: Large Animal Surgery
courses.description: Clinical training in general large animal surgery with emphasison equine soft tissue, musculoskeletal, soft tissue disease, foodanimal lameness, alimentary surgery, diagnosis andpathophysiology of disease.

courses.subject: LAMS
courses.title: Large Animal Farm Practice
courses.description: Clinical training in farm animal medicine. Pathophysiologicalmechanisms of disease in the individual animal.  Examination,evaluation, and treatment of domesticated animals in the farmenvironment.

courses.subject: LAMS
courses.title: Clinical Focus on Small Ruminants and Camelids
courses.description: Provides students the opportunity to experience and discuss management issues and diseases of small ruminants and camelids and to perform common procedures on these species.

courses.subject: LAMS
courses.title: Advanced Farm Animal Husbandry and Clinical Medicine
courses.description: Clinical training in farm animal medicine. Pathophysiological mechanisms of disease in the individual animal. Examination, evaluation, and treatment of domesticated animals in the farm environment. Medical and surgical principles of Farm Practice will be studied and practiced. Students will be exposed to farm/exotic animals and honey bees in a clinical situation which has inherent dangers.

courses.subject: LAMS
courses.title: General Theriogenology
courses.description: The didactic and clinical aspects of animal reproduction in bovine, canine, equine, and other species. Content includes the management of normal and abnormal reproductive cases and assigned reviews for clinical rounds.

courses.subject: LAMS
courses.title: Small Animal Theriogenology
courses.description: This is a comprehensive clinical rotation that encompasses the didactic and clinical aspects of small animal theriogenology. Emphasis is on the practical implementation of the specialty. The course is only available to fourth-year students.

courses.subject: LAMS
courses.title: Advanced Equine Theriogenology
courses.description: A comprehensive course encompassing the didactic and clinicalaspects of equine theriogenology.  The emphasis is on practicalimplementation of the specialty.  The course is only available tofourth year students during the equine breeding season.

courses.subject: LAMS
courses.title: Large Animal Emergency and Critical Care
courses.description: Clinical rotation in large animal emergency medicine and surgery. Students will participate in the admission, work-up, and treatment of large animal emergencies after hours. Additionally, participants will help with treatments on critical patients in the hospital and take part in topic and case based rounds.

courses.subject: LAMS
courses.title: Equine Diagnostic Imaging and Lameness
courses.description: The object of this course is to provide students with an in-depthunderstanding of equine lameness, and the diagnostic imagingtechniques used and their interpretation.

courses.subject: LAMS
courses.title: Equine Clinical Nutrition
courses.description: Discussion of equine nutrition concepts and journal articlesregarding equine nutrition.

courses.subject: LAMS
courses.title: Equine Ophthalmology
courses.description: Provides students with a strong foundation in equine ophthalmology by providing in-depth experience performing equine ophthalmic examinations, common medical and surgical procedures, and diagnosing and treating common diseases affecting the equine eye.

courses.subject: LAMS
courses.title: Equine Sports Medicine, Rehabilitation, and Podiatry
courses.description: Clinical rotation in equine sports medicine and podiatry. Students will predominantly see cases related to equine sports medicine and podiatry. Assigned responsibilities include case involvement, record keeping, and primary case care for patients hospitalized through the service (may include weekend treatments). This rotation is appropriate for students pursuing equine practice.

courses.subject: LAMS
courses.title: Seminar in Large Animal Medicine and Surgery
courses.description: Seminar is presented by the student under the direction of a faculty member.  The seminar can consist of a literature review or a review of clinical cases. After the presentation, the group asks questions of the student, who then leads the discussion.

courses.subject: LAMS
courses.title: Studies in Clinical Large Animal Medicine
courses.description: Studies involving different areas of large animal medicine, surgery, population medicine, or theriogenology.

courses.subject: LAMS
courses.title: Clinically-Based Concepts I
courses.description: This is the first of a series of three courses that are designed to achieve two goals. First, to apply foundational basic science concepts from cell biology, chemistry, anatomy, and physiology in a clinical context to better prepare students for careers in healthcare. In addition, this course will introduce strategies for studying and learning that have been proven to reinforce long-term recall. Students will complete three modules, two of which will address biomedical concepts encountered by healthcare professionals. These modules will be presented in a clinical context and will use four learning modalities to address them: reading text, viewing animations and illustrations, watching videos, and answering questions. The third module will describe the neuroanatomy behind memory and learning techniques that target and strengthen these pathways and provide the students opportunities to use these techniques during the course.

courses.subject: LAMS
courses.title: Clinically-Based Concepts II
courses.description: This is the second of a series of three courses that are designed to achieve two goals. First, to apply foundational basic science concepts from cell biology, chemistry, anatomy, and physiology in a clinical context to better prepare students for careers in healthcare. In addition, this course will introduce strategies for studying and learning that have been proven to reinforce long-term recall. Students will complete three modules, two of which will address biomedical concepts encountered by healthcare professionals. These modules will be presented in a clinical context and will use four learning modalities to address them: reading text, viewing animations and illustrations, watching videos, and answering questions. The third module will introduce the students to specific strategies proven to enhance long-term learning and mastery of the learned concepts.

courses.subject: LAMS
courses.title: Clinically-Based Concepts III
courses.description: This is the third of a series of three courses that are designed to achieve two goals. First, to apply foundational basic science concepts from cell biology, chemistry, anatomy, and physiology in a clinical context to better prepare students for careers in healthcare. In addition, this course will introduce strategies for studying and learning that have been proven to reinforce long-term recall. Students will complete three modules, two of which will address biomedical concepts encountered by healthcare professionals. These modules will be presented in a clinical context and will use four learning modalities to address them: reading text, viewing animations and illustrations, watching videos, and answering questions. The third module will introduce the students to specific strategies proven to enhance long-term learning and mastery of the learned concepts.

courses.subject: LAMS
courses.title: Graduate Student Seminar
courses.description: Advanced supervised experience in an applied setting.  Thiscourse may not be used to satisfy a student's approved program ofstudy.

courses.subject: LAMS
courses.title: Large Animal Internship
courses.description: Clinical training for the graduate veterinarian desiring in-depth knowledge and skills relative to the diagnosis and treatment of diseases affecting food animals and horses.
courses.prerequisiteText: DVM degree and permission of department

courses.subject: LAMS
courses.title: Large Animal Residency I
courses.description: This course provides clinical training during year one of a residency for graduate veterinarians desiring to specialize in large animal medicine, surgery, theriogenology, or anesthesiology.
courses.prerequisiteText: DVM degree and permission of department

courses.subject: LAMS
courses.title: Large Animal Residency II
courses.description: This course provides clinical training during year two of a residency for graduate veterinarians in large animal medicine, surgery, theriogenology, or anesthesiology.
courses.prerequisiteText: DVM degree and permission of department

courses.subject: LAMS
courses.title: Large Animal Residency III
courses.description: This course provides clinical training during year three of a residency for graduate veterinarians in large animal medicine, surgery, theriogenology, or anesthesiology.

courses.subject: LAMS
courses.title: Large Animal Residency IV
courses.description: This course provides clinical training for graduate veterinarians in the fourth year of a large animal residency in animal medicine, surgery, theriogenology, or anesthesiology.
courses.prerequisiteText: DVM degree and permission of department

courses.subject: LAMS
courses.title: Problems in Large Animal Pathophysiology
courses.description: Designed to allow graduate students the opportunity to explore, under supervision, problems pertaining to the pathophysiology oflarge animals. These may be, but are not limited to, the areas of large animal surgery and medicine. Open to graduate students in the biological sciences meeting the course prerequisites.
courses.prerequisiteText: Student must be enrolled in the veterinary curriculum or be enrolled in a graduate (MS or PhD) within the College of Veterinary Medicine

Focus is on the design of the built environment as an ongoing activity integrating ecological, social, and cultural values.  Topics include land use patterns and policies, development and resource management, community design issues, and strategies for improving environmental integrity and quality of life.
courses.course_objectives: Students will describe, understand, interpret, and critique the designed/built environment from a variety of cultural, artistic, and scientific perspectives. Students will be able to prepare a construction cost estimate based on construction drawings using published material and labor costs. Students will be able to identify and describe key characteristics and typical applications of materials common to landscape construction.

courses.subject: LAND
courses.title: History of the Built Environment I: Landscape
courses.description: Landscape architecture from ancient times to the present.  Emphasizes the relationship between landscape architecture and culture, aesthetics, and the environment.
courses.course_objectives: Students will be able to demonstrate an ability to define a set of concepts, principles, techniques, and physical features that constitutes a basic vocabulary for environmental planning and design. Students will be able to demonstrate an ability to identify significant movements and prominent persons in the history of the built environment and in the development of the professions of architecture, landscape architecture, and city planning. Students will be able to demonstrate an ability to describe, analyze, and compare various historic styles and periods in the history of environmental planning and design, and the guiding principles that characterized them. Students will be able to demonstrate an ability to identify and describe the environmental, social, cultural, and economic conditions that shaped various historic styles and periods of environmental planning and design. Students will be able to demonstrate an ability to analyze and critique the visual and spatial qualities of exemplary works of environmental design through writing and simple diagramming. Students will be able to demonstrate an ability to infer and interpret how human history and cultural traditions shape present-day built environments and contemporary environmental design practice.

courses.subject: LAND
courses.title: Landscape Engineering Processes and Materials
courses.description: The forming and building of landscapes with emphasis on the values of "sustainability."  Includes introduction to landscape engineering:  grading, drainage, and roadway alignment.
courses.course_objectives: Students will be able to explain the relationships between contour lines, land forms, and water flow. Students will be able to discuss the role grading and drainage play in landscape architectural design. Students will be able to define the acceptable slope ranges needed for accessibility, water drainage, and erosion control. Students will be able to identify landforms on a contour map and create scaled cross sections from a contour map. Students will be able to prepare basic grading plans for roads, parking lots, and building swales. Students will be able to calculate horizontal and vertical curves for roadway design. Students will be able to calculate the amount of storm water runoff on a site and size drainage structures accordingly. Students will be able to calculate cut and fill volumes for grading plans. Students will be able to list the consequences of selecting either surface or subsurface drainage systems. Students will be able to create grading plans that respond sensitively to the existing landscape as well as considering human use of the landscape.

courses.course_objectives: Students will demonstrate skills learned in prerequisite studio courses, which may include, but are not limited to, the following: design fundamentals; design process; graphic and written communication; site inventory and analysis; illustrative analog and digital graphics; construction detailing; construction documents; site engineering and stormwater management; plant selection; and planting design. Students will demonstrate through their design solutions an understanding of the various factors and elements that influence and shape the experiential quality of the built environment.

Proper site design, the sizing and placement of stormwater components and systems, and the design of soil erosion and sediment control practices are addressed. NPDES standards are identified and practices described in the Georgia Stormwater Manual and the Manual for Soil Erosion and Sediment Control in Georgia are applied.
courses.course_objectives: Students will be able to explain the role of site planning and design in the protection of soil and stormwater quality and identify planning and design principles critical to sustainable and responsible site development. Students will be able to identify planning and design principles critical to sustainable and responsible site development. Students will be able to describe the role of pertinent Federal, State, and Local regulations, ordinances and manuals for stormwater and erosion and sediment control in protecting natural resources and influencing site design and development practices. Students will be able to model watershed runoff rates and volumes using various methods and identify the strengths, weaknesses, and limitations of each method. Students will be able to select and apply stormwater best management practices to achieve required site stormwater targets and assess their effectiveness. Students will be able to select and apply appropriate erosion and sediment control best management practices to minimize erosion and to protect downstream water quality.

Students will be able to apply earthwork and storm water management techniques to a specific site. Students will be able to demonstrate an understanding of construction surveying and layout techniques by creating a construction layout plan. Students will be able to create a planting plan that demonstrates an understanding of planting design, proper selection based upon site conditions, horticultural principles, and design objectives. Students will be able to identify and explain basic construction techniques. Students will be able to identify and apply new construction technologies to their design solutions. Students will be able to calculate quantities of materials needed to build a specific design and calculate overall construction costs.

courses.subject: LAND
courses.title: Ecological Landscape Restoration
courses.description: Principles and techniques associated with the enhancement and restoration of degraded landscapes within an aesthetic framework. Case studies focus on stream and wetland systems in southeastern United States. Field trips allow participants to observe and critically analyze projects at the site scale.
courses.course_objectives: Students will summarize and justify ecological benefit of enhancement or restoration case studies of grassland, savanna, forest, stream, and wetland areas.  Measurement: Applied project. Students will explain principles of landscape restoration and techniques of restoration design. Measurement: Applied project. Students will recognize and describe the aesthetic values that contribute to ecological design. Measurement: Applied project. Students will read the landscape to classify and explain ecological functions. Measurement: Applied project. Students will prioritize interventions to improve ecological function. Measurement: Applied project. Students will combine the art of landscape restoration and human dimensions to underpin designs for project sites. Students will gain a basic understanding of principles and techniques of landscape restoration and enhancement at the site scale. Students will relate and balance ecological processes with the art of landscape restoration. Students will understand landscape trajectories and critically analyze associated restoration and enhancement success criteria. Students will understand the site inventory, analyses, design, and mechanics of implementing stream and wetland restoration and enhancement projects. Students will become familiar with selected case studies in grassland, savanna, forest, stream, and wetland restorations. Students will understand adaptive management and associated management practices.

courses.description: The plant communities of the southeastern United States, with emphasis on botanical and aesthetic characteristics, factors affecting community composition, and community dynamics.

courses.description: Field instruction in the techniques of drawing and painting in the outdoors. Topics covered will include correct perspective drawing, value mapping, scale and proportion, interpreting color as value, and processes for watercolor painting, including color mixing and wash techniques for use as fine art or design presentation.

courses.subject: LAND
courses.title: Design Build
courses.description: Emerging sustainable design-build practices integrating community involvement, design, development, fabrication, and installation, with an emphasis on low-impact design and adaptive reuse. Through "design-build," students will work with community members to design and physically construct chosen designs.

courses.subject: LAND
courses.title: Landscape Photography
courses.description: This course investigates the relationship between photography and landscape and centers on a simple question: how can studying landscape photography make you a better landscape architect? Students will investigate answers to this question from a variety of technical, creative, and design points of view.
courses.course_objectives: Students will learn and show proficiency in basic camera functions and the exposure triangle including: shutter speed, aperture, and ISO. Students will compare and contrast photographic and landscape architectural design elements and principles to enhance their own design style and philosophy. Students will be able to explain how photographers creatively approach and depict landscape through their work. Students will document their ability to critically see and evaluate landscape through an individual photographic portfolio of images.

courses.subject: LAND
courses.title: Plant Communities of the Cherokee Landscape
courses.description: A field study of the native plants of the Cherokee landscape and their historical and contemporary uses.  The Cherokee landscape describes the region consisting of the eastern Cherokee Homeland, the route westward along the Trail of Tears, and the Cherokee Nation in Oklahoma.

courses.subject: LAND
courses.title: Plants for Temperate Landscapes
courses.description: A continuation of Plants of the South/Plant Communities. Native and introduced species, including trees, shrubs, grasses, herbaceous annual, and perennial plants.
courses.course_objectives: Students should be able to identify both the common and botanical names of approximately 200 trees, shrubs, and herbaceous plants on weekly quizzes, and midterm and final field exams. Students will assemble a compilation (notebook) or sketchbook of the plants studied during the semester in a format required by the professor at the beginning of the semester. The book will include the significant ornamental attributes of  each plant, as well as their cultural requirements and native habitat. This notebook will serve as a resource for the students in subsequent LAND courses and in their professional careers, and will be evaluated for accuracy and completeness at the end of the semester. Students shall demonstrate an understanding of the ornamental attributes and cultural requirements of the plants presented in class through assessment on the midterm and final written exams.
courses.topical_outline: Plant Morphology, Classification and Nomenclature, Ornamental Attributes, Cultural Requirements, Ecological Systems, Plant Communities, Plant Identification

courses.subject: LAND

courses.description: Investigation of the relationship between lighting and landscape, centering upon the question: how does light, including its source, location, and character, change the perception of and engagement with the landscape? Students will investigate this question from a variety of technical, creative, and design points of view.

courses.subject: LAND
courses.title: Introduction to Construction Project Management
courses.description: Providing basic understanding of concepts of construction management and alternate methods for contracting project management, such as traditional design-bid-build and design build methodologies. Includes discussions of field operations, contract administration, outlining process of project management from beginning of procurement of project through submittals, contract processes, closeout procedures, and final completion documentation.
courses.course_objectives: A student successfully completing this course will be able to describe of the issues and practices used in project management. A student successfully completing this course will be able to assess the various methodologies used to contract for project management. A student successfully completing this course will be able to explain all aspects of the construction administration processes. A student successfully completing this course will be able to evaluate whether field operations or project management is an individual’s preferred career pathway.

courses.description: Introduction to history of American architecture from colonial period to nineteenth century. Emphasis on evolution of building technologies, materials, and social and economic currents influencing architectural expression of covered period. Coursework includes lectures, readings, field excursions, class discussions, exams, research paper on subject related to American architecture of period.
courses.course_objectives:
Readings (2 books at Bookstore and a reader from Bel-Jeans); midterm and final; paper; 10-minute presentation (with slides) from your paper The Paper (15 pages, double-spaced, not including pictures) will be on a topic of your choice -- e.g., an
architect, some aspect of theory, a building type, a city or region in a certain period -- and should have as a significant focus one or two projects or building that you describe and analyze in detail. Talk to instructor about a topic by week 3. We will schedule student presentations depending on the topics and how they fit into the course of lectures. A PowerPoint presentation will be required. Readings from Roth, American Architecture: A History, are to supplement and reinforce lectures. Handbook readings deal with architectural theory and will be discussed in class. Poppeliers and Chambers, What Style is It? A Guide to American Architecture, is also required reading.

courses.title: (Re)Structuring the American Landscape
courses.description: The course explores significant changes to the American Landscape, pre-European settlement to today, including transportation systems, cities, agricultural and resource extractive landscapes, and iconic dam and bridge projects.  All of those interventions are informed by a sociological and environmental critique suggesting a more equitable and ecologically healthy way to build.

Students will be able to demonstrate minimum competency in professional assignments and activities over the internship period. Students will be able to assess the quality of the internship experience provided by an employer. Students will be able to identify important internship experiences related to professional life and activities.

courses.subject: LAND
courses.title: Professional Practice
courses.description: The legal environment of business focusing on public and private law.  Professional relations during project management, resolution of disputes, the court system, torts, real property/liens, contract law, specification writing, insurance bonds, business organizations, ethics, and professional registration.
courses.course_objectives: Students will use a version of the BMTI to determine one’s personality type. Students will develop an understanding of the different types of landscape architecture practice and the opportunities and constraints of each. Students will determine which types of landscape architecture practice best suits your personality type. Students will explain the opportunities and challenges your personality type presents when working at the type of practice you have chosen. Students will transform personality strengths into an “elevator pitch” that can be used during a job search. Students will learn how to conduct an informational interview. Students will use professional social media sites (handshake and linked in) to locate UGA CED Alums who are working for firms that align with your chosen career path. Students will conduct informational interviews with the alumni who work at the firms you are interested in. Students will conduct informational interviews at a professional networking event attended by landscape architects. Students will utilize what has been learned from informational interviews and self-discovery exercises to prepare an “elevator pitch” for the CED Career Fair. Students will participate in the CED Career Fair to locate a summer internship. Students will work with a team of students to develop initial concepts for a landscape architecture firm. Students will research demographic projections and public/private sector business opportunities in the firm’s home city. Students will prepare an initial “pitch” for the firm using market research, demographics, and preliminary company organizational chart. Students will research median salaries for all the company employees using a job search/salary app (glass door, indeed, salary.com) Students will use industry standard multipliers to determine payroll costs for the firm. Students will research the cost of equipment and office space needed for the firm to conduct operations in its home city. Students will prepare a power point presentation that presents payroll costs and “startup” expenses for office space and equipment. Students will demonstrate an understanding of the different phases of a landscape architecture project. Students will use industry standard multipliers and salaries to determine billing rates and projected income for the firm. Students will prepare a preliminary profit and loss statement for the firm using projected billing rates and expenses. Students will demonstrate an understanding of the different phases of construction for a landscape architecture project. Students will prepare a contract proposal for a hypothetical project using the firm’s billing rates. Students will prepare a three-year income statement for the firm. Students will develop a “pitch” for potential investors to contribute startup funding to the firm. Students will present preliminary pitch for the firm to an initial investor, and obtain feedback from the investor for how to improve the presentation. Revise presentation per comments received. Students will present final pitches to group of alumni investors (aka sharks.)
courses.topical_outline:
1. ‎ Students will discover their Briggs-Myers personality type using an online personality testing app.
2.  Learn about the 7 different types of landscape architecture practice
3.  Utilize personality test results to identify what types of opportunities and constraints for different personalities in landscape architecture.
4.  Practice basic networking and informational interview skills by participating in a variety of networking/mentorship events with professionals.
5.  Utilize networking skills at the CED career fair to begin the search for an internship. 
6.  Work with a team of classmates to research and develop an idea for a hypothetical landscape architecture firm. 
7.  Develop a business plan for the landscape architecture firm.
8.  Understand the phases of a landscape architecture design project.
9.  Use the design phases to develop a fee proposal for professional services. 
10.  Understand the phases of a construction project and the landscape architect's role in each phase. 
11. Understand how to obtain a professional license and keep that license active through continuing education.
12. Prepare a final pitch and three year financial statement for the hypothetical landscape architecture firm.
 13. Present the plan and financial statement to a panel of professional judges.

courses.subject: LAND
courses.title: Landscape Studio Engagement
courses.description: Concepts of environmental and community engagement with emphasis on potential of landscape architecture to act as liaison and operative framework. Projects selected to engage contemporary, critical issues in marginal locations at several scales, ranging from ecological urbanism to site and system-specific details.
courses.course_objectives: Students will understand current theories and concepts of environmental and community engagement in landscape architecture. Students will understand systems theories related to environmental and community dynamics. Students will understand contemporary systems urbanisms, including new urbanism, landscape urbanism, and ecological urbanism. Students will understand the role and potential for infrastructure and frameworks to act as leveraging devices in design. Students will have the capability to utilize system dynamics to inform site scales in landscape and urban design. Students will be able to engage community and stakeholder liaisons and to utilize sensitive research methodologies. Students will be able to conduct intensive landscape assessments of ecological, cultural, and aesthetic systems and sites. Students will have the confidence to use generative techniques to derive landscape ability to develop concepts and designs which incorporate intentional symbolism and meaning. Students will have a sense of the importance of symbolism—implied and explicit— in landscape architectural design. Students will have an appreciation for the multiple values, needs, and preferences held by pubic-oriented landscape architecture. Students will have a regard for the role and potential of synthesis as design driver in landscape architecture.
courses.topical_outline:
This course applies a project-driven studio format with integrated lectures, seminars, and workshops on relevant concepts, skills, and techniques. Advanced application of foundational skills and methods is expected in order to develop strategies and designs for complex issues and sites. Critical course components include topical research, class discussions on assigned readings, site visits, stakeholder engagement, and progress and juried project critiques. Course and Project Schedule:
Week 1 – 4: Understanding Systems – Instrumental Mapping Week 5 – 10: Nested Scales – Leverages and Linkages Week 11 – 16: Engaging Site – Strategies and Forms Projects will apply these course-acquired skillsets to the design of a real-world site in Georgia in service to actual clients. Students will gain experience in working with clientele while providing Georgia citizens/businesses/communities with implementable deliverables.

courses.course_objectives: Students will demonstrate knowledge of the relationship between architecture, landscape architecture, and urban design. Students will demonstrate knowledge of appropriate and sustainable design elements. Students will demonstrate a comprehension of spatial concepts, organizational frameworks, and ordering principles in architecture and urban design. Students will become familiar with urban design and planning terminology and how it relates to the physical form and function of a city. Students will demonstrate knowledge of the pressures that affect the built environment. Students will demonstrate the ability to recognize, analyze, and reinforce spatial structure in urban and sub-urban contexts. Students will incorporate various human-behavior research methods into the design process. Students will demonstrate the ability to site buildings and structures, adaptively reuse existing features and incorporate circulation systems (pedestrian, bicycle, automobile, bus, rail) into a responsive urban design plan. Students will demonstrate the ability to apply urban design concepts through a range of scales from an urban design scale plan to its articulation in site scale and detail design. Students will further develop design skills and creativity in landscape architecture. Students will further develop abilities to effectively communicate design ideas through advanced visualization techniques, graphics (hand and computer), models, written documents, and presentations. Students will become more aware of how community values are manifested in landscapes and design. Students will gain a deeper understanding of the complexity involved with community development and participation. Students will recognize the relationships between aesthetics, community values, cultural diversity, ecological quality, and sound urban design and planning. Students will understand the importance of recognizing and reinforcing community values through design forms. Students will develop an appreciation for the importance of creating human-scaled, pedestrian-friendly environments. Students will develop an appreciation for the need to design for human health, safety, and welfare.

courses.subject: LAND
courses.title: Landscape Ecology: Materials and Processes
courses.description: Landforms, geology, hydrology, soils, and biotic communities, with an examination of ecological concepts and their application at the landscape scale.
courses.course_objectives: Students will define central ecological concepts within the landscape planning context: environment, biomes, energy exchange, ecosystems, connectivity, and biodiversity. Measurement: Discussion, exams Students will recognize how disturbance processes shape the structure of natural ecosystems and the challenges that disturbance regimes pose for urban and regional planning. Measurement: Discussion, exams, field exercises Students will describe the processes in which land use relates to environmental health and biotic diversity and the central role of land use planning in the protection of these societal values. Measurement: Discussion, exams, essay Students will develop a working definition and philosophy of sustainability that integrates multiple perspectives at local, regional, and global scales. Measurement: Discussion, exams, essay Students will recognize and evaluate ecological concepts and landscape theory in designs, policies, and plans that better maintain environmental integrity at a variety of scales, from single sites to watersheds and regions.  Measurement: Discussion, exams, field exercises, essay Students will develop a sense of our responsibility, as citizens and as professionals, for preserving biotic diversity. Measurement: Discussion, essay Students will understand the impact of resource consumption on future generations and develop a sense of our responsibility to act as stewards of natural and social resources.  Measurement: Discussion, exams, essay Students will gain an understanding of central ecological concepts: environment, biomes, energy exchange, ecosystems, and ecotypes. Students will gain an understanding of processes of disturbance and recovery in ecosystems. Students will gain an understanding of the relationship of land use and land use planning to environmental health and protection of biotic diversity. Students will understand the concept of sustainability, with local, regional, and global implications. Students will be able to apply ecological concepts in the establishments of policies and plans which will preserve environmental integrity at a variety of scales, from single sites to watersheds and regions. Students will gain a sense of our responsibility, as citizens and as professionals, for preserving biotic diversity. Students will gain a sense of our responsibility to future generations in terms of resource use.

courses.subject: LAND
courses.title: Plant Communities
courses.description: The history and ecology of plants and related materials associated with architectural landscape design.
courses.course_objectives: Students will strengthen and expand their plant materials vocabulary. Students will understand the role of plants as major landscape design materials. Students will understand the plant characteristics that affect their use as design elements in the landscape (form, texture, line, color, and scale). Students will understand the basic cultural requirements of the plants studied. Students will have the ability to recognize and identify the plant palette of both courses in various environments and in varied microclimates. Students will have an appreciation of the value of plant communities/associations of the southeastern U.S. in analyzing environmental factors and as landscape settings. Students will have an appreciation of plant materials as a reflection of a site's condition and history. Students will have an appreciation of the varied uses environmental designers make of plants (architectural, engineering, functional, as well as aesthetical). Students will identify by both the common and botanical names approximately 350-400 trees, shrubs, and herbaceous plants. Measurement: Exams and lab specimen tests Students will develop observation skills. Measurement: Students will maintain and turn in sketchbooks containing drawings of plant forms and leaf characteristics for all plants covered Students will demonstrate an understanding of the ornamental attributes and cultural requirements of the plants presented in class. Measurement: Exams and lab specimen tests
courses.topical_outline:
Laboratory emphasizing the design characteristics of plants during various seasons of the year. Lecutures to focus on terminology, plant nomenclature, design elements, principles of design, and cultural aspects of plant materials. Plant materials presented in class laboratory periods, through field trips and through slides. Field trips around campus may be supplemented by off-campus field trips. 

All exams shall be in the field taken on 3 x 5 note cards or test booklets. Correct Latin name with correct spelling is required to receive full credit.

courses.subject: LAND
courses.title: Landscape Construction
courses.description: Introduction to materials of landscape architectural construction; their physical characteristics; their effects on people, environment, and economy; their installation methods; their purposeful use in design; sources of information about them and their use; and their documentation in contract documents.
courses.course_objectives: Students will know materials of landscape architectural construction (their origins and physical characteristics; their effects on people, environment, and economy; and their installation methods). Measurement: Specification of materials which are functional, buildable, durable, and economical, in pavements, walls, and elevated (frame) structures. Students will document materials’ arrangement in construction drawings. Measurement: Creation of construction drawings which are complete, clear, and unambiguous. Students will find and apply information about landscape construction as needed in developing technologies and emerging project needs. Measurement: Discovery and direct use of web-based sources of information in the creation of construction specifications and drawings. Students will convey the professional basics of landscape construction drawing and specification. Students will bring interests, motivations, and decision-making activities to landscape construction, so that theycan discover their own minds in application to landscape architecture. Students will be in direct working contact with sources of landscape construction information. Students will experience the design and specification of three common types of landscape construction systems: pavement, wall, and details, in their full context of site-specific concerns.
courses.topical_outline:
The experiential (lab) aspect of the course is organized around
a single design project. The intent is to make, by the end of
the semester, a complete, coherent set of construction drawings
suitable for use in contractor bidding and implementation.

An initial site design project sets each student’s template for
the specific construction that will be documented. Then a
sequence of construction design completes the documentation for
each fundamental type of landscape structure within that
template: pavement, wall, and frame structure.

courses.subject: LAND
courses.title: Landscape Engineering
courses.description: Applications of landscape construction and engineering through inquiry into their ability to implement values of community and place.
courses.course_objectives:
Students will select and design appropriate and functional solutions to mitigate stormwater quality degradation and the increased rate and volume of runoff on a site due to development. Measurement: Exercises, exams, and applied project Students will give a prescribed development program, model a watershed’s hydrologic conditions (including pre and post development runoff) and generate a site plan that minimizes increased runoff. Measurement: Exercises and applied project Students will use and identify standard notational and graphic conventions for grading and stormwater management plans. Measurement: Exercises, exams, and applied projects Students will properly size, grade, and diagram stormwater management structures. Measurement: Exercises, exams, and applied project Students will demonstrate the use of horizontal and vertical alignment criteria and formulae for road design. Measurement: Exercises and exams Students will demonstrate the use of horizontal and vertical alignment criteria and formulae for road design. 
Measurement: Exercises and exams Students will manipulate the earth results in changes that are both quantitative and qualitative; implications of landscape engineering choices are addressed. Landscape forms and flows have both functional and aesthetic properties; this course  focuses on the functional aspects, but aesthetics are presented and discussed for further application in the design studio sequence. Students will determine site watershed stormwater rates and volumes, managing them using a variety of techniques. Students will manipulate landforms in applied landscape architectural projects to achieve functional, environmental, and aesthetic goals, Students will properly integrate required structures (pavements, buildings, roads, etc.) into a site landscape. Students will respond to required site structures and earthwork volumes as constraints upon site grading. As an applied skill, landscape engineering is both intuitive and analytical. It is near the core of applied landscape architectural skills. Landscape engineering is considered an essential component in your landscape architectural training, in the professional licensure exam and in professional practice. This course provides the essential skills and knowledge necessary for the landscape architect to begin to shape the landscape. Achieving sustainability in landscape design is the product of careful and practiced application of these skills  and knowledge.
courses.topical_outline:
Most class sessions will consist of exercises to prepare
students for exams and applied design projects that will be
graded. In addition, homework that consists of similarly
important exercises will be assigned frequently. Students are
advised to do class work both during the studio session and at
other times in the building where they can learn from other
students.

I. Landscape Level (Weeks 1-4)

A. Visualizing the Landscape
1. Mapping, scales & units
2. Topography: contours
3. Plan, Section & Profile

B. Landscape Structure
1. Landforms
2. Watersheds
3. Water bodies

C. Landscape Function
1. Components & Interactions
2. Hydrologic Cycle and Water Balance
3. Systems of Flows – example: soil loss

D. Landscape Quantification
1. Determining area, distance & slope
2. Determining watershed water balance (Thornthwaite
method)
3. Determining watershed runoff volume and rate
a. Rational Formula
b. Modified Rational Formula
c. SCS Method (WinTR-55)


II. Site Level (Weeks 5-15)

A. Volumes
1. Grading Basins and Ponds
2. Grading Berms and Dams
3. Point and Contour Interpolation
4. Storage Volume & Earthwork

B. Infiltration and Runoff Volume Management
1. Soils and Infiltration rates
2. Rain gardens, bioswales and subsurface infiltration
3. Infiltration Modeling

C. Surface Conveyance and Runoff Velocity Management
1. Grading Swales and Channels
2. Velocity and Erosion Control
3. Sizing Swales and Channels

D. Structural Pads, Walkways and Foundation Walls
1. Grading Pads & Warped Pads
2. Grading Foundation Walls
3. Incorporating Drainage Swales
4. Earthwork

E. Subsurface Conveyance
1. Grading for Pipes
2. Piping Systems
3. Plan & Profile
4. Pipe Sizing
a. Inlet control
b. Outlet control

F. Detention and Runoff Rate Management
1. Sizing Detention Basins
2. Outlet Structure Devices
3. Grading Detention Basins
4. Grading Emergency Spillways
5. Temporary Sediment Basins

G. Vehicular Pavements
1. Grading Parking Lots
2. Roads and Rights of Way
3. Horizontal and Vertical Alignment
4. Plan & Profile
5. Earthwork

H. Staking Plans
1. Grid Staking
2. Base Line
3. Radial Staking
4. Coordinates
5. Stationing

courses.description: Site design and construction have direct impacts upon the exposure of soils to erosion and the quantity and quality of stormwater runoff. Proper site design, the sizing and placement of stormwater components and systems, and the design of soil erosion and sediment control practices are addressed. NPDES standards are identified and practices described in the Georgia Stormwater Manual and the Manual for Soil Erosion and Sediment Control in Georgia are applied.

courses.description: Landscape design theory of the late 19th, 20th and 21st centuries. Beginning with Olmsted's theories on social democracy and urban park design, will trace how architectural, artistic, social, and scientific theory, along with cultural ideas and values, have influenced our discipline, design, and built environment to present.

courses.subject: LAND
courses.title: Design Research
courses.description: Instructs in design concepts, theories, and precedents in the use of design as a primary research methodology. Iterative and problem-solving process of design including inventory, analysis, design development, and design synthesis is presented as a primary research methodology for discovering and communicating information to the discipline of landscape architecture. Design is presented as a research method and communication tool.

courses.subject: LAND
courses.title: Research Strategies
courses.description: Introduces research strategies for landscape architecture students and thesis as vehicle for documenting research in landscape planning, design, and management. Course will include an overview of state of research in the field and introduce tools of research used in landscape planning and management.  Introduces methods of inquiry appropriate to discipline.
courses.course_objectives: Students will describe and differentiate nine methods of inquiry appropriate to the discipline of landscape architecture as defined by Deming and Swaffield (2011). Students will write a research thesis proposal using a required format based on Turabian (2013). Measurement: Preliminary research proposal. Students will critically analyze an MLA thesis using structure mapping. Students will present a short summary of research thesis proposal using PowerPoint software. Measurement: PowerPoint presentation. Students will evaluate research strategies in peer-reviewed research papers of the discipline Measurement: Group discussion and short papers. Students will differentiate between landscape research activities and other design, planning, and management undertakings. Students will have the ability to describe and differentiate nine methods of inquiry appropriate to the disciplines of landscape architecture, planning, and management. Students will identify and choose appropriate research methods or strategies for research questions. Students will have the ability to plan and design a research thesis project. Students will critically evaluate published, peer-reviewed, research studies. Students will demonstrate the ability to conduct a key word search. Students will identify the issues of current concern within a specific area of interest. Students will define a focus for a research inquiry and develop a research question. Students will develop a research question or hypothesis. Students will demonstrate the ability to formulate a strategy or strategies for research. Students will demonstrate the ability to write grammatically correct English. Students will understand the importance of research to the creation of new knowledge for the discipline and profession. Students will understand the reciprocity between research and creativity and problem-solving in landscape design, planning, and management. Students will understand the importance of appropriate ethical considerations in research.
courses.topical_outline:
1. Prepared PowerPoint presentations will introduce nine research strategies
or “strategies of inquiry” commonly used in the field of landscape architecture as
specified in Deming and Swaffield’s textbook, Research Strategies: Inquiry, Strategy,
and Design. John Wiley and Sons, 2011, and other relevant topics.
2. Mid-term exam will test for each student’s understanding of the nine research
strategies and when they can be used.
3. Out-of-class assignments that facilitate student’s ability to critically evaluate
published research.
4. Class discussions focused on current published research projects.
5. Student presentations, including the presentation of each student’s research thesis
proposals.
6. Invitations to outside professionals to discuss various topics.

Every student will have developed a preliminary research thesis proposal by the end of
class.
