courses.subject: POLS
courses.title: Politics and Technology
courses.description: Through political theory, political science, and science fiction, this course attempts to understand the role that technology plays in shaping and maintaining the state in democratic and authoritarian nations.
courses.course_objectives: Students will try to understand what the role of technology is in shaping the state in democratic and authoritarian nations in the past through philosophy, social science, and fiction. Students will then turn their attention to the future, exploring technological innovations hatched during the digital revolution, such as artificial intelligence and blockchain, that are reshaping society. Students will gain an understanding of the role of technology in politics, as well as a warning about some of the very real dangers that technology poses to human freedom if we are not vigilant.

• Blockchain

However, there is no single definition of the term and no clear standard for measuring what constitutes "good" representation. Students will be asked to consider competing definitions of representation, and the implications that these standards have for democracy in the U.S.
courses.course_objectives: Students will understand the central concepts and debates in the political science literature on representation. Students will understand how institutions influence who is represented (and who becomes a representative). Students will understand how competing interests work together/against each other in American democracy and how this influences democratic governance. Students will understand how institutional structures influence the role of sex/gender in American politics. Students will be able to identify testable hypotheses in political science research. Students will be able to formulate testable hypotheses for political questions. Students will be able to synthesize arguments and produce evidence to support and refute empirical claims.

courses.title: The United States Presidency
courses.description: The president of the United States, including the president's constitutional position, theories of executive dominance and executive privilege, the president's attempt to control the executive branch, and presidential-congressional relations.
courses.course_objectives: Students will learn about the evolution of the presidency, with critical attention given to historical events that shaped the development of the executive branch. Students will analyze the president's role in the separation of powers system, through the analysis of contemporary and historical examples. Students will analyze and understand the promise and limits of presidents' ability to influence both domestic and foreign policy, through the analysis of contemporary and historical examples. Students will apply lessons from history to contemporary political issues. Historical examples of presidential attempts to influence policy will be examined, and the lessons from these examples will be used to analyze presidents' ability to influence policy in current issues of interest. Students will learn to analyze quantitative data relevant to the presidency. Students will learn to access and analyze primary source documents relevant to the presidency.

At the end of this course, students should be equipped to identify and access tools associated with the tracking of bills and policies. courses.course_objectives: Students will understand and summarize foundational theories in urban politics and economics. Students will understand the challenges facing present-day city leaders. Students will be able to apply their knowledge as the semester’s “resident expert” on a major city of their choice. Students will be able to identify where course material can inform ongoing debates on urban governance. Students will write detailed briefings justifying the student’s conclusions on the day’s readings. Students will be able to interpret quantitative results from published academic papers in urban politics and economics. Students will lead in-class discussion to help classmates understand and apply information from the day’s readings to contemporary urban governance issues. Students will understand foundational theories in urban politics and economics. Students will complete a project in which you propose a solution to a contemporary urban governance problem, applying lessons learned during the course.

courses.title: Applied Civic Engagement - Service Learning
courses.description: Through online and experiential learning, students explore definitions of civic engagement as it relates to democratic citizenship and its historical context, identify and demonstrate methods of civic engagement that encourage civic life individually and within a community, and understand limits of engagement in society.
courses.course_objectives: Students will be able to identify and apply course techniques and readings in community settings. Students will be able to demonstrate understanding through critical reflection activities such as discussion posts. Students will participate in experiential learning throughout the course. Students will be able to develop working knowledge of civic engagement scholarship as it relates to political science and other related fields. Students will be able to recognize and analyze personal values, experiences, and potential for becoming civically and politically engaged. Students will be able to demonstrate methods of civic engagement individually and in community. Students will be able to identify engagement opportunities with a particular issue and relate local, national, and global social policy to the issue. Students will be able to relate personal academic interests with civic interests and plan steps to pursue these interests simultaneously.
courses.topical_outline: • What is civic engagement? courses.title: The Politics of Climate Change
courses.description: Examination of the politics of addressing climate change, and the effects of climate change on politics and governance itself. The course will examine how policies get constructed and implemented and considers local and national contexts.
courses.course_objectives: Students will evaluate and respond to research and policy arguments regarding the climate change problem. Students will critically evaluate the scientific evidence for global warming and put recent changes in the context of historical climate trends. Students will explore climate change from the perspectives of policymakers, commercial interests, and the public to understand how science informs legislation and agreements on climate change mitigation. Students will identify proposed policies and actions for climate change mitigation and generate ideas to support or oppose these policies in written reports and group discussions.

courses.subject: POLS
courses.title: Constitutional Law: Powers
courses.description: Supreme court cases on the separation of powers, national and state regulatory powers, the federal system, and the role of the courts.
courses.course_objectives: Students should be able to understand the concept of “constitutionalism” and how a written constitution promotes the rule of law. Students should be able to understand the origin, purpose, strengths, and weaknesses of judicial review. Students should be able to understand the basics of constitutional interpretation (such as the difference between judicial activism and judicial restraint, the arguments for and against the use of “original intent” to clarify ambiguous constitutional language, and whether the constitution should be read literally or not). Students should be able to understand the constitutional underpinnings of the separation of powers between the legislative, executive, and judicial branches of the U.S. government and be able to describe how and why the powers of the three branches have evolved as they have. Students should be able to understand the concept of federalism and be able to explain the tensions between “states’ rights” and the concept of national supremacy. Students should be able to understand the significance of the 10th Amendment of the U.S. Constitution, the concept of state “police powers,” and Congress’s use of the Commerce Clause to regulate both the transportation and production of goods. Students should be able to understand and critique the role of the U.S. Supreme Court in determining the balance of power among the various branches and levels of government.
courses.topical_outline: 1. The Supreme Court, Judicial Review, and Constitutional Politics 2. The Development of Law: Comparative Constitutional Interpretation 3. Jurisdiction and Decision Making 4. Congress: Membership and Immunities 8. Federalism 9. Economic Rights

courses.title: Law and Politics of Public Land
courses.description: Course examines legal and political forces that affect public land policy in the United States, offering an in-depth analysis of environmental regulations such as the Wilderness Act of 1964, Endangered Species Act, and National Environmental Protection Act. It will also incorporate the role of science in policy formation and implementation.
courses.course_objectives: Students will identify and summarize the statutory and constitutional law relevant to public land regulation in the United States. Students will understand the connection between environmental policy and public land regulation in the United States. Students will understand the political forces that have shaped public land policy in the United States over time. Students will understand the political and cultural forces that have shaped environmental regulations in the United States over time. Students will analyze the history of environmental problems and how these have shaped public land policy in the United States. Students will investigate the role of relevant policies (NEPA, ESA, Wilderness Act) on U.S. public land and environmental regulation. Students will evaluate and respond to research and policy arguments regarding the climate change problem.

courses.course_objectives: Students will understand the original purpose of the U.S. Constitution’s Bill of Rights and its philosophical bases. courses.description: As part of a course sequence dealing with the theory and practice of American constitutional law, this segment will deal with separation of powers and federalism. Constitutional law is considered in historical perspective, and emphasis placed on American political development over time.
courses.course_objectives: Students will be able to understand institutional power as derived from the U.S. constitution. Students will be able to understand the origin, purpose, strengths, and weaknesses of judicial review. Students will be able to understand separation of powers in historical context. Students will be able to understand federalism and how it has evolved over time. Students will be able to explain the tensions between “states’ rights” and national supremacy, in historical context. Students will be able to understand the significance of the Commerce Clause and how Congressional use has evolved over time. Students will be able to critique the role of the U.S. Supreme Court in determining the balance of power among the various branches and levels of government over time.

courses.subject: POLS
courses.title: American Electoral Development
courses.description: This research seminar is intended as a survey on American electoral development. It is part of a certificate program on Applied History designed to introduce students to the topic of elections and electoral systems and how they have been shaped by political actors over the course of American history.
courses.course_objectives: Students will be able to understand how political elites have attempted to use elections to influence political outcomes over the course of our nation's history. Students will be able to explain how elections have consequences in terms of the types of policies that elected officials pursue once in office. Students will be able to understand how elections have evolved over the course of our nation's history and how some established "facts" are subject to interpretation. Students will be able to evaluate how political actors have sought to influence or manipulate election outcomes for political gain. Students will be able to formulate an argument in a research paper that is supported by evidence and show that alternative hypotheses are not correct. Students will be able to understand why an election outcome occurred and how specific events contributed to that specific outcome. Students will be able to evaluate, interpret, and critique arguments presented in scholarly articles and books. Students will be able to think critically about arguments and evidence that is presented in both written and graphical form. Students will be able to offer alternative explanations for historical events supported by political science concepts. Students will be able to understand and explain concepts related to elections to fellow class members and the instructor when called upon to do so. Students will be able to conduct original research on elections and communicate their findings to the class and instructor in an end-of-the semester project. Students will be able to offer verbal and written critiques of scholarly work relating to historical analyses of elections. Students will be able to explain why political actors seek to influence election outcomes in an effort to gain advantage within the political system. Students will be able to do a critical assessment of a scholarly article or book at the end of the class that illustrates the knowledge they have gained during the semester.
courses.topical_outline: Studying American Electoral Development Political Parties Partisan Realignments Balloting and Primaries Voter Registration Antebellum Politics and Elections Postbellum Elections Electoral Governance Presidential Elections and Congressional Elections Redistricting

courses.title: Presidential Power: Lessons from History
courses.description: An introduction to the American presidency, examining how the president is elected, influences public opinion, competes for power with Congress and the courts, and influences public policy. Special emphasis placed on the historical use of presidential powers and how they are utilized on contemporary political issues.
courses.course_objectives: Students will learn about the historical origins of the presidency through historical documents and contemporary commentary. Students will analyze the president's role in the separation of powers system, through the analysis of contemporary and historical examples. Students will analyze and understand the promise and limits of presidents' ability to influence both domestic and foreign policy, through the analysis of contemporary and historical examples. Students will apply lessons from history to contemporary political issues. Historical examples of presidential attempts to influence policy will be examined, and the lessons from these examples will be used to analyze presidents' ability to influence policy in current issues of interest. Students will learn to analyze quantitative data relevant to the presidency. Students will learn to access and analyze primary source documents relevant to the presidency.

Students completing the Applied Politics Internship should learn what skills and information are important for entry level practitioners in the area. Students completing the Applied Politics Internship should develop skills in interpersonal and professional communication and best practices in the workplace, generally.

courses.subject: POLS
courses.title: Applied Politics Internship Research
courses.description: Research project completed as part of Applied Politics internship that is tailored to the student's experience with elements of applied politics.
courses.course_objectives: Students completing this Applied Politics Internship should gain a basic understanding of the area in which they are interning, with an emphasis on deeper analysis of trends, practices, and important questions in the field. Students completing this Applied Politics Internship should learn to gather general information and data on subject matter related to their internship area and utilize it for academic and professional development. Students completing this Applied Politics Internship should gain skills and practice in the process of analyzing information and data on subject matter content related to their internship field. Students completing this Applied Politics Internship should produce a research memo or paper that will help them gain greater understanding and knowledge in an applied area of their internship. For example, a student interning with a party organization in their communications office may decide to investigate the impact of divisive messages on turnout with a greater focus on state turnout if they are focused on Georgia politics. Or a student may be working for an advocacy organization and decide to develop an advocacy campaign based on current research trends in information dissemination and mobilization.
courses.topical_outline: Internship
courses.prerequisiteText: POLS 5030 and (POLS 4150 or POLS 4150H) and ADPR 3860
courses.offeredText: Not offered on a regular basis.

courses.course_objectives: Students completing this Applied Politics Internship should gain a basic understanding of the area in which they are interning. Students completing this Applied Politics Internship should learn what skills and information are important for entry level practitioners in the area. Students completing this Applied Politics Internship should enhance their ability to create the materials utilized most in this area while gaining experience with the tools that are generally used for analysis or production, including various software applications. Students completing this Applied Politics Internship should develop their own critical evaluation skills as they compare and contrast best practices in their field as well as compare how course work compares to the real-world work they are doing.

courses.subject: POLS
courses.title: American Political Thought
courses.description: Ideas about human nature and government that have shaped political practice and debate in America.  The principles of the Declaration of Independence and the Constitution as developed especially by Jefferson, Madison, and Hamilton, and the interpretation of these principles by such statesmen as Lincoln and Wilson.  Other topics include Black political thought and current liberal-conservative debate.
courses.offeredText: Not offered on a regular basis.

courses.subject: POLS
courses.title: Political Philosophy:  Hobbes to the Twentieth Century
courses.description: Development of modern political philosophy through the analysis of selected works of such writers as Hobbes, Locke, Hume, Rousseau, Mill, Marx, and Nietzsche.
courses.offeredText: Not offered on a regular basis.

courses.subject: POLS
courses.title: Problems in Democratic Theory
courses.description: Major problems that arise in theoretical discussions of democracy, such as the nature of democratic government, its purposes, its justification, its limitations, and the conditions necessary for its maintenance.
courses.offeredText: Not offered on a regular basis.

courses.subject: POLS
courses.title: Theories of Social Justice
courses.description: Introduction to the theoretical and philosophical literatureregarding the nature, justification and practical implications ofdistributive justice.  The focus is on introducing the majortheoretical approaches to justice and designing researchquestions relating to theoretical and practical aspects of thesubject.

courses.subject: POLS
courses.title: Theories of Equailty
courses.description: Examination of the contemporary theoretical and philosophicalliterature regarding the nature, justification, and practicalimplications of egalitarian justice.  The focus is on introducinggraduate students to the major theoretical approaches toegalitarian justice and designing research questions relating totheoretical and practical aspects of the subject.

courses.subject: POLS
courses.title: Pre-Seminar in American Politics
courses.description: The study of American politics.  Recommended for students considering advanced work in the field.

courses.subject: POLS
courses.title: Constitutional Law:  Powers
courses.description: The substantive law of separation of powers; powers among branches of government and between national and state governments defined; historical coverage is emphasized.
courses.offeredText: Not offered on a regular basis.

courses.subject: POLS
courses.title: Master's Research
courses.description: Research while enrolled for a master's degree under the direction of faculty members.

courses.subject: POLS
courses.title: Graduate Student Seminar
courses.description: Advanced supervised experience in an applied setting.  Thiscourse may not be used to satisfy a student's approved program ofstudy.

courses.subject: POLS
courses.title: Research Design
courses.description: Basic scientific methods, broadly defined, to include problems of definition, concept formation, hypothesis testing, explanation and prediction, and theory construction.

courses.subject: POLS
courses.title: Writing for Publication in Political Science
courses.description: Preparation and revision of manuscripts suitable for publicationin political science journals.
courses.offeredText: Not offered on a regular basis.

courses.subject: POLS
courses.title: Graduate Teaching Seminar
courses.description: Provides graduate students with knowledge and skills ofpedagogical approaches for teaching various types of courses inpolitical science and information about the support systems that are available to support teaching and learning at UGA.

courses.subject: POLS
courses.title: Introduction to Rational Choice Theory
courses.description: Formal analysis of strategic behavior in various politicalsettings. Factors leading to competition and cooperation. Coursecontent includes social choice theory, game theory, and otherforms of rational choice analysis.
courses.offeredText: Not offered on a regular basis.

courses.subject: POLS
courses.title: Survey in Political Theory
courses.description: Course provides graduate students an overview of political theory as a field of study. Course should prepare graduate students for more advanced courses in political theory, as well as equip them with a basic grasp of the field to potentially teach introductory courses in political theory.
courses.course_objectives: At the end of this course, students will have sharpened analytical thinking and debating skills. At the end of this course, students will have developed writing skills. At the end of this course, students will have learned the arguments of canonical texts in political theory. At the end of this course, students will understand contemporary scholarship in the political theory.
courses.topical_outline: a. Plato b. Aristotle c. Hobbes d. Utilitarianism e. Marx f. Rawls g. Nozick
courses.offeredText: Not offered on a regular basis.

courses.subject: POLS
courses.title: Game Theory
courses.description: Game theoretic analysis of politics.  The role of information and uncertainty about preferences and beliefs.
courses.offeredText: Not offered on a regular basis.

courses.subject: POLS
courses.title: Spatial Voting Models
courses.description: Examination of the building blocks of spatial voting theoryand its application to studies of legislative process, judicialpolitics, and parliamentary procedure.  Topics include the median voter theorem, properties of the majority preferencerelationship, multidimensional voting, and a brief introductionto empirical estimation of ideal points, among others.
courses.offeredText: Not offered on a regular basis.

courses.subject: POLS
courses.title: Political Economy
courses.description: Various ways of analyzing the interaction between government and the economy.
courses.offeredText: Not offered on a regular basis.

courses.subject: POLS
courses.title: Systems of Political Philosophy
courses.description: Writings of a leading political philosopher, aimed at seeing howthe elements of his/her thought form a comprehensive and unifiedview of political life. Philosophers to be studied will includePlato, Aristotle, St. Thomas Aquinas, Machiavelli, Hobbes, Locke, Rousseau, Hegel, Marx and Nietzsche. Classic works in American thought, such as the Federalist, will also be considered.
courses.offeredText: Not offered on a regular basis.

courses.subject: POLS
courses.title: Seminar in Ancient, Medieval, and Renaissance Political Thought
courses.description: Survey of Western political thought from ancient Greece and Rometo Renaissance Europe. Reading of major texts, as well asimportant scholarly literature.

courses.subject: POLS
courses.title: Problems in Political Philosophy
courses.description: Selected problems in political philosophy, including the nature of justice; the functions of government; the ground of legitimate authority; the scope of individual rights; the foundations of democratic government; political obligation, civil disobedience, and revolution; the meaning of responsibility; and views of human nature and their political relevance.
courses.offeredText: Not offered on a regular basis.

courses.subject: POLS
courses.title: Recent Political Thought
courses.description: Important and influential recent political theories, including ideologies and scientific theories as well as contributions to political philosophy.  The aim will be to understand both the approaches to political theory that have emerged in the contemporary period and the alternative interpretations that have been given of contemporary individuals and society.
courses.offeredText: Not offered on a regular basis.

courses.subject: POLS
courses.title: American Political Development
courses.description: Emphasis will be on historical development, politicalinstitutions, and government branches.  Political change duringthe past 200+ years will be examined in light of theories ofdevelopment.  Course is principally for PhD-level studentsemphasizing advanced material and empirical research.  Studentswill generate an original research paper during the semester.

courses.subject: POLS
courses.title: Research on Electoral Behavior
courses.description: Factors which contribute to electoral choice and the dynamics of voting in the American political system.

courses.subject: POLS
courses.title: Race, Ethnicity, and Politics
courses.description: Students will be introduced to both canonical and contemporary work in the field of REP using a variety of methodological approaches. In addition to examining the substantive themes in the area of REP, we will review and discuss the different methodological approaches taken in each of the works to address the topic of race in America.

courses.subject: POLS
courses.title: Southern Politics
courses.description: The politics of individual states, the emergence of the Republican Party, Black mobilization, the consequences of reapportionment, and selected civil rights topics.
courses.offeredText: Not offered on a regular basis.

courses.subject: POLS
courses.title: Political Behavior
courses.description: Provides a broad introduction to research in American political behavior. Some of the major topics that we will cover include political participation and turnout, citizen competence, political attitudes and attitude change, party identification, vote choice, campaigns, and mass media effects.

courses.subject: POLS
courses.title: Government and Interest Groups
courses.description: Theories of interest group formation and maintenance.  Lobbying and the role of interest groups in the United States governmental process, including traditional literature on pluralism and interest groups as well as modern literature addressing traditional questions and problems.
courses.offeredText: Not offered on a regular basis.

courses.subject: POLS
courses.title: Gender and U.S. Politics
courses.description: Survey of some of the central topics in the study of gender and politics, focusing particularly on the American politics literature, but also works from the comparative literature, and discuss how comparative politics can influence our understanding of women in American politics and vice-versa.
courses.course_objectives: After taking this course, students will have an understanding of major themes in the gender and politics literature and how our understanding of gender has evolved over time. After taking this course, students will have an understanding of gender as an analytic lens that can be applied to understanding political phenomena. After taking this course, students will have an understanding of how gender structures public opinion/behavior among the American public. After taking this course, students will have an understanding of the gendered nature of political institutions and what this means for outcomes. After taking this course, students will have developed research hypotheses and empirical tests for these hypotheses. After taking this course, students will have developed written skills needed to produce an academic article or book chapter.
courses.topical_outline: Gender as an Analytic Tool Candidate Emergence and the Decision to Run for Office Political Recruitment and Institutional Design Women as Candidates Attitudes and Opinions Female Politicians in Elected Office Policy Representation The Constituent Connection Gender Egalitarianism and Symbolic Representation Women in the Judiciary Women in Executive Politics Gender and Participation Intersectionality

courses.subject: POLS
courses.title: The Legislative Process
courses.description: The United States Congress, with emphasis on recruitment and composition of leadership, procedures, and the role of parties and interest groups.  Recent changes in the Congress will be examined in light of theories of representation.
courses.offeredText: Not offered on a regular basis.

courses.subject: POLS
courses.title: The United States Presidency
courses.description: Powers of the United States Presidency.  The President's constitutional position, including theories of executive dominance and executive privilege.  Attention will also be given to the President's attempts to control the executive branch, presidential-congressional relations, and the president's leadership over domestic and foreign policy.
courses.offeredText: Not offered on a regular basis.

courses.subject: POLS
courses.title: Mass Media and American Politics Research
courses.description: Examination of the theory and research in the area of mass media and American politics.  Primary focus will be on the major theories in the area as well as classics and controversies in media research.
courses.offeredText: Not offered on a regular basis.

courses.subject: POLS
courses.title: American Political Parties
courses.description: Research on political parties in the United States, with an emphasis on empirical analysis and theories of parties.
courses.offeredText: Not offered on a regular basis.

courses.subject: POLS
courses.title: Readings and Research in American Government
courses.description: Independent study of selected topics and problems in American government.
courses.offeredText: Not offered on a regular basis.

courses.subject: POLS
courses.title: Campaign Politics
courses.description: Presidential selection processes, including impact of rules, money, media, and voting in primaries.  Focus on campaign dynamics and strategy.
courses.offeredText: Not offered on a regular basis.

courses.subject: POLS
courses.title: Public Opinion
courses.description: Research on public opinion, including the formation, expression, and measurement of opinions.

courses.subject: POLS
courses.title: Public Opinion and Democratic Institutions
courses.description: Exploration of public attitudes towards democratic principles, institutions, and processes, with a primary focus on the United States. The consent of the governed is essential to a properly functioning democracy, so an understanding of public support (e.g., trust, confidence, legitimacy perceptions) of government and political processes provides insight into the health of a democracy.

courses.subject: POLS
courses.title: Political Psychology
courses.description: Central to political psychology is information processing, the mental operations that explain how people think, reason, and feel about the political world. Covers a variety of cognitive approaches, focusing on deliberative, automatic, and effective mental processes. Topics such as implicit attitudes, memory, personality, identity, priming, framing, heuristics, and motivated reasoning will be covered.

courses.subject: POLS
courses.title: Modern Legal Theory
courses.description: Theoretical approaches to analyzing the role of courts in a democracy, including methods for interpreting and applying constitutional and other legal texts.
courses.offeredText: Not offered on a regular basis.

courses.subject: POLS
courses.title: Judicial Politics
courses.description: Judicial processes, policy-making, and policies, with emphasis on judicial selection, models of judicial decision-making, institutional constraints on judicial choice, and the implementation and impact of judicial decisions.
courses.offeredText: Not offered on a regular basis.

courses.subject: POLS
courses.title: Courts and the Executive Branch
courses.description: Graduate seminar with a focus on the institutional relationship between judicial and executive branch actors. Areas of emphasis include the success/failure of executive branch litigants in court, constraints on judicial and executive decision-making and power, and executive-judicial relations from a comparative perspective (U.S. states and cross-nationally).
courses.course_objectives: By the end of this course, students will be able to understand the historical and contemporary engagement between judicial and executive authority in the U.S. context and the context of comparative/global research. By the end of this course, students will be able to effectively review, summarize, and report the theoretical frames and empirical approaches of executive-judicial scholarship. By the end of this course, students will develop an original research project that uses empirical data to answer falsifiable research questions centered in executive and judicial politics.
courses.topical_outline: Introduction Researching the Judiciary Researching the Presidency Theories of Judicial Deference to the Executive Executives and Judicial Appointments Judicial Constraints on the Executive Branch Executive Branch Constraints on Judicial Decision-Making Courts, Executives, and Public Opinion Administrative Agency Litigants in Court Defending the Executive: Solicitor General and Court Outcomes Judicial Monitoring of Executive Branch Transparency Judicial-Executive Interactions in the U.S. States Judicial-Executive Relations in Comparative Perspective Workshop Presentations
courses.offeredText: Not offered on a regular basis.

courses.subject: POLS
courses.title: Special Topics in Law, Courts, and Judicial Process
courses.description: Special topics relating to law, courts, and the judicial process (such as "Women and the Law," "State Legal Systems," "Comparative Legal Systems," "Research Seminar on Trial Courts," etc.).
courses.offeredText: Not offered on a regular basis.

courses.subject: POLS
courses.title: Constitutional Law:  Rights and Liberties
courses.description: The substantive constitutional law of rights and liberties, with emphasis on political freedom of speech and press, religious freedom, freedom from discrimination, and protection of due process in criminal justice.
courses.offeredText: Not offered on a regular basis.

courses.subject: POLS
courses.title: Special Topics in Research Methods
courses.description: Special topics in advanced research methodology.

courses.subject: POLS
courses.title: Measurement Theory for Political Science
courses.description: Methods of estimating latent dimensions of preference and similarity from individuals' observed choices and judgments.  Factor analysis, multidimensional scaling, and related techniques are studied both with classical maximum likelihood and Bayesian methods.
courses.offeredText: Not offered on a regular basis.

courses.subject: POLS
courses.title: Applied Bayesian Modeling for the Social Sciences
courses.description: Introduction to the basics of Bayesian modeling by focusing mostly on real world applications. The course highlights the strengths of the Bayesian modeling paradigm for social science data.  Topics covered include:  generalized linear models, measurement models and IRT, multi-level modeling, and missing data imputation.
courses.offeredText: Not offered on a regular basis.

courses.subject: POLS
courses.title: Survey Research Methods
courses.description: Introduction to research using surveys. Topics covered include random sampling, non-probability sampling, sample bias, and questionnaire design.

courses.subject: POLS
courses.title: Experimental Methods in Political Science
courses.description: Course provides an in-depth exploration of experimental methods used in political science research. Students will learn how to design, conduct, and analyze experiments to investigate political phenomena. The course covers both laboratory and field experiments, emphasizing the strengths and limitations of experimental approaches in understanding causal relationships.
courses.course_objectives: By the end of the course, students will be able to design and implement rigorous experiments to test political science theories. By the end of the course, students will be able to analyze experimental data using appropriate statistical techniques. By the end of the course, students will be able to critically evaluate the validity and reliability of experimental research. By the end of the course, students will be able to apply experimental methods to real-world political science questions and policy issues.
courses.topical_outline: Introduction to Experimental Methods: Understanding the basics of experimental design, including randomization, control groups, and treatment effects Types of Experiments: Exploring different types of experiments such as laboratory experiments, field experiments, survey experiments, and natural experiments Design and Implementation: Practical guidance on designing experiments, including hypothesis formulation, operationalization of variables, and ethical considerations Data Collection and Analysis: Techniques for collecting and analyzing experimental data, including statistical methods for causal inference Applications in Political Science: Case studies and examples of how experimental methods have been applied to study voting behavior, public opinion, policy evaluation, and other political phenomena Critiques and Limitations: Critical examination of the limitations and potential biases in experimental research, and discussions on how to address these challenges

courses.subject: POLS
courses.title: Causal Inference
courses.description: In this class, we introduce the workhorse methods for inferring causal relationships from observational data, with a focus on building the skills students need to develop convincing research designs, identify useful variation in data, and write error-free, reproducible code.
courses.course_objectives: By the end of this course, students will be able to critically evaluate research that employs canonical causal inference designs. By the end of this course, students will be able to conduct research that leverages one of the designs introduced in class to credibly argue that a pattern observed in data is evidence of a causal relationship.
courses.topical_outline: Week 1: Garbage Cans & Causal Salads Week 2: The Fundamental Problem of Causal Inference Week 3: DAGS Weeks 4-5: Experiments (Natural & Unnatural) Weeks 6-7: Selection on Observables (Regression & Matching) Weeks 8-9: Fixed Effects Weeks 10-11: Difference-in-Differences Weeks 12-13: Instrumental Variables Weeks 14-15: Regression Discontinuity

courses.subject: POLS
courses.title: Computational Data Analysis
courses.description: Course introduces Ph.D. students to a range of computational methods commonly used in data-driven research within the social sciences. Through programming in R, students will learn to collect, clean, analyze, and communicate data effectively. Topics include data wrangling, data visualization, text analysis, database management, web scraping, and programming fundamentals.
courses.course_objectives: Students will gain proficiency in statistical programming. Students will learn to collect, clean, analyze, and communicate data effectively. Students will build a foundation for data-driven research in the social sciences.
courses.topical_outline: I. Workflow, presentation, documenting II. Importing data III. Transforming data IV. Visualizing data V. Storing data VI. Text as data VII. Dates and time as data VIII. Geographic data IX. Loops and iteration

courses.subject: POLS
courses.title: Special Topics in American Politics
courses.description: Seminar focusing on selected topics in American politics.  This course will expose graduate students to extensive scholarly research using sophisticated econometric techniques.
courses.offeredText: Not offered on a regular basis.

courses.subject: POLS
courses.title: Doctoral Graduate Student Seminar
courses.description: Advanced supervised experience in an applied setting.  Thiscourse may not be used to satisfy a student's approved program ofstudy.

courses.subject: POPH(IDIS)(MIBO)
courses.title: Molecular Virology and Experimental Design
courses.description: Molecular techniques to study viruses of veterinary importance.

courses.subject: POPH(IDIS)
courses.title: Vector Ecology Field Course
courses.description: Students will develop skills and acquire knowledge of arthropod vectors in the southeast. Students will be exposed to and perform a variety of standard entomological techniques for vector identification and taxonomy, field-based techniques for capturing or attracting vectors, and how these techniques are used by various agencies and personnel for vector control.
courses.prerequisiteText: [(BIOL 1103 or BIOL 1103E or BIOL 2103H) and BIOL 1103L] or [(BIOL 1107 or BIOL 1107E or BIOL 2107H) and BIOL 1107L]

courses.subject: POPH(IDIS)
courses.title: Decoding Disease: Computational Tools for Pathogen Analytics
courses.description: Course explores computational and quantitative methods including genomics, transcriptomics, and machine learning to understand the epidemiology, ecology, and evolution of infectious diseases. Students will use omics and epidemiological data to investigate pathogen dynamics. Graduate students will lead an independent project applying skills learned in the course to their own research.
courses.course_objectives: By the end of this course, all students will be able to analyze pathogen genomic and epidemiological data through completing infectious diseases-focused problem sets that utilize programming in R and advanced computational methods. By the end of this course, all students will be able to evaluate the credibility of statistical analyses of infectious disease data and support conclusions about pathogen evolution and transmission processes through comprehensive evaluation of results. By the end of this course, graduate students will be able to design and implement an independent investigation into population health problems by applying computational tools learned in the course and by communicating findings in written reports and oral presentations.
courses.topical_outline: Introduction to R R for biological data Data visualization and manipulation Introduction to Unix command line Introduction to viral genomics Introduction to bacterial genomics Sequencing technologies, assembly, and annotation Studying host pathogen interactions using transcriptomics Metagenomics for pathogen discovery Exploring evolutionary relationships with phylogenetics Genomic epidemiology to investigate transmission Introduction to ML/AI Applications of ML to molecular data Applications of ML to forecast disease dynamics Applications of computational tools to real world data
courses.prerequisiteText: (BIOL 1107 or BIOL 1107E or BIOL 2107H) and (BIOL 1108 or BIOL 1108E or BIOL 2108H)

courses.subject: POPH(MIBO)(IDIS)
courses.title: Introduction to Virology
courses.description: Introduction to basic principles and concepts of virology, viralreplication and pathogenesis for undergraduate and graduatestudents. Class topics will include classification, replication,diagnosis, quantification, pathogenesis, and epidemiology of viruses.

courses.subject: POPH(MIBO)
courses.title: RNA Virus Genomic Diversity
courses.description: Use of recent publications on molecular characterization and analysis of RNA viruses to give students insight on virus genome diversity and evolution.
courses.prerequisiteText: BCMB 3100 or BCMB 3100E or BCMB 3100H or BCMB 4010/6010 or permission of department

courses.subject: POPH(POUL)
courses.title: Poultry Health
courses.description: Common infectious, parasitic, and nutritional diseases of poultry: the cause, diagnosis, prevention, and control.  Offered to students majoring in poultry science and others who are qualified.
courses.prerequisiteText: POUL 2020-2020L or [(BIOL 1107 or BIOL 1107E) and BIOL 1107L]

courses.subject: POPH(VPHY)
courses.title: Scientific Writing - Communication Across Audiences
courses.description: This writing-intensive course is designed to introduce, develop and refine scientific writing skills for undergraduate and graduate students. Students will write and evaluate scientific literature, critiquing language and effectiveness across audiences. Fundamentals of citing references, peer reviews, and developing a personal style and literary voice will be covered.
courses.prerequisiteText: [(ENGL 1101 or ENGL 1101E or ENGL 1101S) and (BIOL 1103 or BIOL 1103E or BIOL 2103H or BIOL 2103S or BIOL 1104 or BIOL 2104H or BIOL 1107 or BIOL 1107E or BIOL 2107H or ECOL 1000 or ECOL 1000E or ECOL 1000H)] or permission of department

courses.subject: POPH
courses.title: Infectious and Vector-Borne Diseases Associated with Wildlife in a Changing World
courses.description: The world is experiencing tremendous changes that have ramifications for numerous diseases. This course will focus on the effects of climate change, habitat loss, and other factors on the transmission of infectious and vector-borne diseases that impact wildlife or use wildlife as reservoirs. We will also discuss intervention strategies.
courses.prerequisiteText: [(BIOL 1103 or BIOL 1103E or BIOL 2103H or PBIO 1210) and BIOL 1103L] or [(BIOL 1107 or BIOL 1107E or BIOL 2107H) and BIOL 1107L]

courses.subject: POPH
courses.title: Introduction to Wildlife Health
courses.description: Wildlife health is intricately connected to wildlife biology, veterinary medicine, and infectious diseases, necessitating a specialized educational track to equip students with the unique knowledge and skills required to address these issues. This course will examine the key concepts involved in an interdisciplinary and collaborative approach to wildlife health.
courses.course_objectives: By the end of this course, students will have learned to work together as a member of a problem-solving team to research and evaluate assigned Wildlife Health topics and consider the roles of wildlife biologists, veterinarians, and environmental health professionals in approaching solutions to these issues. By the end of this course, students will have learned to examine the relationship between human activity and the impact on habitat quality and wildlife health. By the end of this course, students will have learned to understand the ecological and financial costs of disease on wildlife populations. By the end of this course, students will be familiar with various strategies across fields in response to wildlife health issues. By the end of this course, students will have developed management and research plans in response to emerging wildlife health challenges.
courses.topical_outline: What is disease? What is health? What causes disease? How can disease be detected, described, and measured? Damage, Pathogenicity, and Virulence Defense, Resistance, and Repair Environmental Interactions Transmission and Perpetuation of Infectious Disease Noninfectious Disease: Nutrients and Toxicants Effects of Disease on the Individual Animal and on Populations of Wild Animals Diseases Shared with Humans and Domestic Animals Disease Management Climate and Wildlife Health Wildlife Rehabilitation Wildlife Health Policy
courses.prerequisiteText: [(BIOL 1103 or BIOL 1103E or BIOL 2103H or PBIO 1210) and BIOL 1103L] or [(BIOL 1107 or BIOL 1107E or BIOL 2107H) and BIOL 1107L]

courses.subject: POPH
courses.title: Current Topics in Wildlife Health
courses.description: Introduces students to current issues and the multi-disciplinary responses to pressing wildlife health problems via a series of guest lecturers and readings from peer-reviewed manuscripts. This class will be heavily discussion-based.
courses.course_objectives: By the end of this course, students will be able to explain factors that contribute to and detract from wildlife health and examine the relationship between human activity and the emergence of novel pathogens. By the end of this course, students will be able to differentiate approaches used by veterinarians, wildlife biologists, ecologists, and environmental health practitioners when attempting to control, detect, and diagnose disease in wildlife. By the end of this course, students will be able to critique current issues, management plans, and strategies used in response to current issues in wildlife health.
courses.topical_outline: Climate change Pathogens of population consequence (e.g., BHS pneumonia, WNS, chytrid, HPAI on threatened species, CWD, plague) Habitat restoration and management Environmental/ecosystem health Ecotoxicology Zoonotic disease Federal and state agency responses to wildlife disease issues Deforestation and development impacts on human and animal health Antibiotic usage and antimicrobial resistance Impact of public policy/global economy on environmental and animal health Illegal wildlife trade Invasive species
courses.prerequisiteText: [(BIOL 1103 or BIOL 1103E or BIOL 2103H or PBIO 1210) and BIOL 1103L] or [(BIOL 1107 or BIOL 1107E or BIOL 2107H) and BIOL 1107L]

courses.subject: POPH
courses.title: Advanced Topics in Wildlife Health
courses.description: Advanced Topics in Wildlife Health is a dynamic, experiential learning course designed to immerse undergraduate students in the forefront of wildlife health research and management. Students will engage in hands-on experiences and will gain an understanding of the intricacies involved in wildlife health research.
courses.course_objectives: Students will be able to discuss and demonstrate hands-on skills essential for wildlife health research such as vector sampling through tick dragging and light trapping, mist-netting for avian studies, and chemical immobilization. Students will be able to describe various laboratory diagnostic techniques relevant to wildlife health, including sample collection, analysis, and interpretation of results. Students will also compare and contrast best use-case scenarios for different assays in wildlife health. Students will be able to understand the role of various agencies in wildlife health management and research, and examine how collaborative efforts contribute to effective conservation practices. Students will be able to design and implement a surveillance program to detect and manage potential threats to wildlife populations. Specifically, students will participate in the Student Network for Amphibian Pathogen Surveillance program with the United States Geological Survey, producing new and original work for a nationwide program.
courses.topical_outline: Wildlife Health Techniques Laboratory Diagnostics Collaborative Multi-agency Partnerships Application of Surveillance Techniques Ethical and Sustainable Wildlife Management Communication and Reporting Policy Implications and Conservation Professional Development
courses.prerequisiteText: [(BIOL 1103 or BIOL 1103E or BIOL 2103H or PBIO 1210) and BIOL 1103L] or [(BIOL 1107 or BIOL 1107E or BIOL 2107H) and BIOL 1107L]

courses.subject: POPH
courses.title: Comparative Parasitology and the Changing Global Climate
courses.description: Focuses on the biology of parasites responsible for diseases in domestic animals, humans, and wildlife in the face of global climate change. The course is organized by parasite group providing an overview of major parasite taxa, presentation of the disease, and management and control responses for each major parasite group.
courses.prerequisiteText: [(BIOL 1103 or BIOL 1103E or BIOL 2103H) and BIOL 1103L] or [(BIOL 1107 or BIOL 1107E or BIOL 2107H) and BIOL 1107L]

courses.subject: POPH
courses.title: Comparative Parasitology Lab
courses.description: The lab portion of this course will supplement the lecture by providing a hands-on, skills-based practicum in the identification of parasites responsible for diseases in domestic animals, humans, and wildlife in the face of global climate change. Students will learn a variety of parasitological techniques and navigate dichotomous keys to identify key features of specimens discussed in the lecture.
courses.prerequisiteText: [(BIOL 1103 or BIOL 1103E or BIOL 2103H) and BIOL 1103L] or [(BIOL 1107 or BIOL 1107E or BIOL 2107H) and BIOL 1107L]

courses.subject: POPH
courses.title: Infectious and Vector-Borne Diseases Associated with Wildlife in a Changing World
courses.description: The world is experiencing tremendous changes that have ramifications for numerous diseases. Investigation of the effects of climate change, habitat loss, and other factors on the transmission of infectious and vector-borne diseases that impact wildlife or use wildlife as reservoirs. Discussion of some of the most common vectors and their associated diseases, as well as the effects on wildlife populations. Intervention strategies, management applications, and the successes and failures of previous wildlife disease and mortality responses.
courses.prerequisiteText: [(BIOL 1103 or BIOL 1103E or BIOL 2103H or PBIO 1210) and BIOL 1103L] or [(BIOL 1107 or BIOL 1107E or BIOL 2107H) and BIOL 1107L]

courses.subject: POPH
courses.title: Critical Review of Research in Population Health
courses.description: Critical analysis and discussion of recent advances in population health research through oral presentation. Specific topics may vary but will emphasize management, surveillance, and disease control in populations of animals.
courses.course_objectives: Students learn how to communicate research results orally in an effective manner. Students who successfully complete the course should be able to discuss and critically analyze the results of their original research as well as prepare an oral presentation of their work. Students will learn to assimilate information through a combination of approaches that include discussions with the instructor, practice in front of a group of peers, and observation of experienced presenters in a lab meeting setting.
courses.topical_outline: Specific topics will vary according to the faculty assigned to the course but may include any of the following in accordance with the research instructors are currently conducting: I. Food safety II. Infectious diseases III. Bacterial pathogenesis IV. Viral pathogenesis V. Wildlife management VI. Pathogen surveillance VII. Genomics VIII. Isolation of novel microorganisms IX. Parasitology X. Management of food animal and poultry production XI. Development of animal models of disease XII. Handling and care of research animals
courses.prerequisiteText: Permission of department | Graduate Prerequisite | Permission of department | Undergraduate Pre or

courses.subject: POPH
courses.title: Directed Research for Undergraduate Students
courses.description: Independent laboratory research in infectious diseasepathogenesis and epidemiology under the direction of a facultymember.

courses.subject: POPH
courses.title: Directed Research
courses.description: Students will work on various research related to populationgenetics and ecology of bacterial pathogens. Students will learna specific laboratory technique and apply this method towards aspecific research project.  In addition, students will learnbasic laboratory skills, including making solution, bacterialcultivation, etc.

courses.title: Faculty-Mentored Undergraduate Research I
courses.description: Faculty-supervised independent or collaborative inquiry into fundamental and applied problems within a discipline that requires students to gather, analyze, synthesize, and interpret data and to present results in writing and other relevant communication formats.

courses.subject: POPH
courses.title: Faculty-Mentored Undergraduate Research II
courses.description: Faculty-supervised independent or collaborative inquiry into fundamental and applied problems within a discipline that requires students to gather, analyze, synthesize, and interpret data and to present results in writing and other relevant communication formats.

courses.subject: POPH
courses.title: Faculty-Mentored Undergraduate Research III
courses.description: Faculty-supervised independent or collaborative inquiry into fundamental and applied problems within a discipline that requires students to gather, analyze, synthesize, and interpret data and to present results in writing and other relevant communication formats.

courses.subject: POPH
courses.title: Undergraduate Research Thesis (or Final Project)
courses.description: Faculty-supervised independent or collaborative inquiry into fundamental and applied problems within a discipline that requires students to gather, analyze, synthesize, and interpret data. Students will write or produce a thesis or other professional capstone product, such as a report or portfolio that describes their systematic and in-depth inquiry.

courses.subject: POPH
courses.title: Conservation Medicine - Conservation Biology
courses.description: Conservation medicine is an emerging field concerned with the interface between human health, animal health (both wild and domestic), and ecosystem health. This course provides veterinary students with the opportunity to learn and practice the principles of conservation medicine using the ecology and fauna of Costa Rica.
courses.prerequisiteText: Must be first- or second-year vet student
courses.offeredText: Offered summer semester every odd-numbered year.

courses.subject: POPH
courses.title: Techniques in Laboratory Animal Medicine
courses.description: Humane methods of animal maintenance and experimentation; thetesting methods which minimize animal distress; use ofanaesthetics, analgesics, and tranquilizers for commonly used labspecies.

courses.subject: POPH
courses.title: Animal Welfare
courses.description: Background concepts and principles of animal welfare.  Studentswill be provided with information regarding current issues ofanimal welfare pertinent to veterinary medicine.

courses.subject: POPH
courses.title: Special Topics in Population Health
courses.description: Presentation and discussion of published research and new developments in population health.

courses.subject: POPH
courses.title: Epidemiology and Preventive Medicine
courses.description: The applications of epidemiology to veterinary clinical medicine. The zoonotic diseases of topical interest, with special emphasis on the foodborne diseases associated with red meat and poultry.

courses.subject: POPH
courses.title: Applied Preventive Health
courses.description: Study of preventive health management programs common across animal species.

courses.subject: POPH
courses.title: Production Management
courses.description: Foundational concepts preparing students for veterinary practice within cattle and swine production systems. Exploration and evaluation of common management systems to optimize the health and productivity of swine, dairy cattle, and beef cattle. Major drivers of health and production, how they can be measured and managed, and how the veterinarian fits into the management plan will be discussed.
courses.course_objectives: By the end of this course, students will be able to describe the major drivers of profitability for swine and cattle agricultural enterprises. By the end of this course, students will be able to recognize high risk times for disease for each species covered. By the end of this course, students will be able to describe how common preventive management practices affect health and productivity in swine, dairy cattle, and beef cattle. By the end of this course, students will be able to recognize common measures of animal health and product quality, interpret results, and be able to critique and construct standard operating procedures. By the end of this course, students will be able to use their knowledge of biology and mechanics to design and appraise animal housing, and its effects on health and production.
courses.topical_outline: What is production medicine? Food animal veterinary practice models Economics: profit, throughput, marginality Swine production, housing, animal flow, biosecurity Swine high risk times: neonates, post-weaning, finishing Swine reproductive management Dairy production, housing, animal flow, product quality Dairy high-risk times: calves, transition, udder health Dairy reproductive management Beef production, housing, animal flow, product quality Beef high risk times: calves, weaning, finishing Beef reproductive management

courses.subject: POPH
courses.title: Wildlife Diseases
courses.description: This is an introductory course in conservation/wildlife biology designed for DVM students.  Emphasis will be placed on wildlife diseases and their potential impacts on free-ranging wildlife populations.
courses.course_objectives: Students will develop an understanding of basic conservation/wildlife biology and an appreciation of the major factors impacting free-ranging wildlife populations. Students will develop an understanding of approaches utilized in wildlife disease investigations. Students will understand the veterinarian's potential role in conservation/wildlife biology.
courses.topical_outline:
I. Conservation/Wildlife Biology
A. The conservation infrastructure. Who is responsible for wildlife?
B. Working at the population/ecosystem level
C. Wildlife disease problem definition II. Disease and the Conservation of Free-ranging Wildlife Populations
A. Wildlife diseases and the actions of human
B. Common diseases of Southeastern wildlife
C. Field techniques
D. The domestic animal, human, and wildlife health interface
E. Current and emerging issues in wildlife conservation
courses.prerequisiteText: Enrollment in Doctor of Veterinary Medicine curriculum

courses.subject: POPH
courses.title: Laboratory Animal Medicine: Husbandry, Diseases, and Management of Laboratory Animals
courses.description: This is an elective course for students who are interested in learning about the care and use of common laboratory animals as well as being introduced to the specialty of laboratory animal medicine.
courses.course_objectives: Students will be able to describe the biology, husbandry, and requirements for housing and care for common laboratory animal species. Students will be able to identify, diagnose, manage, and prevent common diseases of laboratory animal species. Students will be able to outline appropriate sedation, analgesic, anesthetic, and euthanasia methods for laboratory animal species. Students will be able to demonstrate proper handling, restraint, injection sites, and sample collection from common laboratory animal species. Students will be able to understand the basics of animal welfare, ethics, and the basics of regulatory compliance considerations. Students will be able to propose appropriate animal models for research studies and experimental protocols.
courses.prerequisiteText: Enrollment in Doctor of Veterinary Medicine curriculum

courses.subject: POPH
courses.title: Ruminant Internal Medicine: Digestive Diseases
courses.description: This course will use a case oriented approach to review common digestive disorders in ruminants.  Students will be expected to generate a tentative etiologic list, and a diagnostic and therapeutic (preventive health) plan after being presented with a clinical situation involving cattle, sheep, or goats.

courses.subject: POPH
courses.title: Poultry Diseases
courses.description: The etiology, epidemiology, pathogenesis, diagnosis, prevention,control, and treatment of infectious diseases of poultry. General aspects of biosecurity, food safety, welfare, andpopulation medicine in commercial poultry.
courses.prerequisiteText: Enrollment in Doctor of Veterinary Medicine curriculum

courses.subject: POPH
courses.title: Public Health
courses.description: An introduction to the important role of veterinarians inprotecting public health. An emphasis on the relationship betweenanimal and human health, and current national and internationalissues in human health and public health policy that impactveterinary medicine will be presented.  Computer modules,didactic lecture material and student presentations will covervarious aspects of veterinary medicine and emerging human diseases.
courses.course_objectives: Students will be familiar with important public health issues impacting veterinary medicine and practice. Students will understand the interaction between veterinary and human medicine and the important role of the veterinarian in human health, zoonotic disease control and surveillance, education, and public health policy.
courses.topical_outline: Veterinary interfaces with state and federal agencies Food safety Antimicrobial resistance Emerging animal diseases Zoonoses Global public health

courses.subject: POPH
courses.title: Diseases of Swine
courses.description: Review of diseases encountered in swine practice.
courses.course_objectives: Students will learn to differentiate reproductive, enteric, respiratory, CNS, skin, musculoskeletal, polysystemic, and parasitic diseases of swine.
courses.topical_outline: 1. Diseases of reproduction 2. Enteric diseases 3. Respiratory diseases 4. CNS diseases 5. Skin diseases 6. Musculoskeletal diseases 7. Polysystemic diseases 8. Parasitic diseases 9. Disease associated with toxic agents 10. Disease associated with nutritional deficiencies

courses.subject: POPH
courses.title: Avian Medicine Clinical Rotation
courses.description: In-depth study of a speciality area of avian medicine.

courses.title: Wildlife Population Health
courses.description: Exposure to the many aspects of wildlife population health.Students will participate in field and laboratory projects,attend meetings of staff to discuss research projects, andconduct a library project on a salient disease topic.
