courses.title: Emergency and Critical Care Basics
courses.description: Introduction to basic concepts and monitoring techniquesnecessary for care of critical patients.  This course preparesstudents for the advanced ECC elective and the clinical emergencyand ICU blocks.

courses.subject: SAMS
courses.title: Small Animal Infectious Disease
courses.description: This course will emphasize diagnosis and treatment of various infectious diseases of dogs and cats.  Didactic information will be presented on a variety of the most commonly associated viral, bacterial, fungal, and protozoal diseases.  In addition, sessions involving case presentation by students will occur.
courses.prerequisiteText: Completion of first year veterinary curriculum or equivalent experience

courses.subject: SAMS
courses.title: Zoological, Wildlife, and Aquatic Medicine
courses.description: An introduction to the fields of institutional zoo medicine, especially larger exotic species, wildlife triage and rehabilitation, aquatic mammal medicine, and fish medicine.

courses.subject: SAMS
courses.title: Wildlife Medicine Clinical Elective
courses.description: Students will assume case responsibility for all wildlifepresented to the hospital.  Duties may include morning andevening treatments, emergency care, maintenance of medicalrecords, and diagnostic workup followed by medical or surgicaltreatment under supervision of the Zoological Medicine Staff.

courses.subject: SAMS
courses.title: Communications Skills for Veterinarians
courses.description: Introduce students to the skills necessary to become an effectivecommunicator.  Topics include: engaging the client, roles of theveterinarian, discussing euthanasia, client compliance, financialmatters, and interactions with difficult clients. This course is made up of didactic lectures.

courses.subject: SAMS
courses.title: Introduction to Clinical Thinking
courses.description: First-year veterinary students utilize their current knowledge base to evaluate case examples. The students learn and use the problem-based medical record method for SOAPing patients in a classroom setting. The final weeks of the course are spent in small groups going into the small animal clinic to evaluate clinical cases.

courses.subject: SAMS
courses.title: Reading for Evidence-Based Veterinary Medicine
courses.description: This course combines a lecture format with a journal club smallgroup meeting to introduce the concept of evidence-basedmedicine, to teach a systematic approach to evaluation ofevidence, and to foster an appreciation for lifelong professional learning.

courses.subject: SAMS
courses.title: Veterinary Ophthalmology
courses.description: Introduces students to the basic medical information necessary to deal with the common ophthalmology problems of dogs, cats, and large animals.  This class is designed to help students develop the problem-solving skills necessary to diagnose and treat the most common ophthalmic problems.

courses.subject: SAMS
courses.title: Small Mammal Medicine
courses.description: The husbandry and management, reproduction, disease diagnosis, and treatment of rabbits, rodents (including guinea pigs,chinchillas, hamsters, mice, rats, and gerbils), ferrets, sugargliders, prairie dogs, and hedgehogs.

courses.subject: SAMS
courses.title: Polysystemic Diseases: Hematology and Endocrinology
courses.description: Core course for sophomore veterinary students that will prepare the student in the diagnosis and treatment of large and small animal hematologic and endocrine disorders.  It will also include an introduction to oncology.

courses.subject: SAMS
courses.title: Small Animal Clinical Endocrinology
courses.description: Diagnosis and treatment of endocrine disorders of dogs and cats.

courses.subject: SAMS
courses.title: Small Animal Urology
courses.description: The medical and surgical disorders of the urinary system important in dogs and cats.

courses.subject: SAMS
courses.title: Principles of Surgery
courses.description: Principles of surgical asepsis, wound healing, and instrumenthandling.

courses.subject: SAMS
courses.title: Topics in Small Animal Dentistry
courses.description: Introduction to the fundamentals of small animal dentistry.  Discussion of anatomy and terminology, professional periodontal therapy, dental radiography, extractions, feline issues, and case examples.  Labs will allow students to practice radiograph, cleaning, and extraction techniques.

courses.subject: SAMS
courses.title: Small Animal Oncology
courses.description: Familiarization of the principles of cancer diagnosis and multimodality therapy in small animal patients.  Development of an approach to diagnosing cancer in pets and determining how advanced the cancer is (clinical staging).  Introduction to treatment options available and appropriate for different types of cancer in cats and dogs.

courses.subject: SAMS
courses.title: Small Animal Advanced Digestive Diseases
courses.description: Instructors will present specific small animal digestive diseases in an advanced problem- and case-oriented format; students will practice applying a rational, problem-oriented approach to the diagnosis and management of specific canine and feline digestive diseases.

courses.subject: SAMS
courses.title: Reptile, Avian, and Small Mammal Medicine
courses.description: Designed to prepare students for the senior clinical rotation in exotic pet, wildlife, and zoo medicine and for general practice. This clinically oriented elective course concentrates on husbandry and nutrition, diagnostic techniques and disease diagnosis, and medical and surgical therapy.
courses.prerequisiteText: Enrollment in Doctor of Veterinary Medicine curriculum

courses.subject: SAMS
courses.title: Small Animal Advanced Anesthesia
courses.description: To allow veterinary students to become more proficient in the anesthetic management of small animal patients (dogs, cats, small exotics, birds, etc.).
courses.course_objectives: Students will choose a safe, appropriate anesthetic protocol for routine small animal and small exotic animal cases, including pediatric and geriatric animals. Students will choose a safe, appropriate anesthetic protocol for more critical small animal cases, including patients with cardiac, pulmonary, endocrine, renal, hepatic, GI, neurological, ophthalmic disease, and ASA status of III, IV, or V. Students will become familiar with the techniques of anesthetic monitoring and be able to determine the appropriate level of monitoring for each case. Students will anticipate the common complications seen under general anesthesia, and know how to prevent, recognize, and treat them. Students will know how to appropriately use anticholinergics, sympathomimetics, anti-dysrhythmics, crystalloids, colloids, blood products, and oxyglobin perioperatively. Students will know the indications and techniques for IPPV. Students will know how to appropriately stabilize and perioperatively manage patients for emergency anesthesia (GDV, c-section, acute abdomen, trauma, airway emergencies. Students will know how to manage pain in small animal and exotic patients, including the use of regional and local blocks.
courses.topical_outline:
1. Review of Options for Anesthesia (TIVA), balanced anesthesia,
inhalation anesthesia. Muscle relaxants. Common anesthetic
protocols used in small animal patients. (1 lecture = 1 contact
hour). 2. Regional and Local Anesthesia/analgesia techniques (brachial
plexus blocks, digit blocks, retrobulbar blocks, dental blocks,
epidural blocks, IV regional). (1 lecture = 1 contact hour). 3. Monitoring under anesthesia. Causes and implications of
complications occurring in veterinary patients under anesthesia.
(2 lectures = 2 contact hours). 4. Management of complications under anesthesia and through
recovery (anticholinergics, inotropic support, anti-arrhythmics,
crystalloid and colloid administration, oxyglobin and blood
transfusions, ventilation, oxygen therapy, etc). (2 lectures = 2
contact hours). 5. Anesthesia for specific conditions in small animal patients:
(2 lectures = 2 contact hours)
Cardiac disease; Pulmonary disease; Endocrine disease; Renal
disease; Hepatic disease; Gastrointestinal disease;
Neurological disease; Ophthalmic disease; Pediatric and
geriatric patients; and Dealing with aggressive patients. 6. Anesthesia for small exotics: ferrets, rabbits guinea pigs,
birds, etc. (1 lecture = 1 contact hour) 7. Emergency anesthesia: stabilization, protocols, specific
problems: Gastric dilation and volvulus, sepsis, trauma,
ceasarian section, airway emergencies, etc. (2 lectures = 2
contact hours). 8. Pain management (1 lecture = 1 contact hour) 9. AQS - case-based (1 lecture; 2 contact hours) 10. Mid-term examination (1 lecture = 1 contact hour) 11. Anesthesia laboratory (= 1 lecture period; 2 laboratory
hours). The class will be broken up into 6 small groups (3
groups in the first 2 hour session and 3 groups in the second 2
hour session). Each group will have the opportunity to observe:
the effects of premedication, induction and maintenance of
general anesthesia, placement of intravenous catheters, fluid
administration, placement and correct usage of monitoring devices
and the principles of monitoring a patient under general
anesthesia. In addition, students will be given an exercise to
calculate drug dosages (to milligrams and milliliters) and fluid
administration rates for their group's dog. Small group sizes
will allow students more "hands-on" experience for this
laboratory.

courses.subject: SAMS
courses.title: Small Animal Clinical Neurology
courses.description: Instruction in small animal neurology. This clinically orientedclass teaches students how to perform a neurological exam andestablish a correct anatomic diagnosis. In addition, the coursecovers disease pathophysiology, diagnostic testing, andtherapeutic treatments.  Didactic lectures are accompanied byvideo presentations.

courses.subject: SAMS
courses.title: Advanced Ophthalmology
courses.description: This elective course offers interested students the opportunityto deepen their knowledge in veterinary ophthalmology.  A basicknowledge in veterinary ophthalmology is required for successful participation in this course.

courses.subject: SAMS
courses.title: Small Animal Musculoskeletal Diseases
courses.description: Musculoskeletal diseases of dogs and cats are presented.

courses.subject: SAMS
courses.title: Small Animal Cardiology
courses.description: The recognition, physical examination, pathophysiology, diagnostic procedures, and management of cardiac disorders in dogs and cats.

courses.subject: SAMS
courses.title: Small Animal Digestive Diseases
courses.description: The diagnosis and management of the medical and surgical digestive disorders affecting dogs and cats.

courses.subject: SAMS
courses.title: Advanced Topics in Feline Medicine and Surgery
courses.description: Building on the first three years of the Doctor of Veterinary Medicine program, this course prepares students for clinical practice. Using system-based and integrated approaches, students advance their knowledge and skills in diagnosis, medicine, anesthesia, surgery, and professionalism, focusing on feline patients.
courses.course_objectives: Students will be able to apply core diagnostic, medical, anesthetic, and surgical knowledge to recognize and treat diseases and presenting complaints of cats. Students will be able to provide plans for preventative health and wellness care for cats.
courses.topical_outline: 1.	Course introduction 2.	Expansion on the systems-based approach to recognition, diagnosis, and treatment of clinical and clinicopathologic problems encountered in cats 3.	Further expansion on presenting problems in cats that do not belong to a defined body system 4.	Application of the principles of clinical pharmacology to cats

courses.subject: SAMS
courses.title: Advanced Topics in Canine Medicine and Surgery
courses.description: Building on the first three years of the Doctor of Veterinary Medicine program, this course prepares students for clinical practice. Using system-based and integrated approaches, students advance their knowledge and skills in diagnosis, medicine, anesthesia, surgery, and professionalism, focusing on canine patients.
courses.course_objectives: Students will be able to apply core diagnostic, medical, anesthetic, and surgical knowledge to recognize and treat diseases and presenting complaints of dogs. Students will be able to provide plans for preventative health and wellness care for dogs.
courses.topical_outline: 1.	Course introduction 2.	Expansion on the systems-based approach to recognition, diagnosis, and treatment of clinical and clinicopathologic problems encountered in dogs 3.	Further expansion on presenting problems in dogs that do not belong to a defined body system 4.	Application of the principles of clinical pharmacology to dogs

courses.subject: SAMS
courses.title: Advanced Clinical Reasoning in Domestic Small Animal Medicine
courses.description: This course focuses on diagnosing and managing complex domestic small animal cases. Through case discussions and advanced diagnostics, students refine clinical reasoning, develop treatment plans, and enhance client communication skills, preparing them to deliver high-quality care in real-world veterinary settings.
courses.course_objectives: For the cases discussed in the course, students will diagnose complex cases: demonstrate the ability to identify and diagnose complex medical conditions in small animals (including exotics/wildlife) using advanced diagnostic techniques. For the cases discussed in the course, students will develop treatment plans: formulate evidence-based and comprehensive treatment plans tailored to individual patient needs. For the cases discussed in the course, students will refine clinical reasoning: apply advanced clinical reasoning skills to evaluate diagnostic findings and adapt management strategies effectively. For the cases discussed in the course, students will enhance communication: improve client communication skills, including discussing diagnostic options, treatment plans, and prognoses clearly and empathetically. For the cases discussed in the course, students will prepare for clinical practice: integrate theoretical knowledge with practical skills to deliver high-quality, real-world veterinary care for small animal patients.
courses.topical_outline: 1.	Course introduction 2.	Expansion on the systems-based approach to recognition, diagnosis, and treatment of clinical and clinicopathologic problems affecting small animal species (including small exotics and wildlife) 3.	Expansion on presenting problems that do not belong to a defined body system 4.	Application of the principles of clinical pharmacology to small animal species
courses.prerequisiteText: Enrollment in the third year of the Doctor of Veterinary Medicine curriculum

courses.subject: SAMS
courses.title: Advanced Techniques in Small Animal Medicine and Surgery
courses.description: Building on the first three years of the Doctor of Veterinary Medicine program, this course prepares students for domestic small animal clinical practice. Students practice common techniques for small animal patients in a lab-based setting, including diagnostic, medical, anesthetic, and surgery skills.
courses.course_objectives: Students will be able to practice diagnostic, medical, anesthetic, and surgical skills common in small animal patients (including exotics and wildlife). Students will recognize limitations, adjust plan(s) to address unexpected complications, and identify when consultation or referral is warranted.

a. Splenectomy 6. GU laboratory
a. Male and female cat and dog urinary catheter
b. Dystocia
c. Cystotomy 7. Orthopedics laboratory
a. Bandaging lab 8. Dermatology 9. Ophthalmology 10. Neurology 11. Open wound management 12. Respiratory laboratory
a. ETW/TTW, tracheostomy 13. Anesthesia laboratory 14. Exotics/wildlife laboratory 15. Oncology laboratory
courses.prerequisiteText: Enrollment in the third year of the Doctor of Veterinary Medicine curriculum

courses.subject: SAMS
courses.title: Shelter Medicine and Companion Animal Population Health
courses.description: Students will learn foundational concepts in animal sheltering and companion animal population health to understand the critical role of veterinarians in protecting community animal health and welfare. This course will emphasize preventive healthcare protocols, behavioral health, enrichment, animal housing, population management, sanitation, outbreak response, community cat management, and spay/neuter techniques.
courses.course_objectives: By the end of this course, students should recognize different types of shelters with different missions, facilities, and resources. By the end of this course, students should be able to describe the role of animal shelters in society, including public safety and animal social services. By the end of this course, students should be able to demonstrate understanding and knowledge of pathophysiology, risk factors, clinical signs, diagnosis, and management of infectious diseases common in the shelter environment. By the end of this course, students should be able to outline strategies for managing populations of animals within the shelter and how to monitor key metrics including length of stay and capacity for care in order to improve outcomes and promote One Health. By the end of this course, students should be able to recognize methods, laws, guidelines, and management surrounding euthanasia and how to create a humane plan for a patient to provide euthanasia safely. By the end of this course, students should be able to discuss the importance of behavioral care and enrichment in the shelter and describe the relationship between stress and disease. By the end of this course, students should understand procedures and techniques in pediatric and high quality, high volume spay/neuter (HQHVSN) anesthesia, surgery, and analgesia. By the end of this course, students should be able to describe the veterinarian’s role in recognition and reporting of suspect animal abuse and perform basic steps in a forensic medical examination, including physical exam, evidence collection, photography, and documentation. By the end of this course, students should be able to assess the impact of housing and environment on animal health, behavior, and welfare. By the end of this course, students should understand current challenges in animal shelters and be familiar with innovative strategies to maximize welfare and protect the human-animal bond, including intake diversion programs, community cat management programs, and improving access to veterinary care and resources for underserved members of the community.
courses.topical_outline: 1. Introduction to Shelter Medicine and History of Animal Sheltering 2. Population Management 3. Facility Design and Housing 4. Sanitation 5. Behavioral Health and Enrichment 6. Preventive Healthcare for Companion Animal Populations 7. Public Health 8. Outbreak Investigation 9. Forensic Veterinary Medicine and Recognition of Animal Abuse 10. Disaster Response and Animal Hoarding 11. Infectious Respiratory Diseases 12. Euthanasia 13. Community Cat Management 14. High-Quality High-Volume Spay/Neuter (HQHVSN)
courses.prerequisiteText: Enrollment in Doctor of Veterinary Medicine curriculum

courses.title: Zoological Anesthesia
courses.description: To allow veterinary students to become more proficient in theanesthetic management of zoological species (e.g., exotic pets, wildlife, zoo, and aquatic).

courses.subject: SAMS
courses.title: Advanced Topics in Small Animal Emergency and Urgent Care
courses.description: Building on the first three years of the Doctor of Veterinary Medicine program, this course prepares students for clinical practice. Using system-based and integrated approaches, students advance their knowledge and skills in the diagnosis and treatment of emergency, urgent care, and trauma-related scenarios affecting small animal patients.
courses.course_objectives: Students will be able to apply core diagnostic, medical, anesthetic, surgical, and professional skills to recognize and treat common emergency, urgent, and trauma-related complaints of small animals. Students will be able to triage problems and address in order of importance. Irrespective of the species, body system(s) affected, or presenting clinical complaints, students will be able to collect patient information, synthesize, and prioritize problems to arrive at differential diagnosis(es). Students will be able to create and adjust diagnostic and therapeutic plans that present a spectrum of options. Students will recognize limitations, adjust plan(s) to address unexpected complications, and identify when consultation or referral is warranted.
courses.topical_outline: 1. Course introduction 2. Expansion on the systems-based approach to triage and stabilization of urgent/emergent and traumatic clinical and clinicopathologic problems affecting small animal species 3. Expansion on the systems-based approach to recognition, diagnosis, and treatment of urgent/emergency and traumatic clinical and clinicopathologic problems affecting small animal species 4. Application of the principles of clinical pharmacology to small animal species

courses.subject: SAMS
courses.title: Small Animal Clinical Anesthesia
courses.description: Clinical training in small animal anesthesiology.  Students willexamine, evaluate, and provide anesthesia and analgesia forclinical patients.  Practical skills and knowledge ofproblem-solving techniques will be emphasized.
courses.prerequisiteText: Must be a fourth year veterinary student | Pre or

courses.subject: SAMS
courses.title: Academic Veterinary Medicine Rotation
courses.description: Clinical rotation designed to expose the veterinary student to academia.  The student will learn what an academic veterinarian does, what roles they fulfill, what tasks they engage in, and how the professional life of academia is structured.  Students will gain an insight into teaching, research, and service through this rotation.

courses.subject: SAMS
courses.title: Zoological Medicine (Exotic Pets, Wildlife, and Zoo)
courses.description: Exposure to exotic pets, wildlife, aviculture, and zoo animal medicine.  Focus on the medical and surgical problems of exotic pets (with some wildlife and zoo animal medicine).  Animals seen will primarily be first opinion and referrals. There will also be regular visits to an aviary and local zoo/nature reserve.

courses.subject: SAMS
courses.title: Small Animal Vet: Bees
courses.description: An in-depth overview of the apiary industry in Georgia. Topics to be covered range from the individual difference of different breeds of bees to the management of a large apiary. Students will work on live beehives and learn how to examine a hive and individual bees for diseases. Students will learn how bees are currently being used in research. Course will include multiple field trips to a variety of institutions and locations which are drivers of the apiary industry in Georgia.
courses.prerequisiteText: Student has to be an active member of the Vet Bee Club and priority is given to zoo med track students

courses.subject: SAMS
courses.title: Small Animal Orthopedic Surgery
courses.description: This elective senior clinical rotation provides students with the opportunity to be an integral part of the initial examination, diagnostic work-up, surgical procedures, and postoperative care involved with referral orthopedic cases.
courses.prerequisiteText: Must be a fourth-year veterinary student

courses.subject: SAMS
courses.title: Small Animal Dermatology Clinical Rotation
courses.description: Provides clinical experience in the examination, work-up,diagnosis, and management of dogs and cats with skin diseases.Performance of dermatologic consultations for the large animaland exotic services.
courses.prerequisiteText: Must be a fourth year veterinary student

courses.subject: SAMS
courses.title: Small Animal Oncology Clinical Rotation
courses.description: Provides clinical experience in the diagnosis, staging, and treatment of canine and feline patients with cancer.

courses.subject: SAMS
courses.title: Small Animal General Surgery
courses.description: Provides students with the opportunity to be an integral part of the initial examination, diagnostic work-up, surgical procedures, and postoperative care involved with referral soft tissuesurgical cases.
courses.prerequisiteText: Must be a fourth year veterinary student

courses.subject: SAMS
courses.title: Small Animal Cardiology Rotation
courses.description: Instruction in the recognition, evaluation, and treatment ofcardiac disorders of the dog and cat.  Emphasis is onauscultation, electrocardiography, echocardiography, diagnosis,and therapy.
courses.prerequisiteText: Must be a fourth year veterinary student

courses.subject: SAMS
courses.title: Small Animal Ophthalmology
courses.description: Development of students' skills in ophthalmolgy so that studentscan understand common ocular diseases in animals as they arepresented to a small or large animal practitioner, requiringcorrect diagnosis, appropriate treatment and, if necessary,referral of the case.
courses.prerequisiteText: Must be a fourth year veterinary student

courses.subject: SAMS
courses.title: Small Animal Clinical Neurology/Neurosurgery
courses.description: This is a clinical rotation.  Provides students with a strongfoundation in performing the neurological exam and understandinghow it establishes an accurate neuroanatomic diagnosis.
courses.prerequisiteText: Must be fourth year veterinary student

courses.subject: SAMS
courses.title: Small Animal Community Practice
courses.description: Instruction in routine preventative care for dogs and cats, theproblem-oriented approach to medical problems commonly seen indogs and cats, and how to anesthetize and perform surgicalprocedures on healthy animals (neutering, variohysterectomy,small cutaneous mass removal, and routine dentistry).
courses.prerequisiteText: Must be a fourth year veterinary student

courses.subject: SAMS
courses.title: Small Animal Internal Medicine
courses.description: This clinical rotation focuses on internal medicine problems of dogs and cats.
courses.prerequisiteText: Must be fourth year veterinary student

courses.subject: SAMS
courses.title: Emergency and Critical Care
courses.description: Clinical problem solving in daytime emergency, critical care,basic and advanced monitoring, diagnostic procedures, andtreatment. Students will have primary case responsibility forcritical patients in ICU and assist with triage, admission, andworkup of emergency cases.
courses.prerequisiteText: Must be fourth year veterinary student | Pre or

courses.subject: SAMS
courses.title: Small Animal Internship
courses.description: Clinical training for the graduate veterinarian desiring in-depth knowledge and skills relative to the diagnosis and treatment of small animal medical and surgical disorders.
courses.prerequisiteText: DVM degree and permission of department

courses.subject: SAMS
courses.title: Small Animal Residency I
courses.description: Clinical training during year one of a residency for graduate veterinarians desiring specialization in internal medicine, surgery, ophthalmology, dermatology, or other clinical specialties.
courses.prerequisiteText: DVM degree and permission of department

courses.subject: SAMS
courses.title: Small Animal Residency II
courses.description: Clinical training during year two of the residency in internal medicine, surgery, ophthalmology, dermatology, or other clinical specialty.

courses.subject: SAMS
courses.title: Small Animal Residency III
courses.description: Clinical training during year three of the clinical residency in internal medicine, surgery, ophthalmology, dermatology, or other clinical specialty.

courses.subject: SAMS
courses.title: Small Animal Residency IV
courses.description: Clinical training during year four of a residency program in internal medicine, surgery, ophthalmology, dermatology, or other clinical specialty.

courses.subject: SAMS
courses.title: Seminar in Small Animal Medicine and Surgery
courses.description: This course is a seminar series presented by the student under the direction of a faculty member.  The seminar can consist of a literature review or a review of clinical cases. After presentation, the group has questions and discussion.

courses.subject: SAMS
courses.title: Studies in Clinical Small Animal Medicine
courses.description: Specific approved problems in clinical small animal medicine and/or surgery.

courses.subject: SAMS
courses.title: Special Problems
courses.description: Problems defined by a faculty member with the student with approval of the department head.  These are usually focused studies or projects by veterinarians entered in a clinical residency program.

courses.subject: SAMS
courses.title: Personal and Professional Development for the Graduate Student
courses.description: An introduction to the personal and professional competencies required of the veterinary specialist. Topics will include, but not be limited to, communication skills, financial planning strategies, conflict resolution styles, teaching skills, contract negotiation, interview skills, and discussion of medical errors. This course will provide an interactive forum for learning.

courses.subject: SAMS
courses.title: Zoological Medicine Residency I
courses.description: Direction of students by faculty members as they receive cases side-by-side in the Zoological Medicine Service of the Veterinary Teaching Hospital. Daily case rounds are conducted to provide didactic instruction on clinical topics and case management. In addition, visits to local zoological institutions and field veterinary medicine are included.

courses.subject: SAMS
courses.title: Zoological Medicine Residency II
courses.description: Residents are trained by adjunct faculty members as they receive cases side-by-side in the veterinary department at Zoo Atlanta. Daily case rounds are conducted to provide didactic instruction on clinical topics and case management. Students conduct a research project and publish from that project.

courses.subject: SAMS
courses.title: Zoological Medicine Residency III
courses.description: Resident students are trained by adjunct faculty members as they receive cases side-by-side in the veterinary department at The Georgia Aquarium. Daily case rounds are conducted to provide didactic instruction on clinical topics and case management.

courses.subject: SAMS
courses.title: Seminar in Medicine and Surgery
courses.description: Graduate students and staff members will regularly participate in review and discussion of current research findings and methodology concerning medical and surgical disorders of animals.
courses.prerequisiteText: (DVM degree or equivalent degree) and permission of department

courses.subject: SAMS
courses.title: Advanced Seminars in Clinical Veterinary Medicine
courses.description: Weekly seminar course for graduate students in the College ofVeterinary Medicine to discuss clinical physiology andpathophysiology at an advanced level.

courses.subject: SAMS
courses.title: Neurosurgery
courses.description: Neurological surgery at an advanced level.

courses.subject: SAMS
courses.title: Advanced Small Animal Internal Medicine
courses.description: Seminar course for graduate students in the College of Veterinary Medicine to discuss physiology, pharmacology, and disease-related information (e.g., pathophysiology, clinical pathology, diagnosis, treatment, prognosis, and prevention).

courses.subject: SAMS
courses.title: Advanced Zoological Medicine: Clinical Management and Advanced Procedures
courses.description: Course focuses on advanced zoological medicine at the post-residency level. Utilizing the advanced facilities and equipment available within the teaching hospital, the student will be trained to manage an academic zoological medicine service and perform advanced medical, surgical, and endoscopic procedures.

courses.subject: SCAN
courses.title: Elementary Scandinavian Language and Culture I
courses.description: Fundamentals of grammar, conversation, pronunciation, reading,and writing of one of the Scandinavian languages, together withan introduction to the culture of the people in question.

courses.subject: SCAN
courses.title: Elementary Scandinavian Language and Culture II
courses.description: A continuation of Elementary Scandinavian Language and Culture I.

courses.title: Faculty-Mentored Undergraduate Research I
courses.description: Faculty-supervised independent or collaborative inquiry into fundamental and applied problems within a discipline that requires students to gather, analyze, synthesize, and interpret data and to present results in writing and other relevant communication formats.

courses.subject: SEMI
courses.title: Studies in Semitic Linguistics
courses.description: Introduction to northwest Semitic languages, which may includePhoenician, Punic, and inscriptional ancient Hebrew, as well asto the principles of Semitic epigraphy.
courses.offeredText: Not offered on a regular basis.

courses.subject: SEMI
courses.title: Studies in Semitic Linguistics II
courses.description: Introduction to a northwest Semitic language, such as Aramaic,Syriac, Ugaritic, Amorite, or "Canaanite" as reflected in the Amarna letters and inscriptions.
courses.prerequisiteText: HEBR 2003 or HEBR 4000 or SEMI 4001/6001 or permission of department

courses.subject: SEMI
courses.title: Akkadian, The Babble in Babylon
courses.description: A survey of Akkadian grammar, permitting readings from Mesopotamian literature, such as the Gilgamesh Epic and the Code of Hammurabi.  After a semester, students are prepared to read creation stories, imperial records from Assyria and Babylon, and manuals of astronomy, medicine and witchcraft, to explore a universe of rediscovered thought.
courses.offeredText: Not offered on a regular basis.

courses.subject: SEMI
courses.title: Ancient Semitic Inscriptions
courses.description: Readings in a body of ancient Semitic inscriptions, whether royal (annals, monuments, correspondence, treaties) or widespread (epitaphs, offerings, contracts, myths).  The selection varies from semester to semester and may focus on a language, a coherent corpus, or a theme, depending on interest.  Students will be directed to appropriate lexicons and grammars for the task.
courses.offeredText: Not offered on a regular basis.

courses.subject: SEMI
courses.title: Written Languages of Early Empires
courses.description: Introduction to one of the written languages from Old World Bronze Age empires, for example, hieroglyphic Egyptian, Sumerian, or Hittite. Texts reflect the conduct of administration, political relations, propaganda, and religion. Study of their grammar affords primary access both to the languages as such and to these ancient cultures.
courses.offeredText: Not offered on a regular basis.

courses.subject: SLAV(LING)
courses.title: Introduction to Slavic Linguistics
courses.description: An overview of the Slavic family of languages, aspects of their historical development, and characteristics of their modern linguistic systems. Selected topics in the phonology, morphology, syntax, and sociolinguistics of individual Slavic languages will be addressed. No prior knowledge of any Slavic language is required. All readings and discussions will be in English.

courses.subject: SLAV
courses.title: Elementary Slavic Language and Culture I
courses.description: Fundamentals of grammar, conversation, pronunciation, reading, and writing of a Slavic language other than Russian, together with an introduction to the culture of the people in question. This course cannot be used in partial fulfillment of the foreign language requirement in the core curriculum.

courses.subject: SLAV
courses.title: Elementary Slavic Language and Culture II
courses.description: A continuation of Elementary Slavic Language and Culture I.

courses.subject: SLAV
courses.title: Slavic Folklore
courses.description: Slavic folklore and belief systems in different historicalperiods and their representation and adaptation in historical accounts, legends, customs, fairy tales, literature, film, and art. No background knowledge required. All readings and discussions are in English.
courses.course_objectives: By the end of this course students should be able to identify and interpret key components of Slavic folk culture and beliefs through the study of scholarly texts, historical accounts, and examples of verbal folklore. By the end of this course students should be able to compare and contrast representations and adaptations of folklore in various media, including literature, film, art, and music. By the end of this course students should be able to decipher symbolic meanings of images from Slavic folklore and identify culture-specific features of folkloric genres. By the end of this course students should be able to examine how folklore is transmitted across generations in Slavic regions and assess its role in shaping societal values and identities. By the end of this course students should be able to construct informed, well-researched oral and written statements that effectively communicate analysis of Slavic folklore to a variety of audiences.
courses.topical_outline:
Following is a representative outline of topics and possible readings. The actual choice and sequencing of materials may vary.

Introduction to basic terminology and concepts (Natalie Kononenko, Slavic Folklore)

Who are the Slavs? Interplay of culture, religion and folklore (Linda Ivanits, Russian Folk Belief)

Ancient Slavic belief systems: Hierarchy of pagan gods (Jan Machal, Slavic Mythology)

Ancient Slavic belief systems: Lower mythology (Ivanits)

The Slavic family: Values and customs (Ivanits)

Slavic rituals: Birth, marriage, and death (Kononenko)

Slavic holidays: Ceremonies and songs (Kononenko)

Slavic taboos (Kononenko)

Slavic riddles and proverbs (Kononenko)

Magic acts and magic words (Ivanits; W. F. Ryan, The Bathhouse at Midnight: An Historical Survey of Magic and Divination in Russia)

East European vampires (Felix J. Oinas, East European Vampires)

The fairy tale: Heroes and villains (Vladimir Propp, Morphology of the Folktale; Aleksandr Afanasyev, Russian Fairy Tales)

Folk epics (William Bascom, Forms of Folklore: Prose Narrative;
Vasa D. Mihailovic, Songs of the Serbian People: From the Collections of Vuk Karadzic; Skaftymov, "The Structure of the Byliny"; various byliny - "Svyatogor", Ilya Muromets", and "Kalinin Tsar")

Children's folklore (Halina Weiss, Draznilkas: Russian
Children's Taunts)

Slavic literature and folklore (Nikolai Gogol, Viy)

Folklore in cinema (Films: Shadows of Forgotten Ancestors [Paradjanov, 1964], Night Watch [Bekmambetov, 2004])

Folklore in classical music (Rimsky-Korsakov, Kitezh; Stravinsky, Firebird, Borodin, Prince Igor)

Folklore in art (palekh, khokhloma, Ivan Bilibin, Viktor Vasnetsov, Mikhail Vrubel)

courses.subject: SLAV
courses.title: The Balkans: Culture, Conflict, and the Construction of Identity (Honors)
courses.description: The peoples and cultures of the Balkans from the Byzantine period to the present, with a focus on the social, historical, and cultural factors that have played a role both in the formation of ethnic/national identity within the region and in the perceptions of outsiders.

courses.subject: SLAV
courses.title: Literature and Moral Life: The Ethics of Fiction and Non-Fiction in East European Literature
courses.description: Exploration of the connection between ethics and literature and how narrative influences the formation of our ethical character, based on key theory, fiction, and non-fiction texts from East European literature. Investigation of the relationship between authors and readers and differences between fiction and non-fiction. All readings and discussions in English.
courses.offeredText: Not offered on a regular basis.

courses.subject: SLAV
courses.title: Kind of Human: Animals, Children, and Robots in Russian and East European Literature and Art
courses.description: The representation of non-human and children’s lives in Russian and East European literatures. Articulation of the human through comparison with lives considered less than human. Philosophy and ethics of non-human subjectivity. Survey of a wide range of sources, including literature, visual art, music, film, philosophical treatises. All readings in English.

courses.subject: SLAV
courses.title: Special Topics
courses.description: Seminar focusing on specific topics in Slavic languages,literatures, or cultures.

courses.subject: SOCI(AFAM)(WMST)
courses.title: Colorism and Hairism in Communities of Color
courses.description: We will use empirical data to analyze how inter- and intra-racial discrimination based on skin color and hairstyles are forms of discrimination apparent in virtually every social institution, such as marriage rates, media, imprisonment, holding political office, educational attainment, wages, and more.
courses.course_objectives: Students will understand how colorism and hairism impact communities of color. Students will learn the history and rationale behind colorism and hairism. Students will gain knowledge of contemporary research on skin tone, colorism, and hairism. Students will learn how to fight against colorism and hairism. Students will consider and engage with different viewpoints from voices and groups of people in the U.S. and around the world to gain knowledge of contemporary research on skin tone, colorism, and hairism by reading and analyzing writings.
courses.topical_outline: 1. History of colorism and hairism 2. Legality of colorism and hairism 3. Colorism and hairism in the criminal justice system 4. Colorism and hairism in politics 5. Colorism x hairism x gender and marriage 6. Colorism x hairism x gender in the media 7. Chemically altering skin and hair 8. Colorism x hairism x body type 9. Colorism and hairism in sports 10. Colorism and hairism on socioeconomic status

courses.subject: SOCI(AFAM)
courses.title: African American Society
courses.description: The class, status, and power relations of African Americans as part of both the United States social structure and the African diaspora.
courses.offeredText: Not offered on a regular basis.

courses.subject: SOCI(AFAM)
courses.title: Race and Ethnicity in America
courses.description: The causes and consequences of race and ethnic discrimination in America, with a focus on ethnic competition and conflict.
courses.course_objectives: Students will develop one’s own informed perspective on American racial problems. Students will introduce the ways that sociologists deal with race, ethnicity, race relations and racism. Students will introduce students to the history, cultures and issues faced by some of the racial and ethnic groups in the U.S. Students will learn more about these groups and consider what their experiences reveal with respect to the challenges racial and ethnic formations present for conventional understandings of citizenship, group membership and social justice. Students will consider race both as a source of identity and social differentiation as well as a system of privilege, power, and inequality affecting everyone in the society in different ways.

1.Theoretical Approaches: The Problematic of Race and Ethnic Formations in Post-Civil Rights America
2.Constructionist Approaches to US Race Relations

courses.subject: SOCI(AFAM)
courses.title: Race, Technology, and the Body
courses.description: This course uses sociological approaches and popular films to examine theories and concepts relating to race, technology, and the body. Topics include beauty, reproduction, work, labor, sports, surveillance, policing, and new media.

courses.subject: SOCI(AFAM)
courses.title: History of Race, Crime, and Justice in the United States
courses.description: Course uses a sociological approach to examine the intersection of race and the criminal legal system in the United States from a historical perspective. Topics include criminal law, policing, sentencing, incarceration, and capital punishment in the U.S. between the 17th and 21st centuries.
courses.course_objectives: Students will develop a keen understanding of the historical relationship between race, inequality, and the American criminal legal system. Students will explore these topics further by critically evaluating how historical and contemporary social phenomena have shaped and continue to influence the system. Students will communicate about course theories, concepts, and themes using written and oral forms.
courses.topical_outline: 1. The Colonial Period 2. The Early Republic 3. The Antebellum Period 4. The Civil War and Reconstruction 5. The Jim Crow Era 6. The Rise of Mass Incarceration 7. The Era of Mass Incarceration to the Present
courses.prerequisiteText: SOCI 1101 or SOCI 1101E or SOCI 1101H or SOCI 2600 or permission of department

courses.subject: SOCI(AFAM)
courses.title: Global Perspectives on Racism and Sexism
courses.description: Race and gender relations and discrimination around the globe; the origins and practice of race and gender domination and empowerment in the Americas, Africa, Asia, Europe, the Middle East, and the Pacific Rim.
courses.prerequisiteText: SOCI 1101 or SOCI 1101H or SOCI 2600 or permission of department

courses.subject: SOCI(AFAM)
courses.title: Race and Culture
courses.description: Evolution of cultures among racial groups as part of, and in contrast to, Western civilization.  Particular attention is given to the ways race and culture intersect to provide styles, practices, and patterns of living for individuals in contemporary society.
courses.prerequisiteText: SOCI 1101 or SOCI 1101H or SOCI 2600 or permission of department
courses.offeredText: Not offered on a regular basis.

courses.subject: SOCI(AFAM)

courses.description: Special topics in race and ethnicity for advanced undergraduates.
courses.prerequisiteText: SOCI 1101 or SOCI 1101H or SOCI 2600 or permission of department
courses.offeredText: Not offered on a regular basis.

courses.subject: SOCI(AFAM)
courses.title: Health Among Black Americans
courses.description: A within ethnoracial group approach to illuminate how social factors contribute to health among self-identified Blacks in the United States. The course will utilize theory and evidence from sociology, biodemography, epidemiology, and psychology to introduce students to health disparities research among aging Blacks in the United States.

courses.subject: SOCI(AFAM)
courses.title: Theories of Race and Ethnicity in the U.S.
courses.description: Analysis of classical and contemporary theories that have been developed specifically to understand race and ethnicity in the United States.

courses.subject: SOCI(AFAM)
courses.title: Sociology of Race and Ethnicity
courses.description: The relationships of racial and ethnic groups with each other and with social institutions and processes.

courses.title: Environmental Sociology
courses.description: The social causes and consequences of resource scarcity and environmental depletion.  Topics include world population growth, pollution, depletion of energy sources, species extinction, and environmental movements.

courses.subject: SOCI(ANTH)
courses.title: Sociopolitical Ecology
courses.description: The relationship between humans and the environment; ecological and social theories about environmental policies and problems.

courses.subject: SOCI(INTL)
courses.title: Italian Society
courses.description: Examination of major changes affecting Italian society over the past century, including unification, migration, economic development, globalization, and modernization. Consideration of how these changes influence how Italians live and work.

courses.subject: SOCI(INTL)
courses.title: Globalization and Work
courses.description: The impact of globalization (the spread of economic policies andpractices across national boundaries) on work, jobs, and careersin different countries.
courses.prerequisiteText: SOCI 3750 or SOCI 3850 or SOCI 3950 or INTL 3200 or INTL 3300 or permission of department
courses.offeredText: Not offered on a regular basis.

courses.subject: SOCI(INTL)
courses.title: Globalization and Work
courses.description: The impact of globalization (the spread of economic policies andpractices across national boundaries) on businesses, jobs, andworkers in different countries.
courses.prerequisiteText: SOCI 3750 or SOCI 3850 or SOCI 3950 or INTL 3200 or INTL 3300 or permission of department

courses.subject: SOCI(INTL)
courses.title: South African Society
courses.description: Social problems and issues in post-apartheid South Africa and how these have been addressed by government and civil society.
courses.prerequisiteText: SOCI 1101 or SOCI 1101H or SOCI 2600 or INTL 1100 or INTL 1100H or permission of department

courses.subject: SOCI(INTL)
courses.title: Global Terrorism
courses.description: Terrorism and its control from a sociological perspective.  Topics include the definition of terrorism, history and contemporary patterns of terrorism, reasons for joining terrorist groups, social conditions under which terrorist violence occurs, whether terrorism works, and the effectiveness of counterterrorist strategies.
courses.course_objectives: Students will be expected to understand why definitions of terrorism are so controversial, how terrorism has evolved as one type of political violence, where across the globe terrorism is most prevalent, which organizations are most heavily involved in terrorist attacks, the links between terrorist and criminal organizations, why people become terrorists, what effects terrorism has, including its effects on terrorists’ strategic goals, which broad strategies are most effective in countering terrorism, and how terrorism might evolve in the future. Students will demonstrate their mastery of the course content in written work that is appropriate for an academic context. Students will demonstrate their mastery of the course content in speech that is appropriate for an academic context.
courses.topical_outline: 1. Defining “terrorism” 2. History of terrorism 3. Contemporary patterns of terrorism 4. Terrorist organizations 5. Terrorism and crime 6. Becoming a terrorist 7. Causes of terrorist violence 8. Does terrorism work? 9. Countering terrorism 10. The future of terrorism
courses.prerequisiteText: SOCI 1101 or SOCI 1101H or permission of department

courses.subject: SOCI(LACS)(POLS)
courses.title: Social Policy Storytelling: In and Around Athens
courses.description: Examination of local and national politics through the lived experience of local Athens area residents, social policymaking processes, and the role of research and storytelling for policy. Students will conduct fieldwork and create policy-relevant digital stories. Students will present their findings to community stakeholders in the Athens area.

courses.subject: SOCI(LACS)
courses.title: Sociology of Latin America
courses.description: Exploration of the social history and contemporary questions ofrace, class, gender, and nation in Latin America. Case studiesdrawn from throughout the region. Topics may includesocioeconomic development, poverty and inequality, socialmovements, institutions, and change.  Latin America intransnational context.
courses.prerequisiteText: SOCI 1101 or SOCI 1101H or SOCI 2600 or permission of department
courses.offeredText: Not offered on a regular basis.

courses.subject: SOCI(NAMS)
courses.title: Native American Social Politics
courses.description: An overview of social and political issues confronted by Native American nations in the contemporary U.S. The primary objectives of the course include recognizing the diversity of experiences among Native American nations and understanding and applying central analytical frames to explain Native American and indigenous realities.

courses.prerequisiteText: SOCI 1101 or SOCI 1101H or permission of department

courses.subject: SOCI(WMST)
courses.title: Seminar in Global Perspectives on Gender

courses.subject: SOCI
courses.title: Introductory Sociology
courses.description: Basic concepts, theoretical approaches, and methods of sociology, with an emphasis on culture, socialization, social organizations, and major institutions.
courses.course_objectives: Students will be able to summarize and critique a piece of sociological research. Students will be able to examine and articulate the complex relationship between structure, culture, and interaction. Students will be able to illustrate the methods of studying social groups and society. Students will compare, contrast, and categorize types of common data collection methods in sociology. Students will be able to articulate why and how each method could be useful to collect sociological data. Students will be able to assess the validity of research findings through a variety of forms, such as charts, figures, and text. Students will be able to infer differences between qualitative and quantitative research findings and assess their validity and reliability. Students will be able to assess the logic and assumptions of major sociological theories. Students will be able to understand, summarize, and express the centrality and significance of research, what research is and what it involves, in the context of a research university such as the University of Georgia where one studies. Students will be able to apply sociological ways of viewing the world; and to understand sociology’s configuration within the social sciences; and articulate how the social sciences in turn fit into the broader organization of knowledge in universities. Students will evaluate how various social locations such as class, gender, race, and deviance are continually influencing their own lives and outcomes as well as people from different cultures or geographical locations than their own. Students will be able to examine the major macro-level dimensions of social stratification and the micro-level processes through which stratification manifests. Students will be able to relate their own experiences with contrasting experiences through classroom discussions, lectures, readings, experiential activities, and research papers. Students will analyze how events and relationships in their own social lives are shaped and constrained by the larger social structure, how individuals create and transform social structures, and how social structures interact with one another.
courses.topical_outline:
The following topics may be covered in this course:
1. The Sociological Perspective
2. Methods of Sociology
3. Culture and Social Structure
4. Socialization and Social Interaction
5. Gender
6. Crime and Deviance
7. Groups, Organizations, and Work
8. Childhood, Families, and Marriage
9. Stratification and Social Class
10. Education and Schooling
11. Race and Ethnicity
12. Age and Aging
13. Religion
14. Population and Urbanization
15. Technology and Environment
16. Social Movements and Collective Action
17. The Political Institution
18. Globalization and the Capitalist World System

courses.subject: SOCI
courses.title: Challenges Facing College Students
courses.description: Key topics that affect the lives of college students. The topics reflect dynamics of the modern university in interaction with broader society. The topics range from alcohol and drug use, mental health, gender and race relations, to college costs, student debt, and the transition from college to work.

courses.subject: SOCI
courses.title: Class, Status, and Power
courses.description: Modern social status systems, with a focus on the United States. The use of prestige, occupational skills, and economic assets to create classes; the impact of class on life chances; and the interaction of class with race, gender, and belief systems to shape individual earnings, wealth, and power.

courses.subject: SOCI
courses.title: Deviance and Social Control
courses.description: The nature, extent, and correlates of deviance and its control by social institutions and agencies; theories of deviance and societal reactions to deviance.

courses.subject: SOCI
courses.title: Social Problems
courses.description: The causes, consequences, and social construction of American social problems, including poverty, crime and delinquency, environmental degradation, and race and ethnic relations.
courses.offeredText: Not offered on a regular basis.

courses.subject: SOCI
courses.title: Social Interaction
courses.description: The relationship between individuals and groups, as it shapes the development of social competence, personality, self-concept, motivation, attitudes and cognition.

courses.subject: SOCI
courses.title: Sociology in Film
courses.description: Popular Hollywood films as they illustrate culture, social class, race, gender, identity, and other sociological concepts.  The ideological and utopian aspects of film are emphasized.
courses.course_objectives: Students will use film and other texts to analyze contemporary (and past) American cultures and subcultures in order to better understand the ways in which forces of social reproduction and social transformation continually operate to make and remake human societies. Students will analyze the Hollywood film industry in terms of its organizational structure (production, financing, advertising, and distribution) and its role in contemporary global culture. Students will be able to conceptualize and describe movies not simply as a form of entertainment but as a powerful cultural force that contains within it many of the themes and contradictions that are part of the larger society. Students will be asked to demonstrate their mastery of the course content in written work that is appropriate for an academic context. Students will be asked to demonstrate their mastery of the course content in speech that is appropriate for an academic context.
courses.topical_outline:
1. How do sociologists look at film?
a. The cultural diamond
b. Ideological and utopian themes
c. Political issues: Can movies have be political even when they’re not about politics?

2. The Structure of the Film Industry
a. Movie Distribution Works
b. The Art of the Deal
c. How Theaters Get A Movie
d. The Need for Concessions
e. First Run vs. Second Run

3. Film criticism and critics

4. Social Class in the Movies

5. Ethnicity, assimilation, and nostalgia

6. Gender Relations and romance in the movies and in life

7. Blacks, whites, conflict, and romance

8. Alienation, Autonomy, and the Self

9. The State and Social Conflict
courses.prerequisiteText: SOCI 1101 or SOCI 1101H or SOCI 2600 or permission of department

courses.title: Sociology of Culture
courses.description: Recent trends in American culture, focusing on traditions, practices, and products, including books, music, and film.  Organizing themes are culture as both a source of social integration and an arena of strife, and the reciprocal effects of culture and human agency.

courses.offeredText: Not offered on a regular basis.

courses.subject: SOCI
courses.title: Lives in Time and Place
courses.description: Examines the sociological study of lives: socialization over the life span, the stratification of lives, cross-cultural comparisons of aging and human development, family patterns across time, careers in crime, health across life, religious expression in lives, and lifetime consequences of education.
courses.course_objectives:
Students will develop a comprehensive understanding of this sociological specialty, including characteristic modes of inquiry, key arguments and debates, and prevailing societal trends. Students will be expected to engage themselves in the scholarly practice of reading, criticism, and argumentation. Students will complete a term research project in which they collect and analyze two life histories based on comparing and contrasting original interview data. The research component places a special emphasis on analysis, evidence, and argument to direct and develop the creative, analytical, and interpretive skills of research. Students will be asked to demonstrate their mastery of the course content in written work that is appropriate for an
academic context. Students will be asked to demonstrate their mastery of the course content in speech that is appropriate for an academic
context.
courses.topical_outline: 1. Introduction 2. Development of the Life Course as a Field of Sociological Inquiry 3. Life Phases 4. Methods of Life Course Research 5. Methodological Considerations in Life Course Research 6. Cultural Constructions of the Life Course 7. Age Norms 8. Cross-Cultural Comparisons of Age and Aging 9. Aging across the Life Span: Stratification 10. Childhood and the Life Course 11. The Family and the Life Course 12. Deviance and the Life Course 13. Health and the Life Course 14. Education and the Life Course 15. Research Projects in Life Course Analysis
courses.prerequisiteText: SOCI 1101 or SOCI 1101H or SOCI 2600 or permission of department

courses.subject: SOCI
courses.title: Sociology of Religion
courses.description: The relationship between social phenomena and religiouspractices. Topics include classic perspectives on religion; secularization; religious resurgence; religion and health; religion, race and ethnicity; religion and politics; religion and social mobilization; religion and immigration; globalization and religion.
courses.prerequisiteText: SOCI 1101 or SOCI 1101H or SOCI 2600 or permission of department
courses.offeredText: Not offered on a regular basis.

courses.title: Sociology of Education
courses.description: Overview of teachers and teaching of students and learning. Focuses on the structure and culture of schools; socialization; stratification; gender and schooling; as well as special problems areas as reflected in society. Materials based on all levels of schooling, but emphasis is on higher education.

courses.subject: SOCI
courses.title: Juvenile Delinquency
courses.description: The juvenile justice system, including the measurement of delinquency, contexts of adolescent socialization, and techniques of evaluation research.
courses.course_objectives: Students will understand Supreme Court rulings and technical aspects of the juvenile court that separate it from the adult criminal court. Students will understand official statistics, self-report data, and victimization data in trying to grapple with trends in juvenile misconduct. Students will understand the theories of delinquency ranging from the biological to the sociological. Students will understand the treatment and prevention of delinquency with an emphasis on institutionalization and probation. Students will understand the evaluation of treatment programs currently being used by the juvenile courts. Students will be asked to demonstrate their mastery of the course content in written work that is appropriate for an academic context. Students will be asked to demonstrate their mastery of the course content in speech that is appropriate for an academic context.

courses.title: Youth Subcultures
courses.description: Theoretical and empirical work on youth subcultures in terms of deviance, gender, identity, media, societal reaction, and style. Various subcultures considered: Cybercultures, Deadheads, Gay/Lesbian, Goth, Hackers, Motorcyclists, Punk/Hardcore, Riot Girls, Skinheads, and Straightedgers.
courses.course_objectives: Students will learn to define the key terms and concepts related to the sociology of deviance. Students will understand the connections between macro-level subculture and micro-level individual identity formation. Students will understand truths around youth subcultures and inaccurate myths related to them. Students will learn to apply sociological theory to youth subcultures. Students will understand intersectionality as a theory, methodological framework, and concept.
courses.topical_outline: 1. Overview of Sociology of Deviance 2. Theories and perspectives to explain, understand, critique, and/or analyze deviance and normalcy 3. History of Subcultural Research: American Chicago School vs University of Birmingham's Centre for Contemporary Cultural Studies 4. Defining a subculture: core components 5. Intersectionality and Identity Formation 6. Witches, Metalheads, Goths, and Gangs 7. Virginity Pledgers, Hackers/Gamers, Hip Hop Heads, and Hippies 8. Recent Subcultures

courses.title: Youth Subcultures in Global Perspective
courses.description: A cross-national perspective to understand youths’ attraction to deviance, through a focus on youth subcultures that emerged in the United Kingdom. Course begins with an overview of deviance, followed by a focus on youth who participate in subcultures, and how youth identity forms within these groups.

courses.subject: SOCI
courses.title: Medical Sociology
courses.description: An exploration of topics such as the social sources of illness, the social distribution of illness and health conditions, the social meanings of illness, and the increasing use of medical frameworks to understand and cope with what used to be considered non-medical, everyday experiences.
courses.course_objectives:
By the end of this course, students will understand the role that sociological factors play in the definition and treatment of illness and disease. By the end of this course, students will be able to demonstrate their mastery of the course content in written
work that is appropriate for an academic context. By the end of this course, students will be able to demonstrate their mastery of the course content in speech
that is appropriate for an academic context. By the end of this course, students will analyze and explore how the health and well-being of people are connected and interdependent in our social networks, communities, countries, and globally.

courses.title: Sociology of Rural Health
courses.description: A sociological consideration of rural health in the contemporary United States and Georgia. Attention is paid to both the provision of health care, such as the challenges facing health care facilities and the recruitment and retention of healthcare providers, and the distinctive health risks, conditions, and needs of rural populations.

courses.subject: SOCI
courses.title: Sociology of Health Care
courses.description: Topics include doctor-patient interactions; complementary and alternative medicine; the training and work of physicians; the work of allied health fields (e.g., nurses); hospitals, assisted living facilities, and nursing homes; the problem of pricing health care and the role of markets; and efforts to reform health care in the United States.
courses.course_objectives: Students will understand the role that sociological factors play in shaping health care in the United States and other countries. Students will understand how to engage in the scholarly practices of reading, focused discussion, and writing. Mandatory writing projects place special emphasis on analysis, evidence, and argument in order to further develop the creative, analytical, and interpretive skills of students. Students will be able to demonstrate their mastery of the course content in written work that is appropriate for an academic context. Students will be able to demonstrate their mastery of the course content in speech that is appropriate for an academic context.

courses.title: Development of Sociological Theory
courses.description: Pivotal sociological theorists from classic theorists such as Marx, Weber, and Durkheim to the present.
courses.course_objectives: Students will review the work of classic sociological theorists (e.g., Marx, Weber, and Durkheim) and contemporary theorists through the use of original texts. Students will review the derivation and history of many concepts, discourses, and dilemmas that are still current in social scientific debate. Students will analyze social problems and assimilate sociological research. Students will be asked to demonstrate their mastery of the course content in written work that is appropriate for an academic context. Students will be asked to demonstrate their mastery of the course content in speech that is appropriate for an academic context.

courses.subject: SOCI
courses.title: College and Social Life
courses.description: Overview of higher education as an institution.  Focuses onstudents, faculty, and the organizational characteristics ofcolleges and universities.  Topics cover the structure and culture of higher education and range from socialization andstratification to achievement, attrition, and athletics.
courses.course_objectives: Students will be expected to acquire an understanding of how higher education operates as a social system. Students will be expected to engage themselves in the scholarly practices of reading, critique, and argumentation with classical and contemporary texts and as part of interaction and discussion with others. In addition, the course incorporates a term research project in which each student conducts an empirical study of two professors. The research component places a special emphasis on assembly, analysis, and argumentation of evidence to direct and develop the creative, analytical, and interpretive abilities of students. Students will demonstrate their mastery of the course content in written work that is appropriate for an academic context. Students will demonstrate their mastery of the course content in speech that is appropriate for an academic context.

courses.subject: SOCI
courses.title: Research Methods in Sociology
courses.description: An introduction to the main research methods used in sociology and the other social sciences. Exploration of surveys, experiments, qualitative interviews, fieldwork, and mixed-methods approaches. Emphasis is placed on basic logic, general strengths and weaknesses, and a critical analysis of applications of each method in published sociological research.
courses.course_objectives: This course introduces students to the main research methods used in sociology and the other social sciences. The course explores surveys, experiments, interviews, fieldwork, and mixed-methods approaches. Emphasis is placed on basic logic, general strengths and weaknesses, and a critical analysis of applications of each method in published sociological research. Issues common to all approaches such as validity, reliability, values, generalizability, and ethical concerns are also explored. For each method, students will be expected to learn how to describe main features and to consider in a critical way the various strengths and weaknesses of each method. Students will be expected to identify, interpret, and critique examples of published sociological research that makes use of each method. In addition, students will be expected to engage in the scholarly practices of reading, focused discussion, and writing. Mandatory writing projects place special emphasis on analysis, evidence, and argument in order to further develop the creative, analytical, and interpretive skills of students. Students will be asked to demonstrate their mastery of the course content in written work that is appropriate for an academic context. Students will be asked to demonstrate their mastery of the course content in speech that is appropriate for an academic context.

1. Social Research Methods: Overview and Common Concerns
2. Surveys: Basic Logic, Aims, Strengths, and Weaknesses
3. Surveys: Presentation and Critique of Published Studies
4. Experiments: Basic Logic, Aims, Strengths, and Weaknesses
5. Experiments: Presentation and Critique of Published Studies
6. Qualitative Interviews: Basic Logic, Aims, Strengths, and Weaknesses
7. Qualitative Interviews: Presentation and Critique of Published Studies
8. Fieldwork: Basic Logic, Aims, Strengths, and Weaknesses
9. Fieldwork: Presentation and Critique of Published Studies
10. Mixed-Methods: Basic Logic, Aims, Strengths, and Weaknesses

12. Wrapping it Up: Comparing Approaches to Social Research

courses.subject: SOCI
courses.title: Qualitative Methods of Social Research
courses.description: Qualitative sociological analysis that emphasizes participant observation, intensive interviewing, and analysis of text; examples of field work studies; the design and completion of an independent field research project.
courses.course_objectives:
Students will read and critique classical and contemporary research studies using a variety of qualitative approaches. 
Students will determine when a qualitative research approach is appropriate, and which approach best fits a question. Through short-term projects, students will practice a number of qualitative research data collection and analysis techniques, including the use of analysis software such as MAXQDA. 
Students will learn to assess the quality and validity of qualitative social research and to understand research ethical issues as they apply to qualitative inquiry. 
Students will learn to write up results of qualitative research studies. Students will be asked to demonstrate their mastery of the course content in written work that is appropriate for an academic context. Students will be asked to demonstrate their mastery of the course content in speech that is appropriate for an academic context.
courses.topical_outline:
I. Choosing and Designing a Fieldwork Project
Fitting methods to questions
Designing qualitative studies
Assessing the validity of qualitative research
Assessing ethical risks in participant Observation

II. Evidence-collection in qualitative research
Participant observation
Grounded theory approaches and their critiques
Interviewing-structured and unstructured
Focus-group interviewing
Content analysis
Analysis of media, discourse, text and historical materials
Analysis of cultural documents
Combining qualitative and quantitative analysis

III. Data analysis and presentation in qualitative research
Grounded theory approaches and their critiques
Interpretive approaches
Issues of validity, reliability and persuasibility
Oral presentations of qualitative research
Written presentations of qualitative research
Nonwritten presentations of qualitative research

IV. Interviewing
Structured versus unstructured approaches
Group and focus group interviewing
Oral history and narrative approaches

V. Analysis of text, documents, media and content

VI. Analysis of Qualitative Data

VII. Writing and Presenting Qualitative Accounts

VIII. The relation of theory to evidence in qualitative research

courses.subject: SOCI
courses.title: Criminology
courses.description: The nature, extent, and correlates of crime; theories of criminal behavior and victimization.
courses.course_objectives: Students will learn about empirical patterns of crime (when, where, how, and by whom crime is committed), as well as the major theories of crime (why crime occurs). Students will analyze and describe the fundamental assumptions and causal mechanisms of theories of crime. Students will evaluate the applicability of theories of crime to everyday life based on the plausibility of assumptions and causal mechanisms. Students will compare major theories of crime to each other by analyzing their implications on public policy, justice, and the criminal legal system. Students will recognize theories of crime, evaluate how each explains crime, and describe strengths and weaknesses as they synthesize literature on these theories. Students will recognize a wide array of causes of crime that likely go beyond what they have learned from their own social circles. This requires reflecting on what the scientific record shows about causes and patterns of crime and how their worldview may be challenged by this. All of this occurs in the context of ethical considerations about crime and justice.

courses.subject: SOCI
courses.title: Communities and Crime
courses.description: Examines sociological theories and research on communities and crime, including spatial variation in crime rates and the impact of efforts to control crime on the structure and well-being of communities.
courses.prerequisiteText: SOCI 1101 or SOCI 1101H or SOCI 2600 or permission of department

courses.subject: SOCI
courses.title: Violence and Society
courses.description: Theory and research on the relationship between criminal violence and social structure and processes.
courses.course_objectives: This course draws on qualitative and quantitative materials to describe and evaluate sociological perspectives on violence in modern societies. Students will learn basic concepts, principles, and theories of violence and apply those ideas to incidents of violence that may occur in their community or society. Students will evaluate different research methods and approaches to assessing the validity of violence hypotheses and research findings. Students will learn how violence differentially impacts demographic groups and what steps might reduce such impacts.
courses.topical_outline:
The following topics may be covered in this course:

1. Violence and the Law
2. Measures of Violence
3. Violence in Other Times and Places
4. Theories of Violence
5. Homicides and Assaults
6. Intimate Partner and Family Violence
7. Robbery and Other Instrumental Aggression
8. Rape and Sexual Assault
9. Mass Murder and Serial Murder
10. Hate Crimes
11. The Role of Guns, Drugs, and Alcohol
12. Prevention and Intervention Strategies
13. Riots and Other Violent Collective Behavior
14. Terrorism and Violent Social Movements
courses.prerequisiteText: SOCI 1101 or SOCI 1101H or SOCI 2600 or permission of department

courses.subject: SOCI
courses.title: Family Violence
courses.description: Data, methods, and theories used in the study of various forms of family violence, including child maltreatment and intimate partner violence. Focuses on the causes and consequences of violence as well as prevention and intervention strategies, including the social welfare and criminal justice responses.
courses.course_objectives: Students will understand the types and limitations of data used by researchers who study domestic violence. Students will have an in-depth understanding of the theoretical perspectives applied to the study of domestic violence. Students will be able to critically analyze and evaluate the results of empirical research on domestic violence. Students will be able to integrate and synthesize research findings from their readings for assigned essays. Students will be able to apply course material to policy and practice designed to address domestic violence.
courses.topical_outline:
Family Violence from an Historical Perspective
Theories of Family Violence
Child Abuse
Sibling Violence
Intimate Partner Violence
Elder Abuse
Social Welfare and Criminal Justice Responses
courses.prerequisiteText: SOCI 1101 or SOCI 1101E or SOCI 1101H or SOCI 3620 or permission of department
