courses.subject: SOCI
courses.title: Sociology of Alcohol and Drug Use
courses.description: Sociohistorical analysis of cultural and policy changes regarding alcohol and psychoactive drugs; theoretical approaches to defining abuse and addiction; causes of substance abuse; treatment strategies, especially Alcoholics Anonymous; and intervention strategies, especially those based in the workplace.
courses.course_objectives: Students will examine psychoactive substance use and abuse, and related policies and issues, primarily in North America. There is particular emphasis on the sociopolitical sources of models of addiction and treatment that have been dominant at different points in history. Students in this course are required to engage themselves in the scholarly practices of reading and evaluating current work in the field of substance abuse and to participate in class discussions. Students who apply themselves fully to this course should leave with a broad understanding of the issues surrounding substance abuse. Students will be asked to demonstrate their mastery of the course content in written work that is appropriate for an academic context. Students can submit their work on out of class assignments for feedback throughout the semester. Students will be asked to demonstrate their mastery of the course content in speech that is appropriate for an academic context.
courses.topical_outline:
The Creation of Deviance and Normality
The Creation of Illness and Health
Socio-Historical Overview
An Epidemiological Overview
Cultural Dimensions
Drug Use and Social Context
courses.prerequisiteText: SOCI 1101 or SOCI 1101H or SOCI 2600 or permission of department

courses.subject: SOCI
courses.title: White Collar Crime
courses.description: Overview of the common forms of white-collar crime, their impact on society, and efforts by law enforcement and other actors to control and punish them. Covers familiar criminological theories in the context of white-collar crime, as well as basic methods for protecting oneself and others from fraud and misinformation.
courses.course_objectives: By the end of this course, students will be able to recognize the common types of white-collar crime (WCC) and their likely victims. By the end of this course, students will understand the methods and impacts of WCC. By the end of this course, students will be able to evaluate theories used to explain WCC. By the end of this course, students will be able to analyze cases of WCC and explain the relevant facts to uninformed readers. By the end of this course, students will be able to apply this knowledge to identify WCC "in the wild" and hopefully avoid it.
courses.topical_outline: Forms of workplace, corporate, and political crime Theories of crime Patterns of criminal behavior Social characteristics of offenders and victims Debates and criticism within criminology
courses.prerequisiteText: SOCI 1101 or SOCI 1101E or SOCI 1101H or SOCI 2600 or permission of department

courses.subject: SOCI
courses.title: Sociology of the American South
courses.description: An analysis of the cultural, social class, economic, and ethnic features of the American South, and investigation of the historical and contemporary forces which shape the unique character of the southern United States.
courses.prerequisiteText: SOCI 1101 or SOCI 1101H or permission of department

courses.subject: SOCI
courses.title: Sociology of the American South
courses.description: An analysis of the cultural, social class, economic, and ethnicfeatures of the American South, and investigation of thehistorical and contemporary forces which shape the uniquecharacter of the southern United States.
courses.prerequisiteText: SOCI 1101 or SOCI 1101H or permission of department

courses.subject: SOCI
courses.title: Sociology of Leadership
courses.description: Explores leadership from a sociological perspective. The structural, human resource, cultural, and symbolic aspects of organizations, and their implications for organizational leadership, will be studied. Key topics will include: conformity, obedience, social identity, status construction, authority, legitimacy, influence, power, and the impact of networks and gender.
courses.prerequisiteText: SOCI 1101 or SOCI 1101H or SOCI 2600 or permission of department

courses.subject: SOCI
courses.title: Sociology of Organizations
courses.description: Research and theories emphasizing organizational structures and cultures; bureaucracies and their alternatives; the control of workers; and the role of gender in organizations.
courses.prerequisiteText: SOCI 1101 or SOCI 1101H or SOCI 2600 or permission of department

courses.subject: SOCI
courses.title: Witches in Modern Society
courses.description: This course focuses on modern day women who are labeled deviant based on socially constructed norms. Students will understand the process and mechanisms that lead to the creation of norms and sanctions of those norms through experiential learning in Salem, Massachusetts where the Salem Witch Trials occurred.
courses.course_objectives: Students will explain different theories of the social construction of deviance. Students will collect qualitative data, analyze, and present basic qualitative findings. Students will complete their CITI training and receive certificate Students will understand and articulate the impact of moral panics on society Students will critique popular culture and media narratives that contribute to inaccurate stereotypes Students will reflect on their experiences with modern day “deviant” women
courses.topical_outline: 1. Social Construction of Deviance 2. Qualitative Research Methods 3. Moral Panics 4. Salem Witch Trials of 1692 5. Modern Day Witches and Ramifications of the Witch Trials 6. Critique/Analysis of Deviant Women in Popular Culture

courses.subject: SOCI
courses.title: Society, Bodies, and Health
courses.description: Exploration of emerging conceptualizations and research on links between social conditions and experiences, biological characteristics and processes, and various aspects of our physical health. It introduces, explains, and assesses biologically-informed medical sociology and highlights the promise and challenges of interdisciplinary collaboration between sociologists, biologists, and bench scientists.
courses.prerequisiteText: SOCI 1101 or SOCI 1101H or SOCI 3100 or permission of department

courses.subject: SOCI
courses.title: Seminar in Culture
courses.description: Special topics in culture for advanced undergraduates.
courses.prerequisiteText: SOCI 1101 or SOCI 1101H or SOCI 2500 or SOCI 3010 or permission of department
courses.offeredText: Not offered on a regular basis.

courses.subject: SOCI
courses.title: Media and Criminal Justice
courses.description: Focuses on the impact of inaccurate stereotypes within the criminal justice institution. Provides a historical overview of court cases that were popular in the media and engages students in reflective, service-learning projects that give back to the local community.
courses.prerequisiteText: SOCI 1101 or SOCI 1101H or SOCI 1101E or SOCI 3810 or SOCI 3810W or SOCI 3810E or permission of department

courses.subject: SOCI
courses.title: Global Inequality and Social Change
courses.description: A survey course of sociological concepts of poverty, inequality, and social change within a global context. Themes explored include basic food security, poverty, and hunger; population and resource distribution; foreign aid and development institutions; and social policies and movements for change. Course approach is historical and transnational, including case studies from Africa, Asia, Latin America, and the United States.
courses.course_objectives: Students will become familiar with the ways different nations differ in the power and resources available to them, and the sociological processes contributing to this inequality. Students will read in a variety of academic styles in preparation for an independent research paper at the end of the semester.
courses.topical_outline:
1 – Globalization
2 – Development and Underdevelopment
3 – Poverty
4 – Transnational and International Crime
5 – Migration
6 – The Global Gender Gap
7 – War and Displacement
8 – International Terrorism
courses.prerequisiteText: SOCI 1101 or SOCI 1101E or SOCI 1101H or permission of department

courses.subject: SOCI
courses.title: Social Control and Behavior Disorders
courses.description: Behavior disorders (BD) include non-criminal andnon-developmental persistent behaviors that typically lead toformal interventions. Shifting boundaries define strategic actionfields wherein BD are both directly and reactively controlled.Expanded from psychoses and substance addictions, BD now includesADHD, depression, autism spectrum, behavioral addictions, tobaccouse, and eating disorders.
courses.prerequisiteText: [(SOCI 1101 or SOCI 1101H) and (SOCI 3100 or SOCI 3810 or SOCI 3810W or SOCI 3860)] or permission of department

courses.subject: SOCI
courses.title: Social Networks
courses.description: Focuses on the causes and consequences of interpersonal relationships and introduces students to analytic tools for understanding patterns in relationships. Considers how online and face-to-face networks help us understand phenomena ranging from career outcomes, musical tastes, criminal behavior, disease transmission, rumor propagation, and the course of social movements.

courses.subject: SOCI
courses.title: Seminar in Work and Occupations
courses.description: The organization of work and occupational processes, such as the emergence of temporary and contract work, the decline of manufacturing jobs and the rise of the service sector, and the impact of technology on the structure of work and the experiences of workers.
courses.prerequisiteText: SOCI 1101 or SOCI 1101H or SOCI 3750 or SOCI 3850 or SOCI 3950 or permission of department
courses.offeredText: Not offered on a regular basis.

courses.subject: SOCI
courses.title: Seminar in Deviance and Social Control
courses.description: Special topics in deviance and responses to deviance, with an emphasis on theoretical perspectives.
courses.prerequisiteText: [(SOCI 1101 or SOCI 1101H or SOCI 2600) and SOCI 2470] or permission of department
courses.offeredText: Not offered on a regular basis.

courses.title: Special Topics in Sociology
courses.description: Course content will be specified by the faculty member offeringthe particular section of this course.

courses.offeredText: Not offered on a regular basis.

courses.subject: SOCI
courses.title: Sociology of Prisons
courses.description: This course provides an overview of sociological theories and research on prisons in the United States and globally. Topics will include theories of punishment; historical origins of the prison as a form of state punishment; prison conditions and social life; imprisonment and social stratification; and the collateral consequences of imprisonment.
courses.course_objectives: Students will be able to evaluate the major sociological theories of imprisonment. Students will be able to analyze how incarceration is affected by diverse social forces historically and cross-nationally. Students will be able to investigate the history of imprisonment in the U.S. using primary source materials.
courses.topical_outline: 1. Are prisons inevitable? The social construction of punishment 2. Penal change: Of pendulums and plate tectonics 3.  Early prison reform in global perspective, 1750-1850 (U.S. and Italy) 4. Prison architecture & model prisons in historical perspective 5. Prisons and social solidarity 6. Prisons and political economy 7. Prisons and power/rationalization/bureaucratization 8. Prisons and culture 9. Social structure and culture in “The Big House” 10. The experience of “doing time” 11. Mass incarceration as a “grand social experiment” 12. Mass incarceration and social stratification 13. The long reach of imprisonment (reentry and collateral consequences) 14. Prisoner rights and the future of prison reform 15. Research project & presentations: Guthrie v. Evans

courses.subject: SOCI
courses.title: Crime in Global Context
courses.description: Cross-national variation in definitions, incidence, andprevalence of crime; the role of culture, structure, andglobalization on crime and crime control.

courses.subject: SOCI
courses.title: Sociology of Aging
courses.description: The status, roles, and demographic aspects of the aging population and its relationship with social institutions.
courses.offeredText: Not offered on a regular basis.

courses.subject: SOCI
courses.title: Seminar in Social Psychology
courses.description: Special topics in social psychology for advanced undergraduates.
courses.prerequisiteText: SOCI 1101 or SOCI 1101H or SOCI 3270 or SOCI 3730 or permission of department
courses.offeredText: Not offered on a regular basis.

courses.subject: SOCI
courses.title: Gender and Interaction
courses.description: Examination of the role that everyday interaction plays in the creation, maintenance, and change of our system of genderdifference and gender inequality in contemporary United States society. To address these questions, we will critically examine current sociological theory and research on gender, inequality, and interaction.
courses.prerequisiteText: SOCI 1101 or SOCI 1101H or SOCI 2600 or PSYC 1101 or permission of department

courses.subject: SOCI
courses.title: Gender and Interaction
courses.description: Examination of the role that everyday interaction plays in thecreation, maintenance, and change of our system of genderdifference and gender inequality in contemporary United Statessociety. To address these questions, students will critically examine current sociological theory and research on gender, inequality, and interaction.
courses.prerequisiteText: SOCI 1101 or SOCI 1101H or SOCI 2600 or PSYC 1101 or PSYC 1101E or PSYC 1030H or permission of department

courses.subject: SOCI
courses.title: State Violence
courses.description: Focuses on violence committed by agents of the state, such as police and military officials, against their civilian populations. Particular attention is paid to the contemporary United States, though patterns of state violence across diverse state systems, including democracies, oligarchies, and autocracies, are also reviewed. The object of the course is to describe and explain variation in the amount and type of violence inflicted by the state against those it is said to serve.
courses.course_objectives: Students will analyze how, and which, structural characteristics of society promote and inhibit the amount and type of violence civilians experience at the hands of state officials as they police crime and respond to protest or counterterrorism.
courses.topical_outline: 1. Introduction: What is State Violence? 2. Types of States 3. Theories of State Violence 4. The United States: Police Violence 5. The United States: Counterterrorism 6. Oligarchy: Brazil 7. Oligarchy: Iran 8. Autocracy: Nazi Germany 9. Autocracy: North Korea 10. Conclusions: Sociological Principles of State Violence
courses.prerequisiteText: SOCI 1101 or SOCI 1101E or SOCI 1101H or permission of department

courses.subject: SOCI
courses.title: Sociology of Morality
courses.description: Analyzes the definition and response to right and wrong in humansocieties. Moral conflict occurs throughout social life, thoughit varies greatly in intensity and type. This course asks: Whyare some groups highly tolerant, while others are highly repressive?

courses.subject: SOCI
courses.title: Sociology of Morality
courses.description: Analyzes the definition and response to right and wrong in humansocieties. Moral conflict occurs throughout social life, thoughit varies greatly in intensity and type. This course asks: Whyare some groups highly tolerant, while others are highly repressive?
courses.prerequisiteText: SOCI 1101 or SOCI 1101H or SOCI 2600 or permission of department

courses.subject: SOCI
courses.title: Sociology of Law
courses.description: The nature of law, and the ways the legal system reflects its broader social context.
courses.prerequisiteText: SOCI 1101 or SOCI 1101E or SOCI 1101H or permission of department

courses.subject: SOCI
courses.title: Sociology of Law
courses.description: The nature of law and the ways the legal system reflects itsbroader social context.
courses.prerequisiteText: SOCI 1101 or SOCI 1101E or SOCI 1101H or permission of department

courses.subject: SOCI
courses.title: Supervised Research in Sociology
courses.description: Research conducted under the direction of a faculty member; includes a review of the literature, data collection and analysis, and interpretation of research findings.
courses.prerequisiteText: SOCI 1101 or SOCI 1101H or permission of department

courses.subject: SOCI
courses.title: Experimental Research in Sociology
courses.description: An experimental research methods course emphasizing hands-on experience in the lab.  Readings and weekly seminar meetings focus on ethics in human research, sociological theories of social interaction, experimental design, experimental procedures, data interpretation, and scholarly writing. Students will work in collaborative teams to conduct original research in the Laboratory for the Study of Social Interaction.
courses.prerequisiteText: Permission of department | Graduate Prerequisite | Permission of department

courses.subject: SOCI
courses.title: Internship Experience
courses.description: Application of sociological theory and research to public and private sector enterprises. Emphasis on observation and analysis of sociological issues that serve as the foundation for an original research paper. Students are responsible for identifying the internship setting and having it approved by the Sociology Undergraduate Coordinator.
courses.prerequisiteText: (SOCI 1101 or SOCI 1101H or SOCI 2600) and permission of department

courses.subject: SOCI
courses.title: Faculty-Mentored Undergraduate Research I
courses.description: Faculty-supervised independent or collaborative inquiry into fundamental and applied problems within a discipline that requires students to gather, analyze, and synthesize and interpret data and to present results in writing and other relevant communication formats.

courses.subject: SOCI
courses.title: Faculty-Mentored Undergraduate Research II
courses.description: Faculty-supervised independent or collaborative inquiry into fundamental and applied problems within a discipline that requires students to gather, analyze, synthesize, and interpret data and to present results in writing and other relevant communication formats.

courses.subject: SOCI
courses.title: Faculty-Mentored Undergraduate Research III
courses.description: Faculty-supervised independent or collaborative inquiry into fundamental and applied problems within a discipline that requires students to gather, analyze, synthesize, and interpret data and to present results in writing and other relevant communication formats.

courses.subject: SOCI
courses.title: Undergraduate Research Thesis (or Final Project)
courses.description: Faculty-supervised independent or collaborative inquiry into fundamental and applied problems within a discipline that requires students to gather, analyze, and synthesize and interpret data. Students will write or produce a thesis or other professional capstone product, such as a report or portfolio that describes their systematic and in-depth inquiry.

courses.subject: SOCI
courses.title: Sociological Approaches to Culture
courses.description: Case studies of art, music, literature, rituals and ceremony, food, dress, and other cultural objects.  Topics include the dimensions of cultural objects; structuralist, postmodern, functionalist and semiotic perspectives; and basic issues such as  consensus and diversity, ideology, collective memory and tradition, religion, social solidarity, conflict, and change.

courses.subject: SOCI
courses.title: Sociology of Work and Family
courses.description: The relationship between paid work and family life.  How work and family have changed over time, how they conflict with or support each other, and how individuals, families, organizations, and governments have approached the need for both.

courses.subject: SOCI
courses.title: Proseminar in Sociology
courses.description: An introduction to the profession of sociology. Faculty members describe their intellectual work and discuss issues of professionalization, including selecting a major professor, preparing for comprehensive exams, writing for publication, and preparing for the job market.

courses.subject: SOCI
courses.title: Development of Sociological Theory
courses.description: Pivotal theories from classic theorists such as Marx, Weber, and Durkheim to the present.

courses.subject: SOCI
courses.title: Sociological Theory: The German Tradition
courses.description: The German theoretical tradition, beginning with Marx and continuing with Wilhelmine-era sociologists, particularly Simmel and Weber; the Weimar and Nazi periods; and postwar critical theorists, notably Habermas.
courses.offeredText: Not offered on a regular basis.

courses.subject: SOCI
courses.title: Sociology of Higher Education
courses.description: Overview of higher education as an institution.  Focuses onstudents, faculty, and the organizational characteristics ofcolleges and universities. Topics cover the structure and culture of higher education and range from socialization andstratification to achievement, attrition, and athletics.

courses.subject: SOCI
courses.title: Sociology of Gender
courses.description: Feminist theories and methodologies on gender, with an emphasis on contemporary American society and the intersection of gender, race, and class.  Topics include socialization, sexual orientation, reproduction, violence, family and household, work and global restructuring, and politics.

courses.subject: SOCI
courses.title: Current Trends in Sociological Theory
courses.description: The concepts of community, authority, rank, the sacred, and alienation to examine conflict and consensus, modernity and postmodernity, classical theory, and the problem of meaning. The role of ideas in social integration and change, the problem of legitimation, civil religion in politics, "postmodern" society, and symbolism and moral order.

courses.subject: SOCI
courses.title: Structured Inequality
courses.description: Social stratification in the United States. The perception of class distinctions; prestige and power; the criteria of status evaluation; and the consequences of class for social relationships, lifestyles, and personality development.

courses.subject: SOCI
courses.title: Research Methods
courses.description: Sociological research methods.  Topics include conceptions of research, the philosophy of science, formal and grounded theory construction, and qualitative and quantitative approaches to research design.

courses.subject: SOCI
courses.title: Analysis and Interpretation of Sociological Data I
courses.description: Univariate, bivariate, and multivariate analyses of non-experimental quantitative evidence.  Topics include frequency distributions, central tendency and dispersion, cross tabulation, mean difference analyses, statistical inference, regression, and the use of microcomputers and statistical software to conduct quantitative data analysis.

courses.subject: SOCI
courses.title: Analysis and Interpretation of Sociological Data II
courses.description: Multivariate data analysis; the design and execution of an independent research project using such techniques.

courses.subject: SOCI
courses.title: Qualitative Methods of Social Research
courses.description: Qualitative approaches to research, with an emphasis on participant observation, intensive interviews, and analysis of text.  Students must complete a major fieldwork project.

courses.subject: SOCI
courses.title: Social Deviance and Mental Health
courses.description: Theory and research relating to various types of deviant behavior, including crime, family violence, substance use, and mental and physical illness. Social structural, cultural, social psychological, evolutionary, and biosocial theories will be examined.

courses.subject: SOCI
courses.title: Master's Research
courses.description: Research while enrolled for a master's degree under the direction of faculty members.

courses.subject: SOCI
courses.title: Graduate Student Seminar
courses.description: Advanced supervised experience in an applied setting.  Thiscourse may not be used to satisfy a student's approved program ofstudy.

courses.subject: SOCI
courses.title: Master's Thesis
courses.description: Thesis writing under the direction of the major professor.

courses.subject: SOCI
courses.title: Special Topics in Sociology
courses.description: Theory and research on advanced topics selected by the student.

courses.subject: SOCI
courses.title: Seminar in Culture
courses.description: Approaches to culture, including the critical traditions of Frankfurt and Birmingham; the Durkheimian tradition of collective memory and social integration; and interactionist emphases on cultural products and structuration.

courses.subject: SOCI
courses.title: Sociology of Higher Education
courses.description: Overview of higher education as an institution. Focuses on students, faculty, and the organizational characteristics of colleges and universities. Topics cover the structure and culture of higher education and range from socialization and stratification to achievement, attrition, and athletics.

courses.subject: SOCI
courses.title: Sociology of Religion
courses.description: Contemporary social scientific approaches to the analysis ofreligion. Classic perspectives on religion and secularizationcontrasted to varied attempts to move beyond secularizationtheory in response to religious resurgence around the world.Other topics include attempts to reconceptualize the relationshipbetween religion and politics in (post-)modernity.

courses.subject: SOCI
courses.title: Sociology of the Life Course
courses.description: An examination of the sociological study of lives. Covers socialization over the life span, the stratification of lives, cross-cultural comparisons of aging and human development, family patterns across time, careers in crime, health across life, religious expression in lives, and life-time consequences of education.
courses.course_objectives: Students will develop a comprehensive understanding of this sociological specialty, including characteristic modes of inquiry, key arguments and debates, and prevailing societal trends. Students will engage themselves in the scholarly practice of reading, criticism, and argumentation. Students will develop a paper in conjunction with his/her specific interests. Students will demonstrate their mastery of the course content in written work that is appropriate for an academic context. Students will demonstrate their mastery of the course content in speech that is appropriate for an academic context.
courses.topical_outline: Introduction Development of the Life Course as a Field of Sociological Inquiry Life Phases Methods of Life Course Research Methodological Considerations in Life Course Research Cultural Constructions of the Life Course Age Norms Cross-Cultural Comparisons of Age and Aging Aging Across the Life Span: Stratification Childhood and the Life Course The Family and the Life Course Deviance and the Life Course Health and the Life Course Education and the Life Course Research Projects in Life Course Analysis

courses.subject: SOCI
courses.title: Criminal Punishment and Society
courses.description: The relationship between contemporary American punishment and social organization and processes.  Topics include historical features of, and justifications for, punishment; the death penalty debate; prisoner rights; and prison conditions.

courses.subject: SOCI
courses.title: Seminar in Sociological Theory and Research
courses.description: Selected topics on theory and research.
courses.offeredText: Not offered on a regular basis.

courses.subject: SOCI
courses.title: Social Theory Now
courses.description: New intellectual developments have significantly challenged the landscape of social theory in the twenty-first century. Social Theory Now examines recent trends in social theory - often ignored in traditional sociological theory courses - focusing on work by living sociologists and theorists in related fields.

courses.subject: SOCI
courses.title: Seminar in Critical Theory
courses.description: Critical social theory from its origins in Germany in the 1920s to its present development in Europe and the United States.  Includes Frankfurt theorists such as Horkheimer, Marcuse, and Adorno; second-generation Frankfurters, especially Habermas; and contemporary critical theories of identity, culture, justice, and politics.

courses.subject: SOCI
courses.title: Seminar on Social Movements
courses.description: Analysis of methodologies and theories used in the study ofsocial movements.  Case studies may include local, national,(United States and other) and transnational movements.

courses.subject: SOCI
courses.title: Sociology of Gender
courses.description: Feminist theories and methodologies on gender and intersectionality, with cases drawn from the U.S. and other national contexts. Topics may include socialization, reproduction, sexual identities, violence, family, and other social institutions, work, politics, and social movements.

courses.subject: SOCI
courses.title: Seminar in Gender Stratification
courses.description: Research and theories of gender equality and inequality in America and other cultures.  Topics include gender stratification in public and private domains, and the intersection of gender with race, ethnicity, social class, and sexual orientation.
courses.prerequisiteText: SOCI 6280 or WMST 8010 or permission of department

courses.subject: SOCI
courses.title: Sociology of Physical and Mental Health
courses.description: Theory and research regarding the avenues whereby social factors influence the onset, course, and treatment of various emotionalproblems and physical illnesses. Special emphasis upon statusgradient, fundamental cause, social stress, and biologicalembedding perspectives on health. Issues relating to thereliability of diagnoses, the methodological challenges of drugresearch, and the efficacy of pharmacological treatments are alsoconsidered.

courses.subject: SOCI
courses.title: Social and Biological Aging
courses.description: The social, cultural, and biological context of aging. Topics include age-related changes in biology, social relationships, religiosity, psychological well-being, and health; social determinants of accelerated and decelerated biological aging; death and dying; cultural, social class, and racial differences in aging.

courses.subject: SOCI
courses.title: Deviance and Social Control
courses.description: Theories and research on the nature of deviant behavior and its control by social institutions, agencies, and groups.

courses.subject: SOCI
courses.title: Seminar in Political Sociology
courses.description: Issues of class, gender, and race.  Topics include power and state formation; competing paradigms of state action; the relationship between the state and economy; collective action; democratization, legitimacy and revolution.
courses.offeredText: Not offered on a regular basis.

courses.subject: SOCI
courses.title: Seminar in Organizations and Social Control
courses.description: Organizational processes that control behavior, including work performance, career development, and off-job attitudes, orientations, and behaviors.

courses.subject: SOCI
courses.title: Research Training
courses.description: Students acquire advanced research skills that will help them intheir professional careers.  Student duties will vary but mayinclude designing questionnaires, conducting interviews,undertaking library research, planning and executing experiments,and analyzing data.

courses.subject: SOCI
courses.title: Sociological Analysis and Interpretation of Categorical Data
courses.description: An introduction to regression models for categorical and limiteddependent variables.  The objective is to provide students withan understanding of (a) when particular models are appropriate,(b) the basic logic of various models, (c) how results areinterpreted and evaluated, and (d) how to conduct analyses usingstatistical software.

courses.subject: SOCI
courses.title: Empirical Model-Building in Social Research
courses.description: Simultaneous equations and confirmatory factor methods to evaluate structural and measurement models.  Emphasis on the interplay between theory and the construction and evaluation of empirical models.
courses.prerequisiteText: SOCI 6630 or STAT 6220 or permission of department

courses.subject: SOCI
courses.title: Introduction to Multilevel Modeling
courses.description: Focuses on applications of hierarchical linear and nonlinear models (HLM).  Reviews the logic and estimation principles of HLM. Two-level models are illustrated, including estimatingorganizational effects on individuals and examining individualchange over time.  Generalizations to three-level models and tononlinear models for discrete outcomes are considered.

courses.subject: SOCI
courses.title: Social Network Analysis
courses.description: Social network analysts consider relations to be the focal unitsof analysis – and the bases of social structure. This coursesurveys a mixture of mathematical and statistical techniques foranalyzing social networks. Students will gain a working knowledge of relevant software packages and common approaches to network analysis.

courses.subject: SOCI
courses.title: Life Course Research Methods
courses.description: Explores methods of life course research to address questions in health, crime, education, and family while enhancing students' understanding of this interdisciplinary field and their analytic tools.
courses.course_objectives: By the end of this course, students will demonstrate the ability to identify Life Course Approaches and Methods: Identify and criticize life course approaches and methods to understand social phenomena. By the end of this course, students will demonstrate the ability to translate Knowledge into Social Questions: Effectively translate acquired knowledge into addressing diverse social questions. By the end of this course, students will demonstrate the ability to Demonstrate Statistical Modeling Proficiency: Proficiency in estimating and analyzing statistical models to investigate research questions related to life course approaches. By the end of this course, students will demonstrate the ability to conduct Well-being Research Over Time: Develop research skills and design research models to examine the evolution of various well-being aspects over time using life course approaches.
courses.topical_outline: Introduction and Overview of the Life Course Paradigm Lives in Time and Place: Age, Birth Cohorts, and Neighborhood Influences Life Course Models, Methodologies, and Data Sources Retrospective vs. Prospective Measurement in Longitudinal Research Path Analysis with Longitudinal Data Fixed-Effect Models Random-Effect Models Growth Curve Modeling Age-Period-Cohort Analysis Event History Analysis
courses.prerequisiteText: SOCI 6620 or SOCI 6630 or permission of department

courses.subject: SOCI
courses.title: Role, Self, and Identity
courses.description: Focuses on the relationship between society, identity, and social action. Students become familiar with the sociological research literature on self and identity, explore various measurement tools and analytic techniques for theoretical exploration, data collection, and qualitative data analysis, and refine specific professional skills, including academic reviewing, presenting, and proposal writing.

courses.subject: SOCI
courses.title: Interaction and Inequality
courses.description: Designed to provide a broad introduction to the theoretical and empirical approach of contemporary social psychology to problems of inequality. This course examines literature from both sociology and psychology, but places an emphasis on sociological perspectives for understanding how interpersonal interaction reproduces race, gender, and class inequality.

courses.subject: SOCI
courses.title: Theories of Social Psychology
courses.description: Major classic and contemporary theories, including Freudian theory, exchange theory, dramaturgy, phenomenology, and ethnomethodology.

courses.subject: SOCI
courses.title: Sociology of Emotion
courses.description: How personal are your emotions? This seminar examines the role of emotion and affect in sociological theory and surveys empirical research on how social structure shapes individual and collective emotional experience. Involves reading empirical research, designing, and interpreting computer simulations, delivering research presentations, and writing a research proposal.
courses.course_objectives: On completing the course, students will be able to articulate the core concepts and arguments in principal theories in the field of the sociology of emotions. On completing the course, students should be able to critically evaluate the evidence for different sociological theories of emotions and offer some original insight into the debates. On completing the course, students should demonstrate an ability to apply their knowledge and skills to understanding practical examples of how emotions are expressed in different social, structural, and cultural contexts. On completing the course, students will gain the ability to clearly communicate, orally and in written form, their own research ideas relating to the sociology of emotions. On completing the course, students will acquire team-work skills in organizing and leading seminar discussion with a group of peers.
courses.topical_outline: 1.	Emotions in Classical Sociological Theory 2.	Emotion Management Theory 3.	Emotions in Identity Theory 4.	Emotions in Affect Control Theory 5.	Emotions in Justice Theories 6.	Emotions in Ritual Theories 7.	Emotions in Status Theories 8.	Emotions in Exchange Theories 9.	Emotions and Inequality 10.	Emotions and Gender 11.	Emotions and Race 12.	Emotions and Morality 13.	Emotions and Social Movements 14.	Research paper presentations
courses.offeredText: Not offered on a regular basis.

courses.subject: SOCI
courses.title: Sociology of Crime
courses.description: The nature, extent, and correlates of crime; theories of criminal behavior and victimization.

courses.subject: SOCI
courses.title: Communities and Crime
courses.description: Urban crime and spatial variation in crime rates.  The impact of crime on the structure of communities and its role in neighborhood decline.
courses.offeredText: Not offered on a regular basis.

courses.subject: SOCI
courses.title: Gender, Crime, and Justice
courses.description: This course uses sociological and feminist theories to examinecrime, criminology, and the criminal justice system from agendered perspective.  In doing so, the class is organized around three basic themes: the gendered nature of perpetration; gender variation in victimization; and women as participants in the legal process.

courses.subject: SOCI
courses.title: Sociology of Law
courses.description: The nature of law and the ways the legal system reflects its broader social context.

courses.subject: SOCI
courses.title: Doctoral Research
courses.description: Research while enrolled for a doctoral degree under the direction of faculty members.

courses.subject: SOCI
courses.title: Doctoral Graduate Student Seminar
courses.description: Advanced supervised experience in an applied setting.  Thiscourse may not be used to satisfy a student's approved program ofstudy.

courses.subject: SOCI
courses.title: Sociology Job Market Seminar
courses.description: Provides students with the knowledge and skills necessary to navigate the academic and non-academic job market in sociology. Students produce professional products, including their application materials, practice job talks, and interviews talks. They will also learn about opportunities for nonacademic jobs and postdocs.

courses.subject: SOCI
courses.title: Doctoral Dissertation
courses.description: Dissertation writing under the direction of the major professor.

courses.subject: SOWK
courses.title: The Social Welfare Institution
courses.description: History and current status of social welfare programs and services in the United States.  Philosophical, religious, economic, and political perspectives on social welfare. A comparison of approaches to social welfare in the United States and other developed nations.

courses.subject: SOWK
courses.title: Introduction to Social Work
courses.description: History and current status of the profession of social work. The role of the social worker in various fields of practice.  The profession's commitment to social and economic justice for vulnerable and oppressed populations.  The person-in-environment perspective. Communication and interviewing skills lab.
courses.course_objectives: Student will learn to demonstrate familiarity with the history, knowledge base, roles, values, and ethics of generalist social work practice. Student will learn to demonstrate understanding of the history and issues of the American social welfare system and institutions and their relevance to social work. Student will learn identify the role conflicts that arise in providing social programs and social services that are designed to meet basic human needs. Student will learn to explain how the American political and economic policies and systems influenced the ways in which resources are allocated to meet basic human needs. Student will learn to analyze the potential impacts of opposing philosophies that influence political decisions; in particular, decisions that affect present and future provisions for human needs. Student will learn to identify and explain the impacts of racism, discrimination, and oppression on the accessibility of jobs, economic opportunities, and the allocation of resources for meeting human needs attentive to an individual’s race, color, religion, creed, gender, ethnic or national origin, disability, age, political orientation, or sexual orientation. Student will learn to demonstrate a knowledge of seven different fields of practice within the social work profession as discussed through course content and learning experiences. Student will learn to demonstrate an ability to identify and analyze one’s personal positions on issues, values, and thoughts concerning the profession of social work.
courses.topical_outline:
1. Introduction to Social Work and Social Welfare
A. Distinctive aspects of social work and social welfare
B. Content areas of the social work curriculum
C. The social work profession’s similarities and differences with other professions
D. Social work in various fields of practice 2. Social Work Values and Ethics
A. NASW Code of Ethics
B. The social worker’s ethical responsibilities and obligations
C. Personal values and professional social work values 3. Empowerment and Human Diversity
A. Discrimination, oppression, stereotypes, and prejudice
B. Populations at risk
C. Social and economic justice
D. Racial, ethnic, and cultural diversity in the United States 4. The Process of Generalist Practice
A. The definition of generalist practice
B. Social work roles in generalist practice
C. The planned-change process
D. Cultural issues in nonverbal communication and the strengths perspective 5. Practice Settings
A. Social work practice in organizations and communities
B. Micro, mezzo, and macro practice in social work
C. Group practice, social work licensure, and professional organizations
D. Careers in social work 6. An Overview of Social Welfare and Social Work History
A. European approaches to social welfare
B. History of social welfare in the United States
C. The development of the social work profession 7. Policy, Policy Analysis, and Policy Advocacy: Foundations for Service Provision
A. Social welfare policy and its development
B. Structural components of social welfare programs
C. Values perspectives on social responsibility and social welfare programs
D. Policy analysis and policy advocacy 8. Policies and Programs to Combat Poverty
A. Poverty in the United States
B. Social welfare policies and programs
C. Social work roles, social insurance policy, and public assistance 9. Social Work and Services for Children and Families
A. Historical perspectives on family and children’s services
B. Social work’s current role within the child welfare system
C. Self-determination, diverse family structures, and cultural competence
D. Child maltreatment, adoptions, family preservation, supportive and substitute services 10. Social Work and Services for the Elderly
A. Discussion of this population noting demographics, needs, issues, and challenges
B. Older adults and their families
C. Social work’s history in working with this population
D. Social welfare policy and legislation for older adults 11. Social Work and Services for People with Disabilities
A. Mobility, developmental, and cognitive disabilities
B. Discrimination against people with developmental disabilities
C. Services for people with disabilities
D. Disabilities, the ADA of 1990, empowerment, and ethical dilemmas 12. Social Work and Services in Health Care
A. Educational preparation for health care social work practice
B. Social work’s current role in health care settings
C. Cultural competence and social welfare policy in health care
D. The politics and economics of health care 13. Social Work and Services in Mental Health
A. Mental health and mental illness
B. Social work employment settings in mental health
C. Managed care in mental health
D. Cultural competence in mental health settings 14. Social Work and Services for Youth and in the Schools
A. Social work roles in the schools
B. The impact of cultural diversity in the schools
C. Creative empowerment for youth through macro practice
D. Issues of teenage sexuality, pregnancy, and parenting 15. Social Work and Services in the Criminal Justice System
A. Components of the criminal justice setting
B. Social work’s role within this system
C. Juvenile justice and social welfare policies
D. Value dilemmas in criminal justice settings for social workers

courses.subject: SOWK
courses.title: Communication as a Helping Professional
courses.description: A study of the values, knowledge, and skills of effective human communication and interpersonal relations as necessary for planned change with individuals, groups, families, and communities. Includes observation, collection, and description of data, verbal and non-verbal communication, and their relevance to social work practice. Issues in communication regarding minority and oppressed populations are integrated in all course content.
courses.course_objectives: Students will be able to describe interpersonal communication as a transactional event, identifying both verbal and non-verbal communication. Students will be able to describe the social work value base, which undergirds both personal and professional interpersonal relationships including racial, cultural, ethnic, sexual, and disability issues. Students will be able to define and exemplify the concepts of self-awareness, self-acceptance and self-disclosure and their interrelationship with human communication. Students will be able to discuss roles and identify skills for the management of conflict in interpersonal relationships. Students will be able to identify interpersonal relationships and communication within a group and begin to understand its relationship to group dynamics. Students will be able to articulate the elements of a professional relationship and contrast such relationships with personal encounters, understanding the difference between an interview and informal communication.
courses.topical_outline: 1. Social work values: Foundation for communication 2. Understanding communication: The challenge of human discourse 3. Listening: A guide for hearing 4. Perception: Seeing though the prism of truth 5. Verbal and non-verbal communication 6. The self: The journey inward 7. Self-disclosure: The journey outward 8. Emotions: Discovering our deeper selves 9. Relationships: The bridge to others 10. Conflict: From struggle to resolution

courses.subject: SOWK
courses.title: Intro to Power, Oppression, Social Justice, Evidence-Informed Practice, Advocacy, and Diversity
courses.description: Exploration of the complex concerns that emerge in diverseenvironments in order to understand the historical, political,and sociological realities of perceived and genuine differencesthat can lead to ethnocentrism, biases, prejudice,discrimination, exploitation and oppression within, among, andbetween groups.  Students will be challenged to expand theirvisible and invisible perceptions of those who are different fromthemselves.
courses.course_objectives: By the end of this course, students will achieve a heightened ability to understand social justice, marginalized populations, and oppression other nationally and internationally. By the end of this course, students will achieve a heightened ability to comprehend the value diversity within the profession of social work. By the end of this course, students will achieve a heightened ability to increase their personal awareness of their own biases regarding race, gender, religious beliefs, age, sexual orientation, disabilities, socioeconomic differences, political ideologies, and regional differences. By the end of this course, students will achieve a heightened ability to understand their implicit assumptions which contribute to biases and prejudices. By the end of this course, students will achieve a heightened ability to acquire and display behaviors that are consistent with social work values and attitudes that are respectful of human diversity as well as strategies for addressing discrimination and oppression personally and professionally. By the end of this course, students will achieve a heightened ability to control their biases, stereotypes, prejudices.

Week 1: History of the profession, social justices, marginalized populations Week 2: The human condition, perception theory, sociology of oppression Week 3: Differences of self/identifying self (normal v. not normal, attribution theory
Assignment Autobiography (difference and sameness) Week 4: Differences of self/identifying self (normal v. not normal, attribution theory Assignment Autobiography (difference and sameness) Week 5: Race & ethnicity- break gap between unique, ownership v. what is part of them Week 6: Race & ethnicity- break gap between unique, ownership v. what is part of them

courses.subject: SOWK
courses.title: Service Learning in Social Work
courses.description: Experiential learning with reflective and analytical components.  Students will observe and analyze how social service agencies empower individuals and social well-being of clients/people and how community agencies attempt to alleviate social and economic injustices.
courses.course_objectives: Students will outline and interpret the meaning, both personal and pre-professional, of caring for others in a human service agency. Students will analyze and assess the affective, cognitive, and performance dimensions during the volunteering. Students will evaluate personal interest and fit in the profession of social work.
courses.topical_outline: 1. Service-learning and volunteerism. 2. The role of the volunteer. 3. The service-learning plan. 4. Observing and reflecting upon experiences. 5. Evaluating self as a professional helper. 6. The community context of the human service agency.

courses.subject: SOWK
courses.title: Social Action and Social Justice: A Service-Learning Approach
courses.description: An examination of contributors to bias, prejudice, racism, and exploitation nationally and globally through a process of continuous reflection and community-based engagement. Students spend thirty hours in a community agency to understand and critique its social change efforts, and develop a social change project of their own.
courses.offeredText: Not offered on a regular basis.

courses.subject: SOWK
courses.title: Professional Social Work Communication
courses.description: Builds a foundation for effective communication for generalist social work practice. Emphasizes meta-competencies to ground learning of basic communication and interviewing skills, effective professional writing and presenting, and some spoken eloquence. Social work values, norms, and expectations are embedded in the multiple dimensions of professional communication.
courses.prerequisiteText: SOWK 2154 or SOWK 2154S or SOWK 2156 or SOWK 2160S
courses.offeredText: Not offered on a regular basis.

courses.subject: SOWK
courses.title: Gender-Based Violence Among College Students
courses.description: Introduces students to the problem of gender-based violence among college students. Students will critically think about gender-based violence, prevention strategies, and how to advocate for change. Students will develop skills to address gender-based violence and learn how to apply those skills to promoting gender equality.

courses.subject: SOWK
courses.title: Gender-Based Violence Among College Students
courses.description: An introduction to the problem of gender-based violence among college students. Students will critically think about gender-based violence, prevention strategies, and how to advocate for change. Students will develop skills to address gender-based violence and learn how to apply those skills to promoting gender equality.

courses.subject: SOWK
courses.title: Social Work, Sports, and Athletes
courses.description: Exploration of the interpersonal collaboration among athletic professionals and the role the social worker would provide to a team. Also, a discussion of direct practice approaches for youth, collegiate, and professional athletes from a micro mezzo and macro level.

courses.subject: SOWK
courses.title: Social Work, Sports, and Athletes
courses.description: Exploration of the interpersonal collaboration among athletic professionals and the role the social worker would provide to a team. Also, a discussion of direct practice approaches for youth, collegiate, and professional athletes from a micro mezzo and macro level.

courses.subject: SOWK
courses.title: Faculty-Mentored Undergraduate Research I
courses.description: Faculty-supervised independent or collaborative inquiry into fundamental and applied problems within a discipline that requires students to gather, analyze, synthesize, and interpret data and to present results in writing and other relevant communication formats.

courses.subject: SOWK
courses.title: Undergraduate Research Thesis (or Final Project)
courses.description: Faculty-supervised independent or collaborative inquiry into fundamental and applied problems within a discipline that requires students to gather, analyze, synthesize, and interpret data. Students will write or produce a thesis or other professional capstone product, such as a report or portfolio that describes their systematic and in-depth inquiry.

courses.subject: SOWK
courses.title: Foundations of Social Work Research
courses.description: Basic principles of social science research based on the scientific method.  Analytical and evaluative methods of knowledge building and application in social work and social welfare settings. Empirically based practice and the evaluation of the individual social worker's own practice interventions.
courses.course_objectives: demonstrate the nature of the scientific method and its relevance to professional practice in social work. Students will be able to demonstrate basic knowledge about research methodology (e.g., different stages of research; quantitative vs. qualitative) and its importance to social work practice. Students will be able to demonstrate the ability to analyze critically a social work research study regarding its methodological soundness and contribution to social work knowledge building. Students will be able to demonstrate skills that are necessary to design an evaluation of one’s own practice. Students will be able to demonstrate knowledge of program evaluation and the ethical use of scientific inquiry. Students will be able to demonstrate an ability to interpret the relevance to social work research of such client characteristics as age, race, gender, socioeconomic status, disabilities, and other factors.
courses.topical_outline:
Basic principles of social science research based on the
scientific method. Analytical and evaluative methods of
knowledge building and application in social work and social
welfare settings. Empirically-based practice and the evaluation
of the individual social worker's own practice interventions.
courses.prerequisiteText: (SOWK 2154 or SOWK 2154S) and SOWK 2155 and (SOWK 2156 or SOWK 2156E) and permission of department

courses.subject: SOWK
courses.title: Human Behavior in the Social Environment
courses.description: An ecological systems perspective for understanding human development and behavior in contemporary contexts. Students will acquire an understanding of foundational theories of human behavior, biological, psychological, and social dimensions of normative development over the lifespan, and the effects of oppression across multiple social systems.
courses.course_objectives: Students will be able to state the rationale for theory and research based social work practice. Students will be able to critically evaluate several theories used to describe human behavior. Students will be able to define human diversity and identify the risks to and strengths of several non-majority identificational communities. Students will be able to identify and describe key terms associated with the ecosystems perspective. Students will be able to analyze the well-being of individuals from an ecosystems perspective. Students will be able to analyze the well-being of families from an ecosystems perspective.
courses.topical_outline:
I. The ecosystems perspective and social work practice II. Community as a context for human development
A. Types of communities
B. Ethnic communities in America
C. The gay and lesbian community
D. Religious communities
E. Place-based communities III. Family as a context for human development
A. Family as an enduring social institution
B. Diversity in family lifestyles
C. Family as a social organization
D. Family in space and over time IV. Life course and transitions of living
A. Parental influences and early life
B. Childhood and early adolescence
C. Early and middle adulthood
D. Later adulthood

courses.subject: SOWK
courses.title: Disability and Social Justice: Practice, Policy, Research, and Advocacy Across the Lifespan
courses.description: Focuses on the diversity of disability and promoting social justice for people with disabilities and their families across the lifespan. Content includes disability models, U.S. disability history, challenges, available services, and social work’s role in supporting and advocating with disability subpopulations to improve access, equity, quality of life, and well-being.
courses.course_objectives: By the end of this course, students will be able to apply proper disability language and etiquette. By the end of this course, students will be able to contrast differing models of disability. By the end of this course, students will be able to examine ethical issues pertaining to the past, present, and future treatment of people with disabilities in society. By the end of this course, students will be able to identify and apply the principles of the disability justice framework. By the end of this course, students will be able to define and apply concepts of self-determination, community integration, and inclusion. By the end of this course, students will be able to understand the role of advocacy in shaping U.S disability policy. By the end of this course, students will be able to interpret policies that impact people with disabilities. courses.description: Social insurance, public assistance, and social service programs in the United States.  Social welfare within a capitalist economy and an individualistic, democratic society.  The influences of American economics and politics on social services and social work practice.  Introduction to models of policy analysis.
courses.course_objectives:
Students will learn to develop a working understanding of American social policy and the social
welfare system, its response to human need and its relation to the organized profession of social work. Emphasis is placed on identifying and examining social, political, economic, legal and cultural concepts that influence policy formation, program development and service delivery. The emergence of social work and the profession’s role in social welfare policy is emphasized.
courses.topical_outline:
1. Apply critical thinking skills and knowledge within professional contexts, especially with respect to theories and
knowledge about alternative paradigms for viewing individuals, families, groups, and communities. Practice Behaviors 2. Articulate the historical development of American social policy/social welfare system and the emergence and role of the social work profession. Practice Behaviors 3. Demonstrate an understanding of major historical events which influenced social thought and preceded the development of shifts in policy development. Practice Behaviors 4. Demonstrate an understanding of the role of government in the formulation, design, and implementation of social welfare programs. Practice Behaviors 5. Identify and apply principles of policy analysis to social problems for the purpose of problem resolution. Practice
Behaviors 6. Demonstrate an understanding of forms of oppression and discrimination that impact communities, families and
individuals and prepare to offer social and economic justice positions for those individuals and/or groups who are most vulnerable in those systems. Practice Behaviors 7. Demonstrate an understanding of values that under-gird social welfare policies and the social work profession.
Practice Behaviors

courses.title: Technology, Health Equity, and Social Transformation: Insights from South Korea
courses.description: Exploration of the transformative potential of digital health technologies in South Korea. With a focus on the intersection of technology, social determinants of health, and vulnerable populations, students will critically examine how innovations such as mobile health applications, telemedicine, wearable devices, and artificial intelligence are reshaping access to care.
courses.course_objectives: Students will be able to analyze the structural, social, and cultural determinants contributing to health disparities in South Korea. Students will be able to evaluate the effectiveness and limitations of digital health technologies (e.g., mobile health, telemedicine, wearables, AI) in improving health equity. Students will be able to apply policy and ethical frameworks to assess the implications of digital health interventions for underserved and vulnerable populations. Students will be able to critically examine case studies to identify best practices and barriers in implementing digital health strategies within Korean communities. Students will be able to integrate social work values and principles to design culturally responsive and socially just digital health interventions aimed at reducing disparities. Students will be able to reflect on personal and professional values to articulate the role of social workers in shaping equitable digital health futures.
courses.topical_outline: •	Historical overview of health disparities in South Korea •	Social determinants of health and their impact on vulnerable populations •	The rise of digital health technologies: mobile health, telemedicine, wearables, and AI •	Policy frameworks guiding digital health adoption in South Korea •	Ethical issues in digital health: equity, privacy, and accessibility •	Digital health applications in rural communities and underserved populations •	Case studies: successes and challenges of digital health in South Korea •	The role of social work in advancing digital health equity •	Integrating digital health into community-based care models •	Future directions: innovation, sustainability, and culturally responsive digital health strategies

courses.subject: SOWK
courses.title: Mental Health, Substance Use and Technology in South Korea
courses.description: Exploration of mental health and substance misuse in South Korea, with emphasis on technology as a tool in prevention, treatment, and policy. Students will engage with community organizations, health professionals, and policy leaders working to address gaps, while examining how technologies are leveraged to improve prevention, treatment, and recovery.
courses.course_objectives: Students will develop cultural awareness and understanding of South Korea through direct immersion in its communities, institutions, and social systems. Students will increase knowledge about the rising trends of depression, anxiety, and suicide in South Korea, and the societal factors contributing to these mental health challenges. Students will gain insight into the prevalence of substance misuse and co-occurring diseases, and critically examine the gaps in prevention, treatment, and recovery services. Students will explore the transformative role of technology—including digital health tools, AI, and mobile platforms—in addressing mental health and substance misuse disparities. Students will critically reflect on the intersections of culture, technology, and health equity, and how lessons learned in South Korea can inform global responses to mental health and addiction. Students will reflect on their group experience abroad, connecting it to personal and professional values, and identifying ways to integrate these lessons into future practice or research.
courses.topical_outline: •	The rising prevalence of depression, anxiety, and suicide in South Korea: historical and socio-cultural context •	Social stigma, systemic barriers, and inequities in mental health and substance misuse treatment •	The role of families, schools, and communities in shaping mental health outcomes •	Substance misuse in South Korea: trends, risk factors, and social implications •	Comparative perspectives: examining disparities in access to care between South Korea and other OECD countries •	Innovative models of prevention, treatment, and recovery support •	The transformative role of digital health technologies (e.g., telehealth, mobile apps, AI-based interventions) in addressing mental health and substance misuse •	Case studies of technology-enabled interventions for vulnerable and underserved populations •	Ethical considerations in applying technology to mental health care, including privacy, equity, and accessibility •	Policy and programmatic responses to mental health and substance misuse: gaps, opportunities, and future directions •	Reflections on cross-cultural perspectives and the implications for professional practice in health and social services

courses.subject: SOWK
courses.title: Human Behavior in the Social Environment
courses.description: An overview of typical and divergent developmental trajectories over the life course. This includes how biological, psychological, spiritual, interpersonal, family, community, socio-cultural, historical, and economic factors shape these trajectories. It also surveys major theoretical frameworks for explaining typical and divergent development in an environmental context.
courses.course_objectives: The student will be able to summarize key concepts and theories of human behavior in social environments. The student will be able to utilize critical thinking to: (a) evaluate and enhance existing theories of human behavior, person-in-environment and other interprofessional conceptual frameworks; and (b) propose innovative ethical solutions to address social work challenges in contemporary settings. The student will be able to apply knowledge of human development across the lifespan to address the diverse needs of social work clients and constituencies, with specific attention to neurobiological, psychological, cultural-historical, and socio-economic/socio-structural factors. The student will be able to explain the impact of family, group, community and broader systemic contexts on individual development, including both typical and divergent trajectories, and identify key risk and protective factors within these environments. The student will be able to demonstrate cultural humility by applying critical reflection and self-awareness of how personal experiences, values, biases and beliefs influence professional judgement and behavior.
courses.topical_outline: Process of social work: Importance of theory,  assessment, and intervention The Person-In-Environment: Systems Theory, Ecological/Transactional & Resilience Frameworks Biopsychosocial Dimensions: Psychodynamic, Behavior/Learning, Humanistic Theories Sociocultural Dimensions: Critical Theories, Social Constructionism Social Change Dimensions: Critical Race Theories, Feminist Theories, Queer Theories Biological, psychological, social, and spiritual dimensions of typical and atypical development over the lifespan (pre-pregnancy through late adulthood) and the interplay among these dimensions

courses.subject: SOWK
courses.title: Generalist Social Work Practice with Individuals and Families
courses.description: Course covers generalist micro-level social work practice emphasizing race, culture, gender, oppression, and social justice within an ecological systems framework. It develops essential skills, values, and professional relationships through discussions, role-plays, and case studies, focusing on client assessment and practice effectiveness evaluation using various models.
courses.course_objectives: The student will be able to demonstrate an understanding of the NASW Code of Ethics and models of ethical decision-making The student will be able to recognize the presence of bias, power, and oppression; use reflection and self-awareness to manage the influence of personal biases and values The student will be able to develop a strengths-based, culturally responsive, research informed biopsychosocial assessment that reflects understanding of the role of power, oppression, diversity and social justice in the client’s experiences. The student will be able to develop a family assessment and intervention plan that incorporates different theories of family processes in a culturally responsive manner. The student will be able to demonstrate an understanding of culturally responsive and research informed practice evaluation with individuals and families.

courses.subject: SOWK
courses.title: Introduction to the Social Work Profession and Practicum Education
courses.description: Course combines classroom learning and practicum experience to develop generalist social work skills. Covers interviewing, ethics, documentation, professional relationships, and agency policies. Students apply skills like communication, assessment, and organization in a practicum.
courses.course_objectives: The student will be able to apply social work values and ethical behavior in a social service agency. The student will be able to recognize personal values and exact professional social work values in practice situations. The student will be able to demonstrate understanding of a variety of social work roles associated with generalist practice. The student will be able to analyze three ways your practicum agency contributes to human and community well-being. The student will be able to manage ambiguity, challenges, communication, and conflict with clients and colleagues in a learning-centered, respectful, and productive way. The student will be able to develop self-awareness including managing personal bias, striving toward cultural humility, identifying strengths and areas for improvement, reconciling personal and professional values, and identifying the impact of personal experiences with privilege, power and oppression on development as a professional social worker.

courses.subject: SOWK
courses.title: Social Work with Groups
courses.description: This generalist practice course is designed to develop skills andtechniques necessary for practice in group settings. It willfocus on group dynamics and processes, group formation, and groupdevelopment. Other content areas include mutual aid, groupconflict, diversity, group facilitation, and values and ethics ingroup work practice.
courses.course_objectives: The student will be able to describe the historical, philosophical, ethical, and value- based context for the interface between group work and the field of social work. The student will be able to identify, select, apply, and evaluate appropriate theoretical frameworks for the use in groups. The student will be able to identify, select, apply, and evaluate appropriate group facilitation techniques for group work with diverse client populations and constellations. The student will be able to demonstrate understanding of basic concepts in group dynamics and the various stages in group development The student will be able to demonstrate understanding of the leader's role in group facilitation. The student will be able to articulate a beginning understanding of your personal group leadership style.

courses.subject: SOWK
courses.title: Generalist Social Work Practice with Communities and Organizations
courses.description: Theories and practices related to social work practice in communities and organizations are introduced by exploring several themes, including history of macro practice; understanding community and organizational problems; understanding and analyzing communities and organizations; building support for proposed change; selecting change strategies and tactics; and designing an implementation and evaluation plan.
courses.course_objectives: The student will be able to analyze a social issue/problem by calling upon relevant research, theory, and data sources (e.g., census data, interviews) to explore the prevalence, root causes, and related impacts on individuals, families, communities, and/or society. The student will be able to summarize the empirical and theoretical literature on interventions, policies, programs, etc. that have been used to address the identified social issue/problem. The student will be able to develop a macro intervention plan to address the identified social issue/problem, to include goals, objectives, required resources, stakeholders, and anticipated barriers to implementation.

courses.subject: SOWK
courses.title: Social Welfare Policies, Programs, and Issues
courses.description: Assists students in developing a working understanding of American social policy and the social welfare system and these systems’ responses to human need in relation to social work. Emphasis is placed on examining social, historic, political, economic, legal, and cultural concepts that influence service delivery.
courses.course_objectives: The student will be able to articulate the historical development of American social policy/social welfare system and the emergence and role of the social work profession. The student will be able to demonstrate an understanding of major historical events which influenced social thought and preceded the development of shifts in policy development. The student will be able to demonstrate an understanding of the role of government in the formulation, design and implementation of social welfare programs. The student will be able to identify and apply principles of policy analysis to social problems for the purpose of problem resolution. The student will be able to demonstrate an understanding of forms of oppression and discrimination that impact communities, families and individuals and is prepared to offer social and economic justice positions for those individuals and/or groups who are most vulnerable in those systems. The student will be able to demonstrate an understanding of values and ideologies that undergird social welfare policies and the social work profession. The student will be able to identify and apply policy action skills such as analysis, advocacy and policy development to enhance human rights, economic justice, social well-being and/or quality of social services.

courses.course_objectives: The student will be able to demonstrate professional behavior in a practicum setting, including the ability to utilize supervision and feedback. The student will be able to apply person-in-environment perspective to assess and intervene with clients, with an emphasis on external conditions that undermine social justice, economic justice, and environmental justice. The student will be able to embraces diversity and difference as sources of strength in assessment and intervention processes.

courses.subject: SOWK
courses.title: Social Work Research Methods
courses.description: This foundation course is designed to help students gain an understanding of and appreciation for the use of research as a tool for professional evidence-based practice.
courses.course_objectives: The student will be able to examine how research design choices such as conceptualization, sampling, instrumentation, data collection, and data analysis inform the validity and ethics of research evidence. The student will be able to apply insights from the research literature to inform social work policy and practice. The student will be able to evaluate the generalizability of research evidence to clients and communities that differ by age, gender, sexual orientation, race, ethnicity, and socioeconomic status and other characteristics. The student will be able to critique the presentation and synthesis of research evidence by popular media sources. The student will be able to assess the usefulness and limitations of emerging artificial intelligence tools in retrieving research evidence. The student will be able to the student will be able to plan and propose a project seeking to answer a key research question in an area of interest.
courses.topical_outline: Introduction to Social Work Research & Research Ethics Scientific inquiry in social work and the ethical, political, and cultural context of social work research Conceptualization: Literature Review, Theory, & Research Questions Research Designs I: Experimental & Quasi-Experimental Designs Research Designs II: Non-Experimental, Qualitative, & Mixed Methods Designs Measurement, Instrumentation and Data Collection Quantitative Analysis Planning Qualitative Analysis Planning Writing, Disseminating, and Translating Research Special Topics: Engaged and Participatory Research Special Topics: Internet and Data Science Research
