of the Swahili peoples Basic sound patterns and their cultural base Basic conversational structures: greetings, introducing oneself, how to start a
conversation, cultural and social codes in conversations Basic parts of speech: noun, pronoun, verb, adverb, adjective, preposition,
conjunction Basic sentence structure (focusing on pragmatics, grammatical relations of
sentence units that build up simple and complex sentences and their cultural base
interpretations) The cultural implications of voice: active and passive, causative, reflexives
(these will be introduced with reference to the different verb forms that affect
the overall meaning of a statement/utterance)

courses.subject: SWAH
courses.title: Intermediate Swahili I
courses.description: Introduction to complex linguistic and cultural structures, role of culture in language learning, reading and writing of literary texts, social history of the language.
courses.course_objectives: Students will create extensive spoken and written dialogues. Students will comprehend readings on the lifestyles, culture, customs, and traditions of the Swahili-speaking people. Students will demonstrate the ability to use their vocabulary-bank and computer assisted exercises to critique and advance their written and reading comprehension of literary texts, video, films, and slide shows. Students will show mastery of the language at an intermediate level with a proficiency testing level of Intermediate Mid/High, such as sustaining fifteen minutes of conversation with a native Swahili speaker. Students will evaluate key cultural issues associated with the language that were introduced in level one and reinforced at this level. Students will construct complicated sentences that are grammatically correct and pragmatically acceptable by native speakers, write a 1,000-word essay that may include a critical analysis of literary texts, reports/summaries.
courses.topical_outline:
Additional information on the history, culture, geography, environment,
and globalization issues Intermediate conversational structures: cultural and social codes in
conversation, understanding the role of metaphors, idioms, and proverbs in everyday
language use. More on parts of speech: noun, pronoun, verb, adverb, adjective, prepositions,
conjunctions as used in simple literary texts Sentence structure (focusing on complex grammatical relations of the units that
build up simple and complex sentences) Advanced use of voice: active and passive, causatives, reflexives Goal- and culture-based reading and writing tasks

courses.subject: SWAH
courses.title: Intermediate Swahili II
courses.description: A continuation of Intermediate Swahili I. Practical application of Swahili language skills and culture with native Swahili speakers residing within or near the Athens local community. Introduction to literary texts, poetry, newspapers and magazines, and everyday language use.
courses.course_objectives: At the end of this course, students will understand how to serve the local and broader community by assisting Swahili-speaking refugees with their day-to-day needs. At the end of this course, students will have gained hands-on experience communicating effectively with Swahili speakers. At the end of this course, students will be able to reflect on language and cultural experiences communicating with non-English speaking multi-age population. At the end of this course, students will be able to understand issues relating to the daily needs of Swahili speakers within an English-speaking context.
courses.topical_outline: Introduction to intercultural communication and principles of interpretation Additional information on the history, culture, geography, environment, and globalization issues Intermediate conversational structures: cultural and social codes in conversation, understanding the role of metaphors, idioms, and proverbs in everyday language use More on parts of speech: noun, pronoun, verb, adverb, adjective, prepositions, conjunctions as used in simple literary texts Sentence structure (focusing on complex grammatical relations of the units that build up simple and complex sentences) Advanced use of voice: active and passive, causatives, reflexives Goal- and culture-based reading and writing tasks

courses.subject: SWAH
courses.title: Intermediate Swahili II
courses.description: A continuation of Intermediate Swahili I. Practical application of Swahili language skills and culture with native Swahili speakers residing within or near the Athens local community. Introduction to literary texts, poetry, newspapers and magazines, and everyday language use.
courses.course_objectives: At the end of this course, students will understand how to serve the local and broader community by assisting Swahili-speaking refugees with their day-to-day needs. At the end of this course, students will have gained hands-on experience communicating effectively with Swahili speakers. At the end of this course, students will be able to reflect on language and cultural experiences communicating with a non-English speaking, multi-age population. At the end of this course, students will be able to understand issues relating to the daily needs of Swahili speakers within an English-speaking context.

courses.description: Faculty-supervised independent or collaborative inquiry into fundamental and applied problems within a discipline that requires students to gather, analyze, synthesize, and interpret data and to present results in writing and other relevant communication formats.

courses.description: Faculty-supervised independent or collaborative inquiry into fundamental and applied problems within a discipline that requires students to gather, analyze, synthesize, and interpret data and to present results in writing and other relevant communication formats.

courses.subject: SWAH
courses.title: Undergraduate Research Thesis (or Final Project)
courses.description: Faculty-supervised independent or collaborative inquiry into fundamental and applied problems within a discipline that requires students to gather, analyze, synthesize, and interpret data. Students will write or produce a thesis or other professional capstone product, such as a report or portfolio that describes their systematic and in-depth inquiry.

courses.subject: THEA(AFAM)
courses.title: History of African American Drama and Theatre
courses.description: The emergence of a distinct and conscious African American theatre in the United States.

courses.subject: THEA(AFST)
courses.title: History of Dramatic Art: Special Topics
courses.description: The history of dramatic art in the context of studies abroad programs.  Must be registered in the Studies Abroad Program and participate on-site.  Offered only in conjunction with Studies Abroad.
courses.offeredText: Not offered on a regular basis.

courses.subject: THEA(AFST)
courses.title: African Theatre: An Historical Overview
courses.description: The course will survey some of the major areas of theatreactivity, as well as provide a general history of African theatreand performance.  Playwrights well known in the West, such asWole Soyinka, Ngugi wa thiong'o, Femi Osofisan, and others willbe discussed, primarily within the context of their contributionsto African theatre on the continent itself.

courses.subject: THEA(LACS)
courses.title: Latin American and Caribbean Theatre and Performance
courses.description: Theatre and performance from several Latin American and Caribbean countries. Study of the history of theatre and performance in the region and a selection of plays by some of the best artists. Emphasis will be placed on theatre’s cultural influences and its sociopolitical role.

courses.subject: THEA
courses.title: Appreciation of Theatre
courses.description: Aesthetics and craft of the theatrical experience on stage, screen, and television. Discussions and analyses of all aspects of the theatrical arts; critical viewing of performances both in and out of class with written analyses. May not be used for credit towards the theatre major.
courses.course_objectives: Students will develop a working vocabulary pertinent to and descriptive of the elements and methodology of theatrical production. Students will study representative dramatic literature in its historical and theatrical contexts. Students will critically analyze selected theatrical productions.
courses.topical_outline:
A. Theatre Spaces: A look at the theoretical aesthetic and physical architecture of
entertainment.

B. Comedy: The history and theory of what makes us laugh.

C. Dramatic Structure; The mechanics of the script.

D. Writing on Theatre: How to write a basic theatrical review.

E. Acting: Techniques, theories, and history of the primary dramatic agent.

F. Direction: Techniques, theories and history of the director as artist.

G. The Playwright: Methods, theories and the people who write the script.

H. Multimedia: The current trends involving live performers and technology.

I. Lighting Design: The art of lighting in entertainment.

J. Costume Design: The aesthetics and practical aspects of what the actor wears.

K. Scenic Design: The physical environment of the entertainment experience.

L. The Craftspeople: Technicians, trade unions and the profession of technical
production.

M. Today's Theatre: Current trends in live theatre.

courses.subject: THEA
courses.title: Introduction to Acting
courses.description: Basic acting skills for non-theatre majors and theatre minors.
courses.course_objectives: Students will apply the actor's observational skills to daily life and its experiences towards the end of becoming a more artistically sensitive and informed audience member. Students will deploy basic imaginative, physical, and vocal skills necessary for acting. Students will organize a scripted scene for rehearsal. Students will appreciate and understand the cooperative nature of acting
courses.topical_outline:
A. The actor's instrument
B. Actor's process
C. Beginning text analysis
D. Character analysis
E. Rehearsal process
F. Actor critique skills

courses.subject: THEA
courses.title: Applied Drama Laboratory
courses.description: Individual production crew assignments for theatre majors.

courses.subject: THEA
courses.title: Applied Drama Laboratory
courses.description: Individual production crew assignments for theatre majors.

courses.subject: THEA
courses.title: Applied Drama Laboratory
courses.description: Individual production crew assignments (open to non-majors).

courses.subject: THEA
courses.title: Appreciation of Theatre (Honors)
courses.description: All aspects of the theatrical experience on stage and screen, emphasizing the role of the audience as well as that of the artist. May not be used for credit towards the theatre major.

courses.subject: THEA
courses.title: Voices of Diversity in American Drama and Theatre
courses.description: Survey of dramatic literature that foregrounds issues of race, gender, culture, and/or ethnicity.  Emphasis is placed on African American, Asian American, Latino/Latina, and Native American drama and theatre.  The origin and development of these theatre movements are contextualized within the social and cultural milieu of the times.
courses.course_objectives: Students will appreciate theatre and drama by, for, and about artists from diverse American backgrounds performing in various venues from Broadway, off-Broadway, off-off-Broadway and regional theatres in the United States. Students will understand theatre as an important facet of expression of all of the cultures under consideration in this class. Students will interpret and analyze how a play offers different possible meanings within multiple cultural contexts. Students will respond thoughtfully and critically to live performance and written scripts by playwrights and performers identifying with underrepresented social groups in American culture, using the vocabulary of the theatre.
courses.topical_outline:
Week One: Introduction and Historical Overview of American
Drama and Theatre

Week Two: African American Theatre History and Development

Week Three: Plays: Charles Gordone's NO PLACE TO BE SOMEBODY,
George C. Wolfe's THE COLORED MUSEUM, and August Wilson's JOE
TURNER'S COME AND GONE

Week Four: Plays: Alice Childress' WEDDING BAND: A LOVE/HATE
STORY IN BLACK AND WHITE and Ntozake Shange's FOR COLORED GIRLS
WHO HAVE CONSIDERED SUICIDE WHEN THE RAINBOW IS ENUFF

Week Five: Latino/Latina Theatre History and Development

Week Six: Plays: Luis Valdez' ZOOT SUIT, Jose Rivera's THE
HOUSE OF RAMON IGLESIA

Week Seven: plays: Milcha Sanchez-Scott's ROOSTERS and Nilo
Cruz's ANNA IN THE TROPICS

Week Eight: Asian American Theatre History and Development

Week Nine: Plays: Frank Chin's THE CHICKENCOOP CHINAMAN, David
Henry Hwang's M BUTTERFLY

Week Ten: Plays: Wakka Yamauchi's AND THE SOUL SHALL DANCE and
Philip Kan Gotanda's YANKEE DAWG YOU DIE

Week Eleven: Plays: Anuvab Pal's CHAOS THEORY, Aasif Mandvi's
SAKINA'S RESTAURANT, and Shishir Kurup's MERCHANT ON VENICE

Week Twelve: Selected plays by Filipino and Vietnamese authors

Week Thirteen: Native American Theatre History and Development

Week Fourteen: Selected plays by Native American playwrights

Week Fifteen: Research and Writing Projects and Conclusions

courses.subject: THEA
courses.title: American Ethnic Cinema (Honors)
courses.description: Cultural history of the most important ethnic film makers in the American cinema from the 1920's to the present, with emphasis on stories and styles of the films, as well as on the underlying economic and social contexts.
courses.offeredText: Not offered on a regular basis.

courses.subject: THEA
courses.title: Athletes and Artists: The Drama of Sports
courses.description: A theatre appreciation course for non-theatre majors who have an interest in sports. This course will investigate representations of athletes and/or athletic events and will also discuss the ways in which sports are a form of live performance/theatre.
courses.course_objectives: Students will understand how to effectively write response papers to department production in which they demonstrate critical thinking. Students will understand how to experience sports more critically as an important expression of American culture. Students will understand their own study and learning habits and how to improve upon them.
courses.topical_outline: A. Theatre Spaces: A look at the theoretical aesthetic and physical architecture of both entertainment and sports B. Dramatic structure: The Expectations of a Script, The Expectations of a Game, including thoughts on protagonists and antagonists and how these character “types” relate to favorite home teams vs. rivals C. Writing on Theatre: How to write a basic theatrical review D. Performance: From an Acting Standpoint: techniques, theories, and history of the primary dramatic agent. For the sports figure: this includes performance on the field, as well as behaviors in the public eye. We will also consider modes and definitions of performance using the performance studies paradigm(s). E. Direction: Techniques, theories, and history of the director as an artist, in relation to those who execute the playbook F. The Playwright: Methods, theories, and the people who write the script, in relation to those who create a playbook G. Multimedia: The current trends involving live performers, live performances, and live theatre and sports events, and how technology shapes the reception of a performance H. Lighting Design: The art of lighting in entertainment, including theatre spaces, nontraditional spaces, and sports venues (indoors and outdoors) I. Costume Design: The aesthetics and practical aspects of what the performer wears – including both the actor as well as the team colors and jerseys that codify a home team. J. Scenic Design: The physical environment of the sports and entertainment experience. K. The Craftspeople: Technicians, trade unions, and the profession of the technical production of a live performance event (theatre, concerts, fashion shows, operas, and sports events) L. Today's Athletes and Artists: Current trends in live theatre and how various sports are represented by twenty-first century plays and productions

courses.subject: THEA
courses.title: Theatre as Discipline and Profession
courses.description: Designed to help theatre majors navigate their college careers at UGA as well as prepare them for life post-graduation, while situating theatre in the liberal arts tradition. Theatre majors develop skills that can be applied to many professional arenas, both in the entertainment industry and beyond.
courses.course_objectives: Students will appreciate theatre as an art form and profession. Students will set ambitious goals for pursuing a career in the theatre. Students will understand the theatre-specific resources and opportunities available at UGA in order to make the best use of them on the path towards working in the theatre industry.
courses.topical_outline:
Unit 1: Theatre, Its Aesthetic, Its Process

A. An introduction to the theatre major and an understanding of
the different degrees offered at UGA and beyond (B.A., B.F.A.,
M.A., M.F.A., D.F.A., Ph.D.)

B. What is art? How do we define art? How do we differentiate
between art that is “good” and “bad”?

C. Elements of Drama

D. Creating a Cohesive Production/Collaboration in a Safe,
Respectful, Working Environment

Unit 2: What Does our Department Offer During Your Time Here?

A. Generalist Track; Department Opportunities and Career Options

B. Acting Track; Department Opportunities and Career Options

C. Directing/Stage Management Track; Department Opportunities and
Career Options

D. Design Track; Department Opportunities and Career Options

E. Writing Track; Department Opportunities and Career Options

F. Animation Track; Department Opportunities and Career Options

G. Theory/History/Dramaturgy Track; Department Opportunities and
Career Options

Unit 3: Planning Your College and Career Goals

A. Planning Your College Career - Student Groups, Leadership
Roles, Roles of Faculty, Staff, and Administration; Choosing a
Mentor

B. Resumes, Portfolios, Headshots, CV

C. Planning Goals Post Graduation - Five-Year Plan, Finances,
Life Skills, Budgeting

D. Interview Skills, Using the Career Center

courses.description: Creating costumes for performance. Study andexperience in methods of notetaking for costume fittings, production meetings, and rehearsals will be examined.

courses.description: Safety, scenery, lighting, audio, painting, props, budgeting, scheduling, management, projection, and more. courses.description: Participation in a series of group and individual activities designed to develop basic acting skills. The course also includes exercises for the actor's voice and body. Open only to Theatre majors, who should contact the department or instructor of record for permission to register.

courses.subject: THEA
courses.title: Voice and Movement Fundamentals
courses.description: Voice and movement fundamentals for the actor. Essential topicsinclude diagnosis of vocal and physical misuse; re-alignment ofthe spine; re-education of breathing, phonation, and physicalprocess toward healthy, connected use for stage; conditioning ofthe instrument; and broadening of vocal/physical repertoire forversatility in character development.

courses.subject: THEA
courses.title: Ensemble Acting and Devising
courses.description: Using various solo and ensemble-based collaborative techniques, students work together to create and perform devised works. The focus is on productive communication within groups of artists with the goal to foster bravery of imagination, and to empower these artists to create and produce their own work.
courses.course_objectives: Students will create original work in both collaborative ensemble settings and as solo pieces. Students will learn the dynamics of devising work in the complex community of other imaginative artists. Students will learn to devise methods from The Open Theater, Tectonic Theater Project, and Viewpoints. Students will gain the skills and confidence to share their ideas in a public performance. Students will discover effective ways to stage compelling performance pieces. Students will understand the strengths they bring to a collaborative ensemble and feel empowered to realize their vivid imaginations for an audience.
courses.topical_outline: 1. Exercises to foster ensemble: Group games and warm-ups help the ensemble feel comfortable with vulnerability and group creativity 2. Free Writing/Bringing Ideas to an Audience: Through journaling and writing prompts, students will discover the topics that are important to them, and practice ways to bring these ideas into performance 3. Solo Devised Projects: Each student will perform a short solo work of their own devising 4. Workshopping and Critical Reflection: Through discussion and observation, students discover effective devising strategies 5. Exercises to deepen the ensemble connection: Further games and activities embolden students to try unique things and make brave performance choices 6. Small Group Devised Projects: in groups of 3-5, students devise and perform pieces 7. Workshopping and Critical Reflection (see #4) 8. Full Ensemble Devised Project: Students are tasked with one devised piece that incorporates the voices of the entire class 9. Workshopping and Critical Reflection (see #4) 10. Final Project Presentation: Students share the full ensemble piece for an audience

courses.subject: THEA
courses.title: Improvise Your Way to Better Communication!
courses.description: This lively, experiential course uses improvisation techniques and games to help students in any major tap into spontaneity and impulses, communicate ideas more effectively, and build confidence in leadership and teamwork. Whether the student wishes to develop as an artist, teacher, scientist, manager, or writer, these fun improvisational tools will help students respond more authentically, boost creativity and imagination, and become more effective public speakers, actors, leaders, or collaborators.
courses.course_objectives: Students will develop proficiency in the basic principles of successful Improvisation. Students will experience basic long and short forms of Improvisation. Students will develop and hone ability to communicate ideas clearly and effectively. Students will enhance public speaking skills to confidently present in front of any audience. Students will strengthen capacity to listen and respond thoughtfully. Students will cultivate effective collaboration and teamwork abilities. Students will improve ability to adapt communication and behavior to various audiences and contexts. Students will build confidence in taking risks and embracing challenges. Students will practice the art of saying “Yes, and…” to foster creativity and progress. Students will boost spontaneity and quick-thinking skills. Students will develop the ability to be more flexible, present, and adaptable in any situation. Students will understand and leverage failures as opportunities for growth. Students will learn to accept and grow from constructive criticism. Students will conquer the inner “No” voice to achieve greater self-assurance.
courses.topical_outline: · Fundamentals of Improvisation: Guidelines to responding to impulses, generating ideas, and collaborating with spontaneity · Fundamentals of Clear and Effective Communication by knowing the Who, What, and Where: Understand your audience, yourself and everyone’s goals and how to make the adjustments needed to deliver you message confidently and have your voice heard · Building a Conversation through Collaboration: Listening to your partner, ego, and allowing yourself to accept and make offers through “Yes..and!” · Explore Improvisational Territories and Build Confidence: Develop spontaneity, confidence, and team skills through the exploration of different Improvisation territories including long form, short form, and improv “sports” games · Research Improvisation Companies, Important Figures, Cultural Practices, and Topics: Through individual research and presentation, students will become familiar with the important historical and cultural improvisational people and practices
courses.prerequisiteText: THEA 2000 or THEA 2010 or THEA 2500 or THEA 3500 or permission of department or permission of major

courses.description: Fundamental principles and practices in makeup for stage and media.  Drawing and face painting skills as well as practice in use of cosmetics, wigs, hair pieces, and  work with departmental productions.

courses.subject: THEA

courses.description: A foundation in acting for TV, film, and internet. Covers on-camera acting techniques, industry protocols, equipment, and terminology required to create successful screen performances. Also covers casting and audition strategies as well as how to work effectively with actors, directors, and cinematographers in production.

Other topics include the various roles of the art department, production cycles, and camera work.

courses.subject: THEA
courses.title: Theatre and Modernity
courses.description: Traces the history and legacy of key Modernist movements including psychological realism, epic theatre, symbolism, expressionism, theater of the absurd, theatre of cruelty, and postmodern theatre, among others. Explores the way the innovations, ideals, and controversies stemming from these movements continue to shape and inspire theatre artists in diverse ethnic communities across the world.

courses.subject: THEA
courses.title: Theatre and Society
courses.description: Examines theatre as a cultural form crucially interwoven with systems of social organization and government. As a forum for debate, a dangerous location to be regulated, a tool for molding citizens, or a revolutionary force; studies theatrical practices and dramatic literature across historical periods; global in scope.

courses.subject: THEA
courses.title: Theatre and Ritual
courses.description: Examines theatre as a cultural form crucially interwoven with systems of ritual as didactic and community bonding events. Exploration of ritual as an origin for theatre, although othertheories of theatre origin will be explored.  Studies theatrical practices and dramatic literature (global in scope).

courses.subject: THEA
courses.title: Women in Performance
courses.description: Women's contributions to the performing arts, focusing on contemporary American artists in such fields as theatre, film, dance, performance art, and other contemporary performance genres.
courses.course_objectives: Students will evaluate the human experience through the critical perspective of feminist drama, theatre, and performance. Students will critique theatre, drama, and performance from a feminist perspective. Students will appreciate plays, playwrights, performers, and directors who have contributed to the history of feminist theatre, performance, and theory. Students will apply histories and theories of feminist performance in the formulation of performance interventions into social issues.
courses.topical_outline:
I. The representation of women on the stage
a. Representative female characters in drama
b. A brief history of performance art
c. Feminism and performance art

II. Feminist theatre practice
a. From theory to practice
b. Representative feminist theatres

III. Women in performance, representative performance artists
a. Groundbreakers and pioneers
b. The contemporary scene

IV. Women and contemporary theatre
a. Playwrights
b. Directors

courses.subject: THEA
courses.title: Queer Theatre and Film
courses.description: Overview of the presentation of gay, lesbian, bisexual, andtransgendered characters in theatre, film, and television. Through readings of theoretical texts and dramatic scripts andthrough viewings of films and theatre productions, students willexamine the social, historical, artistic, and political contextin which queer performance has been created and the manner inwhich the queer character has been presented in dramatic formsfrom prehistoric ritual drama to the present day sitcom.
courses.course_objectives: Students will research a project and give a final presentation on Aspect of Queer Theatre and Film. Students will engage with LGBT history through Theatre and film throughout history. Students will create a performative response to text studies during course.
courses.topical_outline:
1. Defining Queer Drama
A. Manner and Style in which the following are presented
1.Sex
2. Sexuality
3.Gender
4. Sensibility/Camp
5.Closet Drama/Overtone
B. Looking through Queer Eyes
1. The Shift in “Reading” what is Queer: Pre Stonewall to Post
Stonewall to Post AIDS
2. The Need for a Mirror..Chasing Role Models
3. The Mirror Has Two Faces…Subversion
4. The Mirror Cracks…..Redefining the Queer
5. Is Queer always Gay? The Birth of the Homosexual vs. The
Birth of the Queer
2. Queer Theatre History: Pre 20th Century
A. Pre Christian Ritual
B. Greco/Roman Drama
C. Medieval Mystery Plays
D. Renaissance …Shakespeare, Marlowe
E. Restoration Comedies
F. Victorian….Wilde
3. Queer Theatre Film and TV: 20th Century
A. Early 20th Cent Themes
1.The Forbidden Love
2.The Predator
B. Mid 20th Cent Themes
1.The Closet
2. Better Off Dead
C. Late 20th Cent Themes
1.Gay Power and Pride
2. AIDS
4. Present Day Presentation of the Queer
A. Drag
C. Bisexuality
D. The power of the gay demographic…the queer TV Explosion
E. Where to now?

courses.subject: THEA
courses.title: Asian Theatre and Drama
courses.description: Genres of performance in India, China, Japan, and Southeast Asia.  Focus on social and cultural significance of performances, including examples of Noh, Kabuki, Beijing Opera, Kathakali, Kutiyattam, Wayang Kulit, and Topeng.
courses.offeredText: Not offered on a regular basis.

courses.subject: THEA
courses.title: Sustainable Theatres
courses.description: This class explores how theatre participates in multiple aspects of sustainability. Students will investigate how theatre engages with cultural diversity, social justice, and environmental activism. Students learn about theatre’s historical participation in these areas of sustainability and related theories. The course culminates in an immersive project of the students’ design.
courses.course_objectives: Students will understand how to contextualize the pillars of sustainability (environmental, economic, and social) within the framework of theatre and performance praxis. Students will understand how to discover twentieth- and twenty-first century theatre and performance artists who have contributed to a sustainable society. Students will understand how to explore sustainable models of theatrical production. Students will understand how to apply theories of sustainability through writing about contemporary theatre and performance. Students will understand how to synthesize sustainability histories and theories in the creation of an activist theatre project.
courses.topical_outline: Theatre and Environmental Activism Theatre and Society Sustainable Theatre Models Green Theatre
courses.prerequisiteText: THEA 2000 or THEA 2010 or THEA 2100H or THEA 2110 or THEA 2110E or THEA 3290 or THEA 3291H or ECOL 1000 or ETAP 5700 or FANR 1500 or LAND 2310 or permission of department

courses.subject: THEA
courses.title: The Broadway Musical and American Culture
courses.description: Studies the Broadway musical as one of the most quintessentially American forms of performance. Explores the history of musical theatre and its relationship to other entertainment media. Analyzes the messages about gender, race and ethnicity, sexuality, and the meaning of "America" that musicals have conveyed.

courses.subject: THEA
courses.title: Dramaturgy
courses.description: A dramaturg is a theatrical literary advisor, whoseresponsibilities include play development (including new plays,adaptations, or translations), production research and support,and educational support. Students will learn that set of skillsand how to communicate their knowledge productively.

courses.subject: THEA
courses.title: Performance Studies
courses.description: Performance studies human activity as culturally meaningful, from performance art to rituals of the everyday. A combination of critical perspectives can be used to study performance. This course introduces students to diverse approaches to performance studies through a variety of live, digital, historic events, written reflection, and immersive projects.
courses.course_objectives: Students will understand how to develop a working vocabulary pertinent to and descriptive of the elements and methodology of Performance Studies as a field distinct from theatre. Students will understand how to investigate representative historic, contemporary, and daily performances from the perspective of performance studies. Students will understand critical and creative methods used in performance creation and performance studies research. Students will understand how to apply performance studies methods in class and individual research projects.
courses.topical_outline: Foundations of Performance Studies Ritual, Identity, and Lived Experience Performance Art and Performance Research Play, Performance, and Performativity Performance Methods for Activism New Horizons in Performance Studies

courses.subject: THEA
courses.title: Topics in History
courses.description: Topical issues in theatre or cinema, combining history and critical analysis of specific significant topics (e.g., national theatre or cinema, animation, authorship, genre).

courses.subject: THEA
courses.title: Performance and Simulation
courses.description: Simulating physical, vocal, and psychological limitations in dramatic performances in addition to standardized and simulated patient and client encounters. Practice skills in live encounters with professional students training to become doctors, pharmacists, and veterinarians.
courses.course_objectives: This course encompasses acting technique and training of transferrable life skills such as empathy, communication, and presentation. Students will also learn how acting techniques inform their understanding of communication and how strong communications skills will enhance their acting. Students in this class will work with the College of Pharmacy, College of Veterinary Medicine, School of Social Work, and other UGA professional disciplines performing as standardized and simulated patients/clients for students studying to be our future health care professionals. In the latter half of the semester, we will work with students in a science writing course to develop scenarios related to the dangers of vaping. These scenarios will then be performed for a group of community members who are stakeholders in UGA's Archway Partnership program. The goal is to apply the research that the science writing students have done on vaping to scenario development, highlighting important issues about vaping and leaving space for audience participation.
courses.topical_outline:
• At least four class sessions focused on the nature of simulation across disciplines, defining key terms, and establishing a safe space to discuss issues around physical and mental illness.
• At least three class sessions focused on body awareness.
• At least nine class sessions of acting training focusing on portraying emotion as well as physical and psychological ailments.
• At least six class sessions at the medical, pharmacy, and vet schools performing in encounters. Students will portray patients/clients with emotional responses such as anger, anxiety, fear, shock, emotional shutdown, and physical ailments such as sore throat, abdominal pain, and ankle pain.
• At least five class sessions developing empathy and communications skills and working on ways students can give useful and effective feedback to students training to be doctors, pharmacists, and veterinarians.
• At least five class sessions analyzing plays, films, television, performance art, and news items related to issues surrounding physical, vocal, and psychological limitations.

Students will learn collaboration, creative problem-solving, and synthesis of skills as they gain practical experience in managing the logistics of a production. Students will prepare portfolios, resumes, and a digital showcase which will be made available online for production companies and casting directors.

Focusing on process, praxis, and synthesis, students mount workshop productions of original or known work. Opportunity for collaboration, with solo projects possible. Prepare post grad portfolios, websites, and create digital showcase. Meant to be taken in final semester.

Course participants are required to tour localperformance facilities.

Standard theatreorganizational structure, terms, scheduling, unions, stagemanagement, and technical coordination.

courses.subject: THEA
courses.title: Performing Physical Violence and Weaponry
courses.description: Students will explore the performance of physical conflict, learning basic techniques to stage violence and use prop weapons safely, accurately, and truthfully as an integral part of a storytelling. All terminology, skills, and assessments for staged combat will meet the Society of American Fight Directors’ standards, advancing students toward professional competency and successful S.A.F.D. proficiency test completion.
courses.course_objectives: Students will develop proficiency in the safety, performance, and weapon standards set by the Society of American Fight Directors through hands-on exploration of unarmed combat, quarterstaff, and single sword techniques. Students will confidently and skillfully collaborate in creating believable and safe staged physical violence choreography with scene partners and choreographers, with specific use of body and movement. Students will cultivate the discipline, specificity, and creativity needed to integrate and perform physical acting choices safely and accurately. Students will devise, notate, and perform choreography beats, rhythms, and story arcs with clarity. Students will enhance advanced performance skills through the deliberate and specific use of body and movement.
courses.topical_outline: 1. The Illusion of Conflict: Master the principles of safely and believably staging and performing violence that is consistent with the world of the script and its characters and tells a compelling story 2. Weapon Proficiency: Learn fundamental skills of unarmed staged combat 3. Weapon Proficiency: Learn fundamental skills of quarterstaff and pole arms 4. Weapon Proficiency: Learn fundamental skills of rapier sword play 5. Choreographing Staged Combat: Learn the construction and notation of staged violence choreography 6. Overview of Additional Theatrical Weapons and Fight Styles: Broadsword, Rapier and Dagger, Knives, Pole Arms, Found Objects 7. Firearms Safety: Explore standards for safety and use of firearms established by the Actors unions (AEA, SAG-AFTRA) 8. Overview of National and International Stage Combat and Stunt Organizations: Explore organizations that define the standards of safety and offer additional training and certifications in stage and film physical conflict, stunts, weapons, and firearms

courses.subject: THEA

courses.subject: THEA
courses.title: Musical Theatre Performance Styles
courses.description: Students will study and perform a range of musical theatre styles,including operetta, tin pan alley, and the modern musical. Students will learn how to analyze libretto and lyrics throughthe psychological lens of a character. Through readings, lecture,and practice they will understand how to better attack thevarious elements, structure, style, content, and purpose ofmusical theatre performances.

courses.subject: THEA
courses.title: Acting Styles

courses.subject: THEA
courses.title: The Meisner Technique
courses.description: An intensive study of the Repetition Exercise developed by Sanford Meisner.  By the end of the course, the student should have mastered the basic exercise, begun to respond honestly, impulsively, and with full emotional, vocal, and physical engagement to a partner and have applied the technique to thestudy of text and character.

courses.subject: THEA
courses.title: Acting for the Camera
courses.description: Applying theatre acting techniques to the demands of modern media.  Practical work in class with emphasis on the vocal and physical demands of dramatic material designed for television and cinema.
courses.course_objectives: To allow students freedom to creatively explore their vocal creation, placement, range, and strength To further develop student's knowledge of the role which relaxation, breath, articulation, and vocal production play in the development of character, intensity, mood, and style of a performance piece Through exercises done in and out of class, students shall experience the discipline required to keep the voice strong and pliable as required for performance Students shall be able to identify and correct specific breath and vocal habits which may be impeding their own growth as a performer and acknowledge the steps which must be taken to improve them Through the use of scene work and monologues, the students shall become aware of the importance that relaxation, breath, resonance, and articulation have in bringing deeper strength and personal meaning to their performance Students will be introduced to basic phonetics and the role it plays in researching and learning a stage dialect and will become proficient in the use of three standard stage dialects
courses.topical_outline:
The class time will be divided into two parts. The first half will involve relaxation, breath, and vocal exercises. These exercises will be built upon with each subsequent class session so that upon leaving the course, the student has established a full vocal warmup to be used outside of class. The second part will involve monologue and scene work concentrating on specific vocal goals that have been agreed upon through private meetings between teacher and student. The student shall prepare and perform two monologues and three scenes (final scene requires a dialect.) There will also be outside reading from the following texts:
Rodenburg, Patsy. The Right to Speak, Routledge, 1992
Rodenburg, Patsy, The Need for Words, Routledge, 1993
Blumenfeld, Robert. Accents: A manual for actors, Limelight, 2000 A. An overview of the vocal process and the mechanics of voice production

Topics include: light sources,luminaries, design considerations, lighting codes, andrecommended standards of architectural and landscape lighting. Practical exercises related to lighting a selection ofarchitectural environments (interior and exterior) as well asdesign documentation and specification practices.

courses.description: Practice and theory of interactive multimedia as a dramatic medium.  Multimedia hardware and software, principles of interactive design, and comparison of development tools and delivery systems including CD-ROM and the World Wide Web.

courses.subject: THEA
courses.title: Interactive Media as Drama II
courses.description: Advanced exploration of interactive media as a dramatic form, with an emphasis on algorithmic structures, self-generating media, adaptive behaviors, and object-oriented programming techniques.
courses.offeredText: Not offered on a regular basis.

courses.subject: THEA
courses.title: Performing with Media
courses.description: Explores how live performers interact with digital media to create dynamic performances. Students create original works and participatory environments incorporating interactive media, and study directors, designers, and artists who have integrated media into performance in innovative ways. No prior technical or performance experience required.
courses.course_objectives: Students will develop original performance works—including writing, acting, and directing—that creatively integrate live performance with digital media, demonstrating the ability to experiment, take risks, and refine work through iterative development and feedback. Students will distinguish among a range of functions that media can fulfill in live performance contexts, analyzing different modes of performer-media interaction and evaluating how these choices shape dramaturgical meaning and audience experience. Students will understand the development of digital performance from experimental practice to contemporary professionalization, critically examining the work of innovative theatre companies, directors, designers, and artists who have pioneered media integration in performance. Students will use digital media tools and technologies—including projection, interactive video, and sound design software—to create performance works, gaining hands-on skills in the technical processes required to realize creative concepts. Students will articulate creative concepts and technical requirements clearly in written, oral, and visual form, and give and receive constructive feedback to strengthen collaborative work and individual projects.
courses.topical_outline: Modes of interaction between live performers and media. Survey of innovative theatre companies, directors, designers, and artists who have pioneered media integration in performance. Scripting interactive and participatory events incorporating media. Performing interactively with media. Interactive media programming: creating linear and non-linear cues. Interactive media programming: audio and video effects. Interactive media programming: motion and audio tracking. Interactive media programming: particles. Interactive media programming: projection mapping.
courses.prerequisiteText: THEA 2000 or THEA 2500 or THEA 3300 or THEA 3500 or FILM 2120
courses.offeredText: Not offered on a regular basis.

courses.title: The Moving Body Expresses
courses.description: The course begins by diagnosing the individual's accustomed use of the body, employing the theories of F.M. Alexander to examinealignment and conditioning of the body in neutral. Drawing fromdiverse vocabularies such as Feldenkrais, modern dance, andcontact improvisation, we explore the organic use of the body inmotion.
courses.offeredText: Not offered on a regular basis.

An exploration of movement and gesture for blue-screen,green-screen, and motion-capture work comprises one unit of the class.

courses.subject: THEA
courses.title: Creating Physical Performance
courses.description: Exploration of essential movement and characterization usingneutral and character masks and techniques adapted primarily fromtheories of masters of theatrical mask, such as Jacques LeCoq.

courses.description: Voice II focuses on speech and dialect addressing issues such asarticulation, diction, dialect reduction, standard Americanspeech, and dialect using IPA and Lessac's vocal notion as tools.

courses.subject: THEA

Learn tools to document theircreative work as applied scholarship. Develop critical assessmenttools for artistic process. Create CV's, teaching philosophies,and practice academic interviews.

courses.description: Development of consistent acting process through partner work, exercises, scenes, play and character analysis, scoring a role,and Stanislavski's method of physical action.  Additional majorfocus will be on the actor's creative self and development of theinner instrument.

Through readings of theoretical texts, dramaticscripts, and practical application, students will be introducedto the concepts of ritual drama, playmaking through group theatretechniques, solo performance, and postmodern deconstruction asapplied to performance.

courses.subject: THEA
courses.title: Art Direction for Film and Television
courses.description: Provides a foundation in taking a script through the transformative process from written word to visual image. Explores the workings of a typical art department and the working relationships between the director, director of photography, and production designer. Other topics include the various roles of the art department, production cycles, and the scenery design and build process.
courses.course_objectives: By the conclusion of this course, the student will understand the world of design and how it impacts the effectiveness of storytelling. By the conclusion of this course, the student will have the ability to watch, analyze, and discuss design choices in a film or television show and describe how those choices contribute to the overall whole. By the conclusion of this course, the student will have the ability to respond to a script through visual research and sketches, creating a unified design approach. By the conclusion of this course, the student will understand budgeting and standard paperwork used in production. courses.description: The theoretical concepts of ecofeminism and ecowomanism applied to the four pillars of sustainability. A survey of the environmental, economic, social, and cultural concerns of the global fashion industry and the current tools and methodologies available to improve it.
courses.course_objectives: Students will be able to understand the four pillars of sustainability and their application within the fashion industry. Students will be able to analyze and apply sustainability theories and corporate social responsibility principles to the fashion industry. Students will be able to critique diverse approaches to sustainable fashion design, production, consumption, and disposal, with a focus on environmental and social justice. Students will be able to evaluate the challenges and opportunities fashion brands face when adopting sustainable business models and implementing corporate social responsibility. Students will be able to develop and communicate innovative sustainability projects and ideas through written, oral, and visual formats, using relevant technology for professional development.
courses.topical_outline: What do ecofeminism and ecowomanism have to do with fashion ethics and sustainability? Overview of sustainability and social change; Colonization, the root of the problem Diversity, equity, inclusion, and social justice Product life cycle; What’s in your closet Longevity of use Cultural sustainability Supply chain assurance and transparency Sustainable business logistics and distribution Sustainable communities Goals, plans, and trends in creating sustainable supply chains Corporate social responsibility

Students will analyze personal design direction and effectively communicate and target potential brands and/or companies for job search. Students will cultivate the ability to work up color palettes and schemes in a variety of methods to apply to both hand and digital surface designs.

courses.subject: TXMI
courses.title: History of Dress and Fashion: Nineteenth Century to the Present
courses.description: Interrelationship of dress and social, cultural, political, and economic environments from the late nineteenth century to contemporary times.
courses.course_objectives: Students will participate in an active learning community. Students are expected to take responsibility for their own learning and to encourage one another as well as the instructor to constantly improve the learning environment in the classroom. Students will develop critical thinking skills that would allow them to interpret and analyze relevant information related to the history of dress while they apply this knowledge to their specific majors and using adequate terminology. Students will communicate and express opinions, ideas, and concepts in an organized manner, thus making important contributions to the learning process of the class. Students will comprehend the historic development of clothing and textiles in the context of a specific time period and geographical location with an emphasis on the study of the history of clothing from the mid 1800s thru contemporary times. Students will identify the influence of cultural values, ethnic background, class, and gender in the development of clothing and textiles during the 20th century with some knowledge building in the 19th and 21st centuries. Students will identify the influence of customs, art, religion, economy, politics, and technological advancements in the historic development of clothing and textiles. Students will develop an appreciation for historic clothing and textiles as an inspiration for contemporary designs and trends. Students will identify specific contributions of the figure of the designer and other fashion innovators in the historical development of clothing and textiles. Students will determine the relation between specific cultural background and contemporary trends in clothing and textiles. Students will gain understanding of the interrelatedness of cultural diversity and the development of twentieth century fashion by recognizing multi-cultural influences on fashionable dress. (For the graduate-level course). Students will develop original research on historic dress demonstrating appropriate research and writing skills. Students will analyze, evaluate, and cite published research in the historic dress field and evaluate relevant theoretical frameworks.

Methodology and Historical consideration. Functions of Clothing. Overview of the Eighteenth Century and its relationship to the development of the
modern fashion system of design and merchandising Introduction to Romantic Period, Crinoline Period, Bustle Period Movement through decades of merchandising, design, and lifestyle development in the
20thc Charles Frederick Worth and the development of Haute Couture Mass market development of ready to wear, mass sizing, factories Subculture, pop culture, media developments and advancements Designers names and accomplishments including projects on under recognized
designers/brands Art movements such as Art Nouveau, surrealism, pop art, op art, art deco, graffiti Major designers and brands of Europe and the US also with projects that expand
students knowledge into global design history parallel to the same time period chapters Gender, war, youth culture, commerce, sport, technology, art, all impacting design and
merchandising history

Overview of the Eighteenth Century and its relationship to the development of the modern fashion system of design and merchandising Introduction to Romantic Period, Crinoline Period, Bustle Period Movement through decades of merchandising, design, and lifestyle development in the 20thc Charles Frederick Worth and the development of Haute Couture Mass market development of ready to wear, mass sizing, factories Subculture, pop culture, media developments and advancements Designers names and accomplishments including projects on under recognized designers/brands Art movements such as Art Nouveau, surrealism, pop art, op art, art deco, graffiti Major designers and brands of Europe and the US also with projects that expand students knowledge into global design history parallel to the same time period chapters Gender, war, youth culture, commerce, sport, technology, art, all impacting design and merchandising history

courses.subject: TXMI
courses.title: Studio V: Innovative Residential Interior Design
courses.description: Evaluation, design, and advanced space planning of residentialenvironments with consideration of new and current architecturaland interior design industry trends, including sustainability,prefabricated, temporary, and multifamily.

courses.subject: TXMI
courses.title: Professional Practices in Interior Design
courses.description: Explore relationships between the designer, wholesaler, and retailer in the home interiors industry. Particularly, designer and client relationships that emphasize retailing practices and economic resources in the interior design firm. Additionally, introduce business concepts, models, and professional skills associated with interiors. Students furthermore will develop a professional portfolio.
courses.course_objectives: To become familiar with business principles and practices of the interior designer To become familiar with the interaction that takes place between the client, the designer, and the trade sources To become familiar with current issues in the furnishings and interiors field Examine professional skills necessary to work in the furnishings and interiors industry Develop understanding and application of presentation software Complete projects and activities designed to prepare students for internships in furnishings and interiors Understand client issues and consumer behavior related to furnishings and interiors
courses.topical_outline: Relationship between designer, wholesaler, and retailer in the home interiors industry Understand client issues and consumer behavior related to furnishings and interiors Residential space planning Selection of fabrics, finishes, and furnishings Economic resources Introduction to professional skills Current issues in the furnishings and interiors field Presentation and portfolio software for the industry Entrepreneurship and the furnishings and interiors industry Company culture Developing a professional portfolio

courses.subject: TXMI
courses.title: American Historic House Museums
courses.description: In-depth study of the history of and relevant issues related to historic house museums in America.  Small- and large-scale,privately and publicly owned, non- and for-profit house museumswill be covered.  Restoration practices for historic interiorsand homes will also be applied into several projects.

courses.subject: TXMI
courses.title: History of Design, Interiors, and Furnishings I
courses.description: The architecture, interiors, and furnishings in the western world from the ancient Egyptian era to the industrial revolution.
courses.course_objectives: Students will gain an understanding of the influence social sustainability has on the re-use and re-purpose of architectural furniture design. Students will gain an understanding of elements through the ages. Students will begin a personal visual reference library of classical architectural elements that have been re-purposed throughout various historical periods.
courses.topical_outline: Thonet, Shakers Arts and Crafts Art Nouveau and De Stilji Pre-World War I Modern Movement Post Modernism Deconstructivism Sustainability/Eco Design Present Day

courses.subject: TXMI
courses.title: Decorative Arts and Antiques
courses.description: Historical and cultural development of accessories used in the home including ceramics, metals, and textiles.  Design and characteristics of materials in these accessories will be covered.

courses.subject: TXMI
courses.title: Interior Fabrics and Materials: Specifications and Estimations
courses.description: Construction, fibers, and finishes for fabrics with emphasis on quality, durability, and utilization of current materials for soft floor coverings, window treatments, and upholstery.  Estimations and specifications.
courses.course_objectives: Students will become aware of the factors to consider when evaluating and selecting textile materials for interiors and to use these factors to make appropriate choices. Students will be able to accurately estimate amounts of textile products needed for a given situation.
courses.topical_outline: 1. Codes and Regulations 2. Window Treatments - Functions Criteria for Selection and Estimations 3. Floor Coverings - Functions Criteria for Selections and Estimations 4. Upholstery - Functions Criteria for Selection and Estimations 5. Analysis of Performance and Criteria of Textiles for Interiors
courses.prerequisiteText: TXMI 3500 | Graduate Prerequisite | TXMI 3500 or permission of department

courses.subject: TXMI
courses.title: Studio VI: Advanced Residential Design Method
courses.description: In-depth study of the design process as it applies to the designof residential spaces, advanced space planning techniques,analysis/synthesis methods used in designing interiors, anddesigning within specified economic constraints.  Application ofthis knowledge to comprehensive studio projects.

courses.subject: TXMI
courses.title: Studio VI: Advanced Universal and Sustainable Residential Design with Service Learning
courses.description: Students will apply program of study and course knowledge/skills to service projects to solve real-world problems. Over half of assignments will pertain to service learning to enhance students' practical design experiences working with real clients. Topics explored range from sustainability to adaptive reuse and aging-in-place to cultural adaptation.

courses.subject: TXMI
courses.title: Entrepreneurship for Product Development
courses.description: Explores the basics of the entrepreneurial process in the field of textiles, merchandising, interiors, and product development. Students engage in hands-on projects, empathize with stakeholders, define challenges, prototype solutions, and scale ideas into impactful ventures. The course bridges social and business entrepreneurship to innovate and create meaningful, market-ready solutions.
courses.course_objectives: Students will be equipped with the tools and knowledge to ideate, prototype, and develop market-ready products. Students will foster an entrepreneurial mindset, focusing on innovation, market fit, and scalability. Students will be able to teach practical applications of interdisciplinary collaboration for product development. Students will participate in experiential learning opportunities through projects that address social and market challenges.
courses.topical_outline: 1.	Introduction to entrepreneurship and product development. 2.	Ideation, prototyping, and market research. 3.	Building business models and identifying market opportunities. 4.	Strategies for scaling and launching products. 5.	Social impact and sustainable product development. 6.	Collaboration and presentation of final projects.
courses.prerequisiteText: Permission of department | Graduate Prerequisite | Permission of department

courses.subject: TXMI
courses.title: History of Design, Interiors, and Furnishings II
courses.description: The architecture, interiors, and furnishings in the western world from the ancient Egyptian era to present day.
courses.course_objectives:
Students will understand the historical, social, political, economic and industrial influences upon the evolution and development of architecture, interiors, and furniture design. Students will become familiar with the various eras and styles of historic architecture and interior design by recognizing significant works and understanding the philosophies and influences of the contributors. Students will gain knowledge of and identify individual characteristics and structural details of historic architecture, interiors, and furnishings. Students will become familiar with the various areas of contemporary furniture design by recognizing significant works and understanding the philosophies of the contributors. Students will effectively assimilate, analyze, and present course content in written forms. Students will develop the ability to present academic material in a professional manner. Students will gain an understanding of the influence social sustainability has on the re-use and re-purpose of architectural elements through the ages.
· Begin a personal visual reference library of classical architectural elements that have been re-purposed throughout various historical periods.
courses.topical_outline: 1. Eighteenth-Early Nineteenth Centuries 2. Thonet, Shakers 3. Arts and Crafts 4. Art Nouveau and De Stilji 5. Pre World War I 6. Modern Movement 7. Post-modernism 8. Deconstructivism 8. Deconstructivism 9. Sustainability/ Eco design 10. Present Day

courses.subject: TXMI

courses.description: A study of the various segments of the textile and apparel industry, including analysis of the market structure and how each segment functions. Also includes factors currently affecting the industry.
courses.prerequisiteText: TXMI 3210 or TXMI 3210E | Graduate Prerequisite | Permission of department

courses.subject: TXMI
courses.title: Virtual Garment Prototyping
courses.description: Course provides a comprehensive introduction to 3D apparel design, focusing on garment simulation and its applications in the fashion industry. Students will develop skills in using specialized 3D CAD software to create and visualize designs and explore how physical textile properties affect the drape and fit of virtual garments.
courses.course_objectives: Students will gain a foundational understanding of 3D garment simulation concepts and their application in the fashion industry. Students will develop proficiency in using specific 3D virtual garment simulation software for creating and visualizing fashion designs. Students will understand how to simulate various fabric types and textures in 3D software, including color, print, and other material properties. Students will master 3D modeling techniques for creating realistic garments, including complex structures and details. Students will learn to adjust and fine-tune garment sizing and fit in a virtual environment for different body types. Students will acquire skills in rendering high-quality images of 3D garments for presentations, including understanding lighting and camera angles.
courses.topical_outline: •	Interface •	Stitch and 3D Simulation •	Pattern Drafting and Modification •	Styling and Layering •	Material Properties and Library •	Colorways and Tech pack •	Rendering and Showcase
courses.prerequisiteText: TXMI 3540 or permission of department | Graduate Prerequisite | Permission of department

courses.description: An overview of the fashion product development process and brand management tactics used in fashion industry. Integrating hands-on activities and projects, methods by which apparel companies create and manage their fashion products for the target customers will be discussed.

courses.description: Retailing, retail organizational structures, merchandising, and organization of market resources from national and global perspectives. Emphasizes concepts applicable to the apparel and textile industry.

courses.title: Retailing Apparel and Textiles
courses.description: Retailing, retail organizational structures, merchandising, and organization of market resources from national and global perspectives. Emphasizes concepts applicable to the apparel and textile industry.

courses.title: UX/UI Design Fundamentals in Fashion Branding
courses.description: Course combines design, technology, and branding. Human factors, usability, user experience (UX), and creating efficient, high-quality user interfaces (UI) for current fashion brands will be covered.

courses.subject: TXMI
courses.title: Retail Entrepreneurship
courses.description: Targeted to students interested in creating and growing their own retail business. This course is approached from a business perspective by combining the practical realities of creating and running a retail business through the operation of Couture a la Cart with the imaginative process that only successful entrepreneurs can cultivate.
courses.course_objectives: Students will demonstrate the knowledge and skills to implement and sustain a business concept, Couture a la Cart on the UGA campus. Students will compare and contrast the successes and challenges of past iterations of CALC to inform decision making and set realistic goals. Students will act as a CALC employee working individually and cross-functionally in a team environment. Students will understand the necessity of vulnerability, risk taking, and failure as components of innovation and critical problem solving.
courses.topical_outline:
•	Entrepreneurial endeavors and job responsibilities
•	Metrics of success, mission statement, entrepreneurial vision
•	Consumer analysis and budget proposals
•	Product mix, procurement, and vendor relations
•	Location analysis, permissions, and golf cart preparation
•	Marketing and merchandising
•	Go to market, selling season and ongoing analysis
•	Concluding selling, vendor payouts, budget finalization, and final reporting

courses.subject: TXMI
courses.title: Textile Design and Fabrication
courses.description: This course explores the design and creation of woven and knitted textiles using digital tools. Students will learn to design textiles through specialized software and translate their designs into physical form using textile machinery. The course emphasizes understanding fabric structures, properties, and the process of moving from design to fabrication.
courses.course_objectives: Students will gain a foundational understanding of woven and knitted textile design principles and their applications in fashion industries. Students will develop proficiency in using software tools for designing digital woven and knitted textiles. Students will fabricate creative textile structures and interpret their behaviors. Students will understand the process of translating digital textile designs into physical fabrics. Students will acquire the skills to work with textile machinery and understand the key factors in achieving quality and troubleshooting.
courses.topical_outline: Principles of woven and knitted textile structures Digital textile design software Design translation for production Machine operation and fabrication techniques Industrial textile machinery Nonwovens and braids

courses.description: An on-location study of clothing, textiles, fashion merchandising, and residential interiors and furnishings.  Includes lectures by recognized leaders in the fields; meetings with designers, manufacturers, merchants and field trips to designers' showrooms or studios, manufacturing plants, distribution centers, retail stores, and museums.

courses.subject: TXMI
courses.title: Fashion Merchandising Capstone
courses.description: Represents a final experience for Fashion Merchandising majors. Students work in teams that reflect the roles and functions in the industry, showing a balanced input from design and merchandising. Students develop their professional identity and apply the knowledge and skills they have gained throughout the major for industry readiness.
courses.course_objectives: Students will understand how to analyze the current market, competitive landscape, and marketing and promotional strategies for an apparel brand or fashion retail business. Students will understand how to develop a market-responsive apparel product line for an apparel brand or fashion retail business. Students will understand how to create merchandising and assortment recommendations for an apparel brand or fashion retail business. Students will understand how to examine various factors from the FACS Body of Knowledge and assess the impact on consumers fashion choices and merchandising strategies. Students will understand how to demonstrate cross-functional team collaboration and effective communication and presentation skills for fashion industry professional settings. Students will understand how to compose a professional persona representing the culminating experience of the fashion merchandising major in preparation for post-graduation industry placement.
courses.topical_outline: Cross-functionality: How each role works in tandem Analyzing the market and competitive landscape Product Development: From concept to creation Responding to the Market: Making choices that reflect what consumers want Merchandising: Choosing what goes to sale and how The professional sphere

courses.subject: UNIV
courses.title: Introducing English Composition
courses.description: This course intends to help students develop skills necessary forsuccess in English Composition I.
courses.course_objectives: By the end of this course, students will develop and understand transferable reading and writing skills necessary for success in English Composition I and beyond. By the end of this course, students will compose written products that reflect a critical thought process and focused revising. By the end of this course, students will construct written products demonstrating critical development and creative support for an argument. By the end of this course, students will respond to nonfiction text and documentary film through writing and active learning processes. By the end of this course, students will employ formal academic English.
courses.topical_outline: Understanding sentence grammar, structure, and syntax Review of MLA format, its construction, and use Reading texts and constructing an argument from text-based analyses Four major writing assignments Four shorter writing activities

courses.subject: UNIV
courses.title: Essentials of Math Modeling
courses.description: This course intends to help students develop skills necessary forsuccess in Introduction to Mathematical Modeling.
courses.course_objectives: By the end of this course, students will develop and understand transferable math modeling skills necessary for success in Introduction to Mathematical Modeling and beyond. By the end of this course, students will use graphing calculators to solve, graph and analyze functions. By the end of this course, students will understand functions and be able to use and interpret function notation. By the end of this course, students will create and use linear, quadratic, exponential, and logarithmic functions to solve real world problems. By the end of this course, students will analyze and interpret real world data by choosing the appropriate functional model.
courses.topical_outline: Functions definitions Domain and range Functions defined by tables, graphs, and formulas Average rate of change Increasing and decreasing functions Modeling with linear functions Constant rate of change and linear growth Equations of lines Linear functions Fitting linear models to data Modeling growth with quadratic functions Quadratic functions, graphs, maxima and minima, and applications Fitting quadratic models to data Modeling with exponential and logarithmic functions Percent increase and decrease Simple interest Exponential functions and their graphs Natural growth and decline Fitting exponential models to data Continued/compound interest

courses.subject: UNIV
courses.title: Introduction to Pre-Calculus
courses.description: This course intends to help students develop skills necessary forsuccess in Precalculus.

courses.subject: UNIV
courses.title: Supplemental Instruction for Precalculus
courses.description: Students will develop skills to be successful active learners within a variety of instructional modalities in this course that serves as a co-enrollment for Precalculus. Students will learn to engage peers and instructors; embrace collaborative learning and study groups; reflect on their progress and strategies; and adapt based on self-reflection and results. This course will fuse these topics with the curriculum of Precalculus to help students develop the skills they need to successfully complete Precalculus.
courses.course_objectives: By the end of this course, students will identify oscillatory, exponential/logarithmic, and polynomial behavior and derive appropriate functions to approximate the behavior. By the end of this course, students will state the definition of a function and determine the domain and range of a function as well as determine if the function has an inverse and be able to define the inverse. By the end of this course, students will provide and defend arguments for conclusions using correct mathematical notation and justify intermediate steps. By the end of this course, students will read a problem statement and determine a set of steps to answer the question using a formal and effective problem-solving strategy. By the end of this course, students will manipulate relationships to correctly and efficiently isolate a variable of interest.
courses.topical_outline: - Review of algebra topics - Functions and function notation. Finding intercepts, domain, and range - Average rate of change and forms of lines, modeling problems with linear relationships - Basic graphs and transformations. courses.subject: UNIV
courses.title: Learning for Success at the University
courses.description: This course provides students opportunities to obtain skills thatlead to success in college and beyond including learning how tolearn, motivation, critical and creative thinking,decision-making, identity development, wellness, and careerchoice. The hallmark of this course will be an active-learningenvironment focused on application of skills and content.
courses.course_objectives: By the end of this course, students will independently acquire and practice evidence-based learning strategies, increasing their skills as learners. (e.g., metacognitive learning strategies, active learning techniques, collaborative learning). By the end of this course, students will demonstrate greater academic engagement within the behavioral, psychological, and cognitive domains. By the end of this course, students will practice self-regulated learning skills and employ self-directed learning behaviors. By the end of this course, students will assess and increase their current competencies in developmentally based life-skills across several domains germane to success in college and beyond (e.g., Chickering’s Vectors, Gazda’s life-skills).
courses.topical_outline: •Academic motivation for learning and engagement •Identity Development •Time-management •Stress-management •Metacognition: understanding learning and using memory strategies •Self-regulated learning •Getting the most out of campus resources and support services •Organization for the “best self”: goal setting, boosting concentration, limiting distractions, and managing personal wellness

courses.title: Becoming Active Learners
courses.description: Students will develop skills to be successful active learners within a variety of instructional modalities. Students will learn to engage peers and instructors; embrace collaborative learning and study groups; reflect on their progress and strategies; and, adapt based on self-reflection and results.
courses.course_objectives: Students will be able to capitalize on a personal understanding of the culture and expectations of higher education, particularly those of a research university. Students will be able to engage in self-motivation practices to maintain interest in academic content given common instructional modalities in college (lecture, online, seminar). Students will be able to maintain behavioral, psychological, and affective engagement in common educational delivery modalities (small and large-group discussion, game-based learning environments, student-led seminars). Students will be able to engage active learning strategies conducive to success in specific content-courses. Students will be able to thrive in out-of-class active learning strategies conducive to success in specific content-courses (group projects, case studies).
courses.topical_outline: Psychological, behavioral, and affective aspects of engaged learning Theory and practice of science of motivation Maintaining interest and locating personal success in innovative academic environments Active learning environments, expectations, and techniques for success
