courses.subject: UNIV
courses.title: Starting Strong: Introductory Seminar for Scholars
courses.description: This course provides first-year Scholars opportunities to practice skills regarding motivation, academic, and careerexploration; develop academic and professional skills; and,prepare for academic success at UGA. A cohort-based approach, the class builds a sustainable community during students' entry to the University.
courses.course_objectives: By the end of this course, students will articulate their educational goals and future academic goals. By the end of this course, students will develop and sustain a strategic academic plan using requisite coaching and advising resources (e.g., Academic Coaching, Academic Advising, DegreeWorks, Exploratory Center, Mentors, and Career Center). By the end of this course, students will utilize learning strategies to maintain high levels of active cognitive engagement within varied academic environments, and with complex scholarly content to sustain necessary academic momentum and progress. By the end of this course, students will regulate their productive, growth mindset when confronted with ideas, beliefs, attitudes, and behaviors that are different from their own. By the end of this course, students will apply understandings of motivational and attitudinal concepts as they relate to academic work and endeavors including, but not limited to self-determination, motivation, mindsets, tenacity, grit, resilience, and perseverance.
courses.topical_outline: Goal setting Mindset Grit Achievement behaviors Professional communication skills Motivation Evidence-based Academic Success Strategies Metacognition

courses.subject: UNIV
courses.title: Preparing for Peer Learning: Undergraduate Facilitator Training
courses.description: The purpose of this course is to teach and enhance the skillscharacteristic of peer instruction, explore relevant research andevidence-based practices, and create dialogue on peer-to-peerlearning at the University.
courses.course_objectives: By the end of this course, students will evaluate and apply metacognitive learning strategies to their learning. By the end of this course, students will illustrate the different approaches to learning and identify the mechanisms to support their learning and the learning of their peers. By the end of this course, students will effectively communicate ideas, thoughts, and knowledge to their peers to support their learning. By the end of this course, students will identify and explain the appropriate academic and non-academic campus resources to their peers depending on the circumstances/situations they disclose.
courses.topical_outline: Orientation to the higher education classroom and the peer-to-peer instructional experience Preconceptions and their influence on learners Understanding (meta)cognition Exploring and enhancing student motivation Factors affecting classroom climate Addressing challenging classroom scenarios Modeling teaching evaluations with mid-term course evaluation How do students develop mastery? Promoting self-directed learning in students How does feedback improve learning? The various skills and roles of teachers Discussion of emerging identity and teaching philosophies Presentations of capstone teaching philosophies Program evaluations

courses.subject: UNIV
courses.title: Learning Online: Strategies, Skills, and Success
courses.description: This course prepares students enrolled in UGA online courses how to use the web for successful college experiences. The course covers navigating online resources and services; using online tools for time management and organization; developing strategies for online learning; searching for content; and, evaluating the credibility of online information.

courses.subject: UNIV
courses.title: Professional Development Abroad
courses.description: This course provides OSSA Scholars opportunities to practice skills regarding motivation, academic, and career exploration; develop academic and professional skills; and prepare for academic success at UGA and abroad. This course builds a sustainable community for students to achieve academic success while exploring the professional landscape abroad.
courses.course_objectives: Students will articulate their educational goals and future academic and career goals. Students will develop and sustain time management and project management skills. Students will independently acquire and practice evidence-based learning strategies, increasing their skills as learners. (e.g., metacognitive learning strategies, active learning techniques, collaborative learning). Students will demonstrate greater academic engagement within the behavioral, psychological, and cognitive domains. Students will develop appropriate and effective formal and informal interpersonal communicative professional skills and etiquette within an academic setting and the professional landscape.

courses.subject: UNIV
courses.title: Developing Literacies in the Humanities
courses.description: An introduction to focus areas that comprise the humanities (e.g., literature, philosophy, history, and the arts). An overview of the different modes of expression that scholars utilize to make sense of the world and to document the human experience. Additionally, a survey of scholarship and introduction to humanist writing allows students to critically examine forms of expression; present well-reasoned arguments; explore what it means today to be a practitioner; and, consider necessary skills across these fields.

courses.subject: UNIV
courses.title: Developing Literacies in the Social Sciences
courses.description: This course offers an interdisciplinary introduction to varioussocial science disciplines by providing an overview of the development of the social sciences and their approaches to investigating social phenomena and analyzing results. Students learn how to critically consume social science research and evaluate the skills necessary to be a practitioner in the field of social sciences while developing and presenting their arguments in a range of formats.

courses.subject: UNIV
courses.title: Developing Literacies in the STEM Fields
courses.description: An introduction to the fields of Science, Technology, Engineering, and Mathematics (STEM) and the skills students need to be successful within these domains. The course presents fundamental principles, applications, and processes of becoming literate within STEM fields as students explore some of the world's problems from the perspectives of STEM inquiry, learn to use various problem-solving strategies, and practice effective communication.

courses.subject: UNIV
courses.title: Developing Literacies in the Pre-Professional Majors
courses.description: An overview of professions that require advanced level education for entry into the profession (e.g., medicine, pharmacy, business). Students will explore how practitioners in these professions create and interpret written/delivered information and communication norms. Multiple sections of this course may be offered to accommodate different pre-professional majors.

courses.subject: UNIV
courses.title: Digital Literacies and Documentary Media
courses.description: This course will expose students to the various forms of digitalmedia and will allow students to explore the communicativepossibilities unique to digital media production.

courses.subject: UNIV
courses.title: Preparation for Calculus I
courses.description: A review of selected topics includes a brief review of college algebra, variation, equations, functions (including exponential and logarithmic), systems of equations, multi-step solving application problems, an introduction to limits and piecewise functions, and other related topics from pre-calculus to prepare students for calculus.
courses.prerequisiteText: MATH 1113 or MATH 1113E or permission of department

courses.subject: UNIV
courses.title: Supplemental Instruction for Calculus I
courses.description: This is a co-enrollment course for Calculus I for Science and Engineering, where students will develop skills to be successful active learners in Calculus I for Science and Engineering. Students will learn to engage peers and instructors; embrace collaborative learning and study groups; reflect on their progress and strategies; and adapt their learning based on self-reflection and performance results.
courses.course_objectives: By the end of this course, students will calculate and interpret basic trends, rate, and accumulation using the limit, the derivative, and the integral, respectively. By the end of this course, students will use a function’s graph to identify increasing/decreasing behavior and critical numbers of the first or second derivative of the function, identify extrema, determine limits, identify points of continuity/discontinuity, identify asymptotes, and identify points where the function is/is not differentiable. By the end of this course, students will use information (a formula or table and/or first or second derivative) about a function to predict behavior of the function and/or its first or second derivative, extrema, limits, points of continuity/discontinuity, asymptotes, and identify points where the function is/is not differentiable. By the end of this course, students will apply calculus to solve an application problem by selecting an appropriate model, identifying an appropriate calculus technique, using the calculus technique on the model to solve the problem, and interpreting the solution in context.
courses.topical_outline: Review of problem-solving/critical thinking strategies and techniques Review of course materials from Calculus I for Science and Engineering (limits, continuity, rates of change) Review of course materials (finding derivatives using definition) Prep for Exam 1 in Calculus I for Science and Engineering Review of Exam 1 (How did you do? If you missed a problem, what went wrong? How do we make sure we don’t make the same mistake on the final exam?) Review of course materials (finding derivatives using rules) Review of course materials (finding derivatives using rules) Review of course materials (related rate problems) More related rate word problems Review of course materials (finding extreme values and curve sketching) Prep for Exam 2 in Calculus I for Science and Engineering Review of course materials (optimization problems) Review of course materials (finding antiderivatives and area approximation) Review of course materials (the definite integral and finding area between curves) Review of course materials (integration using substitution) Review for Final Exam in Calculus I for Science and Engineering

courses.subject: UNIV
courses.title: Supplemental Instruction for Calculus II
courses.description: This is a co-enrollment course for Calculus II for Science and Engineering, where students will develop skills to be successful active learners in Calculus II for Science and Engineering. Students will learn to engage peers and instructors; embrace collaborative learning and study groups; reflect on their progress and strategies; and adapt their learning based on self-reflection and performance results.
courses.course_objectives: By the end of this course, students will apply various integration techniques. By the end of this course, students will recognize and evaluate improper integrals. By the end of this course, students will apply the definite integral to problems of the area, volume, arc length, surface area, and work. By the end of this course, students will solve separable differential equations. By the end of this course, students will understand the concept of convergence and apply tests for convergence of sequences and series. By the end of this course, students will apply calculus to functions in parametric form and to functions in polar coordinates.
courses.topical_outline: Review of derivatives from Calculus I for Science and Engineering Review of course materials (integration techniques) Prep for Exam 1 in Calculus II for Science and Engineering Review Exam 1 in Calculus II for Science and Engineering Review of applications of the integral Review of volumes and arclength Review of surface area and work Review of separable differential equations Prep for Exam 2 in Calculus II for Science and Engineering Review Exam 2 in Calculus II for Science and Engineering Review sequences and series Review convergence tests Review Taylor series Prep for Exam 3 in Calculus II for Science and Engineering Review Exam 3 in Calculus II for Science and Engineering Review parametric and polar equations Review vectors Prep for Exam 4 in Calculus II for Science and Engineering Prep for Final Exam in Calculus II for Science and Engineering

courses.subject: UNIV
courses.title: Transformative Learning Strategies
courses.description: Course will assist students in developing skills needed to learn across academic disciplines and career fields. Students will investigate how the brain works, deep learning strategies, and how to integrate the new science of learning. The hallmarks of the course will be the development of transferable skills beyond academics.
courses.course_objectives: By the end of this course, students will critically analyze primary literature to inform their research ideas. By the end of this course, students will practice steps of question formulation and refinement. By the end of this course, students will communicate their research interests and ideas in written and oral formats.

courses.description: This service-learning course assists students in developing the skills needed to learn intentionally across academic disciplines and career fields. Students will investigate how the brain works, deep learning strategies, and how to integrate the new science of learning. The hallmarks of the course will be the development of transferable skills beyond academics.
courses.course_objectives: By the end of this course, students will define metacognition and apply fundamental metacognitive principles for their academic success within their program(s) of study. By the end of this course, students will employ reflective learning strategies to recognize flaws in their thinking, articulate their thought processes, and revise their efforts (key elements of success through reflection-centered metacognition). By the end of this course, students will evaluate research on creative and critical thinking. By the end of this course, students will create an integrative, life-long strategic learning plan using strategies that are congruent with metacognitive learning principles. By the end of this course, students will engage in service projects in the local community by assisting various nonprofits with fulfilling their missions while completing various learning tasks linked to developmentally based life-skills research.

courses.title: Success for Transfer Students
courses.description: Provides transfer students opportunities in writing, reading,research, and communication strategies for success within theUniversity's unique learning environments. To enhance the transfer experience, students will examine resources and themissions, purpose, and character of the University. Selected texts, guest speakers, and campus events will provide materials for seminar exchanges. Hallmark of the course will be attention to the importance of attendance, preparation, and engagement in University classrooms.
courses.course_objectives: By the end of this course, students will be knowledgeable about the resources on campus. By the end of this course, students will engage with campus resources including academic, social, and health services. By the end of this course, students will connect with the UGA community in and outside the classroom. By the end of this course, students will understand of the college academic expectations. By the end of this course, students will be skilled in how to gain research experience. By the end of this course, students will be prepared for future opportunities at UGA and beyond.

courses.subject: UNIV
courses.title: Propelling Success: Exit Seminar for Scholars
courses.description: This course allows Scholars from division programs to reconvene (from year one) as a cohort for successful transition from the University to life after college. Special emphasis placed on  reflecting and synthesizing knowledge, skills, and traits developed during their first two years at the University; transitioning into programs of study; visioning where paths are headed post-University; updating strategic learning plans; building relationships around resources, e.g. the Career Center and Alumni Association.
courses.course_objectives: By the end of this course, students will engage campus and community resources to support transition from student identity to that of a professional in their chosen program of study. By the end of this course, students will practice skills required for academic success as a third-year student. By the end of this course, students will develop a plan for coping with transition and maintaining wellness after college. By the end of this course, students will articulate financial values, professional goals, and future plans in collaboration with the Career Center and Alumni Association. By the end of this course, students will apply understandings of motivational and attitudinal concepts as they relate to academic work and endeavors.
courses.topical_outline: Developing a professional identity Accessing campus resources to aid in developing a professional identity and post-University network of support and contacts Factors related to successful life-transitions Coping strategies for successful life-transitions Reflection and presentation of skills acquired through formal curriculum Student Wellness and Well-being Financial Literacy and Well-being Navigating life goals associated with emerging adulthood

courses.subject: UNIV
courses.title: Joy and Achievement in Learning
courses.description: Investigation of the paths connecting deep learning to one’s career objectives, leading to the pursuit of a joyful life. Provides scholars opportunities to practice skills regarding academic and professional purpose, success at UGA, and the building and maintenance of a joy-infused life.
courses.course_objectives: By the end of this course, students will articulate their educational, professional goals in relation to their pursuit of a joyful life. By the end of this course, students will apply understandings of well-being literature to their own goal pursuit, motivational attitudes, and behaviors. By the end of this course, students will practice behaviors conducive to achieving high levels of well-being, based on scientific research. By the end of this course, students will develop a personalized career development plan, supported by steps in their academic goals. By the end of this course, students will identify the main ideas and arguments of the well-known research of happiness and well-being.

(e.g., metacognitive learning strategies, active learning techniques, collaborative learning). By the end of this course, students will demonstrate greater academic engagement within the behavioral, psychological, and cognitive domains. By the end of this course, students will practice self-regulated learning skills and employ self-directed learning behaviors. By the end of this course, students will demonstrate a positive growth mindset approach to their academics and foster an attitude of resilience and perseverance from their prior academic shortcomings. By the end of this course, students will practice behaviors conducive to achieving high levels of academic performance in light of their return from academic suspension (i.e., productive mindsets regarding impulse control and anxiety and stress management).

courses.description: Introduces students to current research on how people learn, reviews strategies for engaging them in active learning, and develops strong learning strategies to be successful at the University level upon returning from Academic Suspension. Students participate in small group discussions of the course readings and materials, brainstorm solutions to common learning challenges, and share personal reflections of their own experiences. The hallmark of this course is an active learning environment focused on the application of strengths-based skills and content.

courses.subject: VETM
courses.title: Foundations of Veterinary Medicine Ia
courses.description: Foundational concepts preparing students for the study of organ systems, including cell structure and function, cellular respiration, membrane physiology, distribution of water in the body, cells, and components found in the blood, basics of the immune response, chemical mediators, the autonomic nervous system, and introduction to imaging.
courses.course_objectives: Describe the major intrinsic and extrinsic cell pathways and organelles involved in cell activation (i.e., protein synthesis, cell proliferation, cell death) Describe how cells make energy required for cellular function Explain the importance of the cell membrane in cell to cell communication Identify how the body maintains fluid homeostasis Describe the source and function of circulating cellular and non-cellular components found in the bloodstream Define the basic function of the immune system, delineate the actual role of both the innate and adaptive immunity, and be able to apply this knowledge to explain the importance of the use of vaccines in disease prevention Explain how cellular mediators affect cells either locally, within the same cell, or somewhere else in the body Describe the components of the autonomic nervous system and their general function Describe fundamental concepts of imaging
courses.topical_outline: Cellular Respiration Membrane Physiology Distribution of Water in the Body Cells and Components Found in the Blood Basics of Immune Response Chemical Mediators Overview of the Autonomic Nervous System Introduction to Imaging

courses.subject: VETM
courses.title: Foundations of Veterinary Medicine Ib
courses.description: The body under stress, introducing pathophysiology to consolidate basic physiologic and structural principles the students have learned throughout year one. This course will also introduce foundational concepts of bacteriology, mycology, parasitology, and immunology.
courses.course_objectives: Students will be able to gather and assimilate signalment and historical information to elicit both important patient information and client goals, values, and resources in domestic animals. Students will be able to recognize and interpret normal and abnormal physical examination findings in the domestic animals. Students will be able to describe the comprehensive wellness, preventative care, and nutrition of domestic animals. Students will be able to describe the complete diet and nutritional needs across species. Students will be able to recognize interactions between body systems and clinical manifestations during physiologic disturbances. Students will be able to describe the steps involved in problem-oriented medicine. Students will be able to apply relevant factors including cost, logistics, quality of life, animal welfare, and owner priorities/expectations to guide clinical decision making. Students will be able to relate each of the following to the study of unhealthy organ systems in animals: Concepts of infectious disease, including bacteriology, mycology, virology, and parasitology. Students will be able to relate concepts in immunology to the study of unhealthy organ systems in animals.
courses.topical_outline: Introduction to infectious diseases Inflammatory processes, response to infection, and principles of vaccination Foundations of animal nutrition across the lifespan Cases using varying species, differing mechanisms of disease, and the integration of body systems

courses.prerequisiteText: Enrollment in the first year of the doctor of veterinary medicine curriculum

courses.subject: VETM

courses.subject: VETM
courses.title: Personal and Professional Development Ia
courses.description: Introduction to professional competencies for veterinary medicine, including communication, collaboration, learning skills, well-being, and personal finance.
courses.course_objectives: By the end of this course, students will be able to apply written communication skills for intended audiences. By the end of this course, students will be able to demonstrate collaboration, while respecting each other's differences. By the end of this course, students will be able to apply behaviors expected of the veterinarian, including reflective practice, self-regulation, professional and career development, ethical decision-making, and personal wellbeing. By the end of this course, students will be able to apply financial acumen to manage personal decisions, specifically budget planning. By the end of this course, students will be able to apply core verbal communication skills for intended audiences.
courses.topical_outline: 1. Course Introduction 2. Introducing strategies for written communication with clients and colleagues 3. Introducing skills that promote teamwork, collaboration, community, and social competence 4. Introducing study skills, time management, and self-directed learning 5. Introducing skills that promote self-regulation including self-reflection and metacognition 6. Introducing strategies and resources for wellbeing and resilience 7. Introducing personal financial management strategies 8. Introducing career planning strategies 9. Introducing strategies for verbal communication with clients and colleagues, including core skills
courses.prerequisiteText: Enrollment in the first year of the doctor of veterinary medicine curriculum

courses.subject: VETM
courses.title: Personal and Professional Development Ib
courses.description: Expanding on professional competencies introduced in Professional Skills in Veterinary Medicine Ia, including communication, collaboration, and professional development. Introducing foundations of ethical reasoning and evidence-based practice.
courses.course_objectives: By the end of this course, students will be able to apply written communication skills for intended audiences, specifically professional documentation. By the end of this course, students will be able to demonstrate teamwork and collaboration, while respecting each other's differences. By the end of this course, students will be able to apply behaviors expected of the veterinarian, including professional and career development. By the end of this course, students will be able to acquire and evaluate appropriate health-related information. By the end of this course, students will be able to advocate for animal welfare.
courses.topical_outline: 1. Course Introduction 2. Strengthening and expanding verbal communication strategies for clients and colleagues, including enhancing client adherence, setting the framework for interactions, and obtaining informed consent 3. Strengthening and expanding on written communication strategies for clients and colleagues, including completing requisition forms and preparing cases in a problem-oriented format 4. Strengthening and expanding collaborative skills, including management of conflict 5. Strengthening and expanding career planning strategies 6. Introducing skills for acquiring and evaluating health-related information 7. Introducing animal welfare of the individual and herd animal

courses.title: Foundations of Veterinary Medicine IIa
courses.description: Foundational concepts preparing students for the study of unhealthy animals, including basic concepts from infectious disease, immunology, anatomic and clinical pathology, clinical pharmacology, nutrition, and anesthesia and diagnostic imaging.
courses.course_objectives: By the end of this course, students will understand how to relate each of the following to the study of unhealthy organ systems in animals: Concepts of infectious disease, including bacteriology, mycology, virology, and parasitology. By the end of this course, students will understand how to relate concepts in immunology to the study of unhealthy organ systems in animals. By the end of this course, students will understand how to relate foundational principles of anatomic and clinical pathology to the study of unhealthy organ systems in animals. By the end of this course, students will understand how to relate foundational principles of diagnostic imaging to the study of unhealthy organ systems in animals. By the end of this course, students will understand how to relate foundational principles of clinical pharmacology, nutrition, and anesthesia to the study of unhealthy organ systems in animals.

courses.subject: VETM
courses.title: Foundations of Veterinary Medicine IIb
courses.description: Foundational concepts preparing students for the study of unhealthy animals, with a focus on populations and public health: expanding on basic concepts from anatomic and clinical pathology, infectious disease, epidemiology, parasitology, clinical pharmacology, diagnostic imaging, nutrition, anesthesia, and immunology.
courses.course_objectives: Students will be able to describe the structure and function of the dairy, swine, poultry, and beef industries. Students will be able to identify issues that limit animal productivity in different industry segment. Students will be able to identify issues in population, food safety, and public health. Students will be able to assess likely cause(s) of disease in populations. Students will develop surveillance and testing strategies to manage diseases in populations. Students will be able to design basic disease prevention programs for animal facilities and populations. Students will be able to effectively communicate health information to stakeholders.

courses.subject: VETM
courses.title: Clinical Skills in Veterinary Medicine IIa
courses.description: For specific organ systems, expand knowledge and skills in clinical safe practices, performing diagnostics, therapeutic procedures, surgical skills, and physical examination techniques, interpreting radiographs/ultrasound, setting up and using an anesthetic system, creating medical plans, administering medications, applying bandages, splints, nerve blocks, and using medical records systems.
courses.course_objectives: Students will be able to appropriately integrate clinical safe practices as skills grow. Students will be able to appropriately integrate good patient handling practices as skills grow. Students will be able to properly use a microscope for diagnostic requirements/testing. Students will be able to properly obtain patient samples as they expand testing options coordinating with the system. Students will be able to properly assess radiographs and perform Focused Assessment with Sonography for Trauma (FAST) ultrasound (abdominal). Students will be able to properly perform physical examination techniques in the abnormal patient. Students will be able to properly set up an anesthetic circuit and set up a patient on the system understanding how to monitor the patient. Students will be able to properly intubate a patient. Students will be able to perform surgical skills from suturing to methods for performing procedures coordinating with systems. Students will be able to perform proper placement of IV catheter, and establishment and maintenance of fluid therapy. Students will be able to properly perform standard medical mathematics when creating diagnostic and therapeutic plans. Students will be able to properly administer medication as appropriate for organ system. Students will be able to properly apply and maintain bandaging/splints/supportive wraps. Students will be able to properly perform nerve blocks for diagnostic and therapeutic reasons. Students will be able to use basic features of medical records software.
courses.topical_outline:
Microscope usage for diagnostic procedures: Urinalysis in the abnormal patient, vaginal cytology, artificial intelligence tools for cytologic examination Obtaining and handling biological samples coordinated with systems Physical exam: in parallel with organ systems courses with emphasis on abnormalities, including models and live animals Anesthesia: How to set up and proceed with a patient, including Intubation/establishment/maintenance Interpreting radiographic images (in parallel with organ systems courses) IV catheter placement using models Fluid therapy: using models and learning pumps and medical math involved Administering medications (in parallel with organ systems courses) Suturing
Continued practice of square knot, surgeon’s knot, buried knot, simple interrupted suture pattern, simple continuous suture pattern, circumferential knot, modified miller’s knot, modified transfixation knot, 
Addition of ford interlocking pattern, intradermal pattern, mattress sutures. Creation of a formal Diagnostic/Therapeutic plan/orders with all elements of delivery/medical mathematics/intervals Introduction to the use of medical records software

courses.subject: VETM
courses.title: Clinical Skills in Veterinary Medicine IIb
courses.description: For specific organ systems, expand knowledge and skills in clinical safe practices, performing diagnostics, therapeutic procedures, surgical skills, and physical examination techniques, interpreting radiographs/ultrasound, performing mock surgeries, performing feline castration, cleaning and extracting teeth, creating medical plans, administering medications, applying bandages/splints/nerve blocks, and using medical records systems.
courses.course_objectives: Students will be able to continue to appropriately integrate clinical safe practices as skills grow. Students will be able to continue to appropriately integrate good patient handling practices as skills grow. Students will be able to properly use a microscope for diagnostic requirements/testing. Students will be able to properly obtain patient samples as they expand testing options coordinating with the system. Students will be able to properly assess radiographs and perform Focused Assessment with Sonography for Trauma (FAST) ultrasound (thoracic). Students will be able to properly perform physical examination techniques in the abnormal patient. Students will be able to perform surgical skills from suturing to methods for performing procedures coordinating with systems. Students will be able to perform a live patient surgery (feline castration). Students will be able to properly perform standard medical mathematics when creating diagnostic and therapeutic plans. Students will be able to properly administer medication as appropriate for organ system. Students will be able to properly apply and maintain bandaging. Students will be able to properly perform dental skills: ultrasonic scaling, hand scaling, charting, probing for gingival pockets, radiographs, nerve blocks, and simple extractions (Comprehensive Oral Health Assessment and Treatment - COHAT).
courses.topical_outline:
Microscope usage for diagnostic procedures- fecals, differentials, artificial intelligence tools for cytologic examination Obtaining and handling biological samples coordinated with systems Physical examination in parallel with organ systems courses with emphasis on abnormalities using models and live animals Rectal Palpation Models: Equine Colic, Bovine Reproductive Interpreting radiographic images in parallel with organ systems courses Ultrasound training: Introduction of Global FAST Dental Skills- ultrasonic scaling, hand scaling, charting, probing for gingival pockets, radiographs, nerve blocks and simple extractions (COHAT) Administering medications in parallel with organ systems courses. Suturing
Revisit and improve: square knot, surgeon’s knot, buried knot, simple interrupted suture pattern, simple continuous suture pattern

courses.subject: VETM
courses.title: Core Medicine and Surgery:  Integrated Animal Care and Management I
courses.description: Building on the skills and foundational knowledge gained in the first two years of the Doctor of Veterinary Medicine program and using both system-based and integrated approaches, students will continue to acquire knowledge and practice diagnostic, medical, anesthetic, and surgical skills for health, wellness, and treatment of unhealthy animals.
courses.course_objectives: Students will be able to apply core diagnostic, medical, anesthetic, and surgical knowledge to recognize and treat common diseases and presenting complaints of domestic animals. Students will be able to provide plans for preventative health and wellness care for common domestic animal species. Students will be able to provide general anesthesia for common elective surgical procedures. Students will be able to complete common elective surgical procedures using a variety of species models. Students will be able to apply non-technical competencies to different clinical situations (in a didactic setting).
courses.topical_outline: Course introduction Recommendations for preventative care and wellness visits for common domestic species Expansion on the systems-based approach to recognition, diagnosis, and treatment of common clinical and clinicopathologic problems across veterinary species Introduction to presenting problems that do not belong to a defined body system Application of the principles of clinical pharmacology Routine and common emergency anesthetic protocols across veterinary species Routine and common surgical emergency protocols across veterinary species

courses.subject: VETM
courses.title: Clinical Reasoning, Decision Making, and Preparation for Practice
courses.description: Building on skills and knowledge from the first two years of the Doctor of Veterinary Medicine program and using an integrated and case-based approach, students will practice critical thinking and problem-solving skills to arrive at evidence-based decisions that consider animal, herd, and client needs, available resources, ethics, and social context.
courses.course_objectives: Students will be able to collect patient information, synthesize, and prioritize problems to arrive at differential diagnosis(es), irrespective of the species, body system(s) affected, or presenting clinical complaint. Students will be able to triage problems and address in order of importance. Students will be able to create and adjust diagnostic and therapeutic plans that present a spectrum of options. Students will be able to recognize limitations, adjust plan(s) to address unexpected complications, and identify when consultation or referral is warranted. Students will be able to apply hospital policies in the clinical setting. Students will be able to efficiently and effectively navigate the University of Georgia’s veterinary teaching hospital’s patient management and treatment software programs. Students will be able to apply non-technical competencies to different clinical situations (in a didactic setting).
courses.topical_outline: Course introduction Review of clinical reasoning, use of diagnostic algorithms, and differentials lists Triage and emergency decisions Spectrum of care Practice with cases Orientation to hospital policies Patient management and treatment software training and application

courses.course_objectives: Students will be able to apply core diagnostic, medical, anesthetic, and surgical knowledge to recognize and treat common diseases and presenting complaints of domestic animals. courses.subject: VETM
courses.title: Personal and Professional Development IIIa
courses.description: To prepare students for clinical practice, this course will provide information and training on tasks that are necessary to practice veterinary medicine upon graduation. Through reflection and self-assessment to increase self-awareness, students will learn how to poise themselves for future success in completing the tasks necessary to practice veterinary medicine.
courses.course_objectives: Students will know the veterinary accreditation program including the roles and responsibilities of an accredited veterinarian and the process for obtaining USDA APHIS Veterinary Accreditation status. Students will be able to describe how to ensure animals move legally, the role of health certifications and certificates of veterinary inspection, and government agencies involved. Students will be able to describe the roles the veterinary profession plays in preventing, detecting, and responding to emerging and foreign animal diseases. Students will be able to describe disease conditions in various species which would be suggestive of an emerging disease, transboundary animal disease, and/or warrant a call to an animal health official. Students will be able to locate the World Organization for Animal Health listed diseases, the CDC’s Category ABC diseases, the USDA High Consequence Foreign Animal Diseases and Pests, the USDA-APHIS National List of Reportable Animal Diseases, and the reportable diseases in Georgia, as well as indicate which of these diseases pose threats to human health. Students will be able to describe the steps needed to obtain a license to practice veterinary medicine. Students will be able to explain the application process, content of, and preparation methods for the North American Veterinary Licensing Exam (NAVLE). Students will be able to identify personal areas of clinical strengths and areas on which to focus continued study and improvement.
courses.topical_outline: Course overview Reflections on clinical experiences USDA APHIS Transboundary and Emerging Diseases of Animals online training USDA APHIS Initial Accreditation Training in-person training Everything you need to know about the North American Veterinary Licensing Exam How to obtain a license to practice veterinary medicine Self-assessment exercise for NAVLE readiness

courses.subject: VETM
courses.title: Personal and Professional Development IIIb
courses.description: How to apply financial principles to personal and professional decisions, explain work-related insurance, and describe the relationship between revenue generation, expense categories, and compensation including benefits.
courses.course_objectives: Students will be able to discuss trends and earnings in different veterinary sectors. Students will be able to define financial terms used on North American Veterinary Licensing Exam. Students will be able to recognize barriers and limitations to production and pay. Students will be able to develop communication and marketing strategies based on a practice’s culture, client needs, standard of care, branding, and systems. Students will be able to identify work flow inefficiencies that contribute to reduced earnings and negatively impact effective communication and patient care skills. Students will be able to appreciate the benefits of professional liability insurance. Students will be able to lead staff through hiring, training, and delegating. Students will be able to create a strategy to properly manage debt. Students will be able to set future personal and budgeting goals. Students will be able to identify positive and undesirable components to a job contract and how to negotiate needs.
courses.topical_outline: Course introduction Industry trends Introduction to financial terminology Common practice barriers for professional compensation First year compensation, benefits and budget Practice culture, leadership, and performance Professional liability insurance Human resource law, leadership and employee relationships Getting yourself in financial order before you graduate Thinking strategically about your debt Mentorship - who, what, when, where, why? Students will be able to understand financial commitments after graduation and construct their financial plan. Students will know the licensing requirements for the state in which they are applying and start the application process when applicable. Students will be able to apply for a job and complete an interview.

courses.topical_outline:
The Vertically Integrated Projects for Research (VIPR) Program operates in a research and development context. Each research experience is an independent collaboration between the faculty member and multidisciplinary teams of undergraduate students. As such, there is no set topical outline.

Undergraduate students that join VIPR teams earn academic credit for their participation in design/discovery efforts that assist faculty and graduate students with research and development issues in their areas of expertise. The teams are multidisciplinary, drawing students from all disciplines on campus; vertically-integrated, maintaining a mix of undergraduates and graduate or professional students each semester; long-term, each undergraduate student may participate in a project for up to three years.

The VIPR course will aim to provide enough structure for the student to learn and make progress with the research but not so much that each team can't pursue new and fruitful directions. Students will have “assignments” like one would have for completing a project as part of a team. They will be important for students to understand and make progress on the research. Assignments may include but are not limited to:
- Reading and summarizing research articles, including those in the primary literature
- Documenting progress in writing and through presentations in meetings with peers and faculty
- Constructively respond to feedback on their papers or presentations from faculty mentors
- Reporting the student's/team’s progress during weekly meetings
- Participating during weekly discussions and following through on the weekly time commitment to the research and the team 
- Writing an end-of-semester research brief or full research report

Student time commitment for 1 credit = ~3 hours/week. Some weeks the student may have to spend more time to make sure time-sensitive research tasks get done. Other weeks the student may spend less time because of other student time commitments.

courses.topical_outline:
The Vertically Integrated Projects for Research (VIPR) Program operates in a research and development context. Each research experience is an independent collaboration between the faculty member and multidisciplinary teams of undergraduate students. As such, there is no set topical outline.

Undergraduate students that join VIPR teams earn academic credit for their participation in design/discovery efforts that assist faculty and graduate students with research and development issues in their areas of expertise. The teams are multidisciplinary, drawing students from all disciplines on campus; vertically-integrated, maintaining a mix of undergraduates and graduate or professional students each semester; long-term, each undergraduate student may participate in a project for up to three years.

The VIPR course will aim to provide enough structure for the student to learn and make progress with the research but not so much that each team can't pursue new and fruitful directions. Students will have “assignments” like one would have for completing a project as part of a team. They will be important for students to understand and make progress on the research. Assignments may include but are not limited to:
-	Reading and summarizing research articles, including those in the primary literature
-	Documenting progress in writing and through presentations in meetings with peers and faculty
-      Constructively respond to feedback on their papers or presentations from faculty mentors
-	Reporting the student's/team’s progress during weekly meetings
-	Participating during weekly discussions and following through on the weekly time commitment to the research and the team 
-	Writing an end-of-semester research brief or full research report

Student time commitment for 1 credit = ~3 hours/week. Some weeks the student may have to spend more time to make sure time-sensitive research tasks get done. Other weeks the student may spend less time because of other student time commitments.

courses.subject: VPAT(IDIS)
courses.title: Virology and Viral Pathogenesis
courses.description: Introductory virology includes viral structure, replication, genetics, and immunity.  The mechanism(s) by which viruses enter, spread, and cause diseases in humans and animals.  Virus-cell interactions include structural and functional alterations of hosts after virus infection and viral components responsible for these alterations.

courses.subject: VPAT(POPH)
courses.title: Avian Histopathology
courses.description: Detailed microscopic studies will be made of avian tissues and the effects of specific diseases and their processes on them.  A working knowledge of tissue processing and differential staining will be included.

courses.subject: VPAT
courses.title: Introduction to Disease (Honors)
courses.description: Introduction to the many ways disease can be caused in the body, how they happen and, in some cases, how they can be prevented.
courses.prerequisiteText: BIOL 1107 and BIOL 1108 and permission of Honors

courses.subject: VPAT
courses.title: Basic Veterinary Medical Terminology
courses.description: Designed for students entering veterinary medical fields or animal/poultry science/production to learn and understand the basic terminology used in veterinary medicine. Taught by veterinary pathologists, the learning experience will be augmented by visual examples, including fresh tissue specimens and gross and microscopic lesions.

courses.subject: VPAT
courses.title: Introduction to Histology and Histopathology
courses.description: Students will learn pattern recognition of normal tissue and organ structure (histology), correlation of tissue architecture with normal physiologic function, and comparison to microscopic processes observed in disease (histopathology). Comparative histology of human and animal tissues and across fundamental disease processes, such as inflammation, necrosis, and neoplasia will be emphasized.
courses.course_objectives: By the end of this course, students will be able to define and correctly use terminology related to cellular morphology (shape), tissue architecture, component parts of cells, tissues and organs, and basic disease processes. By the end of this course, students will be able to distinguish normal tissues and organs by microscopic appearance when shown a microscopic image. By the end of this course, students will be able to categorize tissues into organ systems based upon cell type(s) visualized and other unique characteristics. By the end of this course, students will be able to compare and contrast known tissues across species or across diseased states. By the end of this course, students will be able to identify or describe the diseased area of a given tissue when given a tissue diagram or photomicrograph and a comparison “normal” tissue. By the end of this course, students will be able to correlate anatomic and microscopic tissue structure with functional purpose in a given organ or tissue and the pathologic processes occurring to produce lesions observed.
courses.topical_outline: Cell structure and function Mesenchymal tissues Epithelial tissues Inflammatory cells Heart and blood vessels Respiratory system Oral and gastrointestinal tissues Liver and pancreas Urinary system Nervous system Special senses Bone and muscle Reproductive system Skin Endocrine system Hematopoietic and lymphatic
courses.prerequisiteText: BIOL 1107 or BIOL 1107E or BIOL 2107H or BIOL 1108 or BIOL 2108H

courses.subject: VPAT
courses.title: Introduction to One Health
courses.description: One Health is the collaborative integration of human, veterinary, and environmental sciences to attain optimal health for people, animals, and our environment. This course examines the key concepts of the One Health Initiative and the benefits of utilizing an interdisciplinary approach to disease prevention and elimination.
courses.prerequisiteText: (BIOL 1107 or BIOL 1107E or BIOL 2107H) and (BIOL 1108 or BIOL 2108H)

courses.subject: VPAT
courses.title: Current Topics in One Health
courses.description: Introduces students to substantive issues and knowledge to pursue a career in health-related science.

courses.subject: VPAT
courses.title: One Health Capstone
courses.description: Faculty-supervised service-learning capstone project for students pursuing the undergraduate certificate in One Health.  Provides students the opportunity to engage in inquiry into an area highlighting a One Health approach to solving a disease problem. Students will be expected to apply theoretical knowledge acquired in their seminars and coursework in a real-life setting. Students will work closely with their faculty mentor(s) to identify a project, create a proposal, gather information/data, analyze results, create a project summary, and present their findings to others.
courses.course_objectives: By the end of the course, students will be able to critically research and evaluate a problem and propose a multidisciplinary solution. By the end of the course, students will be able to work together in cross-disciplinary teams. By the end of the course, students will be able to appreciate the importance of collaboration and disciplinary diversity in effective problem-solving. By the end of the course, students will be able to analyze data and summarize results. By the end of the course, students will be able to effectively communicate findings to others. By the end of the course, students will be able to explain the importance of effective leadership in project management.
courses.topical_outline: The capstone project will be developed collaboratively by the student(s) and faculty mentor(s). Specific topics will vary depending on the individual capstone project. Weeks 1-3: Develop project and pre-proposal with the faculty mentor(s) and host site. Weeks 4-12: Launch, conduct, and conclude the project. Weeks 13-15: Create a written summary of the project and present project findings in a seminar format to student peers and faculty.
courses.prerequisiteText: VPAT 3700 and permission of department | Pre or

courses.subject: VPAT
courses.title: On the Origins of Disease
courses.description: A comparative and evolutionary perspective on the origins andpathogenesis of disease. Topics include: Darwinian medicine,pathology, natural selection and infectious disease, evolution of host defenses, evolutionary models of cancer, selectivebreeding and disease susceptibility, and relationships betweendiet and toxins.  Diseases of both man and animals will be studied.
courses.prerequisiteText: BIOL 1108-1108L or permission of department | Graduate Prerequisite | Permission of department | Undergraduate Pre or

courses.subject: VPAT
courses.title: Common Diseases of Production Animals
courses.description: Designed to help students entering veterinary medical fields or animal production learn the common diseases of production animals. The course focuses on infectious, toxic, nutritional and metabolic conditions, as well as important neoplastic and congenital conditions that impact animal production. Learning is augmented through clinical case material.

courses.subject: VPAT
courses.title: Basics of Pathology
courses.description: Gives students an overview of the basic mechanisms of disease in Veterinary Medicine.

courses.subject: VPAT
courses.title: Directed Readings and/or Projects
courses.description: A directed study in one of the basic sciences in the College of Veterinary Medicine.  Includes library and laboratory learning experiences not otherwise available to undergraduate students. For the research, the student will complete a project under the direction of the professor which includes the writing of the results and the presentation as appropriate.

courses.title: Faculty-Mentored Undergraduate Research I
courses.description: Faculty-supervised independent or collaborative inquiry into fundamental and applied problems within a discipline that requires students to gather, analyze, and synthesize and interpret data and to present results in writing and other relevant communication formats.

courses.subject: VPAT
courses.title: Undergraduate Research Thesis (or Final Project)
courses.description: Faculty-supervised independent or collaborative inquiry into fundamental and applied problems within a discipline that requires students to gather, analyze, synthesize, and interpret data. Students will write or produce a thesis or other professional capstone product, such as a report or portfolio that describes their systematic and in-depth inquiry.

courses.subject: VPAT
courses.title: General Animal Pathology
courses.description: The reactions of the body to disease processes, specifically disturbances of circulation, cell injury, inflammation and disturbances of growth.  Recognizing lesions grossly and microscopically, determining the pathogenesis of the lesions, and making lesion and disease diagnosis.

courses.subject: VPAT
courses.title: Systemic Pathology I
courses.description: This course is designed to give students an organ-system relatedapproach to disease processes as manifested by morphologic,physiologic, and biochemical changes.

courses.subject: VPAT
courses.title: Clinical Pathology
courses.description: Hematology, clinical biochemistry, and cytology of domestic animals.  Laboratory testing as an ancillary aid in disease diagnosis.

courses.subject: VPAT
courses.title: Integrated and Advanced Diagnostics in Veterinary Pathology
courses.description: Exploration of diagnostic pathology through interactive, hands-on learning. Students with an interest in clinical practice, specialty medicine, research careers, and beyond will benefit. Students will interpret laboratory and diagnostic tests that encompass a wide range of animal species, in a comprehensive, holistic approach that extends beyond individual organ systems.
courses.course_objectives: The student will be able to analyze a diverse range of laboratory tests and relate the results to history and signalment data, physical examination findings, and post-mortem examination results. The student will be able to identify additional laboratory testing needs based upon the minimum database or previous testing. The student will be able to recognize common microscopic findings of clinical significance. The student will be able to propose differential diagnoses based on initial laboratory test results. The student will be able to explain pathogeneses and how these relate to laboratory test results in common disorders or diseases. The student will be able to communicate interpretations for different audiences. The student will be familiar with types of clinical and anatomic pathology careers, including specific training and job opportunities.
courses.topical_outline: 1. Course introduction 2. Fundamentals of pathology testing 3. Interpretation of laboratory data 4. Interpretation of microscopic findings 5. Interpretation of gross findings 6. Career exploration in pathology
courses.prerequisiteText: Must be a DVM student | Pre or

courses.subject: VPAT
courses.title: Advanced Techniques in Pathology: Anatomic and Clinical Pathology Pathways
courses.description: Course allows students to explore anatomic and clinical pathology through dedicated tracks. Students will learn introductory concepts of cytology, biopsy, and necropsy and gain hands-on experience in one or more of these techniques based on their interests, while investigating disease in a wide range of animal species.
courses.course_objectives: The student will be able to recognize discipline specific knowledge and skills of anatomic and clinical pathologists and their role in diagnostic medicine. The student will be able to demonstrate proficiency in laboratory procedures, including proper cytology, biopsy, and/or necropsy specimen handling and biosafety. The student will be able to understand and perform proper cytology, biopsy, and/or necropsy sample collection and preparation procedures, ensuring quality and accuracy. The student will be able to utilize laboratory equipment and tools effectively for tissue and/or cellular analysis, ensuring safety and precision. The student will be able to recognize common microscopic and/or gross findings of clinical significance. The student will be able to develop critical thinking and analytical skills to correlate pathological findings with clinical symptoms and histories. The student will be able to explain pathogeneses and how these relate to gross and/or microscopic findings or laboratory test results in common disorders or diseases. The student will be able to communicate diagnostic results effectively through verbal communication and by creating at least one written report.
courses.topical_outline:
1.	Course introduction-all students 2.	Anatomic pathology pathway-if selected by student
a.	Necropsy
b.	Biopsy
c.	Cytology optional 3.	Clinical pathology pathway-if selected by student
a.	Cytology
b.	Necropsy optional
c.	Biopsy optional

courses.subject: VPAT
courses.title: Systemic Pathology II
courses.description: This course is designed to give students an organ-system relatedapproach to disease processes as manifested by morphologic,physiologic, and biochemical changes.

courses.subject: VPAT
courses.title: Veterinary Forensics and Forensic Pathology
courses.description: Animal cruelty and forensic investigations from both a clinicaland pathologic point of view and the relationship between theclinician, pathologist, and law enforcement agencies inveterinary medicolegal death investigation.
courses.course_objectives: Students will be able to define common terms and methodologies used in forensic investigations. Students will be able to describe how to collect and properly preserve samples for evidence during a forensic necropsy. Students will be able to describe the key features that distinguish cases involving animal cruelty and abuse from illness and death from naturally occurring disease. Students will be able to write and evaluate a necropsy report. Students will be able to identify resources for medicolegal death investigation. Students will know how to prepare to testify in court.

courses.subject: VPAT
courses.title: Clinical Laboratory Techniques
courses.description: Basic skills in clinical pathology that will be helpful in clinical practice.  The course is designed to make the student think about sample collection, submission, analysis, and interpretation of test results.  In addition, reference interval, laboratory quality control, and solving technical problems will be addressed.

courses.subject: VPAT
courses.title: Diagnostic Pathology
courses.description: Divided into clinical pathology and necropsy pathology sections. The clinical pathology section emphasizes interpretation of cytologic and hematologic data.  Postmortem examinations are performed on cases submitted to the Athens Diagnostic Assistance Laboratory.  Integration of information provided by clinical history, morphologic lesions, and ancillary tests.
courses.prerequisiteText: Must be a fourth year veterinary student

courses.subject: VPAT
courses.title: Anatomic Pathology Clerkship
courses.description: Postmortem examinations are performed on cases submitted to theAthens Diagnostic Laboratory.  Integration of information fromclinical history, gross and microscopic lesions, and ancillarytests are used to formulate a diagnosis.

courses.subject: VPAT
courses.title: Clinical Pathology Clerkship
courses.description: Cytologic and hematologic data from the Teaching Hospital areexamined, interpreted, and diagnoses are reported to clinicians.
courses.prerequisiteText: VPAT 5250-5250L and must be a DVM student

courses.subject: VPAT
courses.title: Studies in Pathology
courses.description: Individual study or project in veterinary pathology.

courses.subject: VPAT
courses.title: Master's Research
courses.description: Research while enrolled for a master's degree under the direction of faculty members.

courses.subject: VPAT
courses.title: Graduate Student Seminar
courses.description: Advanced supervised experience in an applied setting.  Thiscourse may not be used to satisfy a student's approved program ofstudy.

courses.subject: VPAT
courses.title: Necropsy Practicum I
courses.description: Necropsy diagnosis of diseases of animals via gross and microscopic examination of tissues. For residents in their first year.
courses.course_objectives: To become competent in necropsy technique for domestic and exotic mammals, birds, and reptiles To become competent in the gross and microscopic description of diseases of domestic and exotic animals To become competent in the diagnosis of diseases of domestic and exotic animals based on gross and microscopic examination of necropsy specimens Writing necropsy reports
courses.topical_outline: Necropsy laboratory safety Necropsy techniques Interpretation and recognition of gross lesions Interpretation and recognition of microscopic lesions Communication of necropsy findings to veterinarians

courses.subject: VPAT
courses.title: Necropsy Practicum II
courses.description: Necropsy diagnosis of diseases of animals via gross and microscopic examination of tissues. For residents in their second year.

courses.description: Course explores challenges in animal agriculture from a One Health perspective, focusing on impacts on animal, environmental, and human health. Students will learn about management practices, diagnostic systems, and infrastructure, then identify vulnerabilities to food safety and security, developing solutions balancing public health, productivity, and sustainability.
courses.course_objectives: Students will be able to discuss the strengths and weaknesses of the current US infrastructure to support food safety and security. Students will be able to compare and contrast current diagnostic methodologies for pathogen detection and surveillance. Students will be able to describe how animal agriculture has contributed to antimicrobial resistance (AMR) and the implications for animal and human health. Students will be able to utilize a collaborative One Health approach to create innovative solutions to current and emerging challenges impacting animal agriculture.

courses.subject: VPHY(IDIS)
courses.title: Immunophysiology: The Intersection of Immunology and Human Physiology
courses.description: The relationships between the immune system and various physiological systems within the human body. We introduce the mechanisms of immune responses, how they interact with organ systems, and apply the concepts to the implications of immune response to pathologies including mechanisms and causation of diseases.
courses.course_objectives: By the end of this course, students will be able to comprehend basic immunology and acquire different skills to apply this knowledge in understanding advanced immunology topics. By the end of this course, students will be able to integrate information from lectures to identify how the immune system and organ systems work together to maintain health and homeostasis. By the end of this course, students will be able to describe and categorize the immune system's components, including the main mechanisms of innate and adaptive immunity. By the end of this course, students will be able to apply the basic knowledge to identify and predict the immune system's involvement in disease pathophysiology. By the end of this course, students will also evaluate and justify current treatment protocols based on the latest evidence and immunological insights. By the end of this course, students will apply immunological principles to case studies, demonstrating critical thinking to solve problems through the analysis of immune responses in various disease states.
courses.topical_outline: I. Principles of immune response (including organization/anatomy of the immune system, key molecules, functional basis of innate and adaptive response). II. Physiology of immune response in primary and secondary lymphoid organs (including lymphatic system, bone marrow, thymus and tertiary lymphoid structures like BALT, GALT, etc.). III. Immune response in different physiological systems (including integumentary, gastrointestinal, respiratory, cardiovascular, muscular and urinary, etc.). IV. Physiological outcomes of immune responses and tissue damage caused by the immune system. V. Fundamentals of host-environmental interactions (including immunodeficiencies at the extremes of age, microbiota in immunity and inflammation, etc.). VI. Systemic Immune Diseases (mechanisms of autoimmunity, rheumatoid arthritis, muscle disease, etc.). VII. Medical management of immunological diseases.

courses.subject: VPHY(PHRM)
courses.title: Clinical Reasoning in Physiological and Pharmacological Contexts
courses.description: Explores clinical reasoning and structured analysis in the context of physiological and pharmacological disorders. Focuses on identifying, understanding, and solving complex clinical problems using structured analytic techniques and interpreting medical data through case studies.
courses.course_objectives: Students will develop a comprehensive understanding of clinical reasoning and structured analytic techniques. Students will apply structured analysis to dissect clinical cases and interpret medical data. Students will understand and analyze metabolic, physiological, and pharmacological pathways and their implications in clinical settings. Students will compare and contrast different therapies for disorders using structured analytic techniques. Students will utilize primary literature to address complex and ill-defined clinical cases. Students will interpret figures and diagrams related to metabolic events at both whole-body and molecular levels. Explain Clinical Reasoning: Students will be able to explain how and why clinical reasoning differs from other forms of reasoning found in domains such as mathematics and philosophy. Identify Analytic Techniques: Students will be familiar with and able to identify specific structured analytic techniques and how they can be used to enhance the rigor of clinical reasoning. Understand Metabolic Pathways: Students will develop a basic understanding of presented physiological, metabolic, and pharmacological pathways to a degree that they can respond to case study questions. Compare Therapies: Students will use structured analytic techniques to compare and contrast the advantages and disadvantages of different therapies for a given disorder. Utilize Primary Literature: Students will identify and make use of primary literature as a means to address complex and ill-defined cases through written argumentation. Interpret Figures and Diagrams: Students will apply what they learn to interpret figures and diagrams of whole-body or molecular events related to metabolic topics.
courses.topical_outline:
1.	Introduction to Clinical Reasoning
o	Overview of clinical reasoning
o	Differences between clinical reasoning and other forms of reasoning 2.	Structured Analytic Techniques
o	Introduction to structured analytic techniques
o	Application of these techniques in clinical settings 3.	Metabolic Pathways
o	Overview of key metabolic pathways
o	Bioenergetics and biosignaling 4.	Case Studies in Metabolic Disorders
o	Analysis of case studies using structured analytic techniques
o	Interpretation of medical data and clinical scenarios 5.	Therapies for Metabolic Disorders
o	Comparison of different therapies
o	Advantages and disadvantages of various treatment options 6.	Primary Literature and Research
o	Identifying and utilizing primary literature
o	Addressing complex and ill-defined clinical cases 7.	Figures and Diagrams Interpretation
o	Interpreting figures and diagrams related to metabolic events
o	Whole-body and molecular level analysis 8.	Practical Applications
o	Practical applications of structured analytic techniques
o	Real-world examples and case reviews 9.	Midterm and Final Projects
o	Midterm exam focusing on structured analytic techniques
o	Final team-based project on a metabolic case study 10.	Review and Integration
o	Review of key concepts and techniques
o	Integration of knowledge through discussions and presentations

courses.description: The mammalian body as a single functional unit; studies include nervous, muscular, respiratory, circulatory, digestive, renal, endocrine, and reproductive systems.
courses.course_objectives: Students will explain human bodily function through the lens of core concepts of physiology, including homeostasis, flow-down gradients, and structure <--> function. Students will collaborate with peers through active listening and thoughtful contributions to solve physiology-based problems.

courses.subject: VPHY
courses.title: Integrative Concepts in Physiology Laboratory
courses.description: Weekly laboratory experiments in physiology, including cardiovascular, respiratory, neuromuscular, and sensory systems.
courses.course_objectives: The student will be able to hypothesize outcomes of planned experiments based on an understanding of physiologic processes. The student will be able to perform physiologic measurements to gain viable data for subsequent plotting and analysis. The student will be able to accurately tabulate or graphically present experimental data. The student will be able to critically evaluate data to evaluate whether hypotheses are supported or refuted. The student will be able to succinctly and accurately describe relationships between independent and dependent measures based on experimental findings. The student will be able to understand and communicate the physiologic processes that underlie the experimental results. The student will be able to communicate in an accurate and sensical manner the experimental details, findings, and conclusions of each experiment in the form of lab reports. The student will be able to prepare and present experimental details, findings, and conclusions in an accurate and sensical manner using a visual media format (e.g., PowerPoint).

Heart rate variability and respiratory sinus arrhythmia Coordination of ECG, heart sounds, and peripheral pulses Dive response effects on heart rate and peripheral circulation Autonomic effects on blood pressure Cardiovascular effects of exercise Pulmonary function Electromyography (EMG) with peripheral nerve stimulation to determine nerve conduction parameters Muscular twitch summation, recruitment, and fatigue Reflexes and reaction times Sensory physiology Skin conductance with electrodermal responses Glucose absorption Renal concentrating ability Assessment of students will be based on:
1. Laboratory reports
2. Participation in laboratory activities
3. Quizzes on pre-class readings
4. Group preparation of a scientific poster reporting results from one experiment, and presentation of the poster to the class

courses.subject: VPHY
courses.title: Integrative Concepts in Physiology II
courses.description: Emphasizes the physiologic mechanisms by which mammalian body systems function under normal conditions and respond to diseases and changes in the external environment. Includes functional, integrated aspects of nervous, endocrine, metabolic, immune, cardiovascular, respiratory, muscular, digestive, renal, and reproductive systems.
courses.course_objectives: Students will be able to predict responses of different organ systems to alterations in physiologic parameters and predict how responses are integrated systemically. Students will be able to develop explanations of how physiologic events occur based on readings and other information sources. Students will be able to develop scientifically-based arguments to support predictions. Students will be able to effectively communicate their work to faculty and peers, both verbally and in written form. Students will be able to critically evaluate readings relevant to discussion topics to extract salient information. Students will be able to search the scientific literature to identify sources of information relevant to the topic.

courses.subject: VPHY
courses.title: Careers in Biomedical Physiology and Professional Skills
courses.description: Develops written and oral communication skills applicable to professional settings. Fosters skills in leadership and collaboration, workplace-related social skills, time management, and strategic planning. Develops understanding of professionalism and ethical principles.
courses.course_objectives: By the end of this course, students will understand that professionalism is a constellation of behaviors exhibited throughout their professional lives. Students will be able to evaluate situations and respond in a manner that upholds the standards of professionalism. By the end of this course, students will be able to communicate scientific information in a clear, professional manner to a variety of audiences, including other professionals as well as members of the public without a scientific background. This will be practiced through written and video presentations for which peer and instructor feedback are provided, allowing for revisions that incorporate feedback. By the end of this course, students will be able to lead and collaborate according to situational needs in professional settings. This will be accomplished through discussions of qualities exhibited by effective leaders and collaborators and through a semester-long group project and a series of group exercises in which students alternate roles in the group, reflect on each other’s performance, and receive peer and instructor feedback throughout the semester. By the end of this course, students will be able to develop supportive working relationships through collaboration, prosocial behaviors, and considering alternative perspectives. By the end of this course, students will be able to employ time management and strategic planning techniques to balance their personal and professional needs while they progress in their careers. By the end of this course, students will be able to navigate challenges in the work environment, focusing on attention to inclusion, self-awareness, mutual respect, and contributing to a workplace culture of accountability, dignity, and safety.
courses.topical_outline: Written communication, including scientific writing and peer review, writing for the public, and electronic communications. Oral communication, including verbal communication of scientific topics to peers and to the public and professional presentations. Professionalism. Career management, including resumes/curriculum vitae and cover letters/personal statements, electronic presence, networking, and interviewing. Leadership principles and skills. Teamwork/collaboration principles and skills. Workplace skills including emotional intelligence, constructive criticism, active listening, mentor mapping, conflict resolution, and time management.

courses.subject: VPHY
courses.title: Figuring the Human Body Through Drawing
courses.description: This course will cover how structure informs physiological function through anatomical art. Students will engage with this material through readings, activities, drawings, and excursions.
courses.course_objectives: Students will develop an in-depth understanding of how anatomical structure informs physiological function. Students will develop generative learning of the human body through drawing. Students will develop critical thinking on the topics of interdisciplinary collaboration between artists and medical doctors, traditional and non-traditional practices in medical education, and representation in medical illustration.
